docs.title: The Field Guide
docs.text:
A validated curriculum for documentation engineering, developer experience, and KnowledgeOps roles.

A curriculum for a job category that does not have a settled name yet.

Two job postings started this. One from Intel, for a role in Developer Relations that asks for golden paths, curriculum, documentation CI, cold-start testing, and content optimized for SEO and GEO. One from NVIDIA, for something it calls KnowledgeOps, which asks for content modeling, taxonomy, metadata for machine retrieval, RAG packaging, agent skills, and evaluation sets for answer accuracy.

The titles are different. The work is the same work, and it is a real discipline with no agreed curriculum, no textbook, and almost no one deliberately trained for it. This guide is an attempt at the curriculum.

It covers 106 concepts. Every one is here because one of those two postings asks for it, and every one says which posting and in what words. The coverage matrix prints the receipts, including the places where the claim is this author's argument rather than a quotation.

docs.title: Three ways in
docs.text:
• Follow a route

    Nine learning paths, each an ordered sequence with the prerequisites worked out. Start with the first week if you have just taken one of these jobs, or prove it in a weekend if you need a portfolio artifact before Monday.

  • Look something up

    The coverage matrix is every concept with its tier, difficulty, time estimate, and the posting line that put it on the list. Sorted by category, so you can read one domain and ignore the rest.

  • Do all of it

    Everything in order is a dependency-respecting sequence through all 106, generated by topological sort. Longer and less useful than a path, which is why it is third.

docs.title: What a concept page looks like
docs.text:
Every one answers the same seven questions in the same order:

  1. What it is, in two sentences, for someone who has heard the term in a meeting and not admitted they do not know it.
  2. Why the job asks for it, connected to the posting line, explaining the work behind the words.
  3. The golden path: the shortest real exercise that produces a working result, from a clean environment, ending in something observable.
  4. Reference: the facts worth looking up later. Tables, not narrative.
  5. How to talk about it, including the tradeoff, because reciting what a thing does is not the signal.
  6. How to prove it: the artifact that demonstrates it without you having to claim it.
  7. Related: the lateral links the prerequisite graph does not know about, each with a clause saying why a reader would follow it from here.

That consistency is not a stylistic preference. It is a content model applied to a learning corpus, and CI rejects a page that violates it. The payoff is that the thirtieth page costs you nothing to navigate, because you learned the shape on the first.

docs.title: This guide is also an example of its own subject
docs.text:
A guide about information architecture that was itself a folder of unstructured Markdown would be an argument against its own content.

So the curriculum is a validated data file, concepts.yaml, and the pages that describe it are generated from that file. A concept marked complete with no page fails the build. A page nobody planned fails the build. A learning path that teaches a prerequisite too late fails the build. A page missing one of its seven sections fails the build.

Three of those four checks caught real mistakes in this repository within minutes of being written, which is the honest argument for all of it. See why a registry.

docs.title: Where to be sceptical
docs.text:
The postings are not reproduced here. Verbatim quotes were recorded while reading them and are marked quoted. Everything marked derived is a reconstruction of a requirement, and adjacent means neither posting mentions it and this author thinks the named work is impossible without it. 90 of the 106 concepts are quoted. The provenance page explains why that distinction is printed on every row rather than quietly averaged away.

One person wrote this. The golden paths have been run; the career advice is opinion. Where a page recommends a tool over an alternative, it says what the alternative is better at.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
106 of 106 concepts written. 0 drafted, 0 planned.

Each row names the concept, the posting line that put it on this list, and how strong that claim is. quoted is a verbatim phrase from a posting. derived means the posting requires the thing but these are not its words. adjacent means neither posting names it and the named work is impossible without it.

Read that last column as a confidence rating on the concept's right to your time.

docs.title: Where this list comes from
docs.text:
• 90 of 106 concepts are backed by at least one verbatim quote.
  • Claims by provenance: 90 quoted, 4 derived, 12 adjacent.

A concept with no quoted claim is still here on an argument, and the argument is printed next to it so you can reject it.

docs.title: The page contract
docs.text:
Every concept page answers the same seven questions in the same order, and CI rejects one that does not:

  1. What it is
  2. Why the job asks for it
  3. The golden path
  4. Reference
  5. How to talk about it
  6. How to prove it
  7. Related

That is a content model applied to a learning corpus rather than to a product's documentation. The payoff is that the thirtieth page costs a reader nothing to navigate, because they learned the shape on the first.

docs.title: Demonstrated
docs.text:
This guide is prose about how to do a job, and prose is cheap. This page records which concepts are also implemented somewhere you can open, down to the file that does the work.

77 of 106 concepts have a demonstration, 37 of them in full. The rest of this page is the other side of that number, which is the half worth reading.

docs.title: docpack
docs.text:
Turns a documentation tree into retrieval-ready, agent-readable artifacts.

A Python library and the documentation site that documents it, where the site is also the test corpus. Ten CI gates, 142 tests, a 20-case retrieval evaluation, an MCP server, and a cold-start harness that follows the quickstart from an empty virtual environment.

https://github.com/johnallred/docpack · demonstrates 49 concepts

docs.title: fieldguide
docs.text:
This guide, which validates its own curriculum and its own pages.

The repository you are reading. It earns entries here only where it does the work rather than describing it: a two-part fence gate that compares fenced source against the rendered code blocks of the built HTML, and an accessibility property test over generated pages. The fence gate found 127 defects across seven pages that every other check had passed.

https://github.com/johnallred/fieldguide · demonstrates 35 concepts

docs.title: What is demonstrated
docs.text: full means the concept is implemented as this guide describes it. partial means something real is there and the concept page asks for more, and it is used literally: rag is partial because the records are retrieval-ready and nothing embeds them.

docs.title: Information and knowledge architecture
docs.text:
11 of 13.

Concept Extent Artifact What it does Content models full src/docpack/frontmatter.py Five required front-matter fields, two of them closed vocabularies, rejected in CI by docpack docs --check. Diátaxis full docs/ Four directories, one declared type per page, enforced rather than conventional. Information architecture full concepts.yaml All three decisions made and enforced: 106 units with a closed vocabulary for category, tier and Diataxis type, a prerequisite DAG with a cycle check, and generated routes (nine paths, coverage, a topological study plan). No audience, so findability itself is unevidenced. Knowledge architecture full concepts.yaml 106 concepts and 115 prerequisite edges, acyclic and enforced, with a topological order driving the writing sequence. The audit found four supporting concepts carrying more of the graph than the average core concept, and three core concepts correctly isolated because craft skills are not prerequisites. Metadata for navigation and retrieval partial src/fieldguide/dialect.py Front matter must parse as YAML and diataxis must be in a closed vocabulary. Added after 46 pages shipped unparseable front matter and 53 claimed a page type a generator had hardcoded. Playbooks and decision guides full drills/playbook.py A decision guide validated as a graph: dangling targets, dead-end options, orphaned outcomes, unreachable nodes and cycles reported as the looping path. Each class is injected and caught. Committing it found the page's step 4 had been trimmed to one line per class, hiding that two of the four injections cascade, so four defects produce six findings and a findings count is not a repair list. Taxonomy and controlled vocabularies full src/docpack/frontmatter.py DIATAXIS_TYPES and AUDIENCES as frozensets: adding a term is a code change and a review. Findability and search design full hooks/summary.py An audit of the search index found 72 of 73 page summaries absent from it; this hook gives the field three readers (page body, search index, meta description) and a CI step asserts the wiring, because the hook's unit tests pass either way. Security guidance as encoded standard partial drills/security_lint.py A five-rule linter over a quickstart with six planted problems, which finds five. The miss is the demonstration: the credential rule was case-sensitive and environment variables are uppercase, so it missed the commonest shape a secret takes in a shell sample. Tests pin both the findings and the samples to the page. No threat model, no review process, no real product. Single-sourcing and content reuse partial hooks/seo.py One summary field feeds the meta description, Open Graph, JSON-LD, llms.txt and the retrieval snippet. Field-level reuse, not topic-level. Style guides and terminology management partial styles/Showcase/Terms.yml The style guide exists only as enforced rules. There is no prose document for a human to read.

docs.title: Docs-as-code toolchain
docs.text:
7 of 14.

Concept Extent Artifact What it does Choosing a static site generator partial drills/generator_build.py An identical corpus built under bare MkDocs and bare Sphinx at three sizes, cold and warm. It found that the build-time figure quoted on two pages described CI rather than authoring and inverted above about 120 pages, since MkDocs rebuilds everything and Sphinx rebuilds what changed. Docusaurus is not in the comparison; re-measuring it needs an npm install this environment will not do. Docs-as-code full .github/workflows/docs.yml The whole repository is the demonstration: page source, style rules, content model and pipeline all under review. Generated API reference full docs/reference/api.md mkdocstrings over the package, so the reference cannot drift from the signatures. Git authoring workflows for writers full .github/workflows/docs.yml Eight gates on every pull request, each failing independently so one problem does not mask another. Markdown and its dialects partial src/fieldguide/dialect.py A gate for the dialect failure mode. A construct used in prose whose markers survive into the built HTML did not render; covers two constructs, not every dialect. MkDocs and Material full mkdocs.yml Material plus mkdocstrings, built with --strict from the first commit. Sphinx partial drills/sphinx_autodoc.py Autodoc and napoleon pull a typed signature and its parameter docs out of real source, then the function is renamed and nitpicky plus -W turns the unresolvable cross-reference into exit 1. The mechanism is demonstrated; owning a Sphinx corpus is not, and the page says so: no custom extension, no theme fork, no intersphinx across teams. Needs sphinx and myst-parser, which this guide does not depend on.

docs.title: Quality automation and documentation CI
docs.text:
13 of 14.

Concept Extent Artifact What it does Building a doc test harness full tests/test_doc_samples.py The extractor, the skip convention, and an assertion that the skip ratio stays under 25 percent. Code-sample validation full tests/test_doc_samples.py Extracts every Python block from the docs and executes it; # docpack: skip makes an exception visible and countable. That is the easier half, and for a while it was the only half: executing a sample proves it runs and says nothing about whether the output printed beside it is still what it prints. tests/test_published_figures.py closes that, re-deriving every figure the README and the retrieval page quote from live runs rather than duplicating them as constants, which is the same contract this guide's own drills are held to. Cold-start testing full scripts/coldstart.sh Fresh venv, installs the way a reader would, follows the tutorial literally, and asserts the exact output string the tutorial promises. Documentation CI full .github/workflows/docs.yml Content model, links, tests, doc samples, retrieval quality, prose, strict build, and a generated-page wiring check. Freshness monitoring partial src/docpack/frontmatter.py PageMeta.is_stale at 365 days, surfaced as a warning and as an ## Optional section in llms.txt. A property, not a monitor. GitHub Actions for docs full .github/workflows/docs.yml Three jobs, with the slow cold-start check separated so it does not gate fast feedback. Link checking full scripts/check_links.py Internal links and heading anchors, so a renamed heading fails the build rather than silently breaking a deep link. Prose linting with Vale full .vale.ini Vale with terminology errors blocking the build and style warnings advisory, because a build that fails on a hedge word teaches people to skip CI. Accessibility checks partial tests/test_generate.py An audit of the built site found all seven path pages skipping h1 to h3; the generator was fixed and a property test now asserts no generated page skips a level. Five checks, not a compliance claim. Detecting terminology drift partial drills/terminology_drift.py Conformance measured against a glossary two ways, to show that the obvious way flatters: a word-boundary search for the canonical term matches inside its own deprecated variants, scoring drift as conformance, so widget reads 60% when the true figure is 33%. Masking variants before counting fixes it. Three pages, not a corpus, and no team or review process is involved. Doctests and executable docstrings full pyproject.toml --doctest-modules across the package, so every docstring example is executed. One broke a strict build and had to be rewritten. Preview deployments and publishing partial .github/workflows/docs.yml Publishes to GitHub Pages on main, and regenerates the retrieval artifacts alongside the site. No per-pull-request preview. Writing custom linters full src/fieldguide/fences.py A rule no pattern matcher can express, because it models shell heredocs to decide which fence markers are markup and which are data.

docs.title: Golden paths and developer onboarding
docs.text:
8 of 8.

Concept Extent Artifact What it does Designing tutorials full docs/tutorials/getting-started.md Five steps, nine code blocks, one route, no choices before first success; scripts/coldstart.sh runs it from an empty virtual environment and asserts the exact output it promises. Golden paths full docs/tutorials/getting-started.md Clean environment to four generated artifacts, with a deliberate failure step, verified by the cold-start harness on every push. Guided workflows full src/fieldguide/release.py fieldguide release-check: seven named steps over this corpus, each returning a detail on success and a specific remedy on failure, with an explicit GATES set of exactly one, the registry parse every other step depends on. drills/release_rounds.py reproduces the round-trip measurement against the real command: four runs against two for the same three independent defects. Quickstarts that survive contact full scripts/coldstart.sh The quickstart is tested rather than hoped about, including the promise that an invalid content model is rejected. Sample walkthroughs partial drills/walkthrough_transclusion.py Five states with a real MkDocs build behind three of them: a copied block caught drifting, the same block transcluded by line range, the sample edited and the page following it, two lines inserted so the transclusion renders the wrong line while the build exits zero, and a named anchor surviving the same insertion. The silent failure is the finding; a string check cannot catch it, because nothing is quoted any more. Templates and scaffolding full src/docpack/scaffold.py docpack new how-to --title ... writes a conforming page; CI generates one of each type and validates it, so the generator cannot drift from the validator. Reproducible environments partial scripts/coldstart.sh A fresh virtual environment installed the way a reader would, which is level 2 of the five in the page's own table and the right level for a pure-Python project. It would not catch a system library or a platform difference. Sample applications and galleries partial drills/gallery_audit.py A four-entry gallery verified against its manifest, two entries failing in two different ways, plus a coverage table crossing what the samples teach against what readers ask. Committing it found the page's golden path was unreachable: it quoted a checker's output without printing the checker or the samples it ran. The ticket distribution is invented and the page says so; the arithmetic over it is real.

docs.title: AI-ready content and agents
docs.text:
13 of 21.

Concept Extent Artifact What it does Agent-ready content full src/docpack/pack.py Three outputs for three consumers, with the argument for why one file serves none of them. Chunking strategies full src/docpack/chunk.py Heading-aware, fence-state tracking so a # comment inside a bash block is not a heading, and content-derived stable ids. Evaluating retrieval full evals/golden.yaml Twenty cases scored on hit@1, hit@3, MRR, routing accuracy and grounding, with a floor enforced in CI and the unflattering scores published. Generative engine optimization full hooks/seo.py JSON-LD TechArticle carrying the Diátaxis type, so a crawler learns what kind of question the page can answer, not only its subject. Grounding and citation partial src/docpack/evaluate.py grounded@1 checks the top chunk contains the terms an answer must cite. A floor on groundedness, not a citation mechanism. Model Context Protocol full mcp_server/server.py JSON-RPC over stdio, dependency-free, three tools, sharing the same retriever the evaluation scores so the eval measures what ships. RAG pipelines partial src/docpack/pack.py Emits chunks with stable ids and filterable metadata. No embedding, no vector store, no retrieval loop; the README argues that is the replaceable part. Vector stores and hybrid search partial drills/vector_store.py An IVF index over 4000 hashed vectors in 64 dimensions, measuring what an approximate search costs: 0.548 recall@10 probing one cluster of 64, 0.988 probing eight while scanning 13% of the corpus, and slower than brute force past the knee. The vectors are hashed rather than learned, which preserves the recall and latency geometry exactly and preserves nothing about semantics, so the drill also measures what it cannot show and the page tabulates the boundary. llms.txt and llms-full.txt full src/docpack/pack.py to_llms_txt and to_llms_full_txt, generated from front matter and grouped by Diátaxis type, so the index cannot go stale. Crawlability and the agent-ready front door partial drills/crawlability.py A six-check audit over a site with five planted defects, run by writing the page's own crawl.py to a temp directory, so the demonstration and the published code are one artifact. Committing it found the page had quoted no output at all, that five defects yield ten findings, and that the word-count check false-positives on a sixteen-word static page. No real site, no crawler, no search engine. Hallucination and guardrails partial drills/guardrails.py Four guardrail layers run against eight fluent answers, six of them wrong, producing the matrix of which layer catches which failure. The result worth having is a negative one: grounding passes a fabricated flag name as soon as real text surrounds it, so only a known-identifier list catches the convincing fabrications. No model, no retrieval and no live pipeline; the answers are written by hand to isolate the failure modes. SEO for documentation full hooks/seo.py Per-page meta description from the content model's summary, plus a CI step that fails if the hook is ever unregistered. Structured data and JSON-LD full hooks/seo.py Open Graph, Twitter cards and JSON-LD, all derived from one required field rather than hand-written per page.

The loop is now closed rather than open: the corpus was measured, 59 pages carried a sentence over 45 words and six over 60, the worst were edited, and a test holds the ceiling at 55 so it cannot drift back. Two defects fell out of acting on it. The splitter did not treat a sentence ending in bold as a sentence ending, which accounted for as much of the improvement as the editing did, and the metric excluded list items, so a long sentence became compliant the moment somebody bulleted it; both are fixed and both are published beside the result. The effect on a reader is still unmeasured. Ceiling: no-audience. Since then the commitments became enforceable rather than measurable: STRUCTURAL_LABELS declares the wording of all fourteen labelled elements, the scaffold emits them so a new page cannot invent a fifteenth, and the audit reports every repeated label nobody declared. That last check is the one that matters, because this page's own fix had standardised the label that surfaced and asserted that one string, which could not have found the three other variant pairs in use at the time. That second figure was published as 17 per cent for months and the classifier was wrong: it matched the preposition in "run it against a corpus you own" and recognised no conditional, predicted value or author comparison, so the guide's self-declared weakest number was about half the real one. It is now scored against sixty tasks hand-labelled before it was written, held in tests/fixtures/criterion_labels.json. The 40 is after a pass that added a criterion to every core page that had none; the correction was worth more than the pass. It establishes that the instrument is well formed and nothing about whether anyone learns. Ceiling: no-audience. docs.title: Accessibility checks
docs.text:
Automating the subset of accessibility a machine can judge, on the built HTML rather than the source.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

Not a quotation (adjacent)

Neither posting mentions accessibility. It is here because published documentation at either company is subject to it regardless, and because the automatable part costs an afternoon.

Prerequisites: Documentation CI

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A CI gate over the built HTML that catches the mechanically detectable accessibility defects: images without alternative text, heading levels that skip, link text that means nothing out of context, tables with no header cells, a page with no declared language.

The emphasis on built HTML matters. Accessibility is a property of what the browser receives, and a Markdown source file cannot tell you whether your theme emitted a lang attribute or what heading level a generated page landed on.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
It does not, and this page says so in its own banner. It is on the curriculum for two reasons.

The first is that documentation at a large company is published content subject to the same obligations as the rest of the site, whether or not a job posting mentions it. Nobody writes "must not ship inaccessible pages" in a requisition, and everybody expects it.

The second is that the automatable subset overlaps almost exactly with things that are also correctness problems for other readers. A heading structure that skips levels breaks screen reader navigation, and it also breaks your table of contents, your chunking for retrieval, and any tool that infers document structure from headings. Alternative text is what a retrieval system indexes for an image. The accessibility fix and the machine-readability fix are frequently the same fix, which is the honest argument for doing it even where it is not asked for.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Write five checks, run them over a real site, and fix what they find. About thirty minutes. This one found a genuine defect in this guide.

Step 1: the checks

Operating on built HTML with BeautifulSoup, scoped to the content region so the theme's own chrome is not under test:

# a11y.py
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

VAGUE = {"click here", "here", "read more", "this", "link", "more"}


def audit(site: Path) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    issues: dict[str, list[str]] = {}
    for page in sorted(site.rglob("index.html")):
        soup = BeautifulSoup(page.read_text(encoding="utf-8"), "html.parser")
        main = soup.find("article") or soup

        for img in main.find_all("img"):
            if not img.get("alt"):
                issues.setdefault("img-no-alt", []).append(str(page))

        levels = [int(h.name[1]) for h in main.find_all(re.compile(r"^h[1-6]$"))]
        for first, second in zip(levels, levels[1:]):
            if second > first + 1:
                issues.setdefault("heading-skip", []).append(
                    f"{page} (h{first}->h{second})")
                break

        for link in main.find_all("a"):
            if link.get_text(strip=True).lower() in VAGUE:
                issues.setdefault("vague-link-text", []).append(
                    f"{page}: {link.get_text(strip=True)!r}")

        for table in main.find_all("table"):
            if not table.find("th"):
                issues.setdefault("table-no-header", []).append(str(page))

        if not soup.find("html", attrs={"lang": True}):
            issues.setdefault("no-lang", []).append(str(page))
    return issues


if __name__ == "__main__":
    found = audit(Path(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "site"))
    for name, hits in sorted(found.items(), key=lambda kv: -len(kv[1])):
        print(f"  {name:18} {len(hits):4}   e.g. {hits[0][:78]}")
    print(f"{'FAIL' if found else 'ok'}: {sum(len(v) for v in found.values())} issue(s)")
    raise SystemExit(1 if found else 0)

Step 2: run it over this guide's own site

mkdocs build -q
python3 a11y.py site

One run, when the built site held 121 pages. The counts move as pages are added; the ratio between theme defects and content defects is the finding and does not.

pages scanned: 121
  heading-skip          7   e.g. site/paths/content-architect/index.html (h1->h3)

Seven pages. No missing alt text, no vague links, every table has headers, every page declares a language, because the theme handles those. One real defect, in content this guide generates itself.

Step 3: look at what it found

paths/content-architect   h1->h3
    h1: 'The content architect'
    h3: '1. Information architecture'

Every learning path page jumps straight from its title to an h3. The generator emitted ### 1. Concept for each step and never emitted an h2 at all, so there is no second level for the third to sit under.

A sighted reader does not notice: the steps look like a numbered list of sections. A screen reader user navigating by heading hears a jump from level one to level three, which conventionally means a section was skipped, and has to work out whether they missed something.

Step 4: fix the generator, not the pages

# in path_page(), one character
out.append(f"## {position}. {_link(concept, '../concepts/')}\n")

fieldguide build && mkdocs build -q && python3 a11y.py site

heading-skip pages after the fix: 0

Two unit tests failed on that change, because they asserted ### 1.. They were right to fail, and updating them is part of the fix. A third test now asserts the property rather than the string:

def test_path_steps_do_not_skip_a_heading_level(registry):
    for learning_path in registry.paths:
        levels = [...]
        assert levels[0] == 1
        for first, second in zip(levels, levels[1:]):
            assert second <= first + 1

Asserting the property means the next person who changes the heading level for a good reason gets told about the consequence, rather than being blocked by a test that hardcoded the old answer.

What you built. A gate over the built site, and a generated corpus with a heading structure a screen reader can navigate.

docs.title: What automation can and cannot judge
docs.text:
Machine-checkable Needs a human Missing alt attribute Whether the alt text is useful Heading levels skipping Whether the heading structure reflects meaning Link text from a vague list Whether link text makes sense in context Colour contrast ratios Whether colour is the only carrier of meaning Missing form labels Whether the reading order is sensible No lang attribute Whether a diagram's content is available another way

Automated tools are usually reckoned to cover something like a third of accessibility criteria. Treat the gate as a floor that stops regressions, never as a claim of compliance, and say so in that order when asked.

docs.title: Where the defects come from in a docs site
docs.text:
Source Typical defect Fix lives in The theme Contrast, focus states, landmarks, lang Theme config or an override Generated pages Heading structure, as above The generator Authors Missing alt text, vague link text A lint rule and review Diagrams and screenshots No text alternative Authoring guidance, and a check that flags images with no alt Code samples Nothing much; <pre> is fine Not a concern

Scoping the audit to the content region rather than the whole page keeps theme defects out of your authors' failure reports. Audit the theme once, separately, and fix it upstream.

docs.title: The checks worth having, in order of value
docs.text:
Check Why first Heading structure Breaks navigation, chunking and the table of contents at once Image alternative text The only text a retriever has for an image Link text Screen reader users often navigate by a list of links alone Table headers Without th, a data table is an unlabelled grid lang attribute One line, changes pronunciation for every page

The first two pay for themselves outside accessibility, which is what makes them easy to get funded.

docs.title: Tools, when you can install them
docs.text: axe-core, pa11y and lighthouse cover far more than the five checks above and should be preferred where the environment allows. The hand-rolled version earns its place in two situations: a build environment with no Node available, and a defect class specific to your own generated output, which is exactly the case here. A general tool would have found the heading skip too; writing it yourself is how you learn which of its findings matter.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the overlap, not the obligation. "The automatable subset of accessibility overlaps almost exactly with machine readability. Heading structure that skips levels breaks screen reader navigation and also breaks chunking for retrieval; alt text is the only thing a retriever can index for an image. So I run it as a CI gate on the built HTML, and the same fixes improve both."

The follow-up is whether this means the site is accessible, and the only honest answer is no. Automated checks cover roughly a third of the criteria. Say that number, say the gate is a regression floor, and say that a real assessment involves assistive technology and users.

The tradeoff to volunteer. The checks run on built HTML, which means they need a build before they can run, and they report against built paths rather than source lines. An author gets a failure pointing at site/paths/content-architect/index.html and has to work out that the cause is a generator template. That indirection is the cost of auditing the artifact that actually reaches the reader, and it is worth paying, but it needs a mapping back to source to be usable at scale.

One sharper point. Scope the audit to the content region. A gate that reports theme defects on every page in the corpus tells your authors that accessibility is a wall of noise they cannot fix, and it will be switched off. Audit the theme once, fix it upstream, and let the recurring gate cover only what authors and generators control.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A CI step that audits built HTML, plus a commit where it caught something and the fix went into a generator or template rather than into individual pages.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path over a docs site you own. Heading skips are extremely common in generated content and nobody is looking.
  2. When it finds something, fix it where it is generated. A fix applied to output is a fix that regresses.
  3. Convert the finding into a property test rather than a string assertion, so the next change is informed rather than blocked.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Neither of this guide's repositories demonstrated accessibility checking before this page was written, which is recorded on the demonstrated page. What exists now is better evidence than a tool in a workflow file: a check that found seven real defects in generated output, a one-character fix in the generator, two unit tests that correctly failed, and a property test so it cannot come back.

docs.title: Agent-ready content
docs.text:
Structuring a corpus so machines can find, cite and act on it, which is three different consumers rather than one.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

Make knowledge AI-ready: structure and package content for RAG, internal assistants, and agentic workflows

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: Content models, Metadata for navigation and retrieval

Leads to: Agentic workflows, Chunking strategies, Documentation for coding agents, Generative engine optimization, Model Context Protocol, llms.txt and llms-full.txt

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Structuring and packaging a corpus so that machines can find the right part, know what kind of answer it supports, and cite it. The phrase is vague on purpose in job postings and should not be vague in your head: "AI-ready" is three consumers with incompatible needs, and serving one of them is the usual way to fail the other two.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA's bullet is the clearest statement of this work anywhere in either posting: "Make knowledge AI-ready: structure and package content for RAG, internal assistants, and agentic workflows, including llms.txt, MCP-accessible sources, agent skills and context kits, and evaluation sets for answer accuracy."

Read the list of outputs. llms.txt is a map. MCP is an interface. Chunks for RAG are retrieval units. Agent skills are instructions. Those are not four formats of the same thing; they are four different artifacts for different consumption patterns, and the posting is asking for all of them because no one of them covers the others.

Intel's version is the same requirement from the other side: "a crawlable, agent-ready front door" and "agentready, LLMdigestible content".

On a Tuesday this is a question you answer repeatedly: an assistant gave a developer a wrong answer about batch sizing. Was the chunk missing, or was the right chunk retrieved and the wrong one ranked higher, or did the assistant not know which page could answer the question at all? Those have three different fixes, and you can only tell them apart if you built the three artifacts separately and can inspect each.

The reason this concept exists as its own page rather than being absorbed into chunking or RAG: it is the framing that keeps you from building one thing and claiming all of it.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Produce all three artifacts from one corpus and see why each exists. Forty minutes, no dependencies beyond Python.

Step 1: a small corpus with a real content model

mkdir -p agentready-drill/docs && cd agentready-drill
cat > docs/install.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Install the widget CLI
summary: Install the CLI and verify it runs.
kind: how-to
audience: new-user
updated: 2026-10-26
---
# Install the widget CLI

Run `pip install widget`. Requires Python 3.10 or newer.

## Verify

Run `widget --version`. It prints the version and exits 0.
EOF

cat > docs/batch-size.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Choose a batch size
summary: Pick a batch size from latency, memory and quantisation.
kind: how-to
audience: developer
updated: 2026-10-26
---
# Choose a batch size

Set `batch_size` on the client. The default is 32.

## If latency matters

Use 1 or 2. Batching at 32 adds roughly 200ms at p99.

## If the model is quantised

The memory arithmetic differs. Start at 64 and watch memory.
EOF

cat > docs/why-at-least-once.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Why delivery is at-least-once
summary: The reasoning behind at-least-once rather than exactly-once delivery.
kind: explanation
audience: developer
updated: 2026-10-26
---
# Why delivery is at-least-once

Exactly-once requires distributed transactions across the queue and the
consumer's datastore.

## What it costs you

Every consumer must tolerate seeing an item twice.
EOF
ls docs/

Step 2: build the three artifacts

cat > pack.py <<'PY'
"""Produce three artifacts for three consumers from one corpus.

The point of this script is the comment above each function. Each artifact
answers a question the others cannot, and the reason "AI-ready" is slippery as
a phrase is that it gets used for whichever one somebody built.
"""
import json
import re
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

HEADING = re.compile(r"^(#{1,3}) +(.*)$")


def pages(docs: Path):
    for path in sorted(docs.glob("*.md")):
        text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        front, _, body = text.partition("---\n")[2].partition("\n---\n")
        yield path, yaml.safe_load(front), body


def chunks(body: str, title: str):
    """Split on headings, keeping the heading trail with each piece.

    CONSUMER 1: a retriever. It wants small units, each carrying enough
    context to be understood alone, with metadata it can filter on before
    ranking. It never sees your navigation.

    The trail starts empty and the H1 becomes its first element, which is
    why the slice is `depth - 1`. Seeding it with the title instead produces
    "Choose a batch size > Choose a batch size" on every top-level chunk.
    """
    trail, buffer, out = [], [], []
    for line in body.splitlines():
        match = HEADING.match(line)
        if match:
            if buffer:
                out.append((" > ".join(trail), "\n".join(buffer).strip()))
                buffer = []
            depth = len(match.group(1))
            trail = trail[: depth - 1] + [match.group(2)]
        else:
            buffer.append(line)
    if buffer:
        out.append((" > ".join(trail), "\n".join(buffer).strip()))
    return [(crumb, text) for crumb, text in out if text]


def main() -> None:
    docs = Path("docs")
    out = Path("dist")
    out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

    # ---- artifact 1: retrieval records -------------------------------
    records = []
    for path, meta, body in pages(docs):
        for crumb, text in chunks(body, meta["title"]):
            records.append({
                "id": f"{path.stem}::{crumb}",
                "source": path.name,
                "breadcrumb": crumb,
                "text": text,
                "kind": meta["kind"],
                "audience": meta["audience"],
                "summary": meta["summary"],
            })
    (out / "chunks.jsonl").write_text(
        "\n".join(json.dumps(r, sort_keys=True) for r in records) + "\n"
    )

    # ---- artifact 2: a map -------------------------------------------
    # CONSUMER 2: an assistant deciding WHERE TO LOOK. It has not read
    # anything yet. It needs the shape of the corpus and one line per page,
    # grouped so it can tell which pages can answer which kind of question.
    lines = ["# Widget docs", "", "> Documentation for the widget platform.", ""]
    for kind, label in [("how-to", "How-to guides"), ("explanation", "Explanation")]:
        group = [(p, m) for p, m, _ in pages(docs) if m["kind"] == kind]
        if not group:
            continue
        lines += [f"## {label}", ""]
        for path, meta in group:
            lines.append(f"- [{meta['title']}](docs/{path.name}): {meta['summary']}")
        lines.append("")
    (out / "llms.txt").write_text("\n".join(lines))

    # ---- artifact 3: everything, once --------------------------------
    # CONSUMER 3: an assistant that would rather make one request than
    # thirty. Cheap to serve, and it keeps each page's type visible so the
    # model can still tell a recipe from an argument.
    full = ["# Widget docs: complete", ""]
    for path, meta, body in pages(docs):
        full += [
            "---", "", f"# {meta['title']}", "",
            f"*{meta['kind']} for {meta['audience']}*", "",
            meta["summary"], "", body.strip(), "",
        ]
    (out / "llms-full.txt").write_text("\n".join(full))

    print(f"{len(records)} chunks, {len(list(pages(docs)))} pages -> dist/")
    for name in ("chunks.jsonl", "llms.txt", "llms-full.txt"):
        size = (out / name).stat().st_size
        print(f"  {name:<16} {size:>6} bytes")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
PY
python3 pack.py

Step 3: see why one artifact cannot do the others' job

echo "=== The heading trail is not decoration. Search text only: ==="
python3 - <<'PY'
import json
rows = [json.loads(l) for l in open("dist/chunks.jsonl")]
print("  chunks whose TEXT contains 'latency':",
      sum(1 for r in rows if "latency" in r["text"].lower()))
print("  chunks whose BREADCRUMB + TEXT contains it:",
      sum(1 for r in rows if "latency" in f"{r['breadcrumb']} {r['text']}".lower()))
PY

Read that result carefully, because it is the single most useful thing on this page. The chunk that answers a latency question says:

Use 1 or 2. Batching at 32 adds roughly 200ms at p99.

The word "latency" does not appear in it. It appears in the heading above it, If latency matters. A chunker that discards the heading produces a chunk that is the correct answer and is unfindable by the obvious query.

echo "=== Consumer 1 asks: which chunk answers 'latency' for a developer? ==="
python3 - <<'PY'
import json
rows = [json.loads(l) for l in open("dist/chunks.jsonl")]
hits = [r for r in rows
        if r["audience"] == "developer"
        and r["kind"] == "how-to"
        and "latency" in f"{r['breadcrumb']} {r['text']}".lower()]
for r in hits:
    print(f"  {r['breadcrumb']}")
    print(f"    {r['text']}")
print(f"  ({len(rows)} chunks in the corpus, {len(hits)} match after filtering)")
PY

echo
echo "=== Consumer 2 asks: what kind of questions can this corpus answer? ==="
cat dist/llms.txt

echo "=== Consumer 3: one fetch, whole corpus ==="
wc -c dist/llms-full.txt

Step 4: break each one and watch a different failure

python3 - <<'PY'
import json

rows = [json.loads(l) for l in open("dist/chunks.jsonl")]
def haystack(r):
    return f"{r['breadcrumb']} {r['text']}".lower()

# Failure A: no type metadata. Retrieval still "works" and can no longer
# filter, so an explanation chunk competes for a "how do I" question.
print("A) a query about what batching costs you, with no kind filter:")
for r in rows:
    if "cost" in haystack(r) or "200ms" in haystack(r):
        print(f"     [{r['kind']:<11}] {r['breadcrumb']}")
print("   two chunks, two different kinds of answer. Only the how-to one")
print("   can tell a developer what to do.")

# Failure B: a map with no grouping. The assistant cannot tell which page
# supports which kind of answer, so it guesses.
print("\nB) an ungrouped map gives the model three indistinguishable links:")
for source in sorted({r["source"] for r in rows}):
    print(f"     - {source}")

# Failure C: only llms-full.txt. Fine at three pages, impossible at 3,000.
total = sum(len(r["text"]) for r in rows)
print(f"\nC) whole-corpus fetch is {total} chars here;")
print(f"   at 1,000x the corpus that is {total * 1000:,} chars, which no")
print( "   context window makes sense of. The map exists for this reason.")
PY

What you built. Three artifacts and three distinct failure modes.

Failure A is the one worth dwelling on. Both chunks are topically relevant to a question about batching cost. One is a how-to guide telling a developer to use 1 or 2; the other is an explanation page saying every consumer must tolerate duplicate delivery. Only one of them can answer "what should I do", and nothing about better embeddings distinguishes them. The kind field does.

docs.title: The three consumers
docs.text:
Consumer Wants Artifact Fails without it A retriever Small filterable units with context chunks.jsonl Returns whole pages, or fragments with no heading An assistant choosing where to look A map with one line per page, grouped llms.txt Guesses which page is relevant An assistant reading everything The whole corpus in one fetch llms-full.txt Makes thirty requests, or gives up

A fourth consumer, an agent that needs to act rather than read, is served by MCP and agent skills instead.

docs.title: What makes content agent-ready, in order of value
docs.text: Property Why Covered by Every page declares its type Lets a retriever filter by the kind of answer needed Content model, Diátaxis Chunks carry their heading trail The heading is the strongest statement of what the text is about Chunking Every page has a one-sentence summary Serves the map, the snippet and the meta description Metadata Stable chunk identifiers Editing an intro does not force a whole re-index Chunking A freshness signal Lets a consumer discount stale content Freshness monitoring Machine-readable page type in the HTML A crawler learns what the page can answer Structured data, GEO

docs.title: The thing most "AI-ready" claims mean
docs.text:
Claim Usually means Actually needed "Our docs are AI-ready" There is an llms.txt All three artifacts, plus a measurement "We chunked our docs" Fixed-size windows Heading-aware chunks with metadata "We built a RAG pipeline" Embeddings over a scrape A corpus with a content model under it "The assistant works" Somebody tried five questions An evaluation set

The last row is the gap that matters most and the one NVIDIA asks about by name.

docs.title: What agent-ready does not mean
docs.text:
• Not writing for machines instead of people. Every property above also helps a human: a declared page type improves navigation, a summary improves search results, a heading trail improves scanning.
  • Not a separate corpus. A machine-readable copy maintained alongside the human one drifts within a quarter. These are generated views.
  • Not a formatting convention. No amount of cleaner Markdown substitutes for the page declaring what it is.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with the three consumers, because it immediately distinguishes you from the common answer. "AI-ready is three consumers rather than one. A retriever wants small filterable units. An assistant choosing where to look wants a map, which is what llms.txt is. An assistant doing a one-shot read wants everything in one fetch. Serving only one of those fails the other two, and most sites that claim to be AI-ready have published an llms.txt and nothing else."

The follow-up is usually "what is the single highest-value thing to do first", and the answer is not any of the three artifacts. It is the type field on every page, because it is what lets a retriever filter by the kind of answer the question needs, and that is the failure that no ranking improvement fixes. A corpus with a content model can produce all three artifacts later; a corpus without one produces three artifacts over mush.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Every one of these artifacts is a derived view that has to be regenerated, and a stale derived view is worse than none because it looks authoritative. An llms.txt committed by hand six months ago is now actively misleading a model about what your corpus contains. So the real cost of agent-ready content is a build step and a CI gate that fails when a view is stale, and a team that is not ready to own that should publish nothing rather than publish something that will rot.

One sharper point. The strongest version is that the properties that make a corpus agent-ready are mostly the properties that would have made it good anyway, and the arrival of retrieval made them finally worth paying for. A declared page type, a real one-sentence summary, headings that state what is below them: all of this was recommended practice for twenty years and routinely skipped because the cost was visible and the benefit was not. What changed is that the benefit is now measurable with an evaluation set. That framing is both true and reassuring to a documentation lead who fears this is a new discipline.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. All three outputs, generated from one corpus by a script in CI, plus a measurement showing the type filter helps.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path against a real corpus. Twenty pages is enough. The failure-A demonstration, where an explanation chunk answers a how-to query, is the single most convincing two minutes you can show.
  2. Generate the artifacts in CI, never by hand. The gate that matters is one that fails when a committed view is stale. That is the difference between agent-ready and agent-ready-once.
  3. Measure the type filter. Twenty questions, scored with and without filtering on the expected page type. The gap is the value of your content model, in a number. See retrieval evaluation.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. An llms.txt file proves you read a blog post. Three generated artifacts, a CI gate against staleness, and a measured difference from the metadata filter proves you understand why they are three things.

docs.title: Agent skills and context kits
docs.text:
Packaging the conventions an agent needs before it writes anything, so it does not have to infer them from the code.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

including llms.txt, MCP-accessible sources, agent skills and context kits, and evaluation sets for answer accuracy

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: Model Context Protocol, Templates and scaffolding

Leads to: Agentic workflows

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Instructions written for an agent rather than for a person: the conventions, the commands, the things it must not do, loaded before it starts work. A context kit is the bundle of files an agent reads to orient itself in a repository. An agent skill is a narrower thing: instructions for one kind of task, loaded when that task comes up.

The distinction that matters is not the naming. It is that this content is read by something that will act on it immediately and cannot ask a follow-up question.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA names both in the same breath as llms.txt and MCP: "agent skills and context kits". Under ways to stand out, "agent skill and context libraries backed by documentation".

This is the newest concept in the guide and the one with the least settled practice, which is exactly why it is worth having an opinion about. The underlying need is old and the tooling is three years old at most.

What makes it core: it is the only AI-ready artifact aimed at an agent that writes rather than one that answers. An assistant that gets something wrong produces a bad answer. An agent that gets your conventions wrong produces a pull request that looks plausible and violates six rules nobody wrote down, and a reviewer spends longer fixing it than writing it would have taken.

On a Tuesday it is a recurring cost you can see in review comments. Every agent pull request against the docs repo gets the same four notes: the page is missing front matter, it uses "repo" instead of "repository", it was put in guides/ instead of by Diátaxis type, and the code sample is not runnable so CI fails. Those four notes are tribal knowledge about a repository, they are the same four every time, and they are a context kit that nobody has written.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Write a context kit for a real repository, then test it the only way that works: by checking whether the conventions in it are the ones CI enforces. Thirty-five minutes.

Step 1: find the conventions by looking at what CI rejects

Do not write the kit from memory. Derive it from the gates, because a convention that is not enforced is a preference and a gate that is not documented is a trap.

mkdir -p skills-drill && cd skills-drill
mkdir -p docs/how-to .github/workflows styles

cat > .github/workflows/docs.yml <<'EOF'
name: docs
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  quality:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: python validate_frontmatter.py docs/
      - run: vale docs/
      - run: python -m pytest tests/test_doc_samples.py
EOF

cat > validate_frontmatter.py <<'PY'
"""The real content model. Five required fields, two closed vocabularies."""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

REQUIRED = ("title", "summary", "diataxis", "audience", "updated")
DIATAXIS = ("tutorial", "how-to", "reference", "explanation")
AUDIENCES = ("new-user", "developer", "operator", "contributor")
DIRECTORIES = {"tutorial": "tutorials", "how-to": "how-to",
               "reference": "reference", "explanation": "explanation"}


def main(root: Path) -> int:
    failures = []
    for page in sorted(root.rglob("*.md")):
        text = page.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        if not text.startswith("---"):
            failures.append(f"{page}: no front matter")
            continue
        meta = yaml.safe_load(text.split("---")[1]) or {}
        for field in REQUIRED:
            if field not in meta:
                failures.append(f"{page}: missing {field!r}")
        if meta.get("diataxis") not in DIATAXIS:
            failures.append(f"{page}: diataxis must be one of {list(DIATAXIS)}")
        elif page.parent.name != DIRECTORIES[meta["diataxis"]]:
            failures.append(
                f"{page}: a {meta['diataxis']} page belongs in "
                f"{DIRECTORIES[meta['diataxis']]}/"
            )
        if meta.get("audience") not in AUDIENCES:
            failures.append(f"{page}: audience must be one of {list(AUDIENCES)}")
    for failure in failures:
        print(f"CONTENT MODEL  {failure}", file=sys.stderr)
    print(f"{'FAIL' if failures else 'ok'}: {len(failures)} violation(s)")
    return 1 if failures else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(Path(sys.argv[1])))
PY

cat > styles/Terms.yml <<'EOF'
extends: substitution
level: error
message: "Use '%s' instead of '%s'."
swap:
  repo: repository
  PR: pull request
  docs site: documentation site
EOF
ls -R | head -20

Step 2: write the kit, derived from those gates

cat > AGENTS.md <<'EOF'
# Working in this repository

You are editing a documentation corpus with a validated content model. The
checks below run on every pull request and will reject work that ignores
them. Read this before creating or editing any page.

## Before you write a page

Run `python validate_frontmatter.py docs/` to see the current state. It must
pass before and after your change.

## Required front matter

Every page needs exactly these five fields:

```yaml
---
title: Rotate an API key
summary: Replace a key without downtime.
diataxis: how-to
audience: operator
updated: 2026-10-26
---
```

- `diataxis` must be one of: `tutorial`, `how-to`, `reference`, `explanation`.
- `audience` must be one of: `new-user`, `developer`, `operator`, `contributor`.
- Do not invent values for either. Adding one is a change to
  `validate_frontmatter.py` and needs a human.

## Where a page goes

The directory is determined by `diataxis`, not by topic:

| `diataxis` | directory |
|---|---|
| `tutorial` | `docs/tutorials/` |
| `how-to` | `docs/how-to/` |
| `reference` | `docs/reference/` |
| `explanation` | `docs/explanation/` |

There is no `guides/` directory. A page about a task is a `how-to`.

## Terminology

`vale docs/` fails the build on these. Use the right-hand column:

| Do not write | Write |
|---|---|
| repo | repository |
| PR | pull request |
| docs site | documentation site |

## Code samples

Every fenced `python` block in `docs/` is extracted and executed by
`tests/test_doc_samples.py`. A sample that cannot run standalone must be
marked:

```python
# docpack: skip
client.connect(SECRET_TOKEN)
```

Prefer making the sample runnable over skipping it.

## What to do when you are unsure

Stop and say so. Specifically:

- **Do not add a value** to `diataxis` or `audience`.
- **Do not create a new top-level directory.**
- **Do not edit `validate_frontmatter.py` or `styles/`** to make your page
  pass. If a rule is wrong, say which rule and why, and leave it alone.
- **Do not mark a sample `skip`** just because it fails. Find out why first.

The last one matters most: the escape hatches in this repository are load
bearing, and widening one to get a green build defeats the gate for everyone.
EOF
wc -l AGENTS.md

Step 3: test the kit against the gates

A context kit is documentation, so it rots like documentation. The test that matters is whether it still describes what CI enforces.

cat > test_kit.py <<'PY'
"""Check the context kit against the checks it claims to describe.

This is the only test of a context kit that catches the failure that
matters. A kit is read by something that cannot ask a follow-up question, so
a stale instruction in it is not a confusing sentence, it is a wrong action
taken confidently.

Three checks:
  VOCABULARY  every value the kit lists must be in the validator
  COMPLETE    every value the validator accepts must be in the kit
  COMMANDS    every command the kit tells an agent to run must exist
"""
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import validate_frontmatter as validator

kit = Path("AGENTS.md").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
failures = []

# 1. Values the kit lists are real.
for field, allowed in (("diataxis", validator.DIATAXIS),
                       ("audience", validator.AUDIENCES)):
    match = re.search(rf"`{field}` must be one of: (.+?)\.", kit)
    if not match:
        failures.append(f"the kit does not state the allowed values for {field!r}")
        continue
    listed = set(re.findall(r"`([a-z-]+)`", match.group(1)))
    unreal = listed - set(allowed)
    if unreal:
        failures.append(f"{field}: kit lists {sorted(unreal)}, validator rejects them")
    # 2. Values the validator accepts are all in the kit.
    undocumented = set(allowed) - listed
    if undocumented:
        failures.append(
            f"{field}: validator accepts {sorted(undocumented)}, kit omits them"
        )

# 3. Required fields match.
listed_fields = set(re.findall(r"^- `(\w+)`", kit, re.M)) | set(
    re.findall(r"^(\w+):", kit.split("```yaml")[1].split("```")[0], re.M)
)
missing = set(validator.REQUIRED) - listed_fields
if missing:
    failures.append(f"required fields {sorted(missing)} are not shown in the kit")

# 4. Directory mapping matches.
for kind, directory in validator.DIRECTORIES.items():
    if f"docs/{directory}/" not in kit:
        failures.append(f"the kit does not mention docs/{directory}/ for {kind}")

# 5. Every command the kit tells an agent to run exists.
for command in re.findall(r"`(python [\w./]+\.py[^`]*|vale [^`]+)`", kit):
    target = command.split()[1]
    if target.endswith(".py") and not Path(target).exists():
        failures.append(f"the kit says to run {command!r} but {target} does not exist")

for failure in failures:
    print(f"KIT DRIFT  {failure}", file=sys.stderr)
print(f"{'FAIL' if failures else 'ok'}: context kit matches the gates "
      f"({len(failures)} problem(s))")
sys.exit(1 if failures else 0)
PY
python3 test_kit.py; echo "exit=$?"

Step 4: break the gate and watch the test catch the drift

echo "--- someone adds a new audience to the validator and forgets the kit ---"
python3 - <<'PY'
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("validate_frontmatter.py")
p.write_text(p.read_text().replace(
    'AUDIENCES = ("new-user", "developer", "operator", "contributor")',
    'AUDIENCES = ("new-user", "developer", "operator", "contributor", "partner")'))
PY
python3 test_kit.py; echo "exit=$?"

echo
echo "--- and the reverse: the kit promises a command that was deleted ---"
python3 - <<'PY'
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("validate_frontmatter.py")
p.write_text(p.read_text().replace(
    'AUDIENCES = ("new-user", "developer", "operator", "contributor", "partner")',
    'AUDIENCES = ("new-user", "developer", "operator", "contributor")'))
PY
mv validate_frontmatter.py check_model.py
python3 - <<'PY'
# The test imports the validator, so point it at the new name to isolate the
# one thing being tested: the kit's command reference is now wrong.
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("test_kit.py")
p.write_text(p.read_text().replace("import validate_frontmatter as validator",
                                   "import check_model as validator"))
PY
python3 test_kit.py; echo "exit=$?"
mv check_model.py validate_frontmatter.py

What you built. A context kit derived from the gates rather than from memory, and a test that fails when the two disagree in either direction.

That test is the contribution. A context kit is read by something that cannot ask you a follow-up question, so a stale instruction is not a confusing sentence, it is a wrong action taken confidently and then reviewed by a human who assumes the agent was told correctly.

docs.title: Kits, skills, and what goes where
docs.text:
Artifact Loaded Contains Context kit (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) Always, at the start Conventions, commands, directory rules, prohibitions Agent skill When a matching task comes up How to do one kind of work well MCP server On demand, as tool calls Content the agent queries llms.txt By a model that fetches URLs A map of the published corpus

The division is about when it is read. A kit is always-on and therefore has to be short. A skill is loaded on demand and can be long. Putting a thousand words about release notes into the always-on kit spends context on every task that has nothing to do with release notes.

docs.title: What belongs in an always-on kit
docs.text: Include Why The closed vocabularies, listed in full Otherwise it invents a value Where files go, as a rule not examples A rule generalises; examples get pattern-matched The commands CI runs So it can check its own work before opening a pull request Terminology the linter enforces Cheapest possible review-comment elimination Explicit prohibitions The highest-value section. See below What to do when unsure "Stop and say so" needs saying Leave out Why Anything a tool can answer Put it behind MCP instead Long rationale A kit is instructions; link the explanation Content that duplicates the corpus It will drift from the corpus Style advice with no gate behind it Unenforced advice is noise competing with rules

docs.title: Prohibitions are the part people forget
docs.text:
A kit full of positive instructions tells an agent what good work looks like. It does not stop the specific failures that cost the most, which are all of the form widening a constraint to make a failure go away:

Prohibition What it prevents Do not add a value to a closed vocabulary Silent corruption of a facet everything filters on Do not edit the validator or the lint rules A green build that proves nothing Do not mark a sample skip to pass CI Defeating sample validation for everyone Do not create a new top-level directory Structure drift that is expensive to undo Do not invent a flag or version Fabrication in a committed file

Every one of those is a rational move for something trying to get a green build. They have to be named.

docs.title: Writing for an agent, against writing for a person
docs.text:
A person An agent Can ask a follow-up yes no Infers from surrounding code reliably plausibly, which is worse Reads the whole thing rarely yes, every time Skips a rule they disagree with sometimes only if ambiguous Cost of ambiguity a question a confident wrong action

The third row is why brevity matters more here. Every word in an always-on kit is read on every task, and a kit that grows past a page or two is paid for continuously.

docs.title: The honest status of this area
docs.text:
Claim Reality "AGENTS.md is a standard" A convention, and a recent one. Filenames vary by tool "Skills are portable between tools" Partly. The formats differ "A kit replaces a contributing guide" No. A human guide explains why; a kit instructs "More context is better" No. Always-on context is a recurring cost

Present this internally as a cheap, high-return convention rather than as settled practice, because it is moving fast and a claim of standardisation will be challenged by someone who read a different blog post last week.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with derivation and with prohibitions, because both signal you have shipped one. "I derive the kit from what CI enforces rather than writing it from memory, so every rule in it has a gate behind it and every gate is documented. Then I test the kit against the validators in both directions: a value the kit lists that the validator rejects, and a value the validator accepts that the kit omits. And the section that earns the most is the prohibitions, because the costly failures are all an agent widening a constraint to get a green build: adding an audience value, marking a sample skip, editing the lint rules."

The follow-up is "how do you know the kit is working", and the honest answer is review comments. Count the repeated notes on agent pull requests before and after. If the same four comments keep appearing, those four things are either missing from the kit or stated ambiguously in it, and that count is the only real feedback signal available. There is no eval set for a context kit yet, which is worth admitting.

The tradeoff to volunteer. An always-on kit is a recurring cost paid on every task, so it competes directly with the work. A thorough kit that covers every convention crowds out the actual problem, and the failure mode is subtle: the agent follows all your conventions and does the task badly. That tension is why the split between always-on kits and on-demand skills exists, and why a kit should be ruthlessly short. There is also a real risk of a kit becoming a second source of truth that drifts from the validators, which is what step 3 exists to prevent and what nobody builds.

One sharper point. The strongest observation is that a context kit is the tribal-knowledge extraction problem with a new consumer. The four repeated review comments are exactly what extracting tribal knowledge is about, and the output form happens to be a file an agent reads rather than a decision guide a person reads. The skill is the same: notice what recurs, find the decision behind it, and write the thing that stops the question. Framing it that way makes it continuous with the documentation craft rather than a new AI discipline, which is both more accurate and more reassuring to a documentation lead.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A kit with a prohibitions section, and the test that checks it against the validators in both directions.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path, including step 4. The bidirectional drift test is the part nobody builds: an undocumented validator value and a kit promising a deleted command both fail it.
  2. Write a kit for a repository you know, derived from its CI. Read the workflow file first. Any rule you cannot point at a gate for either needs a gate or does not belong.
  3. Count the repeated review comments on the last ten pull requests in any repository. The ones that recur are your kit's contents, and the count is your before number. If no comment recurs across ten pull requests, either the reviews are not about conventions or nobody is reviewing: both are findings, and neither produces a kit.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. An AGENTS.md file proves you read about the convention. One derived from the CI gates, with explicit prohibitions against widening constraints, and a test that fails when a validator and the kit disagree, demonstrates that you treated it as documentation with a consumer that cannot ask questions.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
No agent ran here. This page describes packaging instructions so an agent behaves consistently, and the demonstration needs an agent that loads such packages, which this environment cannot provide.

What you need. An agent runtime that supports loading instruction bundles from a directory, plus a repetitive task with a checkable result. The task matters more than the runtime: the claim being tested is that a written-down procedure makes an agent's behaviour repeatable, so you need something whose output you can compare run to run.

What you would run. Choose a task your team does by hand, such as adding a conforming page or preparing a release note, and run it three ways: with no instructions, with instructions written as prose, and with instructions written as a skill package including the validator the task has to satisfy. Ten runs of each.

What you would see.

Observation Rough magnitude What it tells you Runs passing the validator, no instructions low and highly variable The baseline Same, with prose instructions better, still variable Instructions help and do not bind Same, with the validator named in the package high and stable The gain is the check, not the prose Variance across runs falls sharply with the package Repeatability is the actual product Behaviour on a case the package does not cover reverts to baseline The edges are where packages end

The third row is the finding. Most of the improvement comes from telling the agent what will be checked rather than from telling it what to do, which is the same result the templates and scaffolding page reached for human authors and for the same reason.

How you would know it had failed. No variance at the baseline means the task is too easy to discriminate between conditions. A package that improves results on tasks it does not mention means something else changed, usually context length. And if the package's own instructions are not reflected in the output at all, check that the runtime loaded it, which is the commonest and least interesting failure.

docs.text:
