  • Extracting tribal knowledge, where the kit's contents come from

docs.title: Agentic workflows
docs.text:
Documentation work done by an agent over several steps, and the checkpoints that keep it reviewable.

core · difficulty 3 · 6h

structure and package content for RAG, internal assistants, and agentic workflows

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: Model Context Protocol, Agent skills and context kits

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Documentation work carried out by an agent across several steps, where each step depends on what the previous one found: audit the corpus, pick the stale pages, check each against the code, propose edits, open a pull request.

The distinguishing feature is the agent chooses what to do next. That is what separates it from a script, and it is the entire source of both the value and the difficulty.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA names it as the third consumer of AI-ready content, alongside RAG and internal assistants. Intel's version is "the agentic toolkit" and "coding agents" as a documentation audience.

What makes it core and difficulty 3 is that the usual review model stops working. For a single generated answer you can check the output: grounded, cited, correct. For a twelve-step run you get a pull request and a summary, and the summary is written by the thing you are checking. If step 3 picked the wrong pages, every later step did excellent work on the wrong input, and the pull request looks fine.

On a Tuesday that failure is concrete. An agent was asked to update version references after a 2.6 release. It opened a tidy pull request touching nine pages. Seven were correct. One updated a deliberately pinned example in a migration guide, and one updated a version string inside a quoted error message, where the old version is the whole point. The summary said "updated version references across nine pages", which is true. Review caught it because somebody read the diff, not because any check did.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build an agentic documentation workflow with checkpoints, then watch a wrong decision at step 2 propagate into confident work at every later step. Fifty minutes, dependency-free.

Step 1: a corpus with traps in it

mkdir -p agentic-drill/docs/{how-to,reference,explanation} && cd agentic-drill
cat > docs/how-to/install.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Install the CLI
updated: 2024-01-15
---
# Install the CLI

Requires widget 2.2 or newer.

    pip install widget==2.2
EOF

cat > docs/how-to/migrate-from-2-2.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Migrate from 2.2
updated: 2024-02-01
pinned_versions: true
---
# Migrate from 2.2

This guide is specifically about moving off widget 2.2. Do not update these
version references; they are the subject of the page.

    pip install widget==2.2
EOF

cat > docs/reference/errors.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Error reference
updated: 2024-03-10
---
# Error reference

## E_VERSION_MISMATCH

The server emits this verbatim:

    error: client widget 2.2 is older than server widget 2.4

Match the client to the server.
EOF

cat > docs/explanation/design.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Why batching is opt-in
updated: 2026-09-01
---
# Why batching is opt-in

Batching changes latency characteristics, so it is never enabled by default.
EOF
find docs -name "*.md" | sort

Four pages. One genuinely needs updating, one must never be touched, one contains a version inside quoted output, and one is current and irrelevant.

Step 2: the workflow, with a checkpoint between every step

cat > workflow.py <<'PY'
"""An agentic documentation workflow with inspectable checkpoints.

The structure is the whole lesson. Each step takes the previous step's
OUTPUT as explicit input and records what it decided, so a wrong decision
early is visible as a wrong decision rather than as a confusing diff at the
end.

Steps:
  1 SURVEY    what exists, with the metadata that matters
  2 SELECT    which pages are in scope          <- the decision that matters
  3 INSPECT   what in each page would change
  4 PROPOSE   the edits, as a diff, applied to nothing
  5 GATE      refuse to proceed past declared tripwires

The agent's judgement lives in step 2. Everything after it is mechanical,
which means everything after it will be done competently on whatever step 2
chose. That asymmetry is why step 2 gets its own checkpoint.
"""
import datetime as dt
import difflib
import re
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

CURRENT = "2.6"
STALE_DAYS = 365
VERSION = re.compile(r"widget[ =]{1,2}(\d+\.\d+)")


@dataclass
class Checkpoint:
    """One step's decision, recorded so a human can audit the sequence."""

    step: str
    decided: list = field(default_factory=list)
    skipped: list = field(default_factory=list)
    notes: list = field(default_factory=list)

    def show(self):
        print(f"--- {self.step} ---")
        for item in self.decided:
            print(f"    in:   {item}")
        for item in self.skipped:
            print(f"    out:  {item}")
        for note in self.notes:
            print(f"    note: {note}")
        print()


def survey(root: Path):
    """Step 1: what exists. No judgement here."""
    pages = []
    for path in sorted(root.rglob("*.md")):
        text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        meta = yaml.safe_load(text.split("---")[1]) or {}
        pages.append({"path": path, "meta": meta, "text": text})
    cp = Checkpoint("1 survey")
    cp.decided = [f"{p['path']}  updated {p['meta'].get('updated')}" for p in pages]
    return pages, cp


def select(pages, respect_pins=True):
    """Step 2: which pages are in scope. THE decision.

    `respect_pins` exists so the golden path can run this step wrong and show
    what happens downstream. A real agent gets this wrong by not knowing the
    convention exists, which is what a context kit is for.
    """
    cp = Checkpoint("2 select")
    today = dt.date.today()
    chosen = []
    for page in pages:
        path, meta, text = page["path"], page["meta"], page["text"]
        updated = meta.get("updated")
        if isinstance(updated, str):
            updated = dt.date.fromisoformat(updated)

        if respect_pins and meta.get("pinned_versions"):
            cp.skipped.append(f"{path}  (pinned_versions: true)")
            continue
        if not VERSION.search(text):
            cp.skipped.append(f"{path}  (no version reference)")
            continue
        if updated and (today - updated).days <= STALE_DAYS:
            cp.skipped.append(f"{path}  (reviewed within {STALE_DAYS} days)")
            continue
        chosen.append(page)
        cp.decided.append(str(path))
    if not respect_pins:
        cp.notes.append("respect_pins=False: pinned pages were NOT excluded")
    return chosen, cp


def inspect(chosen):
    """Step 3: what in each page would change, and what must not."""
    cp = Checkpoint("3 inspect")
    findings = []
    for page in chosen:
        path, text = page["path"], page["text"]
        in_block = False
        for number, line in enumerate(text.splitlines(), 1):
            # A version inside quoted program output is not ours to change.
            # Detecting that is step 3's job; step 4 only applies decisions.
            quoted = line.startswith("    ") and (
                "error:" in line or "warning:" in line
            )
            for version in VERSION.findall(line):
                if version == CURRENT:
                    continue
                item = {"path": path, "line": number, "version": version,
                        "text": line, "quoted": quoted}
                if quoted:
                    cp.skipped.append(f"{path}:{number}  quoted output, left alone")
                else:
                    findings.append(item)
                    cp.decided.append(f"{path}:{number}  {version} -> {CURRENT}")
    return findings, cp


def propose(findings):
    """Step 4: build diffs. Writes nothing."""
    cp = Checkpoint("4 propose")
    diffs = {}
    by_path = {}
    for finding in findings:
        by_path.setdefault(finding["path"], []).append(finding)

    for path, items in by_path.items():
        original = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        updated = original
        for item in items:
            updated = updated.replace(item["text"],
                                      VERSION.sub(lambda m: m.group(0).replace(
                                          m.group(1), CURRENT), item["text"]))
        diff = list(difflib.unified_diff(
            original.splitlines(), updated.splitlines(),
            fromfile=str(path), tofile=f"{path} (proposed)", lineterm="",
        ))
        diffs[path] = diff
        cp.decided.append(f"{path}  {len(items)} line(s)")
    return diffs, cp


def gate(diffs, pages):
    """Step 5: tripwires. Declared in advance, checked before anything ships.

    These are not quality checks. They are statements about what this
    workflow is NOT allowed to do, which is the only kind of check that
    survives an agent being competent and wrong.
    """
    cp = Checkpoint("5 gate")
    pinned = {p["path"] for p in pages if p["meta"].get("pinned_versions")}
    failures = []

    for path in diffs:
        if path in pinned:
            failures.append(f"{path} is pinned and must never be edited")
    if len(diffs) > 5:
        failures.append(f"{len(diffs)} files exceeds the 5-file limit for one run")
    for path, diff in diffs.items():
        added = [l for l in diff if l.startswith("+") and not l.startswith("+++")]
        if len(added) > 10:
            failures.append(f"{path}: {len(added)} added lines exceeds the limit")

    cp.notes = failures or ["all tripwires clear"]
    return failures, cp
PY
echo "workflow written"

Step 3: run it correctly

cat > run.py <<'PY'
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from workflow import gate, inspect, propose, select, survey

respect_pins = "--ignore-pins" not in sys.argv

pages, cp1 = survey(Path("docs"))
cp1.show()
chosen, cp2 = select(pages, respect_pins=respect_pins)
cp2.show()
findings, cp3 = inspect(chosen)
cp3.show()
diffs, cp4 = propose(findings)
cp4.show()
failures, cp5 = gate(diffs, pages)
cp5.show()

print("=== what a reviewer would see at the end ===")
print(f"summary: updated version references across {len(diffs)} page(s)")
for path, diff in diffs.items():
    for line in diff:
        if line.startswith(("+++", "---", "@@")) or line.startswith(("+", "-")):
            print(f"  {line}")
print()
print(f"VERDICT: {'BLOCKED' if failures else 'ready for review'}")
sys.exit(1 if failures else 0)
PY
python3 run.py; echo "exit=$?"

Step 4: run it with one wrong decision at step 2

echo "############ step 2 does not know about pinned_versions ############"
python3 run.py --ignore-pins; echo "exit=$?"

What you built. A five-step workflow where every step records its decision, and a tripwire that catches a wrong early decision after four later steps did competent work on top of it.

docs.title: The correct run
docs.text:
Step 2 selects two pages and records why it rejected the other two: one has no version reference, one is pinned_versions: true. Step 3 then finds two updatable lines in install.md and excludes two lines in errors.md as quoted program output. Step 5 passes, and the diff is two lines.

Note that step 3's exclusion is as important as its inclusions. The version inside error: client widget 2.2 is older than server widget 2.4 is the subject of the error reference, not a stale fact.

docs.title: The run with one wrong decision at step 2
docs.text:
--ignore-pins makes step 2 unaware of the pinning convention. Everything downstream then works perfectly on the wrong input:

--- docs/how-to/migrate-from-2-2.md
+++ docs/how-to/migrate-from-2-2.md (proposed)
-This guide is specifically about moving off widget 2.2. Do not update these
+This guide is specifically about moving off widget 2.6. Do not update these
-    pip install widget==2.2
+    pip install widget==2.6

Read that diff. The agent edited a sentence that says not to make this edit, turning a migration guide about moving off 2.2 into a guide about moving off 2.6, which is incoherent. It also left errors.md alone correctly, which is the tell: steps 3 and 4 were working well the entire time.

The summary line reads "updated version references across 2 page(s)", which is accurate. Nothing in the output is self-evidently wrong except the content of one diff hunk.

It was blocked by the tripwire, not by any quality check, and that is the point of the whole page: a run can be competent at every step after the one that mattered.

docs.title: Why review breaks down
docs.text:
Single generated answer A multi-step run One output to check A diff plus a summary written by the agent Wrong is visible Wrong looks like competent work on the wrong input Grounding applies Nothing to ground against; it is an action, not a claim Cheap to re-run Expensive, and the state has changed Failure is one bad answer Failure is nine correct edits and two harmful ones

The asymmetry is the problem. The agent's judgement is concentrated in one or two early steps, and everything after is executed well regardless. So the review has to target the decisions, not the output.

docs.title: Checkpoints: what to record at each step
docs.text:
Step Record Why Survey What was found So scope is auditable Select What was included AND excluded, with reasons The decision that matters Inspect What would change, and what was deliberately left Surfaces the quoted-output case Propose Diffs, applied to nothing A diff is reviewable; an applied change is not Gate Which tripwires were checked Proves the limits ran

The exclusions in step 2 are the single most valuable thing in the log. An agent that skipped a page for a stated reason can be checked; an agent that silently did not consider it cannot.

docs.title: Tripwires, and why they are not quality checks
docs.text:
A tripwire is a statement about what this workflow may never do, declared before the run:

Tripwire Catches Never edit a page with pinned_versions The failure in step 4 above No more than N files per run Runaway scope No more than N added lines per file A rewrite disguised as an edit Never edit CI config, lint rules or validators Widening a constraint to pass Never delete a file Irreversible, and rarely the intent Diff only; a human applies The strongest version, and the slowest

They work precisely because they do not depend on judging the work. A competent, confidently wrong run passes every quality check and still trips a limit.

docs.title: Where to put a human
docs.text:
Placement Cost Catches Review the final pull request low What a reader notices in a diff Approve the step 2 selection low The decision that determines everything else Approve each proposed edit high Everything, slowly Sample runs after trusting it low Drift, eventually

Approving the selection is the best value by a wide margin: it is a short list, it is cheap to read, and it is where the agent's judgement actually was.

docs.title: What makes a task suitable
docs.text:
Suitable Unsuitable Mechanical change, many files A change needing product judgement Reversible Deletion, publication, anything irreversible Verifiable by a gate "Make the docs better" Scoped by a declared rule Scoped by vibes Proposes, does not apply Direct commits to a default branch

Mapped onto judging where AI can be trusted: an agentic workflow belongs in the proposes-for-review cell, and the tripwires are what keep it there when a run goes wrong.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with the review problem, because that is the thing that distinguishes this from "we ran a script". "The usual check does not work on a multi-step run. You get a diff and a summary written by the thing you are reviewing, and if the selection step picked the wrong pages then every later step did competent work on the wrong input and the summary is accurate. So I record what each step decided, including what it excluded and why, put the human approval on the selection rather than on the final diff, and declare tripwires in advance: never touch a page marked pinned, never more than five files, never edit the validators."

The follow-up is "how do you stop it going off the rails", and the answer that lands is that you do not rely on the agent for that. Tripwires work because they do not judge the work: a run that is competent and wrong passes every quality check and still fails a file-count limit. Pair that with proposing diffs rather than applying them, so the worst outcome is a rejected pull request.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Checkpoints and tripwires cost most of the speedup. A run that proposes a diff for human approval, with a five-file limit, is not much faster than doing the work yourself for anything small, and the honest payoff only arrives at volume: a hundred pages, a mechanical change, a rule you can state. Below that it is overhead. There is also a trap in trusting it over time: tripwires get raised because they keep blocking legitimate runs, and a limit raised three times is a limit that no longer limits.

One sharper point. The strongest observation is that an agentic workflow is a forcing function for writing your conventions down. The step 4 failure happens because pinned_versions was a convention in somebody's head; once it is a front-matter field, both the agent and the tripwire can see it. Every failure of this kind turns into a piece of machine-readable metadata that also makes the corpus better for humans. So the real output of adopting agentic workflows is usually a better content model, which is a much more interesting claim than a productivity one and happens to be the one that survives contact with a documentation lead.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A workflow with per-step checkpoints and declared tripwires, plus the run where an early wrong decision produces competent downstream work.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path both ways. The --ignore-pins run is the demonstration: identical-looking output, correct-looking diffs, blocked only by a tripwire.
  2. Write the tripwires for a task you would actually automate. Five lines. Doing this before building anything is the habit worth demonstrating. Write the tripwires before you look at the task's failure modes, then compare. The ones you missed are the ones that will fire in production.
  3. Find a convention that only exists in someone's head and turn it into a front-matter field, so a gate can see it. That is the durable output, and it improves the corpus whether or not the agent ever runs.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Describing agent workflows is cheap. Per-step checkpoints that record exclusions, tripwires declared in advance, and a demonstrated run where everything downstream of a bad decision looked right shows that you have thought about how these fail rather than how they help.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
The checkpointing structure this page describes was demonstrated here with a scripted stand-in; the part that needs a real agent, where a wrong decision at step two propagates into confident work at every later step, was reasoned about rather than observed.

What you need. An agent runtime that can take multi-step actions on a repository, and a corpus with deliberately planted traps: a stale page, a contradictory pair of statements, a sample that does not run. The traps are the experiment. An agentic workflow on a clean corpus demonstrates nothing, because nothing requires judgment.

What you would run. Give the agent a multi-step task over the trapped corpus, such as "find pages contradicting the reference and fix them", with checkpoints after each step, and record not just the outcome but where the first wrong decision happened and what the agent did afterwards.

What you would see.

Observation Rough behaviour What it tells you Tasks completed with no wrong step some fraction, never all The baseline What happens after one wrong step later steps build on it confidently The failure this page is about Whether the agent reports uncertainty rarely, unprompted Why checkpoints are external, not asked for Cost of a checkpoint that a human reads the whole saving The real economics Behaviour when a trap is unflagged the trap propagates silently Why the corpus needs its own checks

The second row is the point. A wrong step does not produce an error, it produces a premise, and every later step is executed competently against it. That is why this page argues for checkpoints at decision boundaries rather than at the end: a review of the final output cannot tell which premise it rested on.

How you would know it had failed. If the agent completes every trapped task correctly, the traps are too obvious and need to be subtler than a wrong word. If it fails at step one every time, the task is underspecified and you are measuring instruction quality. And if checkpoint review takes as long as doing the task, the workflow is theatre, which is a legitimate finding and worth publishing.

docs.title: Measuring AI answer quality
docs.text:
Retrieval quality is a ceiling on answer quality, and when a wider context window stops helping, the failures left are vocabulary rather than ranking.

core · difficulty 3 · 5h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "AI answer quality"

Prerequisites: Output evaluation, Documentation analytics

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Measuring whether an assistant answering from your corpus answers correctly. NVIDIA lists it as a metric the role owns, which makes documentation partly responsible for a system it does not control: the model is someone else's, the prompt is often someone else's, and the only input the documentation team owns is the corpus.

That constraint is clarifying rather than limiting, because the corpus sets a ceiling. If the retrieved context does not contain the fact, a correct answer requires the model to supply it from elsewhere, which is the behaviour you are trying to prevent. Retrieval quality is an upper bound on grounded answer quality, and the bound is measurable without a model in the loop at all.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because readers have stopped arriving at documentation and started arriving at answers about it.

A corpus is now consumed by assistants more often than many teams realise, and the failure mode is new: a confident, fluent, wrong answer, delivered without the reader ever seeing the page that would have corrected it. Link checking, sample execution and prose linting say nothing about this. The page can be perfect and unretrieved, and the answer is still wrong.

The second reason is defensive. When an assistant answers wrongly from your documentation, the question in the room is whether the docs were wrong or the model was. Without a measurement, that argument is settled by whoever is more senior. With one, it is settled by the number.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Measure the ceiling, find the point at which more context stops helping, and fix what is left. About forty minutes, on the companion repository's twenty-case golden set.

Step 1: the ceiling, at one chunk

Each golden case declares the terms a grounded answer must cite. Check whether the top retrieved chunk contains them:

hay = f"{top.breadcrumb}\n{top.text}".lower()
missing = tuple(t for t in case.must_contain if t.lower() not in hay)

grounded@1   16/20  (80%)

That is not an answer-quality score. It is a statement that for four of twenty questions, a model answering from the single best chunk would have to invent the key fact or decline.

Step 2: the ceiling across the window a model actually sees

No real system passes one chunk. Measure the same property across the top k:

  grounded@1    16/20  (80%)
  grounded@3    18/20  (90%)
  grounded@5    18/20  (90%)
  grounded@10   18/20  (90%)

Ten points between one chunk and three, then nothing at all out to ten.

That plateau is the most useful shape in this measurement. While widening the window still helps, the failures are ranking failures, and a reranker or a better embedding model would address them. Once it stops helping, the remaining failures are not retrieval failures at all, and no amount of model or infrastructure will touch them.

Step 3: look at what survived

ungrounded at k=10: 2
   chunk-size      missing ['size']   'how do I make the chunks smaller'
   prose-linting   missing ['vale']   'how do I stop people writing hedge words'

Both are vocabulary gaps. In each, the reader's everyday word was absent from the page that documents the thing, while the page used a precise term the reader had no reason to know. The golden set had even said so in its own why field for one of them: "the reader knows the symptom and not the tool name".

Neither is a ranking problem, which is why k=10 could not help.

Step 4: fix the corpus, not the retriever

One sentence per page, each putting the reader's word beside the corpus's word. Two sentences in total, no code, no model, no reranker:

             before   after
hit@1          60%     65%
hit@3          95%     95%
MRR          0.742   0.775
routing        70%     75%
grounded@1     80%     90%
grounded@3     90%    100%
headroom      +15%    +10%

Four of five scores moved, and the ceiling reached 100 per cent at three chunks. The narrowing headroom is the subtle part: routing headroom measures accuracy sitting unclaimed behind a query router, and some of that gap turned out never to have been a routing problem. It was a word the corpus did not use.

A ten-point hit@1 gap looks like a business case for a reranker. Five points of it were a synonym.

Step 5: the limit, stated plainly

Everything above measures retrieval. No model answered a single question.

So the honest claim is a bound: at three chunks of context, every question in this set can be answered from material that contains the required facts. Which is not the same as saying the answers would be right. A model can misread a correct chunk, blend two chunks into a claim neither makes, or answer correctly from its own pre-training while the retrieved context is irrelevant, and that last case scores as success on every metric here.

Measuring the rest needs a model in the loop and a grader, which is output evaluation, and it costs per run in a way this does not. The division worth keeping is that retrieval grounding is cheap, deterministic and a hard ceiling, so it is where to start and where most of the early wins are.

What you built. A grounding ceiling measured across the context window, a plateau that distinguishes ranking failures from vocabulary failures, a two-sentence corpus fix that moved four metrics, and an explicit statement of what the measurement does not cover.

docs.title: The three layers, and who owns each
docs.text:
Layer Measures Owned by Cost per run Retrieval grounding Could a correct answer be built Documentation Near zero Answer correctness Was it built correctly The system A model call per case Answer usefulness Did it help the reader The product A human per case

NVIDIA's bullet names the second and a documentation role can only move the first, which is a reasonable division: the first is a ceiling on the second.

docs.title: Metrics worth running, in order of cost
docs.text:
Metric Needs a model Catches grounded@1 No The best chunk lacks the fact grounded@k No Whether more context would help hit@k, MRR No Ranking quality Routing accuracy No The right page of the wrong kind Citation validity No A cited chunk that does not support the claim Faithfulness grading Yes Fluent answers the context does not support Refusal rate on absent content Yes Inventing what the corpus lacks Human preference A person Everything, slowly

The first four are free and deterministic. Teams routinely start at the bottom of this table because that is what the tooling advertises, and leave the free ceiling unmeasured.

docs.title: Why grounding and ranking have to be read together
docs.text:
Neither metric contains the other. Cross them over the twenty cases:

                 grounded   ungrounded
  hit@1             13          0
  miss               5          2

  the two metrics agree on 15 of 20 cases (75%)

grounded@1 is 90 per cent and hit@1 is 65, so grounding looks like the healthier number, and the top-right cell explains why that is misleading. Five cases are grounded while retrieving the wrong page: a chunk from a page the question was not about still happened to contain every term the answer must cite. An answer built on it could be correct and cite the wrong source.

The empty cell is the one to watch over time. "Right page, wrong section" was occupied before the vocabulary fix in step 4, by the case whose top chunk came from the correct page's filtering section rather than its sizing section. A reader of hit@1 alone would have scored that case a success.

Cell Means Visible to hit, grounded Working Either metric hit, ungrounded Right page, wrong section grounded@1 only miss, grounded Right terms, wrong source hit@1 only miss, ungrounded Nothing useful retrieved Either metric

Two of those four failures are invisible to one of the two metrics, which is the argument for reporting both and the reason a single headline retrieval number is not worth having.

docs.title: Reading the grounded@k curve
docs.text:
Shape Means Do Rises steadily with k Ranking is the bottleneck Rerank, or improve the index Jumps then plateaus A few ranking wins, then content gaps Fix the content Flat and low from k=1 The corpus lacks the material Write it 100% at k=1 The set is too easy Write harder cases

The second row is the common case and the one people misdiagnose, because the early jump suggests retrieval work is paying off right up to the point where it stops.

docs.title: What inflates these numbers
docs.text:
Hazard Effect A golden question quoted in the corpus That page wins its own test case Terms chosen after seeing the retrieval Grounding checks for what you know is there must_contain terms that are too generic Any chunk satisfies them A set tuned until it goes green Measures nothing A model's own knowledge of the subject Scores as retrieval success

The first is not hypothetical: adding a documentation example that quoted one golden question verbatim cost five points of hit@1, and the note explaining the mistake quoted it again and cost the same five points.

docs.title: What this cannot tell you
docs.text: Question Needs Was the answer correct A model and a grader Did it hedge when it should have refused A model and absent-content cases Did it cite the chunk it actually used Instrumentation in the answering system Would a reader have been satisfied A reader Is the assistant better than the search box Both, measured side by side

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the ceiling, because it reframes the whole problem. "The model and the prompt usually are not mine, and the corpus is. If the retrieved context does not contain the fact, a correct answer means the model supplied it from somewhere else, which is the thing I am trying to prevent. So retrieval grounding is an upper bound on grounded answer quality, and I can measure that bound with no model in the loop and no cost per run."

The measurement worth describing is the curve, not the number. Grounding at one chunk was 80 per cent, at three 90, and then flat all the way to ten. That plateau is diagnostic: while widening the window still helps, the failures are ranking failures and a reranker would address them; once it stops helping, the failures are not retrieval failures and no model or infrastructure will touch them.

Then the finding, which is the part I would want to be asked about. Both surviving failures were vocabulary gaps: the reader's everyday word was missing from the page that documents the thing, while the page used a precise term the reader had no reason to know. The fix was one sentence per page. It moved hit@1 five points, MRR from 0.742 to 0.775, routing five points, grounding at one chunk from 80 to 90 per cent and at three chunks to 100, and it narrowed the routing headroom, which means part of what looked like a routing opportunity was never a routing problem. A ten-point gap looked like a case for a reranker and five points of it was a synonym.

Volunteer the limit before anyone has to ask for it. No model answered a single question in any of this. I can say that at three chunks every question in the set can be answered from material containing the required facts. I cannot say the answers would be right: a model can misread a correct chunk, blend two into a claim neither makes, or answer correctly from pre-training while the retrieved context is irrelevant, and that last case scores as success on every metric I have. Closing that needs a model and a grader, which is output evaluation and costs per run.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A golden set with must_contain terms, a grounded@k curve over your real retriever, and a commit where fixing the corpus moved the numbers.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Compute grounded@k for k of 1, 3, 5 and 10 on a corpus you own. Predict where it plateaus. The plateau tells you whether to buy a reranker or write two sentences, and that is a budget decision.
  2. Take the cases still failing at k=10 and look for the reader's word on the page. In mine, both were synonyms the corpus never used.
  3. Check whether any documentation page quotes one of your evaluation questions. If it does, that page is winning its own test case.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. The grounded@k curve, the plateau, the two-sentence fix and the before-and-after table are all from docpack's twenty-case golden set and reproducible with docpack eval evals/golden.yaml; the recorded scores on its evaluating retrieval page were updated in the same commit, which is how the change shows up in a diff. What does not exist is any measurement with a model in the loop: nothing here grades an answer, there is no faithfulness scoring and no refusal testing, so the whole second layer of the table above is unmeasured and the demonstrated page records the concept as partial on that basis.

docs.title: Documentation-backed AI assistants
docs.text:
Wrapping retrieval in a product, where the hard parts are refusal, conversation state, and what happens when it is wrong in public.

core · difficulty 3 · 8h

structure and package content for RAG, internal assistants, and agentic workflows

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: RAG pipelines, Grounding and citation

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A product built on retrieval: a developer asks a question in prose and gets an answer with citations. NVIDIA's phrase is "internal assistants", which is the common case, since an internal assistant has a known audience and a forgiving failure mode.

The retrieval is the easy half. The hard half is everything around it: when to refuse, what to do with a follow-up question, and how a wrong answer gets noticed and fixed.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA names it twice, in the AI-ready bullet and under ways to stand out ("RAG pipelines, AI assistants, MCP servers"). Intel's version is "makes documentation discoverable and usable by both developers and AI assistants", which is the other side: being the corpus an assistant reads.

What makes it core rather than a product-management concern is that the decisions are documentation decisions. Refusal thresholds, citation display and scope boundaries are all editorial judgements, and a team that treats them as engineering ships an assistant that answers questions about billing because nobody said it should not.

On a Tuesday it is the thing that determines whether people keep using it. The assistant has been live a month. Usage dropped after week two. Looking at the logs: 40% of questions get a refusal, almost all because they are follow-ups that lost the subject ("what about for quantised models?"), and the refusals are indistinguishable from "we have no documentation on this". Nobody filed a bug, they just stopped asking, which is the characteristic failure of this product category and it is invisible without instrumentation.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build the assistant layer on top of a retriever: refusal, follow-up rewriting, scope, and a feedback loop. Fifty minutes, dependency-free.

Step 1: the retriever and a corpus with a scope boundary

mkdir -p assistant-drill && cd assistant-drill
cat > corpus.json <<'EOF'
[
  {"id": "c1", "source": "reference/flags.md", "crumb": "Server flags > batch_size", "kind": "reference",
   "text": "batch_size controls how many requests are grouped per forward pass. The default is 32."},
  {"id": "c2", "source": "how-to/latency.md", "crumb": "Reduce latency > Lower the batch size", "kind": "how-to",
   "text": "If your p99 is too high, set batch_size to 1 or 2. A batch of 32 waits for 32 requests to arrive."},
  {"id": "c3", "source": "how-to/quantised.md", "crumb": "Quantised models > Batch sizing", "kind": "how-to",
   "text": "Quantised models tolerate much larger batches. Start at 64 and raise while watching memory."},
  {"id": "c4", "source": "reference/flags.md", "crumb": "Server flags > max_memory_gb", "kind": "reference",
   "text": "max_memory_gb caps the GPU memory the server will allocate. The default is 16."}
]
EOF
python3 -c "import json; print(len(json.load(open('corpus.json'))), 'chunks')"

Step 2: the assistant layer

cat > assistant.py <<'PY'
"""The layer between a retriever and a person.

The retrieval is taken as given; what follows is the product. Four
decisions, and three of them are editorial rather than technical.

  SCOPE      refuse questions the corpus was never meant to answer, with a
             message that says so, distinctly from "I could not find it"
  FOLLOW-UP  rewrite "what about for quantised models?" into a standalone
             query, or the retriever sees four meaningless words
  REFUSAL    a confidence floor, with the refusal naming WHY it refused
  FEEDBACK   log every answer with its retrieval trace, so a wrong answer is
             a fixable report rather than a complaint
"""
import json
import math
import re
from collections import Counter
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

K1, B = 1.2, 0.75

#: Below this top score, the assistant refuses rather than answering from weak
#: evidence.
#:
#: This number was MEASURED, not chosen. Step 3 of the golden path scores ten
#: questions whose answerability is known, and on this corpus the answerable
#: ones land at 2.29 and above while the gaps top out at 1.59. Any floor
#: between those separates them; 1.9 is the midpoint.
#:
#: The first draft of this page guessed 1.2 and four of five known gaps were
#: answered confidently from an unrelated chunk. A guessed threshold is the
#: single commonest way an assistant fabricates.
CONFIDENCE_FLOOR = 1.9

#: Subjects the corpus does not cover. Refusing these with a DIFFERENT
#: message from "not found" is the whole point: one is a scope boundary and
#: the other is a documentation gap, and conflating them means the gap
#: reports are buried in the noise.
OUT_OF_SCOPE = {
    "billing": ["invoice", "billing", "price", "cost per", "subscription", "refund"],
    "accounts": ["password", "sign in", "login", "my account", "2fa"],
    "legal": ["license", "licence", "terms of service", "gdpr", "sla"],
}

#: A follow-up has no subject of its own. These are the giveaways.
FOLLOWUP_MARKERS = (
    "what about", "and for", "does that", "is it", "what if", "how about",
    "same for", "and if", "why not",
)


def tokenize(text):
    """Tokenize, indexing an underscore identifier both whole and split.

    `batch_size` is emitted as `batch_size`, `batch` and `size`. Keeping only
    the whole form means the question "what is the default batch size" can
    never match the chunk that documents `batch_size`, which is a real defect
    this guide found twice: once on the retrieval-evaluation page and again
    here, where it sent a reference question to a how-to chunk.

    Splitting only is also wrong, since it destroys the exact-identifier match
    that lexical search exists for. Both forms, indexed together.
    """
    out = []
    for token in re.findall(r"[a-z0-9_]+", text.lower()):
        if len(token) <= 1:
            continue
        out.append(token)
        if "_" in token:
            out.extend(part for part in token.split("_") if len(part) > 1)
    return out


class Retriever:
    def __init__(self, chunks):
        self.chunks = chunks
        self.docs = [Counter(tokenize(f"{c['crumb']} {c['text']}")) for c in chunks]
        self.lengths = [sum(d.values()) for d in self.docs]
        self.avg = sum(self.lengths) / len(self.docs)
        df = Counter()
        for d in self.docs:
            df.update(d.keys())
        n = len(self.docs)
        self.idf = {t: math.log(1 + (n - c + 0.5) / (c + 0.5)) for t, c in df.items()}

    def search(self, query, limit=3):
        terms = tokenize(query)
        scored = []
        for chunk, doc, length in zip(self.chunks, self.docs, self.lengths):
            score = 0.0
            for t in terms:
                f = doc.get(t, 0)
                if not f:
                    continue
                norm = 1 - B + B * (length / self.avg)
                score += self.idf.get(t, 0.0) * (f * (K1 + 1)) / (f + K1 * norm)
            if score > 0:
                scored.append((score, chunk))
        scored.sort(key=lambda s: (-s[0], s[1]["id"]))
        return scored[:limit]


@dataclass
class Turn:
    """One exchange, with everything needed to diagnose it later."""

    question: str
    rewritten: str = ""
    outcome: str = ""  # answered | refused_scope | refused_confidence
    reason: str = ""
    retrieved: list = field(default_factory=list)
    answer: str = ""
    cited: list = field(default_factory=list)


def classify_scope(question):
    lowered = question.lower()
    for topic, cues in OUT_OF_SCOPE.items():
        for cue in cues:
            if cue in lowered:
                return topic
    return None


def is_followup(question):
    lowered = question.lower().strip()
    return any(lowered.startswith(m) or f" {m}" in lowered for m in FOLLOWUP_MARKERS)


def rewrite(question, history):
    """Turn a follow-up into a standalone query using the last subject.

    Crude and deliberately so: it appends the previous question's content
    words. A production version asks a small model to rewrite, which is
    better and introduces a failure mode of its own. Either way the point is
    that SOMETHING must do this, because "what about for quantised models?"
    is four words with no subject and the retriever has no memory.
    """
    if not history or not is_followup(question):
        return question
    previous = history[-1].rewritten or history[-1].question
    carried = [w for w in tokenize(previous) if w not in set(tokenize(question))]
    return f"{question} {' '.join(carried)}".strip()


class Assistant:
    def __init__(self, retriever):
        self.retriever = retriever
        self.history: list[Turn] = []
        self.log: list[Turn] = []

    def ask(self, question):
        turn = Turn(question=question)

        topic = classify_scope(question)
        if topic:
            turn.outcome = "refused_scope"
            turn.reason = topic
            turn.answer = (
                f"I only cover the widget platform documentation, and {topic} is "
                f"outside that. Try the {topic} team's own resources."
            )
            self.log.append(turn)
            return turn

        turn.rewritten = rewrite(question, self.history)
        hits = self.retriever.search(turn.rewritten)
        turn.retrieved = [(round(s, 2), c["id"], c["crumb"]) for s, c in hits]

        if not hits or hits[0][0] < CONFIDENCE_FLOOR:
            turn.outcome = "refused_confidence"
            top = hits[0][0] if hits else 0.0
            turn.reason = f"top score {top:.2f} below floor {CONFIDENCE_FLOOR}"
            turn.answer = (
                "I could not find this in the documentation. This may be a gap; "
                "the question has been logged."
            )
            self.log.append(turn)
            self.history.append(turn)
            return turn

        score, chunk = hits[0]
        turn.outcome = "answered"
        turn.answer = f"{chunk['text']} [{chunk['id']}]  (source: {chunk['source']})"
        turn.cited = [chunk["id"]]
        self.log.append(turn)
        self.history.append(turn)
        return turn

    def report(self):
        """What the team looks at weekly. This is the product's real output."""
        total = len(self.log)
        by_outcome = Counter(t.outcome for t in self.log)
        gaps = [t for t in self.log if t.outcome == "refused_confidence"]
        scope = Counter(t.reason for t in self.log if t.outcome == "refused_scope")

        print(f"  turns: {total}")
        for outcome, count in sorted(by_outcome.items()):
            print(f"    {outcome:<22} {count:>2}  ({count / total:.0%})")
        if scope:
            print(f"    out-of-scope topics asked: {dict(scope)}")
        if gaps:
            print("    questions with no good answer (a content backlog):")
            for turn in gaps:
                print(f"      {turn.question!r}  [{turn.reason}]")
PY
echo "assistant written"

Step 3: calibrate the refusal threshold before using it

The confidence floor is the single most consequential number in the product, and it cannot be reasoned to. Measure it.

cat > calibrate.py <<'PY'
"""Measure the refusal threshold instead of guessing it.

Two lists: questions you know the corpus answers, and questions you know it
does not. If the two score distributions separate, any floor between them
works. If they overlap, no threshold can distinguish them and the honest
conclusion is that refusal alone will not save you.
"""
import json

from assistant import Retriever

ANSWERABLE = [
    "what is the default batch size",
    "how do I cap gpu memory",
    "my p99 is too high",
    "batch size for quantised models",
    "what does max_memory_gb do",
]
GAPS = [
    "how do I rotate a signing key",
    "how do I enable tls",
    "what is the retry policy",
    "how do I add a webhook",
    "where are the logs",
]

retriever = Retriever(json.load(open("corpus.json")))


def top(question):
    hits = retriever.search(question)
    return (hits[0][0], hits[0][1]["id"]) if hits else (0.0, "none")


answerable, gaps = [], []
print("ANSWERABLE                             score   top")
for question in ANSWERABLE:
    score, cid = top(question)
    answerable.append(score)
    print(f"  {question:<36} {score:6.2f}   {cid}")

print("GAPS                                   score   top")
for question in GAPS:
    score, cid = top(question)
    gaps.append(score)
    print(f"  {question:<36} {score:6.2f}   {cid}")

low, high = min(answerable), max(gaps)
print(f"\n  lowest answerable {low:.2f}, highest gap {high:.2f}")
if low > high:
    print(f"  clean separation: any floor in ({high:.2f}, {low:.2f}) works; "
          f"midpoint {(low + high) / 2:.2f}")
else:
    print("  OVERLAP: no threshold separates these. Refusal alone cannot fix this.")
PY
python3 calibrate.py

Step 4: a realistic conversation, including the awkward turns

cat > session.py <<'PY'
import json

from assistant import Assistant, Retriever

assistant = Assistant(Retriever(json.load(open("corpus.json"))))

conversation = [
    "what is the default batch size",            # answerable
    "what about for quantised models?",          # follow-up, no subject
    "how do I cap gpu memory",                   # answerable, new subject
    "what about for quantised models?",          # same follow-up, new subject
    "how do I get a refund",                     # out of scope
    "how do I rotate a signing key",             # a real gap
]

for question in conversation:
    turn = assistant.ask(question)
    print(f"Q: {question}")
    if turn.rewritten and turn.rewritten != question:
        print(f"   rewritten -> {turn.rewritten!r}")
    print(f"   [{turn.outcome}] {turn.reason}")
    print(f"   {turn.answer[:88]}")
    print()

print("=== weekly report ===")
assistant.report()
PY
python3 session.py

Step 5: show what the follow-up rewriting is worth

python3 - <<'PY'
import json

from assistant import Assistant, Retriever

chunks = json.load(open("corpus.json"))
pair = ["what is the default batch size", "what about for quantised models?"]

for label, rewriting in (("with rewriting", True), ("without rewriting", False)):
    assistant = Assistant(Retriever(chunks))
    if not rewriting:
        assistant_rewrite = None
        import assistant as module
        module.rewrite = lambda question, history: question
    print(f"=== {label} ===")
    for question in pair:
        turn = assistant.ask(question)
        print(f"  {question!r}")
        print(f"    -> [{turn.outcome}] {turn.answer[:70]}")
    print()
PY

What you built. An assistant layer with a scope boundary, follow-up rewriting, a measured confidence floor, and a weekly report that is a content backlog.

The report is the deliverable, not the answers:

turns: 6
  answered                4  (67%)
  refused_confidence      1  (17%)
  refused_scope           1  (17%)
  out-of-scope topics asked: {'billing': 1}
  questions with no good answer (a content backlog):
    'how do I rotate a signing key'  [top score 1.23 below floor 1.9]

Every low-confidence refusal is a reader telling you, in their own words, about a page you have not written. Every out-of-scope question tells you what people think this thing is for. Neither is available from a search box.

docs.title: Two things the first draft got wrong, both measured
docs.text:
The guessed threshold fabricated. The first version of this page set the confidence floor to 1.2 by eye. At that floor, "how do I rotate a signing key" was answered confidently from the batch_size chunk, and four of five known gaps got answers. Calibration puts the answerable questions at 2.29 and above and the gaps at 1.59 and below, so the floor belongs at about 1.9. A guessed threshold is the commonest way one of these fabricates, and the fix costs ten labelled questions.

The tokenizer sent a reference question to a how-to page. "What is the default batch size" returned the latency guide, because batch_size with an underscore cannot match "batch size" with a space. That is the same defect retrieval evaluation found on its own corpus, showing up a second time in a different component. Indexing underscore identifiers both whole and split fixes it, and it strengthens the exact-identifier case rather than weakening it: "what does max_memory_gb do" went from 1.73 to 6.06.

Finding the same bug twice in two components is the argument for the tokenizer being a shared, tested function rather than six lines copied into each retriever.

docs.title: The four decisions, and which are editorial
docs.text:
Decision Who owns it Failure if wrong Scope boundary Documentation Answers questions about billing from a page about batching Refusal threshold Documentation, with data Too low: fabrication. Too high: people stop asking Citation display Documentation A reader cannot verify, so trust is binary Follow-up handling Engineering Half of all turns fail and look like content gaps

Three of four are editorial. That is the argument for this concept living in a documentation role rather than in a platform team.

docs.title: Two refusals that must not look the same
docs.text:
Refusal Means Action it should produce Out of scope We never intended to cover this Point elsewhere. No backlog item Low confidence We should cover this and apparently do not A backlog item with the reader's wording

Conflating them is the commonest design mistake, and it destroys the single most valuable output of the whole product. A log where both read "I could not find this" cannot be sorted into gaps and non-gaps.

docs.title: Why follow-ups are most of the problem
docs.text:
A standalone-question assistant is a search box with better prose. People immediately use it as a conversation:

Turn Words the retriever sees without rewriting "what is the default batch size" the whole question "what about for quantised models?" about, for, quantised, models "is that per request or per batch?" that, per, request, batch "why?" nothing

Rewriting options, in increasing cost:

Approach Quality Cost Append the previous question's terms crude, better than nothing trivial Keep a running subject and prepend it decent cheap Ask a small model to rewrite into a standalone query good a model call per turn Pass the whole history to the retriever poor; old terms dominate trivial

The last row is what teams do by accident, and it degrades as conversations lengthen.

docs.title: What to log, per turn
docs.text: Field Why The question, verbatim Reader vocabulary, which is your SEO and eval input The rewritten query Otherwise a rewriting bug looks like a retrieval bug The ranked retrieval list with scores The only way to debug Outcome and reason Separates scope refusals from gaps Citations So you can check grounding after the fact Feedback, if any The one signal you cannot reconstruct later

docs.title: The metrics that matter
docs.text:
Metric Healthy What it tells you Refusal rate 5 to 20% Near zero means fabrication; over 40% means people will leave Gap refusals per week declining Whether the backlog is being worked Repeat question rate declining Whether answers are landing Citation click-through nonzero Whether anyone verifies, and whether the pages are good Turns per conversation over 1 If it is 1.0, follow-ups are failing silently

Turns per conversation is the underrated one. An assistant with an average of 1.1 turns is being used as a search box, which usually means follow-ups fail and people learned not to try.

docs.title: Honest limitations
docs.text: Limitation Consequence It inherits every error in the corpus A grounded answer from a wrong page is wrong A stale index is a confident liar Rebuild on publish, and surface the index date Silent abandonment The main failure mode, invisible without the metrics above It cannot say "nobody wrote this yet" without you logging it Gaps look like failures Internal and external need different scope and tone And different visibility filtering

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with the two refusals, because it is the design decision that shows you have operated one. "The retrieval is the easy half. The thing that decided whether ours was useful was separating two refusals: out of scope, which points you elsewhere, and low confidence, which says we should cover this and do not and logs your exact wording. Conflating them throws away the best output of the whole product, which is a content backlog in readers' own words. After that, follow-up rewriting, because people converse immediately and 'what about for quantised models' is four words with no subject."

The follow-up is "how do you set the confidence threshold", and the answer has to be empirical or it signals you guessed. You need a labelled set: questions you know the corpus answers and questions you know it does not, then pick the floor that minimises both fabrication and false refusal. That is output evaluation applied to a product decision, and the threshold moves whenever the corpus or the retriever changes, which is why it belongs in CI rather than in a config file somebody tuned once.

The tradeoff to volunteer. An assistant reduces the number of people who read your documentation, and that is partly a loss. A reader who lands on a page sees the surrounding caveats, the related links, and the thing they did not know to ask about. A reader who gets a paragraph gets exactly what they asked for and none of the context, so the omission failure from grounding gets systematically worse: every answer is correct and narrower than the page. Citations partly compensate, and only if people click them, which is why click-through is on the metrics list.

One sharper point. The strongest framing is that an assistant is a measurement instrument pointed at your documentation. Its refusals are your gaps, its repeat questions are your unclear pages, and its question log is the vocabulary your readers actually use, which is the input SEO, chunking and evaluation sets all need and almost nobody has. A documentation team that ships one and treats the logs as a product feature has acquired the user research it was never funded to do. That reframes the project from an AI initiative into instrumentation, which is both true and a much better pitch.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. An assistant with the two distinct refusals, a turn log, and a weekly report that lists gap refusals with the reader's wording.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. The weekly report is the demonstration: it turns a conversation into a content backlog, which is the thing nobody expects.
  2. Calibrate the threshold on a labelled set. Twenty questions you know are answerable and ten you know are not. Report the refusal rate at three thresholds. That is a small experiment with a real number.
  3. Instrument turns per conversation on anything you ship. If it is near 1.0, your follow-up handling is broken and nobody has told you.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. A working chatbot over docs is a weekend project. A scope boundary, two semantically different refusals, a logged rewriting step, and a report that produces a prioritised content backlog demonstrates that you built it as documentation infrastructure rather than as a demo.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
This environment has the retrieval half, in docpack, and not the generation half. So the pipeline this page describes exists up to the point where an answer would be produced, and stops there.

What you need. The existing retrieval stack plus a model, and one thing that is harder to get than either: a set of questions real readers asked. The twenty-case golden set substitutes for it and is written by the corpus's author, which makes it systematically optimistic, as search log analysis measures.

What you would run. Wire the retrieved chunks into a prompt, generate answers for every case, and then score the system end to end rather than in halves.

question -> retrieve(k) -> prompt -> answer -> grounded? cited? refused?

What you would see.

Observation Rough magnitude What it tells you End-to-end correct answers below your grounded@k Retrieval sets a ceiling generation does not reach Correct answers from wrong chunks a few per cent The model knew it anyway; your corpus got no credit Wrong answers from correct chunks the interesting bucket A generation or prompt problem, not a retrieval one Answers on questions with no corpus answer mostly invented The reason a refusal path is mandatory Effect of raising k from 3 to 10 small, then negative More context is not more accuracy

The second and third rows are why end-to-end evaluation cannot be replaced by retrieval metrics. A system can look healthy on hit@1 and answer badly, or answer well while retrieving nothing useful because the model already knew the answer, and only the paired measurement distinguishes them. On a documentation assistant the second case is the dangerous one: it works until a reader asks about something your product changed last week.

How you would know it had failed. End-to-end accuracy above your grounding ceiling means the model is answering from its own weights, so the test is not measuring your corpus. Accuracy that does not drop when you shuffle the retrieved chunks means the same thing, and it is the cheapest check available: corrupt the context deliberately and confirm the answers get worse.

docs.title: Reading an AI software stack
docs.text:
The newest onnx writes a file the newest onnxruntime refuses to load, and the error message is a C++ function signature and a path on somebody else's build machine.

context · difficulty 2 · 4h

Asked for by name

Intel: "Python literacy sufficient to run and validate AI samples, with working familiarity with the AI software stack"

Prerequisites: Inference serving and microservices

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The layered set of components between a model and the silicon: a framework, an exchange format, a runtime, a kernel library, a driver. Intel's bullet asks for "Python literacy sufficient to run and validate AI samples", which is a precise and modest requirement: not building models, but being able to run a sample and tell whether its output is right.

The reason it needs a page is that the layers have independent version numbers and the compatibility rules between them are the single largest source of support load in this field.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because "run and validate AI samples" is the job description of a person who will spend their first month on version errors.

A documentation engineer in this space does not debug kernels. They do repeatedly answer the question "why does the sample not load", and the answer is nearly always a pair of version numbers that are each individually current and jointly unsupported. Writing that down, once, correctly, is worth more than any tutorial.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Install the newest versions of two adjacent components and try to pass a file between them. About twenty minutes, and the first result is the whole page.

Step 1: what is installed

import onnx, onnxruntime as ort
print(onnx.__version__, onnx.IR_VERSION, onnx.defs.onnx_opset_version())
print(ort.__version__)

onnx          1.23.2   (writes IR 14, knows opset 28)
onnxruntime   1.29.0

Both current, both installed today, nothing pinned.

Step 2: write a two-line model and load it

A single Relu. There is no simpler model.

m = helper.make_model(graph, opset_imports=[helper.make_opsetid("", 17)])
onnx.save(m, "d.onnx")
ort.InferenceSession("d.onnx")

onnx 1.23.2 make_model default ir_version = 14
  onnxruntime 1.29.0 refuses it:
  [ONNXRuntimeError] : 1 : FAIL : Load model from d.onnx failed:
  /onnxruntime_src/onnxruntime/core/graph/model.cc:192
  onnxruntime::Model::Model(onnx::ModelProto&&, const onnxruntime::PathString&,
  const onnxruntime::IOnnxRuntimeOpSchemaRegistryList*,
  const onnxruntime::logging::Logger&, const onnxruntime::ModelOptions&) Un

The default output of the newest writer is not loadable by the newest reader. No flags, no exotic operators, a single Relu, and the two most obvious packages in the ecosystem disagree out of the box.

The message deserves its own look. A reader is handed a path on NVIDIA's build machine, a fully-qualified C++ constructor signature, and then the text is truncated before it says what to do. The fix is one line, m.ir_version = 10, and it is not in the message.

Step 3: the version matrix has more than one axis

Opset and IR version are different numbers that fail differently:

model as written           what onnxruntime does with it
opset 17, IR 10            loads and runs
opset 28, IR 10            FAIL ... ValidateOpsetForDomain ... (load-time)
opset 17, IR 14            FAIL ... Model::Model ... (load-time)
opset 1,  IR 10            loads, warns twice, then:
                           NOT_IMPLEMENTED : Could not find an implementation
                           for Relu(1) node with name ''

Four outcomes from one Relu. Two axes, two directions, and the fourth row is the interesting one: an opset that is too old passes validation, emits a warning saying it "may run depending upon legacy support", and then fails at a different layer with a different error class when the node is bound.

So the same category of problem, a version mismatch, surfaces as a load error in one direction and a runtime error in the other, which means a troubleshooting page organised by error message will put them in different sections.

Step 4: write the table nobody wrote

Everything above fits in six lines, and would have saved the reader the afternoon:

component     version    writes / accepts
onnx          1.23.2     writes IR 14 by default; set ir_version yourself
onnxruntime   1.29.0     accepts IR <= 10, opset 7..23 (guaranteed >= 7)
fix           m.ir_version = 10
symptom       FAIL at InferenceSession(), message names a .cc file

That is the artifact. Not a tutorial, not a conceptual explanation of ONNX: a table of which versions accept which, the one-line fix, and the symptom text a reader will paste into a search box.

What you built. A reproduced incompatibility between two current packages, a mapped two-axis version matrix, and the compatibility table that the error message replaces.

docs.title: The layers, from model to metal
docs.text:
Layer Examples Breaks as Framework PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX Training-time API churn Exchange format ONNX Opset and IR version Runtime ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, TensorRT Unsupported operator Kernel library cuDNN, oneDNN, cuBLAS Version pinned to the runtime Driver and toolkit CUDA, ROCm, Level Zero Minimum driver version Hardware GPU, CPU, accelerator Compute capability

A single sample exercises every row, and an error from any row arrives at the reader as "the sample does not work".

docs.title: Why the errors are bad, specifically
docs.text:
Property of the message Consequence Names a source file on a build machine Looks like an internal defect Includes a C++ signature Unsearchable, unreadable Truncated before the remedy The fix is one line and absent Error class differs by direction Troubleshooting pages split the cause Warnings that say "may work" Readers proceed and fail later

These are the most-read strings in the stack, since a stuck reader is a motivated reader, and they are maintained by nobody. A documentation role that gets the fix into the message has done more good than a dozen pages.

docs.title: What to pin, and where
docs.text:
Practice Why Pin every layer in the sample's requirements A floating version breaks the sample on a schedule State the tested combination in the page The reader's combination will differ Run the sample in CI on the pinned set Otherwise the page's claim rots silently Test the newest set too, and let it fail loudly So you learn before the reader does Record the fix next to the symptom text Readers search symptoms, not causes

Row four is the one teams skip. A sample pinned forever works forever and tells you nothing about the ecosystem your readers actually install into.

docs.title: Validating a sample's output, not just its exit code
docs.text:
Check Catches Exit code Crashes only Output shape and dtype Most integration errors Output against a stored reference Numerical drift between versions Tolerance stated explicitly False failures on different hardware A known-wrong input A sample that cannot fail

Intel's phrase is "run and validate", and the distance between rows one and three is the whole of it. A sample asserted only on exit code passes while producing nonsense, which is the characteristic AI-sample defect.

docs.title: CUDA minor version compatibility, as an example of a promise with carve-outs
docs.text:
NVIDIA's compatibility documentation states that from CUDA 11 onward, applications built with a toolkit in a major release family run on any driver meeting a minimum version, 580 or newer for 13.x, 525 for 12.x, 450 for 11.x. The same page then carves out five exceptions:

  • The feature set is limited, and newer-driver features fail with cudaErrorCallRequiresNewerDriver.
  • Code compiled to PTX does not work on older drivers.
  • A target architecture must be passed to nvcc.
  • The minimum driver must actually be installed, or calls return an initialisation error.
  • Libraries have interdependencies of their own: each cuDNN version requires a particular cuBLAS.

The useful observation is structural rather than about CUDA: the promise fits in one line and its exceptions take five, so any summary short enough to remember is wrong. That is worth knowing before writing a compatibility page, because the instinct is to simplify exactly the thing that cannot be simplified.

(Verified by opening NVIDIA's minor version compatibility page; the figures and carve-outs above are from that page, not from search results.)

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the version problem, because it is the job. "Running and validating AI samples sounds modest, and in practice it means becoming the person who answers 'why does the sample not load'. The answer is nearly always two version numbers that are each individually current and jointly unsupported."

Then the demonstration, which is short enough to say out loud. I installed the newest onnx and the newest onnxruntime, wrote a model containing a single Relu, and onnxruntime refused to load it, because onnx now writes IR version 14 by default and the runtime accepts 10. No flags, no unusual operators, the two most obvious packages in the ecosystem, incompatible out of the box. The fix is one line.

The part a documentation person should care about. The error message hands the reader a path on somebody's build machine, a fully-qualified C++ constructor signature, and no remedy. Those strings are the most-read documentation in the stack, because a stuck reader is a motivated reader, and nobody owns them. I would rather land the fix inside the message than write another page.

The structural point, with a worked example. NVIDIA's CUDA minor-version compatibility page promises that apps in a major family run on any driver above a minimum, and then carves out five exceptions: PTX, feature set, the -arch requirement, the minimum driver actually being installed, and library interdependencies. The promise is one line and the exceptions are five, so every summary short enough to remember is wrong. Knowing that before writing a compatibility page changes what you write, because the instinct is to simplify precisely what cannot be.

Be honest about the depth. CPU only, no GPU, no CUDA, no TensorRT, no OpenVINO, no distributed training. I can run a sample, read a version matrix, and tell whether output is plausible. I would not claim to debug a kernel or tune an accelerator, and context tier is what this is.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A compatibility table for two components you use, with the symptom text, the accepted ranges and the one-line fix.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Install the newest versions of two adjacent components in a stack you care about and pass the simplest possible artifact between them. Predict whether it works; this page exists because the answer was no.
  2. Take the next version error you hit and write the three-line entry that would have saved you: symptom, cause, fix. That is the page the ecosystem is missing.
  3. Check whether a sample you own asserts anything about its output beyond the exit code. "Run and validate" is two verbs and most samples do one.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Every result was executed here against onnx 1.23.2 and onnxruntime 1.29.0, including the full error text and the four-outcome version matrix. The CUDA material is verified by opening NVIDIA's own compatibility page, and is cited as reading rather than as experience: no CUDA, no GPU and no driver work happened on this machine. The demonstrated page records the ONNX half as demonstrated and the accelerator half as not.
