docs.title: Judging where AI can be trusted
docs.text:
Deciding which content tasks an LLM can own, which it can draft, and which it must never touch.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

sound judgment about where AI can be trusted

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: Prompting for content work

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Deciding, per task, whether an LLM can own it, draft it for review, or must not be used on it at all. The judgement rests on one question: what does a wrong output cost, and would anyone notice?

It is a design skill rather than a prompting skill. The output is usually a pipeline with a human in a specific place, not a better prompt.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA asks for it twice, and the second instance is the more revealing one. The qualification is "practical experience applying LLMs to content workflows (prompting, retrieval and grounding, output evaluation) and sound judgment about where AI can be trusted." The responsibility is "Automate the content lifecycle with LLMs and scripting, from drafting and updating to auditing, with checks for freshness, code accuracy, and terminology drift, and human review where judgment matters."

That last clause is the job. They are not asking whether you can get an LLM to write a page. They are asking where you would put the human, and that is a question about failure cost, not about model capability.

On a Tuesday it is a sequence of small decisions that compound. You are auditing 400 pages for stale version references. An LLM can find candidates reliably and cannot decide which are actually wrong, so it proposes and you dispose. Then someone suggests using it to generate the reference tables from the source, and the right answer there is no. A reference table should be generated from the code, deterministically. An LLM that is right 97 per cent of the time on parameter defaults is a worse tool than mkdocstrings being right every time.

That second decision is the one that distinguishes judgement from enthusiasm. The question is not "can the model do this", it is "is a model the right mechanism". A deterministic generator beats a reliable LLM wherever one is available, and a great deal of documentation work has one available.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Classify a real set of content tasks by failure cost, then build the one that sits in the interesting middle. Forty minutes.

Step 1: the two axes that decide everything

mkdir -p trust-drill && cd trust-drill
cat > axes.md <<'EOF'
                    WOULD ANYONE NOTICE A WRONG OUTPUT?

                        Yes, quickly        No, or not for months
                    +-------------------+-------------------------+
  COST   Low        |  LLM OWNS IT      |  LLM DRAFTS, YOU REVIEW |
  OF A              |                   |                         |
  WRONG  High       |  LLM DRAFTS,      |  DO NOT USE AN LLM      |
  OUTPUT            |  YOU REVIEW       |  (generate it instead)  |
                    +-------------------+-------------------------+
EOF
cat axes.md

The bottom-right cell is the one people get wrong. High cost plus invisible failure is where an LLM is most dangerous and most tempting, because the output looks right and nothing contradicts it.

Step 2: classify real tasks

cat > tasks.md <<'EOF'
| Task                                        | Cost | Noticed?   | Verdict |
|---------------------------------------------|------|------------|---------|
| Suggest a page title                        | low  | yes        | owns    |
| Draft a summary for front matter            | low  | yes        | owns    |
| Find pages mentioning a deprecated flag     | low  | yes        | owns    |
| Rewrite a paragraph for clarity             | low  | yes        | owns    |
| Propose which stale pages need review       | low  | yes        | owns    |
| Draft release notes from a changelog        | med  | yes        | drafts  |
| Write a how-to for a feature you know       | med  | yes        | drafts  |
| Audit 400 pages for terminology drift       | low  | no         | drafts  |
| Write a parameter reference table           | high | no         | NEVER   |
| State a default value                       | high | no         | NEVER   |
| Write a security instruction                | high | no         | NEVER   |
| Generate a runnable code sample             | high | yes (CI)   | drafts* |
| Decide what content to retire               | high | no         | NEVER   |
EOF
cat tasks.md
echo
echo "* drafts only because code-sample validation makes the failure visible."
echo "  Without that gate it belongs in the NEVER row."

That footnote is the whole idea: a gate can move a task between cells. Trust is not a property of the task, it is a property of the task plus the checks around it.

Step 3: build the interesting one

Terminology drift is low cost, invisible, high volume. That is the cell where an LLM proposes and a human disposes, and where the design work is in making review cheap.

mkdir -p docs
cat > docs/a.md <<'EOF'
# Getting started
Clone the repo and install the deps. The repo has a sample config.
EOF
cat > docs/b.md <<'EOF'
# Contributing
Fork the repository, then open a pull request against main.
EOF
cat > docs/c.md <<'EOF'
# Troubleshooting
If the PR build fails, check the repo settings and re-run the job.
EOF

cat > terms.yaml <<'EOF'
# The approved term, and the variants that should become it.
repository:
  - repo
  - repos
pull request:
  - PR
  - MR
  - merge request
EOF

cat > audit.py <<'PY'
"""Find terminology drift and emit a reviewable proposal, not an edit.

The LLM-shaped part of this task is judging whether a hit is really drift:
"PR" in prose is drift, "PR" inside a code block or a URL is not. This script
is the deterministic half, and it exists to make the human review cheap enough
to actually happen. That division is the point: automate the finding, keep the
deciding.
"""
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import yaml


def main(docs: Path, terms_file: Path) -> int:
    terms = yaml.safe_load(terms_file.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    proposals = []

    for page in sorted(docs.glob("*.md")):
        lines = page.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
        in_fence = False
        for number, line in enumerate(lines, 1):
            if line.strip().startswith("```"):
                in_fence = not in_fence
                continue
            if in_fence:
                continue
            for approved, variants in terms.items():
                for variant in variants:
                    if re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(variant)}\b", line):
                        proposals.append(
                            (page.name, number, variant, approved, line.strip())
                        )

    for name, number, variant, approved, text in proposals:
        print(f"{name}:{number}")
        print(f"  {variant!r} -> {approved!r}")
        print(f"  {text}")
        print("  [ ] accept   [ ] reject (quoting a UI label, a URL, or a proper noun)")
        print()

    print(f"{len(proposals)} proposals for review. Nothing has been changed.")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(Path("docs"), Path("terms.yaml")))
PY
python3 audit.py

Step 4: check that the design holds where it matters

cat >> docs/c.md <<'EOF'

Run this:

```bash
# clone the repo first
gh repo clone example/widget
```
EOF
python3 audit.py | tail -3
echo
echo "The 'repo' inside the fenced block was not proposed. Fence awareness is"
echo "deterministic; asking a model to respect code blocks is not."

What you built. A pipeline that proposes and never edits, with a review line per proposal and a reject reason prompted. The LLM's job in the full version is pre-filtering the proposals it can tell are false positives, which reduces human review without ever giving the model write access.

Note which half is deterministic. Fence awareness is a parser's job, and handing it to a model would be choosing unreliability for no reason.

docs.title: The decision, as four questions
docs.text:
Question If the answer is bad news What does a wrong output cost? Raise the review level Would anyone notice, and how fast? Invisible failure is the dangerous case Is there a deterministic alternative? Use it. This question outranks the others Can a gate make the failure visible? A gate can promote the task one cell

The third question is the one that gets skipped. Before asking how to prompt well, ask whether the task is a generation problem at all.

docs.title: Tasks by verdict
docs.text: Verdict Tasks LLM owns it Title suggestions, summaries, clarity rewrites, finding candidates, classifying pages, proposing review queues LLM drafts, human disposes Release notes from a changelog, first drafts of how-tos, terminology audits, freshness triage, test-case generation Never an LLM Parameter references, default values, version requirements, security instructions, anything about data handling, retirement decisions, anything a generator can produce

docs.title: Why "never" for the last group
docs.text:
Not squeamishness. Three specific reasons:

Reason Example A deterministic generator exists and is exactly right Generated API reference beats a 97-percent-accurate table The failure is silent and expensive A wrong default costs each reader an afternoon and nothing flags it The failure is unbounded A wrong security instruction is not a documentation defect

docs.title: What makes a gate good enough to promote a task
docs.text:
Gate Promotes Code-sample validation Generated samples, from never to drafts Doc test harness Generated examples in prose Link checking Generated cross-references A human review queue with a reject reason Any high-volume audit Evaluation sets Assistant answers, from unmeasured to measured

A gate only counts if it fails loudly and nobody can merge past it. A gate that produces a warning promotes nothing, because warnings are ignored.

docs.title: Where this judgement usually goes wrong
docs.text: Mistake Consequence Asking an LLM for facts a generator could produce Confident, occasionally wrong reference Trusting a task because the output reads well Fluency is uncorrelated with accuracy Review with no reject reason Reviewers accept everything by the fortieth item No sampling after the pipeline is trusted Model or prompt changes silently degrade it Treating "the model is better now" as a reason to remove the human The failure cost did not change

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with a refusal, because the refusals are the evidence of judgement. "I use an LLM to find candidate pages for a terminology audit and to pre-filter the false positives, with a human accepting each change. I do not use one to write parameter tables, because mkdocstrings generates them from the signatures and is right every time. A model that is right 97 percent of the time on defaults is a worse tool than a generator, even though it is more impressive."

The follow-up is "what about now that models are better", and it is a real question rather than a trap. The answer is that model capability changes which cell a task sits in on the cost axis, slowly, and changes nothing about the visibility axis. The reason not to generate a default value is not that the model cannot usually get it right. It is that when it is wrong, nothing in the system disagrees with it. That property is about the pipeline, not the model, so it does not improve with the model.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Every human review step you add is a step that will be skipped under deadline pressure, and a review queue nobody works is worse than no automation, because the proposals accumulate and the corpus looks audited. So the design constraint is not "where should a human review" but "where can a human review cheaply enough that they will". That is why the golden path's script prints a reject reason prompt: a reviewer who has to think about why rejects less carelessly, and a reviewer facing 400 undifferentiated proposals accepts all of them.

One sharper point. The strongest version of this judgement is that an LLM is the right tool for tasks where the output is a proposal and the wrong tool for tasks where the output is a fact. Proposals are cheap to reject; facts are expensive to be wrong about and nothing rejects them. Almost every good LLM-in-documentation design turns a fact-production task into a proposal-production task, and almost every bad one does the reverse.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A pipeline with the human in a documented place, and a written list of tasks you decided not to automate, with reasons. The second half is rarer and more convincing.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Classify twenty real content tasks on the two axes. An hour. The output is a table you can show, and the "never" rows are the interesting part.
  2. Build the proposal pipeline from the golden path against a real corpus, with a real term list. Measure how many proposals a reviewer accepts; if it is above 95 percent your filter is too loose and the review is theatre.
  3. Write down one thing you refused to automate and why. One paragraph. This is the single most direct answer to NVIDIA's "sound judgment" line, and almost nobody brings one.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Enthusiasm about LLMs is universal and worthless as a signal. A candidate who says "I would not use a model for that, here is the generator I would use instead" is demonstrating exactly the thing the posting asks for, and it is a short sentence that is very hard to fake.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
This is the only concept on the curriculum whose demonstration is a record of being wrong, which is why it has none here: the project has no accumulated history of predictions against outcomes.

What you need. No special tooling. A model, a log, and several months. The instrument is a written prediction made before each delegated task, which is the part that cannot be reconstructed afterwards and the reason this cannot be demonstrated retrospectively.

What you would run. Before handing any task to a model, write down one line: what you expect it to get right, what you expect to have to fix, and how you will check. Afterwards, record what actually happened. Thirty entries is enough to be interesting.

task                       predicted            actual               checked by
draft the API reference     structure ok,       structure ok,        validator
                            names wrong          two names invented

What you would see.

Pattern What it tells you Tasks you predicted well Where your model of the tool is calibrated Tasks it did better than predicted Where you are over-reviewing, and paying for it Tasks it did worse The real boundary, which is narrower than the discourse suggests Tasks you could not check The actual danger: not inaccuracy, unverifiability Drift over months Whether your judgment is updating or hardening

The fourth row is the one worth the exercise. The decisive question is almost never "can the model do this" but "if it does it wrong, will I notice", and a prediction log makes that visible in a way no benchmark does. Tasks whose output you cannot verify are the ones to refuse regardless of how capable the tool looks.

How you would know it had failed. A log where you were right every time is a log written afterwards; genuine prediction produces surprises at a decent rate. A log with no refusals means the judgment is not being exercised, only the tool. And if every entry's check is "I read it and it looked fine", the exercise has recorded confidence rather than accuracy, which is the thing it exists to distinguish.

docs.title: Antora and AsciiDoc
docs.text:
The generator built for documentation spread across many repositories, and the markup that has includes in the base language.

context · difficulty 2 · 3h

Not a quotation (adjacent)

Covered only by "or similar" in NVIDIA's list of generators. Worth recognising, rarely worth choosing for a new project, and the one answer to a problem the others cannot solve.

Prerequisites: Choosing a static site generator

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Two things usually named together. AsciiDoc is a markup language with a real specification, more capable than Markdown and considerably more verbose. Antora is a generator that assembles one documentation site from AsciiDoc content living in several Git repositories, each at a chosen branch or tag.

That second part is its reason to exist, and it is the thing none of the other three generators do.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
It does not, except through "or similar", which the banner above records honestly. This page is context tier for two reasons.

The first is recognition. AsciiDoc shows up in enterprise and Java-adjacent documentation estates, and in the Red Hat ecosystem in particular, so you will meet it if you work across a large organisation's content.

The second is more useful. Antora solves the one problem that genuinely has no good answer in MkDocs, Sphinx or Docusaurus: documentation that lives next to the code in a dozen repositories and has to publish as one coherent site with one navigation and one search index. If you are ever asked how you would do that, Antora is the answer, and knowing it exists is worth more than fluency in its configuration.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Convert a page that uses the features Markdown needs extensions for, and see which ones AsciiDoc has in the base language. About twenty minutes. The honest limits of what was executed here are stated at the end.

Step 1: a page using six constructs

mkdir -p adoc-demo/shared && cd adoc-demo
npm init -y >/dev/null && npm install @asciidoctor/core@3.0.4

cat > sample.adoc <<'EOF'
= Widget Guide
:toc:
:widget-version: 2.4

== Install

Requires version {widget-version} or later.

[NOTE]
====
An admonition with a block body.
====

include::shared/prereqs.adoc[]

[source,python]
----
client = Client()
client.retry(times=5)
----

See <<configure>> and the xref:other.adoc#section[other page].

[#configure]
== Configure

.A table with a title
|===
| Option | Default

| retry
| 5
|===
EOF

printf 'You need Python 3.10 or later.\n' > shared/prereqs.adoc

An attribute used as a variable, an admonition with a block body, a file include, a highlighted source block, an internal cross-reference, and a titled table.

Step 2: convert it with no extensions configured

// t.mjs
const asciidoctor = require('@asciidoctor/core')()
const html = asciidoctor.convertFile('sample.adoc',
  { to_file: false, safe: 'unsafe', standalone: false })

const checks = {
  'attribute substituted': html.includes('2.4'),
  'admonition block':      html.includes('admonitionblock'),
  'include resolved':      html.includes('Python 3.10'),
  'source block':          html.includes('language-python'),
  'internal xref':         html.includes('#configure'),
  'table with title':      html.includes('tableblock'),
}
for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(checks)) {
  console.log('  ' + k.padEnd(24) + (v ? 'yes' : 'NO'))
}

  attribute substituted   yes
  admonition block        yes
  include resolved        yes
  source block            yes
  internal xref           yes
  table with title        yes

All six, with no extensions enabled. Compare that with the Markdown result, where five constructs produced five different answers across five implementations and every one of them was an extension.

The two to notice are includes and attributes. Those are single-sourcing primitives in the base language: content reuse and variable substitution without a plugin, a convention or a preprocessor. In Markdown both require tooling, and the tooling differs per generator.

Step 3: understand the thing Antora adds

Antora's unit is a component version: a named documentation component at a specific version, sourced from a Git repository and branch. The playbook names the sources:

# antora-playbook.yml
content:
  sources:
    - url: https://github.com/example/widget-core
      branches: [main, v2.x]
      start_path: docs
    - url: https://github.com/example/widget-cli
      branches: [main]
      start_path: docs
output:
  dir: ./build/site

One site, two repositories, three branches, and cross-references that resolve across them. xref:widget-cli:install.adoc from a page in widget-core resolves to a page in a different repository, and Antora fails the build if it cannot be found.

What was and was not executed here. Steps 1 and 2 ran, with @asciidoctor/core 3.0.4, and the six results are measured. Step 3 was not executed: rubygems.org is not reachable from this environment, and a real multi-repository Antora build needs published Git sources rather than local directories. The playbook above is the shape of the configuration, not a verified run, and this page says so rather than implying otherwise.

What you learned. Which of AsciiDoc's advantages are in the base language, measured rather than claimed, and where the honest limit of this exercise sits.

docs.title: AsciiDoc against Markdown, on capability
docs.text:
Construct AsciiDoc Markdown Includes Base language Per-generator plugin Attributes and substitution Base language Front matter plus templating Admonitions with block bodies Base language Extension, per-tool syntax Tables with titles, spans, formatting Base language Extension, limited Cross-references by id Base language Link to a generated anchor Conditional content Base language, ifdef Not available A specification Yes CommonMark, plus dialects Contributor familiarity Low High Tooling ecosystem Small Very large

The capability column is one-sided, and it does not settle the question. Familiarity and ecosystem decide most real projects, which is why AsciiDoc remains a minority choice despite being the better language.

docs.title: What Antora is for
docs.text: Problem Antora's answer Docs in many repositories, one site Component versions from multiple Git sources Each repository ships on its own schedule Per-branch, per-tag content Cross-repository references Typed xrefs, resolved and checked at build One navigation across all of it A per-component nav, assembled Versioned docs Versions are branches, not a plugin

docs.title: When to choose it, and when not
docs.text: Choose Antora Do not Content lives in many repositories and must publish as one site It is one repository Versions map to branches or tags already A new project with no AsciiDoc The organisation already writes AsciiDoc Contributors need to start today Java or Red Hat ecosystem conventions You need interactive components

docs.title: If you have one repository and want includes
docs.text: You do not need Antora. You need single-sourcing in whatever generator you already have: a snippet include plugin on MkDocs, .. include:: on Sphinx, or MDX imports on Docusaurus. Reaching for Antora to get includes is a large change for a small feature.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the multi-repository problem, because that is the only reason to choose it. "Antora is the answer when documentation lives next to the code in a dozen repositories and has to publish as one site with one navigation and cross-references that resolve between them. None of the other generators do that, and the common workarounds, submodules or a sync script, are worse."

The follow-up is whether you would pick AsciiDoc for a new project, and the honest answer is usually no. It is the more capable language, and contributor familiarity and tooling ecosystem decide most projects. Say both halves.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Adopting AsciiDoc costs you the Markdown ecosystem: fewer editors and preview tools, a smaller set of linters, and contributors who need to learn a syntax they do not already know. On a project where most content comes from engineers writing occasionally, that friction is the dominant cost and it outweighs the capability gain.

One sharper point. Includes and attributes being in the base language is a bigger deal than it sounds, because it means single-sourcing is portable. In Markdown, content reuse is always a per-generator plugin, so a corpus that relies on it is locked to that generator. In AsciiDoc the reuse mechanism travels with the content.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. Realistically, none. This is a recognition-and-judgment concept, and the deliverable is being able to answer the multi-repository question without reaching for submodules.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run steps 1 and 2. Twenty minutes, and the six-for-six result is the thing worth remembering about the language.
  2. Write down how you would publish one site from five repositories using your current generator. The awkwardness of that answer is Antora's argument.
  3. Find an AsciiDoc page in the wild, a Red Hat or Spring doc, and read its source. Recognition is most of what this concept is for.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Saying plainly which parts you have run. Steps 1 and 2 are measured here with @asciidoctor/core 3.0.4; the Antora playbook is not, because this environment cannot reach rubygems.org and a real build needs remote Git sources. A candidate who separates those two things is more trustworthy than one who presents a configuration file as experience.

docs.title: Integrating with APIs
docs.text:
Writing a client against a real server found three defects: two in the server, and the first one in the client, because the integrator read the wrong field.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Working proficiency in Python or similar to automate content tasks, transform data, and integrate with APIs"

Prerequisites: Python for content automation

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The third job in NVIDIA's sentence: making a program talk to a service it does not control. In a documentation role those services are the ones holding content and process, a CMS, a ticket tracker, a translation vendor, a repository host, a search index, and increasingly the documentation platform is itself the server, answering an agent.

The work divides unevenly. Calling an endpoint that behaves is twenty minutes. Everything after that is deciding what the client does when the service disagrees, and that is where integrations are actually written.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because the content a documentation team needs is almost never in the repository. It is in the issue tracker, the CMS, the analytics product and the localisation vendor, and the only way to ask a question spanning two of them is a program.

There is a second reason that is newer, and it is why this concept is core rather than supporting: the documentation platform is now on the other side of the line. An MCP server over a corpus is an API that other people's agents integrate against, so a documentation engineer writes clients and publishes one. The two halves teach each other, and the fastest way to learn what a published API owes its consumers is to be a bad consumer of your own.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Write a client against a real server, deliberately misuse it, and see what the integration has to survive. About thirty minutes. The target is the companion repository's MCP server, so there is no network and no credential involved.

Step 1: the smallest honest client

JSON-RPC over stdio, which is a pipe, a line of JSON, and a line back:

proc = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, SERVER, "--docs", DOCS],
                        stdin=subprocess.PIPE, stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
                        stderr=subprocess.PIPE, text=True, bufsize=1)

def call(method, params=None, rid=[0]):
    rid[0] += 1
    req = {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": rid[0], "method": method}
    if params is not None:
        req["params"] = params
    proc.stdin.write(json.dumps(req) + "\n")
    proc.stdin.flush()
    line = proc.stdout.readline()
    return json.loads(line) if line else {"__dead__": True}

The __dead__ branch is there from the first version, because the commonest failure of a subprocess transport is the other end exiting, and readline() on a closed pipe returns an empty string rather than raising.

initialize        -> {'name': 'docpack-docs', 'version': '0.3.0'}
tools/list        -> search_docs, get_page, list_pages

search_docs  {"query": "how do I make the chunks smaller"}         3300 chars
search_docs  {"query": "...", "diataxis": "how-to"}                4106 chars
list_pages   {}                                                    1815 chars
get_page     {"path": "how-to/pack-for-rag.md"}                    2253 chars

Four calls, four answers. By the usual standard the integration is finished.

Step 2: misuse it on purpose

The part worth writing is the next table: six requests a real client will eventually make by accident.

  unknown method         rpc-error -32601 method not found: tools/frobnicate
  unknown tool           ok        Error: 'unknown tool: nope'
  missing argument       ok        Error: 'path'
  path outside the tree  ok        Error: path escapes the documentation tree.
  bad diataxis value     ok        No matches for 'x'.
  empty query            ok        No matches for ''.

still alive after all of that: True

The server survives everything, refuses the path traversal, and reports one case as a protocol error. Five come back as successful calls whose text begins "Error:", which would mean a client can detect failure only by string-matching prose.

That reading is wrong, and the mistake is the useful part of this page.

Step 3: the first defect was in the client

MCP reports a tool-level failure as a successful JSON-RPC response whose result carries isError: true. The server was setting it. My client checked only for a JSON-RPC error key, printed ok for everything else, and produced a table that blamed the server for my own bug.

  unknown tool           TOOL-ERR  Error: 'unknown tool: nope'
  missing argument       TOOL-ERR  Error: 'path'
  path outside the tree  ok        Error: path escapes the documentation tree.
  bad diataxis value     ok        No matches for 'x'.
  empty query            ok        No matches for ''.

Worth dwelling on, because it is the characteristic integration bug and it is not a coding mistake. The protocol has two error channels with different meanings, the client implemented one, and every response was still structurally valid. Nothing threw. The client was reading a field that does not carry the answer, and the output looked like evidence.

Step 4: now the two real defects

With the flag read correctly, two rows are genuinely wrong.

A rejected path traversal reports isError: false while its text says "Error:". The flag and the prose disagree, the flag is the documented thing to check, and so a careful client is told that a refused security-relevant lookup succeeded. The cause is that get_page returned an error string instead of raising, bypassing the handler that sets the flag:

if not target.is_relative_to(self.docs_dir.resolve()):
    return "Error: path escapes the documentation tree."    # before
    raise ToolError("path escapes the documentation tree")  # after

And an unknown filter value came back as "No matches", indistinguishable from a question the corpus genuinely cannot answer. A typo in an enum and an empty result set are different answers and were the same response:

if diataxis is not None and diataxis not in DIATAXIS_TYPES:
    raise ToolError(f"unknown diataxis type {diataxis!r}; expected one of ...")

The third row, Error: 'path', was a bare KeyError whose str() is the key name, so the message named the problem without stating it.

  unknown method         rpc-error -32601 method not found: tools/frobnicate
  unknown tool           TOOL-ERR  Error: unknown tool: nope; expected one of search_docs, ...
  missing argument       TOOL-ERR  Error: get_page requires a 'path' argument
  path outside the tree  TOOL-ERR  Error: path escapes the documentation tree
  bad diataxis value     TOOL-ERR  Error: unknown diataxis type 'nonsense'; expected one of ...
  empty query            ok        No matches for ''.

One channel, actionable messages, and the single remaining ok is a real empty result.

Step 5: the finding that only appeared in a test

Writing the test for that empty result produced a surprise. A query of apparent gibberish returned four confident matches, because BM25 tokenises "zzzqqq no such term anywhere" and matches on term and anywhere. A genuinely empty result needs out-of-vocabulary tokens throughout.

#: Genuinely out of vocabulary. "no such term anywhere" matches on `term`.
call(server, "search_docs", {"query": "zzzqqq wwwvvv xxxyyy"})

So an integrator cannot use an empty result set to detect a bad query. Empty is rare, and the normal failure of a search API is a confident low-relevance match: a client branching on if not results has written a branch that practically never runs, against a silent failure that happens constantly.

What you built. A working client, a misuse table, one client bug that produced false evidence, two server defects fixed so failure travels on one channel, and fourteen tests that assert on the flag rather than the prose.

docs.title: What to write before the happy path works
docs.text: Concern Why first The transport dying A closed pipe returns empty, it does not raise A timeout on every call The default in most clients is to wait forever Which field means failure See step 3; there is usually more than one Retry policy, and what is safe to retry A retried write is a duplicate What a partial result looks like Pagination truncates silently Logging the request, not only the error An error without its request is unactionable

docs.title: The two error channels, in any protocol
docs.text:
Channel Means Example Transport or protocol The request was not understood HTTP 400, JSON-RPC error Application or tool Understood, and the answer is a failure isError: true, a 200 with "status": "failed"

Nearly every real API has both, they are easy to confuse, and confusing them produces a client that works until something goes wrong. The question to settle before writing any client: which field do I branch on, and what does the other one mean when it disagrees?

docs.title: Failure modes a client has to handle
docs.text:
Mode Detected by Usually forgotten The service is down A timeout No The service is slow A timeout you set Yes Authentication expired mid-run A 401 on call 400 of 900 Yes Rate limited 429, or silence Yes A partial page of results Comparing count to total Yes An enum value it does not know Only if the server checks Yes, on both sides A confident wrong answer Nothing; only a human Always The response shape changed A schema check Yes

The last four are the ones that cost a day, and three of them are a server choosing to be permissive where it should have refused.

docs.title: Publishing an API, learned from consuming one
docs.text:
Obligation Because One error channel, used consistently A client can only branch on one A flag, not prose, for failure Text is for humans; flags are for code Messages naming the fix, not the symptom Error: 'path' names a key, not a problem Reject unknown enum values A typo otherwise returns a plausible empty set Refuse by raising, not by returning text Any other path bypasses the flag List what you accept, in the error Saves the client reading the schema A test per failure mode, asserting the flag They regress silently

Every row came from being a bad consumer of this server for twenty minutes.

docs.title: Where credentials live
docs.text:
Approach Verdict Environment variable, read once Fine A secrets manager Better, where one exists A config file outside the repository Acceptable In the repository, encrypted No; the history is forever Hardcoded for a quick script Becomes permanent within a week

An integration script's credentials end up in CI eventually, so write it as though they already are: read from the environment, fail loudly when absent, and never log request headers.

docs.title: Rate limits and bulk work
docs.text:
Pattern Use Sequential with a small sleep A few hundred calls; honest and slow Respecting Retry-After Always, when the server sends it Exponential backoff with jitter Anything unattended Checkpointing to disk per batch Any job over a few minutes Concurrency Last; it multiplies every other failure mode

The checkpoint is the one that pays. A four-hour extraction that dies at hour three having written nothing is the most expensive mistake available here, and appending JSONL as you go prevents it.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with where the work actually is. "Calling an endpoint that behaves is twenty minutes. The integration is everything after: which field means failure, what is safe to retry, what a partial result looks like. I write the transport-died branch and the timeout before the happy path, because a closed pipe returns empty rather than raising."

Then the story, which is worth telling precisely because it does not flatter. I wrote a client against an MCP server I also maintain, and produced a table showing five failure modes reported as successes. The server was correct: MCP signals a tool failure as a successful response carrying isError: true, my client checked only the JSON-RPC error key, and my output looked like evidence against the server. That is the characteristic integration bug. Two error channels with different meanings, the client implementing one, nothing throwing, every response structurally valid.

Then what was genuinely wrong, which reading the right field exposed. Two defects. A refused path traversal reported success while its text said "Error:", because that branch returned an error string instead of raising and so bypassed the flag. And an unknown filter value returned "No matches", making a typo in an enum indistinguishable from a question the corpus cannot answer. Both are a server being permissive where it should refuse, and both are now tests that assert on the flag rather than the prose.

One sharper point. A search API almost never returns nothing. Writing the test for an empty result, my gibberish query matched four chunks because BM25 tokenised it and hit on term and anywhere. So a client branching on if not results has a branch that practically never runs, and the real failure, a confident low-relevance match, has no branch at all. That is why retrieval needs evaluation rather than error handling.

The tradeoff to volunteer. All of this was learned against a local server with no auth, no network and no rate limit, which is the easiest integration there is. It taught the contract questions well and taught nothing about credentials expiring mid-run, pagination over a moving dataset, or a vendor whose staging and production behaviour differ. Those need the real service, and I would not claim them from a stdio pipe.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A client of yours with a misuse table, and whichever end you control fixed so that failure travels on one channel.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Take an API you already integrate with and establish which field means failure and what the other does when they disagree. Predict first; this page exists because I got that wrong on a server I maintain.
  2. Send your client six deliberately malformed requests and tabulate the replies. Twenty minutes, and it will find something.
  3. Add a checkpoint to the longest extraction script you own. It prevents the most expensive failure in this area and the fix is an append.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. The client is a short script driving docpack's mcp_server/server.py over stdio. The two server defects are fixed in that file with the reasoning left in comments. tests/test_mcp_server.py holds fourteen tests asserting on isError rather than on message text, including one that a bad filter value is distinguishable from an empty result. What is absent is any integration over a network: no authentication, no rate limiting, no pagination, no third-party service. The operational half of this concept is reasoned about rather than demonstrated, and the demonstrated page records it as partial on that basis.

docs.title: Generated API reference
docs.text:
Pulling signatures from source so they cannot drift, and which half of the drift that actually fixes.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

Asked for by name

Intel: "Write and maintain reference documentation, tutorials, and sample walkthroughs that assume no prior context"

Prerequisites: Docs-as-code

Leads to: OpenAPI and REST reference

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Building the reference layer of your documentation from the source code rather than writing it by hand. A tool reads signatures, type annotations and docstrings and emits pages, so the published signature is the real one by construction.

The part worth understanding precisely is which drift this removes and which it does not. Generation makes signatures correct automatically. It does nothing for prose that describes behaviour, and it does nothing for the links into the reference unless you use the right reference syntax.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Intel asks for reference documentation that assumes no prior context, alongside tutorials and sample walkthroughs. Reference is the layer where hand-authoring fails first and worst: a corpus with two hundred functions cannot be hand-maintained through a refactor, and the failure is silent.

It is also the layer readers trust most. A generated signature carries an implicit promise of being authoritative, which means a stale one does more damage than a stale paragraph of prose. Automating it is less about writer effort than about where the corpus is allowed to lie.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Generate reference in two toolchains, then rename the function and find out exactly what each one catches. About forty minutes.

Step 1: a package worth documenting

mkdir -p apiref/pkg apiref/docs && cd apiref
cat > pkg/widget.py <<'EOF'
"""Widget client."""


def retry(times: int = 5, backoff: float = 1.5) -> int:
    """Retry an operation.

    Args:
        times: How many attempts.
        backoff: Multiplier between attempts.

    Returns:
        The number of attempts made.
    """
    return times
EOF
touch pkg/__init__.py

Google-style docstring, type annotations, a default value. Everything a generator needs.

Step 2: generate it with mkdocstrings

pip install --quiet mkdocs mkdocstrings mkdocstrings-python

cat > mkdocs.yml <<'EOF'
site_name: API
plugins:
  - mkdocstrings:
      handlers:
        python:
          paths: [.]
EOF

cat > docs/index.md <<'EOF'
# API

::: pkg.widget.retry
EOF

python3 -m mkdocs build --strict && echo "exit=$?"

The output contains the signature, pulled from the code:

retry(times: int = 5, backoff: float = 1.5) -> int:

plus the parameter descriptions and the return documentation, parsed out of the docstring sections. The same package through Sphinx with autodoc and napoleon produces the equivalent:

retry(times: int = 5, backoff: float = 1.5) → int

Both read the real signature. Neither can publish a stale one.

Step 3: rename the function and see what breaks

sed -i 's/^def retry(/def attempt(/' pkg/widget.py
python3 -m mkdocs build --strict

ERROR - mkdocstrings: pkg.widget.retry could not be found
ERROR - Could not collect 'pkg.widget.retry'
exit=1

The directive fails hard. Sphinx behaves the same way. The generation side is safe in both: point a generator at a symbol that no longer exists and the build stops.

Step 4: the half that is not safe

Fix the directive to point at attempt, and leave behind an ordinary Markdown link to the old anchor:

cat > docs/index.md <<'EOF'
# API

::: pkg.widget.attempt

See [retry](#pkgwidgetretry).
EOF
python3 -m mkdocs build --strict; echo "exit=$?"

INFO - Doc file 'index.md' contains a link '#pkgwidgetretry', but there is no
       such anchor on this page.
exit=0

Exit 0. The link is dead twice over, because the real anchor mkdocstrings emits is pkg.widget.retry with the dots, and that symbol no longer exists anyway. MkDocs logs INFO and publishes it, exactly as on the link checking page.

So generating the reference did not protect the references into it.

Step 5: use the reference syntax, which is checked

mkdocstrings ships autorefs, where [text][symbol] resolves against the collected objects rather than against a heading slug:

cat > docs/index.md <<'EOF'
# API

::: pkg.widget.attempt

Autorefs style: [attempt][pkg.widget.attempt] and a dead one [gone][pkg.widget.retry].
EOF
python3 -m mkdocs build --strict; echo "exit=$?"

WARNING - mkdocs_autorefs: index.md: Could not find cross-reference target
          'pkg.widget.retry'
Aborted with 1 warnings in strict mode!
exit=1

Caught, and the good one resolved to href="#pkg.widget.attempt". The dead one was left as literal [gone][pkg.widget.retry] in the output, which is the usual Markdown failure mode and the reason the warning matters.

What you learned. Generation fixes signatures. Cross-references into the reference are a separate problem with a separate fix, and the fix is to use the symbol-reference syntax instead of hand-written anchors. Two different gates, and most teams have only the first.

docs.title: What generation fixes, and what it does not
docs.text: Drift Fixed by generation A parameter renamed Yes A type annotation changed Yes A default value changed Yes A function removed Yes, the build fails A link to a removed symbol No, unless you use symbol references Prose describing behaviour No An example that no longer runs No; see sample validation Which functions deserve a tutorial No

docs.title: Toolchains
docs.text:
Tool Reads Checks symbol references Sphinx autodoc plus napoleon Python docstrings, annotations Yes, py:func and the domains mkdocstrings plus mkdocstrings-python The same Yes, [text][symbol] autorefs sphinx.ext.intersphinx Other projects' inventories Yes, across projects typedoc TypeScript Yes, within the project javadoc, doxygen Java, C++ Within the project OpenAPI generators A spec, not code See OpenAPI

The practical upshot: you do not need Sphinx to get checked symbol references for Python. You need a tool that collects symbols, and either of the first two qualifies. What stays distinctively Sphinx is several language domains in one corpus plus intersphinx.

docs.title: Docstring styles
docs.text:
Style Looks like Needs Google Args: and Returns: sections napoleon, or mkdocstrings default NumPy Underlined sections napoleon reStructuredText :param x: Nothing extra in Sphinx Plain prose No structure Nothing, and you get no parameter table

Pick one and enforce it with a linter. A corpus with three styles renders inconsistently and the parameter tables silently stop appearing on the pages that drifted.

docs.title: Where generated reference stops being enough
docs.text:
Generated reference tells a reader what a function's signature is. It does not tell them which function to call, in what order, or why. That is what golden paths and tutorial design are for, and a corpus that is only generated reference is the most common failure mode in developer documentation: complete, accurate, and unusable by a newcomer.

Reference is necessary and it is the easy half.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the split. "Generating reference from source means the published signature is the real one by construction, so a rename fails the build instead of shipping. What it does not fix is the links into the reference: a hand-written anchor to a renamed symbol is a dead link that MkDocs publishes. So I use the symbol-reference syntax, which is resolved against the collected objects."

The follow-up is often whether you need Sphinx for this, and the answer is no for a Python-only corpus. mkdocstrings gives you generation and checked [text][symbol] references on MkDocs. Sphinx wins when you have several language domains or want intersphinx checking across projects.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Generated reference is only as good as the docstrings, and generation creates pressure to write docstrings for the tool rather than for the reader. You end up with two hundred pages that are technically complete and tell nobody how to accomplish anything. The mitigation is to treat reference as the floor and spend the real effort on golden paths, which is a staffing argument as much as a tooling one.

One sharper point. The anchor format is not what you would guess. mkdocstrings emits id="pkg.widget.retry", dots included, so hand-written links to generated pages are usually wrong on the first attempt and usually ship anyway, because MkDocs treats a dead anchor as INFO. That is the specific, checkable reason to use the reference syntax rather than a preference for it.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A repository where reference is generated and where a renamed symbol fails the build, plus the use of symbol references rather than anchors.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Steps 3 and 4 together are the lesson: the directive fails, the link does not.
  2. Grep your own docs for hand-written links into generated reference pages. Each one is an unchecked reference. If you find none, check whether anything links into the reference at all: a generated section nobody links to is a different problem with the same symptom.
  3. Convert the five most important of those to [text][symbol] form and turn on --strict. Whatever fails was already broken.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack generates its reference with mkdocstrings and runs --doctest-modules across the package, so the docstrings that feed the reference are themselves executed. The combination is the thing to point at: generation keeps the signature honest, and doctests keep the examples in it honest, which are two different kinds of lie.

  • Sphinx, one of the two toolchains compared here

  • Golden paths, the half generated reference cannot provide

docs.title: Assessment and checks for understanding
docs.text:
A task without a success criterion is practice, not assessment, and a corpus can be excellent at the first while doing almost none of the second.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

Adjacent, not quoted

Not named in either posting. The counterpart to cold-start testing: how you find out the curriculum worked.

Prerequisites: Instructional design for developers

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Any mechanism that tells you whether a reader can now do the thing. The useful distinction is between a practice task, which gives the reader something to do, and an assessment, which also states what counts as having done it. Almost everything published as assessment in developer documentation is practice with a quiz attached.

Cold-start testing is the mirror image. It runs the documentation in a clean environment and tells you whether the content works. Assessment tells you whether the reader does. A corpus can pass the first perfectly and hold no evidence at all about the second, which is the normal state and worth saying out loud rather than disguising.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because every claim a documentation team makes about outcomes is an assessment claim wearing other clothes.

"A developer reaches a working result in fifteen minutes" is a measurement of readers. So is "our quickstart reduced support tickets". So is every sentence in a performance review about improving onboarding. If nothing in the system observes a reader succeeding or failing, those claims rest on page views and on the absence of complaints, which is the weakest evidence available and the most commonly cited.

The practical reason is sharper. Without assessment you cannot distinguish content that is clear from content that is merely agreeable to read, and those two fail in opposite directions: the agreeable page collects good feedback and produces nobody who can do the task.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Assess a corpus's own assessment. This guide ends every page with three things to do, so there are 318 of them to examine. About thirty minutes, and the measurement is wrong twice before it is right.

Step 1: find the instrument

proof = text.partition("## How to prove it")[2].partition("## Related")[0]
tail  = proof[LABEL.search(proof).end():].partition("**What makes it")[0]
items = [" ".join(m.group(1).split()) for m in ITEM.finditer(tail)]

pages with a proof section:   47/82

Forty-seven, when the page contract makes that section mandatory and a separate check had already reported 82 of 82. One of the two is wrong.

(Steps 1 to 3 were run when the corpus was 82 pages, and are kept because they are what exposed the defect. Step 4 onward is the finished 106-page corpus.)

Step 2: it is two labels again

**Three things to do today:**            46
**Three things to do, in order:**        35
**Three things to do today, in order:**   1

On the finished corpus the split was 70, 35 and 1. The inconsistency outlived the discovery by some months, because standardising the label meant touching every page and the defect was recorded rather than fixed.

It is fixed now, and fixing it found three more. The lesson below says to sweep every structural element at once, and acting on that rather than on the one label that surfaced turned up:

Element Wordings in use Proof-task label "today:" on 70, ", in order:" on 35, a splice of the two on 1 Sharper point "One sharper point." on 47, "A sharper point." on 35 Credibility "...rather than decorative." on 72, "What makes it credible." on 34

Two of the three were decided on accuracy rather than on majority, which is worth saying because the majority was the easier answer both times. The tasks genuinely are ordered, with the first always being to run the golden path, while "today" promises a scope that "compute grounded@k on a corpus you own" does not have, so the minority wording won. And "rather than decorative" is the section's whole argument, so the longer form won.

Then a fourth variant appeared, which is the part worth remembering: after the sweep above pronounced the corpus clean, the label "One sharper point, and the best thing to say here." turned out to be on five more pages. The hand sweep had filtered to labels used ten or more times, so a five-page variant was below the threshold that was supposed to find variants. A frequency floor is a filter on what you are willing to find.

So the fix was not the standardisation. It is STRUCTURAL_LABELS in registry.py, which declares the wording of every labelled element, and the part of fieldguide audit that reports every repeated bolded opener not in that list. Counting declared labels confirms what you already know; counting the undeclared ones is what finds the next one.

The section was present on all 82 pages. The parser was looking for one of three labels, and the corpus had split 47 to 35 on wording, almost exactly along the line between two sittings of writing.

This is the second independent discovery of the same defect in this corpus. The prerequisite label audit found "Prerequisites" against "Read first" and fixed it; this one was sitting underneath, in a different section, undetected, because the fix had been applied to the label that surfaced rather than to the class of defect. A corpus written by one author across several sittings contains several of these, and the lesson is to sweep every structural element for variants at once.

Step 3: classify the 246 tasks, and get it wrong

tasks: 246 across 82 pages, exactly 3 each
begin with an imperative action: 133/246 (54%)

Fifty-four per cent would be a real finding, if true. The unmatched items:

[('**Run', 30), ('**Write', 11), ('**Add', 8), ('**Find', 8), ('**Generate', 7), ...]

They begin with **. The same 35 pages bold the opening of each task, so the classifier was measuring Markdown emphasis rather than verbs. Strip the markup and the inline links:

begin with an imperative action: 232/246 (94%)
unmatched: If 3, On 2, For 1, When 1, Redo 1, Use 1, Publish 1, Track 1

Four of the fourteen remaining, Redo, Use, Publish and Track, are imperatives the verb list omitted, which is the word-list bug from the duration audit in miniature. The real figure is about 96 per cent, and the honest summary is that the corpus is good at telling a reader what to do.

Step 4: the number that matters

Two further properties, both about whether a task is assessable at all. The measurement as it originally stood:

tasks: 318 across 106 pages, exactly 3 each
tasks beginning with an imperative:            303/318 (95%)
tasks naming an inspectable artifact:          203/318 (64%)
tasks stating how the learner knows it worked:  53/318 (17%)

Seventeen per cent, and that number was wrong. It stood on this page for months as the guide's weakest figure, and it was the classifier that was weak.

The keyword list behind it included against. Sixteen of its 53 matches were the preposition in "run it against a corpus you own", which states no criterion at all. Meanwhile it recognised none of the forms the corpus actually uses. Not the conditionals, "if the answer is two, you have the drift". Not the predicted values, "on a client-rendered site the number is near zero". Not the comparisons to the author's own result, "mine said 72 tests and there were 119". It was wrong in both directions at once, and the net error ran against the guide rather than for it.

Sixty tasks hand-labelled against a written definition, in two samples with one held out, put the real rate at about forty per cent of a sample where the old classifier saw seventeen. The rewritten classifier, scored against those labels, reports a third of the corpus.

tasks: 318 across 106 pages, exactly 3 each
tasks beginning with an imperative:            303/318 (95%)
tasks naming an inspectable artifact:          204/318 (64%)
tasks stating how the learner knows it worked: 128/318 (40%)

That last figure is 40 per cent after a pass that added one clause to the best-suited task on every core page that had none, which was 22 of them. The pass moved the measured rate from 33 to 40; the correction moved it from 17 to 33. The instrument was worth more than the work, which is not the lesson anybody sets out to demonstrate on a page about assessment.

Two of the clauses written during that pass were invisible to the classifier the moment they were written: "you will know the gate is wired when..." and "more than roughly one suppression per ten pages means...". Both are criteria, both are now patterns, and both arrived as misses. A classifier for a quantity this open-ended is permanently incomplete, which is the argument for scoring it against labels rather than trusting it.

The labelled set is frozen at tests/fixtures/criterion_labels.json with its definition and method beside it, and tests/test_criterion.py scores the classifier against it on every run. Recall against the labels must be perfect and precision is allowed to be imperfect, because a missed criterion understates the corpus and hides work already done, which is exactly how the seventeen happened.

Take a real one:

Measure the per-page maximum sentence length on your docs, then read the three worst sentences out loud.

A good practice task, and not an assessment, because nothing in it distinguishes a reader who understood from one who ran a script. Compare one that does:

Run the golden path and count the runs in step 3 before reading step 4.

Here there is a number, the reader produces it before being told it, and a wrong answer is visible to the reader themselves. That is the entire difference, and it costs one clause.

Step 5: what a seventeen per cent calls for

Not quizzes. A quiz over this corpus would test recall of its wording, which is the thing nobody needs.

The cheap fix is to give the highest-value tasks a predict-then-check shape, which is what the good example does. The reader commits to an expected answer before running the thing, so feedback is immediate, self-administered and honest; and the writer has to know the right answer, which is its own quality check on the task.

The expensive fix is real learners, for which no amount of corpus analysis substitutes. That limit belongs in the claim: this guide can say its tasks are well formed and cannot say they teach, and the distance between those two sentences is the distance between construct and criterion validity.

What you built. An assessment of 318 practice tasks, a second instance of the two-label defect, a classifier corrected twice, and one number worth acting on.

docs.title: Practice against assessment
docs.text:
Practice task Assessment Says what to do Yes Yes Says what counts as done No Yes Who judges Nobody The criterion, or a reader Tells the writer anything No Yes In this corpus 318 128

The bottom row is this page in one line. The gap is cheap to close on the tasks that matter and not worth closing on all of them.

docs.title: Forms, ranked by what they actually measure
docs.text:
Form Measures Costs Fails by Predict, then check Understanding of mechanism One clause Needs a crisp expected answer Produce an artifact Ability A task design Nobody inspects it A task with an automated check Ability, at scale A test harness Teaching to the harness Cold-start run The content, not the reader A clean machine Says nothing about people Watching one person Everything, slowly An hour Does not scale, is still the best Multiple choice Recall of wording Little Passed without ability "Was this page helpful?" Mood Nothing Measures agreeableness

The last row is the most-deployed instrument in documentation and the least informative, which is not a coincidence: it is the only one that costs nothing and never produces bad news.

docs.title: Predict-then-check, as a pattern
docs.text:
Weak With a criterion "Run the link checker" "Predict how many links break, then run it" "Measure sentence length" "Guess your longest sentence, then measure" "Try the sample" "Say what it will print, then run it" "Audit your gallery" "Name the sample you think is broken, then check"

In every row the writer has to know the answer, which quietly removes tasks that sound instructive and have no determinate result.

docs.title: Validity, in the two senses that matter
docs.text:
Question Name This guide's evidence Is the instrument well formed? Construct 318 tasks, 95% imperative, 64% producing an artifact Does it predict real ability? Criterion None

Reporting the first while implying the second is the usual overreach in education claims, and stating both rows avoids it.

docs.title: When not to assess
docs.text: Situation Instead Reference pages Nobody "learns" a parameter table One-off migration guides Cold-start test the instructions Content with four readers Ask all four A number is wanted for a slide Say what you actually have

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the pairing. "Cold-start testing tells me whether the content works; assessment tells me whether the reader does. Most documentation has the first and treats page views and the absence of complaints as the second, which is the weakest evidence available and the most commonly cited."

The follow-up is what you measured. My corpus ends every page with three things to do, 318 tasks in all, and 95 per cent begin with an imperative while 40 per cent state how the reader would know it worked. More practice than assessment, and the forty is after a deliberate pass. The honest part of that story is that the first measurement said seventeen and was wrong: the classifier matched the word "against" and missed every conditional, so the instrument was worth more than the writing it prompted. The fix on the tasks themselves is predict-then-check, because it costs one clause and forces the writer to know the right answer, which removes the tasks that sound instructive and have no determinate result.

Volunteer the limit before being asked. Corpus analysis establishes that an instrument is well formed. It says nothing about whether anybody learns, which needs real readers. Those are construct and criterion validity, and reporting the first while implying the second is the standard overreach in this area. I would rather say I have one and not the other.

One sharper point. My own measurement was wrong twice inside ten minutes: it found 47 of 82 proof sections because the corpus used three labels for one element, and it put the imperative rate at 54 per cent because it was matching Markdown emphasis rather than verbs. Both produced numbers I would have published. The label one matters more, because it was the second independent discovery of that defect here: the earlier fix had been applied to the label that surfaced instead of to the class, so the right move is to sweep every structural element for variants in one pass.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A classification of your own practice tasks by whether they state a success criterion, and one task rewritten into predict-then-check.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Guess what fraction of your exercises say what the result should look like, write the number down, then measure it. The guess is the point, and the gap between the two is this page's whole subject.
  2. Take your most important exercise and add a prediction step before the command. If you cannot state the expected answer, that exercise has no determinate result, which is more useful to learn than any percentage.
  3. Sit with one person while they follow your quickstart and say nothing for ten minutes. It does not scale, it is still the best instrument available, and it will contradict at least one thing you believe.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. The measurement above runs against this guide's own 106 pages and is reproducible from the repository; what it establishes is that 318 tasks are well formed and that 128 of them are assessable, against a classifier scored on sixty hand-labelled tasks rather than trusted. What it cannot establish is that any of them teach anybody anything, because no reader has been observed, and the demonstrated page records assessment as having no demonstration in either repository rather than claiming this analysis as one.
