docs.title: Chunking strategies
docs.text:
Splitting a corpus into retrieval units without destroying the context that makes them findable.

core · difficulty 3 · 5h

structure and package content for RAG, internal assistants, and agentic workflows

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: Agent-ready content

Leads to: Embeddings

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Splitting documents into the units a retrieval system stores and returns. The unit is what gets embedded, ranked, and handed to a model, so the chunk boundary decides what an assistant can possibly know in one answer.

The entire difficulty is that splitting destroys context, and the context it destroys is usually the thing that made the text findable.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA asks you to "structure and package content for RAG", which is this. It is the lowest-level decision in the whole AI-ready stack and the one that constrains everything above it: no reranker recovers information the chunker threw away.

On a Tuesday it is a debugging question with three possible answers. An assistant gave a developer the wrong batch-size advice. Either the right chunk was never retrieved, or it was retrieved and outranked, or it was retrieved and did not contain enough to answer. The third case is a chunking failure and it is the most common one, because it looks like a model problem.

The reason it is core and difficulty 3: the naive implementation is four lines and is wrong in ways that are invisible until you measure. Fixed-size windows over Markdown produce chunks that split a table from its header, a command from its explanation, and a heading from the text it introduces. Each of those degrades retrieval quietly.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a fixed-size chunker and a heading-aware one, then measure the difference on the same queries. Forty-five minutes.

Step 1: a document with the structures that break naive chunking

mkdir -p chunk-drill && cd chunk-drill
cat > page.md <<'EOF'
# Configure the inference server

The server reads configuration from `server.toml` at startup.

## Batch size

Set `batch_size`. The default is 32.

If latency matters, use 1 or 2. Batching at 32 adds roughly 200ms at p99.

## Memory limits

| Flag | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_memory_gb` | 16 | Hard ceiling before the server refuses to load |
| `reserve_gb` | 2 | Held back for the runtime itself |

Size for peak, not for startup. The common failure is an out-of-memory error
under load, which passes a smoke test and fails in production.

## Starting the server

Run this:

```bash
# start the server in the foreground
widget-server --config server.toml
```

The server prints its listening address and blocks.
EOF
wc -c page.md

That document contains all four hazards: a table, a fenced code block with a # comment inside it, headings that state what is below them, and prose that depends on the heading for meaning.

Step 2: the naive chunker, which is what most people ship

cat > naive.py <<'PY'
"""Fixed-size chunking with overlap. Four lines of logic, widely deployed."""
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

SIZE = 200
OVERLAP = 40


def main(path: Path) -> None:
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    chunks = []
    start = 0
    while start < len(text):
        chunks.append(text[start:start + SIZE])
        start += SIZE - OVERLAP

    records = [{"id": f"naive-{i}", "text": c} for i, c in enumerate(chunks)]
    Path("naive.jsonl").write_text(
        "\n".join(json.dumps(r) for r in records) + "\n"
    )
    print(f"{len(records)} chunks of {SIZE} chars with {OVERLAP} overlap")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(Path(sys.argv[1]))
PY
python3 naive.py page.md

Step 3: look at what it did, which is the whole argument

cat > damage.py <<'PY'
"""Report what the window broke, rather than asserting that it broke things."""
import json
import re

rows = [json.loads(line) for line in open("naive.jsonl")]
print("=== damage report ===")
for r in rows:
    text = r["text"]
    problems = []
    if text.count("```") % 2 == 1:
        problems.append("unbalanced code fence")
    if "|---|" in text and "| Flag" not in text:
        problems.append("table header separated from its rows")
    elif re.search(r"^\| `", text, re.M) and "| Flag" not in text:
        problems.append("table rows with no header")
    if not re.match(r"^\s*(#|\||```|[A-Z])", text):
        problems.append("starts mid-sentence")
    if not re.search(r"^#{1,6} ", text, re.M):
        problems.append("no heading anywhere in the chunk")
    print(f"  {r['id']}: {', '.join(problems) if problems else 'intact'}")
PY
python3 damage.py

One chunk in five survives. Two have no heading at all, which means nothing in them says what they are about. One carries table rows with no column names, so a model reading it sees 16 and 2 with no idea what they measure. One ends having opened a code fence it never closes.

None of that is visible in a retrieval score. It shows up as an assistant that is vaguely unreliable.

Step 4: the heading-aware chunker

Two things make it different: it tracks fence state, and it keeps the heading trail with every chunk.

cat > aware.py <<'PY'
"""Heading-aware chunking that survives Markdown.

Two decisions carry all the value.

FENCE STATE. A `#` inside a fenced code block is a shell comment, not a
heading. Without tracking fences, `# start the server in the foreground`
becomes an H1 and the document structure collapses from that point on. This
is the bug every naive implementation has.

THE HEADING TRAIL travels with the chunk. A heading is an author's explicit
statement of what the text below is about, which makes it the single most
valuable retrieval signal in the document, and a splitter that drops it
throws away the best thing it had.
"""
import hashlib
import json
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

HEADING = re.compile(r"^(#{1,6}) +(.*?)\s*$")
FENCE = re.compile(r"^\s*(```|~~~)")
MAX_CHARS = 1200


def stable_id(source: str, trail: tuple[str, ...], ordinal: int) -> str:
    """Identify a chunk by where it is in the document, not by byte offset.

    Position-based ids change for every chunk after an edit, which forces a
    full re-index for a one-word fix. Deriving from the heading trail means
    editing the introduction leaves every other chunk's id alone.
    """
    basis = f"{source}::{'/'.join(trail)}::{ordinal}"
    return hashlib.sha256(basis.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]


def chunk(text: str, source: str):
    trail: list[str] = []
    buffer: list[str] = []
    in_fence = False
    out = []

    def flush():
        body = "\n".join(buffer).strip()
        if not body:
            return
        # Oversized sections split on blank lines, keeping the same trail, so
        # a long section degrades to several chunks that still know where
        # they came from.
        parts, current = [], []
        length = 0
        for para in body.split("\n\n"):
            if length + len(para) > MAX_CHARS and current:
                parts.append("\n\n".join(current))
                current, length = [], 0
            current.append(para)
            length += len(para)
        if current:
            parts.append("\n\n".join(current))
        for ordinal, part in enumerate(parts):
            crumb = tuple(trail)
            out.append({
                "id": stable_id(source, crumb, ordinal),
                "source": source,
                "breadcrumb": " > ".join(crumb),
                "text": part,
            })

    for line in text.splitlines():
        if FENCE.match(line):
            in_fence = not in_fence
            buffer.append(line)
            continue
        match = None if in_fence else HEADING.match(line)
        if match:
            flush()
            buffer = []
            depth = len(match.group(1))
            trail = trail[: depth - 1] + [match.group(2)]
        else:
            buffer.append(line)
    flush()
    return out


def main(path: Path) -> None:
    rows = chunk(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"), path.name)
    Path("aware.jsonl").write_text(
        "\n".join(json.dumps(r, sort_keys=True) for r in rows) + "\n"
    )
    print(f"{len(rows)} chunks")
    for r in rows:
        print(f"  [{len(r['text']):>4}] {r['breadcrumb']}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(Path(sys.argv[1]))
PY
python3 aware.py page.md

Step 5: measure, do not assert

cat > compare.py <<'PY'
"""Score both chunkers on the same queries.

The queries are phrased the way a reader would ask, which is the only fair
test: a query lifted from the document's own headings proves nothing except
that string matching works.
"""
import json
import re

QUERIES = [
    ("how do I reduce latency", "Batch size"),
    ("what is the memory ceiling", "Memory limits"),
    ("how do I start the server", "Starting the server"),
    ("what is the default batch size", "Batch size"),
    ("why did it run out of memory under load", "Memory limits"),
]


def load(path):
    return [json.loads(line) for line in open(path)]


def score(rows, query, expect, use_breadcrumb):
    terms = [t for t in re.findall(r"[a-z]+", query.lower()) if len(t) > 2]
    best, best_hit = 0, None
    for row in rows:
        hay = row["text"].lower()
        if use_breadcrumb:
            hay = f"{row.get('breadcrumb', '')} {hay}".lower()
        hits = sum(1 for t in terms if t in hay)
        if hits > best:
            best, best_hit = hits, row
    if not best_hit:
        return False, "no match"
    where = best_hit.get("breadcrumb") or best_hit["text"][:40].replace("\n", " ")
    return expect.lower() in where.lower(), where


for label, path, use_crumb in [
    ("naive (fixed 320c)", "naive.jsonl", False),
    ("heading-aware", "aware.jsonl", True),
]:
    rows = load(path)
    correct = 0
    print(f"\n{label}: {len(rows)} chunks")
    for query, expect in QUERIES:
        ok, where = score(rows, query, expect, use_crumb)
        correct += ok
        print(f"  {'OK ' if ok else '   '} {query:<42} -> {where[:46]}")
    print(f"  {correct}/{len(QUERIES)} correct")
PY
python3 compare.py

What you built. Two chunkers and a score. On this page, with these five reader-phrased queries, the result is 0 of 5 for the fixed-size chunker and 4 of 5 for the heading-aware one.

Two honest notes about that comparison, because an unqualified 0 against 4 would be overselling it.

The scoring is asymmetric, and that asymmetry is the finding. The heading-aware chunks are judged by their breadcrumb; the naive ones have no breadcrumb, so they are judged by their opening characters. That is not a rigged test, it is the actual situation: a fixed-size chunk cannot tell you which section it came from, because that information was discarded at split time. There is nothing to be fair to.

The heading-aware chunker misses one. "How do I start the server" routes to the page introduction rather than to the Starting the server section, because the word "server" appears heavily in the intro and crude term overlap rewards that. A real retriever with inverse document frequency would weight "server" down across this document and probably get it right. The miss is worth keeping in the output: a method that scores 5 of 5 on its author's own five queries has usually been tuned to them.

docs.title: What fixed-size chunking destroys
docs.text:
Destroyed Consequence The heading above the text The strongest statement of what the text is about A table's header row Rows of numbers with no column names A code fence's opening A chunk ending mid-block, and a model that invents the rest The sentence boundary A chunk starting with "If latency matters, use" Document position Nothing tells the model where in the corpus this came from

Overlap mitigates the sentence boundary and nothing else. It is widely treated as the fix for all five.

docs.title: The fence bug
docs.text:
Every naive Markdown chunker has it. A # at the start of a line inside a fenced block is a shell comment:

```bash
# start the server in the foreground
widget-server --config server.toml
```

A splitter that matches ^# without tracking fence state treats that comment as an H1, and every chunk after it inherits a wrong heading trail. The symptom is bizarre breadcrumbs appearing in retrieval results, and it is often misdiagnosed as an embedding problem.

docs.title: Strategies, and when each is right
docs.text:
Strategy Use when Cost Fixed-size with overlap The corpus is unstructured prose Destroys structure; the baseline to beat Heading-aware Markdown, RST, HTML with real headings Sections vary wildly in size Heading-aware with a size cap Documentation. This is the default worth starting from Slightly more code Semantic or embedding-based splitting Prose with no structural markers Expensive, non-deterministic, hard to debug One chunk per page Short pages, or a small corpus Poor precision; the model gets a lot of irrelevance Sentence-window Precise fact lookup Loses the surrounding argument

For a documentation corpus, heading-aware with a size cap is correct nearly always, and the interesting decisions are the cap and what carries with each chunk.

docs.title: What should travel with every chunk
docs.text: Field Why The heading trail Context, and often the only place the query's vocabulary appears Source path Citation, and the reader needs somewhere to go Page type (Diátaxis) So a retriever can filter by the kind of answer required Audience Same, for multi-audience corpora The page summary Often the closest text in the corpus to how a reader phrases things A freshness date So a consumer can discount stale content A stable id So an edit does not force a full re-index

docs.title: Stable identifiers
docs.text:
An id derived from byte offset changes for every chunk after an edited paragraph. An id derived from the heading trail plus an ordinal within the section changes only for the section you edited.

On a corpus of a few hundred pages that is the difference between re-embedding everything on each commit and re-embedding three chunks.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with the thing the window destroys and the measured result. "Fixed-size windows split tables from their headers and drop the heading that said what the text was about. On a five-query test against one configuration page, the heading-aware chunker routed every query to the right section and the fixed-size one got most of them wrong, because the words a reader uses often appear only in the heading. I keep the heading trail, the page type and the summary on every chunk, and derive the chunk id from the heading trail so an edit does not force a full re-index."

The follow-up is almost always "what chunk size do you use", which is a trap in the sense that any specific number is the wrong answer. The honest reply: the question presumes fixed sizes. For documentation I split on structure and cap the result, so the size is whatever the section is, usually a few hundred to about 1,200 characters. The cap matters more than a target, because the failure you are preventing is one enormous section rather than a few short ones.

The tradeoffs to volunteer, and there are two real ones.

Heading-aware chunking depends on the corpus having real headings. Pointed at a corpus where every page is one H1 and 2,000 words of prose, it produces one chunk per page and is worse than a window. That dependency is why content models and chunking belong in the same discussion.

And section sizes vary enormously, which means your chunks do too. A retrieval system tuned for uniform chunks will behave oddly: a 90-character chunk and a 1,200-character chunk do not compete fairly under most scoring functions, which is part of why BM25 length normalisation and similar corrections exist.

One sharper point. The strongest framing is that chunking is an information architecture decision wearing an engineering costume. The question "what is a retrievable unit of meaning" is the same question as "what is a page", asked at a finer grain, and a corpus with good page boundaries chunks well almost for free. Teams that treat chunking as a tuning parameter are usually compensating for an information architecture problem one layer up, which is why Diátaxis turned out to be the most useful metadata field anyone had.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. Two chunkers and a scored comparison. The comparison is what makes it an argument rather than an opinion.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path, then point both chunkers at a real page from a project you know. The damage report in step 3 is the demonstration; it takes two minutes and it is visceral.
  2. Add the fence test. Put a # comment inside a code block and confirm your chunker does not treat it as a heading. If you only write one test for a chunker, write that one.
  3. Measure, with the queries phrased as a reader would. Five queries is enough to be informative. Publish the number including the cases you lose; see retrieval evaluation.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Everyone in this field can describe heading-aware chunking. A repository with both implementations, a fence-bug test, and a scored comparison on reader-phrased queries demonstrates that you measured rather than adopted the consensus.

docs.title: Code-sample validation
docs.text:
Executing the examples in your documentation, and asserting their output rather than just their exit code.

core · difficulty 3 · 5h

Asked for by name

Intel: "documentation CI, including link and code-sample validation"

NVIDIA: "Build and run docs-as-code pipelines: Git authoring, CI/CD builds, linting, link and code-sample validation, and publishing"

Prerequisites: Docs-as-code

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Extracting the code blocks out of your documentation and running them, so that a sample which no longer works fails a build instead of failing a reader.

Both postings name it. The distinction that separates a real implementation from a checkbox is whether you assert the output or merely the exit code, and the golden path below makes the difference measurable.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
A code sample is the part of a page a reader trusts most and the part most likely to be wrong. Prose ages gracefully; a sample either runs or it does not, and when it does not the reader concludes that nothing on the page can be relied on.

Samples rot for reasons that have nothing to do with the writer. A parameter is renamed, a default changes, a method moves, a dependency releases a major version. Nobody edited the page, and the page became false. This is the canonical case for automation, because no review process catches it: there is no diff to review.

The reason it is difficulty 3 rather than 1 is that the obvious implementation has a hole in it big enough to drive the entire problem through, which is the subject of step 5.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build an extractor, discover the state problem, add a skip convention, then find out that your passing harness is lying to you. About forty-five minutes.

Step 1: a tutorial and the library it documents

mkdir -p samples-demo/docs && cd samples-demo

cat > docs/tutorial.md <<'MDEOF'
# Tutorial

First create a client:

```python
from widget import Client
client = Client(token="test")
```

Then list the data sets:

```python
sets = client.list_data_sets()
print(len(sets))
```

A snippet that cannot run here:

```python
client.delete_everything()
```
MDEOF

cat > widget.py <<'EOF'
class Client:
    def __init__(self, token): self.token = token
    def list_data_sets(self): return ["a", "b", "c"]
EOF

Step 2: extract the blocks

# extract.py
import re
from pathlib import Path

FENCE = re.compile(r"^```(\w+)?\s*$")


def blocks(path, lang="python"):
    out, cur, cur_lang, start = [], None, None, 0
    for n, line in enumerate(path.read_text().splitlines(), 1):
        m = FENCE.match(line)
        if m and cur is None:
            cur, cur_lang, start = [], m.group(1), n
        elif m and cur is not None:
            if cur_lang == lang:
                out.append((start, "\n".join(cur)))
            cur = None
        elif cur is not None:
            cur.append(line)
    return out

Step 3: run each block, and watch the obvious approach fail

from pathlib import Path
from extract import blocks

for p in sorted(Path("docs").rglob("*.md")):
    for start, code in blocks(p):
        try:
            exec(compile(code, f"{p}:{start}", "exec"), {})
            print(f"  PASS {p}:{start}")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"  FAIL {p}:{start}  {type(e).__name__}: {e}")

  PASS docs/tutorial.md:5
  FAIL docs/tutorial.md:12  NameError: name 'client' is not defined
  FAIL docs/tutorial.md:19  NameError: name 'client' is not defined

Two failures, neither of them a real defect. A tutorial is a sequence: block two uses the client that block one created. Executing blocks in isolation tests a document nobody wrote.

Step 4: one namespace per page

for p in sorted(Path("docs").rglob("*.md")):
    ns = {}   # shared across this page's blocks, fresh for the next page
    for start, code in blocks(p):
        exec(compile(code, f"{p}:{start}", "exec"), ns)

  PASS docs/tutorial.md:5
3
  PASS docs/tutorial.md:12
  FAIL docs/tutorial.md:19  AttributeError: 'Client' object has no attribute 'delete_everything'

Now the two tutorial steps pass and the remaining failure is honest: that method does not exist. Per-page rather than per-corpus, because page order is not a contract and a global namespace makes every page depend on every other.

Step 5: the step that matters

Add a skip convention for the destructive block, declare the expected output of block two, and check it:

cat >> docs/tutorial.md <<'EOF'
EOF
# edit the destructive block to carry a reason
python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("docs/tutorial.md")
p.write_text(p.read_text().replace(
    "client.delete_everything()",
    "# docs: skip (destructive)\nclient.delete_everything()"))
PY

The harness now captures stdout and compares it against an untagged fence following the block:

import io
import re
from contextlib import redirect_stdout

SKIP = re.compile(r"^#\s*docs:\s*skip(?:\s*\((?P<why>[^)]*)\))?\s*$", re.M)
BUDGET = 0.25

# ... for each block:
if m := SKIP.search(code):
    skipped += 1
    print(f"  SKIP {p}:{start}  ({m.group('why') or 'no reason given'})")
    continue
buf = io.StringIO()
with redirect_stdout(buf):
    exec(compile(code, f"{p}:{start}", "exec"), ns)
want = expected_after(p, start + len(code.splitlines()) + 1)
got = buf.getvalue().strip()
if want is not None and want != got:
    print(f"  DIFF {p}:{start}  expected {want!r}, got {got!r}")

  PASS docs/tutorial.md:5  (no expected output declared)
  PASS docs/tutorial.md:12  output matches '3'
  SKIP docs/tutorial.md:23  (destructive)

ran=2 skipped=1 failed=0 mismatch=0
skip ratio 33% (budget 25%)

Step 6: prove why the output assertion is the whole point

Change the library the way a real release would, adding a fourth data set:

cat > widget.py <<'EOF'
class Client:
    def __init__(self, token): self.token = token
    def list_data_sets(self): return ["a", "b", "c", "d"]
EOF
python3 harness.py

  PASS docs/tutorial.md:5  (no expected output declared)
  DIFF docs/tutorial.md:12  expected '3', got '4'
FAIL

Caught. Now run a harness that only checks whether blocks execute:

  runs-only harness: 2 block(s) executed with no error -> would report GREEN

Green. Both blocks ran perfectly. The documentation says the answer is 3, the software says 4, and a validation suite that only executes samples reports no problem at all.

What you built. The distinction between a sample that runs and a sample that is correct. Executing samples catches deletions and renames. Asserting their output catches everything else, which is most of it.

docs.title: What each level of rigour catches
docs.text:
Level Catches Misses Syntax check or lint Typos, syntax errors Anything about behaviour Execute, check exit code Removed functions, renamed parameters, import errors Every changed value, every changed shape Execute, assert output Changed defaults, counts, formats, error messages Behaviour you did not print Execute in a fresh environment Missing install steps, undeclared dependencies Nothing much, and it is slow

Most teams stop at level two and describe themselves as validating samples. Level three is where the defects actually are.

docs.title: Decisions you have to make
docs.text:
Decision Options What this page recommends Namespace Per block, per page, per corpus Per page: a tutorial is a sequence, a corpus is not Non-runnable samples Skip marker, separate tag, exclude by path A marker in the code, carrying a reason Expected output Comment, adjacent fence, separate fixture Adjacent fence, so the reader sees it too Non-determinism Normalise, redact, or skip Normalise timestamps and ids; skip only when you cannot Where it runs Unit test suite, separate CI job Separate job: it is slower than unit tests

Declaring expected output in a fence the reader can see is the choice worth defending. The alternative, a hidden fixture file, means the assertion and the documentation can disagree without anyone noticing.

docs.title: The skip convention, and its budget
docs.text:
A skip marker is necessary and it is also the hole in the system, because the quickest way to make a failing harness green is to skip the failing block. Two mitigations, both cheap:

Mitigation Effect Require a reason in the marker A reviewer can judge it; skip (destructive) is arguable, bare skip is not Cap the skip ratio The suite fails if too much of the corpus is exempt

A budget has one honest limitation, visible in step 5: on three blocks, the ratio can only be 0, 33, 67 or 100 per cent, so the cap fired on a corpus with nothing wrong with it. Budgets mean something at a hundred blocks and nothing at ten. Until then, require the reason and read it in review.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the difference between running and being correct. "Extracting and executing samples catches the obvious rot, renames and deletions. It does not catch a changed default or a changed count, and those are the majority. So the harness captures stdout and compares it against an expected-output block that the reader can also see."

The follow-up is about samples that cannot run, and the answer is a skip marker that carries a reason plus a cap on the skip ratio, with the honest admission that the cap is meaningless on a small corpus.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Output assertions make the harness brittle against legitimate change. Every intentional behaviour change now requires a documentation update in the same pull request, which is the point and is also real friction. On a fast-moving product you will spend time updating expected output for changes you intended. That is the cost of a corpus that cannot silently lie, and it is worth it, but claiming it is free is the tell of someone who has not run it.

One sharper point. The expected-output fence is a documentation improvement before it is a testing one. A sample with no output shown makes the reader run it to find out what happens. Writing the output down helps every reader and happens to give the harness something to assert, which is the best kind of quality mechanism: one that makes the page better even when it never fires.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A test that extracts samples from your own documentation, executes them, and asserts at least some of their output, plus a commit where it caught a real change.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path through step 6. The side-by-side of DIFF and GREEN is the argument.
  2. Point the extractor at a docs site you own and just execute the blocks. Whatever fails first is a page currently lying to readers.
  3. Add an expected-output fence to the one sample readers ask about most. You have improved the page and created an assertion in the same edit.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack extracts every Python block from its documentation and executes it, with # docpack: skip making exceptions visible and a test asserting the skip ratio stays under 25 per cent. The part worth discussing in an interview is the skip ratio assertion, because it shows you understood that the escape hatch is the threat.

docs.title: Documentation for coding agents
docs.text:
Writing for a reader that pastes your example straight into a file and cannot ask whether it was meant to be complete.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

Optimize documentation for search (SEO and GEO) and for AI assistants and coding agents through agentready, LLMdigestible content

Source: intel posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: Agent-ready content

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Writing documentation for a reader that will take your code sample and put it into a file. Not an assistant answering a question, and not an agent running a multi-step task: a coding agent in someone's editor, reading your page to write code with your library.

The distinguishing property is that it acts on your examples directly and cannot ask whether one was meant to be complete.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Intel names this audience explicitly and separately from AI assistants: "optimize documentation ... for AI assistants and coding agents". The separation is correct and worth preserving, because the two want different things from the same page.

An assistant wants to find the chunk that answers a question. A coding agent wants to copy a working example and get the imports right. A page that serves the first well can serve the second badly, and the usual failure is a page full of excellent partial snippets.

On a Tuesday it is a support ticket with a strange shape. A developer reports that the library does not work, and pastes code that looks like your documentation. It is your documentation, from three different pages, concatenated by an agent: the client construction from the quickstart, the retry configuration from a how-to that assumed an existing client, and an import line the agent inferred because none of the three snippets had one. Every fragment was correct and the combination never existed.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a checker for the properties a coding agent needs, run it over realistic samples, and fix a page that passes human review and fails this. Forty minutes.

Step 1: four samples, all of which look fine to a person

mkdir -p agentdocs-drill/docs && cd agentdocs-drill
cat > docs/quickstart.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Quickstart
---
# Quickstart

Create a client and send a request.

```python
from widget import WidgetClient

client = WidgetClient(api_key="sk-...")
print(client.infer("hello"))
```
EOF

cat > docs/retries.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Configure retries
---
# Configure retries

Set `retries` when constructing the client.

```python
client = WidgetClient(api_key="sk-...", retries=3)
```
EOF

cat > docs/batching.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Batch requests
---
# Batch requests

Pass a list instead of a string.

```python
results = client.infer_batch(["a", "b", "c"])
```
EOF

cat > docs/streaming.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Stream a response
---
# Stream a response

```python
for token in client.infer_stream("hello"):
    print(token, end="")
```
EOF
ls docs/

Every one of those is a reasonable snippet and would pass review. Three of the four are unusable to something that cannot infer context.

Step 2: the checker

cat > agentcheck.py <<'PY'
"""Check code samples for the properties a coding agent needs.

Four checks. None of them is about quality; all are about whether a sample
survives being lifted out of its page.

  RUNNABLE   does it define the names it uses, or import them?
  LABELLED   if it is deliberately a fragment, does it say so?
  IMPORTS    are the library's own imports present?
  VERSIONED  does the page say which version this is for?

The LABELLED check is the important one and the cheapest. A fragment is
perfectly fine; an UNMARKED fragment is the defect, because an agent cannot
tell the difference and a reader can.
"""
import ast
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

LIBRARY = "widget"
FENCE = re.compile(r"```python\n(.*?)```", re.S)

#: Comment markers that say "this is deliberately partial".
FRAGMENT_COMMENTS = ("# fragment", "# continues from", "# assumes")


def is_marked(source):
    """True when the snippet declares itself partial.

    An ellipsis counts only as a STATEMENT on its own line. Matching `...`
    anywhere in the text treats `api_key="sk-..."` as a fragment marker,
    which silently exempted the page this checker was written to catch. That
    was a real bug in the first version of this checker, and it is the
    characteristic failure of substring matching over code.
    """
    if any(marker in source for marker in FRAGMENT_COMMENTS):
        return True
    return any(line.strip() == "..." for line in source.splitlines())


def samples(path):
    return FENCE.findall(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def undefined_names(source):
    """Names used but never bound or imported in this snippet.

    Uses the AST rather than a regex so that attribute access, function
    arguments and comprehension variables are handled correctly. Builtins
    are excluded.
    """
    try:
        tree = ast.parse(source)
    except SyntaxError:
        return ["<syntax error>"]

    bound, used = set(), []
    for node in ast.walk(tree):
        if isinstance(node, (ast.Import, ast.ImportFrom)):
            for alias in node.names:
                bound.add((alias.asname or alias.name).split(".")[0])
        elif isinstance(node, ast.Name):
            if isinstance(node.ctx, (ast.Store, ast.Del)):
                bound.add(node.id)
            else:
                used.append(node.id)
        elif isinstance(node, (ast.FunctionDef, ast.AsyncFunctionDef, ast.ClassDef)):
            bound.add(node.name)
        elif isinstance(node, ast.arg):
            bound.add(node.arg)

    builtins = set(dir(__builtins__)) | {"print", "len", "range", "list", "dict"}
    return sorted({n for n in used if n not in bound and n not in builtins})


def check_page(path):
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    front = text.split("---")[1] if text.startswith("---") else ""
    findings = []

    for index, source in enumerate(samples(path), 1):
        label = f"{path.name} sample {index}"
        marked = is_marked(source)
        missing = undefined_names(source)

        if missing and not marked:
            findings.append((
                label, "unmarked-fragment",
                f"uses {missing} without defining or importing them, "
                "and is not marked as a fragment",
            ))
        if f"import {LIBRARY}" not in source and f"from {LIBRARY}" not in source:
            if not marked and missing:
                findings.append((label, "no-import",
                                 f"no {LIBRARY} import, so the agent will guess one"))
        if "version" not in front and "since" not in front:
            findings.append((label, "no-version",
                             "the page does not say which version this is for"))
    return findings


def main(root):
    total = 0
    for path in sorted(root.glob("*.md")):
        findings = check_page(path)
        total += len(findings)
        if findings:
            for label, kind, why in findings:
                print(f"AGENT-READY  {label}: {kind}: {why}", file=sys.stderr)
        else:
            print(f"ok  {path.name}")
    print(f"\n{'FAIL' if total else 'ok'}: {total} problem(s)")
    return 1 if total else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(Path(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "docs")))
PY
python3 agentcheck.py docs; echo "exit=$?"

Step 3: fix the pages two ways, and see which check each fix satisfies

There are two legitimate fixes and they are not interchangeable.

echo "--- fix A: make the sample self-contained ---"
cat > docs/retries.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Configure retries
version: "2.6"
---
# Configure retries

Set `retries` when constructing the client.

```python
from widget import WidgetClient

client = WidgetClient(api_key="sk-...", retries=3)
print(client.infer("hello"))
```
EOF

echo "--- fix B: keep it a fragment, and say so ---"
cat > docs/batching.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Batch requests
version: "2.6"
---
# Batch requests

Pass a list instead of a string.

```python
# continues from the quickstart; `client` is already constructed
results = client.infer_batch(["a", "b", "c"])
```
EOF

echo "--- and one left broken on purpose ---"
python3 agentcheck.py docs; echo "exit=$?"

Step 4: the fix that scales, which is a different artifact entirely

The checker catches unmarked fragments. It does not give an agent a complete, tested starting point, and that is a separate thing worth having.

cat > docs/complete-example.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Complete working example
version: "2.6"
---
# Complete working example

Every snippet elsewhere in these docs is an excerpt from this file. If you
want something that runs, start here.

```python
from widget import WidgetClient

client = WidgetClient(
    api_key="sk-...",      # from the dashboard
    retries=3,             # see how-to/retries
    batch_size=1,          # see how-to/batching
)

# one request
print(client.infer("hello"))

# several requests
print(client.infer_batch(["a", "b", "c"]))

# streaming
for token in client.infer_stream("hello"):
    print(token, end="")
```
EOF
python3 agentcheck.py docs 2>&1 | grep -E "^ok|complete" ; echo
echo "A canonical complete example is one page an agent can always fall back to,"
echo "and it is testable by code-sample validation, so it cannot rot."

What you built. A checker for agent-readability, two kinds of fix, and a canonical complete example.

On the four original pages it reports 10 problems across all four, and every one is invisible to human review:

Page Finding quickstart.md no version declared retries.md uses WidgetClient with no import, unmarked batching.md uses client with no definition, unmarked streaming.md uses client with no definition, unmarked

After fix A on retries.md (self-contained) and fix B on batching.md (marked fragment with a named prerequisite), both pass. streaming.md is left broken on purpose so the checker still fails.

docs.title: The bug the checker found in itself
docs.text:
The first version of this checker treated ... appearing anywhere as a fragment marker. retries.md contains api_key="sk-...", a redacted placeholder, so the checker silently exempted the exact page it was written to catch.

That is the characteristic failure of substring matching over code, and it is why undefined_names uses an AST walk rather than a regex: an ellipsis counts only as a statement on its own line. The fix moved retries.md from one finding to three.

A checker that passes the case it was built for is the most dangerous kind, because the green result is taken as evidence.

docs.title: What a coding agent needs that a human reader does not
docs.text: Need Why a human does not need it Cost of omitting Imports in the sample They infer from the page's other samples The agent guesses an import path Names defined, or marked as assumed They know client came from earlier Code that references undefined names An explicit fragment marker A fragment is obvious to them A fragment treated as complete The version the sample is for They are on the current page An API that changed One canonical complete example They assemble mentally Fragments concatenated into fiction

docs.title: The two legitimate fixes, which are not interchangeable
docs.text:
Fix Use when Cost Make it self-contained The sample is short Repetition across pages Mark it as a fragment and name its prerequisite The setup is long or shared The agent must follow the reference

Do both in different places. A reference page's examples should be self-contained; a how-to in the middle of a sequence should be a marked fragment. The defect is the unmarked fragment, not the fragment.

docs.title: Markers worth standardising on
docs.text:
Marker Meaning # continues from <page> client and friends exist already # assumes <thing> A precondition the snippet does not create # fragment Deliberately partial, no claim of runnability # docpack: skip Excluded from sample validation, with a reason ... on its own line Elided code. Universally understood, including by models

Pick one set and enforce it, because an agent pattern-matches on what it sees and inconsistent markers are worse than none.

docs.title: "LLM-digestible", unpacked
docs.text:
Intel's phrase. It decomposes into things that are checkable:

Property Mechanism Serve Markdown, not only rendered HTML A build step; see llms.txt Headings that state what is below them Chunking depends on it Samples that survive extraction This page Declared page type Content model, so a filter can route Stable URLs A moved page breaks every citation No critical content in images Diagrams need text equivalents

The last row is often the biggest single loss in practice: an architecture explained only in a diagram is invisible to every machine consumer and to screen readers, which is the rare case where accessibility and agent-readiness want exactly the same thing.

docs.title: What does not help
docs.text: Non-fix Why A separate corpus written for agents Drifts from the human one within a quarter Removing prose so the page is "cleaner" The prose is what makes the chunk findable More samples Three unmarked fragments are worse than one complete example An llms.txt alone A map does not make a sample runnable

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with the concatenation failure, because it is specific and nobody expects it. "A coding agent assembles from several pages. Our retries page had client = WidgetClient(..., retries=3) with no import, because every human reader knows client came from the quickstart. An agent took that snippet, the batching snippet and an inferred import and produced code that looked like our documentation and never existed anywhere in it. So I check samples for undefined names with an AST walk, and either make them self-contained or require an explicit fragment marker. The defect is the unmarked fragment, not the fragment."

The follow-up is "does this not just mean repeating the setup everywhere", which is the real objection. The answer is that you choose per page type: reference examples are self-contained because they are read in isolation, and a how-to inside a sequence stays a marked fragment with a named prerequisite. Plus one canonical complete example that every excerpt is drawn from, which is single-sourcing applied to code and is testable by sample validation so it cannot rot.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Self-contained samples are more verbose and worse for a human skimming a reference page, who now reads three lines of setup before the one line they came for. There is a genuine conflict between the two audiences on this specific point, and it does not fully resolve. Marking fragments is the cheaper half of the answer and it costs nothing; making everything self-contained costs readability and should be done selectively, which means somebody has to decide per page.

One sharper point. The strongest observation is that this failure mode was always there and agents made it visible. A junior developer copying from three pages hit exactly the same problem, got stuck, and either asked or gave up quietly, and neither outcome produced a bug report that named your documentation. An agent does it at volume and the resulting code arrives in a support ticket. So the agent-readability work is not a new requirement grafted onto documentation, it is an old defect finally getting measured, which is the same pattern as RAG surfacing content gaps. That framing is both true and much easier to fund.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. The AST-based undefined-names checker in CI, plus a canonical complete example that sample validation executes.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. The checker flagging three of four reasonable-looking pages is the demonstration, and the AST walk is what makes it more than a regex.
  2. Point it at a real library's documentation. Yours, or an open-source project's. Count the unmarked fragments; in most corpora it is most of the samples, and that count is the finding.
  3. Write the canonical complete example and make every other sample an excerpt from it. That is one page, it is tested, and it gives an agent somewhere correct to fall back to.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Saying docs should be agent-friendly is a slogan. An AST checker that distinguishes a marked fragment from an unmarked one, a stated rule about which page types get self-contained samples, and a tested canonical example demonstrates that you found the failure and built the gate.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
No coding agent ran against this documentation. The claim this page makes, that documentation written for a coding agent differs from documentation written for a person in specific ways, is testable and was not tested here.

What you need. A coding agent with repository access, and a task whose success is mechanically checkable: "add a page that passes the validator", "fix the failing sample", "wire a new check into CI". Then two versions of your documentation: the current one, and one with the specific changes this page recommends.

What you would run. The same task, ten times against each documentation variant, scoring by whether the resulting code passes the repository's own gates. The documentation is the independent variable, which is the part people get wrong: it is tempting to vary the prompt, and the prompt is not what you control for your readers.

What you would see.

Change to the documentation Rough effect What it tells you Exact file paths instead of descriptions large Agents cannot browse like a person The command and its expected output large Verification is what unblocks the next step Stating what not to edit large, and underrated Generated files are the usual casualty One worked example of the task largest single gain Same as for human readers Conceptual explanation of why small The agent does not need to be persuaded Prose polish, tone, hedging none measurable The thing writers spend time on

The last two rows are the uncomfortable finding, and the reason this concept is separate from ordinary technical writing. The effort that improves a page for a person is close to orthogonal to the effort that improves it for an agent, and a team can only find that out by measuring both.

How you would know it had failed. Identical pass rates between variants usually means the agent never read the documentation, so check whether it actually opened the files before concluding the content does not matter. A 100% pass rate on both means the task is too easy. And if success depends on which model you used more than on which documentation you supplied, the experiment is measuring the model and has to be re-run with that held fixed.

docs.title: Cognitive load in technical content
docs.text:
The mean sentence length is fine on almost every corpus; the per-page maximum and the unprepared cross-reference are what actually cost the reader.

core · difficulty 2 · 3h

Adjacent, not quoted

Neither posting names it. It is the mechanism behind every claim about reaching first success in minutes.

Prerequisites: Instructional design for developers

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The working-memory cost of following a page. The useful split is into three parts. The intrinsic difficulty of the subject, which you cannot reduce without teaching something easier. The extraneous cost added by the presentation, which is the only part a writer controls. And the germane effort the reader spends actually building a model, which is the part you want them to have capacity left for.

Nearly every documentation complaint that gets reported as "too complicated" is extraneous load, and nearly every attempt to fix it by adding explanation makes it worse.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because "a developer reaches a working result in fifteen minutes" is a claim about working memory, not about word count.

A reader following a quickstart is holding several things at once: what they are trying to achieve, where they are in the sequence, what the last command printed, which of three similar-looking names they are supposed to use, and whether the thing that just appeared on screen is a problem. Every item the page adds to that stack is taken from the capacity they need for the actual subject. Exceed it and they do not report confusion, they close the tab, which is why this shows up in time to first success as a drop-off rather than as feedback.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Measure load on a real corpus, discover that the summary statistic is useless, and find a worse problem the summary statistic hides. About thirty minutes.

Step 1: the obvious measurement

sents = []
for c in complete:
    prose = prose_of((docs / c.page).read_text())
    sents += [len(s.split()) for s in SENT.split(prose) if len(s.split()) >= 3]

sentences: 4847   mean 19.6 words
longest sentence per page: mean 50   max 103 (tutorial-design)

(Steps 1 and 2 were run when the corpus was 82 pages. They are kept as the pair that exposed the bug; every figure from step 3 onward is the finished 106-page corpus.)

A 103-word sentence would be remarkable. Look at it:

103 | The architectural ordering, eight steps, output only at the end:
      mkdir sync && cd sync python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
      pip install widget click mkdir src tests cat > src/config.py <<'EOF' ...

That is a shell session. The prose extractor had re-implemented fence detection as a toggle, and the page opens a four-backtick fence containing heredocs, so the toggle closed early and treated the commands as a sentence.

The repository already contained a correct fence parser, written precisely because this problem is harder than it looks. The audit did not use it.

Step 2: the same measurement, using the parser that already existed

from fieldguide.fences import fence_spans, heredoc_body_lines
lines = text.splitlines()
skip  = heredoc_body_lines(lines)
incode = {n for sp in fence_spans(lines, skip=skip)
            for n in range(sp.open_line, sp.close_line + 1)}

sentences: 5341   mean 16.7 words   median 15
longest sentence per page: mean 46   max 66 (reading-code-to-verify)

Every figure moved, and the sentence count went up by 494, because the broken version had been swallowing real prose into pseudo-sentences as well as inventing them. An audit that re-implements a solved problem inherits exactly the bug the solution exists for.

Step 3: the summary statistic is fine and it is useless

The original run, when the corpus held 7,178 sentences rather than today's 8,541:

mean 17.1 words, median 15
sentences over 45 words: 95 of 7178 (1.3%)

By any style guide that is a healthy corpus. Now count pages rather than sentences:

pages whose longest sentence exceeds 35 words: 100/106
pages whose longest sentence exceeds 45 words:  59/106
pages whose longest sentence exceeds 60 words:   6/106

One and a third per cent of the sentences, and more than half the pages. Those two rows describe the same data, and only the second one describes the reader's experience, because a reader does not meet a corpus average. They meet one page, and on 59 of 106 pages they meet a sentence they have to read twice.

The actionable metric is the per-page maximum. A mean is a measurement of the corpus; a maximum is a measurement of the worst moment a reader has, and load failures are worst-moment failures.

Step 3a: part of that number was the splitter

Acting on the figures above turned up a defect in the thing that produced them, which by now is the expected order of events in this corpus.

The sentence boundary was a terminator followed by an optional closing quote or bracket, then whitespace. This corpus ends dozens of sentences in bold, so .** was not a boundary and every bolded sentence was silently joined to the one after it. Three of the six "sentences over 60 words" were two sentences with a .** between them, and the over-45 sentence count fell from 111 to 56 the moment the class was widened to include markup.

                                  before   after the fix   after editing
sentences over 45 words              111             56              33
pages whose longest exceeds 45        59             43              27
pages whose longest exceeds 60         6              5               0
longest sentence in the corpus        71             71              50

The 111 in that first column and the 95 above it are the same measurement at two different times: the corpus kept growing between them. The page counts are the stable comparison, which is the argument for the per-page maximum made twice over.

The editing pass is real work and it moved the middle column to the right one. The splitter fix moved the left column to the middle without touching a word of prose. Both are in the table because publishing only the second would make the editing look twice as effective as it was.

Step 3b: the metric has a hole, and measuring it closed it

A list item is not a sentence, so the prose measurement excludes list items. That exclusion is also a loophole: a 70-word sentence becomes compliant the moment somebody puts a hyphen in front of it, and the reader is no better off unless the content was genuinely a list.

Four of the five worst sentences here were genuinely lists, and converting them to bullets is the right edit for a reader. It is also an edit that removes them from the metric rather than improving them, and those two facts are independent. So fieldguide audit now reports the longest sentence inside list items alongside the prose figure:

    in list items: longest mean 21, max 34
                   45+ on   0/106 pages

No list item in this corpus hides a long sentence, which is worth knowing rather than assuming. The first version of that measurement counted each item's total words and reported an 81-word item, which was four short sentences in a proof task and not a readability problem at all. Sentences inside items are the comparable unit; item length is not.

Step 4: the cost nobody measures

Sentence length is the cheap half. Count what a page asks the reader to hold by way of cross-references:

distinct concepts linked per page: mean 6.3   max 15 (systems-mindset)   min 4

Then ask whether those links point at anything the reader has been prepared for. For each learning path, classify every link on its pages as backward (already read), forward (later in this path), or off-path:

  first-week           backward   9  forward  14  off-path  52
  content-architect    backward  15  forward  18  off-path  45
  docs-engineer        backward  34  forward  35  off-path  39
  knowledgeops         backward  44  forward  38  off-path  49
  developer-educator   backward  22  forward  27  off-path  32
  writer-who-builds    backward   4  forward   8  off-path  60
  prove-it             backward  22  forward  20  off-path  55
  prove-the-outcomes   backward  15  forward  15  off-path  32
  domain-context       backward   9  forward   7  off-path   8

backward 174   forward 182   off-path 372
links pointing at material the reader has not read: 76%

Nine paths, where this measurement first ran over seven. Two paths were added after it, and the per-path rows moved as well as the totals, because pages gained cross-references. The 76 per cent did not move at all, which is the useful thing about a ratio: it is the shape of the corpus rather than its size, and it is why that figure is the one quoted elsewhere.

On first-week, a reader meets 75 concept links and nine of them point at something they have already read. The other 66 are an invitation to leave, each one carrying a small decision: is this a prerequisite I am missing, or an aside?

That decision is pure extraneous load, and it is invisible to every readability measure. The corpus reads well sentence by sentence and asks its readers to make sixty-six unnecessary judgments per path.

Step 5: what to do about each half

The sentence half is a straightforward editing job against a per-page maximum. The six pages over 60 words took an afternoon, and there are now none.

The link half is not fixed by linking less. A guide whose pages do not cross-reference is a worse guide. It is fixed by making the kind of link visible, so the reader's decision is made for them. A prerequisites line is a link you must follow. A "related" list at the foot is a link you may ignore. An inline link is neither, which is why the inline ones generate the load. This corpus has the first and the last and uses inline links for both jobs, which is the finding.

What you built. A load measurement that uses the corpus's own fence parser, a per-page maximum that replaced a useless mean, and a cross-reference census showing 78 per cent of links point at unread material.

docs.title: The three loads, and what moves each one
docs.text:
Load Source Lever Intrinsic The subject's real difficulty Teach a smaller subject first Extraneous Presentation Everything on this page Germane Model-building Protect capacity for it

The common mistake is attacking intrinsic load by adding explanation, which raises extraneous load and leaves less room for germane effort. The reader reports the same confusion about a longer page.

docs.title: Extraneous load, by source
docs.text:
Source Shows up as Measured by Long sentences Re-reading Per-page maximum, not the mean Unprepared cross-references A decision per link The backward/forward/off-path census Split attention Scrolling between code and its explanation Code and prose adjacency Near-identical names Using the wrong one A terminology inventory Unstated prerequisites Failure three steps later Cold-start testing Options presented before a default Paralysis at step 1 Counting choices before first success Output not shown Uncertainty whether it worked Expected output per command

The last two rows are the highest-yield fixes in most quickstarts and neither is a writing problem.

docs.title: Why the mean misleads
docs.text:
Statistic Describes Useful for Mean sentence length The corpus Reporting Median The corpus Reporting Per-page maximum The reader's worst moment Editing Count of pages over a threshold The size of the job Planning Percentage of sentences over it Nothing a reader experiences Reassuring yourself

Load failures are worst-moment failures, so every statistic worth acting on is a maximum or a count of pages, never a central tendency.

docs.title: Chunking, and its limit
docs.text:
Breaking a long procedure into named steps genuinely reduces load, because the reader can discard the contents of a completed step and keep only its name. That is why golden paths in this guide are numbered and named.

The limit is that chunking only helps when the chunks are independent. Steps that require holding state from three steps back are not chunked, they are merely numbered, and the numbering disguises the problem by making the page look organised.

docs.title: What load is not an argument for
docs.text: Not Because Shorter documentation A page can be long and low-load Removing detail Detail the reader needs is intrinsic Simplified vocabulary The real terms are what they will search for Fewer links The fix is marking their kind, not deleting them One page per idea Fragmentation adds navigation load

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the three-way split, briefly. "Intrinsic load is the subject, extraneous load is the presentation, germane load is the reader actually building a model. Only the middle one is mine, and most attempts to reduce the first by adding explanation increase the second. 'Fifteen minutes to a working result' is a claim about working memory, not about word count."

The follow-up is how you measure it, and this is where to bring the numbers. Mean sentence length on my corpus is 15.6 words, which is healthy and useless. A reader never meets an average, so the metric I act on is the per-page maximum: 59 of 106 pages carried a sentence over 45 words and six carried one over 60. After an editing pass, 27 pages and none. The honest part of that story is that fixing the sentence splitter accounted for as much of the improvement as the editing did, because it had never treated a sentence ending in bold as a sentence ending.

The stronger half, if there is time for one more thing. I classified every cross-reference by whether the reader had reached it yet, and 76 per cent of links point at material they have not read. On the shortest path, nine links of 75 point backwards. Each of the other 66 is a decision about whether something is a missing prerequisite or an aside, which is invisible to every readability score. The fix is not fewer links, it is making the kind of link visible, because a prerequisites line and a "related" footer make the decision for the reader and an inline link does not.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Load is a model, not a measurement, and the numbers above are proxies for something nobody can observe directly. A page with a 60-word sentence may be perfectly clear and a page of short sentences may be unreadable. The measurements earn their place by finding candidates quickly, and the reading still has to happen; treating any of them as a gate produces staccato prose that scores well.

One sharper point. My own load audit was wrong, and wrong in the way this whole area is wrong: it re-implemented fence detection as a toggle, so a page with four-backtick fences and heredocs leaked a shell session into the prose and reported a 103-word sentence. The repository already contained a correct fence parser. The corrected run moved every figure and found 494 more sentences, because the broken version had been merging real prose too. An audit that re-implements a solved problem inherits the exact bug the solution exists for.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A per-page maximum sentence length and a cross-reference census over a corpus you own, both computed with that corpus's own parser.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Measure the per-page maximum sentence length on your docs, then read the three worst sentences out loud. The measurement takes five minutes and the reading is what convinces anybody.
  2. Take your shortest learning path and classify every link on its pages as backward, forward or off-path. The ratio will be worse than you expect.
  3. Open your quickstart and count the choices it presents before the reader's first success. Each one is extraneous load at the worst possible moment.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Every figure in steps 2 through 4 comes from fieldguide audit, a committed subcommand rather than a script that was thrown away, so a reader can run it and get these numbers. fences.py is the parser it uses, and it exists because the naive version was wrong three times; tests/test_audit.py holds a fixture for each of those three failures, including the nested fence that leaked a shell session into the prose.

What the guide does not have is any evidence that lowering these numbers improved comprehension for a real reader, which would need assessment and a population. The demonstrated page records this as partial on exactly that split: the instrument is demonstrated, the effect is not.

docs.title: Cold-start testing
docs.text:
Following the quickstart literally, from an empty environment, so the reader is not the first to try it.

core · difficulty 3 · 5h

Asked for by name

Intel: "Build and maintain docsascode pipelines and documentation CI, including link checking and coldstart testing of quickstarts"

Intel: "Treats setup, runnable samples, and docs as one product ... so a developer reaches first success in minutes with zero help"

Prerequisites: Code-sample validation, Reproducible environments

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Running the quickstart from an environment that has nothing: a fresh virtual environment, a clean container, no caches, no credentials the instructions did not mention. The test is not whether the commands work. It is whether the document is complete.

Intel names it explicitly, which is unusual and tells you something about what they have been burned by.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because a quickstart is the only page whose author is structurally incapable of testing it. The author has the SDK installed, the token exported, the repository cloned, a Python with the right version, and three dependencies they installed last March for something else. They run their own quickstart, it works, and they ship it.

Then a developer who has none of that follows it and hits ModuleNotFoundError on step two. That developer is now evaluating your product on the basis of a document that was never true for anyone but its author.

Intel's phrasing is "first success in minutes with zero help." Cold-start testing is the only mechanism that measures whether that claim holds, and it is why they list setup, samples and docs as one product. A quickstart is not prose with code in it. It is an executable artifact that happens to be readable.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Watch a quickstart that passes on your machine fail from a clean environment. About thirty-five minutes.

Step 1: a quickstart with a hidden assumption

mkdir -p cold-demo/docs && cd cold-demo
cat > docs/quickstart.md <<'MDEOF'
# Quickstart

Install it:

```bash
pip install cowsay
```

Use it:

```bash
python3 -c "import cowsay, requests; print('ok')"
```
MDEOF

The install step mentions one package. The sample imports two.

Step 2: confirm it passes on this machine

python3 -c "import requests; print('system-wide:', requests.__version__)"

system-wide: 2.34.2

requests is already here, because something installed it once. An author testing this quickstart in their normal shell sees it work, and the omission is invisible to them. It is also invisible to sample validation, which runs in the same ambient environment.

Step 3: a harness that starts from nothing

cat > coldstart.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Follow the quickstart literally, from an empty virtual environment.
set -euo pipefail
WORK="$(mktemp -d)"; trap 'rm -rf "$WORK"' EXIT
cd "$WORK"

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

# Extract the bash blocks from the quickstart, in order, and run them as one
# shell so that cd and exported variables persist.
python3 - <<'PY' > script.sh
import re
from pathlib import Path
FENCE = re.compile(r"^```(\w+)?\s*$")
out, cur, lang = [], None, None
for line in Path("DOCS").read_text().splitlines():
    m = FENCE.match(line)
    if m and cur is None:
        cur, lang = [], m.group(1)
    elif m and cur is not None:
        if lang == "bash":
            out.append("\n".join(cur))
        cur = None
    elif cur is not None:
        cur.append(line)
print("\n".join(out))
PY

bash -e script.sh
EOF
chmod +x coldstart.sh

The important properties: a temp directory so nothing touches the repository, a virtual environment with no system packages, and the blocks run in document order as a single shell.

Step 4: run it

./coldstart.sh

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
    import cowsay, requests; print('ok')
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'requests'
exit=1

The defect the author could not see. The page is incomplete, and only an environment with nothing in it can say so.

Step 5: fix the document, not the environment

sed -i 's|pip install cowsay|pip install cowsay requests|' docs/quickstart.md
./coldstart.sh

Successfully installed certifi-2026.10.23 charset_normalizer-3.5.2 cowsay-6.1 idna-3.20 requests-2.34.2 urllib3-2.8.0
ok
exit=0

Note the direction of the fix. The temptation when a cold start fails is to make the harness more permissive, by using --system-site-packages or pre-installing the dependency. That converts the one check capable of finding this class of defect into a check that cannot. The environment is the specification. If the test fails, the document is wrong.

Step 6: know what it costs

cold start (venv + install + run):     ~3.9s
sample execution only (no fresh env):  ~0.04s

Two orders of magnitude on a toy. On a real project, where the install pulls a compiled dependency or a container image, it is minutes against milliseconds. That ratio is why this runs as its own CI job rather than alongside the fast gates.

What you built. A check that reads the quickstart as a reader would, with none of the author's advantages.

docs.title: What each environment can detect
docs.text:
Environment Catches an undeclared dependency Catches a missing step Catches a wrong version pin Speed The author's shell No No No Instant Fresh virtual environment Yes, for Python packages Yes Yes Seconds Fresh container Also system packages, locales, system Python Yes Yes Minutes Fresh container, no network cache Also a dead package index or yanked release Yes Yes Minutes

Pick the weakest environment that catches your actual failures. A virtual environment covers most Python quickstarts; a container is required the moment your instructions say apt install.

docs.title: The assumptions a cold start flushes out
docs.text: Assumption How it shows up An undeclared dependency ModuleNotFoundError, as above A pre-existing credential An auth error on a step the author never authenticated for A cloned repository cd myproject with no preceding git clone A specific interpreter version A syntax error, or a dependency resolving differently A warm cache A timeout, or a surprising first-run message in the expected output A tool installed years ago command not found An implied working directory A path that resolves only from the author's home

docs.title: Rules that keep it honest
docs.text:
Rule Reason Never relax the environment to pass The isolation is the test Run the document, do not reimplement it A separate script drifts from the page Blocks run in document order, as one shell A quickstart is a sequence; cd must persist Assert the final output, not just exit codes "First success" means the reader saw the right thing Pin nothing the document does not pin If the quickstart is unpinned, test it unpinned and accept the flakiness as information Its own CI job Minutes, not seconds; do not gate typo fixes on it

That fifth rule is contentious and worth holding. An unpinned quickstart that breaks because a dependency released a major version has told you something true about what a reader will experience today. Pinning the test environment hides that until a reader reports it.

docs.title: Where it sits among the other checks
docs.text:
Check Question Link checking Do the cross-references resolve? Sample validation Do the examples still run and return the right thing? Doc test harness Can we run samples in several languages with attribution? Cold-start testing Is the document complete?

Only the last one is about omissions, and omissions are what make a quickstart fail for a stranger.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the author's blind spot. "A quickstart is the one page its author cannot test, because their machine already has everything. So it runs from an empty virtual environment in CI, following the document's own blocks in order. The failures it finds are always omissions: an undeclared dependency, a missing clone, a token nobody mentioned."

The follow-up is about cost, and the answer is that it runs as its own job on a schedule or per pull request, never in the fast feedback path, because the ratio is seconds against milliseconds and more like minutes in a container.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Cold-start tests are the flakiest check you will own, because they depend on package indexes and the network, and a flaky required check trains people to re-run CI until green. The mitigations are a separate job, a retry on genuine network failure only, and a clear rule about who investigates a red cold start. Do not pretend it is as deterministic as a unit test.

One sharper point, and the thing to say if you say one thing. When a cold start fails, the fix is in the document, not the harness. Every instinct pushes the other way, because pre-installing the dependency makes the build green in one line. That single decision is the difference between a cold-start test and a cold-start-shaped piece of theatre.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A script that creates a clean environment, extracts the quickstart's own commands, runs them in order, and asserts the final output.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Step 2 and step 4 together are the demonstration: the same page, passing and failing, depending only on what the environment already had.
  2. Write coldstart.sh for a project you own and run it once. Whatever it finds has been in your quickstart for months. If it passes on the first run, check that the environment really was empty: a cold-start script that goes green immediately is usually testing the machine it was written on.
  3. Time it, and put the number in the README. The cost is the reason it lives in its own job, and knowing the number is how you defend that decision.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack's scripts/coldstart.sh builds a fresh virtual environment, installs the way a reader would, follows the tutorial literally, and asserts the exact output string the tutorial promises. The exact-output assertion is the part worth pointing at: without it, the script proves the commands exit zero, not that the reader reached first success.
