docs.title: Transforming content as data
docs.text:
Every transformation drops something; the dangerous ones relocate it instead, so the pipeline is correct and any consumer who forgets the relocation is not.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Working proficiency in Python or similar to automate content tasks, transform data, and integrate with APIs"

Prerequisites: Python for content automation, Content models

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Converting documentation from the form people write into the forms machines consume: Markdown into chunk records, front matter into a search index, a tree of pages into one flat file for a context window. The content model is what makes it possible, because a transformation can only carry fields that reliably exist.

The whole discipline reduces to one question asked at every stage: what did this drop, and who finds out?

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because the artifacts a documentation platform ships are mostly derived, and derived artifacts fail quietly.

A broken page is visible to whoever opens it. A chunk record missing a field is visible to nobody until a retrieval returns something unhelpful, and then it looks like a ranking problem. The team spends a quarter evaluating embedding models for a defect introduced by a transformation that ran correctly.

NVIDIA's sentence puts "transform data" between automating content tasks and integrating with APIs, which is the right order: transformation is where the corpus stops being prose and becomes someone else's input, and the handover is where the accountability gets lost.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Measure a real three-stage pipeline for what each stage drops, then find the drop that is not a drop. About thirty minutes.

Step 1: run the pipeline and account for every character

docpack docs --out dist

stage                     files  chars     of source
  docs/*.md                  12   45751      100%
  chunks.jsonl text          85   40767       89%
  llms-full.txt               1   45308       99%
  llms.txt                    1    2246        5%

Three outputs with three quite different jobs. llms-full.txt keeps 99 per cent, so it is close to a concatenation. llms.txt keeps five, because it is a map rather than a copy: titles, summaries and links, grouped by type. Neither is surprising.

chunks.jsonl keeping 89 per cent is the one to look at, because it is the artifact a retriever actually uses.

Step 2: find out where the eleven per cent went

Reconstruct each page by concatenating its own chunks and compare with the source:

joined = "\n\n".join(c["text"] for c in by_source[rel])
frac = len(joined) / len(body_without_front_matter)

page                                          source  chunks   kept
reference/api.md                                1028     908    88%
how-to/wire-up-ci.md                            1549    1415    91%
how-to/add-a-page.md                            3707    3392    92%
explanation/why-heading-aware-chunking.md       2909    2702    93%

mean kept: 93%

Seven per cent, evenly spread, no page catastrophically worse than another. Even distribution is a clue: a parsing bug would concentrate. Account for it directly:

source body characters:      43285
  in heading lines:           2367   (5%)
  blank lines:                 322

Five per cent is heading lines, and the rest is the blank lines between sections. The transformation is doing exactly what it was designed to do.

Step 3: the drop that is not a drop

The headings are not discarded. They are relocated:

a chunk record:
  breadcrumb: AI-readiness patterns > Why generated and not hand-maintained
  title:      AI-readiness patterns
  text opens: 'A hand-written `llms.txt` is accurate on the day it is written...'

chunks whose text still contains their own heading: 3 of 85

Eighty-two of eighty-five chunks have the heading stripped from the body and promoted to a metadata field. That is the right design: the heading trail is more useful as a filterable, displayable field than as the first line of a text blob, and it is how the breadcrumb gets into a search result.

It also means every consumer that reads text alone silently loses every heading in the corpus. The information is present in the record and absent from the field people reach for.

Step 4: measure what that costs the careless consumer

The grounding check joins the breadcrumb back on before testing. Run it both ways:

  grounded@1, breadcrumb + text (what the pipeline does)   18/20  (90%)
  grounded@1, text alone (a careless consumer)             17/20  (85%)

Five points, one case in twenty, from forgetting a field that is right there in the record.

Five points is small and the shape of the failure is what matters. The transformation is correct, the artifact is complete, the schema is documented, and a reasonable integrator writing record["text"] gets a worse system with no error, no warning and nothing to debug. The defect is not in the pipeline; it is in the contract the pipeline does not state.

Step 5: state the contract, then assert it

The fix is not to stop relocating headings, which would make the records worse. It is to say so where an integrator will see it, and to check that the statement stays true:

#: Fields a consumer must concatenate to reproduce what a reader sees.
RETRIEVAL_TEXT = ("breadcrumb", "text")

A transformation that relocates anything owes its consumers three things: the relocation documented next to the schema, a named constant or helper that does the rejoining so nobody has to remember, and a test that fails if the relocation changes. The third is what stops this from recurring the next time the chunker is improved.

What you built. A character-level account of a three-stage pipeline, a seven per cent loss resolved into headings and blank lines, and a measurement of what one unstated contract costs the consumer who follows the obvious path.

docs.title: The three transformations, and what each is for
docs.text:
Output Keeps Job Breaks when chunks.jsonl 89% Retrieval, with filters A field is missing or renamed llms-full.txt 99% One context window The corpus outgrows the window llms.txt 5% A map for an agent to navigate Summaries go stale A search index Varies In-site search Titles collide An offline bundle 100% Air-gapped reading Links assume a server

Keeping less is not worse. Each figure should match the job, and a number that does not match its job is the actual finding: a map at 89 per cent is a copy, and a chunk set at 5 per cent has lost the content.

docs.title: How a transformation loses something
docs.text:
Mode Example Who notices Discarded Comments stripped from output Nobody, correctly Relocated A heading becomes a breadcrumb field The consumer who reads one field Flattened Nested lists become one paragraph A reader, eventually Truncated A chunk cut at a token ceiling mid-sentence A retriever, as poor grounding Reordered Dict iteration changing record order A diff, as noise Silently empty A page that parsed to zero chunks Nobody, which is the worst case

The second row is this page's subject and the most common real defect, because it looks like success at every point in the pipeline.

docs.title: What a derived artifact owes its consumers
docs.text: Obligation Why A documented schema Otherwise every integrator guesses The relocations stated explicitly See step 4 A helper that does the obvious rejoining Cheaper than documentation nobody reads Stable identifiers So a consumer can diff two runs A record count asserted in CI Catches the silently-empty mode A version or generation timestamp So staleness is detectable downstream

docs.title: Stable identifiers, and why they are hard
docs.text:
A chunk id must change when the chunk's content changes and must not change when something unrelated moves. Hashing the content plus the heading trail gets both; hashing the position gets neither.

Scheme Survives an edit elsewhere Changes on a real edit Position index No Yes Hash of text Yes Yes Hash of text and breadcrumb Yes Yes, and on a retitle hash() builtin No; salted per process Unusable

The third is usually right, and the fourth is a real mistake people make once.

docs.title: Round-tripping as a test
docs.text: You will rarely need to reconstruct the source, and attempting it is still the cheapest audit available: concatenate the chunks of each page, compare lengths, and look at the distribution. An even seven per cent is a design decision. One page at forty per cent is a bug, and nothing else in the pipeline would have told you.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the question. "Every transformation drops something, so the only question that matters at each stage is what it dropped and who finds out. The dangerous answer is that it did not drop the thing, it moved it, because then the pipeline is correct and the consumer is wrong, and nothing errors."

The worked example, which is short. My chunk records keep 89 per cent of the source. Reconstructing each page from its own chunks put the loss at seven per cent, evenly spread, and even distribution rules out a parsing bug. It resolved into five per cent heading lines and the blank lines between sections. Eighty-two of eighty-five chunks have their heading stripped from the body and promoted to a breadcrumb field, which is the right design and means any consumer reading text alone loses every heading in the corpus.

Then the cost, measured. Grounding at rank one is 90 per cent when the breadcrumb is rejoined and 85 when it is not. One case in twenty, from forgetting a field sitting in the same record. Small, and the shape is the point: correct pipeline, complete artifact, documented schema, and a reasonable integrator writing record["text"] gets a quietly worse system. The defect is in the contract the pipeline never stated.

The tradeoff to volunteer. I would not fix that by stopping the relocation, because the records are better with the heading as a field. The fix is a stated contract, a helper that does the rejoining so nobody has to remember, and a test that fails if the relocation changes. That is three small obligations on the producer to save every consumer from the same discovery, and producers resist it because from the inside the artifact looks complete.

One sharper point. Round-tripping is worth doing even when you never need the source back. Concatenating each page's chunks and comparing lengths took ten minutes and converted "89 per cent, presumably fine" into an itemised account. If one page had come back at forty per cent I would have had a bug, and no other check in the pipeline would have mentioned it.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A transformation of yours with a character-level account of each stage, and a stated contract for any field it relocates.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Reconstruct one page from its own derived records and compare the lengths. Predict the percentage first, then explain the gap down to the character class; "probably whitespace" is not an explanation.
  2. Find a field your pipeline relocates and check whether the obvious consumer path picks it up. If there is no helper, write the helper rather than the documentation.
  3. Assert a record count in CI. The silently-empty failure is the only one on this page that nobody notices at all, and one assertion closes it.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack's pipeline is real and every figure above is reproducible from it. Three outputs at 89, 99 and 5 per cent of source. A seven per cent round-trip gap resolved into headings and blank lines. 82 of 85 chunks with relocated headings, and the five-point grounding difference between rejoining the breadcrumb and not. What is absent is a consumer other than this project: nobody has integrated against these records, so the contract problem in step 4 is demonstrated by measurement rather than by a real integrator getting it wrong.

docs.title: Content lifecycle and governance
docs.text:
The states a page moves through, and making the state a field something checks rather than a label.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Automate the content lifecycle with LLMs and scripting, from drafting and updating to auditing, with checks for freshness, code accuracy, and terminology drift, and human review where judgment matters"

Prerequisites: Content models

Leads to: Freshness monitoring, Retiring content

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The states a page moves through from proposal to retirement, who owns it in each state, and what has to be true before it moves. Governance is the part that says who decides.

NVIDIA's phrasing names four activities: drafting, updating, auditing, and human review where judgment matters. That last clause is the governance question, and it is the one that determines whether the first three are worth automating.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because a corpus without a lifecycle has exactly one state, which is "published", and therefore no mechanism for anything. A page cannot be known to be a draft, cannot be flagged for review, and cannot be retired, so the corpus only ever grows.

The automation NVIDIA asks for is downstream of the states. You cannot automate auditing without a definition of what is due for audit, and that definition is a lifecycle state plus a date. Teams that try to add the automation first end up with a script producing a list nobody owns.

The sharper version, and the subject of the golden path: a lifecycle state is only real if something checks it. A status field that nothing validates is a label, and labels drift.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Define a lifecycle, then make each state claim falsifiable. About thirty minutes. This uses this guide's own registry, where the lifecycle is three states and every one of them is checked.

Step 1: the states, as a closed vocabulary

STATUSES = ("planned", "drafted", "complete")

Three states, deliberately few. planned means the concept is on the curriculum with no prose; drafted means prose exists and has not been verified; complete means it satisfies the page contract.

Step 2: decide what each state claims

This is the design work, and it is the whole concept. For each state, write down what a reader is entitled to assume:

State The claim Falsifiable by planned A placeholder exists, carrying its registry metadata A generated page exists drafted Prose exists; nothing is promised about it A file exists complete Six required sections, 450+ words, every golden path executed Section and length check

A state whose claim you cannot write down is a state that does nothing.

Step 3: make each claim fail

  CAUGHT check  complete concept, page deleted
  CAUGHT check  complete page truncated below 450 words
  CAUGHT check  complete page missing a required section
  CAUGHT check  an orphan page with no concept

Each of those is a lifecycle lie: a page claiming a state it has not earned. With the checks in place, status: complete is a statement about the file rather than an opinion.

Note what is not checked, and say so out loud: nothing verifies that the golden path on a complete page was actually executed. That part of the claim rests on the author's discipline, and pretending otherwise would be the sort of thing this page argues against.

Step 4: the state that needs a date, not a check

Three states are enough for authoring and not enough for maintenance, because a page can be complete and wrong. That is the freshness problem, and the lifecycle hook for it is a review date rather than another state:

reviewed: 2026-01-10
documents: src/client.py

Measured on the freshness page: comparing a page's edit date against its subject's finds nothing after a bulk commit, and comparing against an explicit reviewed: date finds the real drift. So the lifecycle field that matters for maintenance is a date somebody sets deliberately, not a timestamp the file system supplies.

Step 5: governance, which is the part with no code

Write down, in the repository, who decides:

## Ownership

| Area            | Owner        | Review cadence |
|-----------------|--------------|----------------|
| Install & setup | Platform     | Each release   |
| API reference   | Generated    | Automatic      |
| Concepts        | Docs lead    | Annual         |
| Playbooks       | Service team | Each incident  |

Four rows and a cadence beat a governance document nobody reads. The useful test is whether a page in your corpus can be traced to a person; if it cannot, the lifecycle has no actor and the states will not move.

What you built. Three states whose claims are checkable, a review date for the one claim a state cannot carry, and a named owner per area.

docs.title: A lifecycle that is worth having
docs.text:
State Means Entry condition Who Proposed Someone asked for it A request, or a gap in a coverage matrix Anyone Planned It is on the roadmap Accepted, with a named owner Docs lead Drafted Prose exists A file in the repository Author In review Awaiting judgment Gates green; see docs review Reviewer Published Readers can rely on it Contract satisfied, merged Author plus reviewer Due for review Its subject moved, or the clock ran out Freshness signal Owner Deprecated Still true for old versions Superseded Owner Retired Gone, with a redirect See retirement Docs lead

Most corpora need fewer than this. The test for each state is whether something different happens because a page is in it.

docs.title: What to automate and what not to
docs.text:
NVIDIA's list, with the honest division:

Activity Automatable What stays human Drafting Partly; an LLM can produce a first pass against a template Whether the page should exist Updating Partly; a mechanical change can be proposed Whether the change is correct Auditing Yes; freshness, drift, code accuracy are all measurable Which findings matter Review No All of it Retiring The mechanics The decision

The pattern across every row: measurement automates, judgment does not. That is also NVIDIA's own framing, "human review where judgment matters", and echoing it back with this division is a strong answer.

docs.title: Making a state real
docs.text:
Requirement Without it Closed vocabulary States accumulate: "mostly done", "needs a look" A written claim per state Nobody knows what the label asserts A check per claim The label drifts from the file An owner per area No actor, so nothing moves between states A trigger out of each state Pages enter "published" and never leave

The last row is the one that produces 4,000-page corpora where a third is wrong. Entry conditions are usually defined and exit conditions almost never are.

docs.title: Governance artifacts that actually get used
docs.text: Artifact Why it works An owner table in the repository Short, versioned, reviewable A review cadence per area, not per page Per-page dates are never maintained A coverage matrix with states Makes the gaps visible, which is what drives work A standing queue of audit findings Converts measurement into a work item A retirement policy Permits deletion, which otherwise never happens

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with falsifiability. "A lifecycle state is only real if something checks it. In my own registry, complete claims seven required sections and a minimum length, and all of those fail a build if they are not true. Before the checks existed, complete was an opinion."

The follow-up is NVIDIA's own clause, human review where judgment matters, and the division to offer is that measurement automates and judgment does not. Freshness, terminology drift and code accuracy are all measurable; whether a page should exist, and whether a proposed correction is right, are not.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Every state is overhead, and a lifecycle with eight states on a corpus of two hundred pages means authors spend their time in a workflow instead of writing. Three states that are checked beat eight that are aspirational. Add a state when something different will actually happen because a page is in it.

One sharper point, and the honest one. Not every claim a state makes is checkable. My complete state asserts that the page's golden path was executed, and nothing verifies that. I can check the section headings and the word count; I cannot check that I ran the code. Being able to say which part of your own claim rests on discipline rather than on a gate is worth more than claiming the gate covers everything.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A closed state vocabulary, a written claim per state, a check per claim, and an owner table.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Write down what each of your current states asserts. Any state you cannot write a claim for should be deleted.
  2. Pick the most load-bearing claim and make it fail a build. One check.
  3. Write the owner table. Four rows is enough, and a page that cannot be traced to a person has no lifecycle.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Neither of this guide's repositories implements a governance process, which the demonstrated page records, because process needs an organisation. What does exist is the falsifiable half: three states, a written claim each, and twelve defect classes that fail a build, plus an explicit note about the one part of the complete claim that no check covers.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
The mechanism is here and the process is not. This repository has three lifecycle states, a written claim behind each, and a validator that checks them, which is the falsifiable half. What it cannot have is a year of the states actually being applied by people with other priorities.

What you need. An organisation, a corpus with more than one owner, and twelve months. Nothing technical.

What a learner would do. Pick the state transition your team already gets wrong, usually "current" to "needs review", and instrument only that one. Record, for three months, how many pages entered it, how many left, and how many were still there at the end. Those three numbers are the whole demonstration.

What you would see.

Observation Typical What it tells you Pages entering review Steady, driven by a date The trigger works Pages leaving review Far fewer The usual finding Pages stuck past a quarter The majority Review is a state, not a process Pages retired Almost none Nobody is rewarded for deleting

The gap between rows one and two is the measurement. A lifecycle that moves pages in and not out is a backlog with a vocabulary, and the number makes that arguable rather than a matter of opinion.

Why it does not commit. The states commit; the transitions are events in people's weeks. A reader of this repository sees three states correctly enforced and cannot tell whether anything ever moved between them, because with one author and no readers nothing has.

  • Retiring content, the exit nobody builds
  • Reviewing documentation, the human stage this schedules

docs.title: Content models
docs.text:
A schema for your content, judged by the specific lies it makes impossible.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Information architecture skills: content modeling, taxonomy, and metadata for both navigation and machine retrieval"

Prerequisites: Information architecture

Leads to: Taxonomy and controlled vocabularies, Metadata for navigation and retrieval, Content lifecycle and governance, Single-sourcing and content reuse

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A schema for your content: what kinds of page exist, what fields each kind carries, which of those fields are required, and which draw from a closed vocabulary. In a docs-as-code project it usually lives in front matter plus a validator.

The way to judge one is not by how elegant the schema is. It is by asking what specific lies it makes impossible, and then checking that each of those lies actually fails a build. The golden path does exactly that, twelve times.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA lists content modeling first in its information architecture requirement, ahead of taxonomy and metadata, which is the right order: the model is the thing the other two attach to.

The reason it is engineering rather than documentation theory is that a model without a validator is a convention, and conventions decay silently. Every corpus has a style guide saying how pages should be structured. Very few can tell you which pages currently violate it.

It is also the foundation of everything in the AI-ready category. Filtering retrieval by page type, chunking by section, assembling an llms.txt by audience: all of those read fields. If the fields are optional, inconsistent or unparseable, none of it works, and the failure looks like a bad retriever rather than a bad schema.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Take a real content model and attack it. Twelve defects, one at a time, and check what survives. About forty minutes.

Step 1: the model under test

This guide's own registry is a content model with a validator. Its closed vocabularies and its page contract:

TIERS      = ("core", "supporting", "context")
PROVENANCE = ("quoted", "derived", "adjacent")
STATUSES   = ("planned", "drafted", "complete")

REQUIRED_SECTIONS = (
    "What it is", "Why the job asks for it", "The golden path",
    "Reference", "How to talk about it", "How to prove it",
)
MIN_COMPLETE_WORDS = 450

Plus structural rules: every concept needs at least one demanded_by entry, prerequisites must resolve to real concepts, and the prerequisite graph must be acyclic.

Step 2: attack the vocabularies and the graph

Mutate a copy of the registry, once per defect, and record where each is caught:

def attempt(label, mutate):
    data = copy.deepcopy(base)
    mutate(data)
    Path("mutated.yaml").write_text(yaml.safe_dump(data, sort_keys=False))
    try:
        registry = load_registry(Path("mutated.yaml"))
    except RegistryError as e:
        print(f"  CAUGHT at parse  {label}")
        return
    findings = validate_against_tree(registry, Path("docs"))
    print(f"  {'CAUGHT at check' if not findings.ok else 'MISSED'}  {label}")

  CAUGHT at parse  tier outside the vocabulary
  CAUGHT at parse  status outside the vocabulary
  CAUGHT at parse  provenance outside the vocabulary
  CAUGHT at parse  prerequisite that does not exist
  CAUGHT at parse  prerequisite cycle
  CAUGHT at parse  duplicate concept id
  CAUGHT at parse  concept with no demanded_by

Seven for seven, all at parse time, with messages that name the offender:

concepts[5] (metadata): tier must be one of ['core', 'supporting', 'context']
prerequisite cycle: content-model -> metadata -> content-model
duplicate concept id 'metadata'

Step 3: attack the page contract

The remaining defects are about the relationship between the registry and the files, so they are caught later, by a validator that reads both:

  CAUGHT check  complete concept, page deleted
  CAUGHT check  complete page truncated below 450 words
  CAUGHT check  complete page missing a required section
  CAUGHT check  an orphan page with no concept

Four for four. Note the last one: a page nobody registered is as much a model violation as a registry entry with no page. A model that only validates in one direction lets the corpus grow pages that no index knows about.

Step 4: find the defect the model did not cover

Twelve caught is a good result, and it is not the interesting part. The interesting part is what was missing from the list.

Parse the front matter of every page with a real YAML parser:

for p in sorted(Path("docs").rglob("*.md")):
    m = re.match(r"^---\n(.*?)\n---\n", p.read_text(), re.S)
    if not m:
        continue
    try:
        yaml.safe_load(m.group(1))
    except yaml.YAMLError as e:
        bad.append(p)

front matter parses: 75 pages
front matter INVALID: 46 pages

Forty-six of 121 pages had front matter that no YAML parser could read. The placeholder generator assembled it with f-strings, so the generated summary read summary: Outline only: Measuring AI answer quality is ... and the unquoted colon started a mapping.

Every check above passed on that corpus. The build passed too, because MkDocs' own metadata parser is more forgiving than YAML. The visible consequence was silent:

meta description: A validated curriculum for documentation engineering, ...

The page's own summary was unreadable, so the description fell back to the site default on all 46 pages.

Step 5: fix the cause, not the pages

def _front_matter(title, summary, audience="new-user"):
    data = {"title": title, "summary": summary, "diataxis": "reference",
            "audience": audience, "generated": True}
    body = yaml.safe_dump(data, sort_keys=False, default_flow_style=False)
    return f"---\n{body}---\n\n"

front matter parses: 118   invalid: 3

The remaining three were hand-written pages with the same mistake, including this one's own summary. Quote them, and add the check so the class cannot return:

ok: every page's front matter parses as YAML

What you learned. A content model is judged by the lies it prevents, and the useful question about any model is which lie is still possible. This one prevented twelve and was blind to the thirteenth, which was the one that mattered most for machine readability.

docs.title: The parts of a content model
docs.text:
Part Example here Enforced by Page types diataxis: tutorial / how-to / reference / explanation Closed vocabulary Required fields title, summary, diataxis, audience Parse-time check Closed vocabularies tier, status, provenance Membership test Relationships prerequisites, acyclic Graph check Structural contract Six required sections, 450 words File check Both-directions coverage No page without a concept, no concept without a page File check Serialisation validity Front matter parses as YAML The check added in step 5

The last row is the one most models omit, and it is the cheapest of all of them.

docs.title: Where each class of defect is caught
docs.text: Caught at Defects Parse Vocabulary violations, dangling references, cycles, duplicates, missing required fields Validation against files Status disagreeing with reality, contract violations, orphan pages Build Nothing structural; the build is not your content model Never, without the step 5 check Front matter that is not valid YAML

docs.title: How to write the model down
docs.text:
Option Good for Cost A data file plus a validator A corpus with structure worth enforcing You write the validator JSON Schema on front matter Standard tooling, editor integration Awkward for cross-page rules A linter with custom rules Teams already running Vale Rules are per-field, not relational A documented convention Nothing; it decays Zero to write, high to maintain

Cross-page rules are the deciding factor. A schema validates one page at a time, so prerequisite resolution, cycle detection and orphan detection need code. That is why this guide's model is a Python module rather than a JSON Schema.

docs.title: Designing one for a real corpus
docs.text:
Question Why it matters What page types exist, really? Count what you have before inventing categories Which fields would change a reader's path? Those belong in navigation Which fields would filter a retrieval query? Those belong in metadata What is required versus optional? An optional field is absent half the time, so nothing can depend on it What vocabulary is closed? Open vocabularies drift; see taxonomy What relationships exist between pages? These need code, not a schema

The fourth row is the one with teeth. A field that is optional is a field your pipeline cannot rely on, so "optional metadata" is usually a decision not to use it for anything.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with lies, not schemas. "I judge a content model by the specific lies it makes impossible. On this guide's own registry I could not mark a concept complete without a page, could not add a prerequisite that does not exist, could not create a cycle, and could not ship a complete page under 450 words or missing a required section. Twelve defect classes, each one a failing build."

The follow-up is about contributor friction, and the honest answer is that every required field is a tax and the right number is small. Four required fields that everything depends on beats twelve that half the corpus omits, because an optional field cannot be built on.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Cross-page rules need code, which means your content model becomes software you maintain, with its own tests and its own bugs. My own validator had a counting bug that double-reported demonstrations and a generator that emitted invalid YAML for 38% of the corpus. A model with a validator is better than a convention, and it is not free.

One sharper point. Front matter is the machine-readable half of a page, and almost nobody checks that it parses. MkDocs' metadata parser is more forgiving than YAML, so a page with an unquoted colon builds cleanly and is invisible to every tool that uses a real parser. I shipped 46 such pages. That check is four lines and it is the cheapest AI-readiness work available, because a corpus that cannot be parsed cannot be filtered, chunked or retrieved.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A content model with a validator, plus the list of defects it catches, each with a test.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run step 4 against a corpus you own. Parse every page's front matter with a real YAML parser and count the failures. This finds something surprisingly often.
  2. Write down the lies your current model prevents. If the list is short or you cannot name one, you have a convention rather than a model.
  3. Pick the most consequential lie that is still possible and make it fail. One check, with a test that proves it fires.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack validates five required front-matter fields, two of them closed vocabularies, rejected by docpack docs --check. This guide's registry adds the relational rules a per-page schema cannot express. The part worth discussing in an interview is step 4: the model that caught twelve things and missed the thirteenth, and how the thirteenth was found.

docs.title: Retiring content
docs.text:
Deleting a page without breaking the links to it, and why corpora only ever grow.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Measure outcomes such as time-to-first-success, support deflection, repeat questions, and AI answer quality, and use the data to decide what to build, fix, or retire"

Prerequisites: Content lifecycle and governance

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Removing a page from the corpus on purpose: deciding it should go, redirecting its URL, and dealing with everything that pointed at it. NVIDIA lists retire alongside build and fix as one of three outcomes of measurement, which is more than most teams do, because most teams have no third option.

The mechanics are easy. The reason corpora only ever grow is not technical.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because an unretired corpus degrades in a way that no amount of writing fixes. Every stale page competes with a current one in search, dilutes retrieval, and costs a reviewer attention. Past a certain size the most valuable documentation work available is deletion, and nobody is authorised to do it.

NVIDIA naming retirement as a measurement outcome is the important part. The decision to retire needs evidence, which means it needs the measurement category to exist first, and it means the answer to "can we delete this" stops being a matter of opinion.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Retire a page properly, then find the configuration that decides whether a mistake is loud or silent. About twenty-five minutes.

Step 1: a redirect

mkdir -p retire-demo/docs && cd retire-demo
pip install --quiet mkdocs mkdocs-redirects

cat > mkdocs.yml <<'EOF'
site_name: R
plugins:
  - redirects:
      redirect_maps:
        old-guide.md: new-guide.md
EOF
printf '# New guide\n\nThe current content.\n' > docs/new-guide.md
printf '# Home\n\nSee the [new guide](new-guide.md).\n' > docs/index.md

python3 -m mkdocs build -q

Step 2: see what the retired URL now serves

python3 -c "
import re
from pathlib import Path
h = Path('site/old-guide/index.html').read_text()
print(re.search(r'<meta[^>]*refresh[^>]*>', h).group(0))
"

<meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0; url=../new-guide/">

A generated page containing a client-side meta refresh. Note what that is not: it is not an HTTP 301. The distinction matters, because a 301 transfers accumulated ranking signals to the new URL and a meta refresh is a weaker, slower signal that search engines treat with more suspicion. On static hosting this is often all you can do; if you control the server or the CDN, prefer a real 301 and keep the meta refresh as the fallback.

Step 3: point the redirect at nothing

sed -i 's/new-guide.md$/gone.md/' mkdocs.yml
python3 -m mkdocs build 2>&1 | grep -i redirect
echo "exit=$?"

WARNING - Redirect target 'gone.md' does not exist!
exit=0

The plugin notices, declines to generate the redirect page, and the build succeeds. So the retired URL becomes a hard 404 rather than a redirect to a 404, which is better than it could have been, and the build still exits zero.

Step 4: make it loud

python3 -m mkdocs build --strict >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "exit=$?"

exit=1

With --strict, a dangling redirect target fails the build. Measured behaviour, all three cases:

Case Build Result Valid redirect exit 0 Meta refresh page generated Dangling target exit 0, with a warning No page; retired URL 404s Dangling target, --strict exit 1 Nothing ships

Step 5: deal with what pointed at the page

The redirect handles external links. Internal references are a separate problem and the one that is usually forgotten:

grep -rn "old-guide" docs/ | grep -v "^docs/old-guide"

Internal links should be rewritten to the new target, not left to bounce through the redirect. A corpus whose internal links all pass through redirects accumulates chains, and a chain eventually contains a broken hop that link checking cannot see, because each individual hop resolves.

What you built. A retirement that redirects, a check that makes a mistaken target fail, and a rule about internal links that keeps chains from forming.

docs.title: The retirement checklist
docs.text:
Step Why Decide, with evidence Traffic, support deflection, repeat questions Pick the successor, or accept there is none A redirect needs a target Rewrite internal links to the successor Prevents redirect chains Add the redirect External links and bookmarks Remove it from navigation and any index Otherwise it is reachable and gone Remove it from retrieval artifacts A deleted page still in a vector store still answers Note the retirement somewhere So the decision is not relitigated annually

The retrieval row is new and easy to miss. A page removed from the site but still present in an index or an llms.txt keeps answering questions from beyond the grave, and the answer looks authoritative.

docs.title: When not to redirect
docs.text:
Situation Do this instead No successor exists A 410 Gone, or a tombstone page explaining the removal The content was wrong, not outdated Say so on the tombstone; a silent redirect looks evasive The page documented a removed feature Point at the migration path, not the nearest page It is one of many pages merged into one Redirect to the anchor, not just the page

Redirecting to a vaguely related page is worse than a 404. A reader who lands somewhere that does not answer their question and shows no sign of knowing what they asked has had their time wasted twice.

docs.title: Why corpora only grow
docs.text:
Obstacle Reality Nobody owns deletion Authoring has owners; removal usually does not It feels like destroying work Git has it forever; this fear is unfounded and real Someone might need it Possibly, and the measurement tells you It might break a link Solved, and it is the stated reason more often than the real one No policy exists So every deletion is a negotiation

The fix is a written policy that makes deletion the default outcome for pages meeting stated criteria, so that removal needs no new argument each time. That is governance, not tooling, which is why this page sits downstream of content lifecycle.

docs.title: Evidence that justifies retirement
docs.text:
Signal Threshold worth discussing Page views Near zero over a full release cycle Search exits People find it and immediately leave Support tickets citing it Readers are being misled by it Its subject no longer exists Automatic candidate Its freshness queue age Perpetually overdue and never claimed

The last row is the useful one in practice. A page that has been in the review queue for four quarters without an owner claiming it is a page nobody is willing to maintain, and that is the evidence.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with why it does not happen. "The mechanics of retirement are a redirect and a link rewrite. The reason corpora only grow is that authoring has owners and deletion does not, so every removal is a fresh negotiation. The fix is a written policy that makes deletion the default for pages meeting stated criteria."

The follow-up is usually about breaking links, and it is worth naming as the stated reason more often than the real one. Redirects solve the external case; internal links get rewritten rather than bounced, because chains accumulate a broken hop that link checking cannot see.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Redirects are not free: each one is a permanent entry in a map that grows forever, and after a few years the redirect map is its own maintenance problem with chains and loops in it. Periodically collapsing chains and dropping redirects for URLs that have had no traffic for years is real work that nobody schedules.

One sharper point. A retired page still in a retrieval index keeps answering questions. The site has deleted it, the vector store has not, and the answer arrives with a citation to a URL that now 404s. Retirement has to reach the retrieval artifacts, and that step is missing from essentially every retirement checklist written before 2023.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A retirement that happened: a redirect, the internal links rewritten in the same commit, and a written policy that authorised it.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Step 3 and step 4 together are the point: the mistake is silent unless you have --strict.
  2. Find your lowest-traffic page and try to retire it. Whatever blocks you is the actual obstacle, and it is probably not technical.
  3. Check whether anything in your retrieval pipeline would notice a deleted page. Usually nothing does.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Neither of this guide's repositories has retired anything, which the demonstrated page records, and a project with no readers has no retirement evidence to act on. What travels is the measured behaviour of the mechanism and the retrieval-index point, which is the part of the checklist most teams are currently missing.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
A project with no readers has nothing to retire, so the mechanism here is measured and the decision is not. Retirement is mostly a political act and the evidence is that somebody agreed to lose something.

What you need. A corpus old enough to contain pages nobody should read, and the authority to remove them. The second is the scarce one.

What a learner would do. Find the five oldest pages in a corpus you own, check whether each still describes a thing that exists, and then try to delete one. Record what happened: who objected, on what grounds, and what the compromise was.

What you would see.

Outcome What it means Deleted with a redirect The healthy case, and the rarest Marked deprecated instead The usual compromise; now you maintain it forever Kept because someone links to it The link is the argument; check whether anyone follows it Kept because removing it feels risky The real reason, and it is not a documentation reason Nobody could say who owns it The finding worth reporting

The last row is what the exercise usually produces, and it is more useful than the deletion: a page nobody owns is a page nobody will update either.

Why it does not commit. A deletion leaves no artifact except an absence and a redirect. The judgment, that this page cost more than it was worth, is a conversation, and the strongest available evidence is a redirect map with a reason beside each entry.

  • Link checking, and why redirect chains defeat it
  • Crawlability, the search-engine side of removing a URL

docs.title: Crawlability and the agent-ready front door
docs.text:
Being fetchable and parseable at all, which is the precondition for every other machine-facing thing you build.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

site navigation, and a crawlable, agent-ready front door

Source: intel posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: SEO for documentation

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Making sure a machine can fetch your pages, follow your links, and find the content in the response. The dull precondition underneath SEO, GEO, llms.txt and every retrieval system: none of them work on a page nobody can fetch.

Intel's phrase "front door" is the useful part. It means there is an entry point a machine arriving with no context can start from.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Intel names it in the role summary, alongside site navigation. It is listed as something the role owns rather than as a qualification, which tells you it is operational work: redirects, sitemaps, render modes, robots rules.

What makes this supporting rather than core is that it is mostly checks rather than judgement. It earns a page because it is the failure that makes every other investment worthless, and it is invisible from inside. Your documentation site looks perfect in your browser, which is running JavaScript, following your redirects, and already signed in.

On a Tuesday it is a discovery that invalidates a quarter. Somebody asks why the assistant never cites the API reference. The reference is client-rendered, so a fetch returns an empty <div id="root">. Every chunk, every embedding and every llms.txt entry for those pages has been built from nothing. No error was raised anywhere because an empty page is a valid page.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a crawlability audit over a site structure with the five common defects, and see which ones are silent. Thirty-five minutes.

Committed as drills/crawlability.py, which runs the whole path in one go. It writes the crawl.py below to a temporary directory and runs it as a subprocess, so the code demonstrated is the code printed here; a test asserts the two have not drifted apart.

Step 1: a site with realistic problems

mkdir -p crawl-drill/site/{docs,api} && cd crawl-drill

cat > site/docs/install.html <<'EOF'
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head>
<title>Install | Widget</title>
<meta name="description" content="Install the CLI with pip and confirm it runs.">
<link rel="canonical" href="https://widget.example/docs/install/">
</head><body>
<h1>Install the CLI</h1>
<p>Run <code>pip install widget</code>. Requires Python 3.10 or newer.</p>
<p>Next: <a href="/docs/configure/">configure the client</a>, or see the
<a href="/api/reference/">API reference</a>.</p>
</body></html>
EOF

cat > site/docs/configure.html <<'EOF'
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head>
<title>Configure | Widget</title>
<meta name="description" content="Install the CLI with pip and confirm it runs.">
</head><body>
<h1>Configure the client</h1>
<p>Set <code>retries</code> and <code>batch_size</code> on the client.</p>
<p>See <a href="/docs/tuning/">tuning</a>.</p>
</body></html>
EOF

cat > site/api/reference.html <<'EOF'
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head>
<title>API reference | Widget</title>
<meta name="description" content="Generated reference for every endpoint.">
</head><body>
<div id="root"></div>
<script src="/assets/app.js"></script>
</body></html>
EOF

cat > site/robots.txt <<'EOF'
User-agent: *
Disallow: /api/
Allow: /docs/
Sitemap: https://widget.example/sitemap.xml
EOF

cat > site/sitemap.xml <<'EOF'
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">
  <url><loc>https://widget.example/docs/install/</loc><lastmod>2026-10-20</lastmod></url>
  <url><loc>https://widget.example/docs/legacy/</loc><lastmod>2024-01-01</lastmod></url>
</urlset>
EOF
find site -type f | sort

Five defects are in there, and only one of them, a dead link, is something a reader would ever notice. They produce ten findings between them, for reasons the audit output below makes clear.

Step 2: the audit

cat > crawl.py <<'PY'
"""Audit a built site for the things that stop a machine reading it.

Each check corresponds to a failure that leaves the site looking correct in a
browser. That is the property they share and the reason they need a check at
all: a human cannot find these by looking.
"""
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path("site")
BASE = "https://widget.example"

TITLE = re.compile(r"<title>(.*?)</title>", re.S | re.I)
DESCRIPTION = re.compile(r'<meta\s+name="description"\s+content="(.*?)"', re.S | re.I)
CANONICAL = re.compile(r'<link\s+rel="canonical"\s+href="(.*?)"', re.I)
LINK = re.compile(r'href="(/[^"#?]*)"')
#: Text outside script, style and tags. What a fetch without JavaScript sees.
SCRIPT = re.compile(r"<(script|style)\b.*?</\1>", re.S | re.I)
TAG = re.compile(r"<[^>]+>")

MIN_TEXT_WORDS = 20


def url_for(path):
    """Map a built file to the URL it is served at."""
    return f"{BASE}/{path.relative_to(ROOT).with_suffix('').as_posix()}/"


def visible_text(html):
    return TAG.sub(" ", SCRIPT.sub(" ", html))


def robots_rules(path):
    disallow = []
    for line in path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
        if line.lower().startswith("disallow:"):
            value = line.split(":", 1)[1].strip()
            if value:
                disallow.append(value)
    return disallow


def sitemap_urls(path):
    return set(re.findall(r"<loc>(.*?)</loc>", path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")))


def main():
    pages = sorted(ROOT.rglob("*.html"))
    findings = []

    disallow = robots_rules(ROOT / "robots.txt")
    listed = sitemap_urls(ROOT / "sitemap.xml")
    served = {url_for(p) for p in pages}

    descriptions = {}
    for path in pages:
        html = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        url = url_for(path)
        label = path.relative_to(ROOT).as_posix()

        # 1. Content present without JavaScript. The silent one.
        words = len(visible_text(html).split())
        if words < MIN_TEXT_WORDS:
            findings.append((label, "no-server-content",
                             f"{words} words of text without running JavaScript"))

        # 2. Blocked by robots while being a real documentation page.
        for rule in disallow:
            if url.replace(BASE, "").startswith(rule):
                findings.append((label, "robots-blocked",
                                 f"served at {url} but robots.txt disallows {rule}"))

        # 3. Canonical present.
        if not CANONICAL.search(html):
            findings.append((label, "no-canonical", "no canonical link"))

        # 4. Description present and distinct.
        match = DESCRIPTION.search(html)
        if not match:
            findings.append((label, "no-description", "no meta description"))
        else:
            descriptions.setdefault(match.group(1), []).append(label)

        # 5. Internal links resolve to something served.
        for href in set(LINK.findall(html)):
            target = href.rstrip("/")
            candidates = {
                ROOT / f"{target.lstrip('/')}.html",
                ROOT / target.lstrip("/") / "index.html",
            }
            if not any(c.exists() for c in candidates) and not href.startswith("/assets"):
                findings.append((label, "dead-link", f"links to {href}, not served"))

    for text, where in descriptions.items():
        if len(where) > 1:
            findings.append((", ".join(where), "duplicate-description",
                             f"share one description: {text[:46]!r}"))

    # 6. Sitemap agrees with what is served.
    for url in sorted(listed - served):
        findings.append(("sitemap.xml", "sitemap-ghost", f"lists {url}, not served"))
    for url in sorted(served - listed):
        findings.append(("sitemap.xml", "sitemap-missing", f"{url} is served but unlisted"))

    for label, kind, why in findings:
        print(f"CRAWL  {label}: {kind}: {why}", file=sys.stderr)
    print(f"{'FAIL' if findings else 'ok'}: {len(pages)} pages, {len(findings)} problem(s)")
    return 1 if findings else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
PY
python3 crawl.py; echo "exit=$?"

CRAWL  api/reference.html: no-server-content: 4 words of text without running JavaScript
CRAWL  api/reference.html: robots-blocked: served at https://widget.example/api/reference/ but robots.txt disallows /api/
CRAWL  api/reference.html: no-canonical: no canonical link
CRAWL  docs/configure.html: no-server-content: 16 words of text without running JavaScript
CRAWL  docs/configure.html: no-canonical: no canonical link
CRAWL  docs/configure.html: dead-link: links to /docs/tuning/, not served
CRAWL  docs/configure.html, docs/install.html: duplicate-description: share one description: 'Install the CLI with pip and confirm it runs.'
CRAWL  sitemap.xml: sitemap-ghost: lists https://widget.example/docs/legacy/, not served
CRAWL  sitemap.xml: sitemap-missing: https://widget.example/api/reference/ is served but unlisted
CRAWL  sitemap.xml: sitemap-missing: https://widget.example/docs/configure/ is served but unlisted
FAIL: 3 pages, 10 problem(s)
exit=1

Ten findings from five defects, which is not a contradiction. One defect can trip several checks: the client-rendered API reference is simultaneously unreadable without JavaScript, blocked by robots.txt and missing a canonical, so it accounts for three lines on its own. A findings list counts symptoms and a repair list counts causes, and conflating the two is how a backlog ends up three times longer than the work.

One line is a false positive, and it is worth more than the nine true ones. docs/configure.html is static HTML with real prose; it is reported as having too little text without JavaScript because it is sixteen words long and the threshold is twenty. The check cannot distinguish a client-rendered shell from a genuinely short page, because from the outside they look identical: both are a fetch that returns almost no words.

That is not a bug to fix by raising the threshold. It is the limit of what a word count can know, and the honest responses are to tune the threshold to the corpus, exempt known-short pages by path, or treat the finding as a question rather than a verdict. Publishing the audit without publishing its false positive would have made the check look more decisive than it is, which is how a check gets switched off the first time it annoys somebody.

Step 3: see which failures a human could have noticed

python3 - <<'PY'
TABLE = [
    ("no-server-content", "No", "The page renders perfectly in a browser"),
    ("robots-blocked",    "No", "Nothing on the page indicates it"),
    ("duplicate-description", "No", "Visible only by comparing two pages' source"),
    ("sitemap-ghost",     "No", "A sitemap entry for a page nobody visits"),
    ("sitemap-missing",   "No", "An unlisted page still works if linked"),
    ("dead-link",         "Yes", "A reader clicking it gets a 404"),
    ("no-canonical",      "No", "Invisible until duplicate URLs split your ranking"),
]
width = max(len(k) for k, _, _ in TABLE)
print(f"{'failure':<{width + 2}} {'noticed by a human?':<21} why")
print("-" * 86)
for kind, noticed, why in TABLE:
    print(f"{kind:<{width + 2}} {noticed:<21} {why}")
print()
print("Six of seven are silent. That ratio is the argument for the check.")
PY

Step 4: fix them and watch the audit go quiet

# 1. Server-render the reference, or prerender it at build time.
cat > site/api/reference.html <<'EOF'
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head>
<title>API reference | Widget</title>
<meta name="description" content="Every endpoint, parameter and response code for the widget API.">
<link rel="canonical" href="https://widget.example/api/reference/">
</head><body>
<h1>API reference</h1>
<h2>POST /infer</h2>
<p>Accepts <code>input</code> and optional <code>batch_size</code>. Returns 200
with a result, 400 on invalid input, 429 when rate limited.</p>
<div id="root"></div>
<script src="/assets/app.js"></script>
</body></html>
EOF

# 2. Stop blocking the reference. Block the asset directory instead.
cat > site/robots.txt <<'EOF'
User-agent: *
Disallow: /assets/
Sitemap: https://widget.example/sitemap.xml
EOF

# 3 and 4. A real description, and a canonical, on configure.
cat > site/docs/configure.html <<'EOF'
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head>
<title>Configure | Widget</title>
<meta name="description" content="Set retries and batch_size on the widget client, with their defaults.">
<link rel="canonical" href="https://widget.example/docs/configure/">
</head><body>
<h1>Configure the client</h1>
<p>Set <code>retries</code> and <code>batch_size</code> on the client. The
defaults are 5 and 32 as of widget 2.6.</p>
</body></html>
EOF

# 5. The sitemap is generated from what is served, never hand-written.
python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
ROOT, BASE = Path("site"), "https://widget.example"
urls = sorted(
    f"{BASE}/{p.relative_to(ROOT).with_suffix('').as_posix()}/"
    for p in ROOT.rglob("*.html")
)
body = "\n".join(
    f"  <url><loc>{u}</loc><lastmod>2026-10-26</lastmod></url>" for u in urls
)
(ROOT / "sitemap.xml").write_text(
    '<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>\n'
    '<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">\n'
    f"{body}\n</urlset>\n"
)
print(f"generated sitemap with {len(urls)} url(s)")
PY

python3 crawl.py; echo "exit=$?"

generated sitemap with 3 url(s)
ok: 3 pages, 0 problem(s)
exit=0

Note how the dead link was repaired: the rewritten configure.html drops the link to /docs/tuning/ rather than creating the page. That is a legitimate fix and a different decision from the one the finding implies, which is worth being explicit about. An audit tells you a link is dead. It cannot tell you whether the answer is to write the missing page or to stop promising it, and that choice belongs to whoever owns the content.

Fixing configure.html also silenced its no-server-content finding, because the repair happened to push the page over twenty words. The false positive went away for the wrong reason, which is exactly how a flaky check earns misplaced confidence.

What you built. An audit for the failures that leave a site looking correct, and a generated sitemap that cannot disagree with what is served.

docs.title: The failures, and which are silent
docs.text:
Failure Noticed by a human? Consequence Client-rendered content No Every chunk, embedding and llms.txt entry built from nothing Blocked by robots.txt No The page is excluded from everything that respects it Duplicate meta descriptions No Every snippet and link preview destroyed Sitemap lists pages not served No Crawl budget spent on 404s Served pages missing from the sitemap No Slower discovery of new pages Missing canonical No Duplicate URLs split your own ranking Dead internal link Yes A 404

Six of seven are silent, which is why this is a check rather than a review item.

docs.title: The render-mode problem, which is the big one
docs.text:
Render mode A fetch without JavaScript sees Static HTML everything Server-rendered everything Prerendered at build time everything Client-rendered an empty div Client-rendered with a prerender service depends on the user agent, which is fragile

A generated API reference is the page most likely to be client-rendered and the page most valuable to a retrieval system, which is an unfortunate coincidence worth checking for specifically.

The test is one command:

curl -s https://example.com/docs/page/ | python3 -c "
import re, sys
html = sys.stdin.read()
text = re.sub(r'<[^>]+>', ' ', re.sub(r'<(script|style)\b.*?</\1>', ' ', html, flags=re.S|re.I))
print(len(text.split()), 'words without JavaScript')"

docs.title: robots.txt, which is where people block themselves
docs.text:
Pattern Effect Disallow: /api/ Blocks your API reference. Very common accident Disallow: / on a staging host Correct, and catastrophic if the config ships to production Blocking /assets/ Usually fine; may block images from image search Allow: with no Disallow: Does nothing. A no-op people treat as permission No robots.txt at all Everything is allowed. Often the right answer

robots.txt is a crawling directive, not an access control and not a noindex. A disallowed URL can still appear in results if linked elsewhere, and disallowing a page prevents a crawler from reading the noindex you put on it, which is the classic way a page you wanted removed stays listed forever.

docs.title: Sitemaps, generated
docs.text: Rule Why Generate from what is served A hand-maintained sitemap is wrong within a month Include lastmod, accurately A lastmod of today on every page is ignored as noise Exclude redirects and non-canonical URLs They waste crawl budget Reference it from robots.txt The only discovery mechanism that needs no submission Split above 50,000 URLs The per-file limit

docs.title: The front door, in Intel's sense
docs.text:
A machine arriving with no context needs somewhere to start:

Artifact Serves / with real links A crawler following links /sitemap.xml A crawler that wants the full list /llms.txt A model choosing where to look /llms-full.txt A model wanting one fetch Markdown sources beside the HTML A model that would rather not parse your nav robots.txt permitting the docs Everything above

Serving the Markdown next to the rendered site is one line in a publish job and removes the render-mode problem entirely for consumers that prefer it.

docs.title: Things worth checking that this audit does not
docs.text:
Check Why it needs a live site Response status codes A build cannot tell you about a 500 Redirect chains More than one hop loses signal Content-Type correctness Markdown served as application/octet-stream is unreadable Time to first byte Crawl rate is budget-limited Pages behind auth Return 200 with a login page, so they look fine

The last one is the nastiest in enterprise documentation: an authenticated page returns a login form with a 200 status, so a crawler indexes the login page and a retrieval system embeds it.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with the silence. "The failures here are almost all invisible from a browser. The one that cost us a quarter was a client-rendered API reference: a fetch returned an empty div, so every chunk and every embedding for those pages was built from nothing and nothing raised an error, because an empty page is a valid page. So I audit the built site for text present without JavaScript, pages blocked by their own robots.txt, duplicate descriptions, and a sitemap that disagrees with what is served. The sitemap is generated, never hand-written."

The follow-up is usually "is this not an SEO job", and the honest answer is that the work overlaps and the stakes changed. Being unfetchable used to cost you search traffic, which somebody else measured. It now also silently poisons your retrieval corpus, your llms.txt and your assistant, and those are yours. The check belongs with whoever owns the machine-facing artifacts, which in both these postings is this role.

The tradeoff to volunteer. An audit over a built site is a second CI job on output that already passed its own tests, and it will produce findings that are deliberate: a page genuinely excluded, a description shared between two near-identical generated pages. So it needs an allowlist, and an allowlist decays into a list of things nobody reviews. The honest version is to keep the checks few and loud rather than many and warning-level, which means accepting that this audit will not be comprehensive.

One sharper point. The strongest observation is that every machine-facing investment in this guide is multiplied by zero if the page is not fetchable, and crawlability is the only one of them with no visible symptom. Chunking badly degrades retrieval; being unfetchable eliminates it, quietly, for a subset of pages that nobody enumerates. So this unglamorous audit should be the first thing built, before llms.txt or embeddings or an assistant, and it almost never is, because the other things are more interesting to work on. That ordering argument is worth making to a lead who is being asked to fund a RAG pipeline.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. The audit in CI over the built site, plus a generated sitemap and the one-line no-JavaScript text check.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the one-line check against a real documentation site. curl it and count words without JavaScript. On a client-rendered site the number is near zero, and that is a two-minute finding.
  2. Read a real robots.txt and check whether it blocks anything you want retrieved. Disallow: /api/ is common and usually an accident.
  3. Generate the sitemap from the build output and diff it against the committed one. The difference is a list of ghosts and omissions nobody knew about.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Mentioning sitemaps and robots.txt is table stakes. A built-site audit whose first check is text-without-JavaScript, a count of how many of its findings are invisible to a human, and the argument that this should precede the interesting work demonstrates that you have been burned by the silent version.

docs.title: Writing custom linters
docs.text:
Building the check no off-the-shelf tool can express, and learning what its first run tells you.

supporting · difficulty 3 · 5h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Content quality automation you've built, such as Vale or custom linters, doc test harnesses, or freshness monitoring"

Prerequisites: Prose linting with Vale

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A check you write yourself because the rule you need is not a pattern. Vale and its relatives match text. Some of the most valuable documentation rules require parsing: knowing which lines are code, which are heredoc data, whether a front-matter field is a member of a closed vocabulary, whether the version mentioned in a sentence is the one in the lockfile.

The phrase in the posting is "content quality automation you've built." Built, not configured.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because the interesting defects in a documentation corpus are structural, and structure is exactly what a text matcher cannot see.

Consider three rules. "Do not write simply" is a pattern, and Vale does it in four lines. "Every page has a kind field whose value is one of four strings" is a schema check against front matter. "No code fence contains a nested fence that closes it early" requires modeling shell heredocs. The second and third are not expressible as patterns at any length, and the third is the one that silently broke seven pages of this guide.

The deeper reason is that a custom linter encodes a decision. Once a rule is code, the convention it enforces becomes explicit, testable and arguable in a pull request, which is NVIDIA's "encode standards into templates, validators and guided workflows rather than static documents."

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Write a plausible rule, measure it against a real corpus, and let the measurement change the rule. About forty minutes. The point of this path is the measurement, not the code.

Step 1: the rule that sounds obviously right

Every code fence should declare its language, so syntax highlighting works. A reasonable house rule, and not expressible in Vale, which excludes code blocks from its analysis by design.

# lint_fences.py
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

MARKER = re.compile(r"^(?P<indent> {0,3})(?P<ticks>`{3,})(?P<info>.*)$")


def spans(lines):
    """Closed fence blocks as (open, close), ignoring heredoc data."""
    out, open_at, open_ticks = [], None, ""
    for n, line in enumerate(lines, 1):
        m = MARKER.match(line)
        if not m:
            continue
        ticks, info = m.group("ticks"), m.group("info").strip()
        if open_at is None:
            open_at, open_ticks = n, ticks
        elif len(ticks) >= len(open_ticks) and not info:
            out.append((open_at, n))
            open_at, open_ticks = None, ""
    return out


def check(root):
    findings = []
    for page in sorted(root.rglob("*.md")):
        lines = page.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
        for open_at, _close in spans(lines):
            if not MARKER.match(lines[open_at - 1]).group("info").strip():
                findings.append(f"{page}:{open_at}: fence has no language tag")
    return findings


if __name__ == "__main__":
    found = check(Path(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "docs"))
    for f in found:
        print(f"LINT  {f}")
    print(f"{'FAIL' if found else 'ok'}: {len(found)} finding(s)")
    raise SystemExit(1 if found else 0)

Step 2: run it against a corpus that is not a toy

python3 lint_fences.py docs/ | tail -4

LINT  docs/concepts/github-actions.md:219: fence has no language tag
LINT  docs/concepts/prose-linting.md:231: fence has no language tag
FAIL: 21 finding(s)

Twenty-one findings out of 207 fences. At this point the instinct is to open twenty-one pages and add language tags. Do not. Read the findings first.

Step 3: read what the findings actually are

sed -n '98,100p' docs/concepts/documentation-ci.md
sed -n '110,112p' docs/concepts/github-actions.md

```
chain exit=1
```

```
DRIFT  CI runs but `make check` does not: python3 gate_links.py
FAIL: 3 CI command(s), 2 local, 1 drifted
```

Those are not code. They are program output, and there is no language tag that is correct for the stdout of a shell script. The rule is firing on exactly the case where no tag is the right answer.

Sample the rest and the pattern holds. The rule has close to a 100 per cent false-positive rate on this corpus, and it would have cost an afternoon of edits that made every page slightly worse.

Step 4: try to fix it with a heuristic, and measure again

An untagged block that directly follows a tagged block is probably that command's output:

# in check(), replace the inner loop
blocks = spans(lines)
for i, (open_at, close) in enumerate(blocks):
    if MARKER.match(lines[open_at - 1]).group("info").strip():
        continue
    prev = blocks[i - 1] if i else None
    if prev and MARKER.match(lines[prev[0] - 1]).group("info").strip() \
            and open_at - prev[1] <= 4:
        continue   # output of the command above
    findings.append(f"{page}:{open_at}: fence has no language tag")

untagged fences that directly follow a tagged block (output): 17
untagged fences that do not:                                  4
    docs/concepts/ai-assistants.md:420
    docs/concepts/geo.md:317
    docs/concepts/llm-content-lifecycle.md:370
    docs/concepts/prose-linting.md:231

From 21 to 4. Better. Now check those four, and two of them are also output, just separated from their command by a paragraph of explanation.

The heuristic improved the rule and did not fix it, and it cannot, because "is this block program output" is a question about intent. No amount of proximity logic answers it.

Step 5: change the convention, not the heuristic

echo 'Tag output blocks explicitly: ```text for stdout, ```console for a session.' \
  >> CONTRIBUTING.md

With that convention adopted, the original rule from step 1 becomes exact: an untagged fence is now unambiguously a mistake, because output has a tag too. The linter went from unusable to correct without the code getting smarter.

What you built. More usefully than a linter: the knowledge that this rule requires a convention your corpus does not yet have. The first run of a custom linter is a measurement of whether your standard is real.

docs.title: When to write one instead of configuring a tool
docs.text: Write your own Use Vale or similar The rule needs a parse, not a pattern The rule is a word or phrase It validates front matter against a schema It is about prose style It compares the doc to something else: a lockfile, an API spec, the built HTML It is self-contained in the text It must model code structure, heredocs, fences It must ignore code, which Vale already does The finding needs a computed fix suggestion A static message is enough

docs.title: What the first run tells you
docs.text:
First run finds Means Do this Nothing The rule is already satisfied, or it is broken Break a page on purpose and confirm it fires A handful of real defects The rule is right and the corpus drifted Fix the pages, add the gate Hundreds of findings The convention was never adopted Decide the convention first, or do not ship the rule Findings that are all legitimate The rule encodes a convention that does not exist Change the convention or drop the rule

The last row is the one this page's golden path lands in, and it is the most common outcome for a rule invented in the abstract.

docs.title: Design rules that make a linter survive contact
docs.text: Rule Why Report file:line: message A finding that cannot be jumped to is a chore Exit non-zero on findings, zero otherwise So CI can use it without parsing output Blank fenced lines rather than deleting them Line numbers stay true Make the unknown case loud A checker that silently passes on "I could not tell" is theater Ship a test that proves it fires Otherwise a refactor can neuter it and nothing fails Say how to fix it, with the exact replacement "Widen the opener to ````" beats "bad fence"

docs.title: The one at scale, in this repository
docs.text:
src/fieldguide/fences.py is the real version of this page. It has two halves: a static check that models heredoc bodies as data rather than markup, and a dynamic check that compares fenced source lines against the <pre> content of the built HTML.

The second one is the interesting design choice. The static check can be fooled, because it reasons about the source; the dynamic one compares against what the reader actually receives, so the only way to pass it is for the sample to genuinely be code on the page. It found 127 defects across seven pages on the day it was written, every one of which had passed a strict build, a hundred tests and a registry validator.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the class of rule, not the tool. "Vale covers anything that is a pattern. I write my own when the rule needs a parse: validating front matter against a closed vocabulary, or checking that a code fence is still a code fence on the published page. That last one needed modeling shell heredocs, which is not a regex."

The follow-up is about maintenance, and the answer is tests. A custom linter without a test that proves it fires is a liability, because a future refactor can silently neuter it and the build stays green. Say that you write the failing fixture first.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Every custom linter is code you now own, with a false-positive rate you are responsible for, and a suppression mechanism people will use. A rule with widespread suppressions is a rule that is wrong, so you have to watch suppression counts as a signal about the rule rather than about the writers.

One sharper point. The first run of a new rule is a measurement of your convention, not of your corpus. A rule that produces hundreds of legitimate findings has discovered that the standard it encodes was never actually adopted, and shipping it anyway converts that into an afternoon of edits plus a permanent tax on contributors. Measure, read the findings, and be willing to conclude that the convention needs changing instead of the pages.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. One linter you wrote, with a test that proves it fires, and a number: how many real defects it found on first run.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path against a corpus you already have. The twenty-one findings are the lesson, not the code.
  2. Write the failing fixture before the rule. If you cannot construct a document that should fail, you do not yet know what the rule is.
  3. Write down the false-positive rate of your rule on your own corpus. That number is the most credible thing you can say about a linter, and almost nobody has it.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. A linter that has never caught anything proves you can write a loop. A linter with a commit history showing a red build followed by a real fix proves the rule is about something. docpack has four hand-written Vale rules, and the one worth discussing is the one that caught the author's own prose.
