docs.title: Developer advocacy
docs.text:
Making documentation part of the definition of done needs a gate at capability granularity, and three plausible gates at the wrong granularity all fail in ways that get them switched off.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

Intel: "Partner with engineering, product, and developer advocates so each new capability ships with tested documentation"

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The part of this job that happens in other people's meetings. Advocacy in the sense Intel's bullet means is not conference talks and not evangelism: it is arranging that documentation is produced as part of shipping, by the people who built the thing, rather than reconstructed afterwards by someone who did not.

The operative phrase is ships with. Everything else in the sentence describes who you have to work with to make that true.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because the alternative does not scale and everyone knows it.

A documentation team that writes everything is a queue. Features ship, the queue lengthens, the docs describe the product of six months ago, and the team is measured on throughput against an inflow it does not control. The structural fix is to move authorship to the point where the knowledge already exists, and that is an organisational change rather than a writing one, which is why it appears in a job posting as "partner with".

The reason it needs a mechanism rather than goodwill is that goodwill does not survive a deadline. A definition of done that includes documentation, enforced in the same place as the tests, is the only version of this that is still true in the fourth quarter.

And the reason the mechanism is hard is the subject of the golden path: a docs gate at the wrong granularity produces failures that engineers correctly identify as noise, and a gate that cries wolf gets switched off within a month. The gate's design is the whole job.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build the "ships with documentation" gate against a real package, four times, getting it wrong three ways. About thirty minutes.

Step 1: the obvious gate, per public symbol

for node in ast.parse(f.read_text()).body:
    if isinstance(node, (ast.FunctionDef, ast.ClassDef)) and not node.name.startswith("_"):
        rows.append((f.name, node.name, ast.get_docstring(node) is not None))

public symbols in the package: 44 across 7 modules
with a docstring: 37/44 (84%)
undocumented:
   cli.py::build_parser
   cli.py::cmd_check
   cli.py::cmd_build
   cli.py::cmd_new
   cli.py::cmd_status
   cli.py::cmd_render
   cli.py::main

Eighty-four per cent, and every failure in one module. Look at what it is accusing:

fieldguide build   named in the documentation 32 times
fieldguide check   named in the documentation  5 times
fieldguide new     named in the documentation  5 times

The functions without docstrings are the command handlers, and the commands they implement are the best-documented part of the entire system. They are documented as commands, in prose, in the place a user looks, which is the correct way to document a command and invisible to a gate that counts docstrings.

This is how docs gates die. An engineer reads that failure, sees it is wrong, and is right.

Step 2: the second gate, per symbol named in the prose

public symbols never named in the documentation: 28/44
   demos.py::DemonstrationError
   demos.py::Demonstration
   fences.py::Span
   dialect.py::front_matter_findings
   ...

Worse. Most of those 28 are internal plumbing whose public-ness is an artifact of Python not having private modules. Span is a dataclass used in one place. Documenting it would be writing documentation nobody will read in order to satisfy a counter, which is the characteristic output of a badly aimed gate.

Both gates are measuring symbols. The posting says capability.

Step 3: the third gate, per shipped capability

Ask the program what it ships, rather than inferring it from the source:

subcommands = sorted(next(a.choices for a in build_parser()._actions
                          if getattr(a, "choices", None) and isinstance(a.choices, dict)))

  build    named in the documentation 32 time(s)
  check    named in the documentation 5 time(s)
  new      named in the documentation 5 time(s)
  render   named in the documentation 1 time(s)
  status   named in the documentation 0 time(s)   <-- ships undocumented

A real finding, apparently: a shipped command documented nowhere. Except the gate searched docs/ and the README has listed fieldguide status in its quick start since the first commit.

Three gates, three wrong answers, and the third was wrong about scope rather than granularity: documentation is not only the thing in the docs directory.

Step 4: the gate that works, and what it actually finds

Capability granularity, every surface a reader looks at:

command      docs/   README.md
  build         32       2
  check          5       1
  new            5       1
  render         1       0
  status         0       2

Every capability is documented somewhere, and two defects are now visible that none of the first three gates could see:

render is absent from the README's quick start, which is the entry point readers actually use; it is mentioned once, deep in a page. And while checking the README against reality:

README.md:59  python -m pytest -q   # 72 tests
actual:       119 tests

The claim had been stale for the length of this project. Both fixed in the same commit as the gate, which is the point: the gate is only worth adding if the first run is allowed to find something.

undocumented = [s for s in subcommands if not re.search(rf"fieldguide {s}\b", prose)]
assert not undocumented, f"shipped but undocumented: {', '.join(undocumented)}"

Step 5: why the granularity argument is the advocacy work

The gate took twenty minutes to write and three attempts to aim. The reason that matters is not the code. It is that the first two versions would have been rejected by engineers, correctly, and the rejection would have been remembered as "the docs team wanted docstrings on everything" for years.

Partnering with engineering on a documentation gate is mostly the work of making sure the gate is right before anyone else sees it, because you get roughly one attempt at a definition of done before the proposal acquires a reputation. Run it on your own repository, let it fail, fix what it finds, and bring the number rather than the principle.

What you built. A documentation gate at capability granularity, wired into the test suite, plus three instructive wrong versions and two real defects the right version found on its first run.

docs.title: Granularity, and what each level gets wrong
docs.text:
Gate Flags Verdict Every public symbol has a docstring Command handlers, documented as commands Wrong unit Every public symbol is named in prose Internal plumbing Wrong notion of public Every capability is named in docs/ A capability documented in the README Wrong scope Every capability is named where readers look render missing from the quick start Usable Every capability has a tested example The honest target Expensive, and correct

The last row is what Intel's sentence actually asks for, and it needs code-sample validation underneath it to mean anything.

docs.title: A definition of done that survives a deadline
docs.text:
Item Enforced by Fails usefully The capability is named in user-facing docs The gate above Yes An example exists A sample manifest Yes The example runs and asserts its output CI Yes The changelog mentions it A release check Yes A page explains when to use it Nothing; needs a person No

The bottom row is the honest limit of mechanisation, and pretending otherwise is how a definition of done becomes a form.

docs.title: Who writes what
docs.text:
Content Best author Why What it does and the first example The engineer who built it They have the knowledge now Reference detail Generated from source Nobody should type it twice When to use it, and when not The docs or advocacy role Needs the comparison across features The quickstart it affects The docs role It is a shared artifact The migration note Both One knows the change, one knows the readers

The common failure is the docs role writing row one, which puts a transcription step between the knowledge and the reader and guarantees the result is late and thinner.

docs.title: What makes a partnership proposal land
docs.text: Do Instead of Run the gate on your own repo first Proposing it in a meeting Bring the defects it found Bringing the principle Make the failure message name the fix A generic "docs missing" Gate capabilities, not symbols Anything that flags working docs Let it fail on your code publicly Exempting yourself Count the false positives before shipping it Discovering them in review

docs.title: What this concept is not
docs.text: Not Belongs to Conference talks Developer relations, a different job Writing all the documentation The queue this is meant to replace Reviewing every pull request for docs Does not scale; gate it Persuasion Mechanism outlives persuasion

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with what "ships with" implies. "A documentation team that writes everything is a queue, and the queue is always behind an inflow it does not control. So the work is moving authorship to where the knowledge already is, and making documentation part of the definition of done in the same place the tests live, because goodwill does not survive the fourth quarter."

The follow-up is how you would enforce it, and this is the part worth telling in detail. I built that gate against my own package and got it wrong three times. Docstring coverage flagged the five CLI handlers, which are the best-documented part of the system because they are documented as commands. Per-symbol prose coverage flagged internal plumbing that nobody should document. Capability coverage over the docs directory flagged a command that had been in the README's quick start from the first commit. The fourth version, capabilities against every surface a reader looks at, passed and immediately found two real things: one command missing from the quick start, and a README claiming 72 tests when there were 119.

The point that makes this advocacy rather than scripting. The first two gates would have been rejected by engineers, correctly, and the rejection would have been remembered as "the docs team wanted docstrings on everything" for years. You get about one attempt at a definition of done before the proposal acquires a reputation, so the real work is aiming the gate before anyone else sees it: run it on your own repository, let it fail, fix what it finds, and bring the number instead of the principle.

The tradeoff to volunteer. A gate can only check that documentation exists, never that it is any good. "When to use this and when not" is the most valuable thing in a reference and no mechanism will ever require it. So the gate buys coverage and the review still has to be human, and a team that mistakes the first for the second ends up with complete documentation nobody can use.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A test in a repository of yours that enumerates shipped capabilities from the program itself and fails when one is undocumented, plus the commit where its first run fixed something.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Write the gate for your own project at capability granularity, run it, and count the false positives before telling anyone it exists. Predict the count first; this page's subject is that the prediction is usually zero and the answer usually is not.
  2. Check your README's claims against reality. Mine said 72 tests and there were 119, and nothing had ever checked, which is the cheapest class of defect there is.
  3. Find the last capability your team shipped and ask who wrote its first example. If the answer is the docs role, there is a transcription step in the pipeline, and that is the thing to propose removing.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. The gate exists, lives in this guide's test suite, enumerates subcommands from the parser rather than from a list, and its first run produced two fixes in the README. What is not demonstrated is the partnership: this is a one-person repository, so no engineering team has been persuaded of anything, and the claims about how a proposal lands are reasoning from the gate's three wrong versions rather than from organisational experience. The demonstrated page records that split.

docs.title: Turning developer feedback into changes
docs.text:
Ten automated gates were green when the first real reader could not tell what the software did; the only signal that catches that arrives once, from a person.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

Intel: "Ability to translate developer feedback into documentation, samples, and product improvements"

Prerequisites: Documentation analytics

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The path from something a developer said to something that changed in the repository. The interesting part is not collection, which every team does, but the translation: a complaint is evidence about an experience, and turning it into an edit means deciding what it is evidence of, which is usually not what the complaint names.

Intel's bullet puts "documentation, samples, and product improvements" in one sentence, which is the right scope. The same report frequently calls for all three, and routing it only to the documentation queue is how feedback gets answered without being used.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because it is the only measurement in this category that no instrument produces.

Everything else here, deflection, repeat questions, answer quality and time to first success, is a number computed from artifacts. Each of them can be green while the thing is unusable, because each measures a property somebody thought to measure. A reader saying "I ran all of this and I do not know what it does" measures the property nobody thought of, and there is no automated substitute.

The practical problem is that the signal is rare and perishable. The first reader is only first once, and the confusion they report is the confusion everyone after them will have and nobody else will mention, because by then the project looks like something they are supposed to already understand.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Two real feedback events, traced from report to shipped change, with what each cost and what no gate could have caught. About twenty minutes of reading and nothing to install.

Step 1: the report

The companion repository had been built, tested and packaged. Its first reader worked through the README's quick start on his own machine, then said:

I ran all the commands and I have no idea what the result is or what I should be looking at. The readme didn't clarify this for me.

Nine commands, all exit zero, no errors.

Step 2: what the gates said at that moment

Content model                       pass
Links and anchors                   pass
Unit tests and doctests             pass
Code samples in the docs            pass
Retrieval quality above the floor   pass
Generated pages pass validation     pass
Prose linting                       pass
Site builds with no warnings        pass
Per-page SEO is rendered            pass
Cold-start the quickstart           pass

Ten gates, ten passes, and the artifact was incomprehensible to its reader.

The cold-start gate is the painful one, because it exists precisely to catch "a quickstart that does not work for a stranger". It runs the tutorial's commands. The reader had followed the README's quick start, a different sequence. The repository had two front doors and one of them was instrumented.

Step 3: diagnose what the complaint is evidence of

The report names the README. The README was a symptom. Counting what the quick start actually offered:

  1. docpack docs --check                   report
  2. python -m pytest -q                    report
  3. python scripts/check_links.py          report
  4. vale docs/                             report
  5. mkdocs build --strict                  artifact: site/
  6. docpack eval evals/golden.yaml         report
  7. bash scripts/coldstart.sh              report
  8. docpack new how-to --title ...         artifact: a page
  9. docpack docs --out dist                artifact: 3 files
 10. python mcp_server/server.py            artifact: a running server

commands producing something: 4 of 10, the first at position 5
the first four, consecutively, produce nothing but reports

The command that makes the library's actual output was ninth. The first impression of a tool whose purpose is packaging documentation was four consecutive validators printing "ok".

One thing was missing altogether: the library's whole point is retrieval, and there was no way to perform a retrieval by hand. eval scores a fixed set of twenty questions, which answers "is retrieval working" rather than "what does this do".

Step 4: the three changes, which belong to three different queues

Change Kind Why this report produced it docpack search Product The capability existed and was unreachable README reordered, making before checking Documentation The ordering was the reported symptom Three tests on the new command Tests So it cannot silently rot

Intel's bullet asks for exactly that split, and the product change is the one that gets missed by treating a README complaint as a README task.

report at 11:56, change delivered at 12:01
elapsed: about five minutes

The latency is not a boast about speed. The point is the ratio: the diagnosis took longer than every edit combined, which is normal and is why feedback handling is a judgment skill rather than a throughput problem.

Step 5: the second loop, which started from a number

A different shape, worth contrasting. The retrieval evaluation reported two cases whose top chunk lacked the terms an answer needs. That is a measurement rather than a complaint, and it named its own cause: the reader's everyday word was absent from the page documenting the thing.

             before   after
hit@1          60%     65%
MRR          0.742   0.775
routing        70%     75%
grounded@1     80%     90%
grounded@3     90%    100%

Two sentences, four of five scores moved, no code at all.

Step 6: what the two loops say together

loop 1   a person, once        found: nothing was measurable
loop 2   an instrument, daily  found: two words

The instrument found a precise, small, actionable defect and would never have found the first one, because "the artifact does not explain itself" is not a property anybody encodes as a check. The person found the structural failure and would never have found the second, because no reader computes vocabulary overlap across twenty questions.

Neither substitutes for the other, and the asymmetry is in supply. Instruments run on every commit. The first reader happens once.

What you built. Two feedback loops traced to shipped changes, a gate audit showing ten passes against one unusable artifact, and one report split into a product change, a documentation change and a test.

docs.title: What each signal can and cannot see
docs.text:
Signal Catches Blind to Supply CI gates Breakage, drift, regressions Whether any of it makes sense Every commit Cold-start test A quickstart that fails for a stranger The quickstart you did not instrument Every commit Retrieval evaluation Unfindable answers, vocabulary gaps Whether the corpus is worth finding Every commit Search logs The words readers use Why they wanted them Continuous, with an audience Support tickets Problems bad enough to report Everything people gave up on Continuous, with an audience A person reading it cold Structural incomprehension Anything needing aggregation Once per person

The bottom row is the only one that catches the top row's blind spot, and the only one you cannot schedule.

docs.title: Translating a report into the right queue
docs.text:
The reader says Often means Goes to "The docs are confusing" The product has no obvious entry point Product "I don't know what this does" The artifact is validated but never shown Docs, and usually product "This didn't work" An undeclared prerequisite Docs, then a cold-start test "Where is X?" X exists and is unfindable Ranking or vocabulary "Can it do X?" It can, and nothing says so Docs "I expected Y" A real design disagreement Product, with a decision record

Taking any of these at face value produces a documentation edit that does not help, which is the most common way feedback is formally honoured and practically wasted.

docs.title: Why the first reader is worth protecting
docs.text:
Property Consequence They have no context They see what the artifact actually communicates They will not be first twice The signal is single-use They assume the confusion is their fault Most of it is never reported They stop at the first wall You learn where the wall is, not what is behind it They are usually polite about it The report understates the problem

The fourth row is the reason to ask what they expected rather than only what happened. The fifth is the reason to treat a mild report as a severe finding.

docs.title: Closing the loop visibly
docs.text:
Practice Effect Name the report in the commit or the comment The reporter sees that it landed Record it in the source, not the ticket It survives the ticket system Add the check that would have caught it The class closes, not the instance Say which queue it went to Product changes get credited as product Say what you did not change, and why Preserves trust for the next report

The third row is the one that compounds. One report produced a new command and a reordered README; the lasting change is a check asserting that the first quick-start command after install produces something rather than reporting something.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the gate audit, because it is the strongest thing here. "The first real reader of my repository ran nine commands, all exited zero, and reported that he had no idea what the software did. Ten CI gates were green at that moment, including a cold-start test that exists specifically to catch a quickstart failing for a stranger. It tested the tutorial's command sequence and he had followed the README's, so the repository had two front doors and I had instrumented one."

Then the diagnosis, which is the actual skill. The report named the README and the README was a symptom. The first four commands produced nothing but reports, the command that makes the library's output was ninth of ten, and the library's whole purpose, retrieval, could not be performed by hand at all. One report became three changes in three queues: a new command, a reordered README, and tests. Treating it as a README task would have missed the product change, which was the real finding.

Contrast it with the measured loop. The same day, the retrieval evaluation found two cases where the reader's word was missing from the page documenting the thing, and two sentences moved four of five scores. That is a precise, small defect an instrument finds daily and a person never would, against a structural failure a person finds and an instrument never will. The difference is supply: instruments run on every commit, the first reader happens once.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Acting on a single report risks building for one person, and one report cannot tell you whether the confusion generalises. What made this one safe to act on is that the fix was additive and the diagnosis was checkable without him: the command ordering and the absent capability are facts about the repository rather than opinions about his experience. When a report cannot be grounded in something checkable, the right move is to collect a second one before building.

One sharper point. Mild reports understate. "The readme didn't clarify this for me" is a polite sentence describing a total failure of an artifact to communicate its purpose, and the politeness is load-bearing: most readers who hit that wall conclude they are missing something obvious and say nothing. The right prior on a gently worded confusion report is that it is severe and under-reported.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A repository where a reader's report is traceable to a commit, and a check that closes the class rather than the instance.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Find the last piece of feedback your team received and ask which queue it went to and which queue it should have gone to. If the answer is the same queue every time, reports are being filed rather than diagnosed.
  2. Count the commands in your own quick start that produce something against the ones that only report, and note the position of the first producing one. Write both predictions down first.
  3. Ask one person who has never seen your project to run its quick start while you watch and say nothing. It is the highest-value hour available in this job and it works exactly once per person, so spend it on the project you care about most.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Both loops are in the repositories: docpack search exists with three tests, the README is reordered into commands that make something and commands that check something with a line saying why, the vocabulary edits are in two how-to pages, and the score movement is recorded in docs/explanation/evaluating-retrieval.md. What cannot be claimed is a process. This is two events, one of them from a single reader, with no recurring intake, no triage policy and no second data point, and the demonstrated page records developer feedback loops as having instances rather than a demonstrated practice.

docs.title: Diátaxis
docs.text:
Four kinds of documentation that serve different needs and must not be mixed on one page.

core · difficulty 1 · 2h

Not a quotation (adjacent)

The dominant framework for documentation structure. Neither posting names it; both describe the problem it solves.

Prerequisites: Information architecture

Leads to: Designing tutorials, Golden paths, Learning paths and curriculum

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A claim that documentation serves four separate needs, and that a page trying to serve more than one serves none of them well. The four are tutorials (learning by doing), how-to guides (achieving a goal), reference (finding a fact), and explanation (understanding why).

It is attributed to Daniele Procida and has been adopted as the organising framework by Canonical, Django, Gatsby, Cloudflare and a long list of others. It is the closest thing this field has to a standard.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Neither posting says "Diátaxis", which is why this concept is tagged adjacent. Both describe the problem it solves, repeatedly. Intel asks for golden paths, curriculum, tutorials, sample walkthroughs and reference documentation as separate deliverables, which is a Diátaxis decomposition written out without the name. NVIDIA asks for content modeling and for content structured for machine retrieval, and the type of a page is the single most useful field in that model.

The reason it earns core status despite being unquoted is that it answers the first question anyone asks when they open an unfamiliar corpus: what is a page? Without an answer, every page drifts toward being the same page: a bit of motivation, some steps, a table of options, and a paragraph about design philosophy. That page is comfortable to write and bad to read, because the reader arrived with exactly one of those four needs and has to filter out three quarters of what is in front of them.

On a Tuesday this shows up as a specific recurring decision. An engineer gives you a page that says "Getting started with the inference server" and it contains an installation sequence, a conceptual overview of the serving architecture, a full table of configuration flags, and three worked examples. Diátaxis is how you explain, without it sounding like an aesthetic preference, that this is four pages, and which four.

The retrieval argument is the newer and stronger one. A page with four jobs produces chunks with four jobs, and a retriever that returns the architecture-overview paragraph to someone who asked "how do I set the batch size" has failed in a way no ranking improvement will fix. Type separation is retrieval hygiene, not just navigation hygiene.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Take one page that does four jobs and split it, then feel the difference. Thirty minutes, no tooling.

Step 1: write the page everybody writes

mkdir -p diataxis-demo && cd diataxis-demo
cat > before.md <<'EOF'
# Getting started with the widget queue

The widget queue exists because synchronous processing could not keep up with
burst traffic during launches. We chose an at-least-once delivery model rather
than exactly-once because exactly-once requires distributed transactions, and
the cost of a duplicate widget is lower than the cost of a dropped one.

## Installation

Run `pip install widget-queue`. You need Python 3.10 or newer and a running
Redis instance.

## Configuration options

| Flag | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--workers` | 4 | Number of worker processes |
| `--batch-size` | 100 | Items pulled per poll |
| `--visibility-timeout` | 30s | How long a claimed item stays hidden |

## Your first queue

Create a queue, push an item, and consume it. By the end you will have seen a
widget travel end to end.

## Draining a queue before a deploy

Call `widget-queue drain --wait`. This stops new claims and waits for in-flight
items. Always do this before a deploy that changes the item schema.
EOF
wc -l before.md

That page is not badly written. It is five pages.

Step 2: sort the content by the reader's state

The test is not "what is this paragraph about". It is two questions about the person reading it:

cat > sorting-test.md <<'EOF'
                 |  Studying            |  Working
-----------------|----------------------|------------------------
Practical steps  |  TUTORIAL            |  HOW-TO GUIDE
Theory, facts    |  EXPLANATION         |  REFERENCE
EOF
cat sorting-test.md

Apply it to each section above:

Section in before.md Studying or working? Steps or facts? Type Why at-least-once Studying Theory Explanation Installation Working Steps How-to Configuration options Working Facts Reference Your first queue Studying Steps Tutorial Draining before a deploy Working Steps How-to

Step 3: split it

mkdir -p tutorials how-to reference explanation

cat > explanation/delivery-guarantees.md <<'EOF'
# Why the queue is at-least-once

Exactly-once delivery requires distributed transactions across the queue and
the consumer's datastore. At-least-once requires only that consumers be
idempotent.

## What this costs you

Every consumer must tolerate seeing the same item twice. That is real work
pushed onto every team that uses the queue, and it is the honest price of the
decision.
EOF

cat > how-to/install.md <<'EOF'
# Install the widget queue

```bash
pip install widget-queue
```

Requires Python 3.10 or newer and a reachable Redis instance.
EOF

cat > reference/configuration.md <<'EOF'
# Configuration reference

| Flag | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--workers` | 4 | Number of worker processes |
| `--batch-size` | 100 | Items pulled per poll |
| `--visibility-timeout` | 30s | How long a claimed item stays hidden |
EOF

cat > tutorials/first-queue.md <<'EOF'
# Your first queue

By the end of this you will have pushed a widget through a queue and seen a
consumer handle it. About ten minutes.
EOF

cat > how-to/drain-before-deploy.md <<'EOF'
# Drain a queue before a deploy

```bash
widget-queue drain --wait
```

Do this before any deploy that changes the item schema.

## If it hangs

A consumer holding an item past its visibility timeout blocks the drain. Find
it with `widget-queue inspect --claimed`.
EOF

find . -name "*.md" -not -name before.md -not -name sorting-test.md | sort

Step 4: see what the split bought you

echo "--- A reader mid-deploy, who needs one command ---"
cat how-to/drain-before-deploy.md
echo
echo "--- The same question against the original ---"
grep -n -A3 "Draining" before.md

The how-to guide is the whole answer and nothing else. In before.md the same answer is four paragraphs down a page that opens with distributed-transaction theory. The content is identical; only the boundaries changed.

One more thing the split bought, which is easy to miss: writing explanation/delivery-guarantees.md as its own page made it obvious that it was missing a "what this costs you" section. A page whose only job is to explain a decision invites the question "and what is the downside", and a page where that argument is buried under an installation command does not.

What you built. One mixed page split into four, and the evidence for why: each piece became checkable in a way the combined page was not, and one of them revealed a section that had been missing all along.

docs.title: The four types
docs.text: Type Reader's state Answers Must not contain Tutorial Learning, no context "Can I get something working?" Options, alternatives, edge cases How-to guide Working, competent "How do I achieve X?" Teaching, motivation, background Reference Working, needs a fact "What are the parameters?" Narrative, opinion, tasks Explanation Studying, wants to understand "Why is it like this?" Instructions

docs.title: The distinguishing tests
docs.text:
Question Tutorial How-to Reference Explanation Who chooses the goal? Author Reader Neither Neither Can the reader fail? No, never Yes n/a n/a Are alternatives offered? Never Sometimes Exhaustively Discussed Is it read start to finish? Yes No No Yes Structure mirrors A lesson A task The code An argument

The "who chooses the goal" row is the sharpest tool here. A tutorial's goal belongs to the author; the reader does not know enough to have a goal yet, and offering them a choice is the commonest way tutorials fail. A how-to guide's goal belongs to the reader, who arrived with it already.

docs.title: Common failures and their fix
docs.text: Symptom Diagnosis Fix Tutorial offers three ways to install Reference leaking into tutorial One way; link the rest How-to guide opens with two paragraphs of context Explanation leaking into how-to Move it; link it Reference page has a worked example with narration Tutorial leaking into reference Keep the example, drop the narration Explanation page lists every flag Reference leaking into explanation Link the reference A page called "Overview" Usually all four Split, then decide if the overview is needed at all A guides/ folder Tutorials and how-tos conflated The most common corpus-level error

docs.title: What Diátaxis does not cover
docs.text:
Worth knowing, because being asked is likely:

  • Release notes and changelogs. Chronological, not topical. Outside the model.
  • Troubleshooting pages. Usually a how-to guide indexed by symptom rather than goal, which the model handles awkwardly.
  • API reference generated from source. Reference, but the type is determined by the generator rather than a choice.
  • Landing and orientation pages. Navigation, not content.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Name the four, then immediately give the discriminating test rather than definitions, because the definitions are googleable and the test is what you use. "The useful question is what state the reader is in: studying or working, and do they want steps or facts. That gives you the four quadrants, and it tells you which of two plausible-looking pages a piece of content belongs on."

The follow-up you will get is "isn't this just rigid?" or some version of an objection to the purity of it. Do not defend the framework as doctrine. The honest answer is that the value is almost entirely in the separation of tutorial from how-to and reference from explanation, because those are the two pairs people conflate by default. Whether a particular page is a how-to guide or a tutorial matters much less than whether anyone asked the question.

The tradeoffs to volunteer, and there are three real ones:

It multiplies page count. One page becomes four, navigation gets wider, and a reader who wanted the old all-in-one page now follows links. For a small product that is a net loss, and Diátaxis applied to a corpus of fifteen pages is overhead with no payoff.

It fragments the thing a reader is holding. Some readers genuinely do want installation, concept, and example in one scroll, and the framework's answer, which is "link them clearly", is weaker than its proponents admit. A good landing page partly compensates. Partly.

The boundaries are genuinely ambiguous in practice. Troubleshooting is the clearest case: it is tasks indexed by symptom instead of by goal, which the model has no slot for. Anyone who tells you the four types partition all documentation cleanly has not migrated a large corpus.

One sharper point. The strongest modern argument for Diátaxis is not navigational at all, and it is the one most candidates miss: type separation is what makes retrieval filterable. If every page declares one of four types, a retrieval system can be told to return only how-to content for a "how do I" question, which is a hard constraint rather than a hope that the embedding noticed the genre. Diátaxis was proposed years before anyone was packaging docs for language models, and it turned out to be the most useful metadata field in the corpus. That is worth saying out loud.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A corpus organised by type, where the type is a declared field and not only a folder name, and something that uses the field.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Keep both files. before.md next to the split tree is a two-minute demonstration in an interview, and showing the before is what makes the after land.
  2. Audit a real corpus by type. Take a project's documentation, classify thirty pages into the four types, and count how many are more than one. The number is usually between a third and a half, and reporting it with the examples is a genuinely useful piece of analysis. Do it on your own project's docs first; doing it on an employer's corpus is a strong interview artifact but check whether you can share it.
  3. Make the type do work. Add it as a required field, validate it in documentation CI, and then use it for something: a faceted navigation, a filter in your retrieval layer, or grouping in llms.txt. A type field nothing reads is a convention; a type field that filters a search is architecture.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Everyone in this field can name the four types. The signal is the migration: having taken a real page apart, and being able to say which boundary was genuinely ambiguous and how you decided. Interviewers in this category have all fought with the troubleshooting question. Having an opinion about it marks you as someone who has done the work.

docs.title: Building a doc test harness
docs.text:
The infrastructure around sample execution: shell state, failure attribution, and a check that cannot be fooled.

core · difficulty 3 · 6h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Content quality automation you've built, such as Vale or custom linters, doc test harnesses, or freshness monitoring"

Prerequisites: Code-sample validation

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The infrastructure that turns sample execution from a script into something a team can rely on. Code-sample validation is the idea: run the examples. A harness is what you need once the corpus has more than one language in it, samples that depend on each other, and contributors who will be reading its failure output at 5pm on a Friday.

Three problems make it real work: shell samples carry state a subprocess does not inherit, concatenating them destroys failure attribution, and any harness built on parsing source can be fooled by the source.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA lists doc test harnesses as a thing you have built. The word is doing work: a harness, not a test. The difference is everything in this page.

A script that executes Python blocks is a weekend. A real harness is not: it handles bash and Python, keeps per-page state, attributes failures to a source line, carries a reviewable skip convention with a budget, and verifies its conclusions against what the reader actually receives. That is a piece of engineering, and it is the most direct evidence you can offer that documentation correctness is something you enforce rather than hope for.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build up the shell half, discovering the two traps that make it harder than Python. About fifty minutes.

Step 1: a quickstart whose steps depend on each other

mkdir -p harness-demo/docs && cd harness-demo
cat > docs/quickstart.md <<'MDEOF'
# Quickstart

```bash
mkdir -p project && cd project
printf 'name = "demo"\n' > config.toml
```

```bash
cat config.toml
```

```
name = "demo"
```
MDEOF

Step 2: isolate each block, the safe-sounding choice

import subprocess
import tempfile

for start, code in blocks(page, "bash"):
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
        r = subprocess.run(["bash", "-e", "-c", code], cwd=d,
                           capture_output=True, text=True)
        print(f"  block@{start}: exit={r.returncode} err={r.stderr.strip()!r}")

  block@3: exit=0 err=''
  block@8: exit=1 err='cat: config.toml: No such file or directory'

Same failure as the Python case: a quickstart is a sequence. Isolation tests a document nobody wrote.

Step 3: share the directory, and watch it still fail

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    for start, code in blocks(page, "bash"):
        r = subprocess.run(["bash", "-e", "-c", code], cwd=d, ...)

  block@3: exit=0 err=''
  block@8: exit=1 err='cat: config.toml: No such file or directory'

Identical. This is the trap that makes shell harder than Python: block one ran cd project, and cd changes the working directory of that subprocess. Block two gets a new subprocess, starting in the shared directory's root, and the file it wants is one level down.

Sharing a directory is not sharing a shell. Environment variables set by a block are lost the same way.

Step 4: one shell per page

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    script = "\n".join(code for _start, code in blocks(page, "bash"))
    r = subprocess.run(["bash", "-e", "-c", script], cwd=d,
                       capture_output=True, text=True)
    print(f"  exit={r.returncode} out={r.stdout.strip()!r}")

  exit=0 out='name = "demo"'

Correct. cd persists, the file is found, and the output matches what the page promises.

Step 5: discover what concatenation cost you

Add a block that fails:

cat >> docs/quickstart.md <<'MDEOF'

```bash
cat missing-file.toml
```
MDEOF

  exit=1  stderr='cat: missing-file.toml: No such file or directory'
  -> no line number, no block identity

The harness knows the page is broken and cannot say where. On a 200-line quickstart with nine shell blocks, that report sends the reader to read the whole page. Concatenation bought shared state and sold failure attribution.

Step 6: buy it back with sentinels

parts = []
for start, code in blocks(page, "bash"):
    parts.append(f'echo "__BLOCK__ {page}:{start}" >&2')
    parts.append(code)

r = subprocess.run(["bash", "-e", "-c", "\n".join(parts)], cwd=d,
                   capture_output=True, text=True)

last = None
for line in r.stderr.splitlines():
    if line.startswith("__BLOCK__"):
        last = line.split(None, 1)[1]
real = [l for l in r.stderr.splitlines() if not l.startswith("__BLOCK__")]
print(f"  exit={r.returncode}  failing block={last}")
print(f"  error={real[-1] if real else ''}")

  exit=1  failing block=docs/quickstart.md:16
  error=cat: missing-file.toml: No such file or directory

A source line and the real error. Because bash -e stops at the first failure, the last sentinel seen is the block that broke, which is all the bookkeeping this needs.

What you built. Shared shell state and per-block attribution at the same time, which were in tension and did not have to be.

docs.title: The decisions a harness has to make, per language
docs.text: Decision Python Bash State sharing One globals() dict per page One shell process per page What cd does Not applicable Persists only inside one process Isolation boundary Per page Per page, in a temp directory Failure attribution Free, via compile(code, filename) Needs sentinels Stopping on first error Natural, exceptions propagate Needs -e Capturing output redirect_stdout capture_output

docs.title: What belongs in a harness that does not belong in a script
docs.text: Feature Why it earns its place Per-page state, per-corpus isolation Pages are sequences; the corpus is not Source-line attribution A failure you cannot locate is a chore, not a fix A skip marker carrying a reason Reviewable in a diff A skip budget The escape hatch is the threat; see below Expected-output fences Catches changed values, which is most rot Language dispatch A corpus is never one language A scratch directory per page Samples that write files must not touch the repo A verification half (below) Because the parsing half can be fooled

docs.title: The escape hatches are the attack surface
docs.text:
Every harness needs a way to exempt a sample, and every exemption is a way to make a red build green without fixing anything. In docpack, the convention is # docpack: skip, the reason is required, and a test asserts the skip ratio stays under 25 per cent.

The honest limitation, measured in code-sample validation, is that a ratio budget is meaningless on a small corpus: with three blocks the ratio can only be 0, 33, 67 or 100 per cent, so the cap fires on a clean corpus. Budgets start meaning something in the low hundreds of blocks. Before that, require the reason and read it in review.

Do not widen a budget to get a green build. The budget is load-bearing, and relaxing it is the one change that converts the whole harness into decoration.

docs.title: Two halves, because the first half can be fooled
docs.text:
The most important structural idea in a harness is that a check which reasons about source can be defeated by the source, so it needs a partner that compares against what the reader receives.

This guide learned that the expensive way. Its static checks, a registry validator, a hundred tests and a strict site build all passed while seven pages rendered code samples as prose, because a heredoc inside a bash sample contained a fence of its own and closed the outer block early. Every tool was looking at the Markdown and reasoning about it correctly; none was looking at the published HTML.

Half Reads Can be fooled by Speed Static Markdown source Anything that makes the source parse differently than you modelled Instant Ground truth Built HTML Very little; it is what the reader gets Needs a build

src/fieldguide/fences.py implements both. The second half compares every fenced source line against the <pre> content of the built page, and found 127 defects on the day it was written. Keep the fast half for feedback and the slow half for truth.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the shell state problem, because it is concrete and most people have not thought it through. "Sharing a temp directory between bash blocks is not sharing a shell. cd and exported variables live in the process, so a quickstart has to run as one shell per page. That buys shared state and costs failure attribution, which you get back with a sentinel echo before each block."

The follow-up is about the skip mechanism, and the strong answer names it as the attack surface: a required reason, a ratio budget, an explicit rule that you do not widen the budget to go green, and the honest caveat that the budget does nothing on a small corpus.

The tradeoff to volunteer. A harness that runs real shell commands is running untrusted-ish code from pull requests. It needs a scratch directory, no credentials in its environment, and ideally a container, and that means contributors cannot easily reproduce the sandbox locally. You are trading reproducibility for safety, and the mitigation is to make the sandbox a script rather than a CI-only incantation.

One sharper point. Any harness built on parsing source can be fooled by the source, so it needs a half that checks the artifact the reader receives. This guide had every static check green while seven pages shipped code as prose, and the fix was a comparison against the built HTML, not a smarter parser. If you can only say one thing about harness design, say that.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A harness in a repository of yours that handles more than one language, attributes failures to a source line, and has a skip convention with a budget.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path to step 6. Steps 3 and 5 are the two surprises.
  2. Add sentinel attribution to any shell-sample runner you already have. It is four lines and it changes the failure report from useless to actionable.
  3. Pick one static check you trust and ask what artifact it never looks at. That gap is your second half. If the answer is that it looks at everything, you have not found the artifact yet: every static check skips something, and what it skips is where the next defect lives.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack's harness extracts every Python block, executes it, requires a reason on every skip, and asserts the skip ratio stays under 25 per cent. The number is the credible part: a harness with no budget and a dozen silent skips is a harness that stopped testing a while ago and did not mention it.

docs.title: Documentation analytics
docs.text:
Corpus-side analytics need no audience and answer a surprising amount; reader-side analytics need one, and cannot see the terminal where most developer documentation is actually read.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

Asked for by name

Intel: "Instrument documentation analytics and convert findings into improvements to docs, samples, and tooling"

Prerequisites: Documentation CI

Leads to: Measuring AI answer quality, Search and query log analysis, Support deflection, Time to first success, Turning developer feedback into changes

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Instrumenting a documentation corpus so that claims about it can be checked. The word covers two activities with almost nothing in common, and conflating them is why most documentation-analytics work goes nowhere.

Corpus-side analytics measure the artifact: how pages connect, what is reachable, what is findable, what is stale, which claims have no evidence. They need no audience and work on day zero.

Reader-side analytics measure behaviour: page views, search queries, scroll depth, exit rates, the path through a funnel. They need an audience, a pipeline, and usually a privacy review.

Intel's bullet says "instrument ... and convert findings into improvements", and that second half is the part that matters: the deliverable is a change, not a dashboard.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because without it every statement about documentation is an assertion, and documentation people make a great many statements.

"The quickstart is too long." "Nobody can find the auth page." "That tutorial is our most valuable asset." Each is testable and almost never tested, so priorities get set by whoever was most recently annoyed. An instrumented corpus replaces that with a number somebody can disagree with, which is a lower bar than being right and a far better starting position.

The reason the split matters is practical. Most teams asking for documentation analytics are imagining the reader-side dashboard, cannot have it yet (no traffic, no pipeline, no consent), and conclude they cannot measure anything. They can measure a great deal. It is all on the other side.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build the analytics available with no audience whatsoever, against a real corpus. About thirty minutes, and the last step changes how you read any documentation dashboard.

Every figure below is one run, when the tree held 121 pages. It holds more now, and the point of the step is the impossible ratio rather than the count, so the output is kept as it was printed rather than restated each time a page is added. fieldguide audit is where to read the current numbers.

Step 1: the link graph, which is most of corpus-side analytics

LINK = re.compile(r"\]\((?!https?:|mailto:)([^)#]+?)(?:#[^)]*)?\)")
for page in sorted(docs.rglob("*.md")):
    for match in LINK.finditer(page.read_text()):
        dest = (page.parent / match.group(1)).resolve()
        ...

pages in the tree: 121
internal links: 1127

pages nothing links to: 1
   index.md

reachable from index.md by following links: 134/121

One hundred and thirty-four reachable out of 121. An impossible ratio, and the signal to fix the measurement rather than publish it.

Step 2: two different populations

The traversal was collecting link targets while the denominator counted pages, so every link pointing at something that is not a page in the tree inflated the numerator. Constrain the traversal to real pages, and report the remainder separately instead of silently absorbing it:

pages: 121   links to real pages: 1108
link targets that are not pages in this tree: 14 distinct
   install.md                                 x9
   guide.md                                   x4
   {BASE}/docs/{path.name}                    x2
   tuning.md                                  x2

Those fourteen are filenames inside golden-path code samples, belonging to the fictional corpora the exercises build. Correct content, and not links, which is why the link checker had never flagged them.

A measurement that counts one population and reports it as another is the most common analytics defect there is, and the hardest to notice, because the number looks like a number.

Step 3: the corrected picture

reachable from index.md: 121/121
clicks from the front door: {0: 1, 1: 8, 2: 111, 3: 1}
unreachable by any link path: 0

Everything is reachable, and the shape is the finding: nine pages in ten sit exactly two clicks from the front door, one at three. That is a flat corpus, which is right for a reference guide and would be a warning in a tutorial series, where depth should track sequence.

One page has nothing linking to it, and it is index.md. Correct: a front door is entered, not linked.

Step 4: what else needs no audience

search index entries:                              1358
pages absent from the search index:                   0
concept pages with a distinct meta description:  106/106
pages whose longest sentence exceeds 45 words:    38/82
golden paths with no stated result:                0/82
demonstrations resolving to real concepts:           50
concepts with no demonstration anywhere:             56

Every line is a finding, each points at specific pages, and none required a pipeline, a cookie banner, or a quarter of accumulated traffic.

Step 5: the limit, which arrived unannounced

On the day this page was written, the project's first real reader followed the README of the companion repository, ran every command in its quick start, watched all of them exit zero, and reported that he could not tell what the library did.

Now ask what reader-side analytics would have shown.

page views in that session:   0
search queries:               0
time on page:                 none
exit page:                    none
funnel step reached:          not applicable

Zero, because he never opened the site. He read a README on a code host and worked in a terminal, which is where developer documentation is mostly consumed and where no analytics system has any visibility whatsoever. The most important documentation failure in this project was invisible to the entire reader-side category, and it surfaced because a person said something.

That is not an argument against reader-side analytics. It is the boundary of the instrument. A dashboard reporting healthy numbers for a corpus nobody can get started with is reporting on the subset of readers who got far enough to be counted.

What you built. A corpus-side analytics report over the whole corpus that needed no audience, a measurement bug caught by an impossible ratio, and a worked example of the failure class the other half of analytics cannot see.

docs.title: The two halves
docs.text:
Corpus-side Reader-side Needs an audience No Yes Available on day zero Yes No Sees terminal and README use Yes No Sees what readers wanted No Partly Points at a specific page Usually Rarely Can be confidently wrong Yes Yes Privacy review No Usually

The fourth row is reader-side analytics' real advantage and the reason to build it eventually: a corpus-side check can tell you a page is unreachable, never that nobody wanted it.

docs.title: Corpus-side measurements, roughly by value
docs.text: Measurement Finds Reachability from the front door Pages that exist and cannot be arrived at Click depth distribution A corpus shaped wrongly for its purpose Inbound links per page Orphans, and accidentally load-bearing pages Presence in the search index Content that is live and unfindable Distinct meta descriptions Pages indistinguishable in results Key terms absent from their own page Findability failures Review age against change rate Freshness candidates Claims with no demonstration Where a corpus overstates itself Per-page maximum sentence length Load outliers

docs.title: Reader-side measurements, and what each is worth
docs.text:
Measurement Worth Caveat Internal search queries High The clearest statement of intent available Zero-result searches Very high A list of content you do not have Support ticket volume High Confounded by everything Entry pages Medium Where people arrive, not whether it helped Page views Low Popularity, not usefulness Time on page Very low Confused and careful reading look identical Scroll depth Very low Mostly measures page length "Was this helpful?" Near zero Measures mood, and never produces bad news

The top two are worth more than everything below them combined, which is why search log analysis is a concept of its own.

docs.title: Where developer documentation is actually read
docs.text:
Surface Reader-side visibility The documentation site Full A README on a code host Almost none A terminal, via --help None An IDE hover or completion None A package registry page Vendor-dependent An assistant answering from the corpus None, unless you built the assistant A snippet copied into somebody's codebase None

Only the first row is instrumented, and it is not obviously the largest. Any claim resting on reader-side analytics alone is a claim about one surface.

docs.title: Converting findings into changes
docs.text:
Intel's bullet ends "improvements to docs, samples, and tooling", and that ordering is a useful discipline: a finding that produces only a documentation edit is often a finding about the tooling.

Finding Weak response Better A page is unreachable Link to it Ask why the navigation omitted it A term is searched and absent Write the page Also fix the vocabulary that hid it The quickstart is abandoned Rewrite the prose Cut the steps before first success The same support question recurs Add an FAQ entry Change the thing people get wrong Nobody runs the samples Promote them Check whether they still work

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the split, because it is the useful idea. "Documentation analytics is two jobs. Corpus-side measures the artifact and needs no audience: reachability, click depth, findability, staleness, which claims have no evidence. Reader-side measures behaviour and needs traffic, a pipeline and usually a privacy review. Teams who want the second and cannot have it conclude they can measure nothing, and they are wrong by a wide margin."

The follow-up is what corpus-side analytics actually caught. On a corpus with no readers: every page reachable, nine in ten exactly two clicks from the front door, nothing missing from the search index, 27 of 106 pages carrying a sentence over 45 words, and 56 concepts whose claims have no demonstration anywhere. Each of those points at a page, which is the property reader-side numbers mostly lack.

The thing to volunteer, and the best point here. The most important failure this project has had was invisible to reader-side analytics. The first real reader followed a README, ran the commands in a terminal, and could not tell what the library did. Page views for that session: zero, because he never opened the site. Developer documentation is read in READMEs, in terminals, in IDE hovers and increasingly through assistants, and the site is the only one of those that is instrumented. A dashboard of healthy numbers describes the readers who got far enough to be counted.

The tradeoff. Corpus-side analytics can be confidently wrong, and mine was: the first reachability run said 134 pages reachable out of 121, because the traversal counted link targets while the denominator counted pages. An impossible ratio is a lucky way to discover that, since most measurement bugs produce a plausible number instead. Every figure here gets a fixture with a known answer before it is quoted anywhere.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A script in your own repository reporting reachability, click depth and orphans, run in CI so the numbers show up in a diff.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Compute reachability and click depth for a corpus you own, predicting the number of unreachable pages first. If the ratio comes out impossible, you have found your measurement bug early and cheaply.
  2. List the surfaces your documentation is read on and mark which are instrumented. The honest answer is usually one of five or six.
  3. Take your most confident claim about your documentation and work out which half of analytics could test it. If it is neither, it is an assertion.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. The corpus-side measurements above run against this guide's own pages and its built search index, and the 134-of-121 bug is recorded rather than tidied away. That page count is deliberately not quoted here: it changes whenever a learning path is added, and a figure that moves for reasons unrelated to the claim is a figure that will be wrong before anyone notices. What does not exist is any reader-side analytics at all: no site has been published, so there are no views, no queries and no funnel, and every reader-side figure in the tables is drawn from general practice rather than from this project. The demonstrated page records the category on that basis.

docs.title: Docs-as-code
docs.text:
Treating documentation as source: same repository, same review, same CI, same release.

core · difficulty 1 · 2h

Not a quotation (derived)

Both postings describe documentation built, reviewed and shipped like software.

Leads to: Code-sample validation, Documentation CI, Generated API reference, Git authoring workflows for writers, Link checking, Markdown and its dialects

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Documentation kept in the same version control as the code, written in plain text, reviewed through pull requests, and built and published by CI. The opposite is documentation kept in a CMS, a wiki, or a shared drive, edited through a web form, and published by someone clicking a button.

It is a workflow decision rather than a tooling decision, though it forces a long chain of tooling decisions afterwards.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Neither posting uses the phrase. Both describe its consequences, which is more telling: Intel asks for Git authoring, CI/CD builds, linting, link validation and publishing as separate bullets, and NVIDIA asks for standards encoded into validators. Those are all things you can only do to documentation that lives in a repository.

The practical reason this matters on a Tuesday is drift. Documentation stored away from the code it describes has no mechanism connecting the two. An engineer changes a function signature and the page describing it stays correct in the CMS forever, because nothing in the engineer's workflow ever touched it.

Docs-as-code does not solve drift. It creates the opportunity to solve drift, by putting the page in the same diff as the change, in front of the same reviewer, gated by the same pipeline. Everything else in this guide's quality automation category is built on that opportunity, and none of it is possible without this step first.

The second reason is contribution. An engineer who will never log into a documentation portal will fix a typo in a Markdown file if the fix is a three-line pull request in a repository they already have cloned.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a documentation site from nothing, publish it, and see the publish happen automatically. About twenty minutes.

Step 1: a repository with documentation in it

mkdir docs-as-code-demo && cd docs-as-code-demo
git init -q
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install --quiet mkdocs
mkdocs new .

You now have mkdocs.yml and docs/index.md. That is the whole structure.

ls -R

Step 2: see it build

mkdocs build --strict
ls site/

--strict turns warnings into errors. Use it from the first build, not later: a project that accumulated five hundred warnings before anyone turned it on never turns it on.

Step 3: break it on purpose, and watch the build catch it

cat >> docs/index.md <<'EOF'

See the [installation guide](install.md) for details.
EOF

mkdocs build --strict

It fails, naming the missing target. That failure is the entire argument for docs-as-code in one line: a dead link is now a build error rather than a reader's problem. Fix it by creating the page:

printf '# Installation\n\nRun the installer.\n' > docs/install.md
mkdocs build --strict

Step 4: put it under review and under CI

mkdir -p .github/workflows
cat > .github/workflows/docs.yml <<'EOF'
name: docs
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install mkdocs
      - run: mkdocs build --strict
EOF

printf 'site/\n.venv/\n' > .gitignore
git add -A && git commit -qm "Documentation site with a strict build in CI"
git log --oneline

What you built. Documentation in version control, with a build that fails on a broken link, running on every push. Every other automated gate in this guide, from prose linting to cold-start testing, is another step in that workflow file.

docs.title: What moves into the repository
docs.text: Artifact Where it lives Reviewed by Page source docs/*.md Pull request Navigation and site config mkdocs.yml, docusaurus.config.js Pull request Style rules .vale.ini, styles/ Pull request The build and publish pipeline .github/workflows/ Pull request Content model and templates Front-matter schema, scaffolding Pull request

docs.title: The vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Single source of truth One canonical location per fact, with everything else referencing it Drift Documentation and implementation disagreeing, silently Gate A check that can fail a pull request Strict build Warnings treated as errors Preview deployment A built copy of the site for one pull request, so reviewers read rendered pages Docs-adjacent code Scripts in the docs repo that validate, generate or package content

docs.title: What it is commonly confused with
docs.text: Not the same as Difference Markdown An authoring format. You can keep Markdown in a wiki and get none of this Static site generators A build tool. Necessary, not sufficient Having docs on GitHub Storage is not review, and review is not CI Writing docs in the code That is docstrings and generated reference, one part of a larger corpus

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with drift and with gates, not with Git. "Documentation in the repository means a page can be in the same pull request as the change it describes, and it means I can fail a build on a dead link or an example that no longer runs. Those two things are most of what keeps a corpus from rotting."

The follow-up you will get is about non-engineer contributors, and it is the real objection. A technical writer without Git, a product manager who wants to fix a sentence, a support engineer with a correction. If you answer that everyone should learn Git, you have failed the question.

Better answer: name the actual mitigations and be honest that they are partial. Web-based editing in GitHub or GitLab handles a typo without a local clone. Preview deployments let a reviewer read the rendered page rather than a diff. A CMS that commits to the repository behind the scenes is a real option for large writing teams. And some organisations genuinely should not do this: if most of your content is authored by people whose job is not software, the workflow tax is real and a content management system may win.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Docs-as-code moves the cost of documentation from publishing time to authoring time. Publishing becomes free and automatic; authoring now requires a toolchain, a review cycle, and a green build. That trade is overwhelmingly worth it for developer documentation, where the audience and the authors both live in repositories. It is much less obviously right for marketing content or end-user help centres, and claiming otherwise in an interview signals that you have only worked on one kind of documentation.

One sharper point if you want to show depth. Docs-as-code is often sold as "engineers will contribute to the docs now". They mostly will not. What actually changes is that you can automate quality, and that a change to the code and a change to its documentation can be made atomic. Pitch it on the automation, not on the contributions, because the contribution promise is the one that disappoints.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A public repository whose documentation build is a CI gate, not a convenience. The specific thing a reviewer looks for is a workflow file with --strict in it and more than one check in the job.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path above and push it. Fifteen minutes, and you now have a repository where a dead link fails CI. That alone is further than most docs sites get. You will know the gate is wired when a deliberately broken link turns the build red and fixing it turns it green. A build that stays green either way is reading something other than the exit code.
  2. Add link checking and prose linting as separate jobs. Separate, so a broken link does not mask a style failure.
  3. Open one pull request that changes a code file and its documentation page together, and link to it. That diff is the argument, and it is more convincing than any description of the workflow.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. A repository where the docs build is green and nothing would fail if the content were wrong proves you can install MkDocs. A repository with a check that has caught something, visible in the history as a red build followed by a fix, proves the gate does work. Keep that commit; it is the most useful thing in the project.
