  • Documentation CI, what to put in the workflow file
  • Markdown and its dialects, what you will be authoring in

docs.title: Treating docs, setup and samples as one product
docs.text:
The unit a developer experiences is not the page; it is everything between arriving and first success.

core · difficulty 2 · 3h

Treats setup, runnable samples, and docs as one product

Source: intel posting, verbatim

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Owning the whole route from a developer arriving to a developer succeeding, rather than owning the pages along it. Setup instructions, the install script, the sample repository and the tutorial are one deliverable with one success criterion, even when three different teams maintain them.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Intel states it in one sentence and the rest of the posting follows from it: "Treats setup, runnable samples, and docs as one product", and then "so a developer reaches first success in minutes with zero help".

The failure this prevents is organisational rather than editorial. The page is correct. The sample repository is correct. The install script is correct. The developer still fails, because the sample assumes a driver version the install page does not mention, and no single owner is responsible for the seam. Each team passes its own tests.

On a Tuesday this is mostly about who owns the seams. A developer reports that the quickstart does not work. Investigating, the cause is that the sample repo pinned a dependency three weeks ago and the docs page predates the pin. In a page-ownership model, that is nobody's defect, and the conversation is about whose ticket it is. In a product-ownership model it is yours, and the fix is a cold-start test that would have caught it, which you also own.

The second reason this is core: it is what makes time to first success a meaningful metric. If you only own pages, the number you can move is small and the number the developer experiences is somebody else's.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Measure one real route end to end, find the seam, and write the thing that watches it. About forty minutes.

Step 1: write the route down as a sequence of artifacts

Not as a page outline. As the things a developer actually touches.

mkdir -p product-drill && cd product-drill
cat > route.md <<'EOF'
# Route: zero to first inference result

| # | Artifact                      | Owner        | Can it fail alone? |
|---|-------------------------------|--------------|--------------------|
| 1 | Landing page                  | docs         | no                 |
| 2 | Install page                  | docs         | no                 |
| 3 | pip package                   | release eng  | yes                |
| 4 | Driver / runtime prerequisite | platform     | yes                |
| 5 | Quickstart page               | docs         | no                 |
| 6 | Sample repository             | engineering  | yes                |
| 7 | Model artifact download       | ml infra     | yes                |
| 8 | First result on screen        | nobody       | --                 |
EOF
cat route.md

The last two columns are the point. Four of eight artifacts are owned by people whose tests do not include this route, and the final row, which is the only one the developer cares about, is owned by nobody.

Step 2: walk it and record where time goes

cat > walk.md <<'EOF'
Walk the route on a clean machine. Record elapsed time per step and every
moment you had to leave the documented path.

| # | Step                  | Minutes | Left the path? |
|---|-----------------------|---------|----------------|
| 1 | Found the quickstart  |     2   | no             |
| 2 | Installed the package |     3   | no             |
| 3 | Ran the sample        |     -   | FAILED         |
| 4 | Searched the error    |    14   | yes: GitHub issue |
| 5 | Installed the runtime |     6   | yes: undocumented |
| 6 | Reran the sample      |     1   | no             |

Total: 26 minutes, of which 20 were off-path.
EOF
cat walk.md

Two numbers matter and neither is the total. Minutes off-path is the real measure of the product, because off-path time is where developers abandon. And which seam produced it: step 4 was caused by step 5's prerequisite being owned by a team that does not read the quickstart.

Step 3: build the thing that watches the seam

The seam is between the install page's claimed prerequisites and the sample's actual ones. That is checkable.

mkdir -p docs sample
cat > docs/install.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Install
requires:
  - python>=3.10
  - widget-runtime>=2.0
---
# Install

    pip install widget
EOF

cat > sample/requirements.txt <<'EOF'
widget>=1.4
widget-runtime>=2.4
numpy>=1.26
EOF

cat > check_prereqs.py <<'PY'
"""Fail when the sample needs something the install page does not promise.

The seam this watches is organisational: the sample's requirements file is
owned by engineering and the install page is owned by docs, and nothing
otherwise connects them. A developer finds the gap by failing.
"""
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

NAME = re.compile(r"^([A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)")


def declared(page: Path) -> dict[str, str]:
    front = page.read_text(encoding="utf-8").split("---")[1]
    out = {}
    for item in yaml.safe_load(front).get("requires", []) or []:
        match = NAME.match(item)
        if match:
            out[match.group(1).lower()] = item
    return out


def required(reqs: Path) -> dict[str, str]:
    out = {}
    for line in reqs.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
        line = line.strip()
        if not line or line.startswith("#"):
            continue
        match = NAME.match(line)
        if match:
            out[match.group(1).lower()] = line
    return out


def main() -> int:
    promised = declared(Path("docs/install.md"))
    needed = required(Path("sample/requirements.txt"))

    missing = sorted(set(needed) - set(promised))
    mismatched = [
        (name, promised[name], needed[name])
        for name in sorted(set(needed) & set(promised))
        if promised[name] != needed[name]
    ]

    for name in missing:
        print(f"UNDOCUMENTED  the sample needs {needed[name]!r}, "
              f"the install page never mentions it", file=sys.stderr)
    for name, page, sample in mismatched:
        print(f"VERSION SKEW  install page promises {page!r}, "
              f"the sample needs {sample!r}", file=sys.stderr)

    failures = len(missing) + len(mismatched)
    print(f"{'FAIL' if failures else 'ok'}: {failures} seam problem(s)")
    return 1 if failures else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
PY
python3 check_prereqs.py

Step 4: close it and confirm the gate turns green

python3 - <<'PY'
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("docs/install.md")
p.write_text(p.read_text()
             .replace("widget-runtime>=2.0", "widget-runtime>=2.4")
             .replace("  - python>=3.10",
                      "  - python>=3.10\n  - widget>=1.4\n  - numpy>=1.26"))
PY
python3 check_prereqs.py

Three findings came out of one check, and the third is the one worth noticing. widget-runtime was a version skew, numpy was undocumented, and widget itself was undeclared: the install page said pip install widget without ever stating which version the sample needs. That is invisible until something compares the two files, and it is the most common form of this defect. A page that tells you to install a thing is not the same as a page that tells you which version of it works.

What you built. A check that fails when two teams' artifacts disagree, and a written route that shows which of the eight steps nobody owns. The check is small; the route document is the thing that changes conversations, because it turns "whose bug is this" into "this seam has no owner and here is the gate I put on it".

docs.title: The shift in the unit of ownership
docs.text: Page ownership Product ownership Is the page accurate? Does the developer succeed? My tests pass The route works on a clean machine The sample repo is engineering's The seam is mine Measured in pages shipped Measured in time to first success A broken route is a routing problem A broken route is a defect with my name on it

docs.title: The seams, and what watches each
docs.text: Seam Typical failure Gate Install page to package Version drift Prerequisite check, as above Docs to sample repository Sample moved or pinned Code-sample validation Docs to runtime prerequisite Undocumented dependency Cold-start testing Sample to model or data artifact Download moved, auth added A smoke test that fetches it Release to documentation Capability ships undocumented Release readiness Page to page Dead cross-reference Link checking

docs.title: What to measure
docs.text: Metric Why it is better than it looks Minutes off-path Where developers actually abandon. Total time hides this Number of artifacts on the route A proxy for how many ways it can break Artifacts owned by teams whose CI excludes the route The real risk register First-attempt success rate on a clean machine The only number that matches the posting's promise

docs.title: The limits of this framing
docs.text: Claim Honest version "I own the route" You own the gates. You do not own engineering's priorities "One product, one owner" Four teams still ship four artifacts on their own schedules "Cold-start testing proves it works" It proves it works on the CI runner's clean machine, not on the developer's

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with the seam, not the philosophy. "The quickstart was accurate and the sample repository was accurate and the route failed, because the sample had pinned a runtime version three weeks earlier. I added a check that compares the sample's requirements against the prerequisites the install page declares, and it fails the build when they diverge. Before that, the gap was nobody's defect."

The follow-up is about authority, and it is the real question: how do you own a product made of other teams' artifacts when you cannot direct those teams? The answer is that you own the detection, not the artifacts. A gate that fails loudly when engineering's pin drifts is available to you without anyone's permission, and it converts an invisible seam into a red build with a named cause. That is usually enough, because the argument changes from "please care about documentation" to "this check is red and here is the commit".

Where it is not enough, the escalation is release readiness: getting documentation into the definition of done, which is a political project rather than a technical one.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Claiming the whole route means owning failures you cannot fix. You will be the person who reports that the model download started requiring authentication, and you will not be the person who can change it back. That is genuinely uncomfortable and it is the job: the alternative is a documentation team that passes all its own tests while developers fail.

One sharper point. The strongest version of this is that the route is the product's actual API for new users, and it is the only part of a platform that every single user touches in the same order. Teams instrument their services heavily and instrument that route not at all. Pointing out that the highest-traffic, least-monitored path in the product is the first ten minutes is a good way to get resources, and it is exactly the argument Intel's posting is making with "setup, runnable samples, and docs as one product".

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A route document and one gate on one seam. The route document is unusual enough to be memorable and takes an hour.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Walk a route on a clean machine and record minutes off-path. Any product, including one you do not work on. The off-path number is the finding, and almost nobody has it. Predict the off-path minutes first. On a route you own the guess is usually low by a factor, and that factor is the number worth reporting.
  2. Build one seam check. The golden path above is a working one. Point it at two real files in a project you know.
  3. Name the artifacts on the route whose owners' CI excludes the route. That list is a risk register nobody has written, and presenting it is a stronger demonstration of product ownership than any page.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. "I think of docs as a product" is a slogan. A table of eight artifacts, four owners, and a measured twenty minutes off-path is not.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
A repository can show that setup, samples and documentation are built and tested together, and this one does. What it cannot show is the organisational half: that they are owned together, planned together and released together, which is what the concept actually asserts.

Where the skill is exercised. In a release meeting, when someone asks whether the docs are ready and the honest answer is a gate rather than an opinion. In the decision to hold a launch for a broken quickstart. In whose backlog a sample lives.

What a learner would do. Take the last three features your team shipped and reconstruct, from records rather than memory, when the documentation work started relative to the code. Then ask who decided it was done. Those two facts describe whether docs are a product or a deliverable, and neither is a matter of opinion once you look.

Then run the cheaper experiment: pick one feature and treat its quickstart as a release blocker for a single release. The interesting output is not the quickstart, it is the conversation that happens when it blocks something.

What competence looks like.

Evidence Why it carries weight A release that waited for documentation Someone had the authority and used it A sample owned by the team that owns the feature The authorship question, answered A definition of done naming documentation It survives a deadline A quickstart in the same CI run as the code The mechanisable half A feature shipped without docs, and the record of why Honest exceptions beat a perfect claim

What this guide and its companion can point at. docpack builds its samples, its site, its llms.txt and its chunk artifacts from one command and gates all of them on one CI run, and its tutorial is executed from an empty virtual environment on every change. That is the product half made real.

Why it is not the demonstration the page needs. One person wrote all of it, so nothing was negotiated, nobody had to be persuaded, and no release was ever held. The hard part of this concept is entirely social and a single-author repository removes it by construction. That is why the entry here is not upgraded past the mechanical half.

docs.title: Prioritizing documentation work
docs.text:
Deciding what to build, fix and retire from evidence rather than from whoever asked most recently.

core · difficulty 2 · 3h

use the data to decide what to build, fix, or retire

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: Repeat-question analysis, A systems mindset

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Choosing which documentation work to do from evidence rather than from whoever asked most recently. The output is a ranked list with a stated basis, and crucially a retire column, which most documentation backlogs do not have.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA's phrasing is one clause at the end of the measurement bullet: "Measure outcomes such as time-to-first-success, support deflection, repeat questions, and AI answer quality, and use the data to decide what to build, fix, or retire."

The three verbs are the content. Most documentation prioritisation has two options, build and fix, and a backlog that therefore only grows. Retire is the one that makes the other two sustainable, and it is in the posting explicitly.

On a Tuesday this is the thing that decides whether you are useful. A documentation backlog at a company this size has a few hundred items: requests from engineers, gaps you found, support escalations, a migration somebody promised, and forty pages marked for review. You can do maybe three things this week. Without a basis, the three you do are whichever came with the most senior request attached, which is a reasonable heuristic and an expensive one.

The reason it is core: the backlog in this field is unbounded. The product ships continuously, every release creates potential gaps, and the corpus ages whether you touch it or not. Prioritisation is not an occasional planning activity, it is the mechanism that converts an infinite queue into a finite week.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a ranking from evidence you can actually get, and see it disagree with your instinct. Thirty minutes.

Step 1: get the inputs that are cheap and the ones that are not

mkdir -p prio-drill && cd prio-drill
cat > inputs.md <<'EOF'
| Input                        | Cost to get        | What it tells you |
|------------------------------|--------------------|-------------------|
| Support ticket topics        | cheap (export)     | what fails in the field |
| Repeat questions in channels | cheap (search)     | what docs failed to answer |
| Page views                   | cheap (analytics)  | demand, not satisfaction |
| Search queries with no click | cheap, underused   | a gap, stated in the reader's words |
| Time to first success        | expensive (study)  | whether the golden path works |
| Staleness by review date     | free (front matter)| risk, not impact |
| Requests from engineers      | free (they arrive) | what a colleague noticed |

The fourth row is the best value in the list and almost nobody uses it.
A query with no click is a reader telling you, in their own words, that
the answer is not there.
EOF
cat inputs.md

Step 2: score on impact and cost, and write down the basis

cat > backlog.csv <<'EOF'
item,action,evidence,affected_per_month,effort_hours,basis
Batch size guidance,build,"12 support tickets, 3 repeat asks",40,4,tickets
Rewrite install page,fix,"search: 'install fails' 60/mo no click",300,6,search
Migrate 40 pages to new model,fix,"migration commitment",0,30,commitment
USD schema reference,build,"2 engineer requests",8,20,request
Retire 2.x upgrade guides,retire,"0 views in 6 months, 11 pages",0,2,analytics
Fix 7 stale pages flagged by CI,fix,"review date >365d",25,5,staleness
Tutorial for the agentic toolkit,build,"product launch in 3 weeks",200,16,launch
EOF
column -s, -t backlog.csv

Step 3: rank it mechanically, then look at what moved

python3 - <<'PY'
import csv

rows = list(csv.DictReader(open("backlog.csv")))
for row in rows:
    affected = float(row["affected_per_month"])
    effort = float(row["effort_hours"])
    # Deliberately crude: people helped per hour of work. The number is not
    # the decision, it is a way to notice when your instinct disagrees with
    # the evidence and to make yourself say why.
    row["score"] = affected / effort if effort else 0.0

rows.sort(key=lambda r: -r["score"])
print(f"{'item':<34} {'action':<8} {'per mo':>7} {'hrs':>5} {'score':>7}  basis")
print("-" * 86)
for row in rows:
    print(f"{row['item']:<34} {row['action']:<8} "
          f"{row['affected_per_month']:>7} {row['effort_hours']:>5} "
          f"{row['score']:>7.1f}  {row['basis']}")
PY

Step 4: argue with the ranking, in writing

The ranking is an input, not a decision. This step is the actual skill.

cat > decisions.md <<'EOF'
# This week

DO  Rewrite install page            (50.0)  highest score, and it is the
                                            first thing every developer touches
DO  Retire 2.x upgrade guides       ( 0.0)  scored zero and I am doing it anyway:
                                            2 hours, removes 11 pages from every
                                            future migration, audit and review
                                            cycle. The score cannot see avoided
                                            future cost.
DO  Batch size guidance             (10.0)  12 tickets is a real number and the
                                            fix is a decision guide, not a page

DEFER  Agentic toolkit tutorial     (12.5)  scored well, but the 200/month is a
                                            forecast rather than a measurement.
                                            Revisit when the launch date is firm.
DEFER  Migrate 40 pages             ( 0.0)  a commitment with no measured impact.
                                            Renegotiate the deadline rather than
                                            spending 30 hours on it this month.
DEFER  USD schema reference         ( 0.4)  20 hours for 8 people. Ask the two
                                            requesters whether a 2-hour decision
                                            guide would do instead.

NOTE  Staleness items scored 5.0 and are genuinely ambiguous: a stale page is
      a risk, not a measured harm. Doing them when they are cheap.
EOF
cat decisions.md

What you built. A ranking, and a written record of the three places you overrode it. The overrides are the deliverable. A score nobody argues with is a score nobody is using; the point of making it explicit is to make the disagreements explicit too, so that next quarter you can tell whether your instincts were better than the number.

Note the retire item: it scored zero and was done anyway, because the scoring function cannot see avoided future cost. That is a known limitation written down rather than a flaw in the method.

docs.title: The three actions
docs.text: Action When Common mistake Build A gap with measured demand Building for forecast demand Fix Existing content failing readers Fixing by staleness date rather than by harm Retire Content with no readers, or superseded Never doing it, so the corpus only grows

docs.title: Why retire is load-bearing
docs.text:
Every page you keep costs something forever, and the costs are invisible individually:

Cost of a page nobody reads Paid by It appears in search results and in retrieval Every reader who gets it instead of the right page It is included in every audit and migration You, repeatedly It must be reviewed to stay in compliance with the model The review cycle It dilutes llms.txt and the chunk corpus Every assistant answer It can be found and followed, and be wrong A reader, expensively

The fourth row is new and is the one worth raising in an interview. In a corpus packaged for retrieval, a stale page is not merely unread, it is competing. That is a materially stronger argument for retirement than it was five years ago.

docs.title: What each input is good and bad for
docs.text: Input Good for Misleads about Page views Demand Satisfaction. A heavily viewed page may be heavily re-read because it is bad Support tickets Real failures Only covers people who asked. Most do not Repeat questions Documentation gaps Biased toward whoever is loudest in a channel Zero-click searches Gaps in the reader's words Volume is low, so weak on frequency Staleness Risk Harm. An old page about something stable is fine Engineer requests What a colleague noticed Impact. Usually reflects their week

docs.title: Honest limits of scoring
docs.text:
Limit Consequence Affected-per-month is usually a guess The ranking is precise about imprecise inputs It cannot see avoided future cost Retirement and tooling always score badly It cannot see strategic commitments A launch has value a ticket count does not capture It optimises for the readers you have Not the readers a new capability might attract Effort estimates are wrong And wrong in the optimistic direction

A scoring function that is treated as a decision is worse than no scoring function, because it launders judgement as arithmetic. Treated as a prompt for disagreement, it is useful.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with an override and with retire. "I score the backlog on people affected per hour of work, and then I write down where I disagree with the score. Last quarter the highest-value thing I did scored zero: retiring eleven pages about a version nobody runs. Two hours, and it removed them from every future audit and from the retrieval corpus, where they were competing with the current pages."

The follow-up is "how do you say no to a senior person", and it is the real question. The answer that works is to make the comparison explicit rather than the refusal. You do not say no; you show the two items and what each is based on, and ask which they want. "This is 20 hours for 8 people, and this is 6 hours for 300 based on search data. I can do the first if it matters more for a reason the data cannot see." That reframes it from your judgement against theirs to a choice they are making with information.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Evidence-based prioritisation systematically underweights new things. Every input you can cheaply measure is about the readers you already have and the content that already exists, so a strict reading of the data never builds documentation for a capability that has not shipped. That is exactly backwards for release readiness, where the whole point is being ready before demand exists. The resolution is to carve out capacity for launch work outside the scored backlog, rather than trying to score a forecast, because a forecast dressed as a measurement corrupts the whole exercise.

One sharper point. The most valuable prioritisation move in this field is usually not choosing between backlog items at all, it is noticing that several items share a cause and that the cause is fixable once. Four tickets about four pages being out of date is not four fix items; it is one freshness monitoring item. That is the systems mindset as a prioritisation technique, and it is how a backlog starts shrinking instead of being triaged forever.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A ranked backlog with a basis column and a written record of the overrides. One page, and it is unusual enough to be memorable.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Export your zero-click search queries for any documentation site you can access. It takes ten minutes, almost nobody does it, and the list is readers telling you the gaps in their own words.
  2. Find something to retire. Pages with no views in six months, or documentation for a version out of support. Propose it with the costs from the table above, including the retrieval-competition argument.
  3. Score a real backlog and write down your three overrides. The overrides are the artifact. A ranking is arithmetic; knowing when to ignore it is the job.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Anyone can say they are data-driven. A backlog with a basis column, and a documented case where you did the thing that scored zero and said why, demonstrates that you use evidence without hiding behind it.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
Prioritisation needs a backlog with competing claims on it and someone who can be overruled. A repository with one author has neither, so what is here is the reasoning and not the decisions.

What you need. A real backlog, a source of demand data, and at least one stakeholder who wants something different from what the data says.

What a learner would do. Take your next ten documentation tasks and give each a basis column: the ticket count, the search volume, the failing check, or "someone asked". Then rank by basis and compare with the order you would have chosen anyway.

What you would see.

Observation Typical What it tells you Tasks with a measurable basis Fewer than half The honest starting point Tasks whose basis is "someone asked" The largest group Not illegitimate, but it should be labelled Agreement between the data order and your instinct Partial Where it disagrees is the interesting part Tasks you did anyway, against the data Some, and that is fine Say why, in the column

The fourth row is the demonstration. Anyone can claim to be data-driven; the specific, unfakeable artifact is a backlog where one item scored zero, was done anyway, and carries the reason.

Why it does not commit. A ranked backlog is a snapshot of an argument. The evidence of skill is in having held the argument and recorded the exception, and that is a document in someone else's planning tool.

docs.title: Reviewing documentation
docs.text:
Spending human attention only on what no check can judge, and shrinking the checklist as automation grows.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Hands-on docs-as-code experience: Git, pull request review, Markdown/RST, static site generators ... and CI/CD"

Prerequisites: Git authoring workflows for writers, Style guides

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Pull request review for documentation, and more usefully, the decision about what a human reviewer should be looking at. Human attention is the scarcest thing in this whole category, so the design question is not "what should a reviewer check" but "what is left once everything checkable has been automated."

That boundary is not fixed. It moves every time you make an artifact executable, and the golden path below moves it.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA lists pull request review alongside Git and CI, in the same breath. That grouping is the point: review is one stage of a pipeline, not a substitute for one.

The failure mode in most organisations is a review checklist that grew by accretion. A reviewer is asked to verify terminology, link validity, heading case, sample correctness and British spelling, all of which a machine does better. By the time they reach the only question that matters, whether the page is true and useful, they have no attention left for it.

A second failure mode is believing review is a safety net it cannot be. Review observes what the reviewer looks at, and a reviewer looks at a diff.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Plant two defects, one that looks automatable and one that looks like it needs judgment, then discover the second one is automatable too. About thirty minutes.

Step 1: a page with two defects

mkdir -p review-demo/docs && cd review-demo
printf 'site_name: Review demo\n' > mkdocs.yml

cat > docs/setup.md <<'EOF'
# Set up the widget

## Steps

1. Run `widget start` to launch the service.
2. Run `widget init` to create the config file.
3. Confirm with `widget status`.

See [the tuning guide](setup.md#tuning) for more.
EOF

Defect one: a dead heading anchor, #tuning does not exist. Defect two: the steps are in the wrong order, because you cannot start a service before its config file exists.

The first looks like a job for CI. The second looks like a job for a reviewer who knows the product.

Step 2: confirm CI catches the first and not the second

mkdocs build --strict 2>&1 | grep -E "INFO.*anchor"

INFO - Doc file 'setup.md' contains a link 'setup.md#tuning', but there is no
       such anchor on this page.

A link checker reports the dead anchor precisely. Nothing in any linter has an opinion about whether step 1 should precede step 2, and no amount of pattern matching will acquire one.

So far this confirms the usual story: machines check mechanics, humans check meaning.

Step 3: make the steps executable and watch the story change

Give the commands a real implementation, where start requires a config:

mkdir -p bin
cat > bin/widget <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
case "$1" in
  init)   printf 'name = "demo"\n' > widget.toml; echo "initialised";;
  start)  [ -f widget.toml ] || { echo "error: no widget.toml; run 'widget init' first" >&2; exit 1; }
          echo "started";;
  status) [ -f widget.toml ] && echo "running" || { echo "error: not initialised" >&2; exit 1; };;
esac
EOF
chmod +x bin/widget
export PATH="$PWD/bin:$PATH"

Now run the documented steps in the documented order, as cold-start testing would:

widget start; widget init; widget status

error: no widget.toml; run 'widget init' first
  step 1 FAILED
initialised
running

The ordering defect is mechanically detectable after all, and the error message even names the fix. In the correct order all three pass.

The lesson is not that reviewers are unnecessary. It is that the boundary between "needs judgment" and "automatable" is a function of how much of your documentation is executable, and it moves whenever you invest. A review checklist written two years ago is asking humans to do work a machine now does.

Step 4: find what is left

Executing the steps proves the sequence runs. It says nothing about whether this is the sequence a real user needs, whether step 3 is reassuring or patronising, whether the page should exist at all, or whether it answers the question people actually arrive with. Those are the review questions, and there are fewer of them than most checklists contain.

What you built. A review checklist with four items instead of fifteen, and a habit of asking, for every finding, whether a machine could have caught it.

docs.title: What only a human can judge
docs.text: Question Why no check can answer it Should this page exist? Requires knowing the corpus and the audience Is the explanation correct? Requires domain knowledge Is this the sequence a user needs? Running is not the same as teaching Is the reader's likely question answered? Requires knowing what readers ask Is this the right Diátaxis type? A tutorial written as reference runs fine Does this duplicate an existing page? Requires judgment about near-duplicates Is the tone right for this audience? Taste, and audience knowledge

docs.title: What should never be in a review checklist
docs.text:
Item Automate with Dead links and anchors Link checking Terminology and banned phrases Prose linting Samples that no longer run Sample validation Steps in an impossible order Cold-start testing Missing front-matter fields Content model validation Heading case A Vale capitalization rule Heading levels skipping Accessibility checks

Every row is something humans do worse than a script, more slowly, and at the cost of the rows in the previous table.

docs.title: What review structurally cannot see
docs.text:
Review observes what the reviewer looks at, which is a diff. Three blind spots follow, and the first one is not theoretical:

Blind spot Example A source-to-render discrepancy Seven pages in this guide shipped code samples rendered as prose. The Markdown source looked correct, because it was correct as text; the defect was in how the parser read a heredoc. No amount of careful reading of a diff finds that. What is missing A reviewer sees the lines that changed, not the step nobody wrote Corpus-level effects A page that is fine alone and duplicates two others

The first blind spot is the general case worth remembering: a human reading source cannot verify a claim about the artifact. That needs a check that reads the artifact.

docs.title: Review mechanics that help
docs.text:
Practice Effect Preview deployments Reviewers read rendered pages; non-engineers can participate CI green before human review Nobody spends attention on what a gate already covers A template naming the four judgment questions Keeps review on the irreducible part Separate "blocking" from "suggestion" in comments An author knows what must change Review the page, not the diff, for structural changes A diff hides reordering

The second row is a sequencing decision with real leverage. A reviewer who opens a pull request with a red build spends their attention triaging CI failures. Make CI pass first, and human review starts where machines stop.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the boundary, not the checklist. "I treat review as the stage that handles what no check can judge: whether the page should exist, whether the explanation is correct, whether it answers the question readers actually arrive with. Everything mechanical belongs in CI, and the review template says so explicitly, because a checklist asking humans to verify links is spending the scarcest resource on the easiest problem."

The follow-up is often a challenge that this trusts automation too much. The strong answer concedes the real limit: review cannot catch a source-to-render discrepancy, and automation cannot catch a procedure that runs but teaches badly. They fail in different directions, which is why you want both and why neither is a safety net for the other.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Shrinking the checklist assumes the automation exists and works. On a corpus with no CI, the fifteen-item checklist is doing real work badly, and taking items off it before building the gates makes things worse. The sequence matters: automate, then shrink, and be able to point at which gate replaced which checklist item.

One sharper point. The boundary between judgment and automation moves. A wrong step order looks like it needs a reviewer who knows the product, and becomes a failing cold-start test the moment the quickstart is executable. So the useful question in a review is not "is this correct" but "could a machine have caught this", and when the answer is yes the fix goes in the pipeline rather than in the page.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A pull request template that names the judgment questions only, plus the list of gates that replaced the mechanical ones.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Step 3 is the one that changes how you think about review checklists.
  2. Take your current review checklist and split it in two columns: automatable and not. Build the gate for the largest automatable item.
  3. Write the four judgment questions into a template. If the template is longer than about five items, something on it is a machine's job.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Neither of this guide's repositories demonstrates review process, which is recorded on the demonstrated page, and process is genuinely hard to evidence in a portfolio. What travels instead is a specific story: a checklist item you deleted, the gate you built to replace it, and one defect that got through review anyway and what you added afterwards. This guide's own answer to the last part is the fence defect in seven pages and the render check that now prevents it.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
Review is two people and a diff, so a single-author repository removes it by construction. The mechanisable part is here, as linters and a page contract; the part that matters is what a human catches that no check can.

What you need. Someone else's draft, and the standing to comment on it.

What a learner would do. Review ten pages you did not write, and for each comment, label it: mechanical, factual, or structural. Then ask which of the mechanical ones a linter could have caught, and automate those instead of making them again.

What you would see.

Comment class Rough share What to do with it Mechanical: style, terminology, formatting Most of them Automate; making these by hand is waste Factual: the claim is wrong or stale Few, and the highest value Needs a reviewer who read the code Structural: the page answers the wrong question Fewest, and the most valuable Only a human finds these Preference with no basis More than anyone admits Drop it, or write it into the style guide

The ratio is the finding. A review culture spending most of its attention on row one is expensive and feels productive, and the fix is a linter rather than a better reviewer.

Why it does not commit. The comments live in someone else's review thread. What a repository can show is the result of the exercise: checks that exist because a reviewer got tired of making the same comment. Several in this project exist for exactly that reason, which is the nearest thing to evidence available here.

docs.title: Doctests and executable docstrings
docs.text:
Making the example in a docstring run, and measuring the examples that are not there.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 2h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Content quality automation you've built, such as Vale or custom linters, doc test harnesses, or freshness monitoring"

Prerequisites: Code-sample validation

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
An example written inside a docstring, in the form of an interactive session, that a test runner executes and checks. The example that appears in your generated API reference is the same text that has to pass CI, so the reference cannot drift from the code it documents.

It is the cheapest form of code-sample validation, because the sample and the implementation are in the same file and cannot be edited separately.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA asks for doc test harnesses. Doctests are the version of that which costs nothing to adopt: one flag in pyproject.toml and every docstring example is executed on every run.

The specific decay they prevent is the worst kind, because it is invisible. A function's behaviour changes, the docstring example still looks plausible, and the generated reference publishes a wrong answer with the authority of auto-generated documentation. Readers trust generated reference material more than hand-written prose, which makes a stale example in it more damaging.

They also change how people write docstrings. An example that must execute cannot be hand-waved, which tends to produce more concrete, more useful documentation than one that only has to look reasonable.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Adopt doctests, hit the trap everyone hits, then measure the examples you do not have. About twenty-five minutes.

Step 1: a module with examples

mkdir -p doctest-demo && cd doctest-demo
cat > money.py <<'EOF'
"""Money helpers."""


def split(total, ways):
    """Split a total into equal shares.

    >>> split(10, 4)
    [2.5, 2.5, 2.5, 2.5]
    >>> split(10, 3)
    [3.33, 3.33, 3.34]
    """
    base = round(total / ways, 2)
    shares = [base] * ways
    shares[-1] = round(total - base * (ways - 1), 2)
    return shares


def fees(amount):
    """Return the fee.

    >>> fees(100)
    2.9
    """
    return amount * 0.029
EOF

Both examples look correct. One of them is not.

Step 2: run them

python3 -m pytest --doctest-modules money.py -q

_____________________________ [doctest] money.fees _____________________________
021 >>> fees(100)
Expected:
    2.9
Got:
    2.9000000000000004

1 failed, 1 passed

100 * 0.029 is not 2.9 in binary floating point. Nobody writing that docstring by hand would have written 2.9000000000000004, and nobody reviewing it would have queried 2.9. This is the entire argument for doctests in four lines: the example was wrong, in a way review does not catch, and execution found it immediately.

Note the split(10, 3) example passed. The uneven split genuinely returns [3.33, 3.33, 3.34], which is worth knowing and is exactly the kind of behaviour a reader wants documented.

Step 3: fix it the right way

python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
t = Path("money.py").read_text()
Path("money.py").write_text(t.replace(
    "    >>> fees(100)\n    2.9\n",
    "    >>> round(fees(100), 2)\n    2.9\n"))
PY
python3 -m pytest --doctest-modules money.py -q

2 passed in 0.02s

Rounding in the example is better than pasting the full float. The reader learns the rounded figure they care about, and the assertion stops being hostage to the last bit of a float.

Step 4: the exit codes, which are not what you expect

printf 'def f(x):\n    """No example here."""\n    return x\n' > empty.py

python3 -m doctest empty.py >/dev/null 2>&1
echo "python -m doctest, module with no doctests: exit=$?"

python3 -m pytest --doctest-modules empty.py -q >/dev/null 2>&1
echo "pytest --doctest-modules, same module:     exit=$?"

python -m doctest, module with no doctests: exit=0
pytest --doctest-modules, same module:     exit=5

python -m doctest is silent and successful on a module with no examples, which is correct behaviour and a trap: if a docstring is reformatted and the >>> lines are lost, nothing fails. Pytest's exit 5 means "no tests were collected", which CI reads as a failure and which you will hit the first time you point --doctest-modules at a single file.

Step 5: measure the examples that do not exist

A doctest that was never written cannot fail, so coverage is the missing number:

import ast
import pathlib

for path in [pathlib.Path("money.py"), pathlib.Path("empty.py")]:
    tree = ast.parse(path.read_text())
    rows = []
    for node in ast.walk(tree):
        if isinstance(node, (ast.FunctionDef, ast.AsyncFunctionDef, ast.ClassDef)):
            if node.name.startswith("_"):
                continue
            rows.append((node.name, ">>>" in (ast.get_docstring(node) or "")))
    covered = sum(1 for _n, ok in rows if ok)
    print(f"{path}: {covered}/{len(rows)} public callables carry a runnable example")
    for name, ok in rows:
        print(f"    {'yes' if ok else 'NO '}  {name}")

money.py: 2/2 public callables carry a runnable example
    yes  split
    yes  fees
empty.py: 0/1 public callables carry a runnable example
    NO   f

What you built. Executed examples, plus the number that tells you how much of your public surface has one. The second is the part most projects never add, and it is the difference between "our doctests pass" and "our public API is documented with examples that pass."

docs.title: Enabling them
docs.text:
# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
addopts = "--doctest-modules"
testpaths = ["tests", "src"]

testpaths must include the source tree, not just tests, or the docstrings are never collected. This is the most common reason a project believes it runs doctests and does not.

docs.title: Directives worth knowing
docs.text:
Directive Use for # doctest: +ELLIPSIS Output containing a path, address or timestamp; ... matches anything # doctest: +SKIP An example that is illustrative and cannot run # doctest: +NORMALIZE_WHITESPACE Wrapped output you do not want to match exactly # doctest: +IGNORE_EXCEPTION_DETAIL An expected exception whose message may change

Reach for +ELLIPSIS before +SKIP. A skipped doctest looks like coverage in the file and provides none.

docs.title: What doctests are good and bad at
docs.text:
Good Bad Small, pure functions with a clear return Anything needing setup or fixtures Showing a return value's exact shape Floating point, unless you round Documenting edge cases, as split(10, 3) does Dict or set ordering Keeping a generated reference honest Multi-step workflows, which belong in a tutorial Error messages a user will see Anything slow, networked or stateful

When a doctest wants fixtures, it has stopped being documentation and become a unit test written in an awkward syntax. Move it.

docs.title: Where this fits against the alternatives
docs.text:
Approach Sample lives Catches drift when Doctests In the docstring The function's behaviour changes Sample validation In Markdown pages A tutorial or how-to goes stale Doc test harness Either, with infrastructure You need skip budgets, output fixtures, reporting Cold-start testing In the quickstart The install path breaks

They are complements. Doctests cover the reference layer, where functions are small and examples are one-liners. They are a poor fit for tutorials, and trying to force a tutorial into docstrings is how projects end up with unreadable module headers.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the generated reference. "Doctests keep the examples in generated API documentation honest, which matters because readers trust generated reference material more than prose and therefore get hurt worse when it is stale. The cost is one line in pyproject.toml."

The follow-up is where they break down, and the answer should be specific: floating point, dict ordering, and anything needing fixtures. Say that you round in the example rather than pasting a full float repr, and that a doctest wanting a fixture should become a unit test.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Doctests make docstrings longer and partly mortgage readability to testability. A module whose header is forty lines of session transcript is worse documentation than one with a clear paragraph, even though the transcript is verified. The honest position is that doctests belong on small functions with interesting return values, not on everything.

One sharper point. A doctest that does not exist cannot fail, so "our doctests pass" is a claim about the examples somebody happened to write. The useful metric is what fraction of the public surface carries a runnable example, which is twenty lines of ast walking and is almost never measured. Bring the number.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A repository with --doctest-modules enabled against the source tree, and ideally a coverage number for runnable examples.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. The fees(100) failure is the whole pitch, and it takes two minutes to reproduce.
  2. Add --doctest-modules to a project you own, with testpaths including the source. Whatever fails was already wrong in your published reference.
  3. Run the step 5 coverage script over your package and write the number down. That is the sentence nobody else in the interview will have.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack runs --doctest-modules across its package, so every docstring example is executed, and one of them broke a strict build and had to be fixed. The broken one is the story: it proves the examples are load-bearing rather than decorative.

docs.title: Documentation CI
docs.text:
The pipeline that decides what counts as a broken page, and fails a pull request over it.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

Asked for by name

Intel: "Build and maintain docsascode pipelines and documentation CI, including link checking and coldstart testing of quickstarts"

NVIDIA: "Build and run docs-as-code pipelines: Git authoring, CI/CD builds, linting, link and code-sample validation, and publishing"

Prerequisites: Docs-as-code, Git authoring workflows for writers

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The set of automated checks that run on every documentation pull request, and the decision about which of them can block a merge. Both postings name it as a thing you build and operate, not a thing you configure once.

The useful framing is not "CI for docs" but a list of ways this corpus can start lying, each with a gate that catches it. The pipeline is the artifact; the list is the thinking.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
A documentation corpus does not decay because people write badly. It decays because the world moves and nothing tells the page. A flag is renamed, a default changes from 3 to 5, a heading is reworded, a sample stops running against the current release. Each of those is a silent, specific defect, and each needs a specific check.

Both postings ask for the pipeline because it is the only mechanism that scales past the size where a human can hold the corpus in their head. NVIDIA's phrase for the philosophy is exact: build systems where the right way is easier than the wrong way. A gate is how you make the wrong way harder.

The part interviewers probe is what you chose to block on. Anyone can add checks. Deciding that a dead link blocks a merge while a style suggestion does not, and being able to defend the line, is the judgment the role is actually hiring for.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a two-gate pipeline, then discover why the gates must be separate steps. About thirty minutes.

Step 1: a corpus with two different defects

mkdir -p ci-demo/docs && cd ci-demo
printf 'site_name: CI demo\n' > mkdocs.yml

cat > docs/index.md <<'EOF'
# Home

A [dead link](nope.md) and a style problem: we will probably maybe fix this.
EOF

One broken link and one hedging phrase. Two defect classes, two gates.

Step 2: a style gate of your own

# gate_style.py
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

BAD = re.compile(r"\b(probably|maybe|should be able to)\b", re.I)

bad = []
for page in sorted(Path("docs").rglob("*.md")):
    for n, line in enumerate(page.read_text().splitlines(), 1):
        if m := BAD.search(line):
            bad.append(f"{page}:{n}: hedging: {m.group(0)!r}")

for b in bad:
    print(f"STYLE {b}")
print(f"{'FAIL' if bad else 'ok'}: {len(bad)} style problem(s)")
raise SystemExit(1 if bad else 0)

Step 3: run them chained, the way people naturally write it first

mkdocs build --strict >/dev/null 2>&1 && python3 gate_style.py
echo "chain exit=$?"

chain exit=1

That is the whole output. The build failed, && short-circuited, and the style gate never ran. You now know about one defect and have no idea the second exists. Fix the link, push again, and learn about the hedging on the next round trip.

Step 4: run them as independent gates

mkdocs build --strict >/dev/null 2>&1; BUILD=$?
python3 gate_style.py; STYLE=$?
echo "build gate exit=$BUILD   style gate exit=$STYLE"

STYLE docs/index.md:3: hedging: 'probably'
FAIL: 1 style problem(s)
build gate exit=1   style gate exit=1

Both defects, one run. In a GitHub Actions workflow this is the difference between one run: with && in it and two run: steps, and it is worth more than it looks. A contributor who gets every problem at once fixes them in one commit. A contributor who gets them one at a time learns that the pipeline wastes their afternoon.

Step 5: name the gates after the lie they prevent

mkdir -p .github/workflows
cat > .github/workflows/docs.yml <<'EOF'
name: docs
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  quality:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install mkdocs

      # A page links somewhere that does not exist.
      - name: Site builds with no warnings
        run: mkdocs build --strict

      # A page hedges where it should state a fact.
      - name: Prose is direct
        run: python3 gate_style.py
EOF
cat .github/workflows/docs.yml | head -5

Each step name describes the failure mode in the reader's terms, not the tool's. "Site builds with no warnings" tells a contributor what broke. "Run mkdocs" tells them nothing.

What you built. Two independent gates whose names describe defects. Adding link checking, code-sample validation and cold-start testing is another step each.

docs.title: A gate per failure mode
docs.text:
This is the real deliverable. The pipeline is downstream of this table.

The lie The gate Blocking? A link goes nowhere Link checking Yes A sample no longer runs Code-sample validation Yes The quickstart fails from scratch Cold-start testing Yes, in its own job A required metadata field is missing Content model validation Yes A term drifted from the glossary Terminology drift Yes The prose hedges or is passive Prose linting Warn only A page is older than its subject Freshness monitoring Warn, or a scheduled report An external URL died Scheduled check, never a merge gate No

docs.title: What to block on
docs.text:
Block the merge Warn only Deterministic Depends on a third party or the clock About correctness About taste Fixable by the author of this diff Fixable only by someone else Fails for one clear reason Produces a list to triage

A gate that is non-deterministic trains people to re-run CI until it passes, and once that habit exists it applies to the trustworthy gates too. That is the reason external link checking stays out of the merge path even though it finds real problems.

docs.title: Where the fast feedback goes
docs.text:
Job Contents Runs in quality Build, links, linters, unit tests, content model Under two minutes samples Executing every code block A few minutes coldstart Fresh environment, install, follow the quickstart Ten minutes or more

Keep them as separate jobs so the slow one does not gate the fast feedback. A writer fixing a typo should not wait on a virtual environment build.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the list, not the pipeline. "I start from the ways the corpus can start lying, and then there is one gate per way. Dead link, sample that no longer runs, quickstart that fails from an empty environment, term that drifted from the glossary. The workflow file is just that list in YAML."

The question you will be asked is what you block on, and the answer has to include something you deliberately chose not to block on, with a reason. Prose style is the usual example: failing a build because a sentence is passive teaches contributors that the pipeline is an obstacle rather than a safety net, so style warns and correctness blocks.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Every gate is a tax on contribution, paid by the next person who wants to fix a typo. A pipeline with fifteen required checks on a corpus nobody contributes to has optimised the wrong thing. The honest version is that you add gates in response to defects that actually shipped, not in anticipation of all possible defects.

One sharper point, and it is the best thing to say here. A gate suite is only as good as its coverage of failure modes, and the count tells you nothing about that coverage. This guide had a fully green pipeline, a hundred-odd tests and a passing strict build while seven of its pages were silently rendering code samples as prose, because a heredoc inside a bash sample contained a fence of its own and closed the outer block early. Nothing in the suite was looking at whether a code block was still a code block on the published page. The fix was one more gate, comparing fenced source against the <pre> content of the built HTML, and it found 127 defects the day it was written.

That sentence used to give the gate count and the new gate's ordinal, which is a figure with no way to stay right: gates have been added since and the arithmetic quietly stopped working. .github/workflows/docs.yml is the count, and this paragraph is a story about a blind spot. The lesson is not "add more gates". It is that every green pipeline has blind spots, and the useful question in a review is which failure mode nothing here would catch.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A workflow file with more than one independent check, step names that describe failure modes, and a commit history that shows a gate catching something real.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path, including the && step. Seeing the chain hide the second failure is the part that changes how you write workflows.
  2. Write the failure-mode table for a corpus you already own. Three columns: the lie, the gate, whether it blocks. The gaps in that table are your backlog. Expect the blocking column to be mostly empty. This guide ran a fully green pipeline while seven of its pages were shipping code samples as prose.
  3. Pick the one failure mode in your table with no gate and build it. That is the one worth talking about, because it came from your corpus rather than from a blog post.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. A reviewer can tell the difference between a pipeline assembled from a tutorial and one grown in response to real breakage. The tell is specificity: a gate that exists because a particular page misled a particular reader, with the commit to prove it. Keep the red build in the history.

docs.title: Docusaurus
docs.text:
A React documentation site with versioning and i18n built in, and 771 packages behind it.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 5h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "static site generators (Sphinx, MkDocs, Docusaurus, or similar)"

Prerequisites: Choosing a static site generator, MDX

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A React-based static site generator aimed specifically at documentation, originally from Meta. Pages are MDX, so prose can contain components, and the things that are plugins or conventions elsewhere are first-class here: versioned docs, internationalisation, a blog, search integration and a sidebar model.

It produces a React application that is pre-rendered to static HTML, and that pre-rendering turns out to matter more than it sounds.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA lists it third. In practice Docusaurus is what you find on product-facing developer sites, especially where the documentation needs interactive pieces or where the front-end team already lives in React.

The judgment being tested is whether you can weigh it honestly. It is the strongest of the four on versioning and translation, which are the two features teams most often discover they need after choosing a generator that makes them hard. It is also the heaviest, and its content is the least portable.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Scaffold, build, and test what the build catches. About forty minutes, most of it waiting for npm.

Step 1: scaffold

npx create-docusaurus@3.10.2 mysite classic --javascript --skip-install
cd mysite && npm install

Pass --javascript or the scaffolder prompts and hangs in CI. Then measure what you just acquired:

du -sh node_modules && ls node_modules | wc -l

349M    node_modules
771

Seven hundred and seventy-one packages, 349 megabytes, for a documentation site. That is not an argument against it, but it is a number worth saying out loud when someone asks why the build is slower than MkDocs.

Step 2: build

npm run build
find build -name "*.html" | wc -l

[SUCCESS] Generated static files in "build".
28

28 pages in about 10 seconds. Per page that is the slowest of the three by a wide margin, because it is compiling and pre-rendering a React application rather than templating HTML.

This page used to put a MkDocs and a Sphinx figure beside that one, from a measurement that ran once and was never committed. drills/generator_build.py now builds an identical corpus under both, and the comparison is more interesting than the numbers were:

  pages   mkdocs   sphinx cold   sphinx warm   warm vs mkdocs
    121     0.50          1.57          0.59   mkdocs 1.2x faster
    240     0.91          2.36          0.58   sphinx 1.6x faster
    480     1.94          4.10          0.65   sphinx 3.0x faster

One machine, one run, and the shape is the claim rather than the seconds. The shape is that MkDocs rebuilds everything every time and Sphinx rebuilds what changed, so MkDocs' time scales with the corpus and Sphinx's warm build is almost flat. The two lines cross just above the corpus size the old figure used, which is why that figure confirmed a conclusion the next data point reverses.

The edit loop, which is what a writer experiences, says the same thing:

  one page edited in 121: mkdocs 0.53s, sphinx 0.59s  (mkdocs 1.1x faster)
  one page edited in 480: mkdocs 1.78s, sphinx 0.70s  (sphinx 2.5x faster)

Two things worth taking from this. A build-time comparison has to say which build, because cold and warm are different questions: CI pays the cold number on every run and an author pays the warm one forty times an afternoon. And a ratio measured at one corpus size is not a property of the tools. The old figure here was reproducible in direction, overstated in magnitude, and describes a regime this guide's own corpus has nearly grown out of.

Docusaurus itself is not in that table. Re-measuring it needs an npm install of a few hundred megabytes, so the 10 seconds above remains one unverified run and is labelled as such rather than quietly standing beside two measured numbers.

Step 3: a broken link

cat > docs/broken.md <<'EOF'
# Broken

See [the missing page](./nope.md).
EOF
npm run build; echo "exit=$?"

[WARNING] Markdown link with URL `./nope.md` in source file "docs/broken.md"
          (7:5) couldn't be resolved.
[ERROR] Error: Docusaurus found broken links!
  Note: it's possible to ignore broken links with the 'onBrokenLinks'
  Docusaurus configuration, and let the build pass.
exit=1

Fails by default, with no strict flag. That is a better default than MkDocs, where --strict is opt-in, and the error message helpfully tells you the escape hatch exists.

Step 4: an undefined component, which is the interesting one

rm docs/broken.md
cat > docs/undef.mdx <<'EOF'
# Undefined

<NoSuchComponent>body</NoSuchComponent>
EOF
npm run build; echo "exit=$?"

[ERROR] Error: Docusaurus static site generation failed for 1 paths:
  [cause]: Error: Expected component `NoSuchComponent` to be defined: you
           likely forgot to import, pass, or provide it.
      at _missingMdxReference (...)
exit=1

Caught, with the component named.

This is worth dwelling on, because it corrects the usual warning about MDX. The MDX compiler itself only emits a runtime guard, so compiling a page proves nothing. Docusaurus catches it anyway, because static site generation renders every page during the build, which executes that guard. The pre-rendering is what converts a reader-facing crash back into a build failure.

What you built. A site whose build fails on a broken link and on a missing component, at the cost of 771 packages and the slowest per-page build of the four.

docs.title: What the build checks, measured
docs.text:
Defect Docusaurus build Link to a missing page Fails, by default Link to a missing anchor Fails, with onBrokenAnchors Undefined MDX component Fails, via pre-rendering Page in no sidebar Passes, unless configured Malformed front matter Fails

The first three are a stronger default posture than MkDocs. Set onBrokenLinks: 'throw' and onBrokenAnchors: 'throw' explicitly anyway, so the behaviour is recorded rather than inherited.

docs.title: What is built in that is a project elsewhere
docs.text:
Feature Docusaurus MkDocs Sphinx Versioned docs Built in, a command mike plugin Build-per-version convention Internationalisation Built in, per-locale builds Plugin, limited gettext workflow Blog Built in Plugin Extension Client-side search Plugin, or Algolia Built in Built in Interactive components Native, MDX No No

Versioning and i18n are the real differentiators. If you know you need either, this is the generator that makes them ordinary rather than a project.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text: Cost Detail Dependency surface 771 packages, 349 MB, measured above Build speed per page Slowest of the four Portability Pages depend on your component library, not just the generator Reviewer skills Diffs contain JSX Machine readability Components are worse input to chunking than prose Upgrade work Major versions have required real migration effort

docs.title: Choosing it
docs.text: Choose Docusaurus Choose something else You need versioned docs and translations Neither is on the roadmap The site needs interactive examples The content is prose and samples A React team maintains the site Nobody on the team writes JavaScript It is a product site, not a library reference It is a Python or C++ API reference

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with what it makes ordinary. "Docusaurus is the one where versioned docs and internationalisation are features rather than projects, and where pages can contain components. The price is a React toolchain: 771 packages in a default install, and the slowest per-page build of the common generators."

The follow-up is often a challenge about weight, and the honest answer concedes it with numbers and then says what it buys. If the project does not need versioning, i18n, or components, the weight buys nothing and MkDocs is the better choice.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Content portability. Pages written against your component library cannot move to another generator without a rewrite, and that coupling grows quietly as the component set grows. It is usually the right bet for a product site with a long life and a front-end team, and it is a genuine commitment rather than a default.

One sharper point. Docusaurus catches undefined MDX components even though the MDX compiler does not, because static site generation renders every page during the build. Most discussions of MDX warn that component typos reach readers; that is true of the compiler and false of this build. Knowing the difference shows you tested the pipeline rather than read about the format.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A Docusaurus site with onBrokenLinks and onBrokenAnchors set to throw explicitly, and a versioned docs directory if versioning is the reason you chose it.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Step 4 is the one to remember, because it contradicts the common warning about MDX.
  2. Measure du -sh node_modules on any Docusaurus site you have. Quote the number rather than an adjective when weight comes up.
  3. Check whether onBrokenAnchors is set on a site you maintain. Links are usually handled; anchors usually are not.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Neither of this guide's repositories uses Docusaurus, which the demonstrated page records. What travels is the measured comparison: fails on a broken link by default where MkDocs needs --strict, catches a missing component where the compiler alone cannot, and costs 771 packages and the slowest per-page build to do it.
