  • Localization and translation pipelines, the other one

docs.title: Embeddings
docs.text:
Turning text into vectors so similar meaning lands nearby, and knowing what that buys and costs.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

Not a quotation (derived)

Required by any RAG pipeline, and NVIDIA names RAG pipelines twice.

Prerequisites: Chunking strategies

Leads to: Vector stores and hybrid search

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A function from text to a fixed-length list of numbers, trained so that text with similar meaning produces vectors that are close together. Closeness is usually cosine similarity, which is the angle between two vectors.

That is the whole idea. Everything interesting is in what "similar meaning" turns out to mean in practice, which is not always what you want.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Neither posting says "embeddings", which is why this is tagged derived. NVIDIA asks for RAG pipelines twice, and there is no RAG pipeline without an embedding step, so the inference is safe.

What makes this core rather than a detail is that embeddings are where documentation people usually stop understanding their own system. The chunker is readable code. The vector store is a database. The embedding model is a black box that turns text into 1,536 numbers, and the temptation is to treat it as magic and move on. That is how you end up unable to explain why your assistant returned the wrong page.

On a Tuesday it is a diagnosis. An assistant answered a question about deprecating a flag using the page about adding one. Lexical search would never have made that mistake, because the words differ. The embedding made it because the two pages are semantically adjacent: same subject, same vocabulary, opposite instruction. Embeddings capture topic much better than they capture polarity, and knowing that is the difference between fixing it and blaming the model.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Embed a small corpus with a real model, see where similarity helps, and find a case where it fails. Forty minutes.

This one needs network access

Steps 2 to 4 download model weights from huggingface.co on first run, roughly 90 MB. Unlike every other golden path in this guide, it will not run in an environment that blocks that host, and the author verified the arithmetic in step 0 rather than the model steps for exactly that reason. If you are behind a restrictive proxy, do step 0 here and steps 2 to 4 on a machine with access.

Step 0: confirm the one piece of arithmetic that matters

Everything in this page rests on cosine similarity equalling a dot product once vectors are normalised. That is checkable with no model and no network, and it is worth seeing once so the rest stops being magic.

mkdir -p embed-drill && cd embed-drill
python3 - <<'PY'
import math

def dot(a, b):
    return sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))

def norm(v):
    return math.sqrt(dot(v, v))

def cosine(a, b):
    return dot(a, b) / (norm(a) * norm(b))

def unit(v):
    n = norm(v)
    return [x / n for x in v]

a = [3.0, 1.0, 0.0, -2.0]
b = [1.5, 0.5, 1.0, -1.0]

print(f"cosine(a, b)            = {cosine(a, b):.6f}")
print(f"dot(unit(a), unit(b))   = {dot(unit(a), unit(b)):.6f}")
print(f"identical?                {abs(cosine(a, b) - dot(unit(a), unit(b))) < 1e-12}")
print()
print(f"norm of a unit vector   = {norm(unit(a)):.6f}")
print(f"cosine(a, a)            = {cosine(a, a):.6f}   (a vector is identical to itself)")
print(f"cosine(a, [-x for x in a]) = {cosine(a, [-x for x in a]):.6f}   (opposite direction)")
PY

That is why every vector store normalises at write time: it turns similarity into one multiply-add per dimension, with no division and no square roots at query time.

Step 1: install a local embedding model

mkdir -p embed-drill && cd embed-drill
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install --quiet "sentence-transformers>=3.0"
python -c "import sentence_transformers; print(sentence_transformers.__version__)"

all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is 384 dimensions, runs on a CPU in milliseconds, and needs no API key. Good enough to learn on and good enough for a lot of production documentation search.

Step 2: embed the chunks and look at the actual numbers

cat > embed.py <<'PY'
"""Embed a handful of documentation chunks and inspect the result."""
import json

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

CHUNKS = [
    "Set batch_size on the client. The default is 32.",
    "If latency matters, use a batch size of 1 or 2.",
    "Size memory for peak load, not for startup.",
    "Run pip install widget to install the CLI.",
    "Exit code 2 means the arguments were invalid.",
    "Exactly-once delivery requires distributed transactions.",
]

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
vectors = model.encode(CHUNKS, normalize_embeddings=True)

print(f"model dimensions: {vectors.shape[1]}")
print(f"one vector, first 8 of {vectors.shape[1]}:")
print(f"  {[round(float(x), 4) for x in vectors[0][:8]]}")
print(f"norm after normalisation: {float((vectors[0] ** 2).sum()) ** 0.5:.4f}")

with open("vectors.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump({"chunks": CHUNKS, "vectors": vectors.tolist()}, f)
print(f"\nwrote {len(CHUNKS)} vectors")
PY
python3 embed.py

Normalising at encode time is worth understanding: once every vector has length 1, cosine similarity is just the dot product, which is one multiply-add per dimension and no division. Every vector store does this.

Step 3: see what similarity actually ranks

cat > search.py <<'PY'
"""Rank chunks against queries by cosine similarity."""
import json

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

data = json.load(open("vectors.json"))
chunks, vectors = data["chunks"], data["vectors"]

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

QUERIES = [
    "my p99 latency is too high",          # no shared words with the answer
    "how do I install it",
    "it ran out of memory in production",
    "what does the argument error mean",
]


def dot(a, b):
    return sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))


for query in QUERIES:
    q = model.encode([query], normalize_embeddings=True)[0].tolist()
    scored = sorted(
        ((dot(q, v), c) for v, c in zip(vectors, chunks)), reverse=True
    )
    print(f"\nQ: {query}")
    for score, chunk in scored[:2]:
        print(f"   {score:.3f}  {chunk}")
PY
python3 search.py

Look at the first query. "my p99 latency is too high" shares no words with "If latency matters, use a batch size of 1 or 2" except "latency", and it ranks first on meaning rather than overlap. That is what embeddings buy, and lexical search cannot do it.

Step 4: find where it fails, which is the part worth your time

cat > failure.py <<'PY'
"""Two failure modes that matter for documentation.

Neither is a bug. Both are consequences of what the training objective
rewards, and both are invisible unless you look for them.
"""
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")


def similarity(a, b):
    v = model.encode([a, b], normalize_embeddings=True)
    return float(sum(x * y for x, y in zip(v[0], v[1])))


print("=== 1. negation and polarity ===")
pairs = [
    ("Enable the cache with cache=True.",
     "Disable the cache with cache=False."),
    ("This flag is supported in version 2.",
     "This flag is deprecated in version 2."),
    ("Retries are safe because writes are idempotent.",
     "Retries are unsafe because writes are not idempotent."),
]
for a, b in pairs:
    print(f"  {similarity(a, b):.3f}  opposite instructions")
    print(f"         {a}")
    print(f"         {b}")

print("\n=== 2. exact identifiers ===")
checks = [
    ("max_memory_gb", "max_memory_mb"),
    ("widget-server", "widget-client"),
    ("error code 2", "error code 3"),
]
for a, b in checks:
    print(f"  {similarity(a, b):.3f}  {a!r} vs {b!r}")

print("\nHigh scores in both sections are the problem, not the reassurance.")
PY
python3 failure.py

What you built. A working embedding search, a demonstration of the thing it does that lexical search cannot, and two measured failure modes.

Run step 4 and read the numbers before continuing, and do not take this page's word for the result. The expected finding is that opposite instructions score high, often above 0.8, and that max_memory_gb against max_memory_mb scores very high. Those similarities are the reason hybrid search exists, and the reason a documentation corpus should never rely on embeddings alone: a version number, a flag name and a negation are exactly the things a developer's question turns on, and exactly the things embeddings blur.

The numbers are not quoted here on purpose. They vary by model, and a page that printed them would be asserting a result the reader should measure on their own vocabulary. Step 4 of "how to prove it" below is where that matters.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Embedding The vector produced from a piece of text Dimensions Length of the vector. 384 to 3,072 typical Cosine similarity Angle between vectors, in [-1, 1]. The usual metric Dot product Equals cosine similarity when both vectors are normalised Normalisation Scaling a vector to length 1, so similarity is one dot product Bi-encoder Query and document embedded independently. Fast, indexable Cross-encoder Query and document scored together. Accurate, cannot be pre-indexed Reranker Usually a cross-encoder, applied to the top k from a fast search Context window Maximum tokens the model embeds. Text beyond it is truncated silently

docs.title: Choosing a model
docs.text:
Consideration What to look at Dimensions More is not better. 384 is often enough and is four times cheaper to store Context window Must exceed your largest chunk, or the tail is silently dropped Asymmetric support Some models embed queries and documents differently; use the prefixes they ask for Local or hosted Local means no key, no per-call cost, and no data leaving. Hosted means less to run Reproducibility Pin the version. A model update silently changes every vector you have stored

That last row causes real incidents. A hosted model updated under you makes new vectors incomparable with stored ones, and the symptom is retrieval quality degrading for no visible reason.

docs.title: What embeddings are good and bad at
docs.text:
Good at Bad at Paraphrase: "latency too high" finding "use 1 or 2" Negation: supported against deprecated Synonyms: "repo" finding "repository" Exact identifiers: max_memory_gb against max_memory_mb Vocabulary mismatch between reader and author Numbers and versions: "2.4" against "2.3" Topic similarity Polarity: enable against disable Short queries with no keyword overlap Rare terms that appear once in the corpus

The right column is most of what a developer question is made of. This table is the single most useful thing on this page.

docs.title: The practical consequences
docs.text: Consequence What to do Embeddings alone will confuse opposites Hybrid search: combine with BM25 Identifiers need exact matching Keep a lexical index; never go vector-only Chunks longer than the context window are truncated Cap chunk size below it, deliberately A model change invalidates your index Pin the version; re-embed on purpose, never by surprise Similarity scores are not comparable across queries Never threshold on an absolute score

docs.title: Cost, concretely
docs.text:
For a 5,000-page corpus at roughly 8 chunks per page:

Item Scale Chunks ~40,000 Storage at 384 dimensions, float32 ~60 MB Storage at 1,536 dimensions, float32 ~245 MB Local embedding on a CPU minutes, free Hosted embedding cents to a few dollars, once Re-embedding on every commit the thing stable chunk ids prevent

Embedding is cheap. Re-embedding carelessly is what costs, which is why chunk identity is a design decision rather than an implementation detail.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with the failure modes, because everyone can describe what embeddings do and far fewer can say where they break. "They buy you paraphrase matching, so a question about high p99 latency finds a chunk that never uses the word 'performance'. What they do not buy is polarity or exact identifiers: 'supported in version 2' and 'deprecated in version 2' embed close together, and max_memory_gb and max_memory_mb are nearly identical vectors. Since developer questions turn on exactly those things, I would not ship vector-only search over a documentation corpus."

The follow-up is "so which model and how many dimensions", and the useful answer resists the premise. Start with a small local model, because it is free and fast enough to iterate with, and let an evaluation set tell you whether a bigger one helps. More dimensions cost storage and latency on every query forever; the gain is usually small on a documentation corpus and is sometimes zero. The point is that this is a measurable question and should not be answered from a blog post.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Adding embeddings makes retrieval better at the queries you cannot anticipate and worse at being debuggable. A BM25 result is explainable: these terms matched, with these weights. A vector result is a number with no account of itself, and when it is wrong the only available fix is changing the inputs and hoping. That loss of debuggability is a real cost in a documentation system, where you will be asked why the assistant said something.

One sharper point. The strongest observation is that embeddings fix a problem documentation teams can also fix with writing. The gap embeddings close is between the reader's vocabulary and the author's. You can also close it by writing summaries and headings in the reader's words, which is free, improves the page for humans, helps lexical search too, and does not degrade when a model is updated. Embeddings are the right tool when you cannot anticipate the vocabulary; they are an expensive substitute for writing when you can. Saying that in an interview for a documentation role lands well, because it is the documentation-specific insight rather than the generic ML one.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A working local embedding search and a measured table of its failure modes on your own corpus's vocabulary.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path, especially step 4. Then redo step 4 with identifiers from your own product: your flag names, your version numbers, your enable/disable pairs. The numbers are usually worse than the generic examples and far more persuasive.
  2. Find a real confusion. Embed your corpus, query it with ten real questions, and find one case where a semantically adjacent chunk beats the correct one. That single example is the whole argument for hybrid search.
  3. Pin the model version and write down why. One line in a README about a model update invalidating a stored index demonstrates operational understanding that most candidates lack.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Describing cosine similarity proves nothing. A measured table showing that your product's own flag names embed nearly identically, and a stated conclusion that you would not ship vector-only search because of it, demonstrates that you tested the tool rather than adopted it.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
Nothing on this page was run. This environment has no model access and the package network allows registries only, so no weights can be fetched. What follows is what the demonstration needs, what you would run, and what you would see, so that the gap is a specification rather than an absence.

What you need. A machine with roughly 2 GB free and any sentence-embedding model small enough to run on CPU; a 384-dimension MiniLM-class model is the usual choice and takes a few hundred megabytes. No GPU. No API key, if the model is local. The whole demonstration is about one afternoon.

What you would run. Embed every heading-bounded chunk of a corpus you own, then embed a set of real reader questions, then score each question against every chunk by cosine similarity and record where the correct chunk ranked.

vectors = model.encode([chunk.text for chunk in chunks], normalize_embeddings=True)
query = model.encode([question], normalize_embeddings=True)
scores = vectors @ query.T          # cosine, because both are normalised

What you would see, and what each number means.

Observation Rough magnitude What it tells you Cosine between a chunk and a paraphrase of it 0.75 to 0.9 The model is doing its job Cosine between two unrelated chunks 0.1 to 0.4, rarely near 0 Why a raw similarity threshold is a bad filter Cosine between --dry-run and --no-commit 0.8 or higher The failure this page is really about Cosine between a question and its answer chunk Often lower than between two chunks Questions and statements are different registers hit@1 against a lexical baseline Better on paraphrases, worse on exact names Why hybrid search exists

The fourth row is the one that surprises people and the reason an evaluation set matters more than a model choice: a question is phrased unlike its answer, so the nearest neighbour of a question is often another question.

The measurement that justifies the page's claim. Take fifteen of your own product's flag, field or endpoint names, embed them, and print the pairwise similarity matrix. On most corpora you will find several pairs above 0.85 whose meanings are opposites, because they share surrounding vocabulary and differ by one token the tokeniser barely registers. That table is the artifact. The conclusion that follows, that you would not ship vector-only retrieval over a corpus whose distinguishing terms are near-identical, is the judgment the table buys you.

How you would know it had failed rather than surprised you. Three signatures. Unnormalised vectors make every cosine implausibly high, usually above 0.9 for everything, so check that the norms are 1.0 before believing any score. A model loaded with the wrong pooling returns near-identical vectors for every input, which shows up as a similarity matrix that is uniform rather than merely high. And if hit@1 is at chance level, the chunk order and the vector order have come apart, which is an indexing bug rather than a model result.

docs.title: Findability and search design
docs.text:
Auditing what your search index actually contains, which is usually less than you think.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

Intel: "The role makes documentation discoverable and usable by both developers and AI assistants through search optimization and agentready content"

Prerequisites: Metadata for navigation and retrieval

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Whether a reader who knows what they want can get to it. On a documentation site that means three overlapping mechanisms: navigation, on-site search, and external search engines. This page is about the middle one, which is the one nobody audits.

The useful move is to stop treating search as a feature your generator provides and start treating the search index as an artifact you are responsible for. It is a file. You can open it.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Intel pairs discoverability for developers with discoverability for AI assistants in one sentence, which is the right pairing: both are retrieval over the same corpus, and both fail for the same reasons.

The reason this is engineering rather than a content concern is that the failure is invisible from the outside. A search box that returns results looks like it works. Whether it returns the right results depends on what went into the index, and what went into the index is a function of your metadata, your chunking granularity, and defaults you probably never looked at.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Open your own search index, find out what is missing from it, and fix the cause. About thirty-five minutes. The measurement in step 3 was wrong the first time, which is part of the lesson.

Step 1: open the index

import json
from pathlib import Path

data = json.loads(Path("site/search/search_index.json").read_text())
docs = data["docs"]
print(f"{len(docs)} entries, {Path('site/search/search_index.json').stat().st_size/1024:.0f} KB")
print(f"keys: {sorted(docs[0].keys())}")

1201 entries, 1177 KB
keys: ['location', 'text', 'title']

Two facts immediately. The index is 1.1 megabytes, downloaded by every visitor who uses search. And each entry has three fields, which tells you what can be matched.

Step 2: find the granularity

by_page = collections.Counter(d["location"].split("#")[0] for d in docs)
print(f"pages: {len(by_page)}  entries per page: "
      f"min={min(by_page.values())} max={max(by_page.values())} "
      f"mean={sum(by_page.values())/len(by_page):.1f}")

pages: 121  entries per page: min=3 max=19 mean=9.9

Section-level, not page-level: roughly ten entries per page, one per heading. That is good news, and it means your heading structure is your search granularity. Headings that are vague or inconsistent degrade search directly, which is a concrete reason the accessibility heading structure work pays twice.

Step 3: check whether your metadata is in there

This is the audit worth running, and my first attempt at it was broken. I tested whether three stopword-stripped words from each summary appeared contiguously in the index text, which they essentially never would, so it reported 83 failures that were an artifact of the test.

The correct test is simpler: normalise both sides and look for the whole summary.

def norm(s):
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", re.sub(r"[^\w\s]", " ", s)).strip().lower()

if norm(summary) in norm(" ".join(index_text_for_page)):
    found += 1

pages with a real summary: 73
summary present in the search index: 1
absent: 72

Seventy-two of 73. Every page in this guide carries a one-line summary in its front matter, and on all but one of them that sentence was not searchable, because front matter is not page content and the search plugin never saw it.

The summary is the single most retrieval-useful sentence on a page. It was written 121 times and indexed once.

Step 4: find out who else was not reading it

grep -rn "summary" src/fieldguide/*.py hooks/*.py mkdocs.yml

Nothing consumed it. Not the search index, not the page body, and not the meta description, because Material falls back to site_description unless a page sets description explicitly. So the field had zero readers while two generators wrote it.

Step 5: one field, three readers

The fix is a hook that puts the summary into the Markdown, early enough for the search plugin to index it:

def on_page_markdown(markdown, page, config, files):
    summary = page.meta.get("summary")
    if not summary or page.meta.get("diataxis") == "placeholder":
        return markdown
    match = TITLE.search(markdown)
    lead = f"\n*{summary.strip()}*\n"
    return markdown[:match.end()] + lead + markdown[match.end():]


def on_page_context(context, page, config, nav):
    summary = page.meta.get("summary")
    if summary and not page.meta.get("description"):
        page.meta["description"] = summary
    return context

summary present in the search index: 73 / 73
distinct meta descriptions:         121 / 121 pages

And the reader now sees it as a standfirst under the title. One field, three consumers, where it previously had none.

Step 6: assert it in CI, because the unit tests cannot

A hook's tests pass whether or not it is wired into mkdocs.yml. So the gate has to read the built output:

assert len(descriptions) > pages * 0.9, (
    f"only {len(descriptions)} distinct descriptions across {pages} pages; "
    f"the summary hook is not wired in")

Verified in both directions: with the hook, 121 distinct descriptions across 121 pages. With the hooks: key removed, 1 across 121, and the assertion fails.

What you built. An audited index, a field with three readers instead of zero, and a gate that fails if the wiring is removed.

docs.title: What to audit in a search index
docs.text:
Question How How big is it? File size; it is downloaded by every searching visitor What granularity? Entries per page Which fields are matchable? The keys on an entry Is page metadata in it? The step 3 comparison Are code samples in it? Search for an identifier only present in a fence Are generated pages in it? They may dominate results while saying nothing

The last row is worth checking on any corpus with stubs or auto-generated indexes. Forty placeholder pages in a 121-page index is a third of the results competing with real content.

docs.title: The three findability mechanisms
docs.text:
Mechanism Serves Fails when Navigation Browsers who do not know the vocabulary Deep or inconsistent hierarchies On-site search Readers who know roughly what they want The index lacks the text they will type External search Readers who start on a search engine See SEO for docs and GEO Assistant retrieval Readers who ask a question See RAG and chunking

Intel's sentence covers the second and fourth. They share an index-quality problem and differ in what they do with the results.

docs.title: What makes a page findable on-site
docs.text:
Factor Why Headings that name what a reader would type Headings are the index's unit A summary in the body What a reader would type is often the summary, not the prose Real terms rather than internal names Your search cannot match a word nobody uses Synonyms somewhere on the page Lexical search has no concept of similarity Code identifiers present as text So searching a flag name finds the page

The synonym row is the one lexical search makes unavoidable. A page about access token does not match a search for "API key" unless the string "API key" appears on it, which is a reason to name deprecated terms once on the page rather than purging them.

docs.title: Index size
docs.text:
Corpus Index Consequence ~120 pages, section-level ~1.1 MB Noticeable on a slow connection ~1,000 pages ~10 MB Prohibitive; use a hosted search

Material supports prebuilding and compressing the index, and beyond roughly a thousand pages the answer is a hosted search service rather than a client-side one. Knowing the crossover exists, and where yours sits, is the point.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the index as an artifact. "I treat the search index as something I am responsible for rather than a feature the generator provides. It is a JSON file; you can open it and find out what is actually matchable. On this corpus it was 1.1 MB, section-level at about ten entries per page, and missing the one field I most wanted searchable."

The follow-up is what you found, and the number is the answer: 72 of 73 page summaries were absent from the index, because front matter is not page content. The fix gave one field three readers, the page body, the search index and the meta description, and the CI gate reads the built output because a hook's unit tests pass whether or not it is wired in.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Putting the summary in the body means every page opens with a sentence that partly repeats its title, which is a small cost in polish for a large gain in findability. And it is a client-side index, so everything that improves matching also grows a file every searching visitor downloads. At this corpus size that trade is clearly worth it; at ten times the size it is not, and the answer becomes hosted search.

One sharper point. Your heading structure is your search granularity. The index here is section-level at roughly ten entries per page, so a vague heading is a bad search result, and the heading-level work that an accessibility audit produces improves search at the same time. Those are usually treated as unrelated chores.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. An audit of your own index with numbers: size, granularity, and one concrete thing you found missing and fixed.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Open site/search/search_index.json and run steps 1 and 2. Most people have never looked.
  2. Run the step 3 comparison for your most important metadata field. Be careful how you test it; my first attempt produced a plausible wrong number.
  3. If you fix it with a hook, add the CI assertion from step 6. Otherwise one mkdocs.yml edit silently reverts the whole thing.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack exposes its corpus through an MCP server with a BM25 index, recorded as a partial demonstration of this concept, and its retrieval evaluation caught summary being unindexed there too. The same defect existed in this guide, which is the part worth telling. I wrote the page about metadata having no readers while shipping a field with no readers, and found it by auditing the index. Every page now carries its own description, with a gate proving it.

docs.title: Freshness monitoring
docs.text:
Measuring staleness against the thing a page documents rather than against the calendar.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Automate the content lifecycle with LLMs and scripting, from drafting and updating to auditing, with checks for freshness, code accuracy, and terminology drift, and human review where judgment matters"

Prerequisites: Content lifecycle, Documentation CI

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: A recurring check that identifies pages likely to have stopped being true. The naive implementation flags pages older than some number of days. The useful one compares a page against the thing it documents, because age is not staleness and the two are only loosely correlated.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA groups freshness with code accuracy and terminology drift as the three things content auditing should cover. They share a shape: correct when written, falsified by something that happened elsewhere.

Freshness is the hardest of the three to measure honestly, which is why most implementations are theatre. A "last updated" date in a footer tells a reader almost nothing: a page edited yesterday to fix a typo is no more accurate than it was the day before, and a page untouched for three years documenting something that has not changed in three years is perfectly correct.

What a reader actually needs to know is whether the page has been verified against its subject since the subject last moved. That is a different question, it needs different data, and the golden path below shows the two answers diverging completely.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build three definitions of staleness, run all three over the same repository, and watch them disagree. About thirty-five minutes.

Step 1: a repository where the code moved ahead of the docs

mkdir -p fresh-demo/docs fresh-demo/src && cd fresh-demo
git init -q && git config user.email d@e.f && git config user.name dev

cat > src/client.py <<'EOF'
def retry(times=3):
    return times
EOF
cat > docs/retries.md <<'EOF'
---
documents: src/client.py
reviewed: 2026-01-10
---
# Retries

The default is 3.
EOF

git add -A
GIT_AUTHOR_DATE="2026-01-10T10:00:00" GIT_COMMITTER_DATE="2026-01-10T10:00:00" \
  git commit -q -m "initial"

# The code changes. The documentation does not.
cat > src/client.py <<'EOF'
def retry(times=5):
    return times
EOF
git add -A
GIT_AUTHOR_DATE="2026-09-01T10:00:00" GIT_COMMITTER_DATE="2026-09-01T10:00:00" \
  git commit -q -m "default retries 3 -> 5"

docs/retries.md now says the default is 3 and the software says 5. Add two more pages: one documenting something genuinely unchanged, and a bulk commit that touches every page's front matter, which is the kind of thing that happens when a team adds a metadata field.

Step 2: three ways to ask the question

TODAY = date(2026, 10, 27)
AGE_LIMIT_DAYS = 180

by_clock  = (TODAY - edited).days > AGE_LIMIT_DAYS   # how old is the page?
by_edit   = subject > edited                         # did the subject move since the last edit?
by_review = subject > reviewed                       # ... since the last actual review?

edited comes from git log -1 --format=%ad, subject from the same query against the file named in documents:, and reviewed from a front-matter field that a human sets only when they have actually checked the content.

Step 3: run all three

python3 freshness.py

page               edited      reviewed    subject      clock  vs-edit  vs-review
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
overview.md        2026-10-20  2026-01-10  2026-09-01   ok     ok       STALE
retries.md         2026-10-20  2026-01-10  2026-09-01   ok     ok       STALE
stable.md          2026-01-10  2026-01-10  2026-01-10   STALE  ok       ok

  clock      flags: ['stable.md']
  vs-edit    flags: (none)
  vs-review  flags: ['overview.md', 'retries.md']

Read that carefully, because all three columns are informative and two of them are wrong.

The clock flags exactly one page, and it is the only correct page in the repository. stable.md documents something that has not changed since January. It is old and it is true. Meanwhile retries.md is actively lying to readers and the clock says it is fine.

Comparing against the last edit flags nothing at all. The metadata commit on 2026-10-20 touched every page, so every page's edit date is now newer than the code change. One bulk commit defeated the entire check. This is not a contrived scenario: adding a front-matter field, running a formatter, or fixing a license header across a corpus all do exactly this.

Only comparing against an explicit review date finds the real problem. retries.md was last verified in January, the code moved in September, so the page needs a human.

Step 4: be honest about the third method too

vs-review also flags overview.md, which contains only general notes and makes no claim about the retry default. That is a false positive, and it is structural: the check knows the page's subject changed but not whether the page says anything about the part that changed. File-level granularity over-reports.

The mitigations, in order of cost: name a narrower subject in documents:, point at a symbol rather than a file, or accept the over-reporting because the output is a review queue rather than a build failure.

What you built. A freshness signal that survives a bulk commit, plus a clear-eyed view of its remaining error mode.

docs.title: The three definitions, and what each is good for
docs.text:
Definition Finds False positives False negatives Age since last edit Nothing reliably Stable, correct pages Any page edited cosmetically Subject moved since last edit Real drift, until a bulk commit Few Every page after a formatting run Subject moved since last review Real drift Pages that mention the subject without claiming anything about it Pages whose subject is not tracked

The third needs a reviewed: field that humans maintain, which is its real cost. A field that nobody updates degrades into the second definition.

docs.title: Why "last updated" in a footer is worse than nothing
docs.text:
What the reader infers What it actually means Someone checked this recently A character changed in this file The content is current Nothing about the content Old date means do not trust it Possibly that nothing needed changing

Publishing an edit date invites a conclusion the data does not support. If you publish a date, publish the review date, and if you do not have one, consider publishing nothing.

docs.title: What to track as the subject
docs.text:
Subject Good for Cost A source file API reference, configuration pages Coarse; any change in the file flags the page A symbol or function Reference pages for one function Needs parsing, or a convention A dependency version Install and compatibility pages Easy, from the lockfile A release tag Release notes, upgrade guides Easy An OpenAPI path Endpoint documentation Easy if the spec is in the repo Nothing trackable Conceptual explanation Fall back to review cadence by importance

Conceptual pages have no mechanical subject, and pretending otherwise produces noise. For those, a review cadence weighted by traffic is the honest answer.

docs.title: Make it a queue, not a gate
docs.text:
Property Freshness A gate like link checking Deterministic Yes, but about likelihood Yes, about correctness False positives Common and structural Rare Right response A human reviews it Fix it now Belongs in the merge path No Yes

Freshness findings are probabilistic. Blocking a merge on "this page may have stopped being true" fails builds for authors who cannot act on them, and the check gets switched off. Run it on a schedule, open issues, and track how long the queue is.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the divergence. "Age is not staleness. A page edited yesterday for a typo is no more accurate, and a three-year-old page about something that has not changed is correct. So I compare against the thing the page documents, using a review date rather than an edit date, because one bulk commit across the corpus resets every edit date and silently defeats the check."

The follow-up is where the review date comes from, and the honest answer is that a human sets it when they verify the page, which means the mechanism depends on a habit. Say that a reviewed: field nobody maintains decays into the weaker check, and that you would rather measure the decay than assume it away.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Subject tracking is coarse. A page flagged because its source file changed may say nothing about the part that changed, which is the overview.md case above. Narrowing the subject to a symbol costs parsing and a convention nobody will follow perfectly. Since the output is a review queue rather than a build failure, over-reporting is the right error to make, but it is still an error and it still costs someone an afternoon.

One sharper point. Publishing a "last updated" date is actively misleading, because readers draw a conclusion about accuracy from a fact about file modification. Either publish a review date that means what readers think it means, or publish nothing and keep the signal internal.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A scheduled job that produces a ranked review queue rather than a pass or fail, with a tracked subject per page.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. The three-column table is the argument, and the vs-edit column flagging nothing is the part people have not considered.
  2. Add a documents: field to twenty pages in a repository you own and run the comparison. Whatever it flags has been wrong for a while.
  3. Measure your queue length twice, a month apart. One measurement is a complaint; two are a trend, and a trend is what gets staffing. Predict the direction before the second measurement. A queue you expected to grow and did not is as useful a finding as the trend you went looking for.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack implements the weak version honestly and says so: PageMeta.is_stale fires at 365 days and is surfaced as a warning and as an ## Optional section in llms.txt. That is recorded as a partial demonstration rather than written up as a complete one, because a clock-based check is exactly what this page argues against. Being able to name the weakness of your own implementation is worth more in an interview than a stronger claim nobody can verify.

docs.title: Generative engine optimization
docs.text:
Being the source an assistant cites, which rewards different things from being the result a human clicks.

core · difficulty 2 · 3h

Optimize documentation for search (SEO and GEO) and for AI assistants and coding agents through agentready, LLMdigestible content

Source: intel posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: SEO for documentation, Agent-ready content

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Making your documentation the source an assistant retrieves, cites and quotes correctly, rather than the result a human clicks. The acronym is new and contested; the underlying question is not.

The useful framing: a search engine ranks pages, an assistant extracts passages. Everything that differs follows from that.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Intel names it twice, in a responsibility and in minimum qualifications, and pairs it with SEO both times. That pairing is the instruction: the same work serves both, and the parts that differ are worth knowing.

What makes it core despite being the newest idea here is that the mechanism is concrete even though the branding is not. An assistant answering a developer question retrieves a passage, not a page, and whether your passage is usable depends on properties you control: whether it stands alone, whether the claim and its qualifier are in the same chunk, whether the exact identifier appears as text.

On a Tuesday it looks like a complaint with an unfamiliar shape. A developer says an assistant told them the retry default is 3. Your page says 3 in the opening sentence and corrects it four paragraphs later, under a heading about version 2.5. The page is accurate and the passage is not, because the correction and the claim ended up in different chunks. No amount of ranking helps; the page needs rewriting so the qualifier travels with the claim.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Take a page that is correct and extracts badly, measure why, and fix it. Thirty-five minutes.

Step 1: a page that is accurate and quotes wrong

mkdir -p geo-drill && cd geo-drill
cat > before.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Configure retries
summary: Retry configuration for the widget client.
diataxis: how-to
updated: 2026-10-20
---
# Configure retries

The client retries failed requests automatically. The default is 3.

## Backoff

Backoff is exponential with jitter. This avoids synchronised retries across
many clients, which was a problem in the 2.3 release.

## Limits

The maximum is 10. Setting it higher is rejected at construction time.

## Changes in 2.5

As of 2.5 the default changed from 3 to 5, because the previous value was
too low for the new upstream timeout.
EOF
wc -w before.md

Every sentence in that page is true. The first sentence of the page is also wrong as of 2.5, and that first sentence is what gets extracted.

Step 2: chunk it and see which passage answers the question

cat > extract.py <<'PY'
"""Chunk a page and show which passage answers a question.

This is the GEO measurement: not whether the page is correct, but whether the
PASSAGE an assistant would lift is correct and self-contained.
"""
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

HEADING = re.compile(r"^(#{1,6}) +(.*?)\s*$")
FENCE = re.compile(r"^\s*(```|~~~)")


def chunks(path):
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    body = text.partition("---\n")[2].partition("\n---\n")[2]
    trail, buffer, out, in_fence = [], [], [], False
    for line in body.splitlines():
        if FENCE.match(line):
            in_fence = not in_fence
            buffer.append(line)
            continue
        match = None if in_fence else HEADING.match(line)
        if match:
            if buffer:
                out.append((" > ".join(trail), "\n".join(buffer).strip()))
            buffer = []
            depth = len(match.group(1))
            trail = trail[: depth - 1] + [match.group(2)]
        else:
            buffer.append(line)
    if buffer:
        out.append((" > ".join(trail), "\n".join(buffer).strip()))
    return [(c, t) for c, t in out if t]


def best(path, question):
    terms = [t for t in re.findall(r"[a-z0-9_]+", question.lower()) if len(t) > 2]
    scored = []
    for crumb, text in chunks(path):
        hay = f"{crumb} {text}".lower()
        scored.append((sum(hay.count(t) for t in terms), crumb, text))
    scored.sort(reverse=True)
    return scored[0]


def audit(path, question, truth):
    score, crumb, text = best(path, question)
    print(f"  question: {question!r}")
    print(f"  passage:  {crumb}")
    print(f"  text:     {text.splitlines()[0][:72]}")
    standalone = truth in text
    contradicted = any(truth in t for _, t in chunks(path)) and not standalone
    print(f"  contains the current answer ({truth!r}): {standalone}")
    if contradicted:
        print("  >>> the correct value is elsewhere on the page, in another chunk")
    return standalone


if __name__ == "__main__":
    path = Path(sys.argv[1])
    print(f"=== {path.name}: {len(chunks(path))} chunks ===")
    for crumb, text in chunks(path):
        print(f"  [{len(text):>4}] {crumb}")
    print()
    # Two questions, because WHICH question decides whether the stale chunk
    # or the corrective one is retrieved. That sensitivity is the point: the
    # page is a coin flip, and you do not control the phrasing.
    for question in (
        "does the client retry automatically",
        "what is the default retry count",
    ):
        audit(path, question, "default is 5")
        print()
PY
python3 extract.py before.md

Step 3: fix it for extraction, not for reading order

cat > after.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Configure retries
summary: Set the retry count on the widget client; the default is 5 as of version 2.5.
diataxis: how-to
updated: 2026-10-20
---
# Configure retries

## The retry default

The client retries failed requests automatically. **The default is 5** as of
widget 2.5. Before 2.5 it was 3, which was too low for the current upstream
timeout.

Set it explicitly to avoid depending on the default:

    client = WidgetClient(api_key="sk-...", retries=5)

## The retry maximum

**The maximum is 10** as of widget 2.5. A higher value is rejected at
construction time, not at request time.

## Backoff behaviour

Retries use exponential backoff with jitter, as of widget 2.5. Jitter avoids
synchronised retries across many clients, which caused a thundering-herd
problem before the 2.3 release.
EOF
python3 extract.py after.md

Step 4: measure the properties, rather than asserting the fix worked

cat > geocheck.py <<'PY'
"""Score a page on properties that decide whether its passages extract well.

Four checks. Each one corresponds to a failure that leaves the PAGE correct
and the PASSAGE wrong or unusable.

  SELF-CONTAINED  does each chunk state its own subject, or does it rely on
                  a sentence in a different chunk?
  QUALIFIED       do claims carry their version or condition in the SAME
                  chunk as the claim?
  NO CONTRADICTION  do two chunks give different answers to one question?
  IDENTIFIERS     do exact names appear as text, not only in prose about them?
"""
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from extract import chunks

VALUE = re.compile(r"\b(?:default|maximum|minimum) is (\d+)", re.I)
#: "the default changed from 3 to 5" states the CURRENT value as the second
#: number. Without this, a page whose correction is phrased as a change rather
#: than as a restatement evades the contradiction check entirely, which is
#: exactly what the `before.md` fixture does.
CHANGED = re.compile(
    r"\b(default|maximum|minimum) changed from (\d+) to (\d+)", re.I
)
QUALIFIER = re.compile(r"\b(as of|before|since|in) (?:widget )?\d+\.\d+", re.I)
PRONOUN_START = re.compile(r"^\s*(it|this|that|these|they|the above)\b", re.I)


def audit(path):
    findings = []
    page_chunks = chunks(path)

    # Claims of the same kind that disagree across chunks.
    claims = {}
    for crumb, text in page_chunks:
        for match in VALUE.finditer(text):
            kind = match.group(0).split(" is ")[0].lower()
            claims.setdefault(kind, []).append((crumb, match.group(1)))
        for match in CHANGED.finditer(text):
            kind = match.group(1).lower()
            claims.setdefault(kind, []).append((crumb, match.group(3)))

    for kind, found in claims.items():
        values = {value for _, value in found}
        if len(values) > 1:
            where = "; ".join(f"{crumb}: {value}" for crumb, value in found)
            findings.append(("contradiction", f"{kind} is given as {sorted(values)} ({where})"))

    for crumb, text in page_chunks:
        first = text.splitlines()[0] if text.splitlines() else ""

        if PRONOUN_START.match(first):
            findings.append(("not-self-contained",
                             f"{crumb!r} opens with a pronoun: {first[:46]!r}"))

        if (VALUE.search(text) or CHANGED.search(text)) and not QUALIFIER.search(text):
            findings.append(("unqualified-claim",
                             f"{crumb!r} states a value with no version or condition"))

    return findings


if __name__ == "__main__":
    total = 0
    for name in sys.argv[1:]:
        path = Path(name)
        findings = audit(path)
        total += len(findings)
        print(f"=== {path.name} ===")
        if not findings:
            print("  ok")
        for kind, why in findings:
            print(f"  {kind}: {why}")
        print()
    print(f"{'FAIL' if total else 'ok'}: {total} problem(s)")
    sys.exit(1 if total else 0)
PY
python3 geocheck.py before.md after.md; echo "exit=$?"

What you built. A chunk-level view of a page, a rewrite aimed at extraction, and a checker for the properties that decide whether a passage survives being lifted out.

docs.title: What the measurement showed
docs.text:
before.md splits into four chunks, and which one answers the question depends on the phrasing:

Question Passage retrieved Contains the current value? "does the client retry automatically" Configure retries No, says 3 "what is the default retry count" Configure retries > Changes in 2.5 No, says "changed from 3 to 5"

Neither passage is usable. The first is stale. The second is correct and phrased as a change rather than a statement, so a reader quoted it gets history instead of an answer. You do not control which phrasing a developer uses, and the page is a coin flip between two bad passages.

after.md returns the same correct passage for both phrasings, because the value, its qualifier and the subject sit in one chunk.

The checker reports three problems on before.md and none on after.md:

contradiction: default is given as ['3', '5']
  (Configure retries: 3; Configure retries > Changes in 2.5: 5)
unqualified-claim: 'Configure retries' states a value with no version
unqualified-claim: 'Configure retries > Limits' states a value with no version

docs.title: The contradiction check almost did not work
docs.text:
In its first version that check never fired on this page. It matched only the form "default is N", and before.md phrases its correction as "the default changed from 3 to 5", so the two claims were never compared.

The pattern is worth sitting with, because it recurs: a checker that recognises only the canonical phrasing misses exactly the pages that are phrased loosely, which are the pages most likely to be wrong. The fix adds the "changed from X to Y" form. Other phrasings will still evade it, and that is a real limitation of lexical checking rather than something to regex away indefinitely. The honest claim is that it catches the two commonest forms, not that it finds every contradiction.

docs.title: What differs between SEO and GEO
docs.text:
SEO GEO Unit the page the passage Goal be clicked be cited, and quoted correctly Reader sees the whole page sees one chunk, usually Reading order matters does not exist A correction later on the page works does not travel with the claim Signals links, titles, freshness self-containment, qualifiers, identifiers as text Measurement rankings, clicks retrieval evaluation, citation checks

The "reading order does not exist" row is the whole discipline. A page is read top to bottom by a human and sampled at a random heading by a machine.

docs.title: The four properties that matter
docs.text: Property Failure if absent Self-contained chunks A passage opening "It defaults to 3" with no subject Qualifiers with their claims The version caveat in a different chunk from the value No contradictions across chunks Two passages, two answers, one gets cited Identifiers as text max_memory_gb only in a table cell or an image

docs.title: Writing habits that follow
docs.text:
Habit Why Put the current value in a heading's own section So the chunk containing it is the one retrieved State the version in the same sentence as the value "The default is 5 as of 2.5" Never open a section with a pronoun The antecedent is in another chunk Replace a "Changes in 2.5" section with inline qualifiers A changes section strands the correction Repeat the subject in each section Mild redundancy for a human, essential for a machine Put exact identifiers in prose, not only tables Tables chunk badly and extract worse

The fourth is the counter-intuitive one. A "what changed in 2.5" section is good documentation practice and actively harmful for extraction, because it separates a correction from the thing it corrects. Keep the section for humans if you like, and also fix the claim where it is made.

docs.title: Mild redundancy is correct here
docs.text:
A human reading three consecutive sections does not need "as of widget 2.5" three times. A machine retrieving one of those sections needs it every time.

That is a real cost: the page is slightly worse to read. For developer documentation where a wrong default costs an afternoon, it is the right trade, and saying so plainly is better than pretending there is no tension.

docs.title: The honest status of the term
docs.text:
Claim Reality "GEO is an established discipline" The term is about two years old and contested "There are GEO best practices" There are retrieval properties, which are measurable "You can rank in an assistant" There is no ranking to see. You can measure citation "It replaces SEO" No. Most documentation traffic is still search "Vendors can do it for you" The work is rewriting your pages

Present it internally as "making passages extract correctly", which is checkable, rather than as GEO, which invites a debate about whether the term means anything. Intel used the word, so use it on your résumé and describe the mechanism in the interview.

docs.title: How to measure it, since the usual metrics do not exist
docs.text: Measurement How Does the right passage come back? Retrieval evaluation with page-level expectations Is the cited passage correct? Grounding checks against the chunk, not the page Do chunks contradict? The checker above, in CI Are identifiers findable? Query your own index for each flag name Does an assistant cite you? Ask it, repeatedly, and record. Crude and the only direct signal

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Define it by the unit, then give the failure. "SEO optimises a page to be clicked; GEO optimises a passage to be quoted correctly. The failure that taught me the difference was a page whose first sentence said the retry default is 3 and whose last section said it changed to 5 in 2.5. The page was accurate, reading order fixed it for a human, and an assistant retrieved the first chunk and gave people the old value. So I check that chunks are self-contained, that a claim carries its version qualifier in the same chunk, and that no two chunks answer one question differently."

The follow-up is "is GEO a real thing or marketing", and the answer should concede the branding and keep the mechanism. The term is contested and about two years old. What is not contested is that assistants retrieve passages, that a passage can be wrong while its page is right, and that this is measurable with a retrieval eval and a grounding check. Lead with the mechanism and the word stops mattering.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Writing for extraction makes pages slightly worse to read. Repeating "as of 2.5" in three consecutive sections is redundant for a human and necessary for a machine, and replacing a tidy "what changed" section with inline qualifiers scatters information a human would rather have in one place. It is a genuine conflict between audiences, it resolves in favour of the machine only where a wrong answer is expensive, and anyone claiming the two audiences always want the same thing has not tried it.

One sharper point. The strongest observation is that GEO is mostly a rediscovery of standalone writing. "Do not open a section with a pronoun" and "state the condition with the claim" are decades-old technical-writing advice that got skipped because a human reader could recover from violating them. Retrieval removed that slack. So the work is less a new optimisation discipline than an old quality bar that finally has a failure mode visible enough to fund, which is the same pattern as RAG surfacing content gaps and coding agents surfacing unmarked fragments. Noticing that pattern three times is worth saying: machine consumers did not create these defects, they made them measurable.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A before-and-after page with the chunk-level audit, plus the checker in CI.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. The before-and-after on one page, measured at the chunk level, is the demonstration and it takes five minutes to show.
  2. Find a real contradiction in a corpus you know. A value stated in an introduction and corrected in a later section. They are common, and the checker finds them automatically. Expect to find one within the first twenty pages. If you do not, you are reading for sense rather than for contradiction, which is the harder habit and the whole exercise.
  3. Add the self-contained and qualifier checks to CI. Thirty lines. The pronoun-opening check alone catches a surprising amount.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Using the word GEO proves nothing and may cost you credibility with a sceptic. A page rewritten for extraction, a chunk-level audit showing which passage gets lifted, and a CI check for cross-chunk contradictions demonstrates that you understand what assistants actually do with your content.

docs.title: Git authoring workflows for writers
docs.text:
How prose is wrapped decides whether diffs are readable and whether two writers conflict.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Hands-on docs-as-code experience: Git, pull request review, Markdown/RST, static site generators (Sphinx, MkDocs, Docusaurus, or similar), and CI/CD"

Intel: "Hands on experience with docs-as-code workflows and documentation CI, including Git, Markdown or MDX, and doc build pipelines"

Prerequisites: Docs-as-code

Leads to: Reviewing documentation

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The practices that make Git work for prose rather than merely tolerate it. Branch and review conventions, commit granularity, and, most consequentially, how you wrap lines, because Git's unit is the line and a paragraph is not one.

Both postings name Git. The thing worth knowing is not git rebase. It is that a formatting decision almost nobody makes deliberately determines whether your diffs are reviewable and whether two writers editing one page collide.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because the objection to docs-as-code is always the same: that it does not work for people whose job is writing. Most of the time the complaint is correct, and the cause is not Git. It is that the repository was set up by engineers who hard-wrapped the prose at 80 columns, so every edit produces a diff that looks like a rewrite and every concurrent edit produces a conflict.

Fix the wrapping and most of the objection dissolves. That is a cheap, high-leverage thing to know, and it is invisible until someone measures it.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Measure what line wrapping does to a diff and to a merge. About thirty minutes, and the second result is the one to remember.

Step 1: the same paragraph, wrapped two ways

mkdir -p git-prose && cd git-prose
git init -q

python3 - <<'PY'
import textwrap
from pathlib import Path

para = ("The retry setting controls how many times the client attempts an "
        "operation before giving up. The default is five attempts. Each "
        "attempt waits longer than the last, multiplied by the backoff "
        "factor. Set it to one to disable retries entirely.")

Path("wrapped.md").write_text("# Retries\n\n" + textwrap.fill(para, 80) + "\n")

sentences = [s.strip() for s in para.split(". ") if s.strip()]
Path("perline.md").write_text(
    "# Retries\n\n" + "\n".join(s.rstrip(".") + "." for s in sentences) + "\n")
PY

git add -A && git commit -qm base

Identical content. One file wrapped at 80 columns, one with a line per sentence.

Step 2: insert a clause, and re-wrap as an editor would

# the edit: a qualifying clause early in the paragraph
# wrapped.md is re-flowed to 80 columns afterwards; perline.md is not
git diff --numstat

  wrapped.md   +5   -4   lines
  perline.md   +1   -1   lines

One inserted clause. Nine changed lines in the hard-wrapped file, two in the other. The re-wrap cascaded through every line of the paragraph, so a reviewer sees the whole paragraph rewritten and has to find the actual change by reading.

The sentence-per-line diff shows exactly the sentence that changed.

Step 3: the result that settles it

Two writers, two branches, editing different sentences of the same paragraph. One changes "The default is five attempts." and the other changes "Set it to one to disable retries entirely."

git merge a-wrapped

Auto-merging wrapped.md
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in wrapped.md
Automatic merge failed

git merge a-perline

Auto-merging perline.md
  merged cleanly

Hard-wrapped prose made two writers conflict over edits that did not overlap. With one sentence per line, Git resolved it without a human.

That is not a small ergonomic preference. On a page several people maintain, it is the difference between a workflow that works and one that produces a conflict every week and teaches writers that Git is hostile.

Step 4: write the convention down

cat > .gitattributes <<'EOF'
# Prose diffs: word-level, so a reviewer sees the changed words.
*.md diff=markdown
EOF

git config diff.markdown.wordRegex '[^[:space:]]'
git diff --word-diff=color -- perline.md | tail -3

.gitattributes is committed and applies to everyone; the diff.markdown driver is local config, so document it in your contributing guide or ship it in a setup script. Word diffs make even a re-wrapped paragraph legible, which is the mitigation when you inherit a hard-wrapped corpus and cannot reflow it today.

What you built. A measured reason to adopt one sentence per line, and a fallback for corpora you cannot change.

docs.title: Wrapping styles
docs.text:
Style Diff on a small edit Concurrent edits Authoring feel Hard wrap at 80 Whole paragraph Conflicts, measured above Familiar to engineers One sentence per line One line Merges cleanly Odd for a day, then invisible One clause per line One line, more lines overall Merges cleanly Fussy No wrapping, one long line One line, unreadable in a terminal Merges, but conflicts are total Fine in a wrapping editor

One sentence per line is the standard answer, sometimes called semantic line breaks. The cost is that the raw file looks ragged; the benefit is measured in steps 2 and 3.

docs.title: Commit and branch conventions that suit prose
docs.text:
Practice Why, for documentation One page or one topic per pull request Reviewers read prose serially, not in parallel Commit message says what changed for the reader "Clarify retry default" beats "update docs" Branch per change, not per person A long-lived personal branch guarantees conflicts Squash on merge The history that matters is the published change Change code and its page in one pull request The atomicity that makes docs-as-code worth it

The last row is the one to defend. Splitting a behaviour change and its documentation into two pull requests reintroduces exactly the drift the workflow exists to prevent.

docs.title: What actually stops non-engineers contributing
docs.text:
Obstacle Mitigation Unreadable prose diffs Semantic line breaks, word diffs Conflicts on concurrent edits Semantic line breaks No local toolchain Web editing in GitHub or GitLab for small fixes Reviewing Markdown instead of pages Preview deployments Git itself Real, and smaller than people assume once the above are fixed

Git is usually blamed and is usually the smallest of these. The first two are formatting decisions and the next two are tooling; all four are fixable without asking anybody to learn rebasing.

docs.title: Things to put in the repository
docs.text:
.gitattributes        # diff driver for prose, and binary markers
.github/
  PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md   # the judgment questions, per docs-review
CONTRIBUTING.md       # wrapping convention, how to run the gates locally

The wrapping convention belongs in writing. It is the one rule that is invisible, consequential, and impossible to infer from the existing files once somebody has broken it.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the measurement, not the practice. "The thing that decides whether Git works for writers is line wrapping. I measured it: one inserted clause in a hard-wrapped paragraph changed nine lines against two, and two writers editing different sentences of the same paragraph conflicted when it was hard-wrapped and merged cleanly with one sentence per line."

The follow-up is what to do about an existing hard-wrapped corpus, and the answer is not a mass reflow on day one, because that destroys git blame for every page. Set the convention for new and edited content, use word diffs meanwhile, and reflow a page when you are substantially rewriting it anyway.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Semantic line breaks make the source look ragged and make some editors' formatting commands actively harmful, since a "reflow paragraph" keystroke undoes it silently. You need the convention documented and ideally a lint rule, or it decays one well-meaning editor at a time.

One sharper point. Git is the usual scapegoat for documentation contribution problems and is rarely the cause. Diff legibility and merge conflicts are formatting decisions; reviewing rendered pages is a preview deployment. Fix those three and the residual difficulty of Git for an occasional contributor is a web editor and one page of instructions.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A repository with a documented wrapping convention, a .gitattributes prose diff driver, and a pull request template that asks the judgment questions rather than the mechanical ones.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path, especially step 3. A conflict over non-overlapping edits is the most persuasive thing in this category.
  2. Check how an existing docs repository you have is wrapped, and write the convention into CONTRIBUTING.md either way.
  3. Set up the word-diff driver and read one recent prose diff with it. If your corpus is hard-wrapped, the difference is immediate.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Numbers. "Semantic line breaks produce better diffs" is a preference; "one inserted clause changed nine lines against two, and the hard-wrapped version conflicted where the other merged cleanly" is a measurement, and it takes half an hour to reproduce on any corpus.

docs.title: GitHub Actions for docs
docs.text:
Implementing the gates so CI and a contributor's laptop run the same checks.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

Not a quotation (derived)

Both postings name CI/CD for documentation. GitHub Actions is the most common implementation of it, and the one both companies' public documentation repositories use.

Prerequisites: Documentation CI

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The YAML that runs your documentation gates on every pull request, publishes the site on merge, and caches enough of the environment that the whole thing finishes before the author has switched tasks.

The interesting problem is not the syntax. It is that the workflow file is a second definition of what the checks are, and a second definition drifts from the first.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Neither posting says "GitHub Actions" and both describe the thing it does. NVIDIA asks for CI/CD builds, linting, link and code-sample validation and publishing; Intel asks for docs-as-code pipelines and documentation CI. Those are the steps in the file.

What makes this a real engineering concern rather than configuration is the gap between CI and the contributor. If the gates live only in the workflow, a writer cannot run them before pushing, so they push, wait four minutes, read a log, fix one thing and push again. That loop is why people stop contributing to documentation, and it is entirely self-inflicted.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Discover drift between CI and the local commands, then remove the possibility of it. About thirty minutes. There is one thing you cannot do locally, named honestly at the end.

Step 1: the shape almost everyone writes first

mkdir -p gha-demo/.github/workflows && cd gha-demo

cat > Makefile <<'EOF'
.PHONY: check
check:
    mkdocs build --strict
    python3 gate_style.py
EOF

cat > .github/workflows/docs.yml <<'EOF'
name: docs
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  quality:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: mkdocs build --strict
      - run: python3 gate_style.py
      - run: python3 gate_links.py
EOF

Two definitions of "the checks": the Makefile and the workflow. Look closely and they already disagree.

Step 2: detect the drift

# drift.py
import re
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

workflow = yaml.safe_load(Path(".github/workflows/docs.yml").read_text())
ci = [s["run"].strip() for job in workflow["jobs"].values()
      for s in job["steps"] if "run" in s]

body = re.search(r"^check:\n((?:\t.*\n)+)", Path("Makefile").read_text(), re.M)
local = [line.strip() for line in body.group(1).splitlines() if line.strip()]

only_ci = [c for c in ci if c not in local]
only_local = [c for c in local if c not in ci]
for c in only_ci:
    print(f"DRIFT  CI runs but `make check` does not: {c}")
for c in only_local:
    print(f"DRIFT  `make check` runs but CI does not: {c}")
n = len(only_ci) + len(only_local)
print(f"{'FAIL' if n else 'ok'}: {len(ci)} CI command(s), {len(local)} local, {n} drifted")
raise SystemExit(1 if n else 0)

python3 drift.py

DRIFT  CI runs but `make check` does not: python3 gate_links.py
FAIL: 3 CI command(s), 2 local, 1 drifted

A contributor runs make check, gets a green light, pushes, and CI fails on a gate they had no way to run. That is the drift, and it is the normal state of most documentation repositories.

Step 3: watch the detector get it wrong

Add the realistic parts to CI, the ones a contributor does not need because their environment already exists:

cat > .github/workflows/docs.yml <<'EOF'
name: docs
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  quality:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
          cache: pip
      - run: pip install -e ".[dev,docs]"
      - run: mkdocs build --strict
      - run: python3 gate_style.py
      - run: python3 gate_links.py
EOF

python3 drift.py

DRIFT  CI runs but `make check` does not: pip install -e ".[dev,docs]"
FAIL: 4 CI command(s), 3 local, 1 drifted

A false positive. pip install belongs only in CI, and the detector has no way to tell a setup step from a gate. You could teach it a list of exceptions, and then the exception list becomes the third definition that drifts.

Step 4: remove the class instead of detecting it

cat > .github/workflows/docs.yml <<'EOF'
name: docs
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  quality:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
          cache: pip
      - run: pip install -e ".[dev,docs]"

      # One definition of "the gates". A contributor runs exactly this.
      - name: Documentation gates
        run: make -k check
EOF

Now there is nothing to compare, because there is one definition. The workflow does environment setup; the Makefile owns what a gate is.

Step 5: the trap in step 4, which this guide walked into

Documentation CI argues that gates must be independent so one failure does not hide another. A Makefile recipe with three command lines short-circuits exactly like &&:

make check

Aborted with 1 warnings in strict mode!
make: *** [Makefile:3: check] Error 1

One failure reported, two gates never run. And make -k does not fix it, because -k keeps going across targets, not across lines inside one recipe. The fix is one target per gate:

cat > Makefile <<'EOF'
.PHONY: check gate-build gate-style gate-links

check: gate-build gate-style gate-links

gate-build:
    mkdocs build --strict

gate-style:
    python3 gate_style.py

gate-links:
    python3 gate_links.py
EOF

make -k check

Aborted with 1 warnings in strict mode!
make: *** [Makefile:10: gate-build] Error 1
STYLE: 1 hedge(s) ['docs/index.md:3']
make: *** [Makefile:13: gate-style] Error 1
LINKS: pretend one is dead
make: *** [Makefile:16: gate-links] Error 1

All three gates reported, overall exit non-zero. One entry point and independent failures, which is what both pages were actually asking for.

What you cannot do locally, stated plainly. You cannot execute a GitHub Actions workflow on your laptop. act runs an approximation in Docker and is useful, but it is not the same runner, the same cache, or the same permissions. What the structure above buys you is that the gates are fully runnable locally and the workflow is thin enough to review by reading. That is the achievable goal, not local Actions fidelity.

What you built. A workflow whose gates cannot disagree with the command a contributor runs, and which reports every independent failure in one pass rather than one per round trip.

docs.title: The jobs a docs repository usually wants
docs.text: Job Triggers on Why separate quality Every push and pull request Fast, under two minutes, blocks merge samples Every pull request Executes code, minutes not seconds coldstart Pull request, or nightly Builds a fresh environment; too slow to gate typos publish Push to the default branch only Needs write permissions the others must not have external-links Schedule Non-deterministic, opens an issue instead of failing

docs.title: Things that bite
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Gate passes locally, fails in CI Drift between two definitions One entry point, as above Only the first failure is reported && or a multi-line recipe One target per gate, make -k Builds take minutes on a typo fix No dependency caching cache: pip on setup-python Publish job can write to the repo on a fork PR pull_request_target, or broad permissions Least-privilege permissions:, publish only on the default branch Generated pages committed stale Generation not checked in CI A --check mode that fails instead of rewriting

docs.title: Permissions worth setting explicitly
docs.text:
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  publish:
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pages: write
      id-token: write

Read-only at the top, elevated only in the job that publishes. A workflow with no permissions: block inherits whatever the repository default is, which on older repositories is write access for every job.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the contributor loop, not the YAML. "The thing I care about in a docs pipeline is that a writer can run every gate locally before pushing. If the gates only exist in the workflow file, people learn the pipeline by failing it, and that is why documentation contribution dies."

The follow-up is about speed. Separate jobs, dependency caching, and the slow cold-start check out of the fast path. Be specific that you would not make a writer fixing a typo wait on a fresh virtual environment.

The tradeoff to volunteer. A single entry point makes the workflow thin and reviewable, and it moves complexity into a Makefile or script that CI cannot see into. If that script is badly structured, you lose per-gate reporting in the Actions UI, where each step is normally its own green or red line. The honest compromise is a target per gate called from a small number of steps, so you keep both the single definition and legible output.

One sharper point. Most documentation workflows have a job that can write to the repository and no permissions: block, so every step in it inherits write access including the ones that run third-party actions against contributor input. Read-only by default, elevated in the publish job only, is free to implement and the kind of detail that signals you have worked next to a security team.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A workflow where the gate step calls the same command a contributor runs, with caching, least-privilege permissions, and the slow check in its own job.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. The valuable part is step 5, where a reasonable structure turns out to hide failures.
  2. Open your own docs workflow and count the definitions of "the checks". If the answer is two, you have the drift.
  3. Add permissions: contents: read at the top of a workflow you own and see what breaks. Whatever breaks is a job that was quietly holding write access.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Anybody can paste a workflow. What a reviewer notices is a repository where make check and CI cannot disagree, because that is a structural decision rather than a copied file.
