docs.title: Golden paths
docs.text:
One route from a clean environment to a working result, and the cost of every alternative you offer alongside it.

core · difficulty 3 · 5h

Asked for by name

Intel: "Design and maintain golden paths and curriculum that take a developer from a clean environment to a working result"

Intel: "Treats setup, runnable samples, and docs as one product, engineering docs-as-code with cold-start and link CI so a developer reaches first success in minutes with zero help"

Prerequisites: Diátaxis

Leads to: Quickstarts that survive contact, Reproducible environments

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
One documented route from nothing to a working result. Not the best route for every reader, not every supported configuration: one route, chosen, written down, and tested end to end.

The word that does the work in Intel's phrasing is a. A golden path is singular. The moment there are two, neither is golden, because you can no longer say "this is the route we test and support".

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Intel asks for it twice, and the second quote gives the acceptance criterion: first success in minutes, with zero help. That is a measurable claim about a specific artifact, which is unusual and worth taking seriously.

The reason golden paths are hard is that they require saying no in a document whose author wants to be helpful. Every reader on a different platform, package manager or deployment model is a temptation to add a branch, and each branch feels like inclusion. The golden path discipline says those belong on a different page, because a path that accommodates everyone is tested for nobody.

That is a judgment call you have to be able to defend, which is why this is difficulty 3 while quickstarts is 2.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Count the routes through a page, which turns a style argument into a number. About thirty-five minutes.

Step 1: two versions of the same quickstart

The accommodating one, written by somebody being helpful:

mkdir -p paths-demo && cd paths-demo
cat > quickstart-bad.md <<'MDEOF'
# Get started

## Install

If you use pip, run `pip install widget`. Alternatively, with conda,
run `conda install -c widget widget`. On macOS you can also use Homebrew.

## Configure

Either set `WIDGET_TOKEN` in your environment, or create `~/.widgetrc`.
Optionally you can pass `--token` on every command instead.

## Choose a backend

Depending on your deployment, use the local backend or the hosted one.
If you are behind a proxy, also set `HTTPS_PROXY`.

## Run

Run `widget sync`. If you chose the hosted backend, add `--remote`.
MDEOF

And the golden one:

cat > quickstart-good.md <<'MDEOF'
# Get started

## Install

```bash
pip install widget
```

## Configure

```bash
export WIDGET_TOKEN="$(cat ~/.config/widget/token)"
```

## Run

```bash
widget sync
```

You should see `synced 0 records`.

Using conda, a hosted backend or a proxy? See [Installation options](install.md).
MDEOF

The second one is not less helpful. It moved the alternatives one click away and kept a single tested route on the page.

Step 2: count the routes

A branch marker only counts if the same sentence also tells the reader to do something, because English reuses those words rhetorically:

MARKER = re.compile(
    r"(?i)\b(if you use|if your|either|alternatively|optionally"
    r"|depending on|or you can|you can also)\b")
ACTION = re.compile(r"(?i)(`[^`]+`|\b(run|use|set|install|create|pass|add)\b)")

for section in re.split(r"^##\s+", text, flags=re.M)[1:]:
    n = sum(1 for s in sentences(section)
            if MARKER.search(s) and ACTION.search(s))
    per.append(n)
routes = math.prod(n + 1 for n in per)

quickstart-bad.md    sections=4 branches=[3, 2, 1, 0] routes=24
quickstart-good.md   sections=3 branches=[0, 0, 0]    routes=1

Twenty-four against one, for pages of roughly the same length. The first page offers twenty-four distinct journeys and the reader has to choose at every section without knowing which combinations anybody has tried.

Step 3: connect the number to testing

This is the argument that settles it. A cold-start test follows the document's commands in order, so it can test exactly one route.

Page Routes Tested Untested quickstart-bad.md 24 1 23 quickstart-good.md 1 1 0

Twenty-three untested routes, each of which a reader will take, and each of which can break without anybody noticing. The branches did not add support; they added unverified surface that looks supported.

Step 4: get a real baseline

docpack getting-started.md     sections=9 branches=[0 x 9]  routes=1

A real, shipped tutorial: nine sections, zero branches, one route. 566 words, five steps, nine code blocks. That is what the discipline looks like in practice, and it is achievable.

Step 5: be honest about the metric

Run it over this guide's own pages and one comes back with 2:

link-checking.md     branches=[0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0]  routes=2

The sentence is: "install.md#tuning does not exist either, because install.md has no Tuning heading." That is "either" as a negative conjunction, not a branch. The narrowed rule removed two of three such false positives from my own corpus and could not remove this one, because English reuses branch words conjunctively.

So the metric is a screening signal, not a precise count. A page at 24 or 72 is unmistakably branchy; the difference between 1 and 2 is noise. Use it to find the pages that need attention, not to certify the ones that do not.

What you built. A number that converts "this page is too accommodating" from an opinion into a finding, plus the testing argument that makes it matter.

docs.title: What makes a path golden
docs.text: Property Why One route So it can be tested; see step 3 From a clean environment The author's machine is not a starting state To a stated, checkable result "You should see synced 0 records" Every command copy-pasteable No placeholders the reader must resolve No decisions A decision is a branch, and a branch is untested surface Tested in CI Cold-start testing Minutes, and the number is known Intel's own criterion

docs.title: Where the alternatives go
docs.text:
Reader Page The default case The golden path A different package manager Installation options A different deployment A how-to per deployment Behind a proxy, air-gapped A networking how-to Wants to understand why An explanation

The link at the bottom of the golden path is what makes this humane rather than exclusionary. One sentence, one link, and the reader who is not in the default case is one click from their case instead of being asked to disambiguate four sections of prose.

docs.title: Choosing the one route
docs.text:
Criterion Pick the option that Population The largest group of readers actually uses Reliability Fails least often, not the one that is newest Speed to result Reaches a working state soonest Fewest prerequisites Needs the least already installed Testability You can run in CI without credentials

These conflict, and the last one wins more often than people expect. A route you cannot test in CI is a route that will be broken and unnoticed, which makes it a worse default than a slightly less popular route you can verify every night.

docs.title: Golden path against its neighbours
docs.text:
Concept Is Golden path The one supported route, the organising decision Quickstart The page that implements it, usually the shortest one Tutorial Teaching; a golden path optimises for working, not learning Sample walkthrough Explaining existing code, not building up to it How-to One task, assumes you are already set up

Golden path and tutorial get conflated most. A tutorial may deliberately take a longer route because the detour teaches something. A golden path takes the shortest route to working and teaches nothing it does not have to.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the number. "A golden path is one route from a clean environment to a stated result. The reason it is one is testability: a cold-start test follows the document's commands, so it tests exactly one route. I measured an accommodating quickstart at 24 distinct routes, which means 23 of them were untested and looked supported."

The follow-up is about excluding readers, and the answer is that the alternatives get a page and a link rather than deletion. The reader who uses conda is one click from their instructions instead of disambiguating four sections, and that reader's page can now be tested too.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Choosing one route means someone's case is not the default, and the person whose case it is will tell you. The honest answer is that this is the cost, it is paid by a minority of readers, and the alternative is a page where every reader's route is untested. Also: testability sometimes beats popularity when picking the default, and that is uncomfortable to defend in a room that wants the most-used option.

One sharper point. My own route-count metric over-counts, because English uses "either", "or" and "if you" conjunctively and rhetorically as well as to branch. Narrowing it to sentences that also contain an action removed two of three false positives in my corpus and not the third. So it is a screening signal: good for finding the 24-route page, useless for distinguishing 1 from 2. Saying which half a metric is good for is worth more than the metric.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A quickstart with one route, a stated expected output, a cold-start test, and a separate options page carrying everything you removed.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the route count over your own quickstart. If it is above about 4, you have found your next piece of work.
  2. Count how many of those routes your CI actually tests. The answer is one.
  3. Move the alternatives to a second page and leave one link behind. The quickstart gets shorter and the alternatives get testable.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack's docs/tutorials/getting-started.md is a single route verified by scripts/coldstart.sh, which builds a fresh virtual environment, follows the tutorial literally and asserts the exact output string the tutorial promises. Measured at one route across nine sections. The combination is the evidence: not that the page is short, but that the one route it offers is the one the nightly build walks.

docs.title: GPU computing and CUDA
docs.text:
No GPU was available, so this page measures arithmetic intensity on a CPU and verifies the compatibility rules by reading them: the promise is one line and its exceptions are five.

context · difficulty 2 · 4h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Documentation experience in graphics, simulation, robotics, or real-time systems"

No GPU was available

This machine has no NVIDIA device, so nothing on this page was run on a GPU. The measurement in step 1 is a CPU analogue of a GPU lesson and is labelled as such; the compatibility material in step 3 was verified by opening NVIDIA's own documentation. Where this page reasons rather than demonstrates, it says so.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Running computation on a processor with thousands of simple cores instead of a few complex ones. The programming model is a grid of threads executing the same instruction over different data, which suits dense regular arithmetic and suits nothing else.

For a documentation role the useful framing is not the hardware. It is that GPU performance is governed by data movement rather than arithmetic, and that the toolchain's compatibility rules are the largest source of reader pain.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA lists graphics, simulation, robotics and real-time systems, and CUDA is underneath all four. The role writes for people whose code already works and is slower than they expected, or does not build at all.

Both of those have documentable causes, and neither is about kernel programming. The first is arithmetic intensity, which is arithmetic a reader can do before porting anything. The second is a version matrix.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Measure why moving work to a faster processor often changes nothing. About twenty minutes.

Step 1: arithmetic intensity, measured on the processor that is here

Four operations on 2048×2048 float32 arrays, timed with their bytes moved and their floating-point operations counted:

ops = [("copy  A -> C", lambda: np.copyto(C, A),        2*N*N*4,  0),
       ("add   A + B",  lambda: np.add(A, B, out=C),    3*N*N*4,  N*N),
       ("2A + B",       lambda: np.add(2*A, B, out=C),  4*N*N*4,  2*N*N),
       ("matmul A @ B", lambda: np.matmul(A, B, out=C), 3*N*N*4,  2*N**3)]

operation                     ms       GB/s      GFLOP/s flops/byte
copy        A -> C          2.06       16.3          0.0       0.00
add         A + B           4.64       10.9          0.9       0.08
scale+add   2A + B          7.48        9.0          1.1       0.12
matmul      A @ B         139.40        0.4        123.2     341.33

The three elementwise operations all land near 9 to 16 GB/s and achieve about one GFLOP/s. The matmul achieves 123 GFLOP/s, over a hundred times more compute, on the same arrays, on the same chip, in the same library.

The reason is the last column. Matmul reuses each byte it loads 341 times; add uses each byte once and a bit. The elementwise operations are not compute-limited at all, they are waiting for memory, and a processor with more arithmetic units would not help them.

That is the GPU lesson, and it is why this CPU measurement is worth publishing. A kernel at 0.08 flops per byte moved to a device with ten times the compute and three times the bandwidth gets roughly three times faster, not ten, and then the transfer across PCIe is subtracted from even that. The question "will the GPU help" is answerable with a division before anybody writes a kernel.

The honest limits of the analogue: a GPU's bandwidth, its memory hierarchy, coalescing rules, occupancy and warp divergence are all absent here. The ratio argument transfers; none of the numbers do.

Step 2: the arithmetic a page should hand the reader

arithmetic intensity = flops performed / bytes moved
if  intensity  <  device_flops / device_bandwidth   ->  memory bound

A page that states the device's ratio and shows the reader how to compute theirs has answered the most common pre-port question in this domain. Most documentation instead explains how to launch a kernel.

Step 3: the compatibility rules, verified by reading them

The second thing readers arrive with is a build or load failure, and the rules are genuinely intricate. From NVIDIA's own compatibility documentation, opened and read rather than recalled:

Minor version compatibility means an application built with a toolkit in a major release family runs on any driver meeting a minimum version, 580 or newer for CUDA 13.x, 525 for 12.x, 450 for 11.x. The page then states five qualifications:

1  feature set is limited; newer-driver features fail with
   cudaErrorCallRequiresNewerDriver
2  code compiled to PTX does not work on older drivers
3  a target architecture must be passed to nvcc, such as -arch=sm_xx
4  without the minimum driver installed, calls return an initialisation error
5  libraries have interdependencies: each cuDNN version requires a
   particular cuBLAS

The promise is one sentence and its exceptions are five. The structural observation is the transferable one: any summary of this short enough for a reader to remember is wrong, so a compatibility page cannot be simplified into a sentence, and the instinct to try is the thing to resist. What works instead is a table with the carve-outs as rows and a symptom column, because readers arrive with a symptom.

(Verified by opening NVIDIA's minor version compatibility page. The driver versions, the error constant and all five carve-outs are quoted from that page. I have not run CUDA on any machine in this project.)

What you built. A measured demonstration that performance follows data movement rather than arithmetic, the division a reader should do before porting anything, and a verified account of why the compatibility story cannot be compressed.

docs.title: The model, in the terms readers will meet
docs.text: Term Means Why documentation mentions it Kernel A function run by many threads The unit of GPU work Thread, block, grid The launch hierarchy Launch configuration questions Warp 32 threads executing together Divergence costs Occupancy Active warps against the maximum The usual tuning knob Coalescing Neighbouring threads reading neighbouring memory The usual performance bug Shared memory Fast memory local to a block The usual optimisation Host and device CPU and GPU, with separate memory The usual correctness bug Stream A queue of asynchronous work Overlapping transfer and compute Compute capability A device's feature level, such as sm_90 Build flags and support matrices

docs.title: Why ported code is often not faster
docs.text:
Cause Check The kernel is memory bound Arithmetic intensity, step 1 Transfers dominate Time the copy separately from the kernel The work is too small Launch overhead exceeds the work Uncoalesced access A profiler, or the access pattern Warp divergence Branches depending on thread index Synchronisation each step Measure with the synchronise removed Timing without synchronising The launch is asynchronous; the timer lies

The last row produces reports of impossibly fast kernels and belongs in any getting-started page, because a reader who measures wrongly will optimise wrongly for a week.

docs.title: The version matrix a reader needs
docs.text:
Axis Example Symptom when wrong Driver version 580, 525, 450 Initialisation error Toolkit version CUDA 13.1 Build failure Compute capability sm_90 No kernel image for device PTX against cubin -arch flags Fails on older drivers Library pairings cuDNN with cuBLAS Load-time symbol errors Framework build A wheel pinned to a CUDA minor Silent CPU fallback

The last row is the quiet one: a framework that cannot see the GPU often falls back to CPU and reports success, so the reader's job runs correctly and twenty times slower with no error anywhere.

docs.title: What a GPU page should contain, and usually does not
docs.text: Should Usually has The arithmetic for "will this help" How to launch a kernel A support matrix with symptoms A prose paragraph on compatibility How to time correctly, with synchronisation Timings with no caveat The transfer cost, separately Kernel time only A detection snippet for silent CPU fallback An assumption it worked The minimum driver, stated numerically "A recent driver"

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the honest boundary, because it is better than bluffing. "I have not shipped CUDA. What I can do is the reasoning a documentation role needs: GPU performance follows data movement rather than arithmetic, and the compatibility rules are the main source of reader pain. I measured the first part on a CPU, which is where the lesson is visible without a device."

Then the measurement. On the same arrays with the same library, elementwise operations hit about one GFLOP/s and a matmul hit 123, a hundredfold difference, because matmul reuses each loaded byte 341 times and add uses it once. So the elementwise work is not compute-limited, it is waiting for memory, and moving it to a device with more arithmetic units does nearly nothing. "Will the GPU help" is a division a reader can do before porting anything, and most documentation teaches kernel launches instead.

The compatibility point, with the source named. NVIDIA's minor version compatibility page promises that applications in a major family run on any driver above a minimum, 580 for 13.x, 525 for 12.x, 450 for 11.x, and then carves out five exceptions: feature set, PTX, the -arch requirement, the minimum driver actually being present, and library interdependencies. One line of promise, five of exceptions. No summary short enough to remember is correct, so the page has to be a table keyed by symptom, since symptoms are what readers arrive with.

The thing I would add to any getting-started page. Kernel launches are asynchronous, so a reader who times without synchronising measures the launch rather than the work and reports an impossibly fast kernel. And a framework that cannot see the device often falls back to CPU and reports success, so the job runs correctly and twenty times slower with nothing in the logs. Both are cheap to document and both cost readers days.

What I would not claim. No kernel I have written, no profiler I have run, no occupancy I have tuned. For a documentation role at context depth that is the right boundary, and I would want an engineer's review on anything past the arithmetic.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. An arithmetic-intensity table for the operations your readers actually run, and a symptom-keyed compatibility matrix.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run step 1 on any machine. Predict the ratio between the elementwise GFLOP/s and the matmul's before you look; a hundredfold gap surprises most people.
  2. Compute arithmetic intensity for one kernel your team is thinking of porting, and compare it with the device's flops-per-byte. That division has cancelled porting projects.
  3. Find a timing claim in GPU documentation you rely on and check whether it synchronised. If the page does not say, assume it did not.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. The intensity measurement ran here on CPU with numpy and is reproducible, and the compatibility figures were verified by opening NVIDIA's documentation, which is cited as reading. No GPU, no CUDA, no kernel, no profiler: the demonstrated page records this concept as having no demonstration in either repository, which is the accurate statement, and context tier is the claim being made.

docs.title: Grounding and citation
docs.text:
Making an answer traceable to the text it came from, and failing it mechanically when it is not.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

Practical experience applying LLMs to content workflows (prompting, retrieval and grounding, output evaluation)

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: RAG pipelines

Leads to: Documentation-backed AI assistants, Hallucination and guardrails, Output evaluation

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Requiring every claim in an answer to be traceable to a specific piece of retrieved text, and checking that requirement mechanically rather than trusting it. Citation is the visible half: the answer names its sources. Grounding is the enforcement: a claim with no supporting text is rejected before anyone reads it.

The distinction matters because a citation is not evidence of grounding. A model will happily attach [c3] to a sentence c3 does not support.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA lists it in the middle of the three-part requirement: "prompting, retrieval and grounding, output evaluation". The ordering is the pipeline, and grounding is the stage that makes the other two auditable.

What makes it core rather than a nicety is the asymmetry described in RAG: a generated answer hides the ranking. A reader looking at a search results page judges five results themselves. A reader looking at a paragraph has no way to tell whether it synthesised two relevant chunks or invented a bridge between two half-relevant ones. Citation restores the reader's ability to check, and mechanical grounding restores yours.

On a Tuesday it is a specific and common defect. The assistant says "Set max_memory_mb to cap GPU memory, with a default of 16. [c3]" That sentence contains two facts from two chunks: the flag name from the legacy page and the default from the current one, fused into a claim that is true of neither. The citation is present. The answer is wrong. Only a check that tests the claim against the cited text catches it, and the check is about forty lines.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a grounding checker, run it against answers that look right, and watch it reject three different kinds of ungrounded claim. Forty minutes, dependency-free.

Step 1: the context, and four answers to judge

mkdir -p ground-drill && cd ground-drill
cat > context.json <<'EOF'
{
  "c3": "max_memory_gb caps the GPU memory the server will allocate. The default is 16. Size for peak load, not startup.",
  "c4": "max_memory_mb was the 1.x equivalent of max_memory_gb. It was removed in 2.0 and is ignored if set.",
  "c1": "batch_size controls how many requests are grouped per forward pass. The default is 32. The maximum is 512."
}
EOF

cat > answers.json <<'EOF'
[
  {"label": "grounded",
   "text": "Set max_memory_gb to cap GPU memory. [c3] The default is 16. [c3]"},
  {"label": "fused",
   "text": "Set max_memory_mb to cap GPU memory, with a default of 16. [c3]"},
  {"label": "half-cited",
   "text": "Set max_memory_gb to cap GPU memory. The default is 16. [c3]"},
  {"label": "uncited",
   "text": "Set max_memory_gb to cap GPU memory. The default is 16."},
  {"label": "invented",
   "text": "Set max_memory_gb to cap GPU memory. [c3] The default is 24. [c3]"},
  {"label": "wrong-source",
   "text": "The default is 32. [c3]"},
  {"label": "dangling",
   "text": "Set max_memory_gb to cap GPU memory. [c9]"}
]
EOF
python3 -c "import json; print(len(json.load(open('answers.json'))), 'answers to judge')"

Read those five. Four of them look like a correct answer at a glance, and three are wrong in ways a reader cannot detect.

Step 2: the checker

cat > ground.py <<'PY'
"""Check that every sentence in an answer is supported by its cited chunk.

Three checks, in increasing strictness, and the second is the one that earns
its keep:

  CITED       does every sentence carry a citation at all?
  SUPPORTED   do the sentence's content words appear in the cited chunk?
  NUMBERS     does every number in the sentence appear in the cited chunk?

The NUMBERS check is separate because numbers are where ungrounded answers do
the most damage and where word-overlap scoring is blindest: "the default is
16" and "the default is 24" differ by one token out of five and by everything
that matters.
"""
import json
import re
import sys

CITATION = re.compile(r"\[(\w+)\]")
STOP = {
    "the", "a", "an", "to", "is", "are", "of", "in", "on", "for", "with",
    "and", "or", "it", "its", "set", "was", "be", "by", "at", "as", "this",
    "that", "will", "can", "you", "your", "not", "from", "which",
}

#: A sentence must have at least this share of its content words present in
#: the cited chunk. Deliberately not 1.0: an answer is allowed to paraphrase
#: and to use connective words the source does not contain.
SUPPORT_THRESHOLD = 0.7


def content_words(text):
    return [
        w for w in re.findall(r"[a-z0-9_]+", text.lower())
        if w not in STOP and len(w) > 1
    ]


def numbers(text):
    return set(re.findall(r"\b\d+(?:\.\d+)?\b", text))


#: A sentence, followed by any citations that trail it. Matching them together
#: is the whole point: splitting on `(?<=[.!?])\s+` first puts a trailing
#: `[c3]` in its own fragment and leaves the sentence it belongs to looking
#: uncited, which made the first version of this checker reject every answer.
SENTENCE = re.compile(r"(.+?[.!?])((?:\s*\[\w+\])*)", re.S)


def sentences(answer):
    """Split into (sentence, citations), with a trailing citation kept.

    A citation applies to the sentence it follows. One citation covering three
    sentences is NOT accepted, which is strict on purpose: a single citation
    spanning several claims is exactly the pattern that hides a fused answer.
    """
    out = []
    for match in SENTENCE.finditer(answer.strip()):
        text = CITATION.sub("", match.group(1)).strip()
        if text:
            out.append((text, CITATION.findall(match.group(2))))
    return out


def check(answer, context):
    findings = []
    for text, cited in sentences(answer):
        if not cited:
            findings.append(("uncited", text, "no citation on this sentence"))
            continue

        source = " ".join(context.get(c, "") for c in cited)
        missing_sources = [c for c in cited if c not in context]
        if missing_sources:
            findings.append(
                ("bad-citation", text, f"cites {missing_sources}, not in the context")
            )
            continue

        source_words = set(content_words(source))
        words = content_words(text)
        present = [w for w in words if w in source_words]
        ratio = len(present) / len(words) if words else 1.0
        if ratio < SUPPORT_THRESHOLD:
            absent = [w for w in words if w not in source_words]
            findings.append((
                "unsupported", text,
                f"{ratio:.0%} of content words in {cited}; missing {absent}",
            ))

        absent_numbers = numbers(text) - numbers(source)
        if absent_numbers:
            findings.append((
                "ungrounded-number", text,
                f"{sorted(absent_numbers)} not in {cited}",
            ))
    return findings


def main():
    context = json.load(open("context.json"))
    for answer in json.load(open("answers.json")):
        findings = check(answer["text"], context)
        verdict = "PASS" if not findings else "REJECT"
        print(f"{verdict:<7} [{answer['label']}] {answer['text']}")
        for kind, text, why in findings:
            print(f"        {kind}: {why}")
        print()
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
PY
python3 ground.py

Step 3: see what each check catches that the others do not

python3 - <<'PY'
import json

from ground import check, content_words

context = json.load(open("context.json"))
source_words = set(content_words(context["c3"]))


def overlap(answer):
    words = content_words(answer.replace("[c3]", ""))
    return sum(1 for w in words if w in source_words) / len(words)


print("=== when does the NUMBERS check earn its keep? ===")
print("A wrong number is itself a missing content word, so on a SHORT")
print("sentence the support check catches it anyway. On a long one it does not.\n")

for answer in [
    "The default is 16. [c3]",
    "The default is 24. [c3]",
    "max_memory_gb caps the GPU memory the server will allocate, "
    "and the default is 16. [c3]",
    "max_memory_gb caps the GPU memory the server will allocate, "
    "and the default is 24. [c3]",
]:
    kinds = [f[0] for f in check(answer, context)] or ["none"]
    print(f"  overlap {overlap(answer):5.0%}   findings {kinds}")
    print(f"    {answer}")

print()
print("=== the fused answer, in detail ===")
fused = "Set max_memory_mb to cap GPU memory, with a default of 16. [c3]"
for kind, text, why in check(fused, context):
    print(f"  {kind}: {why}")
PY

The four-line table is the argument, and it is narrower than the usual claim:

Answer Overlap Fires short, default 16 100% nothing. Correct short, default 24 50% unsupported and ungrounded-number long, default 16 100% nothing. Correct long, default 24 88% ungrounded-number only

On a short sentence a wrong number is a large share of the content words, so the support check catches it without help. On a long sentence the same fabrication sits at 88% overlap, comfortably above any usable threshold, and only the dedicated numbers check sees it. Since real answers are long sentences, that is where the check pays for itself.

The fused answer is rejected for missing max_memory_mb and cap. The first is the finding; the second is a false positive, because c3 says "caps" and this checker does no stemming. Worth noticing: lexical support is a proxy with real noise in it, which is why the threshold is 0.7 rather than 1.0 and why it has to be set from a labelled set rather than reasoned to.

Step 4: the prompt side, which reduces the problem rather than solving it

cat > prompt.txt <<'EOF'
Answer the question using ONLY the numbered sources below.

Rules:
- Put a citation [id] at the end of EVERY sentence, naming the single source
  that supports that sentence.
- If a sentence needs two sources, split it into two sentences.
- Quote exact values (numbers, flag names, version strings) verbatim from the
  source. Never convert, round, or infer a value.
- If the sources do not contain the answer, reply exactly:
  "I could not find this in the documentation."
  That is a correct and expected answer.

Sources:
{context}

Question: {question}
EOF
cat prompt.txt

What you built. A checker that rejects three kinds of ungrounded answer, and the prompt that reduces how often they occur.

The division of labour is the lesson. The prompt makes grounded answers more likely; the checker makes ungrounded ones not ship. Only the second is a guarantee, and the "split it into two sentences" rule exists specifically to make the checker's job possible: one citation covering three claims cannot be verified, so the prompt is designed around what the validator can check.

docs.title: The three failures, and which check catches each
docs.text: Failure Looks like Caught by Uncited claim A plausible sentence with no source Citation presence Fused claim Two true facts from two chunks, combined into a false one Word support against the cited chunk Invented value A number or name that is nowhere in the context The numbers check Wrong source A true sentence citing the wrong chunk Word support Dangling citation A citation to a chunk not in the context Citation resolution

docs.title: Why numbers get their own check
docs.text:
Answer Overlap with c3 Support check Numbers check "…allocate, and the default is 16." 100% passes passes "…allocate, and the default is 24." 88% passes fails

A wrong number is one token. In a sentence of eight content words that is 88% overlap, which sits above any threshold loose enough to allow paraphrase. A grounding check that is only a similarity score will pass fabricated numbers in exactly the answers that are long enough to sound authoritative.

The same argument applies to flag names, version strings and error codes, which is why the checker tokenizes keeping underscores.

docs.title: Prompt rules that make checking possible
docs.text:
Rule Why it exists Citation at the end of every sentence A paragraph-level citation cannot be verified per claim Split a sentence that needs two sources Makes fused claims structurally impossible to express Quote values verbatim, never convert Gives the numbers check something exact to match An explicit refusal string A refusal must be available, or the model fills the gap Sources numbered, not pasted raw The citation needs a stable label

Notice that four of the five are written for the benefit of the validator rather than the reader. That is the right way round: design the output format so it can be checked, then check it.

docs.title: Degrees of grounding, from cheap to strict
docs.text:
Level Check Cost Citation present Every sentence has an [id] trivial Citation resolves The id is in the context trivial Lexical support Content words appear in the cited chunk cheap, what this page builds Exact-value support Numbers and identifiers match verbatim cheap, highest value Entailment A model judges whether the source supports the claim expensive, needs its own evaluation Human review A person checks expensive, the only real ceiling

Lexical plus exact-value is the sweet spot: it runs in CI, costs nothing, and catches the failures that matter most in documentation. Entailment checking is better and introduces a second model whose errors you now also have to measure.

docs.title: What grounding does not give you
docs.text:
Claim Reality "The answer is correct" It is supported by the retrieved text. If the page is wrong, so is the answer "No hallucination" It bounds fabrication to what retrieval returned "The answer is complete" A grounded answer can omit the crucial caveat on another page "The citation is the right one" Lexical support is a proxy; a true sentence can cite a near-miss

The first row is the one to say out loud. Grounding inherits the corpus's errors, so it is a check on the pipeline and not on the documentation. That is what freshness monitoring and reading code to verify are for.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with the fused claim, because it is the failure that proves you have looked at real output. "Citations are not evidence of grounding. The failure I check for is a fused claim: the answer takes a flag name from one chunk and a default value from another and combines them into a sentence that is true of neither, with a citation attached. So every sentence carries exactly one citation, and a checker verifies the sentence's content words and every number against that specific chunk. The numbers check is separate, because a fabricated default inside a long sentence sits at 88% word overlap, which is above any threshold loose enough to allow paraphrase."

The follow-up is "what is your threshold and how did you pick it", and the honest answer is that a fixed word-overlap threshold is crude and you pick it from a labelled set. Too strict and legitimate paraphrase gets rejected, which trains people to disable the check; too loose and fused claims pass. The threshold is a parameter you measure, not a number you reason to, which is why this concept leads directly into output evaluation.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Strict grounding makes answers worse to read. A citation at the end of every sentence is noisy, the one-source-per-sentence rule forbids useful synthesis, and a model constrained this hard produces prose that reads like a quotation anthology. There is a real tension between an answer that is pleasant and an answer that is checkable, and for developer documentation checkable wins, because a wrong command costs more than an awkward paragraph. For a general-audience assistant that trade might go the other way.

One sharper point. The strongest observation is that grounding is the mechanism that makes an assistant's failures legible to the documentation team. An ungrounded-number rejection points at a specific chunk and a specific claim, which means your assistant's failure log is a list of pages where the content and the questions do not line up. Without grounding you have a pile of complaints; with it you have a prioritised content backlog. That reframes the work from AI safety into documentation prioritisation, and it is the framing a documentation lead will actually fund.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. The checker, plus a set of answers it rejects, including one that looks correct. The fused example is the one to show.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Five answers, four of which look right, three rejected for three different reasons. The number check passing "16" and rejecting "24" at 88% overlap is the moment that lands.
  2. Run it against real output. Take thirty answers from any documentation assistant you can query, and check them. Count the fused claims. That number is a finding nobody has.
  3. Put it in CI on a golden set. The checker plus twenty question-and-expected-source pairs, failing the build when the grounded rate drops. That is the step from a script to a gate.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Saying "we require citations" is near-universal and means almost nothing. A checker that rejects a fused claim carrying a valid citation, with the threshold justified from a labelled set, demonstrates that you know citations are not grounding.

docs.title: Guided workflows
docs.text:
A checklist that verifies each item instead of asking, and the sequencing mistake that doubles the round trips.

core · difficulty 3 · 5h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Encode standards (user stories, release readiness, onboarding, security guidance) into templates, validators, and guided workflows rather than static documents"

Prerequisites: Templates and scaffolding

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The third thing on NVIDIA's list, and the most ambitious. A template gives you a correctly shaped artifact. A validator tells you whether an artifact is correct. A guided workflow walks you through a process, checking as it goes, so that completing it is the same act as satisfying the standard.

The concrete form is usually a command rather than a page: release-check, onboard, new-integration. It replaces a checklist page where a human reads an item, decides whether it is done, and ticks it.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because a checklist asks a question the reader is badly placed to answer.

"Every page has a summary" is an item on a release checklist. The person reading it has to decide whether that is true, which means either checking 121 pages or guessing. Under deadline they guess, and the checklist records a yes that means "I did not look". A guided workflow answers the question instead of asking it, and the difference is not convenience: it is whether the record is true.

NVIDIA's phrase is again rather than static documents. The standard that exists as a page is a standard whose compliance is self-reported.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a release workflow, then discover that the obvious sequencing doubles the author's round trips. About thirty-five minutes.

Step 1: steps that verify instead of asking

class Blocked(Exception): pass

@step("every page has a summary")
def check_summaries(root):
    bad = [p.name for p in (root / "docs").glob("*.md")
           if "summary:" not in p.read_text()]
    if bad:
        raise Blocked(f"missing summary: {', '.join(bad)}")
    return f"{len(list((root / 'docs').glob('*.md')))} pages have a summary"


@step("the changelog mentions this version")
def check_changelog(root):
    version = (root / "VERSION").read_text().strip()
    if version not in (root / "CHANGELOG.md").read_text():
        raise Blocked(f"CHANGELOG.md does not mention {version}")
    return f"changelog covers {version}"

Three properties make these workflow steps rather than tests. Each has a human-readable name that reads like a checklist item. Each returns a detail on success, so the output is a record rather than a row of ticks. And each raises Blocked with the specific thing to fix, not an assertion failure.

Step 2: run it against a repository with three real problems

python3 release.py .

  [1/3] BLOCKED  every page has a summary
           missing summary: b.md

stopped at step 1. Fix the above and re-run.
exit=1

Precise and actionable. It names the file.

Step 3: count what that costs

Fix exactly what it reports, re-run, repeat, the way an author would:

  [1/3] BLOCKED  every page has a summary
  [2/3] BLOCKED  the changelog mentions this version
  [3/3] BLOCKED  no TODO markers in published pages
  all steps passed; ready to release
  runs needed: 4

Four runs for three defects. The workflow stopped at the first failure each time, so the author learned about one problem per round trip.

This is the && problem from documentation CI wearing different clothes, and it is harder to see here because a workflow feels like it ought to be sequential. It is a workflow; steps come in an order; stopping at a failure looks like correctness.

Step 4: ask which steps actually gate

A step gates when later steps genuinely cannot run without it. Checking the changelog does not depend on page summaries. Checking for TODO markers does not depend on either. All three are independent, and the sequence was an accident of how they were written down.

# A step gates when later steps genuinely cannot run without it.
GATES = set()

for i, fn in enumerate(STEPS, 1):
    try:
        results.append((i, fn.step_name, "ok", fn(root)))
    except Blocked as e:
        results.append((i, fn.step_name, "BLOCKED", str(e)))
        blocked.append(fn)
        if fn in GATES:
            break   # later steps depend on this one; stop here honestly

  blocked this run: 3
  blocked this run: 0
  runs needed: 2

Two runs instead of four, same defects, same fixes. The author saw all three problems at once and fixed them in one pass.

And GATES is empty here, which is the finding. Three steps in a sequence, and none of them actually gated anything.

Step 5: when a gate is real

Gates do exist. A workflow that creates a resource before configuring it genuinely cannot continue past a failed creation, and pretending otherwise produces a cascade of confusing secondary failures. The rule is that GATES is an explicit, short, justified list, and everything not in it runs.

The default most people write is the opposite: everything gates, because break on failure is the shortest code.

What you built. A workflow whose steps verify rather than ask, and an explicit distinction between sequence and dependency that halved the round trips.

docs.title: The three forms NVIDIA names
docs.text:
Form Gives you Tells you Walks you Template A correct artifact No No Validator No Whether it is correct No Guided workflow Sometimes Yes, per step Yes

A guided workflow is usually built on the other two: its steps call the validators, and some of them scaffold.

docs.title: Checklist against guided workflow
docs.text:
Checklist page Guided workflow Who determines done The reader The step Record Self-reported Observed Under deadline Guessed Unchanged Cost to add an item A line of prose A function Catches a regression No Yes Teaches the standard By being read By blocking

The bottom row is the sneaky benefit. A workflow that blocks with a specific message is the most reliably read documentation you will ever write, because the reader is stuck and motivated.

docs.title: What makes a step a good workflow step
docs.text: Property Why A name that reads as a checklist item The output is a record people trust A detail on success, not just a tick "121 pages have a summary" beats "ok" The specific thing to fix on failure A finding you cannot act on is a chore Deterministic A flaky step destroys the whole workflow's credibility Fast, or explicitly slow A step that takes four minutes needs saying so Independent unless genuinely gating See steps 3 and 4

docs.title: Sequence against dependency
docs.text:
Situation Behaviour Later steps read what this one creates A real gate; stop Later steps need this one's credentials or state A real gate; stop Steps check unrelated properties Not a gate; run them all Steps are ordered by convention Not a gate; run them all

The third and fourth rows are the common case and the one people get wrong.

docs.title: Where guided workflows pay
docs.text:
Process Workflow replaces Release readiness A checklist page Writer onboarding "Getting started for contributors" New integration or service A wiki page of steps Incident response A playbook, when the steps are mechanical Content audit A spreadsheet

The incident row has a boundary worth respecting. When the steps are mechanical, automate them; when the next step depends on judgment about observations, that is a playbook, and forcing it into a linear workflow loses the routing that made it valuable.

docs.title: What this is not
docs.text: It is not a test suite, even though it calls the same checks. A test suite answers "is the repository correct" for a machine; a guided workflow answers "what do I do next" for a person, with names, details and a record. The same function can serve both, and the presentation is the difference.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the self-report problem. "A checklist asks the reader to decide whether an item is done, which means checking 121 pages or guessing, and under deadline it is a guess. A guided workflow answers the question instead of asking it, so the record means something. That is why NVIDIA says workflows rather than static documents."

The follow-up is sequencing, and it is the measurement worth bringing. The obvious implementation stops at the first failure, which looks like correctness and cost me four runs for three defects. Separating sequence from dependency, and finding that none of my three steps actually gated anything, took it to two. Everything not in an explicit GATES list runs.

The tradeoff to volunteer. A guided workflow is a program with a user interface, and that is a bigger commitment than a checklist page. It needs maintaining, its failure messages are documentation that will go stale, and a flaky step poisons trust in the whole thing. On a process run twice a year by one person, the page is the right answer; it starts paying when the process is frequent, or when the cost of a skipped step is high.

One sharper point. The failure messages are the most-read documentation you will ever write. A reader hitting a blocked step is stuck and motivated, which is a state no documentation page ever gets its audience into. Treat those strings as prose, name the specific file, and say what to do, because that is the sentence that actually teaches the standard.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A workflow command in a repository of yours, with named steps, details on success, specific failures, and an explicit GATES list.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path and count the runs in step 3 before reading step 4.
  2. Take your most-used checklist and convert the two items most often self-reported as done. Those are the two that are least true.
  3. Audit any multi-step script you own for the sequence-versus-dependency distinction. Most break-on-failure loops are not gating anything. Expect most of them to be gating nothing. In this guide's own release workflow exactly one step of seven genuinely gates the rest, and the other six were sequential by accident.

docs.title: The same measurement, on a real command
docs.text:
fieldguide release-check is this design built for this repository: seven named steps, each returning a detail on success and a specific remedy on failure, with an explicit GATES set in src/fieldguide/release.py.

  [1/7] ok       the registry parses
           106 concepts and 9 paths loaded from concepts.yaml
  [4/7] ok       every generated page is up to date
           13 generated pages match the registry
  [7/7] ok       every committed drill still prints what its page quotes
           26 page-and-drill contract(s) hold

all 7 steps passed; ready to release

drills/release_rounds.py runs the round-trip experiment against it, by the method above: copy the repository, plant three independent defects (a hand-edited generated page, an unclosed fence, unparseable front matter), then fix exactly what each run reports and count the runs.

everything gates, which is what break-on-failure does:
  run 1: blocked 1 of 6
  run 2: blocked 1 of 6
  run 3: blocked 1 of 6
  run 4: blocked 0 of 6
  runs needed: 4

one real gate, which is what fieldguide release-check does:
  run 1: blocked 3 of 6
  run 2: blocked 0 of 6
  runs needed: 2

Four against two, on the real command, for the same reason. The toy workflow above and a seven-step command over a hundred-page corpus produce the same ratio, because the ratio is a property of the gating decision rather than of the workflow's size.

One thing came out differently, and it is the more useful result. GATES is not empty here. Exactly one step gates: every other step calls load_registry, so a registry that will not parse turns the remaining six into six secondary failures about a file none of them could read. Gates are real. They are just far rarer than sequential code implies, and the honest number for this workflow is one in seven rather than zero in three.

Writing that step also produced a small lesson in naming. The step is called "the registry parses" and its first version caught the registry's own validation error and not yaml.YAMLError, so the commonest way a registry fails to parse walked straight past the step named after it. A test caught it. A step's name is a claim about what it checks, and the two drift apart as quietly as anything else on a page.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. The command exists, runs in CI, and its steps check real properties of a real corpus; the demonstrated page records it. The distinction from fieldguide check is the point: that is a validator, which reports everything at once and says nothing about what to do next, and both are worth having for different readers. What travels beyond this repository is the measurement, four runs against two for the same three defects, and the finding that six of seven steps in an apparently sequential process do not gate the next one.

docs.title: Hallucination and guardrails
docs.text:
Why a grounded system still invents things, and the layered checks that bound the damage.

supporting · difficulty 3 · 4h

sound judgment about where AI can be trusted

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: Grounding and citation, Output evaluation

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A hallucination is a fluent, confident claim with nothing behind it. A guardrail is a mechanism that catches one before a reader acts on it.

The useful framing is not "stop hallucination", which is not available. It is bound the damage and make the failures visible, which is.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA asks for "sound judgment about where AI can be trusted" and for "human review where judgment matters". Both are about this. The posting never uses the word hallucination, which is why the tag is quoted on a different phrase: they are asking about the behaviour rather than the vocabulary.

What makes this supporting rather than core is that most of the work lives in grounding and output evaluation. This page is the taxonomy that tells you which of those mechanisms to reach for, plus the failure modes neither catches.

On a Tuesday it is a specific, nasty class of ticket. A developer says the assistant told them to pass --retry-budget, which does not exist. The flag name is plausible, the sentence was well formed, and the cited page is real. Grounding caught nothing, because the fabricated flag sat inside a sentence otherwise copied from the real page, so it was one unmatched word among several that matched. That is the case the layered guardrails below exist for, and the golden path reproduces it.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a layered guardrail and find what each layer catches that the others miss. Thirty-five minutes, dependency-free.

Committed as drills/guardrails.py, which stages these files and runs this page's run.py in one go. Two tests hold it to the page: the five files must still match what is written here, and the results table below must still be the matrix the code produces.

Step 1: five answers, each wrong in a different way

mkdir -p guard-drill && cd guard-drill
cat > context.json <<'EOF'
{
  "c3": "max_memory_gb caps the GPU memory the server will allocate. The default is 16.",
  "c6": "Pass --dry-run to preview changes without applying them.",
  "c1": "batch_size controls how many requests are grouped per forward pass. The default is 32."
}
EOF

cat > known.json <<'EOF'
{
  "flags": ["--dry-run", "--config", "--verbose", "max_memory_gb", "batch_size"],
  "versions": ["2.0", "2.2", "2.4", "2.6"]
}
EOF

cat > answers.json <<'EOF'
[
  {"label": "correct",
   "text": "Pass --dry-run to preview changes. [c6]"},
  {"label": "flag-bare",
   "text": "Pass --retry-budget to bound retries. [c6]"},
  {"label": "flag-camouflaged",
   "text": "Pass --retry-budget to preview changes without applying them. [c6]"},
  {"label": "flag-appended",
   "text": "max_memory_gb caps the GPU memory the server will allocate, and --memory-strict enforces it. [c3]"},
  {"label": "invented-number",
   "text": "max_memory_gb defaults to 24. [c3]"},
  {"label": "invented-version",
   "text": "This requires widget 3.1 or newer. [c3]"},
  {"label": "plausible-fusion",
   "text": "max_memory_gb defaults to 32. [c3]"},
  {"label": "evasive",
   "text": "Set the memory ceiling in the configuration file. [c3]"}
]
EOF
python3 -c "import json; print(len(json.load(open('answers.json'))), 'answers')"

Read those eight. Every one is fluent. Six are wrong and one is evasive.

The three flag-* cases are the same fabrication, --retry-budget or --memory-strict, surrounded by different amounts of real text. That variation is the experiment.

Step 2: four layers, cheapest first

cat > guards.py <<'PY'
"""Four guardrail layers, in increasing cost, each catching what the
previous one cannot.

The ordering is the design. A cheap deterministic check that runs on every
answer is worth more than an expensive check that runs on a sample, because
the cheap one cannot be skipped under deadline pressure.

  1 GROUNDING    content words and numbers against the cited chunk
  2 VOCABULARY   every flag and version against a KNOWN-GOOD list
  3 SPECIFICITY  an answer that avoids the question rather than refusing
  4 ABSTENTION   was a refusal available, and did the model take it

Layer 2 is the one that catches the flag-name fabrication, and it is the one
most teams do not have, because it needs a list of real identifiers that
nothing else in the pipeline requires.
"""
import json
import re

CITATION = re.compile(r"\[(\w+)\]")
FLAG = re.compile(r"(?<![\w-])(--[a-z][a-z0-9-]*|[a-z][a-z0-9]*(?:_[a-z0-9]+)+)")
VERSION = re.compile(r"\bwidget (\d+\.\d+)\b", re.I)
NUMBER = re.compile(r"\b\d+(?:\.\d+)?\b")

STOP = {
    "the", "a", "an", "to", "is", "are", "of", "in", "on", "for", "with",
    "and", "or", "it", "its", "set", "pass", "without", "by", "this", "that",
    "will", "can", "you", "your", "not", "from", "which", "default", "defaults",
}
SUPPORT_THRESHOLD = 0.6

#: Phrases that describe an action without naming it. A model that cannot
#: find the answer and will not refuse produces these.
VAGUE = (
    "in the configuration file", "in the settings", "as appropriate",
    "the relevant", "accordingly", "as needed", "the appropriate",
)
REFUSAL = "i could not find this in the documentation"


def words(text):
    return [
        w for w in re.findall(r"[a-z0-9_-]+", text.lower())
        if w not in STOP and len(w) > 1
    ]


def guard_grounding(answer, context, known):
    """Layer 1: is the claim supported by the chunk it cites?"""
    findings = []
    cited = CITATION.findall(answer)
    body = CITATION.sub("", answer).strip()
    if not cited:
        return [("uncited", "no citation")]

    source = " ".join(context.get(c, "") for c in cited)
    source_words = set(words(source))
    present = [w for w in words(body) if w in source_words]
    ratio = len(present) / len(words(body)) if words(body) else 1.0
    if ratio < SUPPORT_THRESHOLD:
        findings.append(("unsupported", f"{ratio:.0%} of content words in {cited}"))

    absent = set(NUMBER.findall(body)) - set(NUMBER.findall(source))
    if absent:
        findings.append(("ungrounded-number", f"{sorted(absent)} not in {cited}"))
    return findings


def guard_vocabulary(answer, context, known):
    """Layer 2: does every identifier and version actually exist?

    This is the layer that catches a fabricated flag name. Grounding cannot:
    a plausible flag is a single unmatched content word, which sits inside
    any support threshold loose enough to allow paraphrase.
    """
    findings = []
    body = CITATION.sub("", answer)
    for flag in set(FLAG.findall(body)):
        if flag not in known["flags"]:
            findings.append(("unknown-identifier", f"{flag!r} is not a real flag"))
    for version in set(VERSION.findall(body)):
        if version not in known["versions"]:
            findings.append(("unknown-version", f"widget {version} does not exist"))
    return findings


def guard_specificity(answer, context, known):
    """Layer 3: is the answer avoiding the question?"""
    lowered = answer.lower()
    if lowered.strip().startswith(REFUSAL):
        return []
    for phrase in VAGUE:
        if phrase in lowered:
            return [("evasive", f"says {phrase!r} instead of naming the thing")]
    return []


def guard_abstention(answer, context, known):
    """Layer 4: did it answer when it should have refused?

    Heuristic and deliberately weak: if the answer names no identifier and no
    number and is not a refusal, it has probably asserted something it could
    not support. Reported as a warning, never as a hard failure.
    """
    body = CITATION.sub("", answer).lower()
    if body.strip().startswith(REFUSAL):
        return []
    if not FLAG.search(body) and not NUMBER.search(body):
        return [("unspecific", "no identifier or value; a refusal may have been correct")]
    return []


LAYERS = [
    ("grounding", guard_grounding),
    ("vocabulary", guard_vocabulary),
    ("specificity", guard_specificity),
    ("abstention", guard_abstention),
]


def check(answer, context, known):
    out = []
    for name, layer in LAYERS:
        for kind, why in layer(answer, context, known):
            out.append((name, kind, why))
    return out
PY
echo "guards written"

Step 3: run every layer against every answer

cat > run.py <<'PY'
import json

from guards import LAYERS, check

context = json.load(open("context.json"))
known = json.load(open("known.json"))
answers = json.load(open("answers.json"))

for answer in answers:
    findings = check(answer["text"], context, known)
    verdict = "PASS" if not findings else "REJECT"
    print(f"{verdict:<7} [{answer['label']}] {answer['text']}")
    for layer, kind, why in findings:
        print(f"        {layer}/{kind}: {why}")
    print()

print("=" * 68)
print("which layer caught each failure, and which layers alone would miss it")
print("=" * 68)
header = f"{'answer':<30}" + "".join(f"{n[:9]:>11}" for n, _ in LAYERS)
print(header)
print("-" * len(header))
for answer in answers:
    row = f"{answer['label']:<30}"
    for name, layer in LAYERS:
        hit = layer(answer["text"], context, known)
        row += f"{('CAUGHT' if hit else '-'):>11}"
    print(row)
PY
python3 run.py

What you built. Four layers and a matrix showing which one catches each failure. Here is what it reports:

answer grounding vocabulary specificity abstention correct - - - - flag-bare CAUGHT CAUGHT - - flag-camouflaged - CAUGHT - - flag-appended - CAUGHT - - invented-number CAUGHT - - - invented-version CAUGHT CAUGHT - - plausible-fusion CAUGHT - - - evasive CAUGHT - CAUGHT CAUGHT

The two bolded rows are the whole point, and they are the reason this page needed three variants of one fabrication rather than one.

flag-bare invents --retry-budget in a short sentence that shares almost nothing with its cited chunk, so the fabricated flag is most of the content and grounding catches it at 0% support.

flag-camouflaged invents the same flag inside a sentence otherwise copied from the source: "Pass --retry-budget to preview changes without applying them." Grounding passes it. The fabrication is one unmatched word among several that match, which sits comfortably inside any support threshold loose enough to permit paraphrase.

flag-appended does the same thing by addition: a correct sentence about max_memory_gb with "and --memory-strict enforces it" bolted on. Grounding passes that too.

Only the vocabulary layer catches either, and it catches both trivially, because --retry-budget and --memory-strict are simply not in the list of real flags.

Note also that no row is caught by every layer and no layer catches every row. invented-number and plausible-fusion are invisible to the vocabulary check, since 24 and 32 are not identifiers. That non-overlap is what makes this layered rather than a choice between mechanisms.

docs.title: A taxonomy that maps to fixes
docs.text:
Failure Looks like Caught by Uncited claim A plausible sentence, no source Grounding Fused claim Two true facts combined into a false one Grounding, word support Invented value A number nowhere in the context Grounding, numbers check Invented identifier A flag or method that follows your naming conventions A known-good vocabulary list Invented version "requires 3.1" for a product at 2.6 A known-good version list Stale truth Correct in March, wrong now A freshness field, monitoring Evasive answer "Set it in the configuration file" A specificity check Confident non-refusal An answer where a refusal was correct Abstention rate, sampling Wrong because the page is wrong Perfectly grounded, still wrong Verify against code

The identifier row is the one worth building for. It is the most damaging failure in developer documentation, because a plausible flag name costs a reader twenty minutes of trying it. And grounding catches it only when the fabrication is bare: surround it with text copied from the source and the support ratio stays high, as the golden path's flag-camouflaged and flag-appended cases demonstrate. Grounding is not useless here, it is unreliable here, which is worse, because it looks like coverage.

docs.title: Where the known-good list comes from
docs.text:
You already have it, which is why this check is cheaper than it sounds:

Source Gives you --help output, parsed Every real flag An OpenAPI document Every real endpoint and parameter inspect.signature over the public API Every real function and keyword Git tags Every real version The content model's closed vocabularies Every real page type and audience

Generating that list in CI from the artifact that defines it means it cannot drift, which is the same argument as generated reference.

docs.title: The layers, and what each costs
docs.text:
Layer Catches Cost Runs on Grounding Fusion, invented values trivial every answer Known-good vocabulary Invented identifiers and versions trivial every answer Specificity Evasion trivial every answer Abstention rate Non-refusals, in aggregate cheap a dashboard LLM-as-judge entailment Subtler unsupported claims expensive a sample Human review Everything, including a wrong corpus expensive a sample

Order matters more than coverage. A trivial check on every answer beats a sophisticated check on a sample, because the sampled check is the one that stops running when the team is busy.

docs.title: Why abstention deserves a metric
docs.text:
A model that will not refuse fabricates. Measuring the refusal rate is the cheapest early warning available:

Symptom Likely cause Refusal rate near zero No refusal path in the prompt, or the model is overriding it Refusal rate very high Retrieval is failing, not the generation Refusal rate falls after a prompt change You probably made fabrication more likely

Track it on a dashboard. It is one number, and it moves before the complaints arrive.

docs.title: What none of this fixes
docs.text:
Limit Consequence A wrong page A perfectly grounded answer repeating a wrong default A stale page Confidently correct as of eighteen months ago Missing content The model fills a gap it cannot know is a gap Omission Every claim true, the crucial caveat absent

The last row has no good mechanical check and is the most common real harm: an answer about rotating a key that never mentions the one-hour overlap window. Only a person who knows the subject catches that, which is what review is for and why judging where AI can be trusted keeps high-cost tasks away from models entirely.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with the identifier case, because it shows you have debugged a real system rather than read about hallucination. "Grounding catches fused claims and invented numbers. Where it gets unreliable is a fabricated identifier, and specifically a camouflaged one: invent a flag in a sentence otherwise copied from the source and the support ratio stays high, so it passes. I tested the same fabrication bare, camouflaged and appended; grounding caught one of three. So I check every flag and version in an answer against a known-good list generated in CI from --help output and git tags. That list already exists; nothing else in the pipeline was using it."

The follow-up is "can you eliminate hallucination", and the answer is no, followed by the reframing that matters: you bound it and you make it visible. Bounding is grounding plus vocabulary checks, which confine fabrication to things that exist. Visibility is an abstention metric and a sampled human read, so the failures you cannot check mechanically still get counted. A candidate who claims elimination has not operated one of these.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Every guardrail increases refusals, and refusals have a cost that nobody measures. An assistant tuned hard enough to never fabricate will decline questions it could have answered, and users stop asking, and the project is judged a failure for being useless rather than for being wrong. That failure is quieter and just as fatal. The honest position is that there is a dial between fabrication and unhelpfulness, your guardrails set where it sits, and you should know your refusal rate as precisely as your error rate.

One sharper point. The strongest observation is that a hallucination in a documentation assistant is usually a content report. A model asked about retry budgets with nothing in the corpus about retry budgets will invent --retry-budget, and the invention is shaped by the gap. So the fabrication log, grouped by subject, is a ranked list of the pages you have not written, derived from real reader questions. Teams treat that log as a safety problem; it is also the most honest documentation backlog you will ever get, and reframing it that way is what gets the work funded.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A vocabulary guardrail whose known-good list is generated in CI, plus the layer matrix showing what each catches.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. The matrix is the demonstration: the same fabricated flag caught bare and missed when camouflaged, with only the vocabulary layer catching all three variants. That is the clearest reason layering is not optional.
  2. Generate a real known-good list. Parse --help from any CLI you have, or inspect.signature over a library's public API. Twenty lines, and it turns this page from a concept into a check you own.
  3. Measure your refusal rate. If you have any assistant over documentation, count what fraction of answers are refusals. A rate near zero is the finding, and almost nobody has the number.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Discussing hallucination is unfalsifiable. A vocabulary check against a CI-generated identifier list, a layer matrix showing grounding catching a fabricated flag in one phrasing and missing it in two others, and a refusal-rate number, demonstrates that you measured the failure rather than worried about it.
