docs.title: Giving architecture owners implementation feedback
docs.text:
Reporting what broke when you built someone else's design, in a form they can act on.

core · difficulty 2 · 3h

sharing implementation feedback (what works, breaks, and scales) to refine content models, information architecture, and AI-readiness patterns

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: A systems mindset

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Telling the person who designed a standard what happened when you applied it at scale, specifically enough that they can change the design. Not escalating a complaint, and not quietly working around it.

The useful unit is an instance with a count: this rule, this many pages, this failure, this proposal.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
This is the most distinctive thing in the NVIDIA posting and the easiest to skim past. Read the two bullets together:

"Collaborate with documentation leads on knowledge architecture, sharing implementation feedback (what works, breaks, and scales) to refine content models, information architecture, and AI-readiness patterns."

"A collaborative style: you turn design intent into working systems and give leads clear, constructive feedback grounded in implementation."

The role is explicitly the implementer advising the architects. Documentation leads own the content model; you apply it to thousands of pages and find out where it does not hold. That split is deliberate, and it means the job has a built-in feedback obligation. You are not expected to accept a standard you have discovered is wrong, and you are not authorised to change it unilaterally either.

On a Tuesday this is a specific recurring moment. The content model requires an audience field with four allowed values. You apply it across the Omniverse corpus and find 180 pages that are genuinely for two audiences at once, and another 40 where the honest answer is a fifth value nobody anticipated. You can pick the closest value and move on, which corrupts the data quietly. You can block on it, which stops the migration. Or you can report it in a form the lead can decide from, which is the job.

The reason this is core: the quality of this feedback loop determines whether the standards improve or ossify. A lead who only hears "done" learns nothing from a migration that touched three thousand pages.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Turn a real friction into a report someone can decide from. Thirty minutes, and the artifact is the deliverable.

Step 1: hit the friction and resist both reflexes

mkdir -p feedback-drill && cd feedback-drill
cat > friction.md <<'EOF'
THE STANDARD   Every page declares exactly one `audience`, from:
               new-user | developer | operator | contributor

WHAT HAPPENED  Applying it to 260 pages:
                 - 180 pages are honestly two audiences
                 - 40 pages are for partners, which is not a value
                 - 40 pages fit cleanly

THE TWO WRONG REFLEXES
  Pick the closest value and move on.
      -> the field now contains guesses. Every downstream filter is
         subtly wrong and nobody can tell.
  Block the migration and wait for a decision.
      -> three thousand pages stalled on a taxonomy question.
EOF
cat friction.md

Step 2: get a number, because a number is what makes it a design question

An anecdote is a complaint. A count is evidence.

mkdir -p docs
python3 - <<'PY'
# Stand in for a real corpus scan. In practice this reads your pages and
# classifies them; what matters is that the output is counts, not opinions.
import json, pathlib
findings = {
    "total_pages": 260,
    "single_audience_clean": 40,
    "two_audiences_honestly": 180,
    "audience_not_in_vocabulary": 40,
    "examples": {
        "two_audiences": [
            "install/requirements.md  (new-user and operator)",
            "usd/schema-basics.md     (developer and contributor)",
        ],
        "missing_value": [
            "partners/certification.md",
            "partners/branding.md",
        ],
    },
}
pathlib.Path("findings.json").write_text(json.dumps(findings, indent=2))
print(json.dumps(findings, indent=2)[:400], "...")
PY

Step 3: write the report in the shape a decision-maker can use

Five parts, in this order. The order is the content: the proposal comes after the evidence, and the recommendation comes last so it is clearly separable from the facts.

cat > report.md <<'EOF'
# Content model: the `audience` field does not survive the Omniverse corpus

## What I did
Applied the content model to 260 pages in `omniverse/`, the first corpus large
enough to test the closed vocabulary.

## What happened
| Outcome | Pages |
|---|---|
| One audience, cleanly | 40 |
| Honestly two audiences | 180 |
| Audience not in the vocabulary (partners) | 40 |

69% of pages cannot satisfy the field as written. Examples:
- `install/requirements.md` is read by new users and by operators, and the
  page is correct for both.
- `partners/certification.md` has no available value.

## What I think is happening
The field conflates two things: *who the page is written for* (one answer, a
real editorial decision) and *who reads it* (several answers, an observation).
The vocabulary is right for the first and is being asked to do the second.

## Options, with what each costs
| Option | Cost | Who pays |
|---|---|---|
| Allow a list of audiences | Every filter becomes a set operation; navigation needs a primary anyway | Tooling, once |
| Add `primary_audience` plus optional `also_read_by` | One more field; migration can default the second to empty | Authors, slightly |
| Add `partner` to the vocabulary | Solves 40 pages, not the 180 | Nobody, but it is a partial fix |
| Keep as is, authors pick the closest | Free today; the field silently becomes unreliable | Every downstream consumer, forever |

## What I would do
`primary_audience` plus optional `also_read_by`. It keeps the editorial
decision single-valued, which is what navigation and retrieval filters need,
and it stops authors guessing. I can migrate the 260 pages in a day with the
primary inferred from the directory and `also_read_by` left empty.

I am not blocking on this: I will hold the Omniverse migration for a week and
proceed with the other corpora, which do not hit it.
EOF
wc -l report.md

Step 4: check it against the test that matters

cat > test.md <<'EOF'
Can the lead decide from this without talking to me?

[x] Is there a number?                      69% of 260 pages
[x] Can they see the actual pages?          two examples per case
[x] Is my diagnosis separable from the data? "What I think is happening"
[x] Are the options costed?                  table, with who pays
[x] Is my recommendation last and labelled?  "What I would do"
[x] Do they know what happens if they say nothing?  holding one week
EOF
cat test.md

What you built. A report that is decidable without a meeting. The last line of the checklist is the one people forget: a lead needs to know the default outcome if they do nothing, because that is what converts your report from a question into a decision with a deadline.

docs.title: The five parts, and why the order matters
docs.text:
Part Purpose What I did Scope, so they know how much the finding generalises What happened Counts and examples. No interpretation yet What I think is happening Your diagnosis, clearly marked as yours Options, costed Shows you understand the design space, not just your preference What I would do Last, so it is separable. A recommendation, not a conclusion

Putting the recommendation first reads as advocacy, and a lead who disagrees with it discounts the evidence behind it. Putting it last lets them reach a different conclusion from the same facts without overruling you.

docs.title: What makes feedback actionable
docs.text: Actionable Not actionable "180 of 260 pages are two audiences" "The audience field is awkward" "Here are two example pages" "Lots of pages have this problem" "Option A costs tooling work once" "We should allow multiple values" "I am holding one corpus for a week" "Let me know what you think" "This is the first corpus large enough to test it" "This has always been a problem"

docs.title: Things worth reporting that people do not
docs.text:
Report Why it is valuable A standard that worked better than expected Leads hear only about breakage and over-correct A rule nobody violated in 3,000 pages It may be unnecessary, and removing it is cheap A validator whose warnings are universally ignored A dead gate is worse than none The cost of a rule in author time Nobody measures this and it is the main objection Where the model held under scale "What works" is in the posting's own phrasing

That last row is in the quote and is the part almost everybody drops. "What works, breaks, and scales" is three things.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text: Failure What it causes Silent workaround Data corruption nobody can trace. The worst one Blocking on every ambiguity You become the reason the migration stalled Reporting friction without counts Reads as a complaint, gets deferred Arriving with one option Reads as a demand; leads defend the status quo Reporting only failures The lead over-corrects a working standard No default if they do nothing Your report joins a backlog

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Tell it as a report, with the number first. "The content model required one audience per page. Applying it to 260 pages, 69 percent either had two honest audiences or had none in the vocabulary. I wrote it up with the counts, example pages, three options with their costs, and my recommendation last, and I kept the other corpora moving while the lead decided. We ended up splitting the field into a primary and an optional secondary."

The follow-up is "what if the lead disagrees with you", which is testing whether you can be overruled gracefully. The answer worth giving: implement their decision properly and instrument it. If you believed the field would become unreliable, add a check that measures how often authors pick the closest value rather than a true one, and report the number in six months. That is disagreeing with evidence rather than with insistence, and it is the only form of disagreement that survives a difference in authority.

The tradeoff to volunteer. This kind of report costs an hour to write and it is an hour you are not migrating pages. There is a real version of this job where you write careful reports about everything and ship nothing, and a lead will notice. The filter is scale: report what you found because you did the work at volume, and absorb what is merely awkward. A finding that only appears at 260 pages is worth an hour; a rule you personally find annoying is not.

One sharper point. The structural value of this role is that the implementer sees things the architect cannot. A content model is a hypothesis about a corpus, and the corpus is the only thing that can falsify it. Saying that out loud reframes the feedback obligation from politeness to epistemics, which is much closer to how NVIDIA's posting describes it, and it explains why they wanted this as a named requirement rather than assuming it.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. One written report in the five-part shape, about something real. It can be from any context: a schema you applied, a lint rule you rolled out, a convention you migrated to.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Find a standard you worked around rather than reported. Everyone has one. Write the report retroactively, with the count. The exercise is the point. If the count is zero, you have not looked at a wide enough window: the workaround nobody reported is the one that has been in place longest.
  2. Report something that worked. Harder than it sounds, and the rarest thing in this category. Find a rule that held up under scale and say so with a number.
  3. Find one dead gate. A check whose warnings nobody acts on. Propose removing it. Removing a rule is the clearest possible demonstration that your feedback is about the system rather than about your preferences.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. "I give constructive feedback" is unfalsifiable. A one-page report with a percentage, two example files, a costed options table and a recommendation at the bottom is a thing an interviewer can read in two minutes and immediately recognise as the output of someone who has done this.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
The whole concept is a conversation with someone who owns a design, so the evidence is in their repository, their review threads and their decisions, not in yours.

Where the skill is exercised. When documenting a feature reveals that the feature is confusing, and you have to decide whether to write a clearer page or say the design is wrong. In a review comment that proposes a product change rather than a wording change. In being right about it often enough to be asked next time.

What a learner would do. Keep a log, for a month, of every time documentation work surfaced something that was not a documentation problem:

what I was documenting     what I found                  what I did
the retry flag             two flags do the same thing    filed a bug
the error codes            404 and 410 are inconsistent   wrote around it
the setup steps            step 3 exists for a bug        proposed removal

Then count the third column. Most people find they wrote around nearly all of it, which is the finding: documentation work is the most reliable source of design feedback in an organisation and the least likely to be delivered as feedback, because writing around a problem is faster and feels like the job.

What competence looks like.

Evidence Why it carries weight A product change traceable to a docs review The strongest and rarest A bug filed from writing a page The habit, present A design review you were invited into Earned by prior accuracy Feedback given and declined, recorded without rancour Shows the relationship survived A page you did write around, and said why Honest about the tradeoff

The specific skill, which is what to make checkable. Feedback lands when it is phrased as a reader's observed difficulty rather than as an opinion about the design. "This is confusing" is an opinion. "Documenting this takes four paragraphs to explain which of two flags to use, and here is the draft" is an observation with the evidence attached, and it is hard to argue with because the draft is the argument.

Why it does not commit to a repository. A single-author project has no architecture owner to give feedback to. Even in a team, the artifact is a decision in someone else's system, and the part that demonstrates skill, that the feedback was accepted and acted on, is precisely the part you do not control. This is why the concept stays craft and why this guide claims no demonstration of it.

docs.title: Inference serving and microservices
docs.text:
Batching bought 14x throughput and cost 21x latency, and past a knee at batch 16 it bought nothing and still cost.

context · difficulty 2 · 4h

Asked for by name

Intel: "including inference microservices and the agentic toolkit"

Leads to: Reading an AI software stack

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Putting a trained model behind a network interface so other services can use it. The model is fixed; everything interesting is the serving layer: batching, queueing, concurrency, warm-up, and which number you promise.

Intel's phrase is "inference microservices", which is the current packaging: the model, a runtime, a server and a health check shipped as a container with an endpoint. The documentation obligations follow from that being an operable service rather than a library.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because the thing a reader has to get right is a tradeoff, and tradeoffs are where documentation either earns its keep or misleads at scale.

An inference service has two performance numbers that move in opposite directions. Vendors publish the flattering one. A reader who deploys against the published figure and then watches their p99 is the single most common support path in this area, and the fix is almost always a configuration decision that a page could have explained.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Measure latency against throughput on a real runtime, and find the point where the tradeoff stops being a tradeoff. About thirty minutes, CPU only, no model download.

Step 1: a real model on a real runtime

ONNX Runtime, with two matmuls big enough that compute dominates:

g = helper.make_graph(
    [helper.make_node("MatMul", ["x", "w1"], ["h"]),
     helper.make_node("Relu", ["h"], ["hr"]),
     helper.make_node("MatMul", ["hr", "w2"], ["y"])], "mlp", ...)
sess = ort.InferenceSession("big.onnx", providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"])

model: 33.6 MB of weights, two 1024x4096 matmuls

Step 2: sweep the batch size and report both numbers

The column that matters is the last one. Requests arriving at 500 per second have to wait for a batch to fill before it runs, so the latency a request experiences is that wait plus the compute:

  batch  batch ms   per-req ms   throughput   wait for a full batch   total latency
                    (compute)      req/s      at 500 req/s             p50 ms
      1      1.51       1.51          662                0.0             1.5
      2      1.43       0.72         1398                2.0             3.4
      4      1.45       0.36         2765                6.0             7.4
      8      1.55       0.19         5164               14.0            15.5
     16      1.69       0.11         9448               30.0            31.7
     32      3.42       0.11         9370               62.0            65.4
     64      6.78       0.11         9439              126.0           132.8

Three things are in that table and only one of them usually gets published.

Throughput rises 14x, from 662 to 9,448 requests per second. That is the number in the benchmark.

Per-request compute falls 14x, from 1.51 ms to 0.11 ms. That is the number in the datasheet, and it is true: once a batch is running, each request's share of the work really is 0.11 ms.

The latency a request experiences rises 21x, from 1.5 ms to 31.7 ms, because it spent 30 ms waiting for nineteen strangers to arrive. No request anywhere in the system ever experienced 0.11 ms.

Step 3: find the knee

Past batch 16, throughput stops moving: 9,448, then 9,370, then 9,439. Within noise, identical. Latency keeps climbing: 31.7 ms, 65.4, 132.8.

batch 16 -> 64:   throughput  +0%        latency  +4x

So there is a configuration that is simply wrong rather than a tradeoff. The machine saturated at 16, and every batch size above it pays latency for nothing. A reader cannot deduce where that knee is, because it depends on the model, the hardware and the arrival rate, which is exactly why the documentation's job is to tell them to measure it rather than to publish a default.

Step 4: the number to promise

Given the table, the honest commitment is a pair with an arrival rate attached:

at 500 req/s, batch 16:  ~9,400 req/s capacity, p50 latency 31.7 ms
at 500 req/s, batch 1:   ~660 req/s capacity,  p50 latency 1.5 ms

Either row is defensible. "0.11 ms per request" is not, although it is arithmetically true, which is what makes it the most effective misleading number in this field.

What you built. A measured latency-throughput curve on a real runtime, a saturation knee past which batching is pure loss, and three defensible ways to state the result instead of one flattering one.

docs.title: The numbers, and what each one hides
docs.text:
Number True when Hides Throughput, req/s Under sustained load What any one request waited Per-request compute Inside a running batch The queue p50 latency Half the time The tail that pages someone p99 latency The number users feel Cost, since it drives headroom Time to first token Streaming models Total completion time Cold-start latency The first request after a scale-up Everything, on bursty traffic

A service characterised by one of these is characterised by none of them. The pair worth documenting is a latency percentile at a stated arrival rate.

docs.title: Batching strategies
docs.text:
Strategy Latency Throughput Use None, one request per call Best Worst Interactive, low volume Fixed batch, wait to fill Worst Best Offline and bulk Dynamic batch with a timeout Bounded Most of the gain The usual right answer Continuous or in-flight batching Good Best, for generative Token-by-token models

The timeout in row three is the parameter that makes the tradeoff tunable, and it is the one most often left at a default nobody measured.

docs.title: What an inference microservice has to document
docs.text:
Item Why The latency-throughput curve, with arrival rate Otherwise the reader picks a batch size blind The saturation point Above it, configuration is loss, not tradeoff Cold-start time Determines whether autoscaling can work Warm-up requirement First-call latency is often 10x Input shape and dtype contract The commonest integration failure Health against readiness A loaded model is not a ready one Memory per replica, at the chosen batch Capacity planning needs it Version of model, runtime and server Three numbers, see the stack

Rows six and seven are the ones that turn a demo into something operable, and they are the ones a research-led team is least likely to write.

docs.title: Health against readiness
docs.text:
Probe Should mean Liveness The process is not wedged Readiness The model is loaded and warm

Conflating them produces a service that receives traffic before its weights are in memory, so the first requests after every deploy are the slowest, and the dashboard blames the network.

docs.title: Where latency actually goes
docs.text:
Stage Typically Network and serialisation Small, until payloads are images Queue wait Dominant under batching; see step 2 Preprocessing Often on the critical path, often forgotten Model compute The only part benchmarks measure Postprocessing Same as preprocessing Cold start Enormous, and excluded from averages

Preprocessing is the one to raise in a review. It runs per request, is usually single-threaded Python, and is absent from every published figure.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the two numbers moving in opposite directions. "An inference service has a throughput number and a latency number and batching trades one for the other. I measured it on ONNX Runtime: going from batch 1 to 16 bought 14x throughput, 662 to 9,400 requests a second, and cost 21x latency, 1.5 ms to 31.7, because at 500 arrivals a second a request waits 30 ms for nineteen strangers before any compute happens."

Then the number that is true and misleading. Per-request compute falls from 1.51 ms to 0.11 ms, and that is arithmetically correct: inside a running batch each request's share really is 0.11 ms. No request in the system ever experienced it. That is the figure that ends up on a datasheet, and the support path it creates is a reader deploying against it and then looking at their p99.

The finding I would actually bring to a planning meeting. Past batch 16 the throughput stopped moving, 9,448 then 9,370 then 9,439, while latency went to 65 and then 133 ms. Above the knee it is not a tradeoff, it is a wrong setting. And a reader cannot work out where the knee is, since it depends on model, hardware and arrival rate, so the documentation's job is to tell them to measure it rather than to ship a default that looks authoritative.

Be honest about the depth. This is a CPU runtime, one model shape, no GPU, no real server, no autoscaler and no production traffic. It is enough to reason correctly about the tradeoff and to know which questions to ask, and it is not operational experience of running inference at scale. For a documentation role I would rather state that boundary than imply the other thing.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A latency-throughput sweep on whatever runtime you have, with queue wait included and the knee identified.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the sweep in step 2 on any model you have. Include the queue wait column; it is the one that changes the decision and the one no benchmark prints.
  2. Find a published per-request latency for a service you use and work out whether it is compute-only. If the batch size is not stated next to it, it is.
  3. Time the first request after a restart against the hundredth. The ratio decides whether autoscaling is viable, and it is rarely documented.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. The measurements ran against ONNX Runtime 1.29 with a 33.6 MB two-matmul model on this machine's CPU, and the sweep is a short script. What is absent is everything operational: no GPU, no Triton or comparable server, no containers, no autoscaling, no real traffic and no tail-latency work under contention. The demonstrated page records this as partial on that basis, and context tier is the honest claim.

docs.title: Information architecture
docs.text:
Deciding what the units of your content are, what they are called, and how someone finds the one they need.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

Information architecture skills: content modeling, taxonomy, and metadata for both navigation and machine retrieval

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Leads to: Content models, Diátaxis, Knowledge architecture, Metadata for navigation and retrieval

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Deciding what the units of your content are, what each unit is called, and how someone looking for one of them finds it. It is the structural layer underneath writing: not what a page says, but what the set of pages is.

Three decisions make up almost all of it. What is a page? What is a page about, formally, in a way a machine can read? How does a reader get from not knowing to the right page?

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA names it directly and then does something unusual: it specifies the purpose twice, "for both navigation and machine retrieval". That second half is the whole reason this concept is core rather than historical.

For thirty years information architecture meant navigation design: menus, breadcrumbs, sitemaps, card sorting, where things go so humans can click to them. That work still exists. But a documentation corpus in 2026 has a second audience that does not navigate at all. A retrieval system never sees your menu. An assistant answering a developer's question does not traverse your hierarchy; it matches a fragment of text and returns it with whatever context travelled alongside. Structure that only exists in the navigation is invisible to that reader.

That is the practical shift, and it is what someone in either role deals with on a Tuesday. The decision that used to be "which section does this page go in" is now "what does this page declare about itself, such that both a sidebar and a retriever can act on it". A folder name is a fact about one of those audiences. A metadata field is a fact about both.

The second reason this is core: information architecture is the concept that makes every later concept in this guide tractable. Chunking is a structural decision. RAG packaging is a structural decision with embeddings attached. llms.txt is a navigation artifact for machines. If the corpus has no structure, all of those are operating on mush, and no amount of retrieval sophistication recovers from it.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Take an unstructured pile of pages and give it a structure, then prove the structure is real by querying it. About forty minutes, no dependencies beyond Python.

Step 1: make the mess

This is the realistic starting state: pages that are individually fine and collectively unnavigable.

mkdir -p ia-demo/pages && cd ia-demo
cat > pages/install.md <<'EOF'
# Installing the widget CLI
Run `pip install widget`. Requires Python 3.10 or newer.
EOF
cat > pages/rotate-keys.md <<'EOF'
# Rotating an API key
Call `widget keys rotate`. The old key stays valid for one hour.
EOF
cat > pages/why-keys-expire.md <<'EOF'
# Why keys expire
A long-lived credential is a long-lived risk. One hour of overlap is
the shortest window that does not break deployments mid-rollout.
EOF
cat > pages/cli-reference.md <<'EOF'
# CLI reference
`widget keys rotate` rotates the signing key. `widget keys list` lists them.
EOF
cat > pages/first-deploy.md <<'EOF'
# Your first deploy
By the end of this you will have a running widget. Start by installing.
EOF
ls pages/

Five pages, one flat folder. A reader asking "how do I rotate a key" has to read filenames and guess.

Step 2: decide what a page declares about itself

This is the actual architecture work, and it takes judgement rather than typing. For this corpus, three facts are worth declaring: what kind of page it is, who it is for, and what it is about.

python3 - <<'PY'
import pathlib, json

# The architecture, written down. Deciding this IS the work; the code below
# just applies it.
MODEL = {
    "install.md":        ("how-to",      "new-user",  ["installation"]),
    "first-deploy.md":   ("tutorial",    "new-user",  ["installation", "deployment"]),
    "rotate-keys.md":    ("how-to",      "operator",  ["keys", "security"]),
    "why-keys-expire.md":("explanation", "operator",  ["keys", "security"]),
    "cli-reference.md":  ("reference",   "developer", ["keys", "cli"]),
}

for name, (kind, audience, topics) in MODEL.items():
    path = pathlib.Path("pages") / name
    body = path.read_text()
    title = body.splitlines()[0].lstrip("# ").strip()
    front = (
        "---\n"
        f"title: {title}\n"
        f"kind: {kind}\n"
        f"audience: {audience}\n"
        f"topics: [{', '.join(topics)}]\n"
        "---\n\n"
    )
    path.write_text(front + body)
print("structure applied to", len(MODEL), "pages")
PY
head -8 pages/rotate-keys.md

Step 3: prove the structure is real by querying it

Structure you cannot query is decoration. This is the test:

python3 - <<'PY'
import pathlib, re

def meta(path):
    text = path.read_text()
    block = text.split("---")[1]
    out = {}
    for line in block.strip().splitlines():
        key, _, value = line.partition(":")
        value = value.strip()
        if value.startswith("["):
            value = [v.strip() for v in value[1:-1].split(",")]
        out[key.strip()] = value
    return out

pages = {p.name: meta(p) for p in sorted(pathlib.Path("pages").glob("*.md"))}

print("Q: I am an operator, what should I read about keys?")
for name, m in pages.items():
    if m["audience"] == "operator" and "keys" in m["topics"]:
        print(f"   {m['kind']:<12} {m['title']}")

print("\nQ: I want instructions, not background.")
for name, m in pages.items():
    if m["kind"] in ("how-to", "tutorial"):
        print(f"   {m['kind']:<12} {m['title']}")

print("\nQ: is anything missing?")
kinds = {m["kind"] for m in pages.values()}
topics = {t for m in pages.values() for t in m["topics"]}
for topic in sorted(topics):
    present = {m["kind"] for m in pages.values() if topic in m["topics"]}
    gaps = kinds - present
    if gaps:
        print(f"   {topic}: no {', '.join(sorted(gaps))} page")
PY

What you built. The same five files answer three questions they could not answer before, and the third one is the payoff: the structure found gaps in the content. It reports that installation has no reference or explanation page, that keys has no tutorial, and five more besides. Nobody had to notice any of that by reading.

Two caveats worth holding onto, because this is where a naive coverage check turns into busywork. Not every gap is a gap: security almost certainly does not need its own tutorial, and a checker that demands all four types for every topic will generate a backlog of pages nobody wants. And the gaps it found are only as good as the vocabulary: topics here was assigned by hand, so the report reflects the architecture, not the truth. What the structure gives you is a question worth asking about each cell, which is still far more than a flat folder gives you.

docs.title: The three decisions, and what each one governs
docs.text: Decision Artifact Governs What is a unit of content? Content model Page boundaries, required fields, what may not be mixed What is it about? Taxonomy The closed vocabularies, their terms, who may add one How is it found? Metadata, findability Navigation, facets, search, retrieval filters

docs.title: Two kinds of structure, and which audience sees them
docs.text:
Structure Humans see it Machines see it Folder layout Yes, via navigation Only as a path string Navigation config Yes No Front-matter fields Rarely, as rendered facets Yes, directly Headings Yes Yes, if your chunker keeps them Prose that implies structure Yes No

The lesson in that table is the one claim worth remembering from this page: structure expressed only as folders and menus does not survive retrieval. If it matters, it belongs in a field.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Content model The schema a page must satisfy Taxonomy A controlled set of terms, often hierarchical Facet One independent axis of classification (audience, product, version) Controlled vocabulary A closed list; adding a term is a deliberate act Folksonomy An open tag field. Drifts into howto, how-to and How To within a year Information scent How well a link predicts what is behind it Card sorting Research method: users group content, you learn their categories Polyhierarchy A topic belonging in more than one place at once

docs.title: Where information architecture is usually wrong
docs.text: Symptom Underlying mistake A misc/ or advanced/ folder A category defined by what it is not Pages titled "Overview" in six places No content model; "overview" is doing four different jobs Navigation six levels deep Hierarchy used where faceting was needed Search works better than the menu The structure is in the prose, not in the model Everything tagged api A vocabulary with no discrimination is not a vocabulary

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Do not define the term. Describe a decision you made and what it cost. "The corpus had a guides/ folder that contained tutorials, task instructions and background, so readers mid-task had to wade through motivation. I split the type out as a declared field rather than a folder, which meant the navigation and the retrieval filters could both use it."

The follow-up is almost always hierarchy versus facets, and it is the question that separates people who have done this from people who have read about it. The answer: hierarchy is for one primary reading order; facets are for independent axes. Audience, product, version and page type are facets, because a page has a value on all four simultaneously and no nesting order is right for every reader. Forcing facets into a tree is the single most common information-architecture failure, and the symptom is a deep menu with the same leaf repeated in four branches.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Structure costs authoring friction, permanently. Every required field is a thing a contributor must decide before they can publish, and every closed vocabulary is an occasional argument about whether a term should be added. On a corpus of twenty pages that overhead is not worth paying; the structure is in your head and your head is big enough. The crossover is somewhere around fifty pages or the second author, whichever comes first. Saying this unprompted signals that you have paid the cost rather than only read about the benefit.

One sharper point. The strongest version of the NVIDIA bullet is that navigation and retrieval have different failure modes, so structure designed only for one fails the other quietly. Navigation fails visibly: a reader cannot find the page and complains. Retrieval fails invisibly: a model returns a plausible wrong chunk and the reader never knows there was a better page. That asymmetry is why machine-readable structure is now the more urgent half, and it is a genuinely good thing to say out loud.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A corpus with a declared content model, and something that queries it. The query is what makes it real: anyone can add front matter.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path and keep the gap-finding script. Twenty lines that report "this topic has no reference page" is a more compelling artifact than any diagram of a hierarchy.
  2. Take a real corpus you did not design and write a one-page audit: what the units are, what facets are implicit in the folder names, what is mixed that should be split. Your own project's docs, an open-source project's, or a previous employer's. The skill being demonstrated is seeing the structure that is already there and unstated.
  3. Add a validator that rejects a page violating the model, and wire it into documentation CI. The step from "we have a convention" to "the convention is enforced" is the one that distinguishes information architecture as a practice from information architecture as a document nobody reads.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. A diagram of a proposed hierarchy proves nothing; every candidate has one. A script that reads a real corpus and reports what is structurally wrong with it proves you can do the work on content you did not write, which is the actual job.

This guide's own concepts.yaml is the worked example, recorded on the demonstrated page: 106 units, a closed vocabulary for category, tier and Diátaxis type, a prerequisite graph with a cycle check, and every route generated from it rather than hand-maintained. The honest limit is the third decision. Whether a reader actually gets from not knowing to the right page is a question about readers, and there are none yet.

docs.title: Instructional design for developers
docs.text:
The structural commitments that make a page teach rather than inform, and why auditing your own corpus for them is harder than writing them.

core · difficulty 2 · 5h

Asked for by name

Intel: "Design and maintain golden paths and curriculum that take a developer from a clean environment to a working result"

Leads to: Learning paths and curriculum, Cognitive load in technical content, Assessment and checks for understanding

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The practice of designing content so that a reader can do something afterwards, rather than having read about it. For developer documentation that reduces to a small number of structural commitments: say what the reader will be able to do, say what they need first, give them something to practise on, and give them a way to know it worked.

The reason this is not obvious is that documentation and instruction are different jobs sharing one medium. A reference page is finished when it is accurate. A tutorial is finished when a stranger reaches a working result, which is a claim about the reader rather than about the page.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Intel's bullet is the concept in one line: "from a clean environment to a working result". That is an instructional objective written in behavioural terms, with its starting state named. The posting is describing design, not writing.

It matters on an ordinary Tuesday because most developer documentation is written by people who already know the thing, and expertise is the enemy of instruction. An expert cannot see which of their steps are inferential leaps, having stopped making those leaps years ago. Structural commitments are the defence: if every page must declare its prerequisites, the author is forced to notice what they were assuming.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Audit a corpus for four structural commitments, and find out what auditing your own writing actually costs. About thirty-five minutes.

Step 1: four commitments, chosen because a script can check them

Commitment In this corpus Checkable as Objective What the exercise produces A stated result at its end Entry state What the reader must already know A prerequisites line Practice Something to do, not to read The golden path itself Verification How the reader knows it worked A "how to prove it" section

These are not the only possible commitments. They are four that a program can verify, which is what makes them worth adopting over good intentions.

Step 2: audit the corpus

for c in [x for x in reg.concepts if x.status == "complete"]:
    t = (docs / c.page).read_text()
    if c.prerequisites and "**Prerequisites:**" in t:   has["prereq"] += 1
    if DURATION.search(t):                              has["dur"] += 1
    if re.search(r"\*\*What you (?:built|learned)", t):  has["result"] += 1
    if "## How to prove it" in t:                       has["proof"] += 1

complete pages: 82

  prereq stated      55/73   (75%)
  duration stated    75/82   (91%)
  closing result     78/82   (95%)
  proof section      82/82   (100%)

(The audit below ran when the corpus was 82 pages. On the finished 106 the same four commitments stand at 89/89, 106/106, 106/106 and 106/106.)

Two of those four numbers are wrong, and working out which is the real lesson of this page.

Step 3: the prerequisite number was counting labels, not commitments

prerequisite markers in use:
  **Prerequisites:**   46
  **Read first:**      28
concepts with no prerequisites at all: 9

Coverage was already complete. The corpus was using two labels for one structural element: hand-written pages said "Prerequisites", pages that began in the scaffold said "Read first", because that is the string the scaffold emitted.

A real defect, just not the one the number suggested. A reader meeting both labels does not infer two conventions, they experience inconsistency, and the entry-state commitment stops being recognisable as a commitment at all. Fixed by standardising on one label, changing the scaffold, and asserting it in a test so it cannot drift back.

labels in use after the pass: {'Prerequisites:': 74}
prereq coverage: 73/73

On the finished corpus: 90 occurrences, 89 of 89 concepts that have prerequisites. One page states the label twice, which is a cosmetic inconsistency the check does not care about and a reader would not notice.

What this fix got wrong, which took a while to see. It standardised the label that had surfaced and asserted that one label in a test, and that is exactly as far as it went. Three more elements were carrying two wordings each at the time, in other sections, and the test written here could not have seen any of them, because it was a test about prerequisites rather than about labels.

The assessment page found the second pair independently, months later, by measuring something else entirely. All four are standardised now, against STRUCTURAL_LABELS in registry.py rather than against a string written into a test. A fix applied to the instance is not applied to the class, and the way to tell the difference is whether the check you add afterwards could find a defect you had not already found.

Step 4: the duration number was the line-wrapping bug

Seven pages appeared to state no duration. All seven state one:

docs/concepts/content-lifecycle.md:  "... falsifiable. About thirty
                                      minutes. This uses this guide's own ..."

The number and its unit were separated by a line break, and the pattern's [- ]? does not match a newline. Normalising whitespace before searching:

duration stated: 82/82

This is the third time in this project that measuring wrapped prose per line has produced a confident wrong answer, which is worth more than the result.

Step 5: count the real failures, then fix them

With both measurements corrected, exactly one commitment was genuinely incomplete:

golden paths with no stated result: 4/82
   diataxis, antora, github-actions, mcp

Four exercises that ended without telling the reader what they now had. Writing those four closings took ten minutes, and each one forced the useful question: what did this exercise produce? On diataxis the answer came out sharper than the page's own introduction.

golden paths with no stated result: 0/82

Step 6: the finding worth carrying out of here

Count the attempts. Across this corpus, eight successive audits of my own writing returned plausible wrong numbers:

Attempt Wrong because Golden path structure Split sections on ##, which golden paths write inside heredocs Duration, first try Matched only "About N minutes" Duration, second try Matched per line, and prose wraps Duration, third try Word list omitted the hyphenated numbers Sentence length Front matter counted as prose Sentence length, again ." not treated as a sentence ending Sentence length, third A naive fence toggle counted shell commands as prose Prerequisites Two labels for one element

Every one produced a number a reasonable person would have published. Five of the eight would have gone into this guide as findings.

The instructional-design point is not "be careful". It is that the audit is an artifact with the same defect profile as the corpus it measures, and it needs the same treatment: a fixture with a known answer before you believe any number it gives you about something you care about.

What you built. Four structural commitments, measured honestly, four pages repaired, one label standardised, and a calibrated distrust of your own first number.

docs.title: Objectives in behavioural terms
docs.text:
Weak Behavioural "Understand authentication" "Obtain a token and make an authenticated call" "Learn about retries" "Configure a retry policy and observe a backoff" "Get familiar with the CLI" "Install the CLI and list your widgets" "Know the architecture" "Trace one request through all three services"

The test is whether you could watch someone and tell whether they had done it. "Understand" fails that test, which is why Intel's "to a working result" is better written than most objectives in actual curricula.

docs.title: Where expertise hurts
docs.text:
Expert behaviour Consequence for the reader Omitting a step that is automatic for them A silent prerequisite Using the internal name for a thing Unfindable and unsearchable Explaining why before what The reader has nothing to attach it to Choosing the elegant path over the common one Correct and not useful Assuming the goal is obvious The reader does not know what they are building

Cold-start testing is the mechanical defence against the first row. The others need a human reader, which is why assessment is a separate concept.

docs.title: What instructional design is not
docs.text: Not Because Making content friendlier Tone is not structure Adding more explanation Usually raises load A learning management system That is delivery Quizzes One kind of assessment, often the weakest Writing for beginners It applies at every level of expertise

docs.title: The commitments, and what each one costs
docs.text:
Commitment Costs Buys Every page states its entry state One line, and a real decision Silent prerequisites become visible Every exercise states its duration One phrase Readers can decide whether to start Every exercise names its result Two sentences The author must know what it produced Every page says how to verify A section Separates informing from teaching One label per element A standardisation pass, once The commitments stay recognisable

The last row is the one this page learned the hard way, and the one most corpora get wrong without noticing, because each author is individually consistent.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the difference between the two jobs. "A reference page is done when it is accurate. A tutorial is done when a stranger finishes with a working result, which is a claim about the reader rather than the page. So I hold pages to structural commitments: declare the entry state, state the duration, name the result, say how to verify. Four things a script can check, which is why I chose those four."

The follow-up is usually about expertise. The honest answer is that authors cannot see their own inferential leaps, so this needs mechanisms rather than care. Cold-start testing catches undeclared prerequisites; a required prerequisites line forces the author to decide what they are assuming; the rest needs a real reader, which is the limit of what tooling buys you.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Structural commitments are a tax on every page and they can decay into ritual. A prerequisites line reading "none" on forty pages is noise, and a "what you built" paragraph written to satisfy a checker is worse than none at all. They work while they force a decision and fail once they become a form to fill in, and the only way to tell which has happened is to read what they produced.

One sharper point. Auditing your own corpus is harder than it looks, and the failure is silent. Eight successive measurements of mine returned confident wrong numbers. Front matter counted as prose. A duration pattern defeated by line wrapping. A fence parser that counted shell commands as sentences. And two labels for one structural element, which looked like a quarter of the corpus failing a commitment it had already met. Five would have been published as findings. An audit script has the same defect profile as the corpus it measures, so it gets a fixture with a known answer before any of its numbers are believed.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A corpus whose structural commitments are checked in CI, plus the audit and the fixtures that make the audit trustworthy.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Pick one commitment, audit a corpus you own for it, then verify the measurement by hand against three pages. The hand-check is the step people skip and the only one that catches a wrong number.
  2. Rewrite your three weakest learning objectives in behavioural terms. "Could I watch someone and tell?" is the entire test. The test is falsifiable or the objective is not rewritten: if you cannot name the observation that would show a reader had failed, the words changed and the objective did not.
  3. Find an exercise that never says what it produced, and write that sentence. It is the fastest way to discover an exercise that produces nothing.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. fieldguide audit prints the four commitments on demand, which is the whole of the claim: a seven-section page contract enforced in CI, a prerequisite graph with no cycles, 89 of 89 prerequisite lines, and 106 of 106 golden paths stating a duration and naming a result. Every figure in this page's golden path comes from that command rather than from a transcript, and its test fixtures pin the three measurement bugs described above so they cannot come back.

What that does not establish is the thing the concept is actually about. The commitments are met; whether meeting them teaches anybody is a claim about readers, and there are none. The demonstrated page records this as partial for that reason.

docs.title: Knowledge architecture
docs.text:
Structuring what is known rather than where pages live, and auditing the dependency graph against itself.

core · difficulty 3 · 6h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Collaborate with documentation leads on knowledge architecture, sharing implementation feedback (what works, breaks, and scales) to refine content models, information architecture, and AI-readiness patterns"

Prerequisites: Information architecture

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Information architecture organises pages: where they live, how they are labelled, how a reader navigates between them. Knowledge architecture organises what is known: the concepts, their relationships, which depend on which, and which are load-bearing.

The distinction matters because the two can disagree. A page can sit in the obvious place in a navigation tree while the thing it explains depends on four concepts a reader has not met. Information architecture will not tell you that. A dependency graph will.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA names it directly, and names the relationship precisely: you collaborate with documentation leads on it, and your contribution is implementation feedback, what works, breaks and scales. The architecture is owned jointly; what you bring is evidence from having built it.

That framing tells you what the role is not. You are not being hired to design a taxonomy in isolation and hand it over. You are being hired to implement an architecture, find out where it breaks at scale, and feed that back. Which means the valuable skill is measuring an architecture, and that is what the golden path does.

It also explains why this concept is difficulty 3 while information architecture is 2. Organising pages is a judgment you can make by reading them. Organising knowledge requires making the relationships explicit enough to compute over, and then being willing to find out that your own structure disagrees with itself.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Audit a real knowledge architecture against its own graph. About forty-five minutes. Every number below comes from this guide's registry.

Step 1: make the relationships data

This guide's knowledge architecture is 106 concepts with a prerequisite edge wherever one concept assumes another, a tier recording how much of the reader's time each may claim, and a category for grouping. The prerequisites are the graph:

from fieldguide.registry import load_registry, topological_order

reg = load_registry(Path("concepts.yaml"))
indeg = {c.id: len(c.prerequisites) for c in reg.concepts}
outdeg = collections.Counter()
for c in reg.concepts:
    for p in c.prerequisites:
        outdeg[p] += 1

nodes: 106   edges: 115
roots (no prerequisite):   17
leaves (nothing needs it): 58

Fifty-eight of 106 concepts are terminal: nothing in the curriculum builds on them. That is not necessarily wrong, but it is worth knowing, because a graph that is mostly leaves is closer to a list than to an architecture.

Step 2: find what is load-bearing

for cid, n in outdeg.most_common(6):
    print(f"{n:2} dependents   {cid:26} [{by_id[cid].tier}]")

 8 dependents   content-model              [core]
 6 dependents   docs-as-code               [core]
 5 dependents   metadata                   [core]
 5 dependents   static-site-generators     [core]
 5 dependents   documentation-ci           [core]
 5 dependents   agent-ready-content        [core]

These six are the architecture's spine. The practical consequence is about sequencing: writing a leaf before its prerequisites exist produces a page that has to re-explain its own foundations, and the dependency count tells you which pages to write first without guessing.

Step 3: measure the longest chain

order = topological_order(reg)
depth = {}
for cid in order:
    depth[cid] = 1 + max((depth[p] for p in by_id[cid].prerequisites), default=0)

longest prerequisite chain: 11 deep, ending at 'hallucination-guardrails'

information-architecture -> content-model -> metadata -> agent-ready-content
  -> chunking -> embeddings -> vector-stores -> rag -> grounding
  -> output-evaluation -> hallucination-guardrails

Eleven. A reader who wants hallucination guardrails and takes the architecture literally has ten concepts to get through first.

That is a finding requiring judgment rather than a fix. Either the chain is real, in which case the honest answer is that this material is genuinely deep and a learning path should offer a shortcut, or some of those edges are aspirational and should be removed. Depth is the number that forces the question.

Step 4: check the tiers against the graph

The tier is a claim about importance, assigned by hand. Dependents are a fact about structure, computed. If the claim is sound they should correlate:

mean dependents by tier:
   core        n= 64  mean=1.53  max=8
   supporting  n= 33  mean=0.45  max=3
   context     n=  9  mean=0.22  max=1

They do, cleanly, which is the first evidence that the hand-assigned tiers are not arbitrary. Now look for the disagreements, which is where the value is:

context-tier concepts that something depends on:
   usd-omniverse (1), inference-serving (1)

supporting concepts with more dependents than the core mean:
   content-lifecycle (3), style-guide (3), reproducible-environments (2), seo-for-docs (2)

Four supporting concepts carry more of the graph than the average core concept. They are promotion candidates, identified mechanically rather than by argument.

Step 5: the finding that is not a defect

core concepts that are isolated (no prerequisites, no dependents):
   technical-writing, reading-code-to-verify, docs-as-product

Three concepts are marked core, the highest importance, and sit entirely outside the graph. By the logic of steps 2 and 4 that looks like a contradiction.

It is not. All three are craft skills: writing well, reading code to verify a claim, treating documentation as a product. They are among the most important things on the curriculum and they are not prerequisites for anything, because you do not learn them once and build on them. You get better at them across everything else.

So importance and graph position are different axes, and the mistake is assuming a dependency graph ranks importance. It ranks sequence. Conflating the two produces curricula that teach tooling thoroughly and never mention judgment, because judgment has no prerequisites and therefore no place in a tree.

What you built. An architecture you can interrogate: a spine, a depth measurement, four promotion candidates found mechanically, and one finding that looked like a defect and was a property of the domain.

docs.title: Information architecture against knowledge architecture
docs.text: Information architecture Knowledge architecture Organises Pages and their labels Concepts and their relationships Artifact Navigation, URL structure, taxonomy A concept graph with dependencies Question it answers Where does this page go? What must a reader already know? Failure A reader cannot find the page A reader finds it and cannot follow it Validated by Card sorting, tree testing, search logs Graph properties, and reader drop-off Who owns it Often the docs team alone Jointly, per NVIDIA's bullet

docs.title: What a knowledge graph lets you compute
docs.text:
Property Tells you Out-degree What is load-bearing, and what to write first Depth Whether the material is genuinely deep or over-linked Cycles A circular explanation; always a defect Leaf fraction Whether this is an architecture or a list Tier against out-degree Whether hand-assigned importance matches structure Isolated nodes Either a gap, or a craft skill; see step 5 Topological order A defensible writing and reading order

None of these are available from a navigation tree, which is the argument for making relationships explicit.

docs.title: Patterns worth knowing
docs.text:
Pattern Shape Use Prerequisite graph Directed, acyclic Curriculum, onboarding, learning paths Concept map Undirected, typed edges Explaining a domain's shape Taxonomy Tree, is-a Classification; see taxonomy Topic map Hub and spoke A landing page per area Decision graph Branching on conditions Playbooks

Prerequisite graphs and taxonomies get confused most often. A taxonomy says what a thing is; a prerequisite graph says what you must know first. A corpus with only a taxonomy can be perfectly organised and still impossible to read in order.

docs.title: Keeping it honest
docs.text:
Rule Why Acyclic, enforced A cycle is a circular explanation Every edge means "assumes", not "related to" "Related" edges make everything adjacent and the graph useless Prerequisites resolve to real concepts A dangling edge is a silent gap Tiers are reviewed against out-degree Hand-assigned importance drifts Depth is monitored Over-linking inflates it quietly

The second row is the discipline that keeps the graph meaningful. It is tempting to add an edge whenever two concepts are mentioned together, and the result is a graph with no sequence in it.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the distinction. "Information architecture organises pages; knowledge architecture organises what is known. They can disagree: a page can be in the obvious place while depending on four concepts the reader has not met. The second one is a graph, which means you can compute over it."

Match NVIDIA's framing on ownership. The bullet says collaborate with documentation leads and bring implementation feedback. So the answer is not "I would design the architecture", it is "I would implement it, measure it, and tell the leads what breaks". Then give an example of a measurement: depth of eleven, four supporting concepts carrying more of the graph than the average core concept.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Making relationships explicit is real ongoing cost. Every new concept needs its edges decided, the graph needs validating in CI, and the temptation to add "related to" edges has to be resisted continuously or the graph stops encoding sequence. On a corpus of thirty pages this is overhead for nothing; it starts paying somewhere in the low hundreds.

One sharper point. A dependency graph ranks sequence, not importance, and conflating them is how curricula end up teaching tooling thoroughly and never mentioning judgment. Three of the most important concepts in my own registry are isolated nodes, because craft skills are not prerequisites for anything: you do not learn to write well once and build on it. An architecture that cannot represent those will quietly drop them.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A concept graph for a corpus you own, validated in CI, plus the audit from steps 2 through 5.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Write the prerequisite edges for twenty concepts in a domain you know. The arguments about which edges are real are the work.
  2. Compute out-degree and depth. The spine and the longest chain are both immediately actionable. Predict the spine before you compute it; where your guess and the out-degree disagree, one of the two is the finding.
  3. Compare your hand-assigned importance against out-degree. The disagreements are either mis-tierings or craft skills, and telling those apart is the judgment this concept is about.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Neither of this guide's repositories was recorded as demonstrating this, and the honest position is that the registry itself is the demonstration: 106 concepts, 115 edges, acyclic and enforced, with prerequisite resolution failing the build and a topological order driving the writing sequence. Every number on this page came from running the audit against it, including the one that corrected my own assumption about tiers.

docs.title: Learning paths and curriculum
docs.text:
A path is a route through a graph rather than a self-contained course, and the gap between those two things is what the reader pays for.

core · difficulty 3 · 5h

Asked for by name

Intel: "structured learning paths"

Prerequisites: Diátaxis, Instructional design for developers

Leads to: Workshops and hands-on labs

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
An ordered sequence through existing content, aimed at one audience and one outcome. A path adds no new material. It makes two claims about material that already exists: that this is the right subset, and that this is the right order.

Both claims are checkable, which is what separates a learning path from a list of links with a heading, and almost all published learning paths are lists of links with a heading.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because Diátaxis organises content by its kind, and a reader does not arrive with a kind. They arrive with a job.

A corpus sorted into tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation is navigable and gives no answer to "I started on Monday, what do I read first". The four quadrants are an authoring discipline and a filing system; a path is the reading order that the filing system deliberately does not encode. Intel asks for "structured learning paths" next to golden paths and quickstarts because those are the three shapes of the same obligation at three scales: one command, one page, one career's first fortnight.

The failure mode is specific and nearly universal: a path that is a table of contents, ordered by the order someone wrote the pages in, with no claim about prerequisites that anything verifies.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Validate a real curriculum: nine paths over 106 concepts. Find that the ordering claim holds, the coverage claim does not, and the promise made at the top of every path page is false. About thirty-five minutes.

Step 1: the paths as data, not as pages

paths:
  - id: first-week
    name: The first week
    audience: Someone who has just taken one of these roles and needs to be useful by Friday.
    concepts: [technical-writing, docs-as-product, docs-as-code, markdown,
               git-authoring, diataxis, static-site-generators, mkdocs,
               link-checking, documentation-ci]

A path is a list of concept ids. That is the whole structure, and it is the reason any of what follows is possible: the path page is generated, so a path cannot link to a concept that does not exist, and the sequence can be checked against the prerequisite graph.

  first-week             10 steps  34h
  content-architect      13 steps  43h
  docs-engineer          18 steps  70h
  knowledgeops           17 steps  83h
  developer-educator     15 steps  60h
  writer-who-builds      10 steps  37h
  prove-it               15 steps  59h

Step 2: check the ordering claim

Every path page says the order matters. For each step, every prerequisite appearing in the same path must appear earlier:

for learning_path in reg.paths:
    pos = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(learning_path.concepts)}
    for concept in learning_path.concepts:
        for prerequisite in reg.by_id[concept].prerequisites:
            if prerequisite in pos and pos[prerequisite] > pos[concept]:
                findings.path_order_violations.append(...)

learning paths that teach a concept before its prerequisite: 0

Zero across nine paths and 114 steps, and not because the paths were written carefully. They were reordered twice to satisfy this check when it was first added. That is the check paying for itself: a curriculum nobody validates drifts out of order the first time a concept gains a prerequisite.

Step 3: check the claim the validator deliberately does not make

The validator contains this comment:

# A prerequisite outside the path is fine: a path is a route
# through the graph, not a self-contained curriculum.
if prerequisite in learning_path.concepts and prerequisite not in seen:

A defensible decision, and an unmeasured one. Count the pairs it permits:

  first-week           steps assuming something the path never teaches:  1
  content-architect                                                      1
  docs-engineer                                                          5
  knowledgeops                                                           3
  developer-educator                                                     4
  writer-who-builds                                                      3
  prove-it                                                              10

total step-prerequisite pairs pointing outside their path: 27

Ten of prove-it's fifteen steps depend on something the path does not cover. A reader finishing it has been walked through fifteen concepts and quietly assumed to know seven more.

Step 4: what the path page actually promised

**15 concepts, roughly 59 hours.** The order matters:
each step assumes the ones above it.

"Each step assumes the ones above it" is false for ten of those fifteen steps. Each step did disclose its own outside prerequisites further down the page, so the information was present and arrived after the reader had committed.

This is the entry-state commitment from instructional design, applied to a path rather than a page, and it had been applied at step level and skipped at path level. The fix is to compute the assumed set and state it before step 1:

assumed = []
for concept_id in learning_path.concepts:
    for prerequisite in by_id[concept_id].prerequisites:
        if prerequisite not in learning_path.concepts and prerequisite not in assumed:
            assumed.append(prerequisite)

**Assumed before step 1.** This path does not teach Information architecture,
Choosing a static site generator, Git authoring workflows for writers, Style
guides and terminology management, Reproducible environments, Agent-ready
content, RAG pipelines. Each step below repeats what it assumes.

Seven named concepts, before the hours are committed rather than after. A test asserts it appears above the first step, because the useful version of this information is the one the reader sees while deciding.

Step 5: check the coverage claim, which is the worse number

A path makes a claim about a subset. Ask what the subsets add up to:

concepts reachable through some path: 84/106
concepts in no path at all:           22
   of those, written:                 22
   of those, core tier:                4

Four core-tier concepts are in no path. Not thin pages: core means the curriculum asserts you cannot do the job without them, and every one of the twenty-two is written. They are reachable by search and by the dependency graph, and no curated route goes through them.

That was eleven of thirty-seven when this measurement was first run, over seven paths. Two paths were added afterwards, one over measurement and automation and one over domain context, which is what moved it. The figures here are the current ones and fieldguide audit is where to read them; this page was wrong about them for a while, which is the hazard of a page whose subject is a measurement of the thing it lives in.

Then the mirror image:

concepts in exactly one path: 62
most reused: diataxis 4, docs-as-product 3, docs-as-code 3, link-checking 3

Sixty-two concepts carry one path each. A path that is the sole route to well over half the corpus is doing navigation work, not curriculum work, and that is the honest reading of what nine paths over 106 concepts produces.

Step 6: which of the two gaps to fix

They want opposite things. Closing the prerequisite gaps means lengthening paths, and prove-it at 59 hours would become unrecommendable. Closing the coverage gap means adding paths or widening them, which worsens the prerequisite gaps.

The resolution is to stop treating them as the same defect. Prerequisite gaps are a disclosure problem, fixed in step 4 at the cost of one computed paragraph. Coverage is a curriculum problem, and eleven uncovered core concepts is a decision about whether every core concept deserves a route, which is a judgment the numbers inform and do not make.

What is not defensible is the state before this exercise: both gaps present, neither measured, and a promise at the top of every page that the data contradicted.

What you built. Seven validated paths, an ordering check at zero violations, an entry state stated before step 1 and asserted by a test, and two measured gaps that pull in opposite directions.

docs.title: Path against the alternatives
docs.text:
Diátaxis quadrant Path Study plan Ordered by Kind of content One audience's job The dependency graph Covers Everything, filed A chosen subset Everything Written by The content model Judgment A topological sort Claims This is a how-to This subset, this order No cycles Fails by Miscategorising Omitting, or over-including Being 106 steps long

This guide generates all three from one registry, which is the argument for keeping a path as data. The study plan is the honest fallback for the 37 concepts no path reaches.

docs.title: What a path has to declare
docs.text: Field Why Audience, in one sentence A path for everyone is a table of contents Outcome What the reader can do at the end Entry state See step 4; the one most often skipped Step order And a check that prerequisites precede their dependents Total time A reader commits hours, not steps Per-step time So a path can be paused

docs.title: How paths fail
docs.text:
Failure Detected by A step precedes its prerequisite The ordering check Steps assume material the path omits The closure count, step 3 The entry state is stated only per step Reading the top of the page Core concepts in no path The coverage count, step 5 A path is the sole route to a third of the corpus The reuse count Links to pages that do not exist Generating the page from the registry Ordered by authoring date Nothing; this needs a person

The last row is the common case in the wild, and no check catches it, because authoring order is a valid order. It is just never the right one.

docs.title: Sizing
docs.text:
Length Reads as Risk Under 5 steps A reading list Not worth the page 8 to 15 steps A path Right for most audiences Over 18 steps A syllabus Abandoned partway, invisibly Over 60 hours A qualification Needs checkpoints and a reason

This guide's longest is 18 steps and 83 hours, which is over the line, and the mitigation is that every step is independently useful. That is a weaker answer than splitting it.

docs.title: Keeping it honest
docs.text: Rule Because Paths live in the registry, not in prose Pages generated from data cannot link to nothing Ordering is checked in CI A new prerequisite silently invalidates an order The entry state is computed, not written Hand-written assumptions go stale Coverage is reported Orphaned core concepts are invisible otherwise Reuse is reported A concept in four paths is load-bearing

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with why Diátaxis is not enough. "Diátaxis sorts content by kind, and a reader does not arrive with a kind, they arrive with a job. The four quadrants are an authoring discipline; a path is the reading order the filing system deliberately does not encode. So I keep paths as data in the registry and generate the pages, which means a path cannot point at a concept that does not exist, and the order can be checked against the prerequisite graph."

The follow-up is what the check actually caught, and here the numbers are worth stating precisely. Ordering came out at zero violations across nine paths and 114 steps, and only because two paths were reordered when the check was added. The interesting number is the one the validator deliberately does not check: 32 step-prerequisite pairs point outside their path, and on prove-it ten of fifteen steps depend on something it never teaches.

Then the finding that changed the generator. Every path page promised that each step assumes the ones above it, which was false for those ten steps. The information existed, disclosed per step, further down the page, after the reader had already committed to 59 hours. So the generator now computes the assumed set and states it before step 1, and a test asserts it appears above the first heading, because the useful version of that information is the one visible while deciding whether to start.

The tradeoff to volunteer. The two gaps pull in opposite directions. Closing the prerequisite gaps lengthens paths past the point anyone finishes them; closing the coverage gap, four core concepts currently in no path, means more or wider paths, which worsens the prerequisite gaps. I do not think there is a clean answer. What I would not defend is where this started, with both gaps unmeasured and a promise on every page that the data contradicted.

One sharper point. Sixty-two of the 106 concepts sit in exactly one path. A path that is the sole route to a third of a corpus is doing navigation work rather than curriculum work, and calling it curriculum obscures that the real need was findability.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. Paths held as data, pages generated from them, an ordering check and a coverage report in CI, and an entry state computed per path.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Take your longest learning path and count how many steps depend on something it never teaches. If that number is not zero, the page's promise about ordering is false, and the fix is one computed paragraph.
  2. Count the concepts your paths do not reach, split by whether you consider them essential. The essential ones in no path are your real finding.
  3. Count how many paths each item appears in. Anything appearing once is navigation, not curriculum, and should probably be solved by search instead.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. This guide holds nine paths over 106 concepts in concepts.yaml, generates every path page from them, and fails CI on an ordering violation; the entry-state paragraph and its test were added by the exercise above. The honest limits: no reader has completed any of these paths, so there is no evidence the orders are good, only that they are consistent with the prerequisite graph, and the demonstrated page records that distinction.
