docs.title: Link checking
docs.text:
Failing the build on a dead cross-reference, including the anchors a strict build ignores.

core · difficulty 1 · 2h

Asked for by name

Intel: "documentation CI, including link checking and coldstart testing of quickstarts"

Prerequisites: Docs-as-code

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A build-time check that every cross-reference in the corpus resolves: internal page links, heading anchors, and, separately and more awkwardly, external URLs. A dead link becomes a failed pull request rather than a reader's dead end.

The reason it gets its own page rather than one line in documentation CI is that almost everyone implements the easy half, ships it, and believes the problem is solved. The easy half is missing files. The half that rots a corpus is missing anchors.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Intel names it directly. It is the cheapest gate in this entire category, which is why it is difficulty 1 and why it is usually the first thing added after a strict build.

The reason it matters more than its difficulty suggests is that deep links are the links people actually use. An engineer sends a colleague configure.md#retry-behaviour, not configure.md. Then someone rewords that heading from "Retry behaviour" to "Retries and backoff" in an unrelated pull request, and every deep link to it dies silently. The page is still there. The build is still green. The link lands at the top of the page, and the reader has to guess which of forty sections was meant.

Renaming a heading is the most common way a documentation site breaks its own internal links, and it is invisible to every check that only looks for missing files.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Prove that a strict build is not a link checker, then build the checker that closes the gap. About twenty-five minutes.

Step 1: a site with two defects, one of each kind

mkdir -p linkcheck-demo/docs && cd linkcheck-demo
printf 'site_name: Link demo\ndocs_dir: docs\n' > mkdocs.yml

cat > docs/index.md <<'EOF'
# Home

Read the [install guide](install.md) first.
Then see [configuration options](install.md#configuration-options).
Then see [the tuning section](install.md#tuning).
And the [old FAQ](faq.md).
EOF

cat > docs/install.md <<'EOF'
# Install

## Configuration options

Set the values you need.
EOF

There are two dead references. faq.md does not exist. install.md#tuning does not exist either, because install.md has no Tuning heading.

Step 2: watch a strict build catch one and ignore the other

mkdocs build --strict

WARNING - Doc file 'index.md' contains a link 'faq.md', but the target is not
          found among documentation files.
INFO    - Doc file 'index.md' contains a link 'install.md#tuning', but the doc
          'install.md' does not contain an anchor '#tuning'.
Aborted with 1 warnings in strict mode!

Read those two lines carefully. The missing file is a WARNING, and --strict turns warnings into errors, so the build fails. The missing anchor is an INFO. It is not a warning, so --strict does nothing with it.

Remove only the missing-file link and build again:

cat > docs/index.md <<'EOF'
# Home

Read the [install guide](install.md) first.
Then see [configuration options](install.md#configuration-options).
Then see [the tuning section](install.md#tuning).
EOF

mkdocs build --strict
echo "exit=$?"

INFO    - Doc file 'index.md' contains a link 'install.md#tuning', but the doc
          'install.md' does not contain an anchor '#tuning'.
INFO    - Documentation built in 0.05 seconds
exit=0

Exit 0. The build passed. Now look at what it published:

grep -o 'href="install/#tuning"' site/index.html
grep -c 'id="tuning"' site/install/index.html

The dead anchor is in the shipped HTML, and there is no id="tuning" anywhere in the page it points at. A strict build will ship that every day of the week. This is the gap the rest of the page closes.

Step 3: write the checker

The useful version is about sixty lines, because it has to do two things MkDocs does not: resolve anchors against the heading slugs a page actually generates, and ignore link-shaped text inside code samples.

# check_links.py
import re
import sys
import unicodedata
from pathlib import Path

LINK = re.compile(r"\[[^\]]*\]\(([^)\s]+)(?:\s+\"[^\"]*\")?\)")
HEADING = re.compile(r"^(#{1,6})\s+(.*?)\s*$")
FENCE = re.compile(r"^\s*(```|~~~)")


def strip_fences(text):
    """Blank out fenced code, preserving line numbers so reports stay honest."""
    out, in_fence = [], False
    for line in text.splitlines():
        if FENCE.match(line):
            in_fence = not in_fence
            out.append("")
        else:
            out.append("" if in_fence else line)
    return "\n".join(out)


def slugify(title):
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", title)
    text = re.sub(r"[`*_\[\]()]", "", text)
    text = re.sub(r"[^\w\s-]", "", text).strip().lower()
    return re.sub(r"\s+", "-", text)


def anchors_of(path):
    body = strip_fences(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    return {slugify(m.group(2)) for line in body.splitlines()
            if (m := HEADING.match(line))}


def check(root):
    pages = sorted(root.rglob("*.md"))
    # Keyed by RESOLVED path, because link targets are resolved below.
    anchors = {p.resolve(): anchors_of(p) for p in pages}
    problems = []
    for page in pages:
        body = strip_fences(page.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        for n, line in enumerate(body.splitlines(), 1):
            for target in LINK.findall(line):
                if target.startswith(("http://", "https://", "mailto:", "#")):
                    continue
                file_part, _, anchor = target.partition("#")
                dest = (page.parent / file_part).resolve()
                if dest.suffix != ".md":
                    continue
                if not dest.exists():
                    problems.append(f"{page}:{n}: missing file '{file_part}'")
                elif anchor:
                    # Three states, not two. See the note below.
                    if dest not in anchors:
                        anchors[dest] = anchors_of(dest)
                    if anchor not in anchors[dest]:
                        problems.append(
                            f"{page}:{n}: '{file_part}' has no anchor '#{anchor}'")
    return problems


if __name__ == "__main__":
    found = check(Path(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "docs"))
    for p in found:
        print(f"LINK  {p}")
    print(f"{'FAIL' if found else 'ok'}: {len(found)} problem(s)")
    raise SystemExit(1 if found else 0)

python3 check_links.py docs/

LINK  docs/index.md:5: 'install.md' has no anchor '#tuning'
FAIL: 1 problem(s)

One finding, which is the real defect, on the corpus a strict build had just declared clean.

Step 4: fix it and confirm green

printf '\n## Tuning\n\nAdjust as needed.\n' >> docs/install.md
python3 check_links.py docs/
echo "exit=$?"

ok: 0 problem(s)
exit=0

What you built. A gate that catches the failure mode a strict build is structurally blind to. Add it as a separate CI step rather than folding it into the build, so a dead anchor and a broken build are two different red lights.

docs.title: What each tool actually covers
docs.text:
Check Missing page Missing anchor Fenced false positive External URL mkdocs build --strict Fails Logs INFO, ships it Avoided No The script above Fails Fails Avoided No lychee, linkchecker Fails Fails Varies Yes htmlproofer (post-build) Fails Fails Not applicable, reads HTML Yes

Checking rendered HTML instead of Markdown source is a legitimate alternative and gets anchors right for free, because by then the id attributes exist. The tradeoff is that failures report against built paths rather than source lines, so the author has to translate back.

docs.title: The three states of a link target
docs.text:
This is the part that bites, and it bit the author of this page while writing it. A target is not valid or invalid. It is valid, invalid, or unknown, where unknown means the target exists but sits outside the tree you scanned.

Collapse unknown into You get Consequence Invalid False positives Noise, then someone turns the check off Valid False negatives Silence, and the check is theater

The first version of the script above keyed its anchor cache by relative path and looked it up by resolved path, so every lookup missed. Because the default was an empty set, every anchor in the corpus was reported dead. That was the lucky failure, because it was loud. Had the default been "assume valid", the same bug would have reported a clean corpus forever and nobody would have looked.

A checker's unknown case must fail loudly or be handled explicitly. Never let it default to passing.

docs.title: Why external links are a separate decision
docs.text:
Property Internal External Deterministic Yes No Needs network No Yes Can fail on someone else's outage No Yes Belongs in a blocking gate Yes Usually not

Blocking a pull request because a third-party site returned 503 teaches people to re-run CI until it passes, which destroys the gate's credibility for the internal checks too. Run external checks on a schedule, open an issue, and keep them out of the merge path.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the anchor gap, because it is the part that shows you have run this rather than read about it. "A strict MkDocs build fails on a missing page but only logs an INFO for a missing heading anchor, so it ships dead deep links. Renaming a heading is the most common way a site breaks its own links, and it is exactly the case the build cannot see."

The follow-up is usually about external links. The answer that signals experience is that you deliberately do not gate merges on them, and why: non-determinism in a required check trains people to retry until green.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Slug generation is tool-specific. Your checker reimplements the slug rules of your static site generator, and if those rules drift your checker produces false reports. The honest mitigation is to unit-test slugify against real headings from your own corpus. The better long-term answer is to check rendered HTML, where the id attributes are already decided.

One sharper point. The right failure granularity is the source line. A report that says the site has a broken link is a chore; a report that says configure.md:84 points at an anchor that no longer exists is a fix. That is why the script blanks fenced lines rather than deleting them: line numbers stay true.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A repository with link checking as its own CI step, plus a commit where that step caught something.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Twenty-five minutes, and you will have personally watched a strict build publish a dead anchor.
  2. Point the script at a docs site you already have. On any corpus more than a few months old it will find something, and the first finding is the argument you will use in the interview.
  3. Write one unit test for slugify using the ugliest real heading in your corpus, something with backticks and punctuation. That test is what makes the checker trustworthy rather than approximately right.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Anchors. A link checker that only resolves file paths reimplements something the build already does. Being able to say "mine catches renamed headings, and here is the pull request where it did" is the whole difference.

docs.title: LLMs in the content lifecycle
docs.text:
Drafting, updating and auditing a corpus with models, with the human placed where judgement is actually required.

core · difficulty 3 · 6h

Automate the content lifecycle with LLMs and scripting, from drafting and updating to auditing, with checks for freshness, code accuracy, and terminology drift, and human review where judgment matters

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: Prompting for content work, Content lifecycle and governance

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Using models as one stage in the machinery that keeps a corpus current: proposing drafts, flagging what has gone stale, auditing for drift. The quote above is the most specific bullet in either posting, and it names its own constraint at the end: human review where judgment matters.

The work is deciding where that is.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA's bullet is a job description in one sentence. It names three activities (drafting, updating, auditing), three checks (freshness, code accuracy, terminology drift), and one constraint (human review where judgement matters). Every other page in this category is a piece of it.

What makes it core and difficulty 3 is that the lifecycle is where the economics live. A single good answer from an assistant saves a reader five minutes. An audit that correctly flags 40 of 400 stale pages saves a team a week, every quarter, and it is the only thing in this category that scales with corpus size rather than with traffic.

On a Tuesday it is a pipeline you babysit. The weekly audit ran overnight and produced 180 findings on a 400-page corpus. Nobody will review 180 findings, so by Thursday the queue is untouched and the corpus is no more current than before. The pipeline worked and the lifecycle did not, because the design target was recall and the binding constraint was reviewer attention.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build the three stages, with the human placed deliberately, and discover that the constraint is review capacity rather than model quality. Fifty minutes, dependency-free.

Step 1: a corpus in the state corpora are actually in

mkdir -p lifecycle-drill/docs && cd lifecycle-drill
cat > docs/install.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Install the CLI
updated: 2024-01-15
owner: platform
---
# Install the CLI

Requires widget 2.2 or newer. Simply run the installer.

    pip install widget==2.2
EOF

cat > docs/retries.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Configure retries
updated: 2026-09-20
owner: platform
---
# Configure retries

Set `retries` on the client. The default is 3.
EOF

cat > docs/batching.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Batch requests
updated: 2023-11-02
owner: inference
---
# Batch requests

Pass a list to infer_batch. The repo has examples.
EOF

cat > docs/legacy-upgrade.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Upgrading from 1.x
updated: 2023-03-01
owner: platform
status: superseded
---
# Upgrading from 1.x

The 1.x client reached end of life in 2024.
EOF

cat > facts.yaml <<'EOF'
# Ground truth the pipeline checks against, generated in CI from the real
# artifacts: --help output, git tags, the glossary. Never hand-maintained.
current_version: "2.6"
supported_versions: ["2.4", "2.6"]
retries_default: 5          # changed from 3 in 2.5 and nobody updated the page
terms:
  repository: [repo, repos]
  pull request: [PR, MR]
EOF
ls docs/

Step 2: the three stages, each proposing and never applying

cat > lifecycle.py <<'PY'
"""Audit, update and draft stages for a documentation corpus.

Every stage returns PROPOSALS. Nothing writes to the corpus, because the
constraint named in the posting is "human review where judgment matters" and
a stage that applies its own findings has removed the place to put a human.

The three checks NVIDIA names map onto three different mechanisms, and only
one of them should involve a model at all:

  FRESHNESS         a date comparison. No model. Deterministic
  CODE ACCURACY     compare claims to generated ground truth. No model
  TERMINOLOGY DRIFT a substitution list. No model

The model's job is the fourth thing: DRAFTING a proposed replacement for a
finding a deterministic check already located, and ranking what a human
should look at first.
"""
import datetime as dt
import re
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

STALE_DAYS = 365
VERSION = re.compile(r"widget[ =]{1,2}(\d+\.\d+)")
HEDGES = ("simply", "just", "easy")


@dataclass
class Finding:
    """One proposal. `confidence` decides review order, never whether to apply."""

    page: str
    kind: str
    detail: str
    confidence: str          # mechanical | needs-judgement
    owner: str = ""
    proposed: str = ""


@dataclass
class Report:
    findings: list = field(default_factory=list)

    def add(self, **kwargs):
        self.findings.append(Finding(**kwargs))

    def by_confidence(self, level):
        return [f for f in self.findings if f.confidence == level]


def pages(root):
    for path in sorted(root.glob("*.md")):
        text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        meta = yaml.safe_load(text.split("---")[1]) or {}
        yield path, meta, text


def audit(root, facts):
    """Stage 1: find what is wrong. Entirely deterministic."""
    report = Report()
    today = dt.date.today()

    for path, meta, text in pages(root):
        owner = meta.get("owner", "unassigned")
        updated = meta.get("updated")
        if isinstance(updated, str):
            updated = dt.date.fromisoformat(updated)

        # Freshness: a date comparison.
        if updated and (today - updated).days > STALE_DAYS:
            age = (today - updated).days
            report.add(page=path.name, kind="stale", owner=owner,
                       detail=f"not reviewed in {age} days",
                       confidence="needs-judgement")

        # Code accuracy: claims against generated ground truth.
        # `set()` because findall hits the same version once in prose and once
        # in the install line, and two identical findings is one decision
        # presented as two.
        for version in sorted(set(VERSION.findall(text))):
            if version not in facts["supported_versions"]:
                report.add(page=path.name, kind="unsupported-version", owner=owner,
                           detail=f"references widget {version}, "
                                  f"supported: {facts['supported_versions']}",
                           confidence="mechanical",
                           proposed=f"{version} -> {facts['current_version']}")

        match = re.search(r"default is (\d+)", text)
        if match and int(match.group(1)) != facts["retries_default"]:
            report.add(page=path.name, kind="wrong-default", owner=owner,
                       detail=f"says default is {match.group(1)}, "
                              f"actual is {facts['retries_default']}",
                       confidence="mechanical",
                       proposed=f"default is {match.group(1)} -> "
                                f"default is {facts['retries_default']}")

        # Terminology drift: a substitution list.
        for approved, variants in facts["terms"].items():
            for variant in variants:
                if re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(variant)}\b", text):
                    report.add(page=path.name, kind="terminology", owner=owner,
                               detail=f"{variant!r} should be {approved!r}",
                               confidence="mechanical",
                               proposed=f"{variant} -> {approved}")

        # Prose quality: a hedge list. Mechanical to find, judgement to fix.
        for hedge in HEDGES:
            if re.search(rf"\b{hedge}\b", text, re.I):
                report.add(page=path.name, kind="hedge", owner=owner,
                           detail=f"uses {hedge!r}", confidence="needs-judgement")

    return report


def route(report, capacity):
    """Stage 2: decide what a human sees this week.

    THIS is the stage that determines whether the lifecycle works. A report
    of 180 findings is reviewed by nobody. Mechanical findings batch into one
    approval; judgement findings are rationed to the capacity that exists.
    """
    mechanical = report.by_confidence("mechanical")
    judgement = report.by_confidence("needs-judgement")

    batches = {}
    for finding in mechanical:
        batches.setdefault((finding.kind, finding.proposed), []).append(finding)

    # Judgement items go oldest-first, by owner, capped.
    rationed = judgement[:capacity]
    deferred = judgement[capacity:]
    return batches, rationed, deferred


def draft(finding, text):
    """Stage 3: propose replacement text for a located finding.

    A deterministic substitution stands in for a model call. The important
    property is the INTERFACE: a draft is produced for a finding that a
    deterministic check already located, never from an open instruction to
    improve the page. That bounds what a wrong draft can do.
    """
    if finding.kind in ("unsupported-version", "terminology", "wrong-default"):
        old, _, new = finding.proposed.partition(" -> ")
        if not new:
            # A proposal with no `old -> new` form cannot be applied as a diff.
            # Returning `finding.proposed` here replaced the WHOLE document
            # with the proposal string, which is how the first version of this
            # page produced a diff reading `- ---` / `+ default is 5`.
            raise ValueError(
                f"{finding.kind} proposal {finding.proposed!r} is not in "
                "'old -> new' form, so it cannot be rendered as a diff"
            )
        return text.replace(old, new)
    return ""
PY
echo "lifecycle written"

Step 3: run the audit and look at the shape of the problem

cat > run.py <<'PY'
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

from lifecycle import audit, route

facts = yaml.safe_load(open("facts.yaml"))
report = audit(Path("docs"), facts)

print(f"=== audit: {len(report.findings)} findings on 4 pages ===")
for finding in report.findings:
    print(f"  [{finding.confidence:<16}] {finding.page:<20} {finding.kind:<20} "
          f"{finding.detail}")

print()
print("by kind:      ", dict(Counter(f.kind for f in report.findings)))
print("by confidence:", dict(Counter(f.confidence for f in report.findings)))
print("by owner:     ", dict(Counter(f.owner for f in report.findings)))

CAPACITY = 2   # judgement items one person will actually review this week
batches, rationed, deferred = route(report, CAPACITY)

print(f"\n=== routed, with review capacity {CAPACITY} ===")
print(f"  {len(batches)} batched approval(s) covering "
      f"{sum(len(v) for v in batches.values())} mechanical findings:")
for (kind, proposed), items in batches.items():
    pages_affected = ", ".join(sorted(f.page for f in items))
    print(f"    {kind}: {proposed}   ({pages_affected})")
print(f"  {len(rationed)} judgement item(s) for review this week:")
for finding in rationed:
    print(f"    {finding.page}  {finding.kind}  {finding.detail}")
print(f"  {len(deferred)} deferred")
PY
python3 run.py

Step 4: show the drafting stage, and what bounds it

python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

from lifecycle import audit, draft

facts = yaml.safe_load(open("facts.yaml"))
report = audit(Path("docs"), facts)

print("=== drafts for mechanical findings, applied to nothing ===")
for finding in report.by_confidence("mechanical"):
    original = (Path("docs") / finding.page).read_text()
    proposed = draft(finding, original)
    changed = [
        (a, b) for a, b in zip(original.splitlines(), proposed.splitlines()) if a != b
    ]
    print(f"\n  {finding.page}  ({finding.kind})")
    for before, after in changed:
        print(f"    - {before.strip()}")
        print(f"    + {after.strip()}")

print()
print("=== what the drafting stage is NOT asked to do ===")
for finding in report.by_confidence("needs-judgement"):
    print(f"  {finding.page:<20} {finding.kind:<12} {finding.detail}")
print("  No draft is generated for these. 'This page is 1030 days old' has no")
print("  mechanical fix, and a model asked to refresh it would rewrite content")
print("  it cannot verify.")
PY

What you built. Three stages, a routing step that respects review capacity, and a drafting stage that only ever proposes a fix for a finding a deterministic check already located.

docs.title: What the audit found, and how routing changed its shape
docs.text:
Seven findings on four pages: three stale, one terminology, one unsupported version, one hedge, one wrong default. Split 4 judgement and 3 mechanical.

Routing turns that into:

3 batched approval(s) covering 3 mechanical findings:
  terminology: repo -> repository              (batching.md)
  unsupported-version: 2.2 -> 2.6              (install.md)
  wrong-default: default is 3 -> default is 5  (retries.md)
2 judgement item(s) for review this week
2 deferred

Three glances and two decisions, instead of seven items in a list. At four pages the difference is cosmetic. At four hundred it is the difference between a queue that gets cleared and one that does not, which is the whole argument.

The wrong-default finding is the one worth noticing: the page says the retries default is 3 and the ground truth says 5, because it changed in 2.5 and nobody updated the page. No model was involved in finding that. It is a regex against a value generated in CI.

docs.title: Two bugs the first run exposed
docs.text:
A duplicate finding. install.md mentions widget 2.2 twice, in prose and in the install command, so findall produced two identical findings and the batch read (install.md, install.md). One decision presented as two is exactly the thing routing exists to prevent, so the fix is to deduplicate per page and version.

A draft that replaced the whole document. The wrong-default proposal was "default is 5", with no old -> new form, and draft() fell back to returning the proposal as the entire proposed text. The rendered diff read - --- / + default is 5, which is a page being deleted and replaced by a sentence. The fix puts the proposal in old -> new form, and the fallback now raises instead of returning something nonsensical: a drafting stage that cannot express a change as a diff must fail loudly, because the alternative is a diff a reviewer might approve.

docs.title: Where the model goes, and where it does not
docs.text:
Activity Mechanism Model? Freshness check A date comparison No Code accuracy Claims against generated ground truth No Terminology drift A substitution list No Finding hedges and style issues A linter No Drafting a replacement for a located finding Prompt plus validation Yes Ranking a review queue Classification Yes Summarising a changelog into release notes Prompt plus review Yes Deciding what to retire Judgement Never Confirming a page is accurate Needs the implementation Never

Three of the four checks NVIDIA names involve no model at all. That is the most useful thing on this page: "automate the content lifecycle with LLMs" is mostly automation, with an LLM at two specific points. A pipeline that uses a model for the freshness check is slower, more expensive and less reliable than date.today() - updated.

docs.title: The constraint is review capacity
docs.text:
The failure that kills these pipelines is not a bad model. It is a queue nobody works:

Design target Result Maximise recall 180 findings, zero reviewed, corpus unchanged Respect capacity 12 findings, all reviewed, corpus improves weekly

Three mechanisms make a queue reviewable:

Mechanism Effect Batch identical mechanical findings One approval covers "2.2 to 2.6" on nine pages Separate mechanical from judgement Mechanical needs a glance; judgement needs thought Ration judgement items to real capacity The remainder is deferred visibly, not hidden

Batching is the big one. Nine pages with the same wrong version is one decision, not nine, and presenting it as nine is what makes a queue look impossible.

docs.title: Freshness is a signal, not a defect
docs.text:
A date is not evidence of anything. A page about a stable interface is fine at three years old; a page about a weekly-changing API is suspect at three months.

Better signal Why Last change to the code it documents Actual drift risk Views since last review A stale page nobody reads is not urgent Support tickets referencing it Evidence of real harm An assistant's failed answers citing it Evidence it misleads

Age alone over-reports, which is exactly how a queue reaches 180 items. This is why the golden path tags staleness needs-judgement rather than mechanical.

docs.title: What drafting must be bounded by
docs.text:
Bound Why A deterministic check located the finding first An open "improve this page" instruction has no failure bound The proposed change is a diff Reviewable; an applied change is not Validate the draft before a human sees it Grounding and vocabulary checks Never draft for a judgement finding "This is 1030 days old" has no mechanical fix Never widen a constraint to pass See agent skills

The last two are the ones that go wrong. A model asked to refresh a stale page rewrites content it cannot verify, fluently, and the diff looks like an improvement.

docs.title: Measuring whether the lifecycle works
docs.text:
Metric Healthy Review queue depth Flat or falling. Growing means it is theatre Proposals accepted 80% or more. Below that the precision is wrong Median page age Falling Findings per page per quarter Falling, as classes of defect get fixed at the source Time from finding to merge Days, not months

Queue depth is the one to watch. A growing queue with a good acceptance rate means you built a pipeline that generates work faster than the team absorbs it, which is a worse outcome than not having one, because the corpus now also looks audited.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with how little of it needs a model, then with the capacity constraint. "Three of the four checks in that bullet are not model work: freshness is a date comparison, code accuracy is claims against ground truth generated in CI, terminology drift is a substitution list. The model does two things, drafting a replacement for a finding something else already located, and ranking the queue. And the thing that decides whether any of it works is review capacity: our first audit produced 180 findings on 400 pages and nobody reviewed any of them, so I batched identical mechanical findings into single approvals and rationed judgement items to what one person actually reads in a week."

The follow-up is "how do you stop a model rewriting things it should not", and the answer is the interface rather than the prompt. A draft is only ever produced for a finding a deterministic check located, with the specific change named, as a diff, applied to nothing. An open instruction to improve a page has no bound on what it can change, and that is a design choice rather than a prompting problem.

The tradeoff to volunteer. This pipeline makes the corpus more consistent and can make it blander. Batched terminology fixes are genuinely good; batched anything-else starts flattening the voice of pages that had one, and the reviewer approving a batch of nine is not reading nine pages. There is also a real risk of false confidence: a corpus with a green audit looks maintained, and the audit only checks what you taught it to check. The things it cannot see, omissions and subtly wrong explanations, are the expensive defects, and nothing here touches them.

One sharper point. The strongest observation is that the lifecycle pipeline's real output is a list of defect classes to fix at the source. If the audit reports forty wrong version references every quarter, the answer is not a better audit, it is a single source of truth for the version plus a gate, after which that finding never appears again. Findings-per-page should fall over time, and if it is flat you are paying for a treadmill. That is the systems mindset applied to your own automation, and it is the thing that distinguishes an operator from someone who set up a cron job.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A pipeline that proposes and never applies, with a routing step that batches and rations, and queue-depth numbers over a few weeks.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. The routing step is the demonstration: it turns a raw finding list into a queue a person will actually clear.
  2. Generate your ground truth in CI. Parse --help, read git tags, export the glossary. The audit is only as good as the facts, and hand-maintained facts are the first thing to rot.
  3. Track queue depth and acceptance rate for a month. Two numbers. If depth grows while acceptance is high, you have the capacity problem rather than a precision problem, and that diagnosis is the whole value.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. "We use AI to maintain our docs" is a slogan. A pipeline where three of four checks are deterministic, drafting is bounded to located findings, mechanical findings batch into one approval, and queue depth is a tracked metric demonstrates that you have run one long enough for the review bottleneck to bite.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
No model ran here, so the drafting, review and migration uses this page describes were reasoned about rather than measured. The demonstration is organisational as much as technical: the interesting figures are about review cost, not model quality.

What you need. A model you can call, a corpus with a validator, and, crucially, a human reviewer's time logged honestly. Two afternoons: one to run the model over real work, one to review the output while recording how long each piece took.

What you would run. Pick the three lifecycle stages where a model is plausibly useful and treat each as a separate experiment: drafting a page from an outline plus source material, reviewing an existing page against a style guide, and migrating a page between formats. Score each against the check that already exists for that stage, then record reviewer minutes per page.

What you would see.

Stage Rough outcome What it tells you Drafting from sources structurally correct, factually thin The scaffold is the value, not the prose Drafting without sources fluent and wrong in ways review misses The failure this page warns about Style review against a written guide high agreement with a linter Cheapest real win Style review against taste confident and unusable Guides have to be written down first Format migration high accuracy, with a long tail The tail is where the time goes Reviewer minutes, drafted page often higher than writing fresh The number that decides adoption

The last row is the measurement that matters and the one nobody records. Reviewing a plausible wrong draft is slower than writing a page, because verification requires reading the source material you would have read anyway plus the draft's claims about it. A pipeline that reduces authoring time and increases review time has not saved anything.

How you would know it had failed. If review time per page is not recorded, the experiment has measured nothing, whatever the quality scores say. If the model's drafts pass your validator at a higher rate than your humans' do, suspect that the validator checks structure and the humans are writing content. And if migration accuracy is 100%, the sample did not include the awkward cases, which are the only ones that cost anything.

docs.title: llms.txt and llms-full.txt
docs.text:
A map of your corpus for a model that has not read it yet, and the whole corpus for one that wants it in a single fetch.

core · difficulty 1 · 2h

including llms.txt, MCP-accessible sources, agent skills and context kits, and evaluation sets for answer accuracy

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: Agent-ready content

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
/llms.txt is a Markdown file at the root of a site giving a language model a map of what is there: a name, a one-line description, and sections of annotated links. /llms-full.txt is the other artifact, the whole corpus concatenated into one document for a model that would rather make one request than thirty.

They are a community convention proposed by Jeremy Howard of Answer.AI in September 2024. Not a standard, and that distinction matters when you present it internally.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA names the file explicitly, in a list of four AI-ready outputs. That is the whole justification, and it is a core concept for a cheaper reason than most: it takes an afternoon and it is the single most visible signal that a documentation team has thought about machine consumers at all.

On a Tuesday it is a generation step in your build, and the only interesting part is what the annotations say. A map whose descriptions are page titles restated is useless, because a model reading it still cannot tell which of your forty pages answers the question in front of it. A map whose descriptions say what question each page answers is genuinely useful.

The reason it earns its place alongside much harder concepts: it serves a consumer the other artifacts cannot. Chunks serve a retriever that already has a query. An assistant deciding where to look has no query embedding and no index; it has a URL and a question. llms.txt is the only thing in the stack built for that moment.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Generate both files from a corpus and see what each one is for. Twenty-five minutes.

Step 1: a corpus with real summaries

The summaries are the content here. A generator over pages with bad summaries produces a bad map.

mkdir -p llms-drill/docs && cd llms-drill
cat > docs/install.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Install the widget CLI
summary: Install the CLI with pip and confirm it runs.
kind: how-to
updated: 2026-10-26
---
# Install the widget CLI

Run `pip install widget`. Requires Python 3.10 or newer.
EOF

cat > docs/batch-size.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Choose a batch size
summary: Pick a batch size from latency targets, GPU memory and quantisation.
kind: how-to
updated: 2026-10-26
---
# Choose a batch size

The default is 32. If latency matters, use 1 or 2.
EOF

cat > docs/cli.md <<'EOF'
---
title: CLI reference
summary: Every command, flag, default and exit code.
kind: reference
updated: 2026-10-26
---
# CLI reference

## Exit codes

`0` success, `1` configuration error, `2` bad arguments.
EOF

cat > docs/upgrade-1x.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Upgrading from 1.x
summary: Migration steps from the 1.x client, which reached end of life in 2024.
kind: how-to
updated: 2024-03-01
---
# Upgrading from 1.x

Replace the client import and rename two arguments.
EOF
ls docs/

Step 2: generate both files

cat > gen.py <<'PY'
"""Generate llms.txt and llms-full.txt from front matter.

Generated, never hand-written, for the same reason the API reference is
generated: a hand-maintained index of forty pages is accurate for about a
week, and it is the file a model trusts most.
"""
import datetime as dt
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

SITE = "Widget platform docs"
TAGLINE = "Client library and CLI for the widget inference platform."
BASE = "https://widget.example"
STALE_DAYS = 365

GROUPS = [
    ("how-to", "How-to guides", "Task-oriented. Assume familiarity with the platform."),
    ("reference", "Reference", "Factual description of the interface."),
    ("explanation", "Explanation", "Design reasoning and tradeoffs."),
]


def pages(docs: Path):
    for path in sorted(docs.glob("*.md")):
        text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        front, _, body = text.partition("---\n")[2].partition("\n---\n")
        yield path, yaml.safe_load(front), body


def is_stale(meta) -> bool:
    updated = meta["updated"]
    if isinstance(updated, str):
        updated = dt.date.fromisoformat(updated)
    return (dt.date.today() - updated).days > STALE_DAYS


def main() -> None:
    docs = Path("docs")
    out = Path("dist")
    out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    everything = list(pages(docs))

    # --- llms.txt: the map -------------------------------------------
    lines = [f"# {SITE}", "", f"> {TAGLINE}", ""]
    lines.append(
        "Each link points to the Markdown source rather than the rendered page. "
        "Sections group pages by what kind of question they can answer."
    )
    lines.append("")

    for kind, label, blurb in GROUPS:
        group = [(p, m) for p, m, _ in everything
                 if m["kind"] == kind and not is_stale(m)]
        if not group:
            continue
        lines += [f"## {label}", "", blurb, ""]
        for path, meta in group:
            lines.append(f"- [{meta['title']}]({BASE}/docs/{path.name}): {meta['summary']}")
        lines.append("")

    # The convention reserves `## Optional` for content a model may skip.
    # Stale pages belong there: still true enough to cite, not what you want
    # a model reaching for first.
    stale = [(p, m) for p, m, _ in everything if is_stale(m)]
    if stale:
        lines += ["## Optional", "",
                  "Not reviewed in over a year. Treat with lower confidence.", ""]
        for path, meta in stale:
            lines.append(f"- [{meta['title']}]({BASE}/docs/{path.name}): {meta['summary']}")
        lines.append("")

    (out / "llms.txt").write_text("\n".join(lines), encoding="utf-8")

    # --- llms-full.txt: everything, once -----------------------------
    full = [f"# {SITE}: complete documentation", ""]
    for path, meta, body in everything:
        full += [
            "---", "",
            f"# {meta['title']}", "",
            f"*{meta['kind']} · updated {meta['updated']}*", "",
            meta["summary"], "",
            body.strip(), "",
        ]
    (out / "llms-full.txt").write_text("\n".join(full), encoding="utf-8")

    print(f"{len(everything)} pages, {len(stale)} stale")
    for name in ("llms.txt", "llms-full.txt"):
        print(f"  {name:<16} {(out / name).stat().st_size:>6} bytes")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
PY
python3 gen.py
echo
cat dist/llms.txt

Step 3: check it against the only test that matters

A map is good if a model reading only the map can pick the right page.

python3 - <<'PY'
"""Can a reader pick the right page from the map alone?

This stands in for asking a model. The point is that the test uses only
llms.txt, never the pages, which is exactly the situation the file exists
for.
"""
import re

MAP = open("dist/llms.txt").read()
QUESTIONS = [
    ("my p99 latency is too high", "batch-size.md"),
    ("what does exit code 2 mean", "cli.md"),
    ("how do I get started", "install.md"),
]

entries = re.findall(r"- \[(.+?)\]\((.+?)\): (.+)", MAP)
print(f"{len(entries)} entries in the map\n")

for question, expected in QUESTIONS:
    terms = [t for t in re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", question.lower()) if len(t) > 2]
    best, score = None, 0
    for title, url, summary in entries:
        hay = f"{title} {summary}".lower()
        hits = sum(1 for t in terms if t in hay)
        if hits > score:
            best, score = url, hits
    ok = best and best.endswith(expected)
    print(f"  {'OK ' if ok else '   '} {question:<32} -> {best or 'no match'}")
PY

Step 4: see what a bad summary costs

python3 - <<'PY'
import pathlib
# Replace one good summary with the kind most corpora actually have.
p = pathlib.Path("docs/batch-size.md")
p.write_text(p.read_text().replace(
    "summary: Pick a batch size from latency targets, GPU memory and quantisation.",
    "summary: Information about batch size configuration."))
PY
python3 gen.py >/dev/null
grep "Choose a batch size" dist/llms.txt
python3 - <<'PY'
import re
MAP = open("dist/llms.txt").read()
entries = re.findall(r"- \[(.+?)\]\((.+?)\): (.+)", MAP)
terms = ["p99", "latency", "high", "too"]
best, score = None, 0
for title, url, summary in entries:
    hay = f"{title} {summary}".lower()
    hits = sum(1 for t in terms if t in hay)
    if hits > score:
        best, score = url, hits
print(f"  'my p99 latency is too high' -> {best or 'NO MATCH'} (score {score})")
PY

What you built. Both artifacts, generated, with stale pages routed to ## Optional, and a test that uses only the map.

Step 4 is the point of the whole exercise, and the result is stark: with a good summary, "my p99 latency is too high" routes correctly to the batch-size page. Replace that one summary with "Information about batch size configuration" and the same question returns no match at all. The page is unchanged, the file still looks complete, and the map has stopped working.

The summary is the entire payload of llms.txt. Most published ones restate the title, which produces exactly this failure invisibly.

Two honest notes on the step 3 output. It scores 2 of 3: "how do I get started" routes to the batch-size page rather than to install, because "started" appears in neither summary and the crude term overlap latches onto something else. That is a real finding about the install summary rather than about the method, and the fix is to write the summary in the words a new reader would use. And the test is a stand-in for asking a model, not a substitute for it: it measures whether the vocabulary is there, which is necessary and not sufficient.

docs.title: The format
docs.text:
# Project name

> One-line description of what this is.

Optional prose giving a model orientation it cannot get from the links.

## Section name

Optional blurb explaining what this section's pages can answer.

- [Page title](https://example.com/docs/page.md): what question it answers.

## Optional

Pages a model may skip if it is short of context.
Element Required Notes # Name Yes The only required line in the convention > Description Recommended One line, what the project is Prose after it Optional Orientation, not marketing ## Sections Optional Group by what kind of question, not by product area ## Optional Reserved The convention's name for skippable content

docs.title: The two files, and who each is for
docs.text:
llms.txt llms-full.txt Consumer A model deciding where to look A model reading everything at once Size Kilobytes Megabytes Scales to a large corpus Yes No Contains page content No Yes Breaks when the corpus grows No Yes, into the context window

For a corpus beyond a few hundred pages, llms-full.txt stops being useful and llms.txt plus MCP or retrieval is the answer.

docs.title: What makes a good annotation
docs.text:
Bad Better "Information about batch size configuration" "Pick a batch size from latency targets, GPU memory and quantisation" "Installation guide" "Install the CLI with pip and confirm it runs" "CLI reference" "Every command, flag, default and exit code" "Advanced topics" Split it; this describes nothing

The test: does the annotation contain the words a reader would use when they have the problem? "Latency" and "memory" are those words. "Configuration" is not.

docs.title: Linking to Markdown, not HTML
docs.text:
The convention points at Markdown sources. Serving them alongside the rendered site is a one-line build step and it matters: a model fetching an HTML page spends most of its context on navigation, cookie banners and footers.

# in your publish job, after building the site
cp -r docs site/docs

docs.title: The honest status of this convention
docs.text:
Claim Reality "It is a standard" It is a community proposal from September 2024 "Models read it automatically" Some tools do. Most crawlers do not, and support is uneven "It replaces a sitemap" No. Different consumer, different format. Keep both "It replaces RAG" No. It is a map, not a retrieval system

Adoption is real, including by several developer-tools companies, and scepticism about it is also real. Present it internally as cheap and low-risk rather than as table stakes, because somebody in the room will know it is contested and a claim of standardisation will cost you credibility.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Say what it is for, say what it is not, and lead with the summary quality. "It is a map for a model that has not read your corpus yet: a name, a description, and annotated links grouped by what kind of question each page answers. The only thing that matters is the annotations. A summary that restates the title makes the file useless while leaving it looking done, which is the state most published llms.txt files are in. I generate it from the required summary field so it cannot drift, and I route stale pages to the Optional section."

The follow-up is usually "is this actually a standard", and it is a test. The answer is no: it is a community convention proposed by Jeremy Howard in September 2024, adoption is partial, and some people think it is unnecessary because a well-structured sitemap and clean HTML do much the same job. The reason to do it anyway is that it costs an afternoon, it is generated so it cannot rot, and it forces you to write a real one-sentence summary for every page, which is worth having regardless of whether any model ever reads the file.

The tradeoff to volunteer. A hand-written llms.txt is worse than none. Committed once and forgotten, it actively misinforms a model about what your corpus contains, and unlike a stale page nothing in your site contradicts it. So the real commitment is a build step and a CI gate that fails when the committed file does not match the corpus. A team not ready for that should skip the file.

One sharper point. The most valuable thing about adopting llms.txt usually has nothing to do with models. It makes the quality of your page summaries suddenly legible. Forty summaries in one file, side by side, is a brutal review: the vague ones are obvious at a glance in a way they never are scattered across forty pages of front matter. Several teams have found their content model's weakest field this way, and that is a real benefit independent of whether the convention survives.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A generated llms.txt with annotations that pass the reader-vocabulary test, plus the CI gate against staleness.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path, including step 4. The before-and-after on one bad summary is the demonstration, and it takes two minutes.
  2. Generate it in CI and fail on drift. Regenerate, compare against the committed file, fail if they differ. Ten lines, and it is what separates this from a file somebody added once.
  3. Review all your summaries in one sitting, in the generated file. Rewrite every one that does not contain the words a reader with that problem would use. This is the step with value beyond the convention. Predict how many will need rewriting before you start. The gap between that guess and the count is the measurement, and it is usually in the same direction.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Publishing an llms.txt proves you read about it. A generated one, gated against staleness, with annotations written in reader vocabulary, and an opinion about the convention's contested status, proves you thought about it.

docs.title: Localization and translation pipelines
docs.text:
Segmenting Markdown for translators, protecting what must not be translated, and verifying it came back intact.

supporting · difficulty 3 · 4h

Not a quotation (adjacent)

Neither posting mentions localization. It is here because a platform documentation role at a company selling worldwide meets it eventually, and because the engineering is a content-model problem rather than a language one.

Prerequisites: Content models, Single-sourcing

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The pipeline that gets documentation translated and keeps the translations in sync as the source changes. Mechanically: segment the source into translatable units, protect the parts that must not be translated, send the units out, get them back, verify them, and rebuild.

The reason it is difficulty 3 is that almost all of the difficulty is in segmentation and protection, both of which are decisions about your content model. Translation itself is somebody else's job.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
It does not, and the banner says so. The case for knowing it is that localization is the most unforgiving test of a content model that exists.

A corpus with inconsistent structure, inline HTML, text baked into screenshots and sentences that assemble themselves out of fragments can be published in English indefinitely. Try to translate it and every one of those becomes a cost multiplied by the number of languages. Teams routinely discover their content model is broken only when the localization bill arrives.

So it belongs in this category as the stress test. If your corpus localizes cleanly, it is well modelled.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Extract translatable segments from a real Markdown page, break it the way everybody breaks it first, and verify the round trip. About thirty-five minutes.

Step 1: a page with the usual hazards

mkdir -p l10n-demo && cd l10n-demo
pip install --quiet polib

cat > page.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Rotate a key
summary: How to rotate an access token.
---

# Rotate a key

Run `widget keys rotate` to replace the current token.

The command prints the new token. See [the configuration guide](configure.md).

!!! warning
    The old token stops working immediately.
EOF

Four hazards in eleven lines: front matter with translatable values, an inline code span that must survive untouched, a link whose text is translatable and whose target is not, and an admonition whose marker is syntax and whose body is prose.

Step 2: segment and protect

# extract.py
import itertools
import re

PROTECT = [
    (re.compile(r"`[^`\n]+`"), "CODE"),
    (re.compile(r"\]\(([^)\s]+)\)"), "LINK"),   # this one is wrong; see step 3
]


def protect(s):
    counter = itertools.count(1)
    kept = {}
    for pattern, label in PROTECT:
        def sub(m, label=label):
            key = f"{{{label}{next(counter)}}}"
            kept[key] = m.group(0)
            return key
        s = pattern.sub(sub, s)
    return s, kept

python3 extract.py

extracted 5 segment(s); 2 protected span(s)
  [heading   ] Rotate a key
  [sentence  ] Run {CODE1} to replace the current token.
  [sentence  ] The command prints the new token.
  [sentence  ] See [the configuration guide{LINK1}.
  [admonition] !!! warning
    The old token stops working immediately.

Step 3: read the output properly, because two segments are broken

Look at the fourth segment: See [the configuration guide{LINK1}. The opening bracket has no closing bracket. The placeholder swallowed it, because \]\(([^)\s]+)\) matches the ] as well as the parenthesised URL.

A translator receiving that has been handed malformed Markdown and no way to know where the link text ends. The fix is a lookbehind, so the ] stays in the segment:

re.compile(r"(?<=\])\(([^)\s]+)\)")

naive:   See [the configuration guide{LINK1}.
better:  See [the configuration guide]{LINK1}.

The fifth segment has the same class of problem from the other direction. The admonition is one unit containing both !!! warning, which is syntax and must not be translated, and the body, which must be. Split them:

m = re.match(r"^(!!!\s+\w+.*?)\n(\s+)(.*)$", block, re.S)
# m.group(1) = '!!! warning'                     -> do not translate
# m.group(3) = 'The old token stops working...'   -> translate

Neither bug is exotic. Both are what happens when you write segmentation rules against a few example pages, and both produce segments a translator cannot do anything sensible with. Segmentation quality is the whole job, and the way to check it is to read your own output as if you were the translator.

Step 4: verify the round trip

The returned translation, and the check that matters:

src  = "Run {CODE1} to replace the current token."
de   = "Führen Sie {CODE1} aus, um das aktuelle Token zu ersetzen."
kept = {"{CODE1}": "`widget keys rotate`"}

missing = [k for k in kept if k not in de]
print("placeholders dropped:", missing or "none")

placeholders dropped: none
reinserted: Führen Sie `widget keys rotate` aus, um das aktuelle Token zu ersetzen.

And the failure this check exists for, a translation that dropped the placeholder because it read as noise:

a translation that dropped it: Führen Sie den Befehl aus, um das Token zu ersetzen.
placeholders dropped: ['{CODE1}']

Without that check, the German page tells the reader to run "the command" and never says which. A placeholder-integrity check on every returned segment is not optional.

Step 5: measure expansion, on the right basis

masked segment (what the translator sees):  en= 41 de= 58  +41%
full sentence (what the reader sees):       en= 54 de= 71  +31%

Use the second figure. The masked one is inflated, because {CODE1} is shorter than the code it stands for and so understates the English. Measure expansion on the reinserted string.

Thirty per cent is the usual working figure for German against English, and it is why layouts with fixed-width elements break on translation rather than merely looking different.

What you built. A segmentation pass, two corrected rules, a placeholder-integrity check, and an honest expansion number.

docs.title: What must not be translated
docs.text:
Element Why Code spans and blocks They are executed, not read Command names, flags, API identifiers Same Link targets A URL is not prose File paths and environment variables Same Admonition markers and directive names Syntax Front-matter keys Schema; the values often are translatable Product names Policy; decide once and record it

Front matter is the one teams get wrong in both directions: translating the keys breaks the build, and failing to translate title and summary leaves the navigation in English.

docs.title: What breaks when you actually ship it
docs.text:
Problem What it does Text expansion, roughly 30% for German Breaks fixed-width layouts, truncates nav labels Right-to-left scripts Needs logical CSS properties, not left and right Double-byte scripts Font, line-breaking and input-method issues Screenshots with embedded text Untranslatable without regenerating them Sentences assembled from fragments Word order differs; fragments cannot be reordered Sorting and collation Alphabetical order is language-specific Dates, numbers, units Formats differ; a hard-coded format is a bug

The fragment row is a content-model failure rather than a presentation one. A sentence built as "Set " + field + " to enable " + feature cannot be translated correctly into a language with different word order, and the only fix is to make the whole sentence one translatable unit with named placeholders.

docs.title: Keeping translations in sync
docs.text:
Mechanism Does Translation memory Reuses previous translations for unchanged segments Source hashing per segment Marks a translation stale when its source changes Fuzzy matching Flags near-matches for review rather than silently reusing Fallback to source Shows English rather than nothing for untranslated segments A per-language freshness report The freshness problem, times N

Segment-level staleness is what makes this maintainable. Without it, any source edit invalidates a whole page and you pay to retranslate work that did not change.

docs.title: Where this sits in the generators
docs.text:
Generator Support Docusaurus Built in: per-locale builds and a translation directory Sphinx gettext builder, a mature and conventional workflow MkDocs Plugin, and the least mature of the three Antora Component-based; a locale is usually a separate component

If localization is known to be coming, it belongs in the generator choice, because retrofitting it is substantially harder than starting with it.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with it as a content-model test. "Localization is the most unforgiving test of a content model. A corpus with inline HTML, assembled sentences and text baked into screenshots publishes fine in English and multiplies every one of those defects by the number of languages. Most teams find out their model is broken when the first translation bill arrives."

The follow-up is about keeping translations current, and the answer is segment-level staleness: hash each source segment so a change invalidates only the segments it touched. Without it, a typo fix invalidates a whole page.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Segmentation is where the quality lives and it is never finished. My own first pass produced two broken segments out of five: a placeholder that ate a link's closing bracket, and an admonition whose syntax marker was bundled with its prose. Both would have reached a translator. You have to read your own extraction output as the translator will, and you need a placeholder-integrity check on everything that comes back, because a dropped placeholder produces fluent, confident, wrong instructions.

One sharper point. Assembled sentences are the defect that cannot be fixed downstream. Concatenating fragments is fine in English and impossible to translate correctly where word order differs, so the whole sentence has to be one unit with named placeholders. That decision is made in the content model long before anybody thinks about languages, which is why localization belongs in this category rather than in a translation one.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. An extraction script whose output you have read as a translator would, plus a placeholder-integrity check on returned segments.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path, and read step 2's output before step 3 tells you what is wrong with it. Spotting the malformed segment yourself is the exercise.
  2. Grep a corpus you own for assembled sentences: string concatenation in templates, or one sentence split across a list. Each is untranslatable.
  3. Write the placeholder-integrity check. It is five lines, and it is the difference between a wrong page and a caught error.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Neither of this guide's repositories is localized, which the demonstrated page records. What travels is the specific engineering: a segmentation pass, the two bugs it had on first run, why each one matters to a translator, and an expansion figure measured on the right basis rather than quoted from a blog post.

docs.title: Markdown and its dialects
docs.text:
Markdown is a family, not a format, and unsupported syntax ships to the reader as literal text.

core · difficulty 1 · 2h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Markdown/RST"

Intel: "Git, Markdown or MDX, and doc build pipelines"

Prerequisites: Docs-as-code

Leads to: MDX, reStructuredText, Choosing a static site generator

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A family of plain-text markup dialects that mostly agree about headings, emphasis and lists, and disagree about almost everything else. "Markdown" names the family. What your build actually accepts is decided by the specific parser your static site generator uses and the set of extensions you enabled.

The practical consequence, and the reason this page exists at difficulty 1, is the failure mode. A parser that does not understand a construct does not raise an error. It passes the characters through, so the reader gets ~~struck~~ with the tildes attached.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Both postings name it, Intel alongside MDX and NVIDIA alongside RST, which tells you the expectation is not "can you write Markdown" but "do you understand that these are different dialects with different capabilities."

Nobody is testing whether you can write a heading. What matters on a real corpus is knowing which constructs are safe to use, where the extension configuration lives, and that a dialect mismatch is silent. On a corpus with multiple contributors, somebody will write GitHub-flavoured syntax because GitHub rendered it in the pull request description, and your site will publish the raw characters.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Run one source file through five implementations and watch them disagree. About twenty minutes.

Step 1: a file using five commonly assumed features

mkdir -p md-demo && cd md-demo
cat > sample.md <<'EOF'
# Title

A table:

| a | b |
|---|---|
| 1 | 2 |

Term
: A definition.

~~struck~~ and a footnote[^1].

[^1]: The note.

- [ ] a task
EOF

Tables, definition lists, strikethrough, footnotes, task lists. All five feel like "Markdown".

Step 2: ask five parsers

import markdown
import mistune
from markdown_it import MarkdownIt

src = open("sample.md").read()

feats = {
    "table":    lambda h: "<table" in h,
    "deflist":  lambda h: "<dl" in h,
    "strike":   lambda h: "<del" in h or "<s>" in h,
    "footnote": lambda h: "[^1]" not in h and ('href="#fn' in h or "<sup" in h),
    "taskbox":  lambda h: 'type="checkbox"' in h,
}
impls = {
    "python-markdown core":   markdown.markdown(src),
    "python-markdown +ext":   markdown.markdown(
        src, extensions=["tables", "def_list", "footnotes"]),
    "mistune":                mistune.html(src),
    "markdown-it commonmark": MarkdownIt("commonmark").render(src),
    "markdown-it gfm-like":   MarkdownIt("gfm-like", {"linkify": False}).render(src),
}
print(f"{'implementation':26}" + "".join(f"{n:10}" for n in feats))
for label, html in impls.items():
    print(f"{label:26}" + "".join(
        f"{('yes' if fn(html) else '-'):10}" for fn in feats.values()))

implementation            table     deflist   strike    footnote  taskbox
python-markdown core      -         -         -         -         -
python-markdown +ext      yes       yes       -         yes       -
mistune                   yes       -         yes       yes       -
markdown-it commonmark    -         -         -         -         -
markdown-it gfm-like      yes       -         yes       -         -

No two rows are the same. Five implementations, five answers, one source file. CommonMark, the actual standard, supports none of the five features, because every one of them is an extension. And task lists render nowhere by default, including in the GitHub-flavoured configuration.

Step 3: see what the failure looks like

for label, html in impls.items():
    print(f"{label:26} literal '[^1]' in output: {'[^1]' in html}")

python-markdown core       True
python-markdown +ext       False
mistune                    False
markdown-it commonmark     True
markdown-it gfm-like       True

Three of the five publish [^1] to the reader. Not an error, not a warning. The characters are simply passed through, because to a parser without the extension they are just text.

This is the whole argument for treating dialect as a configuration you know rather than a detail you inherit.

Step 4: ask what your own site accepts

Run the same source through the exact extension list in your mkdocs.yml. For this guide, the answer is:

table                yes
deflist              yes
footnote converted   yes
strike               -
taskbox              -

Then look at what the unsupported half becomes:

<p>~~struck~~ and a footnote<sup id="fnref:1">...</sup>.</p>
<li>[ ] a task</li>

Two constructs that any contributor might reasonably type, shipping as literal characters.

Step 5: make it a gate

The source alone cannot tell you this, so compare source against built HTML, exactly as the fence gate does. A construct used in prose whose markers survive into the output did not render:

CONSTRUCTS = {
    "strikethrough": (re.compile(r"~~[^~\n]+~~"), re.compile(r"~~[^~\n]+~~")),
    "task list": (re.compile(r"^\s*[-*]\s+\[[ xX]\]\s"),
                  re.compile(r"<li[^>]*>\s*\[[ xX]\]\s")),
}

Both halves have to agree: the construct in the source and its litter in the HTML. Requiring both is what stops the check firing on a page that explains the syntax inside a code sample.

fieldguide render

ok: 5147 fenced lines checked, every one renders as code; no unsupported
Markdown construct reaches the reader

What you built. Knowledge of which dialect your site actually speaks, and a gate that fails when someone writes outside it.

docs.title: What is in the base layer, and what is an extension
docs.text:
Construct CommonMark Usually an extension Headings, emphasis, lists, links, code Yes Fenced code blocks Yes Tables No Yes, everywhere Footnotes No Yes Definition lists No Yes Strikethrough No GFM, and some others Task lists No GFM, and a separate extension elsewhere Admonitions and callouts No Highly tool-specific Includes and transclusion No Tool-specific, often a plugin Front matter No Convention, handled before parsing

Front matter is worth singling out: it is not Markdown at all. It is a YAML block that the generator strips before the parser sees the file, which is why its rules differ from everything else on this page.

docs.title: The dialects you will meet
docs.text: Dialect Where Notable CommonMark The specification Strict, small, unambiguous GFM GitHub, and much tooling Tables, strikethrough, task lists, autolinks Python-Markdown MkDocs, Material Extension ecosystem, including PyMdown MyST Sphinx with myst-parser Markdown with reStructuredText's directive power MDX Docusaurus and friends Markdown plus JSX; see MDX AsciiDoc Antora Not Markdown; a different language with a real spec

docs.title: Choosing what to allow
docs.text:
Decision Recommendation Which extensions The fewest that cover your content, chosen deliberately Where it is recorded In the generator config, in version control, reviewed How contributors learn it A short authoring guide, plus a gate that catches mistakes GFM compatibility Worth it if contributors draft in GitHub comments Raw HTML Allow sparingly; it breaks other renderers and most AI pipelines

The last row matters more than it used to. Raw HTML inside Markdown is opaque to anything that consumes your source rather than your HTML, including chunking and llms.txt generation. A corpus with heavy inline HTML is markedly harder to make agent-ready.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the failure mode, not the feature list. "Markdown is a family of dialects, and the thing that bites is that an unsupported construct is not an error. The parser passes the characters through, so ~~struck~~ reaches the reader with the tildes on it. So I treat the extension list as a configuration I know, and I gate on it."

The follow-up is usually about contributor experience. The honest answer is that contributors will write GFM, because GitHub rendered it in the pull request they just opened, and the mitigations are a short authoring guide, a sensible extension set that includes the common GFM constructs, and a check that catches the rest.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Every extension you enable is a construct that will not render elsewhere. Content written against Material's admonitions cannot move to Docusaurus without a rewrite, and the more extensions you adopt the more your corpus is locked to one generator. Portability and expressiveness are genuinely opposed here, and the right answer depends on whether you expect to migrate.

One sharper point. Front matter is not Markdown. It is stripped before parsing, which is why its failures look different: a malformed YAML block can take out the whole page rather than one construct, and it needs a content model validator rather than a Markdown gate.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A documented extension set plus a check that fails when somebody writes outside it.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. The five-row table is the thing to internalise: no two implementations agree.
  2. Run your own site's extension list over the sample file and write down the answer. Most teams cannot tell you whether their site supports footnotes.
  3. Grep your corpus for ~~ and - [ ] outside code fences. If you find any, they are shipping as literal characters right now.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. src/fieldguide/dialect.py is the gate from step 5, with seven tests covering both directions, including the case that keeps it honest: a page discussing the syntax inside a fence must not be flagged for using it. This guide's own corpus is clean, which the test asserts rather than assumes.
