docs.title: Model Context Protocol
docs.text:
A JSON-RPC interface that lets an agent call your documentation as tools instead of being handed a blob of text.

core · difficulty 3 · 5h

Ways to stand out: experience building RAG pipelines, AI assistants, MCP servers, or agent skill and context libraries backed by documentation

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: Agent-ready content

Leads to: Agent skills and context kits, Agentic workflows

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A protocol for exposing data and capabilities to a language model as callable tools. An MCP server declares what it can do, a client connects, and the model decides when to call which tool with which arguments.

For documentation, it means an agent can query your corpus mid-task instead of being given a pre-selected chunk of it. The difference matters: the agent gets to decide what it needs, and to ask twice.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA names it twice. Once in the AI-ready list, "MCP-accessible sources", and once under ways to stand out, "MCP servers ... backed by documentation". That repetition is a signal: they want the interface, not just the content.

The reason this is worth a core slot rather than being filed as a tool choice: it serves a consumer none of the other artifacts do. llms.txt serves a model that can fetch URLs. Chunks serve a retriever that already has a query. An agent working inside an editor, halfway through a task, needs neither of those. It needs to ask a specific question, get a specific answer, and ask a follow-up, with filters it chooses.

On a Tuesday this is the difference between two failure modes. With a flat context dump, a coding agent gets 40,000 characters of your docs and uses the wrong page because it was first. With an MCP server, the agent calls search_docs(query="batch size", diataxis="how-to"), gets three chunks, and if they are wrong it can call again with a different filter. The second system can recover from a bad first guess.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a working MCP server over a documentation tree, dependency-free, and drive it with handwritten JSON-RPC. Forty-five minutes.

Step 1: a corpus with metadata worth filtering on

mkdir -p mcp-drill/docs && cd mcp-drill
cat > docs/batch-size.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Choose a batch size
summary: Pick a batch size from latency targets, GPU memory and quantisation.
kind: how-to
audience: developer
---
# Choose a batch size

Set `batch_size`. The default is 32.

## If latency matters

Use 1 or 2. Batching at 32 adds roughly 200ms at p99.
EOF

cat > docs/why-batching.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Why batching helps throughput
summary: The reasoning behind batched inference and what it costs in latency.
kind: explanation
audience: developer
---
# Why batching helps throughput

A GPU is more efficient per item on a larger batch.

## What it costs

Every request waits for the batch to fill.
EOF

cat > docs/cli.md <<'EOF'
---
title: CLI reference
summary: Every command, flag, default and exit code.
kind: reference
audience: developer
---
# CLI reference

## Exit codes

`0` success, `1` configuration error, `2` bad arguments.
EOF
ls docs/

Step 2: the server

Three tools, JSON-RPC over stdio, no dependencies beyond PyYAML.

cat > server.py <<'PY'
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""An MCP server exposing a documentation tree to an agent.

Deliberately dependency-free and small enough to read in one sitting. It
implements the subset of MCP a documentation server actually needs:
`initialize`, `tools/list` and `tools/call`.

The design decision worth noticing is the tool set. Three tools, not one:

  list_pages    the map. An agent with no idea what exists starts here.
  search_docs   the query, filterable by the kind of answer wanted.
  get_page      the full text, once the agent knows which page it needs.

A single `search` tool forces an agent to guess its query before it knows
what the corpus contains, which is the same mistake as serving only
llms.txt or only chunks.
"""
import json
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

PROTOCOL_VERSION = "2024-11-05"
HEADING = re.compile(r"^(#{1,6}) +(.*?)\s*$")
FENCE = re.compile(r"^\s*(```|~~~)")

KINDS = ["tutorial", "how-to", "reference", "explanation"]

TOOLS = [
    {
        "name": "list_pages",
        "description": (
            "List every documentation page with its title, summary, kind and "
            "audience. Call this first to see what the corpus covers before searching."
        ),
        "inputSchema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"kind": {"type": "string", "enum": KINDS}},
        },
    },
    {
        "name": "search_docs",
        "description": (
            "Keyword search across documentation sections. Filter by kind to get "
            "the right sort of answer: 'how-to' for instructions, 'reference' for "
            "exact values, 'explanation' for reasoning."
        ),
        "inputSchema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "query": {"type": "string"},
                "kind": {"type": "string", "enum": KINDS},
                "limit": {"type": "integer", "default": 3},
            },
            "required": ["query"],
        },
    },
    {
        "name": "get_page",
        "description": "Return the full Markdown of one page by its path.",
        "inputSchema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"path": {"type": "string"}},
            "required": ["path"],
        },
    },
]


def sections(body: str):
    """Split a page into (heading trail, text), ignoring fenced blocks."""
    trail, buffer, out, in_fence = [], [], [], False
    for line in body.splitlines():
        if FENCE.match(line):
            in_fence = not in_fence
            buffer.append(line)
            continue
        match = None if in_fence else HEADING.match(line)
        if match:
            if buffer:
                out.append((" > ".join(trail), "\n".join(buffer).strip()))
            buffer = []
            depth = len(match.group(1))
            trail = trail[: depth - 1] + [match.group(2)]
        else:
            buffer.append(line)
    if buffer:
        out.append((" > ".join(trail), "\n".join(buffer).strip()))
    return [(c, t) for c, t in out if t]


class DocsServer:
    def __init__(self, docs: Path) -> None:
        self.docs = docs
        self.pages = []
        for path in sorted(docs.glob("*.md")):
            text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
            front, _, body = text.partition("---\n")[2].partition("\n---\n")
            self.pages.append((path, yaml.safe_load(front), body))

    # ------------------------------------------------------------ tools

    def list_pages(self, kind=None):
        rows = []
        for path, meta, _ in self.pages:
            if kind and meta.get("kind") != kind:
                continue
            rel = path.relative_to(self.docs).as_posix()
            rows.append(
                f"- `{rel}` [{meta['kind']}, {meta['audience']}] "
                f"**{meta['title']}**: {meta['summary']}"
            )
        return "\n".join(rows) if rows else "No pages match that filter."

    def search_docs(self, query, kind=None, limit=3):
        terms = [t for t in re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", query.lower()) if len(t) > 2]
        hits = []
        for path, meta, body in self.pages:
            if kind and meta.get("kind") != kind:
                continue
            rel = path.relative_to(self.docs).as_posix()
            for crumb, text in sections(body):
                # The heading trail and the summary are searched alongside the
                # text, because the reader's vocabulary is often only there.
                hay = f"{meta['title']} {meta['summary']} {crumb} {text}".lower()
                score = sum(hay.count(t) for t in terms)
                if score:
                    # The crumb already begins with the page's H1, so the
                    # title is not repeated here. Rendering both produces
                    # "Choose a batch size > Choose a batch size > ...",
                    # which wastes the agent's context on every result.
                    hits.append((
                        score,
                        f"## {crumb}\n"
                        f"source: {rel} ({meta['kind']}, for {meta['audience']})\n\n"
                        f"{text}",
                    ))
        hits.sort(key=lambda h: -h[0])
        if not hits:
            return f"No matches for {query!r}."
        return "\n\n---\n\n".join(text for _, text in hits[:limit])

    def get_page(self, path):
        target = (self.docs / path).resolve()
        # Path traversal guard. An agent is an untrusted caller: it will
        # eventually ask for ../../etc/passwd, not maliciously but because a
        # model guessed a path.
        if not target.is_relative_to(self.docs.resolve()):
            return "Error: path escapes the documentation tree."
        if not target.exists():
            available = ", ".join(
                p.relative_to(self.docs).as_posix() for p, _, _ in self.pages
            )
            return f"Error: no page at {path!r}. Available: {available}"
        return target.read_text(encoding="utf-8")

    # --------------------------------------------------------- dispatch

    def call_tool(self, name, args):
        if name == "list_pages":
            return self.list_pages(args.get("kind"))
        if name == "search_docs":
            return self.search_docs(
                args["query"], args.get("kind"), int(args.get("limit", 3))
            )
        if name == "get_page":
            return self.get_page(args["path"])
        raise KeyError(f"unknown tool: {name}")

    def handle(self, request):
        method, req_id = request.get("method"), request.get("id")
        if req_id is None:
            return None  # a notification

        def ok(result):
            return {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": req_id, "result": result}

        if method == "initialize":
            return ok({
                "protocolVersion": PROTOCOL_VERSION,
                "capabilities": {"tools": {}},
                "serverInfo": {"name": "widget-docs", "version": "0.1.0"},
            })
        if method == "tools/list":
            return ok({"tools": TOOLS})
        if method == "tools/call":
            params = request.get("params", {})
            try:
                text = self.call_tool(params["name"], params.get("arguments", {}))
            except Exception as exc:  # report to the client, never crash
                return ok({
                    "content": [{"type": "text", "text": f"Error: {exc}"}],
                    "isError": True,
                })
            return ok({"content": [{"type": "text", "text": text}], "isError": False})

        return {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": req_id,
                "error": {"code": -32601, "message": f"method not found: {method}"}}


def main() -> int:
    server = DocsServer(Path(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "docs"))
    for line in sys.stdin:
        line = line.strip()
        if not line:
            continue
        try:
            request = json.loads(line)
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            continue
        response = server.handle(request)
        if response is not None:
            sys.stdout.write(json.dumps(response) + "\n")
            sys.stdout.flush()
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
PY
echo "server written"

Step 3: drive it by hand, which is how you debug it

cat > session.jsonl <<'EOF'
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/list","params":{}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"list_pages","arguments":{}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"search_docs","arguments":{"query":"latency","kind":"how-to"}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":5,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"search_docs","arguments":{"query":"latency","kind":"explanation"}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":6,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_page","arguments":{"path":"../../../etc/passwd"}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"nonexistent","arguments":{}}}
EOF

python3 server.py docs < session.jsonl | python3 -c "
import json, sys
for line in sys.stdin:
    r = json.loads(line)
    print(f\"--- id {r['id']} ---\")
    if 'error' in r:
        print('  JSON-RPC error:', r['error']['message']); continue
    result = r['result']
    if 'serverInfo' in result:
        print('  initialized:', result['serverInfo'])
    elif 'tools' in result:
        print('  tools:', [t['name'] for t in result['tools']])
    else:
        flag = ' [isError]' if result.get('isError') else ''
        print(f\"  content{flag}:\")
        for line2 in result['content'][0]['text'].splitlines()[:6]:
            print('   ', line2)
    print()
"

Step 4: the thing that makes this worth building

Compare ids 4 and 5 in the output above. Same query, different kind, different answer: the how-to filter returns the instruction, the explanation filter returns the reasoning. An agent can choose which kind of answer it needs, and change its mind. That is not available from a flat context dump, and it is the entire argument for the interface.

Then look at id 6 and id 7. The traversal attempt returns an error string rather than a file, and the unknown tool returns isError rather than killing the server. An agent is an untrusted, unreliable caller and the server has to assume it.

What you built. A server an agent can actually navigate: a map before a search, errors returned as results rather than as crashes, and a traversal attempt that fails safely instead of serving a file outside the corpus.

docs.title: The protocol surface a docs server needs
docs.text:
Method Purpose Required initialize Handshake, declares capabilities and protocol version Yes tools/list What this server can do, with JSON Schema per tool Yes tools/call Invoke a tool, return content blocks Yes resources/list, resources/read Expose documents as addressable resources Optional prompts/list, prompts/get Reusable prompt templates Optional

Tools are enough for a documentation server. Resources are an alternative model where the client browses rather than queries, and for a large corpus querying wins.

docs.title: Tool design, which is where the quality is
docs.text:
Rule Why Three tools: map, search, fetch An agent that cannot list first has to guess its query Put the filter vocabulary in the enum The model sees the valid values and uses them Say in the description when to use each filter "how-to for instructions, reference for exact values" Return the source path with every result The agent needs to cite, and the human needs to verify Return an error string, never raise A crash ends the session; a message lets the agent retry Keep responses small Every result consumes the agent's context

The third row is the highest-leverage thing on this page. The tool description is a prompt. "Filter by kind" tells a model nothing; "'how-to' for instructions, 'reference' for exact values" tells it how to choose, and measurably changes which filter it picks.

docs.title: MCP against the alternatives
docs.text:
Approach Agent can query Agent can filter Scales Needs a running process Paste docs into context No No No No llms.txt Fetches, cannot query No Partly No RAG endpoint Yes If you built it Yes Yes MCP server Yes Yes, declaratively Yes Yes

MCP and RAG are not alternatives. A production docs MCP server usually wraps retrieval: the tool is the interface, the retrieval is the implementation.

docs.title: Security, because an agent is an untrusted caller
docs.text:
Risk Mitigation Path traversal in get_page Resolve and check is_relative_to, as above Leaking restricted content Filter by the caller's tier; see partner documentation Unbounded responses Cap limit, cap returned length Prompt injection from page content Treat page text as data; never let it instruct the server Crash as denial of service Catch everything in tools/call

The third and fifth are the ones people skip, and the first is the one that actually gets attempted, usually by accident.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with the consumer and the recovery property. "MCP serves an agent working mid-task, which llms.txt and a chunk dump do not. It calls search_docs with a kind filter, gets three results, and if they are wrong it calls again with a different filter. A flat context dump cannot recover from a bad first guess. I expose three tools, a map, a search and a fetch, because an agent that cannot list the corpus first has to guess its query before it knows what exists."

The follow-up is "how does the model know which filter to use", and the answer is the thing most people miss: the tool description is a prompt. Writing "'how-to' for instructions, 'reference' for exact values, 'explanation' for reasoning" instead of "filter by kind" changes the model's behaviour, because that text is what it reads when deciding. Tool descriptions are documentation written for a model, which is a genuinely nice thing to point out in a documentation interview.

The tradeoff to volunteer. An MCP server is a running process with an operational burden that a static file does not have: it has to be deployed, monitored, versioned and secured, and it only helps clients that speak MCP. llms.txt is a file on a web server that works with anything that can fetch a URL. For a corpus where most consumption is a model fetching pages, the file is the better investment. MCP earns its cost when agents are doing multi-step work against your docs, which is exactly NVIDIA's "agentic workflows" and is not every situation.

One sharper point. The strongest observation is that MCP makes your content model externally visible, and therefore externally tested. The kind enum appears in the tool schema, so a model's filter choices become a measurable signal about whether your taxonomy makes sense. If agents consistently pick reference for questions your corpus answers in how-to pages, that is evidence about your content model that no internal review would produce. Treating the MCP schema as a probe into your information architecture is a more sophisticated position than treating it as a delivery mechanism.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A working server, driven by a committed JSON-RPC session file, including the traversal attempt and the unknown-tool call. The error cases are what distinguish it from a tutorial copy.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Keep session.jsonl: a committed transcript showing initialize, list, two filtered searches and two failures is a two-minute demonstration and proves it runs.
  2. Write the tool descriptions twice. Once as "filter by kind", once as the guidance version, and connect it to a real client to see whether the filter choices change. That is a small experiment nobody does.
  3. Add the tier filter from partner documentation if the corpus has restricted content. An MCP server over a mixed-visibility corpus with no per-caller filtering is an access-control hole, and noticing that is worth more than the server itself.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Standing up an MCP server from a template proves little. One with three deliberately chosen tools, descriptions written as prompts, a path-traversal guard, errors returned rather than raised, and a committed transcript demonstrates that you designed it.

docs.title: MDX
docs.text:
Markdown that compiles to JavaScript, which moves some failures from build time to render time.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

Intel: "Hands on experience with docs-as-code workflows and documentation CI, including Git, Markdown or MDX, and doc build pipelines"

Prerequisites: Markdown and its dialects

Leads to: Docusaurus

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Markdown with JSX in it. You can import a component and use it as a tag inside prose, which makes interactive examples, tabbed code blocks and live API playgrounds possible in a documentation page.

The fact that matters more than the syntax: MDX does not compile to HTML. It compiles to a JavaScript module. Everything else on this page follows from that, including the one genuinely dangerous property.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Intel names it directly, as an alternative to Markdown. In practice that means their documentation estate includes a React-based generator, almost certainly Docusaurus, and you would be maintaining pages that are partly code.

The judgment being tested is whether you understand the costs. MDX is genuinely better for a developer-facing site that needs interactive examples, and it moves a class of error from your build into your reader's browser. An engineer who has only read about it tends to describe the first half.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Compile six inputs and find out which ones MDX accepts. About twenty-five minutes. Two of the failures are ordinary Markdown.

Step 1: a compiler, and nothing else

mkdir -p mdx-demo && cd mdx-demo
npm init -y >/dev/null
npm install @mdx-js/mdx@3.1.0

Note that require('@mdx-js/mdx') fails: the package is ESM-only, so the examples below use .mjs and top-level await.

Step 2: ask it about six inputs

// t.mjs
import { compile } from '@mdx-js/mdx'

const cases = {
  "undefined component": '# Hi\n\n<Note>body</Note>\n',
  "literal brace":       'Set it to {retry} in the config.\n',
  "less-than in prose":  'Use a value < 5 for safety.\n',
  "html comment":        '<!-- a note -->\n\nText.\n',
  "autolink-ish":        'Mail <a@b.com> for help.\n',
  "plain markdown":      '# Title\n\n| a | b |\n|---|---|\n| 1 | 2 |\n',
}
for (const [name, src] of Object.entries(cases)) {
  try {
    const out = String(await compile(src))
    console.log(`  OK    ${name.padEnd(22)} -> ${out.length} bytes of JS`)
  } catch (e) {
    console.log(`  FAIL  ${name.padEnd(22)} -> ${e.message.split('\n')[0].slice(0, 70)}`)
  }
}

node t.mjs

  OK    undefined component    -> 871 bytes of JS
  OK    literal brace          -> 514 bytes of JS
  OK    less-than in prose     -> 487 bytes of JS
  FAIL  html comment           -> Unexpected character `!` (U+0021) before name
  FAIL  autolink-ish           -> Unexpected character `@` (U+0040) in name
  OK    plain markdown         -> 648 bytes of JS

Read the two failures first. An HTML comment is not valid MDX, and neither is an angle-bracket autolink. Both are ordinary, legal Markdown. If you migrate a Markdown corpus to MDX, every <!-- --> in it breaks the build, and comments are exactly the thing writers leave behind in draft pages.

Note also that "bytes of JS" is not a figure of speech. The output is a JavaScript module, which is the point of step 3.

Step 3: the dangerous one

<Note>body</Note> compiled successfully, and Note was never defined or imported. Look at what the compiler emitted:

// t3.mjs
import { compile } from '@mdx-js/mdx'
const out = String(await compile('# Hi\n\n<Note>body</Note>\n'))
for (const line of out.split('\n')) {
  if (/Note|_missingMdxReference|components/.test(line)) {
    console.log('  ', line.trim().slice(0, 96))
  }
}

   const _components = {
   ...props.components
   }, {Note} = _components;
   if (!Note) _missingMdxReference("Note", true);
   children: [_jsx(_components.h1, {
   }), "\n", _jsx(Note, {
   function _missingMdxReference(id, component) {

The compiler succeeded and emitted a runtime guard. _missingMdxReference throws when the page renders, not when it compiles. So compiling MDX is not sufficient to know a page works.

Step 4: find out whether that actually reaches readers

The obvious conclusion is that a typo'd component produces a green build and a page that crashes in the reader's browser. Test it rather than asserting it, because it depends entirely on what your generator does after compiling.

Put the same undefined component into a Docusaurus site and build:

cat > docs/undef.mdx <<'EOF'
# Undefined

<NoSuchComponent>body</NoSuchComponent>
EOF
npm run build; echo "exit=$?"

[ERROR] Error: Docusaurus static site generation failed for 1 paths:
  [cause]: Error: Expected component `NoSuchComponent` to be defined: you
           likely forgot to import, pass, or provide it.
      at _missingMdxReference (...)
exit=1

Caught, with the component named. Docusaurus does static site generation, which means it renders every page during the build, so the runtime guard fires at build time after all.

So the honest statement is narrower than the obvious one. The compiler defers the error; a generator that pre-renders converts it back into a build failure. The risk is real for any pipeline that compiles MDX without rendering it, or that renders only in the browser, and it is not a problem on a conventional Docusaurus build.

What you learned. MDX rejects two common Markdown constructs outright, and whether an undefined component is a build error or a reader-facing crash depends on your generator rather than on MDX. Check which yours does rather than assuming.

Step 5: so what is the gate

If your generator pre-renders, the build is your render check and you need nothing extra. If it does not, you need one: a production build plus a crawl of the output, or a check that every component referenced in the corpus exists in your library. The question to answer for your own pipeline is simply whether build renders pages or only compiles them.

docs.title: What MDX buys
docs.text: Capability Why you would want it Components in prose Tabs, interactive examples, API playgrounds Imports Share a snippet or a diagram across pages Expressions and props Inject version numbers or config at build time Full React ecosystem Charts, embeds, live editors

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
Cost Detail Component errors defer to render The compiler passes them; only a pre-rendering generator catches them Two Markdown constructs break HTML comments and angle-bracket autolinks The corpus is now code Reviewers need to read JSX; linting is a JS concern Toolchain weight Node, a bundler, and a dependency tree to maintain Machine readability drops A page full of components is hard to chunk Portability Pages are tied to your component library, not just a generator

The machine-readability cost deserves attention in an AI-ready corpus. A retrieval pipeline that reads your source gets <Tabs><TabItem ...> rather than prose, and one that reads your HTML gets whatever the component rendered. Either way, content expressed as components is harder to make agent-ready than content expressed as text.

docs.title: Migrating Markdown to MDX
docs.text:
Construct Fate <!-- comment --> Build error; convert to {/* comment */} <a@b.com> autolink Build error; write a normal link Raw HTML with attributes Often needs JSX attribute names, className not class { in prose Usually fine in MDX 3, historically not Unclosed HTML tags Build error; JSX requires closure

The first two are the ones that will actually bite you, and both are verified above rather than inherited from a migration guide.

docs.title: When to choose it
docs.text: Choose MDX Stay on Markdown The site needs interactive examples The content is prose and code samples You already run a React site You have no JavaScript toolchain A component replaces copy-pasted boilerplate on many pages Pages are mostly unique Your audience is front-end developers Your audience is anyone else

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the compilation target. "MDX compiles to a JavaScript module rather than to HTML, and that is the root of everything. It buys components in prose, and it makes an undefined component a render-time error rather than a compile-time one."

The follow-up is how you would gate it, and this is where the obvious answer is wrong. The compiler emits a runtime guard, so compiling is not enough; but Docusaurus does static site generation, so it renders every page during the build and the error comes back as a build failure naming the component. I verified both halves. The gate you need therefore depends on your generator: if it pre-renders, the build is your render check, and if it does not, you need a crawl of the output or a component-reference check against your library.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Components reduce duplication and increase coupling. Every page using <Tabs> is now tied to your component library, so a refactor of that component is a change to hundreds of pages, and the pages cannot move to another generator without a rewrite. On a corpus you expect to keep for a decade, that is a real bet.

The correction worth volunteering. The widely repeated claim is that MDX turns component typos into reader-facing crashes. That is true of the compiler and false of a normal Docusaurus build, which pre-renders and fails. Saying so unprompted is a better signal than repeating the scare, because it shows you tested the pipeline rather than the format.

One sharper point. An MDX corpus is harder to make machine-readable. Source consumers see JSX instead of prose, HTML consumers see whatever rendered, and both are worse inputs to chunking than plain Markdown. If the same organisation is asking for both MDX and agent-ready content, that tension is worth naming out loud, because it is real and most people miss it.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. Less a repository than a demonstrated understanding of the failure distribution. If you do build something, the valuable piece is the component-reference check.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Steps 2 and 3 are both surprises, and step 3 is the one to remember.
  2. Grep a Markdown corpus for <!--. That count is the size of your MDX migration's first obstacle.
  3. On any MDX site you can reach, find out whether CI renders the pages or only compiles them. If it only compiles, undefined components reach readers.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Neither of this guide's repositories uses MDX, which the demonstrated page records. What travels is the pair of measurements and the correction between them. The compiler emits if (!Note) _missingMdxReference("Note", true), a runtime guard, so compiling proves nothing. A Docusaurus build of the same page exits 1 with Expected component 'NoSuchComponent' to be defined, because static site generation renders every page. Both are checkable in minutes, and the correction between them is the point: the first measurement supported the claim that an undefined component reaches readers, and the second showed that is false for any generator that pre-renders. The page says what the compiler does and what a build does, separately, because conflating them is how the wrong advice gets published.

docs.title: Metadata for navigation and retrieval
docs.text:
Two audiences read your front matter, they want different fields, and a field with no reader is already wrong.

core · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "content modeling, taxonomy, and metadata for both navigation and machine retrieval"

Prerequisites: Content models

Leads to: Findability and search design, Agent-ready content

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The structured data attached to each page, usually in front matter. NVIDIA's phrasing is unusually precise and worth taking literally: metadata for both navigation and machine retrieval. Those are two audiences with different needs, and a single field set rarely serves both well.

Navigation metadata answers "where does this page belong and what do I call it in a sidebar". Retrieval metadata answers "which subset of the corpus should a query search". They overlap and they are not the same, and the mistake is designing one and assuming it covers the other.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because the retrieval half is new and most corpora do not have it.

Navigation metadata is well understood: a title, a position, a section. It has existed as long as documentation sites have. Retrieval metadata is what makes a filtered search possible, what lets a chunk carry its context into a vector store, and what an assistant uses to decide where to look. NVIDIA asking for both in one phrase is a signal that they know the second is a separate design problem.

The uncomfortable part, and the subject of the golden path, is that adding fields is easy and keeping them true is not. A field written by a generator and read by nothing will be wrong within weeks, and nothing will report it.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Audit a real corpus's metadata, find the field that is lying, and work out why nobody noticed. About thirty minutes.

Step 1: measure coverage, not existence

121 pages

field        pages  coverage
title          121      100%
summary        121      100%
diataxis       121      100%
audience       121      100%
concept         64       52%
tags           64       52%
generated      53       43%

Coverage is the first question because an optional field cannot be built on. A filter on tags here would silently exclude 48 per cent of the corpus, and the result would look like a retrieval problem rather than a metadata problem.

Step 2: check that the populated fields are true

Full coverage is necessary and not sufficient. Split each field's values by whether the page was generated:

generated pages by diataxis: {'reference': 53}
hand-written by diataxis:    {'how-to': 22, 'explanation': 46}

diataxis had 100 per cent coverage, three legal values, and was wrong on 53 pages. The placeholder generator hardcoded reference, so that value meant "not written yet" while no real page used it.

A filter for reference documentation would have returned exclusively stubs.

Step 3: count the readers

grep -rn "diataxis" src/fieldguide/*.py hooks/*.py mkdocs.yml

src/fieldguide/generate.py:144:        "diataxis": "reference",
src/fieldguide/scaffold.py:102:        "diataxis: explanation",

Two writers, zero readers. That is the explanation for step 2: nothing consumed the field, so nothing could notice it was wrong.

The reader count is the diagnostic. Write it down for every field you have. A field with more writers than readers is decoration, and decoration rots.

Step 4: check the field is even parseable

m = re.match(r"^---\n(.*?)\n---\n", p.read_text(), re.S)
try:
    yaml.safe_load(m.group(1))
except yaml.YAMLError:
    bad.append(p)

front matter parses: 75 pages
front matter INVALID: 46 pages

Forty-six pages whose front matter no YAML parser could read, because a generated summary contained an unquoted colon. MkDocs' own metadata parser is more forgiving than YAML, so the build was green and the pages looked fine.

The visible symptom was in the wrong place entirely:

meta description: A validated curriculum for documentation engineering, ...

Every one of those 46 pages fell back to the site description, because its own summary was unreadable. A navigation-and-SEO symptom caused by a serialisation bug, which is why this check belongs next to the metadata work rather than in the SEO work.

Step 5: fix all three classes

Problem Fix Unparseable front matter Serialise with yaml.safe_dump, never f-strings A field that lies Add the honest value: diataxis: placeholder A field with no reader Give it one, so drift fails a build 
ok: every page's front matter parses as YAML
all pages by diataxis: {'how-to': 22, 'explanation': 46, 'placeholder': 53}
  FIRES: diataxis is 'refrence', which is not one of [...]

What you learned. Metadata health has three questions and most audits ask only the first: is it present, is it true, and does anything read it.

docs.title: The two audiences, and what each wants
docs.text:
Field Navigation Retrieval title Essential, it is the label Useful, it is high-signal text summary Sidebar hints, meta description Essential, it is what a map lists diataxis or page type Section grouping Essential filter: "how-to only" audience Sometimes a separate route Essential filter position or order Essential Useless product_version A version switcher Essential filter component or area Grouping Essential filter updated or reviewed A date in the footer, with caveats Staleness filter tags Weak; a tag index few people use Weak unless closed and required canonical Not used Deduplication across versions

The asymmetry in the position row is the clearest illustration of the two audiences. Navigation needs ordering and retrieval does not care. Retrieval needs filters and navigation can live without most of them.

docs.title: What a chunk needs that a page does not
docs.text:
When a page is chunked for retrieval, each chunk leaves home without its context. The metadata a chunk has to carry:

Field Why the chunk needs it Source page and anchor So an answer can cite a link a reader can follow Page title A chunk from the middle of a page has no title of its own Heading trail Which section this is, so the chunk is placeable Page type and audience So a filtered query still works at chunk level Version So a 2.3 chunk is not returned to a 2.4 reader

Page-level metadata that is not copied onto chunks is metadata that stops existing the moment retrieval starts, which is the most common reason filtered search works in a prototype and not in production.

docs.title: How many fields
docs.text:
Count Outcome Three or four, required, all consumed Reliable, and the common good answer Eight or more, half optional Half-populated, nothing depends on it Any number with no consumers Decorative, and already wrong

Start from the filter you want and add the field that makes it possible. Fields added because they seem like good practice are the ones that end up lying.

docs.title: Where metadata lives
docs.text:
Location Good for Watch out Front matter Per-page facts authors control Must be valid YAML; see step 4 A registry or data file Relationships, ordering, cross-page rules Must not disagree with the pages Derived at build time Word count, last modified, heading trail Cheap, and invisible to source consumers The file path Section, product area Encoded in a URL, so expensive to change

Deriving is underrated. A heading trail, a word count or a reading time computed at build time cannot drift, because nothing stores it.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Take NVIDIA's phrasing literally. "Navigation metadata and retrieval metadata are different field sets. Navigation needs ordering and a label; retrieval needs filters, and it needs them copied onto every chunk, because a chunk leaves the page without its context. A corpus with good navigation metadata and no retrieval metadata looks fine until you put a search in front of it."

The follow-up is how you keep it honest, and the answer is reader count. A field with more writers than readers will be wrong and nothing will report it. I had a fully populated, closed-vocabulary field that was wrong on 44 per cent of pages for exactly that reason.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Every required field is a tax on contribution and a thing reviewers have to check, so the right number is small. The pressure runs the other way, because each new filter suggests a new field, and the way to resist it is to require a named consumer before adding one.

One sharper point. Check that your front matter is valid YAML. MkDocs' metadata parser is more forgiving than YAML, so an unquoted colon builds cleanly and is invisible to every tool using a real parser. I shipped 46 such pages, and the only visible symptom was their meta descriptions falling back to the site default. Four lines of check, and it is the cheapest AI-readiness work available.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A metadata audit of a corpus you own: coverage per field, value distribution per field, and reader count per field.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Print coverage and value distribution for every field in your corpus. Heavy skew toward one value usually means a default is being written somewhere.
  2. Count readers for each field. Anything with none is either removable or needs a consumer.
  3. Parse all your front matter with a real YAML parser. This takes four lines and finds something more often than it should.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack carries metadata through into its retrieval artifacts, so each chunk keeps its source, heading trail and page type, and summary is indexed for search after an evaluation showed it was being ignored. The more useful story is the audit above: a field at 100 per cent coverage, legal values, zero readers, wrong on 44 per cent of pages, and the serialisation bug underneath it.

docs.title: MkDocs and Material
docs.text:
The fastest route to a good documentation site, and the three checks you have to add yourself.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "static site generators (Sphinx, MkDocs, Docusaurus, or similar)"

Prerequisites: Choosing a static site generator

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A Python static site generator that turns a directory of Markdown into a site, plus Material for MkDocs, a theme so dominant that in practice "MkDocs" usually means both. Material supplies navigation, search, admonitions, tabs, code annotations and the visual design most people recognise as a modern docs site.

It is the easiest of the generators to adopt and the one whose build checks the least. Both halves of that sentence matter, and this page is mostly about the second.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA names it in a list of three. It is the most likely generator to appear on a newer documentation project, because a usable site is about fifteen minutes of work and the theme makes it look deliberate without a designer.

What distinguishes someone who has operated it from someone who has installed it is knowing what its build does not verify. MkDocs will happily publish a dead heading anchor and an unreachable page in its strictest mode, which is measured below, so an MkDocs corpus of any size needs gates that an equivalent Sphinx project would get for free.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a site, turn on the useful configuration, then find out what the build still misses and what the theme costs. About thirty minutes.

Step 1: a site

mkdir -p mk-demo && cd mk-demo
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install --quiet mkdocs mkdocs-material
mkdocs new .
mkdocs build --strict && ls site/

Step 2: the configuration worth having on day one

# mkdocs.yml
site_name: Widget
site_url: https://example.github.io/widget/
theme:
  name: material
  features:
    - navigation.instant
    - navigation.tracking
    - content.code.copy
    - search.suggest

markdown_extensions:
  - admonition
  - attr_list
  - def_list
  - footnotes
  - tables
  - toc: {permalink: true}
  - pymdownx.highlight
  - pymdownx.superfences
  - pymdownx.details
  - pymdownx.tabbed: {alternate_style: true}

# Pages not in the nav are deliberate, not forgotten.
not_in_nav: |
  concepts/*.md

Set site_url from the start. It is what produces the canonical tag and the sitemap, and adding it later means a reshuffle of both.

Step 3: find the three things the build will not tell you

cat > docs/index.md <<'EOF'
# Widget

See [the tuning bit](guide.md#tuning).
EOF
printf '# Guide\n\n## Setup\n\nContent.\n' > docs/guide.md
printf '# Orphan\n\nNobody links here.\n' > docs/orphan.md

mkdocs build --strict
echo "exit=$?"

exit=0

Two defects, strictest mode, exit 0. The anchor #tuning does not exist in guide.md, and orphan.md is reachable from nowhere. The same content fails a Sphinx build with -W on both counts.

The third gap is the one from Markdown dialects: syntax outside your extension list ships as literal characters.

So an MkDocs project needs three gates that are not optional:

Gap Gate Dead heading anchors Link checking with anchor resolution Unreachable pages An orphan check against the nav plus not_in_nav Unsupported syntax A source-versus-HTML dialect check

Step 4: measure what the theme costs

Same generator, same 121 pages, two configurations:

default theme, no extensions    0.6 s
Material theme, 12 extensions  16.0 s

Twenty-seven times slower. MkDocs has no incremental build, so every change pays the full cost. At 121 pages that is sixteen seconds and tolerable; at a thousand it is the reason your contributors stop running the build locally.

mkdocs serve mitigates it for authoring, because it rebuilds on change and reloads, but CI pays full price every time.

Step 5: the extension point people miss

MkDocs hooks are plain Python functions in your repository, with no plugin packaging:

# hooks/seo.py
def on_page_context(context, page, config, nav):
    summary = page.meta.get("summary")
    if summary and not page.meta.get("description"):
        page.meta["description"] = summary
    return context

hooks:
  - hooks/seo.py

That nine-line hook fixes a real defect: Material falls back to site_description for the meta description unless a page sets description explicitly, so per-page summaries in your front matter do nothing for search until something maps them across. Hooks are the right tool for anything site-specific; reach for a published plugin only when the need is general.

What you built. A good-looking site in fifteen minutes, a list of exactly three gates you now owe, and a measured reason to care about your theme.

docs.title: What the build checks
docs.text: Defect mkdocs build --strict Link to a missing page Fails Link to a missing heading anchor Logs INFO, publishes it Page in no navigation Passes Unsupported Markdown construct Passes, ships literal characters Malformed YAML front matter Fails Missing nav target Fails

docs.title: Configuration that earns its place
docs.text: Setting Why site_url Canonical tag and sitemap; painful to add later not_in_nav Makes deliberate omissions explicit instead of silent toc: {permalink: true} Gives readers linkable headings, which is what deep links need pymdownx.superfences Nested fences, which plain fences cannot express strict: true in the config So a local build matches CI without remembering the flag validation: Newer MkDocs can promote some INFO messages; check your version

docs.title: Plugins worth knowing
docs.text: Plugin Does mkdocstrings API reference from Python docstrings mike Versioned deployments mkdocs-redirects URL stability when pages move mkdocs-minify-plugin Smaller output mkdocs-git-revision-date-localized Page dates from Git, with the caveats on freshness

docs.title: Hooks versus plugins
docs.text:
Use a hook Use a plugin The need is specific to this site The need is general It is under about a hundred lines It has its own configuration surface You want it reviewed with the docs You want to publish it

Hooks live in the repository and need no packaging, which makes them the right default for one-off fixes. The whole mechanism is one hooks: key.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the trade, not the features. "MkDocs with Material is the fastest way to a site people want to read, and its build checks less than Sphinx's. In strict mode it still publishes dead heading anchors and unreachable pages, so I add an anchor-resolving link checker, an orphan check and a dialect check. Three gates, and then the easy adoption is a free win."

The follow-up is often about scale. Be specific: there is no incremental build, and the theme dominates build time. Twenty-seven times on the same 121 pages in my own measurement, bare theme against Material plus a dozen extensions. That is the number that decides whether contributors build locally.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Material's extensions are excellent and they lock your content to it. Admonitions, content tabs and code annotations are all Material-specific syntax, so a corpus that uses them heavily cannot move to another generator without a rewrite. That is usually an acceptable bet, and it should be a conscious one.

One sharper point. The hooks mechanism is underused. Most teams reach for a plugin or live with the gap, when a nine-line function in the repository solves it and gets reviewed alongside the content. The description fallback above is a good example: a real SEO defect, fixed in nine lines, with no dependency added.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. An MkDocs site with the three compensating gates in CI, and ideally one hook you wrote.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Step 3 is the one that matters: exit 0 on two real defects.
  2. Check whether your own site sets site_url and not_in_nav. Both are usually missing, and both are one line.
  3. Time your build with and without your theme. Put the ratio in the README so the next person understands where the minutes go.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. This guide and docpack both run on MkDocs with Material, and between them they carry a hand-written anchor-and-heading link checker, a fence gate, a render gate, a dialect gate and a hooks/seo.py that exists because the README once claimed something the theme did not actually do. The compensating gates are the evidence, not the site.

docs.title: OpenAPI and REST reference
docs.text:
A valid spec and an accurate spec are different properties, and only one of them has a tool.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 4h

Not a quotation (adjacent)

Neither posting mentions OpenAPI. It is the standard contract format for any HTTP surface you will document, so it is here on the grounds that the work requires it even where the requisition does not say so.

Prerequisites: Generated API reference

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A machine-readable description of an HTTP API: paths, operations, parameters, request and response schemas, authentication. From it you can generate reference pages, client libraries, mock servers and request collections, which is why it has become the default way to document REST.

The distinction this page is built on: a spec can be valid and wrong. Validity is a property of the document and has good tooling. Accuracy is a property of the relationship between the document and the running service, and has almost none.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
It does not, explicitly, and the banner says so. But reference documentation for an HTTP surface is OpenAPI work in practice, and both postings ask for reference documentation.

The reason it belongs in a documentation-engineering curriculum rather than an API-design one is that the spec is a documentation artifact with the same decay problem as any other page, plus one special property: because it is machine readable, people assume it is machine verified. It usually is not. A spec in a repository with a validator in CI feels trustworthy and may describe an API that no longer exists.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Validate a spec, break it, fix it, and then discover the failure a validator cannot see. About thirty-five minutes.

Step 1: a small spec

mkdir -p oas-demo && cd oas-demo
pip install --quiet openapi-spec-validator

cat > spec.yaml <<'EOF'
openapi: 3.1.0
info:
  title: Widget API
  version: "2.4.0"
paths:
  /widgets/{id}:
    get:
      operationId: getWidget
      summary: Fetch a widget
      parameters:
        - name: id
          in: path
          required: true
          schema: {type: string}
        - name: expand
          in: query
          schema: {type: boolean, default: false}
      responses:
        "200":
          description: The widget
          content:
            application/json:
              schema: {$ref: "#/components/schemas/Widget"}
        "404":
          description: Not found
components:
  schemas:
    Widget:
      type: object
      required: [id, name]
      properties:
        id: {type: string}
        name: {type: string}
        retries: {type: integer, default: 5}
EOF

Step 2: validate it, then break a reference

python3 -c "
from openapi_spec_validator import validate
import yaml
validate(yaml.safe_load(open('spec.yaml')))
print('spec is valid')
"

spec is valid

Now make the single most common editing mistake, a typo in a $ref:

sed -i 's|schemas/Widget"|schemas/Widgets"|' spec.yaml
python3 -c "
from openapi_spec_validator import validate
import yaml
try:
    validate(yaml.safe_load(open('spec.yaml')))
except Exception as e:
    print('INVALID:', str(e).splitlines()[0][:70])
"

INVALID: '/components/schemas/Widgets' does not exist within {'openapi': ...

Caught. Put a validator in CI and structural mistakes stop reaching anyone. This is the easy half, and it is where most teams stop.

Step 3: an implementation that has drifted

Restore the $ref so the spec is valid again, then write the service the way services actually end up:

# app.py, the implementation
# drift: retries is 3 here and the spec says 5,
# and there is an extra field the spec never mentions
self.wfile.write(json.dumps(
    {"id": "w1", "name": "Widget One", "retries": 3, "beta": True}
).encode())

python3 app.py & sleep 1
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8731/widgets/w1

{"id": "w1", "name": "Widget One", "retries": 3, "beta": true}

The spec is valid. The validator is happy. The documented API and the real API disagree in two places, and nothing in the toolchain has noticed.

Step 4: check the contract, not the document

# contract.py
import json
import urllib.request

import yaml

spec = yaml.safe_load(open("spec.yaml"))
schema = spec["components"]["schemas"]["Widget"]
documented = set(schema["properties"])
required = set(schema.get("required", []))

body = json.loads(urllib.request.urlopen(
    "http://127.0.0.1:8731/widgets/w1").read())
actual = set(body)

findings = []
for missing in sorted(required - actual):
    findings.append(f"required field absent from the response: {missing!r}")
for undocumented in sorted(actual - documented):
    findings.append(f"response field absent from the spec: {undocumented!r}")
for name, prop in schema["properties"].items():
    if "default" in prop and name in body and body[name] != prop["default"]:
        findings.append(
            f"{name!r}: spec default is {prop['default']}, "
            f"response has {body[name]}")

for f in findings:
    print(f"CONTRACT  {f}")
print(f"{'FAIL' if findings else 'ok'}: {len(findings)} mismatch(es)")
raise SystemExit(1 if findings else 0)

CONTRACT  response field absent from the spec: 'beta'
CONTRACT  'retries': spec default is 5, response has 3
FAIL: 2 mismatch(es)
exit=1

Step 5: be honest about which of those findings is sound

The two findings are not equally valid, and pretending otherwise would be the kind of thing this guide is written against.

The beta finding is a real contract issue: the service returns a field no reader could know about, so anyone writing against the documentation is working from an incomplete picture.

The retries finding is a heuristic, and strictly a false positive. In OpenAPI, default describes what to assume when a value is absent, not what a response must contain. A response legitimately carrying 3 violates nothing. What it does tell you is that the documentation and the implementation disagree about the normal value, which is usually worth a human look, so the check is useful as a warning and wrong as an error.

Keep it, and keep it out of the blocking set.

What you built. A validator for the document and a contract check for the relationship, plus a clear view of which findings are facts and which are hints.

docs.title: Two different properties, two different tools
docs.text:
Property Question Tooling Validity Is this a well-formed OpenAPI document? Good: openapi-spec-validator, spectral Style Does it follow our conventions? Good: spectral with a ruleset Accuracy Does the service behave like this? Poor, and usually hand-rolled Completeness Is every endpoint described? Poor; compare routes to paths Example validity Do the examples satisfy their schemas? Available, rarely enabled

Rows three and four are where real documentation defects live, and they are the two with no off-the-shelf answer. That asymmetry is the single most useful thing to know about OpenAPI in a documentation role.

docs.title: How the spec gets written, and what each approach costs
docs.text:
Approach Drift risk Notes Hand-written spec Highest Nothing connects it to the code Generated from code annotations Low for shape Follows the implementation, so it documents bugs faithfully Spec-first, code generated from it Lowest Strongest guarantee, biggest process change Generated from tests or traffic Low for reality Describes what happens, not what is intended

Generated-from-code is the common middle. Its weakness is worth naming: if the implementation is wrong, the spec documents the wrong behaviour with total confidence.

docs.title: What to put in CI
docs.text: Gate Blocking Why Spec validates Yes Deterministic, cheap, catches $ref typos Spec passes the style ruleset Yes operationId present, descriptions non-empty Every route has a path in the spec Yes Completeness, and easy if you can enumerate routes Examples validate against their schemas Yes Catches examples nobody checked Contract check against a live service No Needs a running service; a queue, not a gate

docs.title: Generating documentation from it
docs.text:
Tool Produces Redoc, Swagger UI, Scalar A reference site from the spec widdershins Markdown, for embedding in an existing site Prism A mock server from the spec, useful in tutorials OpenAPI Generator Client libraries in many languages

The mock server is underrated for documentation work. It lets a quickstart be followed, and cold-start tested, before the real service is available or without credentials.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the two properties. "A spec can be valid and wrong. Validity has good tooling and catches $ref typos and missing descriptions. Accuracy, which is whether the service actually behaves like the document, has almost none, so that is the check I write: compare a live response against the schema and report fields in one and not the other."

The follow-up is how you would keep them in sync, and the honest answer ranks the options: generated-from-code removes shape drift but faithfully documents bugs; spec-first is the strongest guarantee and the biggest process change; hand-written is what most teams have and is the worst of the three.

The tradeoff to volunteer. A contract check needs a running service, which means it cannot be a merge gate without a test environment that is itself reliable. Gating merges on a check that depends on a deployed service is how you get a team that reruns CI until it passes. So it belongs on a schedule, or in a post-deploy step, producing a queue rather than a red build.

One sharper point. Be careful what you call a violation. Comparing a spec default against a live response value looks like a contract check and is not one: default describes what to assume when a field is absent. It is still a useful signal that the docs and the service disagree about the normal case, so it belongs in the warning set, and knowing the difference is the kind of precision that distinguishes someone who has built one of these from someone who has configured a validator.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A repository with spec validation and a style ruleset in CI, plus a contract check that runs somewhere and produces findings.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Step 3 is the point: a valid spec and a drifted service.
  2. Put openapi-spec-validator in CI for a spec you own. It takes ten minutes and usually finds something.
  3. Write the field-set comparison from step 4 against one real endpoint. The first undocumented field you find is your evidence.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Neither of this guide's repositories documents an HTTP API, which the demonstrated page records. What travels is the distinction and the measurement behind it: a spec that validates cleanly while the service returns an undocumented field, and the honest note that one of the two findings is a heuristic rather than a violation.
