docs.title: Output evaluation
docs.text:
Scoring generated text against labelled examples, so a prompt change is a measurement rather than a feeling.

core · difficulty 3 · 6h

Practical experience applying LLMs to content workflows (prompting, retrieval and grounding, output evaluation)

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: Grounding and citation, Retrieval evaluation

Leads to: Measuring AI answer quality, Hallucination and guardrails

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Scoring generated text against examples you labelled yourself, so that a change to a prompt or a model produces a number instead of an impression.

Retrieval evaluation asks whether the right page came back. This asks whether the text produced from it was any good, which is a harder question because there is no single correct output to compare against.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA lists it third in the required triple: "prompting, retrieval and grounding, output evaluation". The ordering is the pipeline, and this is the stage that tells you whether the first two worked.

What makes it core and difficulty 3 is that it has no obvious answer key. Retrieval has one: the expected page is either in the results or it is not. A generated paragraph can be correct, incomplete, correct-but-unhelpful, or subtly fused, and "does this read well" is not a measurement. Building the answer key is most of the work, and it is work most teams skip, which is why every prompt change in this field is justified by somebody having tried five examples.

On a Tuesday it is the thing that stops a bad change shipping. Somebody tightens the audit prompt to reduce false positives. On the three pages they tried, it looks better. Across the labelled set, precision held at 1.00 and recall fell from 1.00 to 0.43, which means the audit now misses eight of the fourteen real defects while every finding it does report is correct.

Only one of those two numbers is observable by reviewing the output, which is why the labelled set exists.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a labelled set, score two prompt versions against it, and find the tradeoff that eyeballing hides. Fifty minutes, dependency-free.

Step 1: the task and the labels

The labels are the expensive part and the whole asset. Label by hand, record why, and never let a model generate them.

mkdir -p outeval-drill && cd outeval-drill
cat > labelled.yaml <<'EOF'
# The answer key: ten pages, each with the defects a human found by reading.
#
# Rules that keep this usable:
#   - Labelled by a person, recorded with a quote. A model-labelled set
#     measures agreement with that model, not correctness.
#   - Includes CLEAN pages. A set of only defective pages cannot measure
#     false positives, which is the failure that destroys trust in an audit.
#   - `notes` says why a case is interesting, so nobody deletes a hard one.

- page: p01
  text: "Simply set the cache_mode flag. It should work on widget 1.9 or newer."
  requires: "2.4"
  kind: how-to
  defects: [hedge, hedge, stale_version, no_example]
  notes: >
    Two hedges, a version older than the requirement, and no example:
    `cache_mode` is a flag name in backticks, not a command.

- page: p02
  text: "Run `widget keys rotate` to rotate the signing key."
  requires: "2.4"
  kind: how-to
  defects: []
  notes: >
    Clean. A set without clean pages cannot measure precision at all. The
    inline `widget keys rotate` counts as an example: it is a runnable
    command, not an identifier.

- page: p03
  text: "Configure the pool size. This is easy to get wrong."
  requires: "2.4"
  kind: how-to
  defects: [hedge, no_example]
  notes: A how-to with no code block at all.

- page: p04
  text: "The scheduler uses a work-stealing queue to balance shots across nodes."
  requires: "2.4"
  kind: explanation
  defects: []
  notes: Clean, and NOT a no_example defect because it is an explanation page.

- page: p05
  text: "Just pass --force. Requires widget 2.0 or newer."
  requires: "2.4"
  kind: how-to
  defects: [hedge, stale_version, no_example]
  notes: Three defects in two sentences.

- page: p06
  text: "Set `batch_size` to 1 for latency-sensitive endpoints.\n```\nbatch_size = 1\n```"
  requires: "2.4"
  kind: how-to
  defects: []
  notes: Clean how-to with an example. The easy true negative.

- page: p07
  text: "You should see the server start within ten seconds."
  requires: "2.4"
  kind: how-to
  defects: [hedge, no_example]
  notes: >
    "should" here describes an EXPECTATION of observed behaviour, not an
    uncertain claim about the software. A strict hedge rule flags it; a human
    might not. Deliberately ambiguous, kept to expose the disagreement.

- page: p08
  text: "Deployment requires widget 2.6 or newer and a running Redis."
  requires: "2.4"
  kind: reference
  defects: []
  notes: 2.6 is NEWER than the requirement, so it is not stale. Tests direction.

- page: p09
  text: "This simply works out of the box on widget 1.0."
  requires: "2.4"
  kind: explanation
  defects: [hedge, stale_version]
  notes: An explanation page, so no_example must not fire.

- page: p10
  text: "Pass `--dry-run` first.\n```\nwidget apply --dry-run\n```\nIt is easy to verify."
  requires: "2.4"
  kind: how-to
  defects: [hedge]
  notes: Has an example; only the hedge should fire.
EOF
python3 -c "
import yaml
cases = yaml.safe_load(open('labelled.yaml'))
clean = sum(1 for c in cases if not c['defects'])
total = sum(len(c['defects']) for c in cases)
print(f'{len(cases)} pages, {clean} clean, {total} labelled defects')
assert clean >= 3, 'need clean pages to measure precision'
assert all(c.get('notes') for c in cases), 'every case needs notes'
print('set is usable')
"

Step 2: two auditors, standing in for two prompt versions

cat > auditors.py <<'PY'
"""Two auditors, standing in for two versions of an audit prompt.

LOOSE   flags every hedge word anywhere. High recall, flags p07's "should"
        where a human might not.
STRICT  someone tightened it to reduce false positives: it only flags a
        hedge when it describes the SOFTWARE's behaviour, and it stopped
        checking versions it cannot parse confidently.

The point is that `strict` looks better on the pages a person would spot
check, and is worse where it matters. A deterministic stand-in keeps that
reproducible; a real prompt change produces the same shape of result.
"""
import re

HEDGES = ("simply", "just", "easy", "should")
SOFTWARE_HEDGE = re.compile(r"\b(it|this|the \w+)\s+(should|simply)\b", re.I)

#: An inline code span containing a space, or starting with the tool name, is
#: a command. A single identifier in backticks (`cache_mode`) is a flag name
#: and is not an example of anything.
#:
#: This definition exists because the first run of this harness disagreed with
#: the answer key on two pages, and the investigation found that `no_example`
#: had never been defined precisely enough to label against. See the page.
INLINE_COMMAND = re.compile(r"`([^`]*\s[^`]*|widget[^`]*)`")


def _has_example(text):
    return "```" in text or bool(INLINE_COMMAND.search(text))


def loose(case):
    """Flag every hedge; check every version; require an example on how-tos."""
    found = []
    text = case["text"]
    for hedge in HEDGES:
        found += ["hedge"] * len(re.findall(rf"\b{hedge}\b", text, re.I))
    for version in re.findall(r"widget (\d+\.\d+)", text, re.I):
        if _older(version, case["requires"]):
            found.append("stale_version")
    if case["kind"] == "how-to" and not _has_example(text):
        found.append("no_example")
    return found


def strict(case):
    """Tightened: hedges only when describing the software, versions skipped."""
    found = []
    text = case["text"]
    found += ["hedge"] * len(SOFTWARE_HEDGE.findall(text))
    # The tightening that does the damage: version checking was dropped
    # because it produced "false positives" on p08, where 2.6 is newer.
    if case["kind"] == "how-to" and not _has_example(text):
        found.append("no_example")
    return found


def _older(found, required):
    return tuple(int(x) for x in found.split(".")) < tuple(
        int(x) for x in required.split(".")
    )


AUDITORS = {"loose": loose, "strict": strict}
PY
echo "auditors written"

Step 3: score both, as sets of defects per page

cat > score.py <<'PY'
"""Score each auditor against the labelled set.

Multiset comparison, not set comparison: a page with two hedges and an
auditor that finds one is a partial miss, and collapsing to a set would call
it a complete hit.
"""
import sys
from collections import Counter

import yaml

from auditors import AUDITORS


def confusion(cases, auditor):
    tp = fp = fn = 0
    per_type = {}
    for case in cases:
        expected = Counter(case["defects"])
        found = Counter(auditor(case))
        for defect in set(expected) | set(found):
            e, f = expected[defect], found[defect]
            hit, over, under = min(e, f), max(0, f - e), max(0, e - f)
            tp += hit
            fp += over
            fn += under
            bucket = per_type.setdefault(defect, [0, 0, 0])
            bucket[0] += hit
            bucket[1] += over
            bucket[2] += under
    return tp, fp, fn, per_type


def metrics(tp, fp, fn):
    precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 1.0
    recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 1.0
    f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) if precision + recall else 0.0
    return precision, recall, f1


def main():
    cases = yaml.safe_load(open("labelled.yaml"))
    results = {}

    for name, auditor in AUDITORS.items():
        tp, fp, fn, per_type = confusion(cases, auditor)
        precision, recall, f1 = metrics(tp, fp, fn)
        results[name] = (precision, recall, f1)

        print(f"\n=== {name} ===")
        print(f"  true positives {tp}, false positives {fp}, false negatives {fn}")
        print(f"  precision {precision:.2f}   recall {recall:.2f}   F1 {f1:.2f}")
        print("  by defect type:")
        for defect, (hit, over, under) in sorted(per_type.items()):
            p, r, _ = metrics(hit, over, under)
            print(f"    {defect:<14} precision {p:.2f}  recall {r:.2f}"
                  f"   (tp {hit}, fp {over}, fn {under})")

        # Per-page disagreements, which is where you look to fix a prompt.
        print("  pages where it disagreed with the labels:")
        any_diff = False
        for case in cases:
            expected, found = Counter(case["defects"]), Counter(auditor(case))
            if expected != found:
                any_diff = True
                missed = sorted((expected - found).elements())
                spurious = sorted((found - expected).elements())
                parts = []
                if missed:
                    parts.append(f"missed {missed}")
                if spurious:
                    parts.append(f"invented {spurious}")
                print(f"    {case['page']}: {', '.join(parts)}")
        if not any_diff:
            print("    none")

    print("\n" + "=" * 56)
    print(f"{'version':<10} {'precision':>10} {'recall':>8} {'F1':>7}")
    print("-" * 56)
    for name, (precision, recall, f1) in results.items():
        print(f"{name:<10} {precision:>10.2f} {recall:>8.2f} {f1:>7.2f}")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
PY
python3 score.py

Step 4: see what a reviewer can and cannot observe

A reviewer does not read the labelled set. They read the auditor's findings and judge each one. That turns out to decide everything.

python3 - <<'PY'
"""What a human reviewing the OUTPUT can actually see.

A reviewer works through the findings the auditor produced. They can judge
every one of those. They cannot see a defect that was never flagged, because
nothing in their queue refers to it.
"""
from collections import Counter

import yaml

from auditors import AUDITORS

cases = yaml.safe_load(open("labelled.yaml"))

for name, auditor in AUDITORS.items():
    flagged = correct = missed = 0
    for case in cases:
        expected, found = Counter(case["defects"]), Counter(auditor(case))
        flagged += sum(found.values())
        correct += sum((found & expected).values())
        missed += sum((expected - found).values())

    apparent = correct / flagged if flagged else 1.0
    print(f"{name}:")
    print(f"  findings in the review queue      {flagged}")
    print(f"  of those, real                    {correct}")
    print(f"  apparent precision to a reviewer  {apparent:.2f}")
    print(f"  defects the reviewer NEVER SEES   {missed}")
    print()
PY

What you built. A labelled set with clean and ambiguous cases, precision and recall overall and per defect type, the per-page disagreements, and a demonstration of what review structurally cannot catch.

docs.title: What the measurement said
docs.text:
version precision recall F1 loose 1.00 1.00 1.00 strict 1.00 0.43 0.60

The tightened prompt kept perfect precision and lost 57% of its recall. It finds 6 of 14 real defects. Per defect type, the damage is specific: hedge recall fell from 1.00 to 0.29, and stale_version recall went to zero, because the tightening dropped version checking entirely to avoid a false positive on p08.

Now step 4, which is the part that matters:

version findings in the queue real apparent precision never seen loose 14 14 1.00 0 strict 6 6 1.00 8

Both look perfect to a reviewer. Every finding in each queue is real, so a reviewer working through either one concludes the auditor is excellent. One of them is silently missing eight defects, and nothing in the review queue refers to a defect that was never flagged.

That asymmetry is the entire argument for a labelled set. Human review can measure precision, because false positives arrive in the queue and annoy someone. Human review cannot measure recall at any volume, because a false negative is an absence. Only an answer key sees it.

docs.title: Two things the first run found, which were wrong with the answer key
docs.text:
Worth recording, because this is the ordinary experience of building one.

The first run reported false positives on p01 and p02 for no_example, and the auditor was right both times. p01 was mislabelled: it is a how-to whose only backticked text is cache_mode, a flag name, so it genuinely has no example. And no_example had never been defined precisely enough to label against: does an inline `widget keys rotate` count as an example? The answer here is yes, a runnable command counts and a bare identifier does not, and that definition is now in the auditor and in the case notes.

A disagreement between the auditor and the answer key is not automatically an auditor bug. Roughly half the time, early on, it is the labels.

docs.title: The metrics, and which failure each one hides
docs.text:
Metric Measures Blind to Precision Of what it flagged, how much was real Everything it missed Recall Of what was real, how much it flagged Everything it invented F1 The harmonic mean Which of the two moved Per-type precision and recall Where the prompt is weak Nothing; this is the useful view Accuracy Overall correctness Useless here: most pages are mostly clean

Never report F1 alone on a content task. In the golden path above F1 fell from 1.00 to 0.60, which correctly signals that something got worse but hides which thing: precision was untouched and recall collapsed. A change in the other direction, trading recall for precision, can leave F1 roughly flat. The two outcomes are not interchangeable: a reviewer drowning in false positives stops reviewing, and an audit that misses half the defects leaves a corpus that looks checked. Which failure you prefer is a judgement about who pays, and you can only make it if both numbers are on the table.

docs.title: Precision or recall, depending on the job
docs.text: Task Prefer Why Audit with human review recall A human filters false positives; nothing recovers a miss Automated fix with no review precision A wrong automated edit is a defect you introduced Finding candidates for a backlog recall Cheap to discard, expensive to never see Blocking a build precision A flaky gate gets disabled, and then nothing is checked Answering a user precision A confident wrong answer is worse than a refusal

docs.title: Building a labelled set that is worth having
docs.text:
Rule Why Label by hand A model-labelled set measures agreement with that model Include clean cases, at least a third Without them you cannot measure precision at all Include deliberately ambiguous cases They expose where humans disagree, which bounds the achievable score Record a note per case So nobody deletes a hard case for lowering the score Keep it small and real 20 to 50 cases from real content beats 500 synthetic Never tune parameters against it That makes it training data and the score meaningless

The ambiguous cases matter more than they look. p07 uses "should" to describe expected behaviour rather than to hedge a claim, and two careful reviewers will disagree about it. That disagreement is the ceiling on your achievable score, and a set with no ambiguous cases will tell you an auditor is worse than it is.

docs.title: Sample size, again
docs.text:
Cases One defect is worth Honest resolution 10 pages, ~15 defects about 7 points a very large difference only 50 pages, ~70 defects about 1.5 points a few points 200 pages, ~300 defects 0.3 points small differences

A ten-page set catches a change that breaks something. It cannot support a claim that precision improved by four points.

docs.title: What this cannot measure
docs.text:
Not measured Why What to do Whether the writing is good No answer key exists Review by a person Whether the page is accurate Needs the implementation Read the code Whether readers succeeded Needs an audience Time to first success Whether an answer is helpful Partly subjective Thumbs, then sample and read

Two layers above this are worth naming. LLM-as-judge scales labelling by having a model grade outputs against a rubric, and introduces a second model whose agreement with humans you now have to measure, on a labelled set, which is this concept again one level up. Pairwise comparison asks which of two outputs is better, which humans do far more reliably than absolute scoring and which is the right method when the task has no answer key at all.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with the tradeoff that eyeballing hides. "I keep a hand-labelled set of pages, including clean ones, because without clean cases you cannot measure precision at all. When someone tightened our audit prompt, both versions looked perfect to a reviewer, because every finding in both queues was real. Against the labelled set the tightened one had dropped from 1.00 recall to 0.43: it was missing eight of fourteen defects, and version checking had gone to zero. A reviewer can never see that, because nothing in a review queue refers to a defect that was never flagged."

The follow-up is "how do you label enough data", and the honest answer has two parts. You do not need much: twenty to fifty real pages is enough to catch a regression, and it is the resolution rather than the count that you should be honest about. And the way to grow it is to add a case every time a reviewer rejects a finding, so the set accumulates from real disagreements rather than from an afternoon of invention. If someone suggests having a model label the set, that is LLM-as-judge, and it needs its own human-labelled set to validate against, so it does not remove the labelling, it moves it.

The tradeoff to volunteer. A labelled set is a target, and the same Goodhart problem as retrieval evaluation applies more sharply here because prompts are so cheap to iterate. Sweep a few prompt variants against the set and you have fitted the prompt to twenty pages and learned nothing about the other four hundred. The discipline is to change the prompt for a stated reason and then measure, never to search for a prompt that scores well, and to hold back a few cases you do not look at.

One sharper point. The strongest thing to say is that the ambiguous cases set the ceiling, and most teams never find out what their ceiling is. If two careful reviewers disagree about p07, no prompt can score 1.0, and an auditor hitting 0.85 might already be at the limit of the task. Measuring inter-annotator agreement before optimising tells you whether you are chasing a real gap or noise, and almost nobody does it. That observation separates someone who has run an evaluation from someone who has read about metrics.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A labelled set with clean and ambiguous cases, a scorer reporting precision and recall per defect type, and one documented case where the measurement contradicted the spot check.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path, including step 4. The gap between the three-page spot check and the full numbers is the demonstration, and it takes two minutes to show.
  2. Label twenty real pages for one defect type. One type, by hand, with notes. An hour, and it is the only artifact on this page that cannot be faked.
  3. Measure your own agreement with yourself. Label ten pages, wait a week, label them again blind, and count the disagreements. That number is your ceiling, and reporting it alongside a precision figure is unusual enough to be memorable. Expect to disagree with yourself on at least one page in ten. A perfect second pass means you are remembering your labels rather than re- deriving them, and the week was not long enough.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Quoting precision and recall is a definition anyone can recite. A labelled set containing deliberately ambiguous cases, per-type metrics, and a worked example where tightening a prompt halved recall while F1 stayed flat demonstrates that you have been misled by a spot check and built the thing that stops it happening again.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
No model was available here, so no generated output was scored. The procedure below is the one this page argues for, and it is cheap enough that the absence is a scheduling problem rather than a technical one.

What you need. Access to whichever model your readers actually reach your docs through, by API or locally, plus the twenty-case golden set that retrieval evaluation already requires. Budget is small: twenty questions against two or three prompt variants is a few hundred calls, which is cents rather than dollars on any current model.

What you would run. For each question, retrieve context, generate an answer, and score it on three axes that need no human. Whether every claim in it appears in the retrieved context. Whether it cites a source that actually contains the cited fact. And whether it refuses when the corpus has no answer.

answer = model.generate(prompt.format(context=chunks, question=q))
grounded = all(claim_supported(c, chunks) for c in split_claims(answer))
refused  = looks_like_refusal(answer)

What you would see.

Observation Rough magnitude What it tells you Answers whose claims are all in context 70 to 90% The ceiling your retrieval sets Answers citing a chunk that lacks the cited fact 5 to 20% Citation is not grounding; both need checking Refusal rate on questions the corpus cannot answer often near 0% The most dangerous number on the page Agreement between two runs at temperature 0 high but not 1.0 Why n=1 evaluation misleads Effect of a prompt change on grounding several points Larger than most model upgrades

The third row is the finding worth building the harness for. Add five questions whose answers are deliberately absent from your corpus, and measure how often the system invents something instead of saying it does not know. A system that never refuses is not accurate, it is confident, and no retrieval metric exposes that at all.

How you would know it had failed. A grounding score at or near 100% almost always means the claim splitter is too coarse, so whole paragraphs count as one claim that matches loosely. A refusal rate of 100% means the prompt is over-constrained and the system is useless rather than safe. And if scores do not move when you deliberately corrupt the retrieved context, the grader is reading the answer rather than comparing it with anything.

docs.title: Documentation for partners and internal teams
docs.text:
One corpus serving three audiences with different access, different trust, and different consequences for a leak.

context · difficulty 2 · 3h

deliver Simulation Technology knowledge to developers, partners, internal teams, and the AI agents that increasingly sit between them and our documentation

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: Metadata for navigation and retrieval

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Serving several audiences with different access rights out of one corpus: public developers, contracted partners, internal teams, and now the agents acting for each of them. The hard part is not writing differently for each. It is that the same source tree has to produce different outputs, and a mistake publishes something it should not.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
It is the first sentence of the NVIDIA posting, and the list is deliberate: developers, partners, internal teams, and AI agents. Later, among the partner functions, "Partner Programs".

This is tagged context rather than core because you will not design the access model, and most of it is someone else's policy. But being unaware of it is how an audience field becomes a security boundary by accident. On a Tuesday this shows up as a question with a non-obvious answer: this page explains a scheduling behaviour using an example from a named studio's production. Which outputs can it appear in?

The reason it belongs in the guide at all is the fourth audience. An agent inherits the access of whoever it acts for, and a retrieval corpus does not inherit anything unless somebody built that. A single vector index over all four tiers, queried by an assistant, is an access-control failure waiting to happen, and it is a new failure mode that the navigation-era version of this problem did not have.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a corpus with three tiers and a publish step that physically cannot leak. Thirty minutes.

Step 1: declare the tier as a field, with a closed vocabulary

mkdir -p partner-drill && cd partner-drill
mkdir -p docs
cat > docs/install.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Install the SDK
visibility: public
---
# Install the SDK
Run the installer.
EOF
cat > docs/certification.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Partner certification process
visibility: partner
---
# Partner certification process
Submit your build to the certification portal.
EOF
cat > docs/scheduling-internals.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Scheduler internals
visibility: internal
---
# Scheduler internals
The dispatcher uses a work-stealing queue. Studio A's 2026 production hit a
pathological case at 400 concurrent shots.
EOF
ls docs/

Step 2: build the publish step as a whitelist, never a filter

The direction matters more than anything else on this page.

cat > publish.py <<'PY'
"""Publish one visibility tier by COPYING what is allowed in.

The critical design decision is the direction. A filter that excludes
`internal` pages leaks a page whose field is missing, misspelled, or a value
nobody anticipated. A whitelist that includes only `public` pages leaks
nothing when a field is wrong: it fails closed, and the page is simply absent,
which someone notices.

That asymmetry is the whole reason this script is shaped this way. One
direction fails by over-publishing and the other by under-publishing, and only
one of those is recoverable.
"""
import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

# Who may see what. A tier sees its own content and everything less
# restricted, which is the only ordering assumption here.
TIERS = {
    "public": ["public"],
    "partner": ["public", "partner"],
    "internal": ["public", "partner", "internal"],
}


def main(tier: str, docs: Path, out: Path) -> int:
    allowed = TIERS.get(tier)
    if allowed is None:
        print(f"unknown tier {tier!r}; known: {sorted(TIERS)}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2

    if out.exists():
        shutil.rmtree(out)
    out.mkdir(parents=True)

    included, skipped, rejected = [], [], []
    for page in sorted(docs.glob("*.md")):
        text = page.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        try:
            front = yaml.safe_load(text.split("---")[1]) or {}
        except Exception:
            rejected.append((page.name, "unparseable front matter"))
            continue

        visibility = front.get("visibility")
        if visibility is None:
            # Not silently skipped: a missing field is a content-model
            # violation and someone has to fix it.
            rejected.append((page.name, "no visibility field"))
            continue
        if visibility not in TIERS:
            rejected.append((page.name, f"unknown visibility {visibility!r}"))
            continue

        if visibility in allowed:
            shutil.copy2(page, out / page.name)
            included.append(page.name)
        else:
            skipped.append((page.name, visibility))

    print(f"tier {tier!r}: {len(included)} included, {len(skipped)} withheld, "
          f"{len(rejected)} rejected")
    for name in included:
        print(f"  include  {name}")
    for name, visibility in skipped:
        print(f"  withhold {name}  ({visibility})")
    for name, why in rejected:
        print(f"  REJECT   {name}  ({why})", file=sys.stderr)

    # A page nobody can classify blocks the build rather than leaking or
    # vanishing quietly.
    return 1 if rejected else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv[1], Path("docs"), Path(f"site-{sys.argv[1]}")))
PY
python3 publish.py public
echo "---"
python3 publish.py partner

Step 3: prove it fails closed

cat > docs/oops.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Unclassified page
---
# Unclassified page
Something nobody set a visibility on.
EOF
python3 publish.py public; echo "exit=$?"

cat > docs/typo.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Typo page
visibility: publc
---
# Typo page
EOF
python3 publish.py public; echo "exit=$?"
test -f site-public/typo.md && echo "LEAKED" || echo "not published: fails closed"

What you built. A publish step that blocks on any page it cannot classify and publishes only what it was told to. Both the missing field and the misspelled value produce a build failure and an absent page, never a leak.

The misspelling case is the one to notice. visibility: publc under a filter design would not match internal and would therefore be published. Under the whitelist it matches nothing and is withheld. Same typo, opposite outcome.

docs.title: The four audiences and what each changes
docs.text: Audience Access What changes in the content Public developers Anyone No customer names, no unreleased features, no internal URLs Partners Contract Certification, co-marketing, early access. Often under NDA Internal teams Employment Runbooks, incident history, named customers, roadmap Agents Whatever their principal has Nothing, and that is the problem

docs.title: The agent row, in detail
docs.text:
This is the part that is genuinely new and the part worth raising.

Mechanism Access-aware by default? A published site per tier Yes, by URL Navigation and search within a site Yes, same boundary A single vector index over the whole corpus No llms.txt No, unless generated per tier An MCP server over the source tree No, unless it filters per caller

The two bolded rows are where the leak happens. An assistant indexed over everything will answer a public developer's question with an internal chunk, fluently and with no indication that it should not have. The fix is one index per tier, or a filter applied at query time with the caller's tier as a hard constraint, which is the same filter-before-ranking argument the rest of this guide makes for quality reasons, here for a much less forgiving one.

docs.title: Whitelist versus filter
docs.text:
Design A missing field A misspelled value Fails by Include only allowed tiers withheld withheld under-publishing Exclude restricted tiers published published over-publishing

Only one of those failure modes can be undone.

docs.title: What is out of scope for you
docs.text:
Worth saying plainly, since this is context tier:

  • The access model itself is legal and policy work.
  • NDA terms, and what partner content may contain, are Partner Programs' call.
  • Authentication for a partner portal is platform engineering's.
  • Whether a customer can be named is a commercial question.

Your job is that the content model carries the distinction, the publish step fails closed, and the retrieval layer respects it.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with the whitelist and the agent problem. "Visibility is a required field with a closed vocabulary, and the publish step copies in what is allowed rather than filtering out what is not, so a missing or misspelled value withholds the page instead of publishing it. The part I would want to check at a company with partners is the retrieval layer: a single index over all tiers will answer a public question with internal content, and nothing about that failure is visible."

The follow-up is likely about the single-source argument, meaning why not keep internal content in a separate repository entirely. That is a legitimate design and often the right one. The honest comparison: separate repositories make a leak nearly impossible and make reuse nearly impossible too, so the same procedure gets written twice and drifts. One tree with a visibility field keeps content reusable and makes the publish step safety-critical. Which is right depends on how much content genuinely spans tiers, and on whether you trust the gate. For a corpus where most internal content is runbooks and incident history, separate repositories are usually simpler.

The tradeoff to volunteer. A visibility field makes every author make a security-adjacent decision while writing, and most authors are not equipped to make it. The field defaults to nothing on purpose, so an unclassified page blocks the build, but that means an author can be stopped by a question they cannot answer. The mitigation is a default by directory with an explicit override, so the common case needs no decision, and it is a real weakening of the model in exchange for authors not being blocked.

One sharper point. The strongest thing to say is that publishing a corpus for retrieval converts an information-architecture field into an access-control boundary, and almost nobody notices the moment it happens. An audience field used for navigation is a convenience; the same field used to partition a vector index is a security control, and it was designed as the former. Raising that distinction unprompted is the most valuable thing on this page, and at a company with partner programs and simulation customers under NDA it is a live concern rather than a hypothetical.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. The whitelist publish step plus the failing cases. It is forty lines and it demonstrates a design instinct that is hard to claim otherwise.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path, including both failure cases. The typo case is the demonstration: same input, opposite outcome depending on the direction of the logic.
  2. Audit one retrieval layer for tier awareness. If you have access to any corpus with internal content and any search or assistant over it, check whether the index is partitioned. The answer is usually no, and reporting it is a genuinely useful finding.
  3. Write the one-paragraph note on why an IA field became an access control when the corpus was indexed. Short, specific, and it is the kind of observation that gets remembered.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Multi-audience documentation is a common claim. A publish step that fails closed, with a demonstrated typo case, and a stated concern about the retrieval layer, is concrete and shows you have thought about the failure rather than the feature.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
Multi-audience publishing needs more than one audience. This repository has one corpus and no partners, so the mechanism can be built and the consequences cannot be observed.

What you need. Two audiences with different entitlements, and content that must not cross between them. A partner tier and a public tier is the usual shape.

What a learner would do. Build the publish step so it fails closed: a page with no audience field does not publish anywhere, rather than publishing everywhere. Then plant a page tagged for partners only, run the public build, and confirm it is absent.

What you would see.

Test Expected Why it matters A partner page in the public build Absent The basic case A page with no audience field Build fails Fail closed, never open A partner page's heading in the public search index Absent The leak people miss A public page linking to a partner page Build fails The other leak people miss A partner term in a public page's prose Nothing catches it The honest limit

Rows three and four are the ones to design for, because a build that filters pages while leaking their titles into a shared index has told the public exactly what it is not allowed to see. Row five is why this needs a reviewer as well as a gate.

Why it does not commit. The gate commits and the stakes do not. The demonstration that matters is a year of publishing without a leak, and that is an absence of incidents in someone else's organisation.

docs.title: Playbooks and decision guides
docs.text:
Turning what one person knows into a branching path other people can follow, and validating that every branch ends.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Capture tribal knowledge from engineering, product, and operations, and turn it into playbooks, decision guides, and self-service paths"

Prerequisites: Interviewing subject-matter experts

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A page that branches. A tutorial takes one reader down one path; a playbook asks what situation you are in and routes you accordingly. It is the right shape for troubleshooting, for incident response, and for any question whose honest answer is "it depends", because it makes the depends explicit.

The move that turns it from a document into infrastructure is writing the branches as data rather than as prose. Then you can render the page and validate the structure, which is the difference between a playbook and a wiki page with a lot of nested bullets.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA's bullet is the clearest statement of leverage anywhere in either posting: capture what individuals know and turn it into self-service paths, so fewer people have to ask "how do I…?".

The reason this needs a page of its own rather than being a kind of how-to is that tribal knowledge is conditional. The expert does not know one procedure; they know how to tell which of six situations they are in, and the discriminating questions are the knowledge. Writing a linear how-to for each branch loses the part that made the expert valuable, which is the routing.

It is also the output of SME interviews, which is why that is the prerequisite rather than information architecture. You cannot write the branches without having asked somebody "how do you know which one it is?"

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Write a decision guide as data, then validate its structure. About thirty-five minutes.

Committed as drills/playbook.py, which is the complete version of what follows: this page prints the playbook in full and the validator in fragments, so the output below used to come from a check_playbook.py that appears nowhere. A test asserts the drill still prints what this page quotes, and that the playbook it validates is the one below.

Step 1: the branches, as data

The subject is a real one: an integration has failed and you have to work out why. This is the shape of knowledge a Boomi or ETL engineer carries around in their head.

mkdir -p playbook-demo && cd playbook-demo
cat > playbook.yaml <<'EOF'
name: Integration is failing
entry: symptom
nodes:
  symptom:
    ask: What does the failure look like?
    options:
      - {answer: No data arrived at all, go: check-trigger}
      - {answer: Some records missing, go: check-filter}
      - {answer: Wrong values in the data, go: check-mapping}
  check-trigger:
    ask: Did the schedule fire?
    options:
      - {answer: "No", do: fix-schedule}
      - {answer: "Yes", go: check-auth}
  check-auth:
    ask: Are the credentials current?
    options:
      - {answer: "No", do: rotate-credentials}
      - {answer: "Yes", do: escalate-platform}
  check-filter:
    ask: Does the filter reference a field that was renamed?
    options:
      - {answer: "Yes", do: fix-filter}
      - {answer: "No", do: escalate-platform}
  check-mapping:
    ask: Is a dynamic process property set where you expect?
    options:
      - {answer: "No", do: trace-dpp}
      - {answer: "Yes", do: escalate-platform}
outcomes:
  fix-schedule: Re-enable the schedule and note why it was off.
  rotate-credentials: Rotate the token, then re-run the failed window.
  fix-filter: Update the filter to the current field name.
  trace-dpp: Find every get and set of the property, then correct the source.
  escalate-platform: Hand to the platform team with the trace attached.
  orphaned-outcome: Nothing routes here.
EOF

Note the shape. Every node is a question with discriminating answers, and every path terminates in an outcome that says what to do. escalate-platform appears three times, which is correct: "I have ruled out what I can" is a legitimate destination and a playbook that pretends otherwise sends people in circles.

Step 2: the five things that can be wrong with it

# every `go` and `do` target resolves, and no option goes nowhere
for nid, node in nodes.items():
    for opt in node["options"]:
        if "go" in opt and opt["go"] not in nodes:
            problems.append(f"{nid}: 'go: {opt['go']}' is not a node")
        if "do" in opt and opt["do"] not in outcomes:
            problems.append(f"{nid}: 'do: {opt['do']}' is not an outcome")
        if "go" not in opt and "do" not in opt:
            problems.append(f"{nid}: option {opt['answer']!r} goes nowhere")

# every outcome is reachable
reached = {o["do"] for n in nodes.values() for o in n["options"] if "do" in o}
for oid in outcomes:
    if oid not in reached:
        problems.append(f"outcome {oid!r}: nothing routes here")

# every node is reachable from the entry
reachable, frontier = {entry}, [entry]
while frontier:
    for opt in nodes[frontier.pop()]["options"]:
        if opt.get("go") in nodes and opt["go"] not in reachable:
            reachable.add(opt["go"])
            frontier.append(opt["go"])
for nid in nodes:
    if nid not in reachable:
        problems.append(f"node {nid!r}: unreachable from {entry!r}")

# no cycles, because a decision guide that loops never ends

The node-reachability check is the same defect as the outcome one, a level up, and it is the likelier of the two in a guide that has been edited for a year. A question nobody can reach is a branch of the expert's knowledge that has quietly left the playbook, and it is harder to notice by reading than an orphaned outcome, because an unreachable node is perfectly well-formed on its own.

Step 3: run it

python3 check_playbook.py

PLAYBOOK  outcome 'orphaned-outcome': nothing routes here
FAIL: 5 nodes, 6 outcomes, 1 problem(s)

One finding, which is the deliberately planted orphan. Remove it:

ok: 5 nodes, 5 outcomes, 0 problem(s)

Step 4: confirm each defect class is caught

Inject the other four, one at a time, and print every finding each produces:

  dangling-go  a target that does not resolve
    check-trigger: 'go: check-athu' is not a node
    node 'check-auth': unreachable from 'symptom'
  cycle        a path that never ends
    cycle: symptom -> check-trigger -> check-auth -> symptom
  dead-end     an option with no next step
    check-trigger: option 'No' goes nowhere
    outcome 'fix-schedule': nothing routes here
  unreachable  a question nobody can get to
    node 'check-retry': unreachable from 'symptom'

Five classes, five catches. Each is a specific way a prose playbook fails silently:

Defect What a reader experiences Orphaned outcome Advice nobody can reach; usually the most interesting advice Unreachable node A question that has silently left the guide, taking its branch with it Dangling target "See the authentication section", which does not exist Cycle Being sent back to a question already answered Dead-end option An answer with no next step, so the reader is stuck

Every one of those exists in prose troubleshooting guides and none is detectable by reading, because reading follows one path at a time and these are properties of the whole graph.

docs.title: A findings count is not a defect count
docs.text:
Two of those four injections report two findings, and both second findings are consequences of the first.

Removing the do from check-trigger's first option leaves that option dangling and orphans fix-schedule, because that option was the only route to it. Mistyping the go target breaks that edge and strands check-auth, which nothing else routes to.

So four injected defects produce six findings, and two of the six vanish when the other four are fixed. That matters the moment anybody plans work from the number: a graph validator reports symptoms, and in a graph one broken edge produces as many symptoms as there are properties that depended on it. The repair list is shorter than the findings list, always, and the only way to know how much shorter is to fix one and re-run.

This page used to show a single line per class, which hid both cascades. The block above is what the validator actually prints.

What you built. A decision guide whose structure is checkable, the knowledge that the cycle in step 4 is the failure readers complain about without being able to name, and a worked reason to distrust findings counts.

docs.title: When a playbook is the right shape
docs.text: Use a playbook Use something else The answer depends on observable conditions One procedure, one audience: a how-to An expert routes before acting The task is linear Troubleshooting, triage, incident response Explaining why something works: an explanation "It depends" is the honest answer There is a single best path: a golden path Several paths converge on an escalation Nobody ever needs to escalate

docs.title: The questions that make it work
docs.text:
A playbook's quality is in its discriminating questions, and the test for each one is whether a reader can answer it without already knowing the diagnosis.

Good question Bad question "Did the schedule fire?" "Is the trigger misconfigured?" "Are the credentials current?" "Is this an auth problem?" "Is the property set where you expect?" "Is the mapping wrong?"

The bad column asks the reader to make the determination the playbook exists to help them make. This is the single most common defect in hand-written troubleshooting guides, and no validator catches it: it needs a reader who does not already know the answer.

docs.title: Getting it out of somebody's head
docs.text:
Technique Produces Watch them do it, and write down the questions they ask The branch structure Ask "how do you know it is that and not the other thing?" The discriminating questions Ask for the last five times they were wrong The branches a confident expert omits Ask what they check first and why The entry node Ask when they give up and escalate The terminal outcomes

The third row is the one that improves a playbook most. Experts narrate their successful path and omit the branches they have learned to skip, and those skipped branches are exactly where a newcomer gets lost.

docs.title: Playbook as data, and what it buys
docs.text:
Output From the same file A rendered page Generated, so prose and structure cannot disagree Structural validation The four checks above An interactive widget Optional; the data supports it An agent skill A model can walk the graph rather than guess Coverage measurement Which outcomes fire most, from incident records

The last two are why this is worth the extra work. A playbook as prose is a page; a playbook as data is something an assistant can traverse, and the routing is the part an assistant is otherwise worst at.

docs.title: Keeping one honest
docs.text: Rule Why Every path terminates Checked above Escalation is a real outcome Pretending otherwise sends people round again Questions are observable, not diagnostic See the table above Review it after an incident it failed to cover The missing branch is now known Date the outcomes "Rotate the token" changes when the auth system does

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the routing. "Tribal knowledge is conditional. The expert does not know one procedure, they know how to tell which of six situations they are in, and the discriminating questions are the actual knowledge. A linear how-to per branch loses exactly that, which is why these are decision guides and not tutorials."

The follow-up is how you keep one correct, and the answer is to write the branches as data and validate the graph: no dangling targets, no cycles, no dead-end options, no unreachable outcomes. Four checks that catch failures no amount of reading will, because reading follows one path and these are properties of the whole structure.

The tradeoff to volunteer. A playbook as data costs you a generator and a validator, and it makes casual editing harder: a contributor who wants to add a sentence now has to understand a schema. On a guide with four branches that is not worth it, and prose with a diagram is the better answer. It starts paying when the graph is big enough that nobody can hold it in their head, which is roughly the point at which it also stops being maintainable as prose.

One sharper point. The quality of a playbook is entirely in whether its questions can be answered by someone who does not already know the answer. "Is the trigger misconfigured?" is useless and extremely common; "Did the schedule fire?" is useful. No validator catches that, which is why these need testing with a reader who is genuinely stuck rather than review by the expert who wrote them.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A playbook for something you actually know, as data, with the four structural checks and a rendered page from the same source.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Step 4 is worth doing in full, because the cycle finding is the reader complaint you have probably received without recognising it.
  2. Take the thing colleagues ask you most often and write its branches. Not the procedure, the questions.
  3. Give it to someone who does not know the answer and watch where they stop. That is the diagnostic-question defect, and it is the only way to find it.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Neither of this guide's repositories contains a playbook, which the demonstrated page records. The validator above is real and runs, and the honest limit is that it checks structure only: it proves every path ends somewhere, and it cannot tell you whether the questions are answerable. Being clear about which half a tool covers is the point.

docs.title: Preview deployments and publishing
docs.text:
Shipping the site, and giving reviewers a rendered page instead of a diff.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Build and run docs-as-code pipelines: Git authoring, CI/CD builds, linting, link and code-sample validation, and publishing"

Prerequisites: GitHub Actions for docs

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Two related things that are usually built at once. Publishing is the job that puts the built site somewhere readers can reach it when a change lands on the default branch. Preview deployments build the site for a pull request and give reviewers a URL, so review happens against a rendered page rather than against Markdown in a diff.

Publishing is nearly free once a build exists. Previews are where the real decisions are, and most of them are about permissions and search engines rather than about building.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA lists publishing as part of the pipeline. The reason it belongs in a quality category rather than an infrastructure one is that previews are the single most effective fix for the biggest objection to docs-as-code: that non-engineer contributors and reviewers cannot work in diffs.

A product manager asked to review a Markdown diff will approve it without reading it. The same person given a link to the rendered page will find the sentence that is wrong. Previews are what make review by non-engineers real, and that is a documentation-quality outcome, not a deployment convenience.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a preview, discover what the production configuration leaks into it, and fix the part that actually matters. About twenty-five minutes.

Step 1: a site with a production URL

mkdir -p preview-demo/docs && cd preview-demo
cat > mkdocs.yml <<'EOF'
site_name: Preview demo
site_url: https://example.github.io/widget/
theme:
  name: mkdocs
EOF
printf '# Home\n\nSee the [guide](guide.md).\n' > docs/index.md
printf '# Guide\n\nBack [home](index.md).\n' > docs/guide.md
mkdocs build -q

Step 2: check the assumption everyone repeats

The usual warning is that a site built for one base URL breaks when served from another prefix. Test it rather than believing it:

grep -o 'href="[^"]*css[^"]*"' site/index.html | head -3
grep -c 'href="/' site/index.html

href="css/bootstrap.min.css"
href="css/fontawesome.min.css"
href="css/brands.min.css"
0

Relative paths, and zero absolute-root hrefs. The build is portable across prefixes: you can serve this same output at /pr-123/ and the CSS resolves. The warning does not apply to MkDocs output, so do not spend your preview budget solving it.

Step 3: find what site_url does leak

Rebuild as a preview and compare what is URL-dependent:

sed -i 's|site_url:.*|site_url: https://example.github.io/widget/pr-123/|' mkdocs.yml
mkdocs build -q -d site-pr

for d in site site-pr; do
  printf "%-8s " "$d"
  grep -o '<link rel="canonical" href="[^"]*"' $d/index.html | head -1
done

site     <link rel="canonical" href="https://example.github.io/widget/"
site-pr  <link rel="canonical" href="https://example.github.io/widget/pr-123/"

And the sitemap:

for d in site site-pr; do
  printf "%-8s " "$d"
  (gzip -dc $d/sitemap.xml.gz 2>/dev/null || cat $d/sitemap.xml) \
    | grep -o '<loc>[^<]*</loc>' | head -2 | tr '\n' ' '
  echo
done

site     <loc>https://example.github.io/widget/</loc> <loc>.../guide/</loc>
site-pr  <loc>https://example.github.io/widget/pr-123/</loc> <loc>.../pr-123/guide/</loc>

The preview is advertising itself. It declares its own canonical URL and ships a sitemap inviting crawlers to index every page of a draft.

Step 4: confirm nothing stops that

for d in site site-pr; do
  printf "%-8s noindex=%s robots.txt=%s\n" "$d" \
    "$(grep -c 'noindex' $d/index.html)" \
    "$([ -f $d/robots.txt ] && echo yes || echo no)"
done

site     noindex=0 robots.txt=no
site-pr  noindex=0 robots.txt=no

No noindex, no robots.txt. A publicly reachable preview of unmerged documentation is fully indexable, and it is competing with production for the same queries while containing text nobody has approved.

Step 5: fix the real problem

mkdir -p overrides
cat > overrides/main.html <<'EOF'
{% extends "base.html" %}
{% block extrahead %}
  {% if config.extra.preview %}
    <meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">
  {% endif %}
{% endblock %}
EOF
printf 'User-agent: *\nDisallow: /\n' > docs/robots.txt
echo "built previews now carry noindex when extra.preview is set"

Two independent controls, because either alone can be bypassed: a noindex meta tag on every page, and a robots.txt that disallows everything. Set extra.preview only in the preview job.

What you built. A preview that reviewers can read and search engines will not index. That is the whole job, and the hard part was never the base URL.

docs.title: What a preview costs you, by hosting choice
docs.text: Approach Fork pull requests Cleanup Notes GitHub Pages, one site Not supported N/A One site per repo; no per-PR previews Netlify or Cloudflare Pages Supported, sandboxed Automatic on merge Purpose-built for this Upload the build as a CI artifact Works everywhere Automatic expiry Reviewer downloads a zip; no URL to click Self-hosted per-PR subpath Needs secrets You build it Where the permissions trap lives

docs.title: The permissions trap
docs.text:
This is the one worth knowing cold. A workflow triggered by pull_request from a fork gets no secrets, by design, so a deploy step in it cannot authenticate. The tempting fix is pull_request_target, which does have secrets.

Trigger Has secrets Runs code from Safe to deploy from pull_request No The fork Nothing to deploy with pull_request_target Yes The base branch Only if it never checks out the fork workflow_run Yes The base branch Yes, consuming an artifact

pull_request_target that checks out the pull request's head and then runs a build is remote code execution with your deploy credentials. The safe pattern is two workflows: an untrusted one that builds and uploads an artifact with no secrets, and a trusted workflow_run that downloads the artifact and publishes it without ever executing contributor code.

docs.title: Publishing, which is the easy half
docs.text:
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  publish:
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pages: write
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pip install -e ".[docs]"
      - run: mkdocs build --strict
      - uses: actions/configure-pages@v5
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: site
      - uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4

Read-only at the top, write only in this job, and gated on the default branch so a pull request can never publish.

docs.title: What this guide actually does
docs.text: docpack publishes to GitHub Pages on main and regenerates its retrieval artifacts alongside the site. It has no per-pull-request preview, because GitHub Pages hosts one site per repository and adding a real preview means adding a second host. That is recorded as a partial demonstration rather than written up as a complete one, which is the honest state.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with review, not deployment. "Previews are how review by non-engineers becomes real. A reviewer who is handed a Markdown diff approves it; a reviewer handed a rendered page finds the wrong sentence. That is a content-quality mechanism that happens to be implemented in CI."

The follow-up you want is about forks, because the answer separates people who have shipped this from people who have read about it. Fork pull requests get no secrets, pull_request_target has secrets but must never check out contributor code, and the safe shape is build-without-secrets then publish from a workflow_run.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Previews cost a second hosting target, a cleanup story, and a small ongoing bill, and they are worth it in direct proportion to how many of your reviewers are not engineers. On a repository where every reviewer reads diffs comfortably, the CI-artifact approach gets most of the value for none of the infrastructure.

One sharper point. Almost nobody adds noindex to their previews. The default MkDocs preview ships a canonical tag pointing at itself and a sitemap listing every draft page, so unapproved documentation ends up in search results competing with the real thing. It is two lines to prevent, and noticing it is the kind of detail that reads as having operated a real site rather than configured one.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A repository that publishes on merge with least-privilege permissions, plus either a working preview or an explicit written reason there is none.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Step 2 will save you time forever, because the base-URL worry is folklore for MkDocs output.
  2. Check whether any preview you already run is indexable. Fetch a preview URL and grep for noindex. If it is missing, that is a real finding on a real site.
  3. Write down, in your repository, why you do or do not have previews. The written reason is worth as much in an interview as the feature, because it shows the decision was made rather than skipped.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. A publish job that is gated on the default branch and scoped with permissions:, and an answer to the fork question that does not involve pull_request_target checking out the head.

docs.title: Prompting for content work
docs.text:
Writing instructions for a model the way you would write a spec for a contractor, and checking the output the same way.

core · difficulty 2 · 3h

Practical experience applying LLMs to content workflows (prompting, retrieval and grounding, output evaluation)

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Leads to: Judging where AI can be trusted, LLMs in the content lifecycle

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Writing the instruction that produces a usable output on a content task: drafting, auditing, classifying, rewriting. For documentation work the prompt is usually part of a script rather than a conversation, which changes what good looks like: it has to work on the four hundredth input as well as the first.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA lists it first in a three-part requirement: "prompting, retrieval and grounding, output evaluation". The ordering is the pipeline, and prompting is the part people think is the whole thing.

What makes it core in a documentation role rather than a general skill is the shape of the task. You are almost never writing a prompt for one output. You are writing a prompt that will run over 400 pages in a batch, where you will review a sample and accept the rest. That changes every decision: consistency matters more than peak quality, the output format has to be machine-parseable, and the prompt needs to be able to say "no finding here" without being pushed into inventing one.

On a Tuesday it is a specific failure. You ask a model to flag pages whose examples use a deprecated API. It returns a finding for every page, because nothing in the prompt made "nothing wrong with this page" an acceptable answer, and a model asked to find problems will find problems. The fix is in the prompt, not the model, and knowing that is the difference between a usable audit and 400 false positives.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Write a prompt for a real content task, then break it four ways and fix each. Thirty-five minutes. No API key: the exercise is the prompt text and a mock model that exposes each flaw.

Step 1: the task, and the naive prompt

mkdir -p prompt-drill && cd prompt-drill
cat > v1.txt <<'EOF'
Review this documentation page and tell me what is wrong with it.
EOF
cat v1.txt

That prompt has four defects, and they are the four that matter.

Step 2: name them before fixing them

cat > defects.md <<'EOF'
| Defect                 | What it causes at scale                          |
|------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| No definition of wrong | Every reviewer, human or model, invents criteria |
| No output format       | Unparseable. You cannot aggregate 400 of these   |
| No null answer         | "Nothing is wrong" is not an option, so it finds |
|                        | something. This is the expensive one             |
| No grounding rule      | It will comment on things not in the page        |
EOF
cat defects.md

Step 3: the fixed prompt

cat > v2.txt <<'EOF'
You are auditing one documentation page for a specific, closed set of defects.

Report ONLY these defect types:
  stale_version   a version number or requirement that contradicts the
                  `requires` field in the page's front matter
  no_example      a how-to page with no code block
  hedge           the words "simply", "just", "easy", or "should" used to
                  describe what the software does
  undefined_term  a term in backticks that the page never defines and does
                  not link to

Rules:
- Report a defect ONLY if you can quote the exact text from the page that
  demonstrates it. If you cannot quote it, do not report it.
- If the page has none of these defects, return an empty findings list. An
  empty list is a correct and expected answer.
- Do not comment on anything outside the list above. Do not suggest
  improvements. Do not rate the page.

Return JSON only, no prose, matching exactly:

{"findings": [{"type": "<one of the four>", "quote": "<exact text from the page>", "line_hint": "<the heading it appears under>"}]}

Page:
---
{page}
---
EOF
wc -l v2.txt

Step 4: test it against the four failures with a mock model

The mock is not a toy. It encodes the four ways a real model fails on this task, so you can see which ones the prompt closes.

mkdir -p docs
cat > docs/good.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Rotate a key
requires: widget>=2.4
kind: how-to
---
# Rotate a key

Run the rotation command.

```bash
widget keys rotate
```
EOF

cat > docs/bad.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Configure caching
requires: widget>=2.4
kind: how-to
---
# Configure caching

Simply set the `cache_mode` flag. It should work on widget 1.9 or newer.
EOF

cat > mock.py <<'PY'
"""A mock model that fails the way real ones do on audit tasks.

Four behaviours, each switchable, so the prompt can be tested against them
without an API key:

  invents     reports a finding on a clean page (no null answer allowed)
  rambles     wraps the JSON in prose (no format discipline)
  ungrounded  reports a defect it cannot quote from the page
  disciplined obeys a prompt that closes all three holes

The point is not that this mock is realistic in detail. It is that each
behaviour maps to a prompt defect, so you can see which clause prevents
which failure.
"""
import json
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

HEDGES = ("simply", "just", "easy", "should")


def disciplined(page: str) -> str:
    findings = []
    front = page.split("---")[1] if page.startswith("---") else ""
    requires = re.search(r"requires:\s*\S+?>=([\d.]+)", front)
    body = page.split("---", 2)[-1]

    for hedge in HEDGES:
        match = re.search(rf"\b{hedge}\b", body, re.I)
        if match:
            sentence = re.search(rf"[^.]*\b{hedge}\b[^.]*\.", body, re.I)
            findings.append({
                "type": "hedge",
                "quote": (sentence.group(0) if sentence else match.group(0)).strip(),
                "line_hint": "body",
            })
    if requires:
        for version in re.findall(r"widget (\d+\.\d+)", body):
            if version < requires.group(1):
                sentence = re.search(rf"[^.]*widget {re.escape(version)}[^.]*\.", body)
                findings.append({
                    "type": "stale_version",
                    "quote": (sentence.group(0) if sentence else version).strip(),
                    "line_hint": "body",
                })
    if "kind: how-to" in front and "```" not in body:
        findings.append({"type": "no_example", "quote": "", "line_hint": "whole page"})
    return json.dumps({"findings": findings})


def invents(page: str) -> str:
    return json.dumps({"findings": [
        {"type": "unclear", "quote": "the page could be clearer", "line_hint": "intro"}
    ]})


def rambles(page: str) -> str:
    inner = disciplined(page)
    return (
        "Sure! I reviewed the page. Here is what I found:\n\n"
        f"```json\n{inner}\n```\n\n"
        "Let me know if you would like me to suggest improvements!"
    )


def ungrounded(page: str) -> str:
    return json.dumps({"findings": [
        {"type": "stale_version", "quote": "requires widget 1.2", "line_hint": "body"}
    ]})


MODES = {"invents": invents, "rambles": rambles,
         "ungrounded": ungrounded, "disciplined": disciplined}


def parse(raw: str, page: str):
    """Parse a response the way a batch job must: strictly, then report why."""
    try:
        data = json.loads(raw)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return None, "not JSON (prose or fences around it)"
    if "findings" not in data:
        return None, "no findings key"

    kept, dropped = [], []
    for finding in data["findings"]:
        if finding["type"] not in ("stale_version", "no_example", "hedge", "undefined_term"):
            dropped.append((finding, "type not in the closed set"))
        elif finding["quote"] and finding["quote"] not in page:
            dropped.append((finding, "quote not found in the page"))
        else:
            kept.append(finding)
    return (kept, dropped), None


for name in sorted(Path("docs").glob("*.md")):
    page = name.read_text()
    print(f"\n=== {name.name} ===")
    for mode in ("invents", "rambles", "ungrounded", "disciplined"):
        raw = MODES[mode](page)
        result, error = parse(raw, page)
        if error:
            print(f"  {mode:<12} REJECTED: {error}")
            continue
        kept, dropped = result
        detail = ", ".join(f["type"] for f in kept) or "none"
        note = f"  ({len(dropped)} dropped: {dropped[0][1]})" if dropped else ""
        print(f"  {mode:<12} {len(kept)} finding(s): {detail}{note}")
PY
python3 mock.py

What you built. A prompt with a closed defect set, a required quote, an explicit null answer and a strict output format, plus a harness that shows what each clause prevents.

Read the output carefully, because each failure is caught by a different clause and that mapping is the lesson.

Mode Result What caught it invents 0 findings, 1 dropped The closed set. It reported type unclear, which is not one of the four rambles rejected The format rule. Prose and code fences around the JSON make it unparseable ungrounded 0 findings, 1 dropped The quote rule. It fabricated requires widget 1.2, which is not in the page disciplined 4 on bad.md, 0 on good.md nothing; it is correct

The last cell is the one to notice. On the clean page the disciplined mode returns an empty list, which is only possible because the prompt says an empty list is a correct answer. Every other mode returns something on every page.

And the broader lesson: three of the four failures were caught by validating the output, not by improving the prompt. The prompt reduces them; the validator is what makes a 400-page batch safe. That is the same division of labour as judging where AI can be trusted.

docs.title: The five clauses a content prompt needs
docs.text: Clause Prevents A closed set of categories Invented categories you cannot aggregate A required quote from the source Fabrication, which is the expensive failure An explicit null answer A finding on every input A strict output format Unparseable results in a batch An explicit "do not" list Helpful additions you did not ask for

docs.title: Why the null answer matters most
docs.text:
A model asked to find problems finds problems. On an audit over 400 pages, a prompt without an explicit empty-list instruction produces a near-100 percent finding rate, a reviewer who accepts everything by page forty, and a corpus that looks audited and is not.

One sentence fixes it: "If the page has none of these defects, return an empty findings list. An empty list is a correct and expected answer."

docs.title: Patterns worth knowing
docs.text: Pattern Use Closed vocabulary in the prompt Classification into your taxonomy Quote-or-drop Any audit or extraction task Few-shot with a null example When the empty case keeps getting missed; show it Chain of custody Ask for the source line, then validate it mechanically Two-pass propose-then-filter High-volume audits; cheap model proposes, you filter Rubric in the prompt Review tasks, so judgements are comparable across runs Refuse-if-unsure "If you cannot determine this from the text, say unknown"

docs.title: What not to ask a model to do
docs.text:
Task Why not State a default value A generator is right every time Write a parameter table Same Decide what to retire Irreversible, and the failure is invisible Write security instructions Unbounded failure cost Confirm that a page is accurate It has no access to the implementation

See judging where AI can be trusted for the decision procedure behind that table.

docs.title: Operational details that matter in a batch
docs.text: Detail Why Pin the model version A model update silently changes the output distribution Set temperature to 0 for classification Reproducibility; you will rerun this Store the prompt in version control, not in a notebook It is code, and it changes behaviour Log the prompt version with every output You will need to know which prompt produced a finding Sample and review after you start trusting it Quality drifts, and nothing tells you

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with the null answer, because it is the clause that shows you have run a batch rather than written a prompt. "On an audit prompt the clause that matters most is telling the model that an empty findings list is a correct answer. Without it, a model asked to find problems finds one on every page, and by page forty your reviewer is accepting everything. The second is requiring a verbatim quote from the source, which I then check mechanically: if the quoted text is not in the page, the finding is dropped before a human ever sees it."

The follow-up is "how do you know the prompt is good", and the answer is that you do not know from reading it. You need a small labelled set: twenty pages you have reviewed yourself, with the defects you expect, scored for precision and recall. That is output evaluation and it is the only way to tell a prompt improvement from a coincidence. Anyone who answers this question by describing their prompt rather than their measurement has not run one at scale.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Every clause you add constrains the model, and over-constraining produces a different failure: a prompt with a tightly closed defect set will miss real problems that fall outside it, confidently and silently. The quote-or-drop rule has the same shape, since a genuine defect that is structural rather than textual, like a missing section, has no quote and gets dropped. So the closed set has to be revisited as you learn what it misses, and a prompt that has not changed in six months is probably missing things rather than being finished.

One sharper point. The strongest framing is that a prompt is a specification, and the clauses that make it work are the clauses that make any specification work: define the terms, state the acceptance criteria, say what is out of scope, and require evidence for claims. That is why documentation people are often good at this: you already write specifications for human contractors and already know that "tell me what's wrong with it" is a bad brief. Saying that connects the LLM work to the craft rather than treating it as a separate skill, which is exactly how NVIDIA's posting frames the whole role.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A prompt in version control, with the labelled set you scored it against, and the validator that drops ungrounded findings.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. The four-mode mock shows which clause closes which failure, and the quote-check dropping a fabricated finding is the convincing moment.
  2. Build a twenty-page labelled set for one real audit task and score precision and recall. Twenty is enough to catch a prompt that finds something on everything. Predict both numbers before you score. Precision is the one that surprises people, because a prompt that finds everything looks like it is working.
  3. Write the validator before the prompt is good. The quote-must-appear check is ten lines and it catches fabrication regardless of which model or prompt you end up with. Shipping the validator first is the move that shows judgement.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Showing a prompt proves nothing; everyone has prompts. A prompt plus a labelled set plus a mechanical grounding check plus a precision number, including the version where precision was bad, demonstrates that you treated it as engineering.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
No model ran here, so every prompt comparison on this page is reasoning. The demonstration is unusually easy to set up and unusually easy to fool yourself with, which is why the failure signatures below matter more than the procedure.

What you need. Any model you can call repeatedly, and a task with a checkable answer. That second requirement is the whole difficulty: prompting demonstrations are usually run on tasks whose output can only be judged by reading it, which is how everyone concludes their favourite prompt is best.

What you would run. Pick a content task with a mechanical check, such as "rewrite this page's front matter to the content model" where a validator can score it, or "extract every flag name from this reference page" where the true list is known. Then run three or four prompt variants, twenty inputs each, and score with the validator rather than by eye.

for variant in VARIANTS:
    scores = [validate(model.generate(variant.format(page=p))) for p in pages]

What you would see.

Observation Rough magnitude What it tells you Spread between the best and worst variant 10 to 40 points Prompting is worth measuring Spread between two runs of the same variant several points Why single-run comparisons are noise Effect of adding one worked example usually the largest single gain Examples beat instructions Effect of adding three more examples small Where the returns stop Effect of asking for a format you then parse large, and brittle Format compliance is its own metric Effect of politeness, persona, emphasis within noise The things people tune hardest

The second row disciplines everything else. If two runs of one prompt differ by five points, then a five-point difference between two prompts is not a finding, and most published prompt advice is built on exactly that size of difference measured once.

The measurement that changes how you work. Run your current best prompt twenty times on one input and record the variance. That single number tells you how large a difference has to be before you are allowed to believe it, and it is the measurement nobody takes before redesigning a prompt.

How you would know it had failed. Zero variance across runs means temperature is pinned and you are measuring one sample repeatedly, which is fine for regression testing and useless for comparison. A validator that passes every output means it is too lenient to rank anything. And if the best variant changes every time you re-run the comparison, the spread is smaller than the noise and the honest answer is that the variants are equivalent.
