docs.title: Prose linting with Vale
docs.text:
Enforcing the parts of a style guide a machine can check, and leaving the rest alone.

core · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Content quality automation you've built, such as Vale or custom linters, doc test harnesses, or freshness monitoring"

Prerequisites: Style guides

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A linter for prose. Vale reads Markdown, reStructuredText and a dozen other formats, applies rules you write in YAML, and reports violations with a file, line, column and severity, the same shape a compiler uses.

What it is really for is converting the mechanical half of a style guide from a document people are supposed to have read into a check that runs. "Use widget rather than Widget CLI" stops being a sentence in a wiki and becomes a failing build.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA names Vale specifically, in the "ways to stand out" section, alongside custom linters and doc test harnesses. That grouping tells you what they mean by it: not that you have installed a linter, but that you have built content quality automation.

The reason it matters on a large corpus is consistency at scale. One writer with good judgment produces consistent prose. Thirty contributors across engineering, product and support produce thirty dialects, and the terminology drift that follows is what makes a documentation set feel untrustworthy even when every individual page is correct. A linter is the only mechanism that applies the same standard to a pull request from someone who has never read your style guide.

The second reason is review bandwidth. A reviewer who spends their attention on serial commas has none left for whether the procedure is correct. Automating the mechanical layer is what makes human review about substance.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a two-rule house style, run it, and discover what actually controls whether the build fails. About thirty minutes.

Step 1: a config and two rules

mkdir -p vale-demo/docs vale-demo/styles/House && cd vale-demo

cat > .vale.ini <<'EOF'
StylesPath = styles
MinAlertLevel = suggestion

[*.md]
BasedOnStyles = House
EOF

cat > styles/House/Hedging.yml <<'EOF'
extends: existence
message: "Avoid hedging: '%s'"
level: warning
ignorecase: true
tokens:
  - should be able to
  - probably
  - fairly simple
EOF

cat > styles/House/Terms.yml <<'EOF'
extends: substitution
message: "Use '%s' rather than '%s'"
level: error
ignorecase: false
swap:
  Widget CLI: widget
  dataset: data set
EOF

Note the direction of swap. The key is the form you do not want and the value is the replacement. Getting this backwards is the most common Vale mistake, and it fails silently: your rule simply never fires.

Step 2: run it

cat > docs/index.md <<'EOF'
# Getting started

You should be able to install the Widget CLI fairly easily.
Load the dataset, then run the command.
EOF

vale docs/

 3:5   warning  Avoid hedging: 'should be able to'   House.Hedging
 3:35  error    Use 'widget' rather than 'Widget CLI'  House.Terms
 4:10  error    Use 'data set' rather than 'dataset'    House.Terms
✖ 2 errors, 1 warning and 0 suggestions in 1 file.

Three findings, with severities you chose per rule.

Step 3: check that it leaves code alone

cat > docs/code.md <<'EOF'
# Example

```bash
# you should be able to run this
widget install --dataset foo
```
EOF

grep -c "should be able to" docs/code.md
vale docs/code.md

1
✔ 0 errors, 0 warnings and 0 suggestions in 1 file.

A grep finds the phrase in the code comment; Vale does not. Vale parses Markdown rather than scanning lines, so fenced blocks, inline code and URLs are excluded by default. This is the single biggest reason to use it instead of the regex script you were about to write. A naive linter that fires inside code samples gets switched off within a week.

Step 4: find out what actually fails the build

The intuitive assumption is that --minAlertLevel decides. Test it:

printf '# T\n\nThis is probably fine.\n' > docs/index.md
for lvl in suggestion warning error; do
  vale --minAlertLevel=$lvl docs/ >/dev/null 2>&1
  echo "warnings only, gate at $lvl -> exit=$?"
done

printf '# T\n\nInstall the Widget CLI.\n' > docs/index.md
vale --minAlertLevel=error docs/ >/dev/null 2>&1
echo "has an error, gate at error -> exit=$?"

warnings only, gate at suggestion -> exit=0
warnings only, gate at warning   -> exit=0
warnings only, gate at error     -> exit=0
has an error, gate at error      -> exit=1

minAlertLevel controls what is displayed, not what fails. Vale exits non-zero if and only if at least one finding is at error level. So the decision about what blocks a merge is made in each rule's level: field, in the rule file, in version control, reviewable. Not in a CI flag.

That is better than it first sounds. It means "does this block the build" is a property of the rule, decided once, visible to everyone, rather than an argument someone passes in a workflow.

Step 5: set the levels deliberately

sed -i 's/^level: warning/level: warning   # advisory: hedging is a judgment call/' styles/House/Hedging.yml
sed -i 's/^level: error/level: error     # blocking: terminology is not negotiable/' styles/House/Terms.yml
echo "terminology blocks, hedging advises"

What you built. A house style that is executable, where terminology errors stop a merge and stylistic suggestions do not, and where the line between the two is a reviewable field in a rule file.

docs.title: The rule types worth knowing
docs.text:
extends Use it for Example existence Banned words or phrases Hedging, "simply", "just" substitution One term replaced by another Product name casing, "data set" occurrence Too many or too few per scope At most one exclamation mark per file repetition The same word twice in a row "the the" consistency Either spelling, but not both "acknowledgement" vs "acknowledgment" conditional B must appear if A does An acronym must be expanded once capitalization Heading case Sentence case in ## headings readability Grade-level scores Flesch-Kincaid thresholds spelling Dictionary plus your own vocabulary Product vocabulary

consistency and conditional are the two that are hard to replicate with a regex script, and they are the ones worth reaching for when someone asks what Vale gives you that grep does not.

docs.title: What to make an error and what to leave as a warning
docs.text:
Error, blocks the merge Warning, advisory only Product and feature names Hedging and filler Expanding an acronym on first use Sentence length Banned legal or security phrasing Passive voice Deprecated terminology Readability scores Spelling of API identifiers Heading capitalization, early on

The test is whether a reasonable contributor could disagree. If they could, it is a warning, because a build that fails on a defensible stylistic choice teaches people that the pipeline is an obstacle. Terminology is not a matter of taste, so it blocks.

docs.title: Severity semantics, exactly
docs.text: Level Displayed by default Fails the build suggestion With MinAlertLevel = suggestion No warning With warning or lower No error Always Yes

docs.title: Where the rules live
docs.text:
.vale.ini             # config: StylesPath, which styles apply to which files
styles/
  House/              # your rules, in version control, reviewed
    Hedging.yml
    Terms.yml
  write-good/         # third-party packages, installed by `vale sync`

Keep your own rules in a directory named after your organization rather than scattering them into a vendored style, so vale sync cannot overwrite them.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the division of labour. "A prose linter handles the mechanical half of the style guide so human review can be about whether the procedure is correct. Terminology, acronym expansion and deprecated names block the build. Passive voice and sentence length are warnings."

The follow-up is usually a challenge about whether this annoys writers, and the answer is yes, if you set the levels wrong. Say that explicitly. A linter that fails builds over defensible choices gets disabled, and the mitigation is that only non-negotiable rules are errors.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Every rule is a guess about intent, and some fire on correct prose. A terminology rule banning "dataset" will flag a direct quotation from a third-party API that is genuinely called dataset. You need an escape hatch, Vale's <!-- vale off --> comments, and the moment you have an escape hatch you need to watch how often it is used, because widespread suppression means the rule is wrong rather than the prose.

One sharper point. minAlertLevel does not control whether Vale fails; the exit code tracks errors only. That means the blocking decision lives in each rule file under version control instead of in a CI flag, which is the right place for it. Knowing that distinction is a reliable signal of having operated Vale rather than installed it.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A styles/ directory of rules you wrote, with levels set deliberately, and at least one rule that caught something real.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path, especially step 4. The exit-code behaviour is not what most people assume.
  2. Write one substitution rule for a term your own project gets wrong, and run it over your existing docs. The first real finding is your evidence.
  3. Count the suppression comments in any corpus you already lint. A high count is a finding about the rules, not about the writers. More than roughly one suppression per ten pages means the rule is wrong rather than the prose, and the fix belongs in the rule.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack runs Vale with terminology errors blocking the build and style warnings advisory, and one of its four hand-written rules caught the author's own prose. The rule that caught you is the one to talk about: it proves the gate works on the person who wrote it.

docs.title: Publishing in public
docs.text:
Published work is the only evidence of this skillset a stranger can check without taking your word, and the most persuasive page in a repository is the one listing what it does not demonstrate.

supporting · difficulty 1 · 4h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Open source contributions or published work on docs-as-code, AI-assisted documentation, or knowledge engineering"

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Putting work where a stranger can run it. The phrase in the posting is a qualification requirement, and it is unusual among qualification requirements in being verifiable: a reader can clone the thing and find out.

That property is the entire point, and it sets a bar that most published portfolios do not clear. A repository that cannot be run is a claim. A repository a stranger clones, installs and tests in five minutes is evidence.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because nothing else in a hiring process can distinguish someone who has built a documentation pipeline from someone who has read about one.

Every other signal is self-reported. A résumé asserts, an interview answer describes, a reference agrees. Published work is the only artifact where the assessment is performed by the reader rather than conveyed to them, which is why NVIDIA lists it beside formal qualifications rather than under interests.

There is a second reason, specific to this field. Documentation work is mostly invisible in its outcomes: when it succeeds, nothing happens, support volume quietly fails to rise, and the credit accrues to the product. A public repository is the one place the work itself is the object, rather than its absent consequences.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Audit a repository for publication, discover the audit is mostly noise, and fix the audit rather than the repository. About twenty-five minutes. This runs against the two repositories behind this guide, which have not been published yet, so every finding is real.

Step 1: the obvious checks

PLACEHOLDERS = {
    "example-org URL":   re.compile(r"github\.com/example/"),
    "example.com":       re.compile(r"\bexample\.com\b"),
    "TODO or FIXME":     re.compile(r"\b(TODO|FIXME|XXX)\b"),
    "angle placeholder": re.compile(r"<your[- ]"),
    "unfilled year":     re.compile(r"Copyright \[|\[year\]|\[fullname\]"),
    "container path":    re.compile(r"/mnt/user-data|/home/claude|/tmp/claude"),
}

=== fieldguide            (142 files)
  example-org URL      9 hits in 4 files
  example.com          6 hits in 3 files
  TODO or FIXME        7 hits in 4 files
  angle placeholder  clean
  unfilled year      clean
  container path     clean

=== docpack               (42 files)
  example-org URL      1 hit
  example.com          2 hits
  TODO or FIXME        7 hits in 5 files

Twenty-two hits. The two useful results are the clean rows: no unfilled licence fields, and no container paths, the second being the one that would have been genuinely embarrassing.

Step 2: read the hits, and find that four of twenty-two are real

src/fieldguide/scaffold.py:101   summary: 'TODO: one sentence on ...'
docs/explanation/why-a-registry.md:23   "three paragraphs of `TODO`"
tests/test_scaffold.py:101       assert "TODO" in meta.summary
docs/concepts/crawlability.md    curl -s https://example.com/docs/page/

The TODO hits are a scaffold that deliberately writes TODO placeholders, prose about TODO markers, and tests asserting the placeholder exists. The example.com hits are a domain reserved by RFC 2606 for exactly this purpose, so a sample command using it is correct and one using a real domain would not be.

22 hits, 4 real: 82% noise

An audit whose output is 82 per cent noise is an audit nobody runs twice, which is the same failure as a badly aimed documentation gate and for the same reason.

Step 3: the obvious fix makes it worse

Add an allowlist of the files where a hit is legitimate:

not ready to publish, 9 finding(s):
  docs/concepts/mkdocs.md:63             site_url: https://example.github.io/widget/
  docs/concepts/preview-deployments.md:55   site_url: https://example.github.io/widget/
  docs/concepts/preview-deployments.md:91   sed -i 's|site_url:.*|...pr-123/|'
  ... four more in the same page ...
  mkdocs.yml:6                           site_url: https://example.github.io/fieldguide/
  mkdocs.yml:7                           repo_url: https://github.com/example/fieldguide

Seven new false hits. The golden paths on those pages legitimately show site_url: lines for a fictional widget project, and an allowlist cannot anticipate that, because the next page to do the same thing is not in the list yet.

Step 4: scope by file role instead

A placeholder URL is a defect when it is this repository's own published identity, and illustration everywhere else. So read only the files that carry that identity:

OWN_CONFIG = ("mkdocs.yml", "pyproject.toml", "setup.cfg", "README.md", "LICENSE")

examined 143 files under fieldguide

not ready to publish, 2 finding(s):
  mkdocs.yml:6  placeholder URL in this repository's own identity
      site_url: https://example.github.io/fieldguide/
  mkdocs.yml:7  placeholder URL in this repository's own identity
      repo_url: https://github.com/example/fieldguide
exit=1

Two findings, both real: a published site whose canonical URL and whose "edit this page" links point at an organisation that does not exist.

Step 5: the transfer test, which settles the argument

Run the same script, unchanged, against the other repository:

examined 42 files under docpack

not ready to publish, 9 finding(s):
  src/docpack/scaffold.py:255   summary = summary or f"TODO: one sentence ..."
  tests/test_scaffold.py:94     assert "TODO" not in text
  ... five more TODO hits ...
  mkdocs.yml:3                  placeholder URL in this repository's own identity
  mkdocs.yml:4                  placeholder URL in this repository's own identity

The role-scoped check travelled perfectly: two findings, both real, on a repository it had never seen. The allowlist-scoped check did not travel at all, producing seven false hits immediately, because the allowlist named fieldguide's paths.

That is the general lesson and it is not about publishing. A check scoped by what a file is for transfers; a check scoped by a list of exceptions is a record of one repository's history. The same distinction decided the documentation gate on the developer advocacy page, found independently, from the other direction.

Step 6: the gate flags the page describing the gate

Writing this page and re-running the script produced twelve findings, eleven of them in this file: it quotes TODO markers while explaining them, and it quotes the container-path pattern itself.

The pattern-definition case has a role-based answer, since a line that defines a pattern is not a line leaking what the pattern matches, and one condition fixes it everywhere. The TODO case does not. TODO is simultaneously a marker and a word, so no property of a file distinguishes the scaffold that writes placeholders, the tests asserting on them, and the four pages discussing them from genuine unfinished work. The allowlist had reached four files and acquired eleven new false hits the moment another page mentioned the subject.

So the check was deleted, with the reasoning left in the source:

# A TODO check used to live here and has been removed, which is the most
# useful thing this script has to say.
#
# It cannot be scoped by role, because TODO is simultaneously a marker and
# a word. ... A TODO marker is better caught on the diff, by review, where
# the question "is this line new unfinished work" is answerable.

Deleting a check is an unpopular outcome and it was the right one. The three that remain ask about a file's role rather than its vocabulary, and the proof is the same script run on both repositories with nothing changed between them:

examined 143 files under fieldguide        examined 42 files under docpack
not ready to publish, 2 finding(s):        not ready to publish, 2 finding(s):
  mkdocs.yml:6  placeholder URL ...          mkdocs.yml:3  placeholder URL ...
  mkdocs.yml:7  placeholder URL ...          mkdocs.yml:4  placeholder URL ...
exit=1                                     exit=1

Two findings each, both real, zero noise, across a 143-file repository and a 42-file one. Those are the figures from the run that settled the argument, when the URLs were still placeholders and both repositories were smaller; step 8 has the current state.

Step 7: what is left, and why it stays

The two findings cannot be fixed here, because nobody knows the real URL until the repository has a home. That is the correct outcome for a pre-publication gate: it converts "remember to change the URL" into a command that exits 1, and it is deliberately not in CI, because a check that fails every build until publication day is a check people learn to ignore.

Step 8: the findings close, and the roster was incomplete

The repositories have a home, so the four placeholders are real URLs now and both checks pass:

examined 173 files under fieldguide        examined 60 files under docpack
ready to publish                           ready to publish
exit=0                                     exit=0

Closing them found something, and it is the more interesting half of this page's argument rather than a footnote to it.

The script said "ready to publish" while two placeholder repository links sat on a published page. demonstrations.yaml carries each repository's own URL in its projects block, the generated demonstrated page prints both as links, and that file was not in OWN_CONFIG. So the gate cleared a repository whose own index pointed twice at an organisation that does not exist.

Note the shape of that failure against the shape of the allowlist's. The allowlist was wrong in principle: it scoped by a list of exceptions, so it could not travel and could not anticipate the next page. Role-scoping is right in principle and was wrong in fact, because the roster of files that carry the role was incomplete, and nothing in the idea of role-scoping tells you when you have finished enumerating the role. That is a quieter failure and an easier one to make twice: the check looked principled, transferred perfectly to another repository, and still missed two live defects.

So the sharpened lesson is narrower than step 5's. A check scoped by what a file is for transfers, and it is only as complete as your list of what carries that purpose, which is a judgement the scoping cannot make for you. The roster is now six files, and the reason demonstrations.yaml is on it is written beside it, because the next person to add a file that publishes an identity will not think to look here.

What you built. A pre-publication gate at full precision on two repositories, six revisions of it, one check deleted for being unscopeable, a demonstrated transfer test, four findings held open until they could honestly be closed, and then a seventh revision because closing them showed the gate had been passing a repository it should have failed.

docs.title: What a stranger checks in ninety seconds
docs.text:
They look at They conclude Does the README say what this is, in one line Whether to continue Can I install and run it from the README alone Whether it is real Is there a test suite, and does it pass Whether it is maintained Is the CI badge green, or absent Same, faster Does the commit history look like work or like a dump Whether it was built or assembled Does it say what it does not do Whether to trust the rest

The last row is the one people leave out and the one that does the most work, which is the subject of the next table.

docs.title: Honest limits as a feature
docs.text:
This guide publishes a demonstrated page listing every concept for which neither repository contains a working example. It is, on the face of it, a page about what is missing.

Without it With it Every claim is equally weighted The reader knows which claims are evidenced A reader who finds a gap finds a lie A reader who finds a gap finds it already named Trust collapses at the first gap Trust survives, because the gaps are the author's own list

A repository that states its limits is making a verifiable claim about its author's judgment, and that is a stronger signal than any of the work itself. It is also the cheapest page to write and the hardest to write honestly.

docs.title: What counts as published work
docs.text:
Form Evidence of Effort A runnable repository Ability, maintenance, judgment High An upstream contribution that was merged Ability to work in someone else's codebase Medium, and gated by review A written account of a real problem Judgment, and that you can explain Low to medium A published site built by the thing That the thing works Low, once the repo exists A talk recording Communication Medium A list of technologies Nothing Low

An upstream merge is the strongest single signal per unit of effort, because somebody else's maintainer agreed. A repository of your own is the strongest overall, because it shows the parts review never sees: what you chose to check, what you chose to leave out, and whether you wrote down the limits.

docs.title: The README contract
docs.text:
Section Answers One line at the top What is this Quick start, copy-pasteable Can I run it What it is for, honestly scoped Should I How it is organised Where do I look What it does not do Can I trust the rest Licence May I

Every claim in the quick start is a claim a stranger will test within two minutes, which makes it the highest-risk prose in the repository. This guide's README asserted 72 tests when there were 119, uncaught for the project's whole life, until the capability gate read it.

docs.title: Before publishing anything
docs.text: Check Why it bites No container or local paths Reveals the machine, breaks every copy-paste Licence has a real name and year A repository without one is unusable, politely Own repo_url and site_url are real Edit links and canonical URLs point at nothing The README's commands exist The first thing anyone runs The README's numbers are current They go stale silently No credentials, in any file or any commit History is public too A clean clone passes its own tests Cold-start testing, applied to yourself

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with verifiability. "Published work is the only part of an application where the assessment is done by the reader instead of conveyed to them. A repository that cannot be run is a claim; one a stranger clones and tests in five minutes is evidence, and that is a much higher bar than a portfolio usually clears."

The follow-up is what you would check before publishing, and the useful answer is about the checker. My first pre-publication audit produced twenty-two hits across two repositories, four of them real: the rest were a scaffold that deliberately writes TODO placeholders, prose about TODO markers, and example.com, which RFC 2606 reserves for exactly that use. Eighty-two per cent noise, and an audit that noisy is one nobody runs twice.

The part worth telling in full. The fix that looked obvious, an allowlist of files where a hit is fine, made it worse: seven new false hits, because golden paths legitimately show site_url: lines for a fictional project. Scoping by file role instead, a placeholder URL is a defect only in the repository's own identity files, took it to two findings, both real. Then I ran it unchanged against the second repository: the role-scoped check transferred perfectly, the allowlist-scoped one produced seven false hits on first contact. A check scoped by what a file is for travels; a check scoped by exceptions is a record of one repository's history.

And the ending, which is the part I would volunteer. Writing the page about the script made the script fail on the page, eleven times, because the page quotes the markers it explains. One of those had a role-based fix. The TODO check did not, because TODO is simultaneously a marker and a word, so no property of a file separates deliberate placeholders from unfinished work. I deleted the check and left the reasoning in the source. Three checks remain and they produce two findings on a 143-file repository and two on a 42-file one, both real, with nothing changed between the runs.

The counterintuitive point, and the best thing to say here. The most persuasive page in a published repository is the one listing what it does not demonstrate. Mine names every concept with no working example in either codebase. Without that page a reader who finds a gap has found a lie and stops trusting everything; with it, they find the gap already named by the author, and the remaining claims get stronger rather than weaker. It is the cheapest page to write and the hardest to write honestly.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Published work is expensive and its payoff is unpredictable: the repository took far longer than the writing it supports, and most readers will look at it for ninety seconds. If the goal were only to pass a hiring filter, a smaller artifact with one genuinely working demonstration would be the better investment. The reason to build the larger one is that the act of making every claim checkable is what found the defects, and that part was not optional.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A pre-publication script in your own repository, run against a second repository to see whether its checks are about file roles or about your history.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Grep your repository for your own machine's paths before anything else. Predict whether you will find any; this guide found none and that was the only genuinely reassuring result in the first run.
  2. Write the page that says what your work does not demonstrate. If it is difficult to write, that difficulty is the information, and the page is worth more than the next feature.
  3. Check every number in your README against reality. Mine claimed 72 tests against an actual 119, stale for the project's entire life, and nothing had ever looked.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. scripts/prepublication.py is in this repository, runs on it and on docpack, and currently exits 1 with two findings: the placeholder site_url and repo_url in mkdocs.yml, which stay open until the repositories have real homes. Neither repository has been published, so the claims above about what a stranger concludes in ninety seconds are reasoning about readers rather than observation of them, and the demonstrated page records this concept as having the gate but not the audience.

docs.title: Python for content automation
docs.text:
Counting the prose in a corpus five ways: the naive answer is a quarter high, and the last correction is worth 0.2 per cent in aggregate and four per cent on one page in five.

core · difficulty 2 · 5h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Working proficiency in Python or similar to automate content tasks, transform data, and integrate with APIs"

Leads to: Content and data transformation, API integration

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Writing programs whose input is documentation. Not a specialism in the language, which is the ordinary standard library and nothing exotic, but a specialism in the data: documentation is text that carries structure, and structure is invisible to the tools text invites you to reach for.

Every interesting bug in this area comes from that sentence. A Markdown file looks like lines, so you process lines; the meaning lives in nesting, fences and front matter, which lines cannot see.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA's bullet is one sentence naming three jobs: automate content tasks, transform data, integrate with APIs. This concept is the first, and the other two have pages of their own because they fail differently.

The reason it is a requirement rather than a nice-to-have is arithmetic. A corpus of a hundred pages has a few hundred cross-references, a few hundred code samples and a metadata field on every page, and every claim anybody makes about it ("every page has a summary", "no sample is broken", "this concept is unreachable") is a loop over files. Without that, the claims are assertions somebody remembers checking once.

The reason it is harder than it looks is that the loop is easy and the parsing is not, and a wrong parse produces a plausible number rather than an error.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
One task, five implementations, each correcting the last. Count the words a reader would actually read across all 106 pages. About twenty-five minutes, and the interesting part is which corrections turn out to matter.

Step 1: the obvious one

words = sum(len(p.read_text().split()) for p in pages)

corpus: 106 written pages

approach                        words      error
1  split() on the file         224929        27%

Twenty-nine per cent high, and nothing about the program suggests so. It would be reported, used to set a page-length policy, and never questioned.

Step 2: front matter is not prose

Every page opens with a YAML block carrying title, summary, diataxis, audience, concept and tags. A reader sees none of it.

FM = re.compile(r"^---\n.*?\n---\n", re.S)

2  minus front matter          221166        25%

Two points. Worth fixing and not the problem.

Step 3: HTML comments are not prose either

COMMENT = re.compile(r"<!--.*?-->", re.S)

3  minus HTML comments         221101        25%

Sixty-six words across the whole corpus. Three hundredths of one per cent, which looks like a correction not worth writing.

Hold that thought until step 6, because it is the most misleading number on this page.

Step 4: code is not prose, and this is where the error lives

4  minus fences, toggled       191137         0%
5  minus fences, parsed        190748    (truth)

Forty-five thousand words, nineteen per cent of everything outside the front matter, are inside code fences. That single distinction is worth ten times the other corrections combined, and it is the one a line-oriented program cannot make without tracking state.

Step 5: the two fence implementations, and why the aggregate lies

Version 4 toggles a flag on any line that looks like a fence marker. Version 5 uses a parser that tracks marker length and skips heredoc bodies. The difference across the corpus:

corpus-level error of the toggle:  +389 words  (0.2%)

Two tenths of one per cent. By that number the parser was a waste of an afternoon. Now count pages instead of words:

pages where the two agree:      86/106
pages where they disagree:      20/106

page                           parsed    delta    error
coding-agents                    2139      +85       4%
security-documentation           1546      +58       4%
tutorial-design                  1554      +57       4%
agent-skills                     2274      +23       1%
chunking                         1753      +20       1%

A fifth of the pages are wrong, the worst by four per cent, and the corpus total is accurate to two decimal places. The errors are small, one-directional and sparse, so summing them produces a number close to the truth by cancellation of significance rather than by correctness.

Which measurement you believe depends entirely on whether you aggregate, and the aggregate is the one people report.

The pages that disagree have a common shape: a four-backtick fence containing three-backtick fences, because they document Markdown or contain heredocs that write Markdown. The toggle sees the inner marker and closes the outer block, so shell commands become prose. Nothing about that is visible in a 0.2 per cent error.

Step 6: the correction from step 3, measured on a different sample

HTML comments were a few dozen words, three hundredths of one per cent. At the time the corpus still held nine pages the scaffold had generated and nobody had written, so the identical measurement had a second sample to run over:

written pages (106):
  words outside front matter: 235983
  of those, inside comments:       79   (0.03%)

freshly scaffolded pages (9):
  words outside front matter:   3160
  of those, inside comments:    2601   (82%)

The first block is current and moves whenever a page is edited. The second cannot be re-run: all 106 pages are written now, so that sample no longer exists, and it is kept because it is the whole point of the step.

The same term in the same measurement: 0.03 per cent on one sample and 82 per cent on another. Scaffolded pages are mostly authoring prompts inside comments, which is their job, and the prompts are deleted as pages get written.

So the correction I nearly dropped as negligible is the dominant term for any measurement that includes unwritten pages, and a word-count gate that ignored it was once 84 per cent pre-satisfied by the template's own instructions. The honest conclusion is not that comments matter; it is that "this correction is negligible" is a statement about a sample, not about a corpus, and it has to be re-checked whenever the sample changes.

What you built. One measurement in five versions, an error budget showing where the naive quarter actually sits, a demonstration that a 0.2 per cent aggregate error can mean a fifth of pages are wrong, and a negligible correction that becomes dominant on a different slice.

docs.title: The standard library does almost all of it
docs.text:
Need Reach for Not Walking a tree pathlib.Path.rglob os.walk with string joins Front matter yaml.safe_load A regex per field Writing front matter yaml.safe_dump f-strings; they break on a colon Counting and grouping collections.Counter Hand-rolled dicts Stable identifiers hashlib on normalised content hash(), which is salted per process Running a sample subprocess.run(capture_output=True) os.system Structured records json, one object per line A CSV with embedded newlines Fences, nesting, headings A parser you own and test A regex

Only the last row needs writing, and only because no dependency does exactly what a corpus-specific checker needs.

docs.title: What defeats a regex, specifically
docs.text:
Construct Why Nested fences Needs marker length, which is state Heredocs inside fences The body may contain fence markers A # inside a code block A shell comment, not a heading Indented fences in list items Up to three spaces, then content indentation Inline code spans `like this` can contain anything Links with parentheses in the URL Balanced delimiters are not regular A YAML colon in a value Breaks any hand-rolled serialiser

Each of those produced a real bug in this project, and none produced an exception. They produced numbers.

docs.title: Error budgets beat precision
docs.text:
Before optimising a measurement, find out which term dominates:

Correction Worth, on written pages Excluding code fences 25% Excluding front matter 2% A correct fence parser over a toggle 0.2% Excluding HTML comments 0.04%

Then check the same table on the sample you will actually run against, because two of those four rows change by more than an order of magnitude between written and unwritten pages.

docs.title: Aggregate against per-item
docs.text:
Reported as Hides Use for A corpus total Sparse, one-directional, small errors Reporting A per-page figure Nothing; it is the reader's experience Deciding what to fix A count of pages over a threshold The size of each failure Planning A maximum How common the failure is Finding the worst case

A sum is the single worst way to look for a parsing bug, because parsing bugs are sparse and sums are robust to sparse error. That is the opposite of what you want from a check.

docs.title: Habits that prevent the plausible wrong number
docs.text: Habit Prevents A fixture with a hand-counted answer Every bug on this page Printing the worst item, not just the total Aggregate blindness Asserting the measurement on a known-bad input Silent regression Three states, never two: present, absent, out of scope Conflating "no anchors" with "not in the tree" Re-deriving every metric after adding a generator A template satisfying its own gate Normalising whitespace before matching Wrapped prose defeating a pattern

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the data, not the language. "Python for content automation is not a language specialism, it is knowing that documentation is text carrying structure, and that structure is invisible to the line-oriented tools text invites you to use. Every real bug I have had in this area came from that, and none of them raised an exception. They returned numbers."

The follow-up is a worked example, and this one is short. Counting the prose in a 106-page corpus: the naive split() is 27 per cent high. Front matter accounts for two points, HTML comments for four hundredths of one, and code fences for twenty-five. So the single distinction worth making is that code is not prose, and it is exactly the one a line-oriented program cannot make without tracking state.

Then the part that generalises. Replacing a naive fence toggle with a real parser moved the corpus total by 0.2 per cent, which says the parser was not worth writing. Counting pages instead, a fifth of them were wrong and the worst by five per cent. Parsing errors are sparse and one-directional, so a sum is robust to exactly the defect you are looking for. A sum is the worst available instrument for finding a parsing bug.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Writing your own parser is a maintenance liability and I would not recommend it as a default: use a real Markdown library where you can. The case for owning the fence logic in a checker is that it has to answer questions a renderer does not, such as whether a closing fence carries an info string, and that it has to be fast enough to run on every commit. That is a narrow justification and it does not extend to parsing links or tables, which I would not hand-roll.

One sharper point. The correction I nearly discarded as negligible, 65 words across the corpus, is 84 per cent of the text in a freshly scaffolded page. The same term, the same measurement, three orders of magnitude apart depending on which pages are in the sample. "This correction is negligible" is a claim about a sample and not about a corpus, and it needs re-checking whenever the sample changes, which in a growing corpus is constantly.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A measurement over a corpus you own, with its error budget written down and a fixture that pins the answer.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Count something about your own corpus the naive way, then subtract front matter, comments and code in that order, and write down what each correction was worth. Predict the ranking first; most people put code third.
  2. Take any corpus measurement you already trust and report its worst single item alongside the total. If they tell different stories, the total was hiding a bug.
  3. Build a two-page fixture, one ordinary and one with a four-backtick fence containing three-backtick fences, and count both by hand. Every parsing bug in this project would have been caught by that one file.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack is seven modules and 134 tests operating on a documentation tree as data, and this guide's own src/fieldguide/fences.py exists because three successive naive versions returned plausible wrong answers; every figure above is reproducible from the two repositories. What is not demonstrated is scale: the largest corpus here is 106 pages, and nothing on this page has been tested against the tens of thousands where streaming, incremental parsing and caching would start to matter.

docs.title: Quickstarts that survive contact
docs.text:
The page with the shortest half-life in your corpus, and the three claims it makes that can each be checked.

core · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

Intel: "documentation CI, including link checking and coldstart testing of quickstarts"

Intel: "so a developer reaches first success in minutes with zero help"

Prerequisites: Golden paths

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The page that takes a reader from nothing to one working thing as fast as possible. It implements the golden path and it is the single most consequential page in a developer documentation set, because it is where people decide whether to continue.

It is also the page with the shortest half-life, for a reason worth stating plainly: it is the only page whose author cannot test it, because their machine already has everything.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Intel names cold-start testing of quickstarts specifically, out of everything it could have named. That phrasing tells you they have been burned by a quickstart that worked for its author.

The deeper reason is that a quickstart makes several claims at once, and they fail independently. It claims the commands work from an empty environment, that the output you will see is what it shows, and that you will reach a useful result. Most quickstart maintenance treats these as one thing ("is the quickstart working?") when in fact the first can pass while the second quietly fails, and the second failing is the one that destroys trust.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Write the three claims as separate checks, then watch each one fail for a different reason. About thirty minutes.

Step 1: a quickstart

mkdir -p qs-demo && cd qs-demo
cat > qs.md <<'MDEOF'
# Quickstart

```bash
pip install cowsay
python3 -c "import cowsay; cowsay.cow('hi')" | head -1
```

```
  __
| hi |
```
MDEOF

Step 2: the claims, checked separately

claims = {}
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "venv", f"{d}/.v"], capture_output=True)
    script = "\n".join(cmds)  # rewritten to use the venv's pip and python
    r = subprocess.run(["bash", "-e", "-c", script], capture_output=True,
                       text=True, cwd=d)
    claims["commands succeed from empty"] = r.returncode == 0
    claims["output matches the page"] = expected[0].strip() in r.stdout.strip()
    claims["result is non-trivial"] = len(r.stdout.strip().splitlines()) >= 1

python3 check_qs.py

  PASS  commands succeed from empty
  FAIL  output matches the page
  PASS  result is non-trivial

The commands ran. The output did not match. A quickstart harness that only checked exit codes would have reported this page healthy.

Step 3: find out why, because it is not what you expect

The real output of that command begins:

  __
| hi |

Which is exactly what the page shows. So why the mismatch?

The command ends in | head -1, so stdout is one line, while the expected block shows two. The page is internally inconsistent: its command contradicts its own output example.

That is not a drift defect. It is an authoring defect that existed from the first commit, and no amount of reading would catch it, because a reader checking the page against itself would have to mentally execute head.

sed -i 's/| head -1/| head -2/' qs.md
python3 check_qs.py

  PASS  commands succeed from empty
  PASS  output matches the page
  PASS  result is non-trivial

Step 4: now the drift case

Change the page the way a real product change would, so the command produces something else:

  PASS  commands succeed from empty
  FAIL  output matches the page
  PASS  result is non-trivial

Same failing claim, entirely different cause: the first was the page disagreeing with itself, the second is the page disagreeing with the software. Both are caught by asserting output and invisible to a harness that checks exit codes, which is the argument for separating the claims.

Step 5: check what you are actually installing

for i in 1 2; do
  python3 -m venv ".v$i" && ".v$i/bin/pip" install -q cowsay
  echo "run $i: $(".v$i/bin/pip" freeze | tr '\n' ' ')"
done

run 1: cowsay==6.1
run 2: cowsay==6.1

Identical today, and nothing in the quickstart guarantees that. An unpinned install is a claim about the future that the page cannot keep. Whether to pin is a real decision, and reproducible environments is where it gets made; the thing to know here is that the quickstart's reproducibility is inherited from that choice rather than from anything on the page.

What you built. Three independently failing claims, and a demonstration that the same failure has two completely different causes.

docs.title: The three claims, and how each fails
docs.text:
Claim Fails when Caught by The commands work from empty A dependency is undeclared, a step is missing Cold-start testing The output is what the page shows The page contradicts itself, or the software changed Output assertion The result is useful The quickstart "succeeds" into an empty state A substantive assertion

The third is the one nobody checks. A quickstart that ends with synced 0 records has technically worked and taught the reader nothing about whether the product does anything. Asserting something non-trivial about the result is what distinguishes first success from first exit code.

docs.title: What belongs in a quickstart
docs.text: In Out One route; see golden paths Alternatives and platform variants The shortest path to a visible result Explanation of why it works Exact commands, copy-pasteable Placeholders the reader must resolve The output to expect Screenshots that go stale One link to the next thing A list of twelve next things A stated time Vague reassurance

docs.title: The author's blind spots
docs.text:
Assumption How it shows up for a reader A dependency installed years ago ModuleNotFoundError on step two A credential already exported An auth error with no explanation A repository already cloned cd myproject with no git clone A warm cache A timeout, or an unexpected first-run message Knowing which of two outputs is correct Paralysis

Every row is invisible from the author's chair, which is the whole case for automating this page's verification rather than reviewing it.

docs.title: Time to first success
docs.text:
Intel's criterion is minutes. To claim it you have to measure it, which means timing the cold-start run and publishing the number:

What to time Why Install step Usually dominates, and is the easiest to improve Total to stated result The number you publish Each step separately So you know which one to attack

A quickstart with an unmeasured "it only takes a few minutes" is making a claim nobody has checked. See time to first success.

docs.title: Quickstart against tutorial
docs.text:
Quickstart Tutorial Goal Working, fast Understanding Length Shortest possible As long as the lesson needs Explanation Almost none Essential Detours Never Sometimes, if they teach Success Something works The reader can now do it themselves

Merging them produces a page that is too long to be a quickstart and too thin to teach, which is the most common failure in this category.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the claims, not the page. "A quickstart makes three separable claims: the commands work from empty, the output is what the page shows, and the result is useful. They fail independently, and most quickstart maintenance treats them as one thing. Checking exit codes passes a page that is lying about its own output."

The follow-up is why its author cannot test it, and the answer is that their machine already has everything, so the verification has to come from a clean environment in CI rather than from a careful reviewer.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Asserting output makes the quickstart brittle against intentional change: every deliberate behaviour change now requires a documentation update in the same pull request. That is the point and it is real friction, and on a fast-moving product you will spend time updating expected output for changes you meant to make.

One sharper point. The same failing check has two causes worth distinguishing. My own test page failed its output assertion not because the software had drifted but because the page contradicted itself: the command piped through head -1 while the expected block showed two lines. That defect was there from the first commit and no reader would catch it, because catching it requires mentally executing head. Drift gets all the attention; pages that were never self-consistent are at least as common.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A quickstart with a stated expected output, a cold-start test that asserts it, and a published time to first success.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Step 3 is the interesting one, because the failure is not drift.
  2. Add an expected-output block to a quickstart you own, then check it. Pages frequently disagree with themselves.
  3. Time your own quickstart from a clean environment and put the number on the page. If you cannot state it, you cannot claim minutes.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack's scripts/coldstart.sh builds a fresh virtual environment, installs the way a reader would, follows the tutorial literally, and asserts the exact output string the tutorial promises. The exact-output assertion is the part to point at: without it the script proves the commands exit zero, which is the weakest of the three claims.

docs.title: RAG pipelines
docs.text:
Retrieve, assemble, generate: the architecture, and which stage is actually failing when the answer is wrong.

core · difficulty 3 · 8h

Ways to stand out: experience building RAG pipelines, AI assistants, MCP servers, or agent skill and context libraries backed by documentation

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: Chunking strategies, Vector stores and hybrid search

Leads to: Documentation-backed AI assistants, Grounding and citation, Retrieval evaluation

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Retrieval-augmented generation: look up relevant text, put it in the prompt, and have a model answer from it. Three stages, and the whole discipline is in knowing which one is broken when the answer is wrong.

The name oversells the novelty. It is search, with the results handed to a model instead of to a person.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA names it three times: "structure and package content for RAG", "RAG pipelines" under ways to stand out, and implicitly in "internal assistants". It is the single most-repeated technical artifact in either posting.

What makes it core and difficulty 3 is not the code, which is a few hundred lines. It is that a RAG pipeline has five distinct failure modes that all present identically to a user: a wrong answer. Diagnosing which one you have is the job, and you can only do it if you built the stages separately and can inspect each.

On a Tuesday this is the ticket. "The assistant told me to use max_memory_mb and that flag does not exist." Five possible causes, in the order worth checking:

  1. The content does not exist. Nothing can fix this but writing.
  2. It exists and was not chunked usefully, so no chunk contains the answer.
  3. It was chunked and not retrieved, because the query and the page use different vocabulary.
  4. It was retrieved and outranked by something adjacent.
  5. It was retrieved, ranked first, and the model ignored it.

Those have five different fixes and four of them are not prompt changes. A team that cannot tell them apart ends up tuning prompts against a retrieval problem, which is the most common wasted quarter in this field.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build the whole pipeline, dependency-free, then break each stage deliberately and watch the same symptom appear. Fifty minutes.

Step 1: the pipeline, with every stage inspectable

mkdir -p rag-drill && cd rag-drill
cat > corpus.json <<'EOF'
[
  {"id": "c1", "source": "reference/flags.md", "crumb": "Server flags > batch_size",
   "kind": "reference",
   "text": "batch_size controls how many requests are grouped per forward pass. The default is 32. The maximum is 512."},
  {"id": "c2", "source": "how-to/latency.md", "crumb": "Reduce latency > Lower the batch size",
   "kind": "how-to",
   "text": "If your p99 is too high, set batch_size to 1 or 2. A batch of 32 waits for 32 requests to arrive, which adds roughly 200ms at p99."},
  {"id": "c3", "source": "reference/flags.md", "crumb": "Server flags > max_memory_gb",
   "kind": "reference",
   "text": "max_memory_gb caps the GPU memory the server will allocate. The default is 16. Size for peak load, not startup."},
  {"id": "c4", "source": "reference/legacy.md", "crumb": "Legacy 1.x flags > max_memory_mb",
   "kind": "reference",
   "text": "max_memory_mb was the 1.x equivalent of max_memory_gb. It was removed in 2.0 and is ignored if set."},
  {"id": "c5", "source": "explanation/batching.md", "crumb": "Why batching helps > Throughput",
   "kind": "explanation",
   "text": "A GPU is more efficient per item on a larger batch, so batching raises throughput at the cost of latency."}
]
EOF
python3 -c "import json; print(len(json.load(open('corpus.json'))), 'chunks')"

Step 2: retrieve, assemble, generate, as three separable functions

cat > rag.py <<'PY'
"""A RAG pipeline with every stage inspectable.

The structure is the lesson. `retrieve`, `assemble` and `generate` are
separate functions returning separate values, because the only way to debug a
wrong answer is to look at what each stage produced. A pipeline written as one
function that takes a question and returns a string cannot be debugged at all,
and that is how most of them are written.
"""
import json
import math
import re
from collections import Counter
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

K1, B = 1.2, 0.75
CONTEXT_BUDGET = 600  # characters, standing in for a token budget


def tokenize(text):
    # Underscores are kept so `max_memory_gb` survives as one term. Splitting
    # on them turns a flag name into three common words.
    return [t for t in re.findall(r"[a-z0-9_]+", text.lower()) if len(t) > 1]


@dataclass
class Trace:
    """What each stage did. The reason this class exists is diagnosis."""

    question: str
    retrieved: list = field(default_factory=list)
    assembled: str = ""
    dropped_for_budget: list = field(default_factory=list)
    answer: str = ""
    cited: list = field(default_factory=list)


class Retriever:
    def __init__(self, chunks):
        self.chunks = chunks
        self.docs = [Counter(tokenize(f"{c['crumb']} {c['text']}")) for c in chunks]
        self.lengths = [sum(d.values()) for d in self.docs]
        self.avg = sum(self.lengths) / len(self.docs)
        df = Counter()
        for d in self.docs:
            df.update(d.keys())
        n = len(self.docs)
        self.idf = {t: math.log(1 + (n - c + 0.5) / (c + 0.5)) for t, c in df.items()}

    def __call__(self, question, kind=None, limit=3):
        terms = tokenize(question)
        scored = []
        for chunk, doc, length in zip(self.chunks, self.docs, self.lengths):
            if kind and chunk["kind"] != kind:
                continue
            score = 0.0
            for t in terms:
                f = doc.get(t, 0)
                if not f:
                    continue
                norm = 1 - B + B * (length / self.avg)
                score += self.idf.get(t, 0.0) * (f * (K1 + 1)) / (f + K1 * norm)
            if score > 0:
                scored.append((score, chunk))
        scored.sort(key=lambda s: -s[0])
        return scored[:limit]


def assemble(hits, budget=CONTEXT_BUDGET):
    """Build the context block, and record what did not fit.

    Two decisions matter here and both are usually invisible.

    The CITATION LABEL is attached per chunk, so the model can cite and a
    reader can verify. Without it, grounding is unenforceable.

    The BUDGET drops the lowest-ranked chunks, and `dropped` is returned
    rather than discarded, because "the answer was retrieved at rank 3 and
    then truncated away" is a real failure that looks like a retrieval
    failure.
    """
    blocks, dropped, used = [], [], 0
    for rank, (score, chunk) in enumerate(hits, start=1):
        block = (
            f"[{chunk['id']}] {chunk['crumb']}  (source: {chunk['source']})\n"
            f"{chunk['text']}"
        )
        if used + len(block) > budget and blocks:
            dropped.append((rank, chunk["id"]))
            continue
        blocks.append(block)
        used += len(block)
    return "\n\n".join(blocks), dropped


def generate(question, context):
    """Stand-in for a model, extractive and deterministic.

    It answers ONLY from the context and cites the chunk it used, which is
    the behaviour a real pipeline has to get a real model to approximate
    through prompting and then verify. Using a deterministic stand-in keeps
    this golden path reproducible and keeps the lesson on the pipeline.
    """
    if not context.strip():
        return "I could not find this in the documentation.", []

    terms = set(tokenize(question))
    best, best_score, best_id = None, 0, None
    for block in context.split("\n\n"):
        label = re.match(r"\[(\w+)\]", block)
        body = block.split("\n", 1)[-1]
        overlap = len(terms & set(tokenize(block)))
        if overlap > best_score:
            best, best_score, best_id = body, overlap, label.group(1) if label else None

    if not best:
        return "I could not find this in the documentation.", []
    sentence = best.split(". ")[0].strip().rstrip(".") + "."
    return f"{sentence} [{best_id}]", [best_id]


def ask(question, retriever, kind=None, budget=CONTEXT_BUDGET):
    trace = Trace(question=question)
    hits = retriever(question, kind=kind)
    trace.retrieved = [(round(s, 2), c["id"], c["crumb"]) for s, c in hits]
    trace.assembled, trace.dropped_for_budget = assemble(hits, budget)
    trace.answer, trace.cited = generate(question, trace.assembled)
    return trace


def show(trace):
    print(f"Q: {trace.question}")
    print("  retrieved:")
    for score, cid, crumb in trace.retrieved or [("-", "none", "")]:
        print(f"    {score:>5}  {cid}  {crumb}")
    if trace.dropped_for_budget:
        print(f"  dropped for budget: {trace.dropped_for_budget}")
    print(f"  answer: {trace.answer}")
    print(f"  cited:  {trace.cited}")
    print()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    retriever = Retriever(json.load(open("corpus.json")))
    for question in [
        "what is the default batch_size",
        "my p99 latency is too high",
        "what does max_memory_mb do",
    ]:
        show(ask(question, retriever))
PY
python3 rag.py

Step 3: break each stage and watch the symptom stay the same

This is the exercise. Five sabotages, one symptom.

cat > failures.py <<'PY'
"""Five failure modes, one symptom: a wrong or useless answer.

Each block below breaks exactly one stage, so the trace shows where the
pipeline lost the answer. In production you get only the last line of the
trace, which is why the trace has to exist.
"""
import json

from rag import Retriever, ask, show

corpus = json.load(open("corpus.json"))


def banner(text):
    print("=" * 72)
    print(text)
    print("=" * 72)


banner("0. BASELINE: the whole pipeline working")
show(ask("how do I cap GPU memory", Retriever(corpus)))

banner("1. CONTENT MISSING: the max_memory_gb chunk does not exist")
# Nothing downstream can recover from this. The answer is about batch_size.
show(ask("how do I cap GPU memory", Retriever([c for c in corpus if c["id"] != "c3"])))

banner("2. CHUNKING: the heading trail was discarded at split time")
# The word "latency" appears in c2's CRUMB, not in its text, which says "p99".
# Discard the crumb and the only chunk that answers the question becomes
# invisible to the query that asks it.
stripped = [dict(c, crumb="") for c in corpus]
print("  with the heading trail kept:")
show(ask("reduce latency", Retriever(corpus)))
print("  with the heading trail discarded:")
show(ask("reduce latency", Retriever(stripped)))

banner("3. RETRIEVAL VOCABULARY: the question says GPU, the page says VRAM")
reworded = [
    dict(c, text=c["text"].replace("GPU memory", "VRAM")) if c["id"] == "c3" else c
    for c in corpus
]
show(ask("how do I cap GPU memory", Retriever(reworded)))

banner("4. RANKING: a removed legacy flag outranks the current one")
# The dangerous one. Both chunks are retrieved; the wrong one is first.
show(ask("cap memory in mb", Retriever(corpus)))

banner("5. ASSEMBLY BUDGET: the correcting chunk is truncated away")
# Same query as 4. With a full budget the context contains BOTH the legacy
# flag and the current one, so a reranker, a better model or a reader could
# notice. With a tight budget the current flag is dropped and that chance is
# gone, while the answer looks identical.
for budget in (600, 190):
    print(f"  budget={budget}:")
    trace = ask("cap memory in mb", Retriever(corpus), budget=budget)
    show(trace)
    # Check for the CHUNK, not the string: c4's own text mentions
    # max_memory_gb in passing, so a substring test on the context passes
    # even when the current flag's documentation was dropped.
    print(f"    c3 (the current flag's page) in context: {'[c3]' in trace.assembled}")
    print()
PY
python3 failures.py

Step 4: the one filter that fixes a whole class

python3 - <<'PY'
import json

from rag import Retriever, ask, show

retriever = Retriever(json.load(open("corpus.json")))
# The question asks what to DO. Topically, the explanation page about
# throughput is the closest match, and it cannot answer that question.
question = "how do I handle throughput and latency"

print("--- unfiltered ---")
show(ask(question, retriever))

print("--- filtered to how-to, because the question asks what to DO ---")
show(ask(question, retriever, kind="how-to"))
PY

Unfiltered, the top result is the explanation chunk: "A GPU is more efficient per item on a larger batch, so batching raises throughput at the cost of latency." True, relevant, and not an answer to "how do I".

Filtered to how-to, the same corpus returns "If your p99 is too high, set batch_size to 1 or 2."

One metadata field turned a correct non-answer into an answer, with no change to the retriever, the corpus, or the prompt. That is the payoff for the content model, and it is failure mode 4 fixed structurally rather than by reranking.

What you built. A pipeline whose every stage is inspectable, and a demonstration that five different defects produce the same user-visible symptom.

Run step 3 and read the traces rather than the answers. Here is what each sabotage produced:

# Sabotage What the user sees What the trace shows 1 max_memory_gb chunk removed An answer about batch_size The right chunk is not in the ranked list because it does not exist 2 Heading trail discarded An answer about GPU efficiency c2 vanishes from the list entirely: "latency" was only in its crumb 3 Page says VRAM, question says GPU An answer about batch_size c3 scores zero; nothing relevant retrieved 4 None; ranking as it is "max_memory_mb was the 1.x equivalent" c4 at 1.52 beats c3 at 1.41. Both retrieved, wrong one first 5 Context budget 190 instead of 600 Byte-identical answer to #4 c3 dropped for budget; the correcting chunk is gone

Four observations worth taking from that table.

Sabotage 2 is the sharpest. The word "latency" appears in c2's heading trail and nowhere in its text, which says "p99". Discard the crumb at split time and the only chunk that answers "reduce latency" becomes invisible to the query that asks it. That is chunking deciding retrieval.

Sabotage 4 is the dangerous one, and nothing was sabotaged to produce it. The pipeline, working as designed, tells a developer to use a flag that was removed in 2.0. Both chunks were retrieved; the wrong one ranked first by 0.11.

Sabotage 5 is invisible. The answer is identical to #4's, and the trace shows c3 was retrieved and then truncated. With the full budget the context contained both flags, so a reranker, a better model or a reader could have noticed. At the tighter budget that chance is gone, and nothing in the output indicates anything was dropped.

And: the answer line alone cannot distinguish any of these. The trace can. That is the argument for building the stages separately, and it is most of what separates a pipeline you can operate from one you can only restart.

docs.title: The three stages and what each owns
docs.text:
Stage Input Output Owns Retrieve question, filters ranked chunks Recall. If the answer is not here, nothing downstream helps Assemble ranked chunks a context block Budget, ordering, citation labels, deduplication Generate question, context answer, citations Faithfulness to the context

The middle stage is the one people skip and it causes the subtlest bugs: truncation, duplicate chunks from one page crowding out variety, and lost citation labels that make grounding unenforceable.

docs.title: The five failure modes, and what actually fixes each
docs.text:
# Failure Symptom Fix 1 Content does not exist Confident wrong answer, or a refusal Write the page. Nothing else 2 Chunked badly Retrieval finds the page, answer is incomplete Heading-aware chunking 3 Vocabulary mismatch Nothing relevant retrieved Hybrid search, or write the reader's words 4 Outranked Plausible neighbour returned instead Fusion, reranking, metadata filters 5 Model ignored the context Answer contradicts a retrieved chunk Prompting, then output evaluation

Four of the five are not prompt problems. The instinct when a RAG answer is wrong is to edit the prompt, and it is the right move about twenty percent of the time.

docs.title: Diagnosing in order
docs.text:
Question How to answer it Does the content exist at all? Grep the corpus. Do this first; it is free Is it in a chunk, whole? Search your chunk store for the fact, not the page Was the chunk retrieved? Log the ranked list for every query. Non-negotiable At what rank? Rank 4 with a top-3 cutoff looks identical to not retrieved Did it survive assembly? Log the dropped-for-budget list Did the answer use it? Require citations and check them mechanically

Log the ranked list. A RAG system without retrieval logs cannot be debugged, and adding them later means losing the traffic you needed.

docs.title: Things that matter more than they look
docs.text: Decision Why Citation labels per chunk Enables grounding checks and lets a reader verify Deduplicate by source page Three chunks from one page is less useful than three pages Context ordering Models weight the start and end of a long context more heavily A refusal path "Not in the documentation" must be an available answer Filter before ranking A hard constraint, not a hope. See vector stores Return the source path The reader needs somewhere to go, and you need to spot bad pages

docs.title: What RAG does not fix
docs.text:
Claim Reality "It stops hallucination" It reduces it. A model can still contradict its context "It keeps answers current" Only if the index is rebuilt. A stale index is a confident liar "It replaces writing" Failure mode 1 is unfixable by any amount of engineering "It replaces search" It is search, with the results read aloud "More chunks is better" Past a point, relevant content gets diluted

The second row is the one that causes incidents: an index built in March answering questions in September, with nothing in the answer indicating its age. A freshness field in the chunk metadata is cheap insurance.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with diagnosis, not architecture. Everyone can draw the three boxes. "When a RAG answer is wrong there are five candidates, and they look identical to the user: the content does not exist, it was chunked badly, it was not retrieved, it was retrieved and outranked, or the model ignored it. Four of those are not prompt problems. So I log the ranked retrieval list and what got dropped for context budget on every query, because without those two logs the only available debugging move is guessing."

The follow-up is "how do you know it is working", which is retrieval evaluation and is where most teams have nothing. The honest answer: a golden set of questions with their expected source pages, scored on whether the right page came back and at what rank, run in CI. And the number you must have next to it is the lexical baseline, because a dense pipeline that scores worse than BM25 is a quarter spent going backwards.

The tradeoff to volunteer. RAG converts a search problem you could inspect into a generation problem you cannot. A search results page is honest: the reader sees five results and judges them. A generated answer hides the ranking, so a confidently wrong synthesis of two half-relevant chunks reads exactly like a correct answer. You have improved the experience and removed the user's ability to notice you were wrong, which is why citations are not a nicety and why a refusal path has to exist.

One sharper point. The strongest framing for a documentation role is that RAG makes your content quality legible for the first time. Failure mode 1 is unfixable by engineering, and a RAG system is an excellent detector for it: the questions it answers badly are the pages you have not written or have written in the wrong vocabulary. Teams treat a bad RAG answer as a model problem; it is usually a content report, delivered in the reader's own words, for free. Pointing that out reframes the whole project from an AI initiative into a documentation gap analysis, which is a much better pitch to a documentation lead and happens to be true.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A pipeline with a trace object, plus the five-failure demonstration. The trace is what makes it look like something you operate rather than something you assembled.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path, especially step 3. Five sabotages producing one symptom is the most persuasive five minutes available on this topic.
  2. Add retrieval logging to anything you build. The ranked list and the dropped-for-budget list, per query. Ten lines, and it is the difference between operating the system and restarting it.
  3. Use the pipeline as a content audit. Ask it thirty real questions and sort the failures by the five modes. The count in mode 1 is a documentation backlog in the reader's words, and presenting it as such is the move that makes this work visible to people who do not care about retrieval. Predict the distribution first. If mode 1 is not the largest, your corpus is in better shape than most and the retrieval configuration is where to look.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. A working RAG demo is now a weekend project and proves little. A trace object, a five-mode taxonomy with a worked example of each, and a lexical baseline next to your retrieval numbers demonstrates that you have debugged one rather than built one.
