docs.title: Reading code to verify accuracy
docs.text:
Checking a documented claim against the implementation instead of against the person who told you.

core · difficulty 2 · 5h

Enough technical depth to read code and APIs, verify accuracy, and write working examples

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Opening the implementation to check whether a documented claim is true, rather than asking the person who wrote it. Specifically: finding the default value, the validation rule, the error path, and the thing the docstring forgot.

It is not software engineering. The skill is narrow and reading-only: navigate an unfamiliar codebase well enough to answer one factual question, then get out.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA puts this in minimum qualifications, and the phrasing is precise: "enough technical depth to read code and APIs, verify accuracy, and write working examples." The word doing the work is enough. They are not asking you to contribute to the simulation engine. They are asking you to stop being dependent on an engineer's memory.

That dependency is the thing to understand. Here is the default workflow in a documentation team that cannot read code: you notice a page might be wrong, you ask in Slack, an engineer answers from memory, you write down what they said. Every step of that is slow, and the last one is unreliable in a specific way. An engineer's memory of a default value is a memory of what it was when they wrote it. Defaults change in pull requests that nobody thought were documentation changes.

On a Tuesday it looks like this. The page says the visibility timeout defaults to 30 seconds. You open the client, find the constructor, and the default is None, which falls through to a server-side value that is 60 seconds in one region. Nobody lied; the page was right two years ago. You could only find that by looking.

The second reason, and the one that gets you hired: it changes what you are in a room with engineers. A writer who arrives with "the page says 30, the constructor says None, which is right?" gets a different conversation than one who arrives with "can you explain timeouts to me." It is the difference between being a channel and being a reviewer, and it is most of what implementation feedback rests on.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Verify three documented claims against a real codebase you have never read. About forty minutes.

Step 1: get a codebase and its docs

mkdir -p verify-drill && cd verify-drill
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install --quiet requests
python -c "import requests, pathlib; print(pathlib.Path(requests.__file__).parent)"

requests is a good target: widely documented, widely misdocumented in blog posts, and small enough to navigate.

Step 2: pick claims that are checkable

A claim is checkable when it names a value, a type, or a behaviour on a specific input. "Requests is user-friendly" is not checkable.

cat > claims.md <<'EOF'
1. `requests.get()` follows redirects by default.
2. `requests.get()` has no timeout by default.
3. `raise_for_status()` raises on a 4xx or 5xx response.
EOF
cat claims.md

Step 3: find the answer in the source, not in the docs

The technique is three tools in a fixed order: find the entry point, read the signature, follow one level down.

python3 - <<'PY'
import inspect, requests

# Claim 1 and 2: the signature carries the defaults.
print("--- requests.get signature ---")
print(inspect.signature(requests.get))
print()
print("--- requests.request signature (one level down) ---")
print(inspect.signature(requests.Session.request))
PY

Read the output before continuing, because it teaches the lesson better than this page can.

requests.get does not show you the defaults. Its signature is (url, params=None, **kwargs: Unpack[GetKwargs]). The convenience wrapper forwards everything through typed keyword arguments, so the defaults are not visible at the level a reader naturally looks.

One level down, Session.request shows them plainly: timeout=None and allow_redirects=True. Claims 1 and 2 are confirmed, but only from the second signature.

That is the whole technique in one observation. The signature of the function you call is often not the signature that holds the defaults, and a writer who stops at the first one documents a default of "whatever the wrapper does". When you see **kwargs, you are not finished.

An earlier draft of this page asserted that requests.get shows allow_redirects=True. Running the step is what proved otherwise.

Step 4: when the signature is not enough, read the body

Claim 3 is about behaviour, so the signature cannot answer it.

python3 - <<'PY'
import inspect, requests
source = inspect.getsource(requests.Response.raise_for_status)
# Print only the lines that decide something: the conditions and the raises.
for line in source.splitlines():
    stripped = line.strip()
    if stripped.startswith(("if ", "elif ", "raise ")):
        print(stripped)
PY

That shows the actual boundaries: which status ranges produce which error class. Note what you have now that the documentation did not give you, which is the exact condition rather than a summary of it.

Step 5: verify by running it, which is the only check that cannot be wrong

python3 - <<'PY'
import requests

# Claim 3, tested rather than read.
r = requests.Response()
r.status_code = 404
try:
    r.raise_for_status()
    print("404: did NOT raise  <- claim is false")
except Exception as exc:
    print(f"404: raised {type(exc).__name__}  <- claim holds")

r.status_code = 204
try:
    r.raise_for_status()
    print("204: did not raise  <- claim holds")
except Exception as exc:
    print(f"204: raised {type(exc).__name__}  <- unexpected")
PY

What you built. Three claims verified against an implementation you had never opened, using four techniques in increasing cost order: signature, then body, then the conditions only, then execution. That escalation is the skill. Most questions stop at step 3, and a writer who knows to look at the signature first answers in thirty seconds what otherwise becomes a Slack thread.

docs.title: The escalation, cheapest first
docs.text:
Technique Answers Cost Read the signature Defaults, types, required arguments Seconds Follow **kwargs one level down The defaults the wrapper hid Seconds Read the docstring, then distrust it What the author intended Seconds Grep for the constant Where a magic number really comes from A minute Read the function body's conditionals Boundaries, error paths Minutes Read the tests Intended behaviour, including edge cases Minutes Run it The truth Minutes

The tests are the most underrated row. A test suite is executable documentation of intent, it is maintained because it fails otherwise, and it usually contains exactly the edge cases your page is missing.

docs.title: Python tools worth knowing by heart
docs.text:
Tool Use inspect.signature(f) Defaults and parameter names without reading source inspect.getsource(f) The actual body inspect.getfile(m) Where a module lives on disk help(f) Docstring plus signature python -m pdb Step through to see which branch is taken git log -S"30" / git blame When and why a value changed rg "DEFAULT_" Constants, which is where defaults usually hide

git log -S is the one that wins arguments. It finds the commit that introduced a value, which tells you whether the documentation or the code is the thing that drifted.

docs.title: What makes a claim checkable
docs.text:
Checkable Not checkable "The default is 30 seconds" "Performance is good" "Raises ValueError on an empty list" "Handles errors gracefully" "Retries 3 times" "Is resilient to failure" "Requires Python 3.10 or newer" "Works with modern Python"

The right-hand column is not just vague writing. It is unverifiable, which means it can never be found wrong, which means it will rot without any signal. Rewriting an unverifiable claim into a checkable one is a documentation improvement before anyone checks it.

docs.title: Where documented claims go wrong, in order of frequency
docs.text:
1. A default changed and the pull request did not touch the docs.
  2. The documented default is the library's, and a layer above overrides it.
  3. The error class is wrong, usually a parent class named instead of the specific one.
  4. A version requirement is stale, having been raised without a docs change.
  5. The example works only in the author's environment, which is what cold-start testing exists for.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Give a concrete catch. "The page said the visibility timeout defaulted to 30 seconds. The constructor passes None, which falls through to a server-side default that differs by region. The page had been right two years earlier. I found it by reading the signature, and I fixed the class of problem by adding a check that compares documented defaults against the signatures."

That last clause is the one that gets remembered, because it is the systems mindset in the same breath.

The follow-up is "what do you do when you cannot read the code", meaning a compiled component, a service you have no access to, a C++ simulation kernel. This is a real situation at NVIDIA in particular. The honest answer has three parts. Read the public API surface and the tests, which are usually available even when the implementation is not. Verify behaviour by running it and observing, which is slower but authoritative. And when neither is possible, document the claim's provenance in the page, so a future reader knows it came from an engineer's statement in 2026 rather than from the code. The failure mode to avoid is writing an unsourced claim with the same confidence as a verified one.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Verification is slow, and the slowness is not distributed evenly: it is most expensive exactly when you are new, which is when you have the most pages to write. A writer who verifies every claim on every page ships very little. The judgement is about which claims are worth it, and the useful heuristic is verify anything a reader will paste, and anything numeric. A conceptual sentence being slightly imprecise costs a reader some confusion. A wrong default costs them an afternoon.

One sharper point. The real value is not the errors you catch, it is that verifiability becomes a property you can design for. Once you are the person who checks, you start writing claims in forms that a script could check later, which is how you get from manual verification to freshness monitoring and doc test harnesses. The reading skill is the thing that teaches you what is automatable.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A pull request fixing a documented claim, with the source reference in the description. That is a small, specific, unfakeable thing, and open-source projects are full of opportunities for it.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path, then do it for real. Pick a library you use, choose five documented claims about defaults or error behaviour, and check them. In a mature project you will find at least one wrong. File it.
  2. Write the check that would have caught it. If the claim was a default value, write twenty lines that compare documented defaults against inspect.signature and fail if they disagree. This is the step that converts a catch into a system, and it is a genuinely strong portfolio piece.
  3. Add provenance to one page. Take a page with claims you cannot verify and mark which ones came from a conversation rather than from code. Then go verify the two that matter most. The marking is the discipline; the verification is the payoff.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Saying you can read code is unfalsifiable. A merged pull request that says "the docs say 30, the signature says None, here is the commit that changed it" is not. One of those is worth more than a paragraph of self-assessment.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
This is the most nearly demonstrable of the craft concepts, and it still is not, because the artifact is a correction and a correction looks identical whether you found it by reading code or were told about it.

What you need. A codebase you did not write and its documentation. Nothing else. The exercise works better the less you know about the language, which is the counter-intuitive part: verifying a documented default does not require fluency, it requires knowing where defaults live.

What a learner would do. Take ten specific, checkable claims from someone else's documentation, the kind with a value in them, and verify each against the source:

"defaults to 30 seconds"        -> find the constant
"retries three times"           -> find the loop bound
"is idempotent"                 -> find the write path
"returns 404 if absent"         -> find the error branch
"logs at warning level"         -> find the call

Record, for each, whether the claim held and how long it took to settle. The second number is the one that matters: a claim you cannot verify in ten minutes is a claim the documentation should not have made in that form.

What you would find, in rough proportions.

Outcome Rough share What it means Claim correct and easy to verify about half The healthy case Claim correct, hard to verify common The value is now indirect; say where it comes from Claim stale: true of an older version a few The commonest documentation defect of all Claim true of one path, false of another a few The most dangerous kind Claim unverifiable from source alone some Runtime or deployment behaviour

The fourth row is the one worth hunting. "Idempotent" is usually true of the documented endpoint and false of a code path reached under retry, and that distinction is invisible unless somebody reads both.

What competence looks like. A correction with a file and line in it. A documented value that now matches a named constant. A claim rewritten from "is idempotent" to "is idempotent for the documented endpoint; the bulk path is not". And, most persuasive, a generated reference that removed the need for the exercise entirely.

Why it does not commit. The correction commits; the reading does not. A reviewer sees "fix timeout default: 30s not 60s" and cannot tell whether it came from the source, a ticket or a guess that happened to be right. The strongest available evidence is a habit of citing the file in the commit message, which is cheap and still only evidence of a habit.

docs.title: Real-time and graphics systems
docs.text:
The median completion time barely moved while the deadline miss rate went from zero to thirty per cent, and then the system fell off a cliff.

context · difficulty 2 · 4h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Documentation experience in graphics, simulation, robotics, or real-time systems"

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Systems where being late is being wrong. A real-time system is not a fast system; it is one with a deadline, and a result delivered after the deadline has no value, or negative value. Graphics is the familiar case: a frame that misses the display refresh is not a slightly slower frame, it is a dropped frame, and the user sees a stutter rather than a delay.

That one property changes which numbers matter, and it is the thing documentation in this domain most often gets wrong.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because the metric conventions a documentation writer brings from web services are actively misleading here, and NVIDIA lists four domains that all share this property.

In a web service, a slow request is a degraded request and the mean is a reasonable summary. In a real-time system, the mean is close to irrelevant: a system that meets its deadline 99 per cent of the time and misses one per cent has a one per cent failure rate, and the mean will look excellent either way. Writing "average frame time 8 ms" about a 60 Hz target is technically true and tells the reader nothing about whether their frames land.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Run the same work against tightening deadlines and watch the summary statistics stay healthy while the system fails. About twenty-five minutes, pure Python, no hardware.

Step 1: a periodic task, and the work it does

for i in range(N):
    target = start + (i + 1) * period / 1000
    now = time.perf_counter()
    if target > now:
        time.sleep(target - now)
    sum(x * x for x in range(WORK))            # the work
    done.append((time.perf_counter() - target) * 1000)

the work itself: mean 2.068 ms per cycle

About two milliseconds of work. Now give it less and less room.

Step 2: sweep the deadline

One run, on a shared two-core cloud machine:

  period  misses        completion time (ms)
    (ms)              mean     p50     p99     max
    10.0     0/250    2.363   1.762   4.314   4.551
     5.0     0/250    1.702   1.521   3.108   4.332
     2.0    67/250    3.308   1.482  22.912  24.702
     1.5   250/250   39.945  42.665  47.797  49.909

Read the p50 column down the first three rows: 1.762, 1.521, 1.482 ms. It does not rise. It improves.

Now read the miss column beside it: 0, then 0, then 67 of 250.

A quarter of deadlines missed, and the median is better than it was on the row with no misses at all. A dashboard plotting median completion time would show a healthy, improving line. The mean rises from 2.4 to 3.3 ms, which nobody pages anyone about. The columns that noticed are p99, which went to 22.9 ms, fifteen times the median, and the miss count.

Step 3: the numbers move, and the shape does not

Repeating the sweep is itself instructive. At the 2 ms period, across six runs:

misses at period 2.0 ms:  67, 81, 164, 176, 202, 205  (of 250)

A factor of three, from nothing but what else the machine was doing. So the specific counts above are one sample and not a property of the code, which is worth saying before quoting any of them.

Three things were stable across every run:

a loose deadline (10 ms)   0 misses, always
a tight one (1 ms)         250/250, always
the median                 stayed between 1.4 and 4 ms throughout

The median never tracked the miss rate, in any run. That is the transferable finding, and the variance is the second one: a general-purpose machine cannot give a repeatable answer here, which is precisely why real-time work reaches for a dedicated kernel, pinned cores and locked memory rather than better averages.

Step 4: the cliff

Wherever the transition falls, it is not gradual:

  2.0 ms period:   67/250 missed,  p50  1.5 ms
  1.5 ms period:  250/250 missed,  p50 42.7 ms

Completion time goes from 1.5 ms to 42.7 ms, a factor of 28, for a 25 per cent tightening of the deadline. Once the work cannot fit in the period, each cycle starts late, so the next starts later, and lag compounds without limit. There is no gentle region: the system is fine, then it is unrecoverable.

That is the characteristic failure shape of this whole domain, and it is why headroom is discussed differently here. A web service at 80 per cent utilisation is busy. A real-time system at 80 per cent utilisation is one scheduling hiccup from the cliff.

Step 5: what this means for the writing

Three consequences, each a concrete documentation decision:

state the deadline, not the average      "16.6 ms at 60 Hz", never "fast"
publish the miss rate                    the mean cannot express failure
publish the tail, p99 and max            the mean hides a 15 ms max at p50 1.5

And one more that is easy to miss. In the run above, the work took 2.07 ms and median completion at a 10 ms period was 1.76 ms, which looks impossible. They are different statistics, a mean against a median, on a machine whose timings vary by a factor of three. That is the lesson rather than a footnote: on this hardware the overhead of being scheduled is not separable from the noise, so any budget a page offers has to be stated with the margin included and the measurement conditions named.

What you built. A deadline sweep showing a median that improves while a quarter of deadlines are missed, a variance measurement showing the counts are not reproducible, the cliff where lag starts compounding, and the things a page in this domain has to publish instead of an average.

docs.title: Hard, firm and soft
docs.text:
Kind A missed deadline Example Hard System failure, possibly unsafe Flight control, motor commutation Firm The result is worthless, no harm A dropped video frame Soft Value degrades with lateness A UI animation, a game's physics

Most things called real-time are firm or soft. The distinction matters in writing because it decides whether the correct advice is "guarantee it" or "degrade gracefully", and those are different pages.

docs.title: Which numbers to publish
docs.text:
Statistic Says Verdict here Mean Typical throughput Nearly useless; see step 2 Median Typical experience Actively misleading; it was flat at 30% misses p99, p99.9 The tail that fails Essential Max over a run The worst case observed Essential, and not a bound Deadline miss rate The failure rate The number that matters Jitter, max minus min Predictability Often the real requirement Worst-case execution time A provable bound Hard systems only, and expensive

A page that quotes a mean in this domain has chosen the one statistic that cannot express the failure mode.

docs.title: Frame budgets, as the familiar case
docs.text:
Refresh Budget per frame 30 Hz 33.3 ms 60 Hz 16.6 ms 90 Hz 11.1 ms 120 Hz 8.3 ms 144 Hz 6.9 ms

The budget covers everything: simulation, culling, draw submission, present, and the scheduling overhead from step 4. Documentation that gives a per-feature cost without saying what the budget is leaves the reader unable to add up.

docs.title: Why a general-purpose OS is not real-time
docs.text:
Source of lateness Typical scale Scheduler granularity Tens of microseconds to milliseconds Another process being runnable Unbounded Page faults and memory allocation Microseconds to milliseconds Garbage collection, where present Milliseconds, unpredictably Interrupt handling Microseconds Frequency and thermal management Milliseconds, and invisible

Measured here: the same sweep gave between 67 and 205 deadline misses out of 250 across six runs, a factor of three from nothing but neighbouring load. A page claiming a sub-millisecond guarantee on a stock kernel is claiming something the kernel does not offer, and this is why real-time work reaches for PREEMPT_RT, core pinning, locked memory and allocation-free hot paths.

docs.title: Terms worth recognising
docs.text: Term Means Jitter Variation in timing, often worse than latency Determinism The same input gives the same timing Priority inversion A low-priority task blocking a high-priority one Starvation A task that never gets scheduled Admission control Refusing work to protect the deadline Headroom Unused capacity, which is the safety margin WCET Worst-case execution time, a proved upper bound

docs.title: Things to put in a page in this domain
docs.text: Do Instead of State the deadline in milliseconds "Real-time", "fast", "low latency" Publish a miss rate A mean Give the tail and the max A single number Include scheduling overhead in budgets Quoting the work alone Say what degrades when the deadline is missed Leaving the failure mode implicit Name the required kernel or configuration Implying stock hardware suffices

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the definition, because it is the whole thing. "A real-time system is not a fast system, it is one with a deadline, and a result after the deadline has no value. A frame that misses the refresh is not a slow frame, it is a dropped frame. That changes which numbers mean anything."

Then the measurement, which is the part worth bringing. I ran a fixed piece of work against tightening periods. At a 10 ms deadline, no misses and a median of 1.76 ms. At 2 ms, sixty-seven misses out of 250 and a median of 1.48, better than the row with no misses, while p99 went to 22.9 ms, fifteen times the median. A quarter of deadlines missed and every summary statistic looking healthy or improving.

The second finding, which I would not have had without repeating it. The miss count at that period ranged from 67 to 205 across six runs, a factor of three from neighbouring load alone. So the counts are not a property of the code, and the transferable claim is the shape: the median never tracked the miss rate in any run. The variance is itself the argument for why this domain uses dedicated kernels and pinned cores rather than better averages.

The third, which is about headroom. Tightening the deadline by 25 per cent, from 2 ms to 1.5, took it from sixty-seven misses to all 250 and the median from 1.5 ms to 42.7. Once the work does not fit, every cycle starts later than the last and lag compounds, so there is no gentle region. That is why utilisation reads differently here: 80 per cent in a web service is busy, and in a real-time system it is one hiccup from the cliff.

Be honest about the depth. This is Python on a general-purpose kernel, which is the right vehicle for showing why general-purpose kernels are not real-time and the wrong one for anything else. No PREEMPT_RT, no GPU, no frame capture, no graphics pipeline. The reasoning about statistics and budgets transfers; the engineering does not, and context tier is the honest claim.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A deadline sweep over a workload of yours, reported as a miss rate and a tail rather than an average.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the sweep in step 2. Predict the period at which misses begin, then look at what the median does on either side of it.
  2. Take any latency claim in your own documentation and work out whether it could be true while the system fails a third of the time. If the claim is a mean or a median, it can.
  3. Add the scheduling or framework overhead to one published cost figure. On an idle machine it was a third again here, and readers budget with the number you give them.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. The sweep ran on this machine and the script is a dozen lines, so the flat median against a 30 per cent miss rate and the cliff between 2.0 and 1.5 ms are both reproducible. What is absent is the domain's actual engineering: no real-time kernel, no graphics pipeline, no frame profiler, no hardware timing. The demonstrated page records this as the statistics rather than the systems work.

docs.title: Release readiness for documentation
docs.text:
Making a documented path part of what shipping means, rather than something that follows it.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

Encode standards (user stories, release readiness, onboarding, security guidance) into templates, validators, and guided workflows rather than static documents

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: Documentation CI

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Making documentation part of the definition of done for a release, enforced by something other than goodwill. The output is a check, a template field, or a gate in the release pipeline, not a policy document.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA names it inside a list of standards to encode, and the phrasing is the important part: "into templates, validators, and guided workflows rather than static documents". They are explicitly ruling out the usual artifact, which is a wiki page titled "Definition of Done" that everyone agreed to in a meeting two years ago.

The outcome they attach to it is "so every release ships documented, discoverable, and supportable". Intel's version: "so each new capability ships with tested documentation".

On a Tuesday this is the recurring unpleasant conversation. A capability shipped on Thursday. The release notes mention it. There is no page, the sample does not cover it, and the first support ticket arrives Monday. Nobody did anything wrong: the engineer shipped a feature, the release manager cut a release, and documentation was not in anyone's checklist in a way that could block.

The reason this is core rather than a process nicety: without it, every other mechanism in this guide is reactive. You can have excellent cold-start testing and freshness monitoring and still be permanently behind, because they tell you about content that exists. Release readiness is the only mechanism that acts before the gap is created.

The honest difficulty: this is the most political concept in the guide. The others are things you can build alone. This one requires someone else to accept a constraint.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build the gate, in the weakest form that still works, and see it block. Thirty-five minutes.

Step 1: decide what "documented" means, concretely enough to check

A definition that needs a human to interpret it is a policy document again.

mkdir -p release-drill && cd release-drill
cat > definition.md <<'EOF'
A user-visible capability is DOCUMENTED when all four are true:

1. A page exists and is reachable from the navigation.
2. The page has a runnable example, or explicitly states there is none.
3. The example is covered by sample validation (so it cannot silently rot).
4. The page names the release it first shipped in.

Deliberately NOT in the definition:
  - "the page is good"      -> not checkable, belongs in review
  - "the page is complete"  -> not checkable, and complete is not a state
  - "approved by docs"      -> a person, not a gate; becomes a bottleneck
EOF
cat definition.md

Step 2: carry the claim in the artifact that already exists

Do not create a new tracking system. The changelog already lists what shipped.

cat > CHANGELOG.md <<'EOF'
## 2.4.0 (unreleased)

- feat: batch inference endpoint  (docs: how-to/batch-inference.md)
- feat: quantised model loading   (docs: none)
- fix: memory leak in the pool    (docs: n/a)
EOF

mkdir -p docs/how-to
cat > docs/how-to/batch-inference.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Batch inference
since: 2.4.0
---
# Batch inference

Post several inputs in one request.

```python
client.infer_batch(["a", "b"])
```
EOF
ls docs/how-to/

Three entry kinds, which is the whole design: a page, an admitted gap, and n/a for a change with no user-visible surface. The n/a case is what makes the gate acceptable to engineers, because without it every bug fix needs a page and the gate gets disabled within a month.

Step 3: the gate

cat > check_release.py <<'PY'
"""Fail a release when a user-visible change has no documented path.

Reads the unreleased section of the changelog and checks each entry's `docs:`
annotation. Three valid forms:

    docs: <path>   the page must exist and declare `since:` this version
    docs: n/a      no user-visible surface; the author asserts this
    docs: none     a known gap; fails the gate, and is meant to

`none` exists so an author can be honest without lying to the gate. The gate
still fails, which is the point: the gap becomes visible before the release
rather than in a support ticket after it.
"""
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

VERSION = re.compile(r"^## (\S+) \(unreleased\)")
ENTRY = re.compile(r"^- (\w+): (.+?)\s+\(docs: (.+?)\)\s*$")


def main(changelog: Path, docs: Path) -> int:
    lines = changelog.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
    version = next((m.group(1) for m in map(VERSION.match, lines) if m), None)
    if not version:
        print("no unreleased section; nothing to check")
        return 0

    failures = []
    checked = 0
    for line in lines:
        match = ENTRY.match(line)
        if not match:
            continue
        kind, description, claim = match.groups()
        checked += 1

        if claim == "n/a":
            continue
        if claim == "none":
            failures.append(f"{kind}: {description!r} has no documentation")
            continue

        page = docs / claim
        if not page.exists():
            failures.append(f"{kind}: {description!r} points at {claim}, which does not exist")
            continue

        front = yaml.safe_load(page.read_text(encoding="utf-8").split("---")[1]) or {}
        if str(front.get("since", "")) != version:
            failures.append(
                f"{kind}: {claim} has since={front.get('since')!r}, expected {version!r}"
            )

    for failure in failures:
        print(f"NOT RELEASE READY  {failure}", file=sys.stderr)
    print(f"{'FAIL' if failures else 'ok'}: {checked} changelog entries, "
          f"{len(failures)} blocking {version}")
    return 1 if failures else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(Path("CHANGELOG.md"), Path("docs")))
PY
python3 check_release.py

Step 4: close the gap and watch it go green

cat > docs/how-to/quantised-models.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Loading quantised models
since: 2.4.0
---
# Loading quantised models

Pass `quantised=True` when loading.

```python
model = load("widget-7b", quantised=True)
```
EOF
python3 - <<'PY'
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("CHANGELOG.md")
p.write_text(p.read_text().replace(
    "- feat: quantised model loading   (docs: none)",
    "- feat: quantised model loading   (docs: how-to/quantised-models.md)"))
PY
python3 check_release.py

What you built. A gate that blocks a release when a feature has no page, reading an artifact the team already maintains, with an honest escape hatch for changes that need no documentation and a deliberately failing value for gaps the author knows about.

The since cross-check is the part that earns its keep over time. It catches the case where someone points the changelog at a page that exists but documents the old behaviour, which is the failure a simple existence check misses.

docs.title: What a checkable definition looks like
docs.text:
Checkable Not checkable A page exists at this path The page is good The page declares since: 2.4.0 The page is up to date The example is covered by sample validation The example is realistic The page is in the navigation The page is discoverable A changelog entry has a docs: annotation Documentation was considered

The right column is not worthless. It belongs in review, performed by a person. The mistake is putting it in a gate, where it either blocks on judgement or passes on nothing.

docs.title: The three annotation values, and why all three are needed
docs.text:
Value Meaning Gate result <path> A page exists and claims this version passes if true n/a No user-visible surface. An assertion by the author passes none A known gap fails

Omitting n/a is the commonest way this gate dies. Every internal refactor needs an annotation, authors resent it, and someone adds --skip-docs-check to the release script. Omitting none is the second way: without an honest value for a gap, authors point at an unrelated page.

docs.title: Where to put the gate, from weakest to strongest
docs.text:
Placement Blocks Political cost A report emailed after the release nothing none A warning in the release pipeline nothing none A required field in the PR template nothing, but prompts low A failing check on the release branch the release medium A failing check on every PR the merge high

Start at the template and the report. A gate introduced at the top of this table gets removed; one that has been producing an accurate report for two months is much easier to promote, because by then everyone has seen the number.

docs.title: What this cannot do
docs.text:
Limit Consequence It checks existence, not quality A one-line stub passes It depends on the changelog being accurate An unlisted feature is invisible to it It cannot see undocumented behaviour changes A default changing is not a changelog feat: It needs someone to accept the constraint The only concept here you cannot build alone

The third row is the real residual risk, and it is why freshness monitoring and claim checking are not optional complements to this.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with the escape hatch, because it proves you have shipped this rather than proposed it. "I added a docs: annotation to changelog entries and a check that fails the release branch if a feat: entry has no page declaring that version. It takes n/a for changes with no user-visible surface, which is what keeps engineers from disabling it, and none for a known gap, which fails on purpose so the gap is visible before the release instead of in a ticket after it."

The follow-up is "what happened when it blocked a release", and this is the question the whole concept lives or dies on. Have a real answer. The useful shape is: it blocked, someone asked for an override, and the override was granted with the gap recorded. A gate that has never been overridden is either very new or not actually on the critical path. Saying that you granted an override, and that the record of it is what later justified headcount, is a much more credible story than a gate nobody ever fought.

The tradeoff to volunteer. This gate moves documentation work from after the release to before it, which means it sometimes delays releases, and the cost lands on engineers rather than on you. That is a real transfer and it is why the gate needs an owner with authority behind it. There is a version of this that is pure friction: a team that resents the check, writes one-line stubs to satisfy it, and ships documentation that is technically present and useless. The stub-passing problem is genuine and the mitigation is not a stricter gate, it is review by a person on the pages that matter.

One sharper point. The strongest argument for release readiness is not completeness, it is that an undocumented capability is more expensive than an unshipped one. A feature nobody can use generates support load, bad first impressions, and a backlog item that gets harder every month as context is lost. Framing it as a cost-of-delay argument rather than a quality argument is what moves release managers, because quality arguments lose to ship dates and cost arguments do not.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. The gate plus the escape hatch, in a repository, with at least one commit where it failed.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path, then point it at a real changelog. Most projects have one and none of them have a docs: annotation. Adding the annotation retroactively to the last release tells you immediately what the gap rate is, and that number is the argument for the gate.
  2. Write the definition of documented for one project, with the deliberately-excluded list. The exclusions are what show judgement; anyone can write a wish list. If the excluded list is empty, the definition is not finished. Every real one excludes something, and a definition that excludes nothing will be overridden the first time it is inconvenient.
  3. Report before you block. Run the check in report-only mode for a few releases and keep the numbers. A gate proposed with two months of data behind it is a different conversation from a gate proposed on principle.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. A policy document proves nothing, and most people in this field have written one. A check that reads the changelog, takes n/a, and has a commit where it blocked a release is specific, unfakeable, and demonstrates that you have had the political conversation rather than theorised about it.

This repository has the mechanism without the politics, and the distinction is worth stating plainly rather than blurring. fieldguide release-check is a real gate: seven named steps, a remedy on each failure, run in CI, and it does block. It carries --report-only precisely because of the advice above, so it can run for several releases and accumulate numbers before anyone is asked to accept a constraint. What it cannot demonstrate is the constraint being accepted, because the only author here is also the only reviewer. A gate you imposed on yourself is a habit, and a gate somebody else agreed to is a negotiation; the second is the thing this page is actually about, and no amount of code in a solo repository produces it.

So the honest version in an interview is: here is the mechanism, here is the report-only mode that exists for the conversation, and the conversation itself is the part I would be having with your release engineers rather than showing you from a repository of my own.

docs.title: Repeat-question analysis
docs.text:
A question repeats because the corpus answers it in the corpus's words; two words missing from a 1,159-term vocabulary moved four of five retrieval scores.

core · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "repeat questions"

Prerequisites: Support deflection

Leads to: Prioritising documentation work

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The practice of treating a question asked many times as a defect report about the documentation rather than as a support workload. One person asking is a person; forty people asking the same thing is a measurement, and the thing it measures is a specific, locatable failure in the corpus.

The reason it earns a concept of its own, next to deflection, is that the repeat is diagnostic in a way the volume is not. Deflection tells you how much load the documentation could carry. A repeat tells you which sentence to write.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because a repeat question is the cheapest high-quality signal in this entire field, and almost nobody acts on it.

NVIDIA lists it among the things to measure, alongside deflection and answer quality, and it is the one that most directly converts into an edit. The failure mode is organisational rather than technical: repeats are visible to support, the fix belongs to documentation, and the two have separate queues. So the same question is answered individually four hundred times by people who are measured on response time, and nobody is measured on making it stop.

The second reason is subtler and is what this page is mostly about. The usual assumption is that a repeat means the answer is missing. More often the answer is present, correct, well written, and phrased in vocabulary the asker does not have.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Find out why two questions kept failing on a corpus that contained both answers, then fix them and measure what the fix was worth. About thirty minutes.

Step 1: the questions that fail when the answer exists

From the deflection ceiling: every one of twenty questions is answered somewhere in the corpus, and the right page comes back first for thirteen. Two of the failures were not ranking failures at all. They survived widening the retrieved window from one chunk to ten:

  grounded@1    16/20  (80%)
  grounded@3    18/20  (90%)
  grounded@5    18/20  (90%)
  grounded@10   18/20  (90%)

A plateau. More context stops helping, so no reranker and no embedding model would touch the remaining two. Something else is wrong with them.

Step 2: measure the corpus's vocabulary against the questions'

For each question, what proportion of its terms appear anywhere in the corpus at all:

corpus = Counter()
for p in Path("docs").rglob("*.md"):
    corpus.update(tokenize(p.read_text()))

terms = tokenize(case.question)
coverage = sum(1 for t in terms if corpus[t]) / len(terms)

corpus vocabulary: 1159 distinct terms

  chunk-size        5/6   83%   term absent from the corpus: ['smaller']
  prose-linting     6/7   86%   term absent from the corpus: ['hedge']
  ...the other 18 cases: 100%

  mean question-vocabulary coverage: 95%
  questions fully covered: 13 of 20

Two words. smaller and hedge, absent from a corpus of 1,159 distinct terms. The page about chunk sizing said "token ceiling". The page about prose rules named the tool but never the symptom. Both pages were correct, complete and useless to the person asking.

Step 3: fix the vocabulary, not the retriever

One sentence per page, each placing the reader's word beside the corpus's. No code, no model, no reranker:

             before   after
hit@1          60%     65%
hit@3          95%     95%
MRR          0.742   0.775
routing        70%     75%
grounded@1     80%     90%
grounded@3     90%    100%
headroom      +15%    +10%

Four of five scores moved, and the ceiling reached 100 per cent at three chunks. Two sentences.

Step 4: confirm the mechanism rather than the coincidence

Scores moving after an edit is not proof that the edit caused it. Re-measure the vocabulary coverage itself, against the corpus as it was and as it is:

corpus vocabulary: 1159 distinct terms before, 1194 after

  chunk-size         83% -> 100%
  prose-linting      86% -> 100%

  mean coverage:      95% -> 97%
  fully covered:    13/20 -> 15/20

The two cases that moved on the retrieval metrics are exactly the two whose vocabulary coverage moved, and no others. Thirty-five new terms entered the corpus and two of them were the ones being tested, which is as close to a mechanism as a twenty-case sample can get.

Step 5: the generalisation, and its trap

A repeat question is usually a vocabulary gap, and the fix is usually one sentence putting the reader's word next to yours. That is the cheapest documentation work there is.

The trap is where to put the sentence. It belongs on the page that answers the question, and nowhere else. Writing the synonym pair into an explanation page about vocabulary gaps makes that page compete for the query it describes. That happened here. An earlier draft of the companion repository's own explanation page set both pairs out in a table and gave back five points of hit@1, because the explanation outranked the two how-to pages for their own questions. Name the case, not its wording.

What you built. Two repeat failures diagnosed as vocabulary rather than ranking, a two-sentence fix worth four of five scores, and a before-and-after on the vocabulary metric itself that ties the fix to the movement.

docs.title: Why a question repeats
docs.text:
Cause Looks like Fix Cost The answer is absent Nothing matches Write the page High The reader's word is absent Right page, never surfaced One sentence Trivial The answer is buried mid-page Right page, wrong section A heading Low The answer is split across pages Partial answers, repeated asks Consolidate Medium The answer is wrong or stale The reader followed it and came back Fix and test it Medium The question is a product defect Documentation cannot fix it File the bug Not yours

Rows two and three are the majority on a mature corpus and the cheapest to close, which is the opposite of how most documentation backlogs are ordered.

docs.title: Detecting repeats without a ticket queue
docs.text:
Signal Shows Available without an audience Vocabulary coverage per question Terms the corpus lacks Yes grounded@k plateau Failures ranking cannot fix Yes Answerable against findable Load that is avoidable Yes Zero-result search queries Words readers use and you do not No, needs logs Clustered support tickets Frequency, which weights everything No, needs a queue The same question in two channels A genuinely load-bearing gap No

The first three are free and this page is built on them. They identify candidates; only the bottom three tell you which candidate is asked four hundred times a month, which is why search logs are the missing input rather than a nicety.

docs.title: The vocabulary sentence, as a pattern
docs.text:
Corpus says Reader says The sentence "token ceiling" "smaller" "To make chunks smaller, change the token ceiling." "Vale" "hedge words" "Vale fails hedge words here rather than in review." "idempotent" "safe to run twice" Name both, in that order "deprecated" "is this still supported" Answer the question the reader asked

The shape is always the same: the reader's word first or immediately adjacent, the precise term kept, on the page that answers the question. Replacing your term with theirs loses precision; putting them side by side loses nothing.

docs.title: What not to do about repeats
docs.text:
Tempting Why it fails A FAQ page Becomes an unmaintained parallel corpus A glossary Readers do not search glossaries, retrievers do not weight them A synonym list in the search config Invisible to every consumer but one Rewriting the page in plain language Loses the precise term, which experts search for A chatbot over the same corpus Inherits the vocabulary gap exactly

The last row is the current version of this mistake and worth saying out loud: a retrieval-augmented assistant over a corpus that lacks the reader's word fails the same query the same way, with more confidence.

docs.title: Repeats against deflection
docs.text: Deflection Repeat analysis Unit The corpus One question Answers How much load is avoidable Which sentence to write Needs weighting Yes, badly Less: a repeat is self-weighting Output A percentage An edit

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the reframing. "A question asked forty times is a defect report about the documentation, not a support workload. Deflection tells me how much load the corpus could carry; a repeat tells me which sentence to write, which is the more actionable of the two."

The follow-up is the diagnosis, and this is where the measurement lands. The assumption is that a repeat means a missing answer. On my corpus both residual failures had the answer present and correct: the words smaller and hedge were absent from 1,159 distinct terms. One sentence per page putting the reader's word beside the corpus's moved four of five retrieval scores, and took grounding to 100 per cent at three chunks.

How you know it was the vocabulary and not luck. I re-measured vocabulary coverage against the old and new corpus. Thirty-five new terms entered, and the only two cases whose coverage moved were exactly the two whose retrieval scores moved. On a twenty-case sample that is as close to a mechanism as you get, and I would say so rather than claim causation.

The diagnostic worth bringing. The grounded@k plateau tells you when to stop reaching for ranking. Mine went 80 per cent at one chunk, 90 at three, and then flat out to ten. Once widening the window stops helping, the remaining failures are not ranking failures, and no reranker or embedding upgrade will touch them. That is a ten-point gap that looks like a business case for a reranker, and half of it was a synonym.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Repeat analysis without frequency data finds candidates and cannot rank them. My twenty cases are unweighted, so a question asked four hundred times counts the same as one asked twice, and the fix order I would derive is therefore arbitrary. Search logs or a ticket queue supply the weights, and until they exist this is a method rather than a prioritisation.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A vocabulary-coverage measurement over your own golden set or query log, and one page edited to carry a reader's word beside your own.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Take the five questions your support channel repeats most, and check whether each one's own words appear anywhere in the page that answers it. Predict how many fail before you look.
  2. Compute grounded@k for k of 1, 3 and 10 on your corpus. Where the curve flattens is where ranking work stops paying, and that boundary is usually argued about rather than measured.
  3. Add one sentence to one page putting a reader's word beside your precise term, then re-run your retrieval scores. It is the highest return per keystroke available in this job.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Every figure above was executed against docpack: the plateau, the 1,159-term vocabulary, the two absent words, the two-sentence fix, and the before-and-after on both the retrieval scores and the vocabulary metric, all reproducible from the repository. What is missing is frequency: there is no ticket queue and no query log, so these are candidates rather than a ranked backlog, and the demonstrated page records that limit rather than implying the method was validated against real repeat volume.

docs.title: Reproducible environments
docs.text:
What a clean environment costs, which isolation level catches which defect, and the pinning decision nobody makes deliberately.

supporting · difficulty 3 · 4h

Asked for by name

Intel: "golden paths and curriculum that take a developer from a clean environment to a working result"

Prerequisites: Golden paths

Leads to: Cold-start testing

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The "clean environment" half of Intel's sentence. Making it true requires three decisions: what level of isolation a reader is asked to create, whether dependencies are pinned, and what your CI reproduces.

They look like infrastructure decisions and they are documentation decisions, because each one changes what your quickstart can honestly promise.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Intel's phrase is "from a clean environment", and the word clean is doing a lot of work. A clean environment is the only starting state a document can assume, because it is the only one that is the same for everyone.

The difficulty is that reproducibility and speed trade off directly, and both matter to time to first success. A reader asked to build a container before seeing anything work has a slower first success than one who runs a single pip install, and the container reader has a more reliable one. That trade has no universally right answer, which is why this is difficulty 3.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Measure the four isolation levels, then find out what each one can and cannot catch. About thirty-five minutes.

Step 1: measure the cost of isolation

The same trivial task, run four ways:

cat > task.py <<'EOF'
import sys
print("working result:", sys.version_info[:2])
EOF

# level 1: ambient interpreter
python3 task.py

# level 2: fresh virtual environment
python3 -m venv .v1 && .v1/bin/python task.py

# level 3: fresh environment plus one dependency
python3 -m venv .v2 && .v2/bin/pip install -q requests && .v2/bin/python task.py

# level 4: from a lockfile
.v2/bin/pip freeze > requirements.lock
python3 -m venv .v3 && .v3/bin/pip install -q -r requirements.lock

level 1: ambient interpreter        0.02s
level 2: fresh venv, no deps        3.40s
level 3: fresh venv + one dep       4.81s
level 4: pinned, from a lockfile    3.69s

Two things worth noticing. Creating a virtual environment costs about three and a half seconds before any dependency is installed, which is the floor on any cold-start check. And requests turned out to pin five packages, so one documented dependency is five unversioned decisions unless you pin.

Level 4 came out faster than level 3 here, because of a warm wheel cache. Pinning is not inherently slower; it is more predictable, which is the actual property you want.

Step 2: find out what each level can catch

Isolation is not a quality ladder. Each level catches a different class of defect, and choosing one is choosing which defects you are willing to miss:

Level Catches Misses Ambient Nothing about setup Every undeclared dependency Virtual environment Undeclared Python packages, missing steps System packages, interpreter version, locale Container Also system packages, interpreter, locale, apt steps A dead package index Container, no network cache Also a yanked release, a registry outage Very little

The second row is the common choice and its blind spot is specific: a quickstart that says pip install widget while widget needs libpq-dev will pass every virtual-environment check and fail for a reader on a clean machine. If your instructions contain apt install, a virtual environment is not sufficient isolation and you need a container.

Step 3: the pinning decision, stated as a trade

for i in 1 2; do
  python3 -m venv ".p$i" && ".p$i/bin/pip" install -q cowsay
  echo "run $i: $(".p$i/bin/pip" freeze | tr '\n' ' ')"
done

run 1: cowsay==6.1
run 2: cowsay==6.1

Identical today. Nothing on the page guarantees tomorrow, and that is the whole decision:

Pinned Unpinned Reader gets What you tested Whatever is current Breaks when You update the pin Upstream ships a change Cold-start test tells you That your pin still works That reality still matches the page Maintenance Scheduled Unscheduled, and surprising Right for Tutorials, reproducible research Quickstarts, where current is the point

The non-obvious half is in the third row. A pinned cold-start test verifies your lockfile and stops telling you about the world. An unpinned one is flakier and reports something you need to know, which is that a reader following your page today would hit a problem.

The resolution most projects land on: pin the tutorial, leave the quickstart unpinned, and run the unpinned check on a schedule rather than as a merge gate so its flakiness does not block contributors.

Step 4: what to actually write on the page

The reader needs the isolation step to be one command, whatever you chose:

cat > docs/quickstart.md <<'MDEOF'
# Quickstart

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install widget
widget sync
```

You should see `synced 0 records`.
MDEOF

Three lines, and the first one is what makes the other two honest. Omitting it is the most common reason a quickstart works for its author: they are in an environment they created months ago and no longer think about.

What you built. A measured cost for each isolation level, a defect class mapped to each, and a pinning decision made on purpose instead of inherited.

docs.title: Mechanisms, by ecosystem
docs.text:
Ecosystem Isolation Pinning Python venv, virtualenv requirements.lock, uv.lock, poetry.lock Node node_modules per project package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml Any Container image A digest, not a tag Any Nix, devbox Lockfile by construction Hosted Dev containers, Codespaces The image digest

The container row is the one that is usually got wrong. FROM python:3.12 is not pinned; FROM python:3.12@sha256:... is. A tag is a moving reference, so a "reproducible" container built from a tag reproduces whatever the tag means today.

docs.title: Dev containers as documentation
docs.text:
A devcontainer.json is a documentation artifact: it is the setup instructions in a form a machine can execute, which makes it the one setup document that cannot drift from what it describes.

Pays off when Does not Setup is genuinely complex pip install is the whole story Contributors are on mixed platforms Everyone is on the same one Onboarding time is a measured problem Onboarding is already minutes You already maintain an image You would be adopting containers for this

It is not a substitute for written instructions. A reader who cannot use your container still needs the steps, and a repository with only a dev container has hidden its setup rather than documented it.

docs.title: What CI should reproduce
docs.text:
Reproduce So that The reader's environment, not yours The check means something The isolation level you documented You test what you promised The pinning state you documented See step 3 A cold cache, periodically Index and release problems surface

The first row is the discipline. A CI job that installs from a cached pre-built environment is testing your cache, and when the cold-start check fails the temptation is always to make the environment more permissive, which converts the one check that finds this class of defect into one that cannot.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the trade rather than the tooling. "Reproducibility and time to first success pull against each other, and both are things Intel asks for. A reader who has to build a container before seeing anything work has a slower first success and a more reliable one. I pick the weakest isolation that catches my actual failures, and I can say what each level misses."

The follow-up is pinning, and the good answer is that it depends on what the check is for. A pinned cold-start test verifies your lockfile; an unpinned one verifies that a reader following the page today succeeds. Those are different questions, so pin the tutorial, leave the quickstart unpinned, and schedule the unpinned run rather than gating merges on it.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Unpinned cold-start checks are the flakiest thing you will own, and a flaky required check trains people to re-run CI until green, which damages the credibility of every other gate. That is a real cost and the mitigation is scheduling rather than pretending the flakiness is not there.

One sharper point. A virtual environment is not enough isolation if your instructions contain apt install. Python-level isolation will pass a quickstart that depends on an undeclared system library, and the reader on a clean machine fails on step two. Matching the isolation level to the kinds of dependency your instructions actually have is the decision, and almost nobody makes it explicitly.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A cold-start script that creates the isolation level your docs describe, plus a written reason for your pinning choice.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the step 1 measurements. Knowing that a bare virtual environment costs about three and a half seconds sets your expectations for CI.
  2. Grep your setup instructions for apt, brew or yum. Any hit means a virtual environment is insufficient isolation for your checks.
  3. Write down why your quickstart is or is not pinned. The written reason is the deliverable; most projects have the state without the decision.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack's scripts/coldstart.sh creates a fresh virtual environment and installs the way a reader would, which is level 2 in the table above and the right level for a pure-Python project. The honest limit, recorded rather than glossed: it would not catch a system-package dependency, and nothing in that repository needs one. Naming your isolation level and its blind spot is the signal.

docs.title: reStructuredText
docs.text:
The markup with directives and cross-references, and the line between docutils and Sphinx.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Markdown/RST"

Prerequisites: Markdown and its dialects

Leads to: Sphinx

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A plain-text markup language from the Python documentation world, older than Markdown and considerably more capable. Its distinguishing features are directives, which are block-level extensions, and roles, which are inline ones, both of which take arguments and options. That extensibility is what lets reStructuredText express a cross-reference to a Python function, rather than a link to a URL you had to know.

The thing most people get wrong, including in interviews, is where reStructuredText ends and Sphinx begins. The golden path draws the line precisely.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA writes "Markdown/RST", and the reason is almost certainly that their documentation estate includes Sphinx projects. Simulation, robotics and graphics tooling is largely Python and C++, and Python API documentation has been Sphinx territory for twenty years.

You are unlikely to be asked to start a new reStructuredText project. You are quite likely to inherit one, be asked whether to migrate it, and be asked what would be lost. Answering that well requires knowing which of the features are the language and which are the tool, because the migration cost is entirely in the second category.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Run one file through docutils, then through Sphinx, and find out which half of "RST" is actually reStructuredText. About twenty-five minutes.

Step 1: a file using the vocabulary people associate with RST

mkdir -p rst-demo && cd rst-demo
cat > sample.rst <<'EOF'
Title
=====

.. note::
   A directive with a body.

.. versionadded:: 2.4
   The ``retry`` parameter.

See :ref:`configuring` and :py:func:`widget.retry`.

.. _configuring:

Configuring
-----------

.. code-block:: python
   :emphasize-lines: 2

   client = Client()
   client.retry(times=5)
EOF

A note admonition, a version annotation, two cross-reference roles, an internal label, and a highlighted code block. This is what people mean when they say a page is written in RST.

Step 2: ask docutils, which is the reStructuredText implementation

python3 -m docutils --report=2 sample.rst > out.html 2> err.txt
echo "exit=$?"
grep -cE "ERROR|WARNING" err.txt
head -8 err.txt

exit=0
4
sample.rst:7: (ERROR/3) Unknown directive type "versionadded".
sample.rst:10: (ERROR/3) Unknown interpreted text role "ref".
sample.rst:10: (ERROR/3) Unknown interpreted text role "py:func".
sample.rst:17: (ERROR/3) Error in "code-block" directive:

Four of the five constructs are unknown to reStructuredText itself. Only .. note:: is part of the language. versionadded, ref, py:func and code-block are all Sphinx, not RST.

Step 3: notice how docutils failed

grep -o 'class="system-message[^"]*"' out.html | sort | uniq -c
grep -o 'Unknown directive type[^<]*' out.html | head -1

      4 class="system-message"
      4 class="system-message-title"
Unknown directive type "versionadded".

Exit code 0, and the four errors are rendered into the page as system-message blocks the reader can see. This is the same shape as the Markdown dialect failure, with the volume turned up: instead of quietly passing characters through, docutils publishes a visible error box. It still does not fail the build.

Step 4: ask Sphinx, with no extensions at all

mkdir -p sx/src && cp sample.rst sx/src/index.rst
printf 'project = "demo"\nextensions = []\n' > sx/src/conf.py
sphinx-build -q -b html sx/src sx/out
echo "exit=$?"
grep -c "Unknown directive" sx/out/index.html
grep -c "versionadded" sx/out/index.html

exit=0
0
1

Everything resolves, with an empty extensions list. So all four constructs come from Sphinx core, not from third-party extensions, which is the detail that makes the boundary confusing: you do not opt into them, you get them by using Sphinx at all.

What you learned. "RST" in common usage means reStructuredText plus Sphinx's directive and role vocabulary. The language on its own is a structured text format with admonitions and tables. Everything that makes it attractive for API documentation is the tool.

docs.title: Which half is which
docs.text:
Construct reStructuredText Sphinx Section headers, lists, tables Yes .. note::, .. warning:: Yes .. image::, .. include:: Yes Substitutions, |name| Yes .. code-block:: with options Yes :ref:, :doc: Yes :py:func:, :py:class: and the domains Yes .. versionadded::, .. deprecated:: Yes .. toctree:: Yes .. autodoc, automodule Yes, an extension

The second column is the migration cost. A corpus using only the first column converts to Markdown almost mechanically. A corpus using domains and toctree does not convert at all without choosing replacements.

docs.title: What it has that Markdown does not
docs.text:
Feature Why it matters Typed cross-references :py:func:\widget.retry`` resolves to the right symbol and fails the build if it moves A directive model Extensions are first-class, not per-tool syntax hacks Domains Separate namespaces for Python, C++, JavaScript symbols A real specification docutils is the reference implementation, not one dialect of many Substitutions and includes Single-sourcing without a plugin

The first row is the strongest argument for it and the one to cite. A cross-reference to a symbol is checkable in a way that a Markdown link to a generated anchor is not, which makes a large API corpus genuinely more maintainable.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text: Cost Detail Contributor friction Directive syntax, indentation sensitivity, and inline markup rules that surprise people Inline markup is fussy Nested emphasis and adjacent punctuation need escapes Smaller tooling ecosystem Fewer editors, linters and preview tools than Markdown Errors can be invisible As step 3 shows, docutils renders errors into the page Hiring Most writers arrive knowing Markdown

docs.title: If you have an RST corpus and want Markdown
docs.text:
Option Keeps Loses MyST in Sphinx All directives, roles, domains, toctree Nothing structural; contributors write Markdown Convert with pandoc Prose Every Sphinx construct in the right column above Rewrite into another generator Nothing automatic Cross-reference checking, domains

MyST is almost always the right answer, and knowing that is worth more in an interview than an opinion about which syntax is nicer. It lets a Sphinx project accept Markdown without giving up the capability that made Sphinx worth using, so the migration question stops being all-or-nothing.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the boundary. "Most of what people call RST is Sphinx. The language gives you admonitions, tables and substitutions; code-block, ref, the Python domain and toctree all come from Sphinx core. That matters because the migration cost of an RST corpus is entirely in the Sphinx half."

The follow-up is whether you would migrate, and the strong answer is MyST rather than a conversion. It lets contributors write Markdown inside a Sphinx project, keeping typed cross-references and domains, which is the capability nobody wants to lose and most conversions throw away.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Typed cross-references are the real feature, and they are worth friction on an API corpus of any size, because a reference to a symbol that moved becomes a build failure instead of a dead link. They are not worth it for a dozen conceptual pages, where the directive syntax is pure cost and Markdown is the right answer.

One sharper point. docutils exits zero and renders its errors into the published page. So an RST project without -W or an equivalent has probably shipped visible error boxes at some point, and checking for system-message in built output is a two-minute audit that tends to find something.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. Less about a repository than about being able to answer the migration question concretely, with the two-column table above.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. The docutils-versus-Sphinx comparison is the part nobody has actually executed.
  2. Grep any built RST site you can reach for system-message. Published errors are more common than you would expect.
  3. Take ten pages of an RST corpus and classify every directive and role into language or tool. That classification is the migration estimate.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Neither of this guide's repositories uses reStructuredText, which is recorded on the demonstrated page. What travels instead is the boundary itself: being the person in the room who knows that code-block is not reStructuredText is a small thing that reliably signals first-hand experience.
