  • Single-sourcing, which RST substitutions and includes do natively

docs.title: Retrieval evaluation
docs.text:
A golden set of questions with expected sources, scored in CI, because every other check asks whether the docs are correct rather than useful.

core · difficulty 3 · 6h

including llms.txt, MCP-accessible sources, agent skills and context kits, and evaluation sets for answer accuracy

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: RAG pipelines

Leads to: Measuring AI answer quality, Output evaluation

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A set of real questions paired with the page that should answer each, scored automatically so a change to the corpus or the retriever moves a number. The metrics are hit@k, mean reciprocal rank, and whatever else your failure modes demand.

It is the only check in a documentation pipeline that asks whether the corpus is useful rather than whether it is correct.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA names it directly: "evaluation sets for answer accuracy", listed alongside llms.txt and MCP as a required AI-ready output. It is the rarest of the four in practice and the most diagnostic of whether a team is serious.

Here is why it matters more than it sounds. Every other gate in this guide, link checking, code-sample validation, cold-start testing, answers a question of the form "is this broken". A corpus can pass all of them and still fail the only question a reader has: I asked this, did I get the right page. Nothing else measures that, and without measuring it you cannot tell an improvement from a coincidence.

On a Tuesday it is the thing that settles arguments. Somebody proposes adding embeddings. Somebody else proposes a reranker. A third person wants to rewrite the chunker. All three are plausible, all three cost weeks, and without an eval set the decision is made by whoever argues hardest. With one, you measure the lexical baseline, see that routing is the gap rather than ranking, and build the cheap thing.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a golden set, score a retriever on it, and use it to make one real decision. Fifty minutes, dependency-free.

Step 1: write the golden set, with the conventions that keep it alive

mkdir -p eval-drill && cd eval-drill
cat > corpus.json <<'EOF'
[
  {"id": "c1", "source": "reference/flags.md", "crumb": "Server flags > batch_size", "kind": "reference",
   "text": "batch_size controls how many requests are grouped per forward pass. The default is 32."},
  {"id": "c2", "source": "how-to/latency.md", "crumb": "Reduce latency > Lower the batch size", "kind": "how-to",
   "text": "If your p99 is too high, set batch_size to 1 or 2. A batch of 32 waits for 32 requests, adding roughly 200ms."},
  {"id": "c3", "source": "reference/flags.md", "crumb": "Server flags > max_memory_gb", "kind": "reference",
   "text": "max_memory_gb caps the GPU memory the server will allocate. The default is 16. Size for peak load, not startup."},
  {"id": "c4", "source": "reference/legacy.md", "crumb": "Legacy 1.x flags > max_memory_mb", "kind": "reference",
   "text": "max_memory_mb was the 1.x equivalent of max_memory_gb. Removed in 2.0 and ignored if set."},
  {"id": "c5", "source": "explanation/batching.md", "crumb": "Why batching helps > Throughput", "kind": "explanation",
   "text": "A GPU is more efficient per item on a larger batch, so batching raises throughput at the cost of latency."},
  {"id": "c6", "source": "how-to/oom.md", "crumb": "Fix an out-of-memory error > Size for peak", "kind": "how-to",
   "text": "If the server starts cleanly and dies under traffic, raise max_memory_gb or lower batch_size."}
]
EOF

cat > golden.yaml <<'EOF'
# Rules for adding a case, which exist because an eval set rots faster than
# the corpus it measures:
#
#   1. Phrase the question the way a READER would type it, never the way the
#      page is worded. A case lifted from a page's own heading measures that
#      string matching works, which was never in doubt.
#   2. `expect_kind` is the kind of answer the question's PHRASING calls for,
#      which is not always the kind of the expected page. A mismatch is a
#      finding about the corpus, not a mistake in the case.
#   3. `why` says what the case probes. Without it nobody can tell a
#      deliberately hard case from a stale one, and in six months the whole
#      set is untouchable.

- id: default-batch
  question: what is the default batch size
  expect_source: reference/flags.md
  expect_kind: reference
  why: Pure lookup. If this regresses, something is badly wrong.

- id: latency-symptom
  question: my p99 is too high
  expect_source: how-to/latency.md
  expect_kind: how-to
  why: A symptom, not a topic. The reader does not know the fix is batch size.

- id: cap-memory
  question: how do I limit gpu memory
  expect_source: reference/flags.md
  expect_kind: reference
  why: Competes with the removed 1.x flag, which is the dangerous near-miss.

- id: oom-under-load
  question: server dies under traffic but starts fine
  expect_source: how-to/oom.md
  expect_kind: how-to
  why: Phrased as an incident. Shares little vocabulary with the page.

- id: why-batch
  question: why would I batch requests at all
  expect_source: explanation/batching.md
  expect_kind: explanation
  why: A why question. Should route to explanation, not to the flag reference.

- id: legacy-flag
  question: max_memory_mb
  expect_source: reference/legacy.md
  expect_kind: reference
  why: An exact identifier for a removed flag. Must not return the current one.

- id: throughput-action
  question: how do I raise throughput
  expect_source: how-to/latency.md
  expect_kind: how-to
  why: >
    Deliberate tension. Topically the explanation page is closest; the reader
    asked what to DO. Expected to be hard.
EOF
python3 -c "
import yaml
cases = yaml.safe_load(open('golden.yaml'))
print(len(cases), 'cases')
assert all(c.get('why') for c in cases), 'every case needs a why'
print('every case states what it probes')
"

Step 2: the harness

cat > evaluate.py <<'PY'
"""Score a retriever against a golden set.

Five metrics, and the last two are the ones worth arguing about.

  hit@1 / hit@3   the expected page is first / in the top three
  MRR             mean reciprocal rank, so second beats ninth
  routing         the top result is the KIND of page the question needs
  headroom        hit@1 if the retriever were told the right kind

ROUTING matters because topical correctness is not enough: a reference page
and an explanation page about one subject can both be relevant while only one
can answer the question asked.

HEADROOM is NOT an achievable score. At query time nobody knows what kind the
question wants. It measures how much accuracy is sitting behind a query
router, which turns "add a reranker or add a classifier" from an argument into
a measurement.
"""
import json
import math
import re
import sys
from collections import Counter

import yaml

K1, B, DEPTH = 1.2, 0.75, 3


def tokenize(text):
    return [t for t in re.findall(r"[a-z0-9_]+", text.lower()) if len(t) > 1]


class Retriever:
    """BM25 over chunks, searching the heading trail as well as the text."""

    def __init__(self, chunks, use_crumb=True):
        self.chunks = chunks
        self.use_crumb = use_crumb
        self.docs = [
            Counter(tokenize(f"{c['crumb']} {c['text']}" if use_crumb else c["text"]))
            for c in chunks
        ]
        self.lengths = [sum(d.values()) for d in self.docs]
        self.avg = sum(self.lengths) / len(self.docs)
        df = Counter()
        for d in self.docs:
            df.update(d.keys())
        n = len(self.docs)
        self.idf = {t: math.log(1 + (n - c + 0.5) / (c + 0.5)) for t, c in df.items()}

    def search(self, question, kind=None, limit=DEPTH):
        terms = tokenize(question)
        scored = []
        for chunk, doc, length in zip(self.chunks, self.docs, self.lengths):
            if kind and chunk["kind"] != kind:
                continue
            score = 0.0
            for t in terms:
                f = doc.get(t, 0)
                if not f:
                    continue
                norm = 1 - B + B * (length / self.avg)
                score += self.idf.get(t, 0.0) * (f * (K1 + 1)) / (f + K1 * norm)
            if score > 0:
                scored.append((score, chunk))
        scored.sort(key=lambda s: (-s[0], s[1]["id"]))
        return scored[:limit]


def rank_of(hits, expect_source):
    """1-indexed rank of the first hit from the expected PAGE, or None.

    Page-level, not chunk-level: a corpus has several chunks per page and the
    reader wants the page. Scoring per chunk would punish a corpus for
    splitting a page well.
    """
    for position, (_, chunk) in enumerate(hits, start=1):
        if chunk["source"] == expect_source:
            return position
    return None


def evaluate(retriever, cases):
    rows = []
    for case in cases:
        hits = retriever.search(case["question"])
        filtered = retriever.search(case["question"], kind=case["expect_kind"])
        top = hits[0][1] if hits else None
        rows.append({
            "id": case["id"],
            "rank": rank_of(hits, case["expect_source"]),
            "filtered_rank": rank_of(filtered, case["expect_source"]),
            "top_source": top["source"] if top else "",
            "top_kind": top["kind"] if top else "",
            "routed": bool(top) and top["kind"] == case["expect_kind"],
        })
    return rows


def report(rows, label):
    n = len(rows)
    hit1 = sum(1 for r in rows if r["rank"] == 1) / n
    hit3 = sum(1 for r in rows if r["rank"] is not None) / n
    mrr = sum(1 / r["rank"] if r["rank"] else 0 for r in rows) / n
    routing = sum(1 for r in rows if r["routed"]) / n
    fhit1 = sum(1 for r in rows if r["filtered_rank"] == 1) / n

    print(f"\n{label}: {n} cases, top-{DEPTH}")
    print(f"  hit@1      {hit1:6.1%}")
    print(f"  hit@{DEPTH}      {hit3:6.1%}")
    print(f"  MRR        {mrr:6.3f}")
    print(f"  routing    {routing:6.1%}")
    print(f"  hit@1 with kind filter   {fhit1:6.1%}")
    print(f"  routing headroom         {fhit1 - hit1:+6.1%}  (not achievable; see the page)")

    misses = [r for r in rows if r["rank"] != 1]
    if misses:
        width = max(len(r["id"]) for r in misses)
        print(f"\n  {'case':<{width + 2}} rank  top result")
        print("  " + "-" * (width + 32))
        for r in misses:
            rank = str(r["rank"]) if r["rank"] else "-"
            print(f"  ! {r['id']:<{width}} {rank:>4}  {r['top_source']} ({r['top_kind']})")
    return {"hit@1": hit1, f"hit@{DEPTH}": hit3, "mrr": mrr, "routing": routing}


def main():
    chunks = json.load(open("corpus.json"))
    cases = yaml.safe_load(open("golden.yaml"))

    # Validate the set against the corpus BEFORE scoring. A case pointing at
    # a renamed page keeps running and keeps reporting a lower score, and the
    # obvious reading of a falling score is that the retriever got worse.
    # That misdiagnosis is expensive, so it fails loudly instead.
    sources = {c["source"] for c in chunks}
    kinds = {c["kind"] for c in chunks}
    for case in cases:
        if case["expect_source"] not in sources:
            sys.exit(f"stale golden set: {case['id']} expects {case['expect_source']}, "
                     f"which is not in the corpus")
        if case["expect_kind"] not in kinds:
            sys.exit(f"{case['id']}: unknown expect_kind {case['expect_kind']!r}")
    print(f"ok: {len(cases)} cases resolve against {len(sources)} pages")

    report(evaluate(Retriever(chunks), cases), "BM25 with heading trails")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
PY
python3 evaluate.py

Step 3: use it to make a decision

This is the whole point. Three candidate changes, measured instead of argued.

cat > decide.py <<'PY'
"""Measure three proposed changes instead of arguing about them."""
import json

import yaml

from evaluate import Retriever, evaluate, report

chunks = json.load(open("corpus.json"))
cases = yaml.safe_load(open("golden.yaml"))

baseline = report(evaluate(Retriever(chunks), cases), "A. baseline")

# Proposal 1: stop indexing the heading trail, to save index size.
no_crumb = report(
    evaluate(Retriever(chunks, use_crumb=False), cases),
    "B. without heading trails (someone proposed dropping them)",
)

# Proposal 2: retire the legacy flags page, which nobody should be using.
without_legacy = report(
    evaluate(Retriever([c for c in chunks if c["source"] != "reference/legacy.md"]),
             [c for c in cases if c["expect_source"] != "reference/legacy.md"]),
    "C. with the legacy page retired",
)

print("\n" + "=" * 64)
print(f"{'metric':<12} {'A base':>8} {'B no crumb':>12} {'C no legacy':>12}")
print("-" * 64)
for key in baseline:
    print(f"{key:<12} {baseline[key]:>8.1%}" if key != "mrr"
          else f"{key:<12} {baseline[key]:>8.3f}", end="")
    for other in (no_crumb, without_legacy):
        print(f" {other[key]:>12.1%}" if key != "mrr" else f" {other[key]:>12.3f}", end="")
    print()
PY
python3 decide.py

Step 4: set a floor, not a target

cat > gate.py <<'PY'
"""Fail the build when retrieval regresses.

The floor sits BELOW the current score on purpose. It is a regression gate,
not a target: set to the current number, ordinary content edits trip it and
people learn to skip CI. The real scores belong on a published page where a
change to them shows up in a diff and has to be explained.
"""
import json
import sys

import yaml

from evaluate import Retriever, evaluate

MRR_FLOOR = 0.60
HIT3_FLOOR = 0.70

rows = evaluate(Retriever(json.load(open("corpus.json"))),
                yaml.safe_load(open("golden.yaml")))
n = len(rows)
mrr = sum(1 / r["rank"] if r["rank"] else 0 for r in rows) / n
hit3 = sum(1 for r in rows if r["rank"] is not None) / n

failures = []
if mrr < MRR_FLOOR:
    failures.append(f"MRR {mrr:.3f} below floor {MRR_FLOOR}")
if hit3 < HIT3_FLOOR:
    failures.append(f"hit@3 {hit3:.1%} below floor {HIT3_FLOOR:.0%}")

for failure in failures:
    print(f"RETRIEVAL REGRESSION  {failure}", file=sys.stderr)
print(f"{'FAIL' if failures else 'ok'}: MRR {mrr:.3f}, hit@3 {hit3:.1%}")
sys.exit(1 if failures else 0)
PY
python3 gate.py; echo "exit=$?"

What you built. A validated golden set, five metrics, a measured comparison of three proposals, and a CI gate with a floor below the current score.

docs.title: What the measurement actually said, which was not what was expected
docs.text:
Baseline: hit@1 71.4%, hit@3 85.7%, MRR 0.786, routing 71.4%, headroom +14.3%. Two cases miss. default-batch lands at rank 2, and throughput-action is not in the top three at all, which is the case the golden set marked as deliberately hard.

Then the comparison:

metric A baseline B without heading trails C with legacy retired hit@1 71.4% 85.7% 66.7% hit@3 85.7% 85.7% 83.3% MRR 0.786 0.857 0.750 routing 71.4% 85.7% 66.7%

Proposal B scored better. Dropping the heading trail from the index improved hit@1 by 14 points, which directly contradicts the argument made on the chunking page and the argument made earlier in this guide.

That is the result, and the honest response is not to bury it or to accept it.

It is one case. Seven cases means one case is 14.3 percentage points, so this entire difference is default-batch changing places. With the crumb indexed, "what is the default batch size" matches Reduce latency > Lower the batch size and returns the how-to page; without it, the reference page wins. By the sample-size table below, a 14-point difference on a seven-case set is one case and is inside the noise floor. The correct conclusion is "this set cannot answer that question", not "drop the heading trails".

And it points at a real defect that is not about crumbs at all. The reference page's chunk says batch_size with an underscore; the question says "batch size" with a space. The tokenizer keeps underscores so flag names survive, which means the two never match. That is a genuine finding the eval set surfaced, and the fix is a tokenizer that indexes both forms, not a change to chunking.

Proposal C is not a like-for-like comparison, and this is a methodological trap worth naming. Retiring the legacy page also removes the legacy-flag case, so C is scored over six cases instead of seven. Its lower score is partly arithmetic. Any change that alters the corpus and the question set cannot be compared on a single number, and an eval harness will happily let you do it anyway.

Three findings from one measurement, and none of them was the one being looked for. That is what an eval set is for.

docs.title: The metrics, and what each is for
docs.text: Metric Question it answers Watch out for hit@1 Is the top result right? Harsh; a near-miss at rank 2 scores zero hit@3 Is it in the top three? Generous; says nothing about ordering MRR Weighted by position One number, hard to interpret alone Routing accuracy Is it the right kind of page? Needs a type field on every page Grounded@1 Does the top chunk contain the fact? See grounding Headroom What a perfect router would gain Not a score. Explained below

docs.title: Why routing accuracy is worth the extra column
docs.text: Topical relevance is not enough. "How do I raise throughput" and "why would I batch requests" are about the same subject, and only one of them can be answered by an explanation page. A retriever returning the right subject in the wrong genre produces an assistant that confidently answers a different question than the one asked, and hit@1 cannot see it.

docs.title: The headroom number, and why it is not a score
docs.text:
The harness runs every question twice: once normally, once with the retriever told which page kind to search.

That second figure is not achievable. At query time nobody knows what kind a question wants; the harness knows only because the golden set declares it.

What the gap measures is how much accuracy is sitting unclaimed behind a query router. A large gap says your content model carries information the retriever is throwing away, and the cheapest next move is classifying the question rather than embedding the corpus better. A gap near zero says the opposite. Either way it is a measurement rather than an argument.

docs.title: Sample size, stated honestly
docs.text:
Cases One case is worth Smallest meaningful difference 7 14 percentage points enormous 20 5 points about 10 points 50 2 points about 5 points 200 0.5 points a few points

A seven-case set cannot distinguish two retrievers that score within 15 points of each other. It can tell you a page became unreachable, which is most of what a regression gate needs. Any decision closer than that needs more cases, and pretending otherwise is how teams make choices out of noise.

docs.title: Where the questions come from
docs.text:
Source Quality Cost Search queries with no click best: gaps in the reader's words an export Support ticket subject lines real failures, biased to people who ask an export Repeat questions in channels real, biased to the loudest a search Assistant conversation logs exactly your traffic needs the assistant running Hand-written by the author available today, reflects author assumptions an afternoon

The last row is where every eval set starts and is the weakest. Hand-written cases measure whether the corpus answers the questions its author imagined, which correlates with real traffic less than you would hope. The first thing to do with real logs is replace them.

docs.title: Keeping the set alive
docs.text: Rule Why Validate expect_source against the corpus A renamed page makes the score drop for no reason Require a why on every case Otherwise nobody dares delete a stale case Phrase questions as readers do A case quoting the page's heading measures nothing Score at page level, not chunk level Readers want pages; chunk-level punishes good splitting Publish the scores, gate on a lower floor The floor survives edits; the published number gets explained Add a case with every reported failure The set grows from real traffic rather than imagination

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with what it decides, not with the metrics. "Every other documentation check asks whether something is broken. This is the only one that asks whether asking a question returns the right page. I keep twenty-odd cases phrased the way readers actually type, validated against the corpus so a renamed page fails loudly instead of quietly lowering the score, scored on hit@k, MRR and routing accuracy, with a floor in CI set below the current number so content edits do not trip it. The number I insist on having is the lexical baseline, because a dense pipeline scoring worse than BM25 is a quarter spent going backwards."

The follow-up is "how many cases do you need", and the answer that shows judgement is about resolution rather than a number. Twenty cases means one case is five points, so anything under about ten points is noise and should not drive a decision. That is enough to catch a page becoming unreachable, which is what a gate is for, and not enough to choose between two close retrievers. Say that before someone asks, because a candidate quoting a precise improvement from a twelve-case set has told you they do not understand the instrument.

The tradeoff to volunteer, and it is the real one. A golden set becomes a target. Once the number is visible, every change gets evaluated against those questions, and the corpus starts getting optimised for them rather than for readers. The symptom is a rising score and flat support load. Two mitigations, both partial: never tune parameters by sweeping them against the eval set, which turns it into training data; and refresh the cases from real logs regularly so the target moves with the traffic. Neither fully solves it. Goodhart's law is not avoidable, only managed.

One sharper point. The strongest observation is that an eval set is a content report, not a retrieval report. A case that fails because the corpus has no page on the subject is a documentation gap stated in a reader's own words, and that is the most valuable output of the whole exercise. Sorting your failures by the five RAG failure modes tells you how much of your problem is engineering and how much is writing, and in most documentation corpora the answer is mostly writing. That reframes an AI project into a documentation gap analysis, which is both true and a much better pitch to a documentation lead.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A golden set in version control, a harness, published scores including the bad ones, and a CI floor.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path, including step 3. The three-proposal comparison is the demonstration: it shows the set earning its keep by settling a decision rather than by producing a number.
  2. Publish the unflattering score. A page with your real hit@1, the cases you lose, and why each is hard is far more credible than a good number with no failures listed. Nobody believes a retrieval system that works.
  3. Replace your hand-written cases with real queries. Export zero-click searches or ticket subjects and rebuild the set from them. Then report how much the score changed, because that delta is the measure of how wrong your assumptions about your readers were, and it is usually a large number.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Describing hit@k and MRR is reading a blog post. A committed golden set with a why on every case, a validator that fails on a renamed page, a lexical baseline next to every other number, and a published score you are not proud of demonstrates that you ran it rather than built it.

docs.title: Robotics simulation, Isaac Sim and ROS
docs.text:
Two frames, both required, that disagree on purpose: one drifts without bound and never jumps, the other stays accurate and jumps, and differentiating the wrong one invents 1.2 m/s of velocity.

context · difficulty 2 · 4h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Documentation experience in graphics, simulation, robotics, or real-time systems; familiarity with USD, Omniverse, Isaac Sim, or ROS"

No simulator was run

No ROS, no Isaac Sim and no robot were available here. The measurement in step 2 is a simulation of the frame properties that ROS specifies, written to demonstrate why the specification says what it does; the specification itself in step 1 was verified by opening it. Nothing on this page is experience of operating a robot.

Prerequisites: OpenUSD and Omniverse

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Running a robot's software against a simulated body and world instead of hardware. Isaac Sim is NVIDIA's simulator, built on Omniverse and therefore on USD; ROS is the middleware most robot software is written against, and the two meet through a bridge.

For a documentation role the domain's defining difficulty is not physics. It is that a robot's software maintains several descriptions of where it is, those descriptions disagree, and the disagreement is deliberate.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because the concept that costs readers the most is a choice between two things that both look correct.

NVIDIA groups robotics with graphics, simulation and real-time systems, and documentation in all four has to explain a model before it can explain an API. In robotics, the model is the transform tree, and the specific thing that bites is which frame to read a position from. Getting it wrong produces software that works in a demo and misbehaves on a robot, which is the most expensive class of documentation failure in this domain because the feedback arrives late and looks like a hardware fault.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Read what ROS actually specifies about coordinate frames, then demonstrate why it specifies it. About twenty-five minutes.

Step 1: the specification, opened and read

ROS standardises this in REP 105, which names four frames and a strict single-parent tree:

earth  ->  map  ->  odom  ->  base_link

Each frame has exactly one parent, so attaching base_link to both map and odom is forbidden. The two interesting frames carry opposite guarantees:

odom   the pose of a robot in the odom frame is guaranteed to be continuous,
       and can drift over time, without any bounds

map    the map frame is not continuous; its pose can change in discrete
       jumps at any time

And each transform has an owner: an odometry source publishes odom → base_link; the localisation component publishes map → odom, deliberately not map → base_link, by taking the odometry transform and correcting it; earth → map is static.

(Verified by opening REP 105. The frame names, the tree ordering, the continuity language and the ownership of each transform are from that document.)

Two frames, both required, with contradictory properties. That is the model a page has to land before any API appears.

Step 2: why those properties are the way round

Simulate twenty metres of travel with two per cent wheel slip and a localisation fix every twenty-five steps:

odom += V * DT * (1 + rng.normal(0, 0.02))       # integrates slip, smoothly
if fix_arrives:
    map_est = truth + rng.normal(0, 0.03)        # snaps to the fix
else:
    map_est += V * DT * (1 + rng.normal(0, 0.02))

                                 odom frame    map frame
error at the end                   -0.045 m     -0.024 m
worst error                         0.050 m      0.070 m
largest single-step change         0.0065 m     0.1203 m

The last row is the whole point. The odom frame's error never changes by more than 6.5 mm in a step; the map frame's jumps by 120 mm the instant a fix lands.

Now consider a controller that estimates velocity by differentiating position, which is an ordinary thing to do:

a controller differentiating the map frame sees 1.2 m/s of phantom velocity

On a robot travelling at 1.0 m/s, reading the globally-accurate frame produces a 120 per cent velocity error at every localisation update, out of nowhere, with every component behaving correctly. Read odom instead and the velocity is smooth and the position slowly wrong, which for a controller is the right trade.

So the rule a page should state plainly: differentiate odom, navigate in map, and never mix them in one calculation. The specification implies it; saying it outright is the documentation contribution.

Step 3: what this says about writing for the domain

The transform tree is a prerequisite, not a reference topic. A reader who has not understood that two frames disagree on purpose cannot use any of the API correctly, and will write code that passes in simulation, where slip can be zero and fixes can be perfect.

That is the sim-to-real gap in its documentable form: a simulator can be configured so that the distinction this page is about does not appear, which means a tutorial that only runs in simulation can teach the wrong model without ever failing.

What you built. A verified reading of the frame specification, a demonstration of why its two guarantees are opposite, and a one-line rule with a measured consequence behind it.

docs.title: The frames, and who owns each transform
docs.text:
Transform Published by Continuous Drifts earth → map Static, or localisation n/a No map → odom Localisation No, jumps No odom → base_link Odometry source Yes Yes, unbounded

Reading a pose in map composes a jumping transform with a smooth one, which is why the result jumps. Reading in odom omits the correction, which is why it drifts.

docs.title: Choosing a frame
docs.text: For Use Because Velocity, by differentiation odom Continuity; see step 2 Local obstacle avoidance odom Short horizon, needs smoothness Navigation to a goal map Global accuracy Logging a trajectory Both, labelled They answer different questions Anything spanning a localisation update odom, then transform once Mixing invents motion

docs.title: Terms worth recognising
docs.text: Term Means TF, tf2 The transform library and its tree Odometry Pose estimated by integrating motion SLAM Building a map while localising in it URDF, SDF Robot description formats; USD in Isaac Sim Joint state Positions and velocities of the articulated parts Twist A linear and angular velocity command Node, topic, service, action The ROS communication primitives Sim-to-real gap Behaviour that holds in simulation and not on hardware Domain randomisation Varying simulation parameters to close that gap

docs.title: Where the sim-to-real gap comes from
docs.text:
Source How a simulator usually differs Sensor noise Absent or Gaussian, rather than structured Contact and friction Approximated; the hardest part of physics Latency Zero, or constant, rather than variable Timing Simulation time, which can pause Actuator dynamics Instantaneous, rather than ramped Localisation quality Can be made perfect, hiding the step 2 problem

The bottom row is the one that interacts with documentation: a tutorial written and tested entirely in simulation can be correct, reproducible, CI-verified and still teach a model that fails on a robot.

docs.title: Simulation time against wall-clock time
docs.text: A simulator can run faster or slower than real time and can be stepped or paused. Code that reads the system clock instead of the simulation clock behaves differently under simulation, and this is a documentation obligation rather than a footnote: any sample that times anything has to say which clock it uses.

docs.title: What a page in this domain owes the reader
docs.text: Owes Rather than The frame model, before any API A tf2 API reference Which frame to use for which question "Use tf2 to transform" An explicit statement that frames disagree Leaving it implied Which clock a sample reads Assuming wall-clock What the simulator does not model Implying parity with hardware A hardware-verified claim marked as such Mixing simulated and real results

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the boundary and then the model. "I have not operated a robot. What I can do is the documentation reasoning, and in robotics that starts with the transform tree, because a robot maintains several descriptions of where it is and they disagree on purpose."

Then the specification, precisely. ROS's REP 105 defines a single-parent tree, earth to map to odom to base_link, and gives two of those frames opposite guarantees: odom is guaranteed continuous and drifts without bound, map is explicitly not continuous and can jump at any time. Localisation publishes map → odom rather than map → base_link, specifically so the correction is applied in one place.

Then why that matters, with the number. I simulated twenty metres with two per cent slip and periodic fixes. The odom frame's error never moved more than 6.5 mm in a step; the map frame's jumped 120 mm when a fix landed. A controller differentiating position to get velocity sees 1.2 m/s of phantom velocity on a robot doing 1.0, so a 120 per cent error, with every component behaving correctly. The rule is to differentiate odom, navigate in map, and never mix them in one calculation, and that sentence is what most API documentation leaves the reader to infer.

The documentation point I would raise in a planning meeting. A simulator can be configured with perfect localisation, which makes the distinction above invisible. So a tutorial that is correct, reproducible and verified in CI can teach a model that fails on hardware, and nothing in the pipeline notices. That is the sim-to-real gap as a documentation problem rather than a physics one, and the mitigation is editorial: mark which claims were verified on hardware.

What I would not claim. No ROS, no Isaac Sim, no robot. The frame reasoning and the simulated demonstration are mine; the operating experience is not, and context tier is the accurate label.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A short simulation showing the two frames' properties, and a page stating which frame answers which question.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run step 2 and predict which frame has the larger single-step change before you look. People reliably guess the drifting one.
  2. Take any robotics tutorial you have and check whether it says which frame its poses are in. Most say "the pose" and mean one of two incompatible things.
  3. Check whether a sample that times anything reads the simulation clock or the system clock. Under a simulator that can pause, the difference is not subtle.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. REP 105's frame names, ordering, continuity guarantees and transform ownership were verified by opening the specification, and the drift-against-jump measurement is a short script that ran here. What is absent is the entire stack: no ROS installation, no Isaac Sim, no USD robot description driven through a simulator, and no hardware. The demonstrated page records this concept as having no demonstration in either repository.

docs.title: Sample applications and galleries
docs.text:
A gallery is a list of promises, and the two ways it breaks are a sample that stopped working and a sample nobody needed.

supporting · difficulty 3 · 6h

Asked for by name

Intel: "This role owns the developer first experience end to end across the Intel AI stack, including quickstarts, golden paths, reference documentation, tutorials, samples, and structured learning paths, by writing and maintaining developer documentation, the sample-app gallery, site navigation, and a crawlable, agent-ready front door"

Prerequisites: Sample walkthroughs, Code-sample validation

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A set of complete, runnable applications, and an index that presents them. Unlike a code sample in a page, a sample app is a standalone project a reader can clone and run; unlike a walkthrough, it is not primarily there to be read.

Intel names the sample-app gallery as an owned artifact. The word that matters is gallery, because it is the index that creates the obligations. A gallery is a published list of promises: these things exist, they work, and they are worth your time.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because a gallery is where a corpus's maintenance debt becomes visible to readers.

A documentation page that goes stale misleads whoever reads it. A sample app that goes stale wastes an hour of someone's afternoon before failing, and they conclude the product is broken rather than the sample. Then the gallery entry that promised it is still sitting there, with a title and a description, in a list that implies curation.

The quantity makes it worse. Forty samples, each with its own dependencies and its own release cadence, is forty independent decay processes. Which is why this is difficulty 3 and why it depends on code-sample validation: a gallery without automated verification is a liability that grows.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a gallery with a manifest, verify every entry, then ask whether the gallery covers anything readers need. About forty minutes. The second measurement is the one that changes what you build.

Committed as drills/gallery_audit.py, and that is not a convenience here. The page below shows the manifest in full and the checker in fragments, and quotes output from a check_gallery.py whose source it never prints, against three sample programs it never writes. The output block was unreachable: a reader could follow every step and have nothing to run. The drill is the complete version, the manifest in it is the one above, and a test holds the two together.

One row order changed when it was committed. The three zero-ticket topics used to be listed in the order a Python set happened to iterate them, which is to say in no order at all; they are now in the order the manifest introduces them. A table that cannot be regenerated is a screenshot with extra steps.

Step 1: the gallery as a manifest, not a page

mkdir -p gallery/samples/{hello,batch,stale} && cd gallery
cat > gallery.yaml <<'EOF'
samples:
  - id: hello
    title: Hello widget
    teaches: [install, first-call]
    entrypoint: samples/hello/main.py
    expect: "widgets: 3"
  - id: batch
    title: Batch requests
    teaches: [batching]
    entrypoint: samples/batch/main.py
    expect: "sent 2 batches"
  - id: stale
    title: Streaming responses
    teaches: [streaming]
    entrypoint: samples/stale/main.py
    expect: "streamed 10 chunks"
  - id: missing
    title: Webhooks
    teaches: [webhooks]
    entrypoint: samples/missing/main.py
    expect: "received 1 webhook"
EOF

The manifest is the gallery. The page that readers see is generated from it, which means the index cannot list something the manifest does not describe, and every claim in it is checkable. teaches and expect are the two fields that make the rest of this page possible.

Step 2: verify every entry

for s in gallery["samples"]:
    entry = Path(s["entrypoint"])
    if not entry.exists():
        problems.append(f"{s['id']}: entrypoint {entry} does not exist")
        continue
    r = subprocess.run([sys.executable, str(entry)],
                       capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=30)
    if r.returncode != 0:
        problems.append(f"{s['id']}: exited {r.returncode}")
    elif s["expect"] not in r.stdout:
        problems.append(f"{s['id']}: expected {s['expect']!r}, got {r.stdout.strip()!r}")

python3 check_gallery.py

GALLERY  stale: expected 'streamed 10 chunks', got 'streamed 8 chunks'
GALLERY  missing: entrypoint samples/missing/main.py does not exist
FAIL: 2/4 samples verified
exit=1

Two defect classes, and they are different in kind.

stale is drift: the sample runs and its behaviour changed, which only an output assertion catches, exactly as on the code-sample validation page. missing is worse: a gallery entry with a title, a description and no code. Somebody listed a sample they intended to write.

Half the gallery was a promise it could not keep, and the index gave no sign.

Step 3: ask what the gallery covers

A verified gallery can still be useless. Cross the teaches tags against what readers ask about.

The ticket counts below are invented, because this project has no support queue. They stand in for the one input this measurement cannot be run without, and they are the shape such a distribution reliably has: a long head of failure-mode questions and a tail of feature questions. Substitute your own before drawing any conclusion from the arithmetic.

covered = {t for s in gallery["samples"] for t in s["teaches"]}
#: Stand-in for a real support queue. Replace with yours.
asked_about = {"retries": 41, "auth": 33, "error-handling": 28,
               "pagination": 12, "batching": 6, "streaming": 3}

topic             in gallery  tickets
retries                    -       41
auth                       -       33
error-handling             -       28
pagination                 -       12
batching                 yes        6
streaming                yes        3
install                  yes        0
first-call               yes        0
webhooks                 yes        0

tickets about uncovered topics: 114 of 123

On that stand-in distribution, 114 of 123 tickets concern topics with no sample. The gallery covers install, first call and webhooks, which generate no tickets at all, and covers none of retries, auth, error handling or pagination. The arithmetic is only as good as the input; what travels is the shape, and the shape is not an accident.

That is the normal state of a gallery, and the reason is structural rather than negligent. Samples get written when a feature ships, so the gallery documents the happy path of each feature and nothing about the failure modes readers hit in production. Retries and error handling are not features; they are what happens when features meet reality, so nobody is assigned to demonstrate them.

Step 4: what the two measurements tell you to do

verified: 2/4
demand coverage: 9 of 123 tickets

Those numbers point in different directions, and both are actionable. The verification failure says fix or delete two entries today. The coverage gap says the next sample you write should be about retries, not about the feature that shipped last week.

Deleting is the underrated half. A gallery of ten samples that all work and cover the top three support topics beats forty where six are broken, and missing should be removed from the manifest rather than left as an aspiration.

What you built. A manifest whose claims are checked, a verification run that found half the gallery wanting, and a demand measurement that says what to write next.

docs.text:
In-page sample Walkthrough Sample app Length Lines A page A project Read or run Read Read, then run Run, then read Dependencies The docs build The docs build Its own Decay rate Slow Slow Fast, independently Verified by Sample validation Same Its own CI job Right for One API call One task end to end An architecture

A sample app earns its cost when the thing being shown is a shape: how the pieces fit, how configuration is layered, what a real project's structure looks like. For anything smaller, an in-page sample is cheaper to maintain and likelier to be read.

docs.title: The manifest fields that earn their place
docs.text:
Field Enables entrypoint Verification; without it the gallery cannot be checked expect Catching drift rather than only breakage teaches The coverage measurement in step 3 stack or requires Filtering, and a reproducibility check updated or verified Freshness, per sample status Permits a published "unmaintained" state

teaches is the one most galleries omit and the one that makes the gallery analysable. Without it you cannot answer whether the gallery covers anything, only whether it runs.

docs.title: How galleries actually fail
docs.text: Failure Cause Detected by A sample no longer runs Dependency or API change Running it in CI A sample runs and lies Behaviour drifted An output assertion A listed sample does not exist Someone listed an intention Entrypoint check The gallery covers nothing readers need Samples follow feature launches The demand measurement Forty samples, six broken No per-sample ownership All of the above, plus retirement Each sample pins differently No shared environment policy Reproducible environments

docs.title: Running them in CI without the bill
docs.text:
Strategy Cost Every sample on every pull request Prohibitive past a handful Nightly, all samples Good default; failures open issues On pull request, only samples touching changed paths Fast and partial Weekly, with dependency updates Catches upstream drift specifically Smoke only: it starts and exits 0 Cheap, and misses drift

Nightly plus output assertions is the usual right answer. Smoke testing a gallery is the common choice and it catches only the first failure row above.

docs.title: Retiring a sample
docs.text: A gallery needs a documented way to remove an entry, or it only grows. Retirement applies: remove it from the manifest, leave a redirect if it had a URL, and say why. A sample marked unmaintained in a gallery is more honest than one quietly broken, and far more honest than one listed and absent.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the gallery as a promise list. "A sample app that goes stale costs a reader an hour and they conclude the product is broken, not the sample. So the gallery is a manifest rather than a page: each entry declares an entrypoint, an expected output and what it teaches, the page is generated from it, and CI runs every one."

The follow-up is coverage, and this is the stronger half. A verified gallery can still be useless. Crossing the teaches tags against support volume on my own worked example puts 114 of 123 tickets on topics with no sample. I should be clear that those ticket counts are invented, since I have no support queue; the reason to expect that shape is structural. Samples get written when features ship, so a gallery documents each feature's happy path and nothing about retries, auth or error handling. Those are not features, so nobody is assigned to demonstrate them.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Every sample is an independent maintenance commitment with its own dependency tree, and the honest consequence is that the right number of samples is much smaller than teams want. Ten that work and cover the top support topics beat forty with six broken, and getting from forty to ten means deleting, which needs a retirement policy nobody wants to write.

One sharper point. The entrypoint check is the cheapest finding in this whole area. A gallery entry with a title, a description and no code is the easiest thing in the world to create, because the index and the implementation live in different places. One Path.exists() per entry catches it, and on an old gallery it usually catches something.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A gallery driven by a manifest, a CI job that runs every entry and asserts its output, and a coverage measurement against support volume.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Step 2's entrypoint check takes a minute to write and finds real things.
  2. Tag your existing samples with what they teach, then rank your support topics by volume. The gap is your backlog, and it will not look like your roadmap.
  3. Pick the oldest sample nobody has verified and run it. Whatever happens is information.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Neither of this guide's repositories ships a sample gallery, which the demonstrated page records; docpack validates samples embedded in its own documentation, which is the in-page case rather than this one. What travels is one real measurement and one method: half the gallery was unverifiable, which the entrypoint and output checks found, and the coverage cross-tabulation is a method whose ticket counts here are invented and have to come from your own queue.

docs.title: Sample walkthroughs
docs.text:
Explaining code that already exists, and transcluding it so the prose cannot quietly disagree with the file.

core · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

Intel: "Write and maintain reference documentation, tutorials, and sample walkthroughs that assume no prior context"

Prerequisites: Designing tutorials

Leads to: Sample applications and galleries

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A page that explains a sample that already exists. The reader does not build anything; they read working code with a guide pointing at the parts that matter and saying why each is there.

It is the inverse of a tutorial. A tutorial withholds the finished thing and grows it; a walkthrough starts from the finished thing and decomposes it. Both are legitimate, and they fail differently: a tutorial fails on sequencing, a walkthrough fails on drift, because it quotes code that lives somewhere else.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Intel lists walkthroughs alongside reference and tutorials, which is the right company: all three are the explain-this-thing layer rather than the get-started layer.

Walkthroughs matter disproportionately for a sample gallery, which Intel also names. A gallery of twenty samples with no walkthroughs is twenty repositories a reader has to reverse-engineer. The walkthrough is what converts a sample from a thing you can run into a thing you can learn from.

The engineering problem is specific. A walkthrough is prose containing copies of code, and copies drift. Nothing about the prose changes when the sample is edited, so the page becomes wrong silently and confidently.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Catch a drifted walkthrough, fix it with transclusion, then find out how the fix fails. About thirty minutes.

Committed as drills/walkthrough_transclusion.py, which runs all five states with a real MkDocs build behind the three that render. A test asserts it still prints what this page quotes.

Committing it corrected a count. This page used to report three quoted blocks where the walkthrough it tells you to write has two, a figure left over from an earlier version of the sample. The drifted-block finding was right and the total beside it was not, which is a fair illustration of the page's own argument: a quoted figure has no idea what it is describing.

Step 1: a sample and a walkthrough of it

mkdir -p walk-demo/samples && cd walk-demo
cat > samples/sync.py <<'EOF'
"""A minimal sync tool."""
import click

RETRIES = 5


@click.command()
@click.option("--dry-run", is_flag=True, help="Report without writing.")
def main(dry_run):
    """Sync records."""
    mode = "would sync" if dry_run else "synced"
    print(f"{mode} 0 records (retries={RETRIES})")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
EOF

And a walkthrough that quotes it, with one value already stale:

cat > walkthrough.md <<'MDEOF'
# Walkthrough: the sync tool

The retry count is a module constant:

```python
RETRIES = 3
```

The command takes one flag:

```python
@click.option("--dry-run", is_flag=True, help="Report without writing.")
```
MDEOF

Step 2: check every quoted block against the file

sample = Path("samples/sync.py").read_text()
blocks = re.findall(r"^```python\n(.*?)^```", text, re.S | re.M)

for i, b in enumerate(blocks, 1):
    snippet = b.rstrip("\n")
    if snippet not in sample:
        problems.append(f"block {i}: not found in samples/sync.py: "
                        f"{snippet.splitlines()[0]!r}")

python3 check_walkthrough.py

WALK  block 1: not found in samples/sync.py: 'RETRIES = 3'
FAIL: 2 quoted block(s), 1 drifted

Caught. That check is twelve lines and it is the minimum a walkthrough needs, because this failure is undetectable by reading: the prose is internally coherent and the code looks plausible.

Step 3: remove the possibility instead of checking for it

Transclude the lines rather than copying them:

cat > mkdocs.yml <<'EOF'
site_name: W
markdown_extensions:
  - pymdownx.snippets:
      base_path: ["."]
      check_paths: true
  - pymdownx.superfences
EOF

cat > docs/index.md <<'MDEOF'
# Walkthrough: the sync tool

The retry count is a module constant:

```python
--8<-- "samples/sync.py:4:4"
```
MDEOF

rendered:  RETRIES = 5

The page now shows what the file says. Change the file and rebuild:

sed -i 's/^RETRIES = 5/RETRIES = 7/' samples/sync.py

rendered:  RETRIES = 7

Drift is now impossible rather than merely detected.

Step 4: break the fix

Line numbers are a reference into a file that moves. Insert two lines near the top, which is what adding an import looks like:

# insert a blank line and `from __future__ import annotations` after line 1
python3 -m mkdocs build -q

rendered for "the retry count":  import click
rendered for "the command flag": (empty)

Silently wrong. The page confidently presents import click as the retry count, the second block renders empty, and the build exits zero. This is worse than the drift in step 2, because step 2's defect was at least detectable by a string comparison and this one is not: the transclusion is working exactly as instructed.

Step 5: anchor by name

Mark the region in the sample and reference it by name:

# --8<-- [start:retries]
RETRIES = 7
# --8<-- [end:retries]

--8<-- "samples/sync.py:retries"

rendered:  RETRIES = 7

Now insertions anywhere else in the file do not affect it, because the reference is to a named region rather than to a position. The cost is two comment lines in the sample, which is the right price.

What you built. A drift check, a transclusion that removes the drift, and the knowledge that line-range transclusion introduces a quieter failure than the one it fixes.

docs.title: Three ways to put code in a walkthrough
docs.text:
Approach Drift Fails when Cost Copy and paste Likely The sample is edited None up front Transclude by line range Impossible Lines are inserted above A build dependency Transclude by named anchor Impossible The anchor is deleted Two comment lines in the sample

Named anchors are the answer, and the reason to know all three is that you will inherit the first and be tempted to stop at the second.

docs.title: Walkthrough against tutorial
docs.text: Walkthrough Tutorial Starting point Finished sample Empty directory Reader types Nothing, or runs it once Everything Risk Prose drifts from the sample Sequencing hides defects Mitigation Transclusion Output at every step Good for Showing how a real thing is built Teaching how to build one Length Bounded by the sample Bounded by the lesson

docs.title: What to point at, and in what order
docs.text:
Order Explain 1 What the sample does, from the outside, with its output 2 The entry point, so the reader can orient 3 The parts that carry the interesting decisions 4 What was deliberately left out, and why Never Every line

The fourth row is the one that distinguishes a good walkthrough. A sample omits error handling, retries, authentication and configuration, and a reader who is not told that will assume the sample is a template for production. Saying what is missing is part of explaining what is there.

docs.title: Keeping a walkthrough honest
docs.text:
Check Catches Quoted blocks appear in the sample Copy-paste drift Named anchors still exist A deleted region, which transclusion fails loudly on The sample runs See sample validation The stated output matches The sample's behaviour changed Anchor count in the sample matches references An orphaned anchor nobody removed

The last one is cheap and worth having. An anchor left in a sample after the walkthrough stopped using it is a small mess that accumulates.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the failure mode, because it is specific to this form. "A walkthrough is prose containing copies of code, so it drifts: nothing about the page changes when the sample is edited, and the page becomes confidently wrong. So I transclude rather than quote, and the page cannot disagree with the file."

The follow-up is how transclusion itself fails, and this is the part worth having run. Line-range transclusion breaks on insertion, silently: after adding two lines to my sample, the paragraph about the retry count rendered import click and the build exited zero. Named anchors fix it, and the cost is two comment lines in the sample.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Transclusion puts documentation markers in source files, which some teams will not accept, and it means the walkthrough cannot show a simplified version of the code. Sometimes you want to show a cut-down snippet for teaching, and then you are back to copying with a drift check. Both mechanisms have a place; the mistake is using copying by default.

One sharper point. Say what the sample leaves out. A reader who is not told that a sample omits error handling and authentication will treat it as a production template, and samples are copied into production constantly. That sentence costs nothing and prevents the most expensive misreading a walkthrough can produce.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A walkthrough that transcludes by named anchor, plus a check that no quoted block has drifted for anything still copied.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the step 2 check against a walkthrough you own. Copy-paste drift is extremely common and completely invisible to review.
  2. If you already transclude by line range, insert a line above one of the ranges and rebuild. The silence is the finding.
  3. Add one sentence to your most-read walkthrough saying what the sample deliberately omits.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Neither of this guide's repositories contains a sample walkthrough, which the demonstrated page records. What travels is the measured progression: a drift check that caught a stale constant, a transclusion that made drift impossible, and the insertion test showing that the obvious transclusion fails more quietly than the problem it solved.

docs.title: Screencasts and video
docs.text:
A screencast script is a code sample with timestamps, so it can be tested; the recording cannot be fixed, which is the whole cost of the medium.

context · difficulty 2 · 4h

Adjacent, not quoted

Neither posting mentions video. A common secondary deliverable in developer-relations roles.

Prerequisites: Designing tutorials

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A recording of someone doing the thing, usually narrated. It is the only documentation format where the reader can see tacit detail: which pane the output appeared in, how long the build actually took, what the error looked like before it was tidied into a code block.

It is also the only format in this guide that cannot be diffed, searched by phrase, copy-pasted from, link-checked, or corrected without being remade. Each of those is a property the rest of a docs-as-code toolchain depends on, so a screencast sits outside every mechanism described elsewhere here, which is the reason this concept is tier context rather than core.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because some things genuinely do not survive being written down, and because people ask for video regardless.

The legitimate case is narrow and real: an unfamiliar interface where the hard part is knowing where to look, a workflow whose shape only becomes obvious when you watch someone move through it, or a result so visual that describing it is absurd. For those, thirty seconds of video beats a page.

The illegitimate case is more common. Video is requested because it feels more approachable, produced because it is satisfying to make, and watched by far fewer people than a page, having cost ten times as much and become wrong within a quarter with nothing to detect it. That failure is not a reason to refuse; it is a reason to build the half of the artifact that can be maintained.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Treat the script as code and test it, then watch the recording become wrong anyway. About twenty-five minutes, and the second half is the point.

Committed as drills/screencast_script.py, which walks all three states in one run. A test asserts it still prints the lines quoted below.

Step 1: the script as a structured artifact

Not a document. A list of beats, each with what is said, what is run, and what appears:

title: Listing your widgets
beats:
  - at: "00:12"
    say: "First we list the widgets, and you should see three of them."
    run: "python3 widget.py"
    expect: "widgets: 3"
  - at: "00:41"
    say: "Now the same thing as JSON."
    run: "python3 widget.py --json"
    expect: '{"widgets": 3}'

The at field is what makes this worth doing. Everything else is an ordinary validated code sample; the timestamp is what turns a failure into an instruction about which four seconds of video are wrong.

Step 2: test it like a code sample, because that is what it is

for beat in script["beats"]:
    r = subprocess.run(beat["run"].split(), capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=30)
    if beat["expect"] not in r.stdout.strip():
        bad.append(f'  {beat["at"]}  expected {beat["expect"]!r}, got {r.stdout.strip()!r}')

DRIFT  00:41  expected '{"widgets": 3}', got 'widgets: 3'
1/2 beats still match what the video shows
exit=1

The second beat was never true. The --json flag the narration describes did not exist, and the script was written from what the author expected the tool to do. Had this gone to recording, the video would have shown a narrator confidently describing output nobody can reproduce.

That is the cheapest and most common video defect, and twenty lines of script-checking catches it before the microphone is switched on.

Step 3: implement the flag, and get a clean run

2/2 beats still match what the video shows
exit=0

Now the recording would be accurate. Record it, publish it, move on.

Step 4: upstream changes the output, as upstream does

sed -i 's/print("widgets: 3")/print("3 widgets found")/' widget.py

DRIFT  00:12  expected 'widgets: 3', got '3 widgets found'
1/2 beats still match what the video shows
exit=1

Twelve seconds in, the video shows output the tool no longer produces. The check caught it the next time CI ran, which is exactly what you want, and now compare what that detection is worth in each medium:

A page A screencast What is wrong Three characters Four seconds of footage Cost to fix An edit Re-record, or re-record everything after it Until then Fix it in the next commit It is live and wrong Reader's experience None Follows along, output differs, loses confidence

The detection is the same. The remedy is not, and the asymmetry is the entire argument about when to use video.

Step 5: what the checked script actually buys

Three things, none of which is a corrected video:

It stops wrong recordings being made, which is where most of the value is. It tells you, by timestamp, exactly which recordings are now stale and how badly, so a stale-video audit becomes a report rather than an afternoon of watching your own back catalogue. And it is a text artifact: searchable, diffable, and the thing you publish next to the video so that readers who want to copy a command, or skim in forty seconds, can.

Step 6: the measurement that decides this for a corpus

pages with code:  106
fenced blocks:    727
lines of code and output: 9982

Every one of those 727 blocks is checked: it renders as code, its structure is validated, and the samples with assertions are executed. The equivalent video corpus would have nine thousand lines of commands with nothing checking any of them, and no way to fix one without re-recording.

A screencast collection is only maintainable at a size where you are willing to re-record it. That number is small, and knowing it before you start is the difference between a useful handful of videos and a back catalogue nobody dares audit.

What you built. A script format that tests like a code sample, a drift check that reports by timestamp, two caught defects (one before recording and one after), and a clear-eyed account of what detection is worth in a medium you cannot patch.

docs.title: What video is actually better at
docs.text:
Situation Why video wins An unfamiliar GUI Knowing where to look is the hard part The shape of a workflow Sequence and rhythm do not survive prose A visual result Describing it is absurd Convincing someone it is easy Watching someone succeed is persuasive A conference talk recording The artifact already exists

Everything else is a page that someone wanted to be a video.

docs.title: What video cannot do
docs.text:
Property Consequence Not searchable by phrase Invisible to readers who search, and to retrieval Not copy-pasteable Viewers retype commands and mistype them Not diffable No review, no history of what changed Not link-checkable A URL on screen rots silently Not patchable A three-character fix means re-recording Not skimmable No way to find the one part you need Not agent-readable Absent from every retrieval pipeline

The last row is newly expensive. A corpus whose answers live in video is a corpus an assistant cannot answer from, which in practice means those answers have stopped existing.

docs.title: The companion-text rule
docs.text:
Every screencast ships with a text twin: the commands, the expected output, and the narration's substance. It costs little once the script exists in the format above, and it is what makes the video findable at all, since in practice the page is what people arrive at and the video is what some of them play.

Artifact Maintained Found by search Copy-pasteable Video alone No Barely No Video plus auto-transcript No Poorly No Video plus checked script The script is Yes Yes

docs.title: Production decisions that matter, briefly
docs.text: Decision Default Length Under four minutes, or chapter it One task per video Yes; compilations get abandoned partway Show the failure Yes, briefly; it is the tacit knowledge video is for Terminal size and font Large enough for a phone, which is where it is watched Narration Scripted; unscripted costs more in edit than it saves Captions Always, and they double as the transcript

docs.title: When to refuse
docs.text:
Request Better answer "Can we have a video of the quickstart?" Fix the quickstart "A video series for the whole product" One video, then count plays "Video because the docs are confusing" The confusion will be in the video too "Record the workshop and publish it" Publish the handout; the recording is three hours long

The third row is the one worth saying out loud in a planning meeting. Video does not fix unclear material, it embeds it in a format you cannot edit.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the asymmetry. "A screencast script is a code sample with timestamps, so I test it in CI like any other sample. What that buys is not a corrected video: a three-character change to a tool means four seconds of footage are wrong, and the fix is re-recording. The detection is identical to a page's and the remedy is not, which is the whole argument about when video is worth it."

The follow-up is what the checking caught. Two things, and the order matters. Before recording, a beat whose narration described a flag that did not exist, which is the commonest video defect and is free to catch. After recording, an upstream output change twelve seconds in, which the check flagged by timestamp, so a stale-video audit is a report instead of an afternoon rewatching your own back catalogue.

The scale point. My corpus has 727 code blocks over 9,982 lines, all checked. A video corpus of that size would have nothing checking any of it and no way to fix one line. Screencasts are maintainable only at a size you are willing to re-record, that number is small, and deciding it before you start is what separates a useful handful from a back catalogue nobody dares audit.

The tradeoff to volunteer. I am sceptical of video and it does win sometimes: an unfamiliar interface where knowing where to look is the hard part, or a workflow whose shape does not survive prose. For those, thirty seconds beats a page. What I would not do is answer "the docs are confusing" with a video, because the confusion ends up in the video too, in a format nobody can edit.

One sharper point. Video is now absent from retrieval. A corpus whose answers live in recordings is one an assistant cannot answer from, and since that is increasingly how people reach documentation, those answers have effectively stopped existing. The companion text is no longer a courtesy.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A script format with timestamps, expected output and narration, plus a CI job that runs every beat and reports drift by timestamp.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Take your most-watched screencast and run its commands by hand. Predict first whether they still produce what the video shows; the prediction is the exercise.
  2. Write the script for your next video in the beats format and run the checker before recording anything. Step 2 above caught a narration describing a flag that did not exist, which is the defect this prevents for free.
  3. Count the videos you currently publish and ask honestly whether you would re-record all of them for a three-character output change. The number you would re-record is the number you should maintain.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. The script checker above was executed, caught a beat that was never true, passed cleanly after the flag was implemented, and caught the upstream output change by timestamp; the corpus figures of 727 blocks and 9,982 lines come from this guide's own pages. What does not exist is a screencast: no video has been recorded, so the production guidance is conventional practice rather than measured, and the demonstrated page records screencasts as having no demonstration in either repository.
