docs.title: Search and query log analysis
docs.text:
Query logs are the only direct statement of what readers wanted, and an attempt to substitute a hand-built retrieval proxy for them measures the proxy.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

Adjacent, not quoted

Not named in either posting. The input that turns a hand-written evaluation set into a representative one.

Prerequisites: Findability and search design, Documentation analytics

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Reading what people typed into your search box. It is the highest-value reader-side signal in documentation and among the cheapest to collect, and it differs in kind from everything else on a dashboard: page views say what people found, queries say what they were looking for, including every time they did not find it.

The most useful single output is the zero-result list, which is a list, in readers' own words, of content you do not have.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because every other way of deciding what readers want is the author guessing.

A documentation roadmap is usually assembled from support escalations, the loudest internal stakeholder, and what the team believes is missing. Queries are the only input coming from readers who were not motivated enough to file a ticket, which is almost all of them.

The reason this sits beside retrieval evaluation in this curriculum is narrower and more interesting. A golden set of questions is hand-written, so it encodes the author's model of what readers ask. Query logs are what turn that set from plausible into representative, and without them there is no way to know which it is.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Try to do this without logs, fail, and work out what the failure is worth. About thirty minutes. The first measurement gets published nowhere.

Step 1: attempt the substitute

With no query logs, the obvious move is to simulate the reader. Take the most basic query anyone would type, a page's own name, and check whether that page comes back first. Score it over the site's real search index of 1,358 entries:

def search(q, limit=5):
    qt = toks(q)
    for loc, t in docs:
        tf = Counter(t)
        s = sum((tf[w] / len(t)) * math.log(N / (1 + df[w])) for w in qt if w in tf)

concepts searched by their own title: 90
rank of their own page: {1: 7, 2: 14, 3: 10, '4+': 42, 'none': 17}

not first for their own name: 83
   Information architecture   rank 9     top: paths/content-architect/#1-information-architecture
   Diátaxis                   rank None  top: paths/developer-educator/#5-designing-tutorials
   Content models             rank None  top: concepts/content-data-transformation/#read-first

Seven of ninety pages rank first for their own title. A catastrophic findability result with an obvious story attached: generated navigation pages carry concept names as headings, they are short, and a short document with the term in its heading beats the long page that explains it.

The story is wrong.

Step 2: check the mechanism before believing the number

That story claims generated pages duplicate concept titles and compete with them. The claim is structural, so it can be checked with no scorer at all:

concept titles appearing as an index entry's title outside their own page: 1 distinct
total such competing entries: 1
   Time to first success   concepts/quickstarts/#time-to-first-success   77 words

One. There is no duplication problem. The 7-of-90 figure came from my own length normalisation: dividing term frequency by document length rewards short sections, and a path page's one-line entry for a concept is about as short as a document gets. MkDocs Material uses lunr, with boosted title fields and different length handling, and does not rank this way.

I had built a proxy for search in order to avoid needing query logs, and the proxy measured itself. That is this page's lesson, reached the expensive way: a hand-built retrieval model is not a substitute for knowing what readers typed, because its failures are indistinguishable from findings.

Step 3: measure what does not depend on a ranking function

Three properties are structural, so no scorer can corrupt them:

complete pages whose own title words are absent from their text: 0/106
pages absent from the search index:                                 0
index entry titles that are not unique:                            42

The first two are clean. The third is the real finding:

Related                   x109
What it is                x107
Why the job asks for it   x107
The golden path           x107
Reference                 x107
How to talk about it      x107
How to prove it           x107

entries carrying one of those seven titles: 751 of 1505  (50%)

Half the search index carries one of seven titles. The page contract that makes this corpus consistent, and that CI enforces, has produced 751 sections indistinguishable by title.

The disambiguating information exists: every entry carries its location, so the page is recoverable, and Material's search UI uses it and shows the parent page, so a human browsing the site is fine. Any consumer using title alone is not, and that now includes retrieval pipelines and assistants reading an index directly. It is the same defect as a grounding report naming the page when it checked the chunk: the identifier has to carry the section, or ninety-one things look like one thing.

Step 4: the test logs would have passed

A golden set is meant to be representative. Twenty cases, hand-written by the author of the corpus. Then a real reader arrived with a real question, the only genuine query this project has ever received:

what is docpack actually creating or doing, and what should I be looking at

Scored against the twenty:

closest golden case: llms-txt-what   what is llms.txt and who proposed it      shared key terms: 1
closest golden case: install         how do I install docpack                  shared key terms: 1
closest golden case: exit-codes      what exit codes does the command return   shared key terms: 1

One shared key term, at best. A twenty-case set written specifically to represent reader questions held nothing resembling the first real one, and the missing case was not exotic: it was "what does this thing do", which is the question every reader has first.

One query is not a sample. The direction is not ambiguous either. The author wrote twenty questions about what the corpus explains, and the reader asked about what it had not thought to say.

Step 5: so collect them from day one

Internal search logging is a few lines of configuration and the only instrumentation in this field that reports content you do not have. Everything else measures the content you do.

What you built. A retrieval proxy that produced a plausible wrong finding, the structural check that disproved it, three measurements that survive without a scorer including 47 per cent of an index sharing seven titles, and a demonstration that a hand-written query set missed the first real question it met.

docs.title: What queries say that nothing else does
docs.text:
Signal Means Zero-result queries Content you do not have, in readers' words High volume, low click-through The page exists and the result looks wrong Queries that are error messages Readers arrive with a symptom, not a topic Words your docs never use A vocabulary gap, not a content gap Queries repeated within a session The first result failed A query straight after a page view That page did not answer

The fourth row is the most commonly misread. A term you do not use is usually not a missing page, it is a missing synonym on a page you already have, and writing a new page is the expensive way to fix it.

docs.title: What to do with each finding
docs.text: Finding Response Zero results, concept missing Write it Zero results, concept present Add the reader's words to the page High volume, wrong page first Fix titles, summaries and headings Error-message queries Index error strings; readers paste them verbatim A query refined twice in a session Watch the session, not the query Queries for things you removed A retirement redirect is missing

docs.title: Without logs, what is still honest
docs.text:
Check Needs a ranking function Does each page contain its own key terms No Is every page in the index No Are index entry titles unique No Are meta descriptions distinct No Do synonyms for each concept appear anywhere No Does each page rank first for its own name Yes, see step 2 Which of two retrievers is better Yes

Everything above the line is worth doing on day zero. Everything below needs either the real search engine or real queries, and a scorer you wrote yourself will answer confidently and wrongly.

docs.title: Privacy, briefly
docs.text: Query strings are user-submitted text, and people paste surprising things into search boxes: internal hostnames, tokens, customer names. Aggregate before storing, keep a short retention window, and do not log queries alongside an identity unless someone agreed to that. None of this is a reason to skip collection; it is a reason to collect the aggregate rather than the transcript.

docs.title: Why this concept is adjacent rather than quoted
docs.text: Neither posting names search logs, and both ask for measurement that depends on them. NVIDIA's "AI answer quality" and "repeat questions" are each evaluation over a question set, and a question set without query data is the author's guess about readers, which is exactly the gap step 4 measures.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the asymmetry. "Page views tell me what people found. Queries tell me what they were looking for, including every time they did not find it. The zero-result list is the only artifact in documentation analytics that describes content you do not have, and it costs a few lines of configuration to start collecting."

The follow-up is what I did without logs, and the honest answer is that I got it wrong. I built a scorer over my own search index to check whether each page ranks first for its own name, and got seven of ninety, which looked like a catastrophe with a tidy explanation about generated pages competing for terms. The explanation was structural, so I checked it, and exactly one competing entry existed. The seven-of-ninety was my own length normalisation rewarding short sections. I had built a proxy for search to avoid needing query data, and measured the proxy.

What survives without logs is worth saying too. Structural checks cannot be corrupted by a scorer: every page contains its own key terms, every page is in the index, and 751 of 1,505 entries carry one of seven titles because the page contract gives every page the same seven sections. A human browsing Material is fine, since the UI shows the parent page, but anything consuming title alone, a retrieval pipeline included, sees ninety-one identical things.

The point to close on. My golden set has twenty hand-written questions and was meant to be representative. The first real reader asked what the thing actually produces and what he should be looking at, and that shared at most one key term with any of the twenty. One query is not a sample, but the direction is not ambiguous: I wrote twenty questions about what the corpus explains, and the reader asked about what it had not thought to say. Logs close that gap and nothing else does.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. Search logging enabled on a corpus you own, and a weekly zero-result list somebody actually reads.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Turn on internal search logging if it is off. It is the cheapest instrumentation in this field and the only one that reports absence.
  2. Compare your evaluation question set against the last ten real questions you received from anybody, counting shared terms. Predict the number first; mine was one.
  3. Check whether your index entry titles are unique. If your pages share a template they are not, and any consumer reading titles without locations is presenting duplicates.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. The structural measurements run against this guide's built search index and are reproducible; the failed proxy and its disproof are both recorded above rather than tidied away. What does not exist is a single query log: no site has been published, so there are no queries, no zero-result list and no click-through data, and the one real reader question in step 4 arrived in conversation rather than through a search box. The demonstrated page records the concept as having no demonstration on the log side.

docs.title: Security guidance as encoded standard
docs.text:
Documentation samples get copy-pasted into production, so the security review belongs in CI rather than in a wiki page.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Encode standards (user stories, release readiness, onboarding, security guidance) into templates, validators, and guided workflows rather than static documents"

Prerequisites: Style guides and terminology management

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Turning the security rules your documentation must follow into checks that run, rather than a page telling authors to be careful. NVIDIA's bullet is explicit about the preference: templates, validators and guided workflows rather than static documents.

The specific problem is that documentation code samples are the most copy-pasted code in any organisation. A sample is read as a recommendation, so an insecure sample propagates the insecurity into every project that follows the quickstart.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because a documentation site is a distribution channel for patterns.

An engineer who writes verify=False in their own code has made a local mistake. A documentation page that writes verify=False has made that mistake in every project that follows it, with the authority of official guidance, for as long as the page lives. The blast radius is the difference, and it is why security guidance belongs on the list of standards worth encoding.

The second reason is in NVIDIA's own phrasing: you will "interface with Security". A security team can give you a policy document. Converting that into a validator is the part they cannot do for you, and arriving with one is a much better opening than arriving with questions.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Write a linter for documentation samples, find out it misses one of the things it was written to catch, and fix the quickstart it ran against. About thirty minutes.

Committed as drills/security_lint.py, which walks all three states in one run. A test asserts the drill still prints the findings quoted below, and that its two sample quickstarts are the ones this page tells you to write.

Step 1: a quickstart with six realistic problems

mkdir -p sec-demo/docs && cd sec-demo
cat > docs/quickstart.md <<'MDEOF'
# Quickstart

Install and configure:

```bash
curl -sSL https://example.com/install.sh | sudo bash
export WIDGET_TOKEN=sk-live-abc123def456
```

Connect from Python:

```python
import requests
r = requests.get("https://api.example.com/widgets", verify=False)
client = Client(token="sk-live-abc123def456")
```

Grant access:

```bash
chmod 777 /etc/widget
aws s3api put-bucket-acl --bucket widgets --acl public-read
```
MDEOF

None of this is exotic. Every line appears in real documentation.

Step 2: the rules, as data

RULES = [
    ("pipe-to-shell", re.compile(r"curl[^|\n]*\|\s*(sudo\s+)?(ba)?sh"),
     "piping a downloaded script into a shell teaches an unverifiable install"),
    ("tls-disabled", re.compile(r"verify\s*=\s*False|--insecure\b|InsecureSkipVerify"),
     "disabling certificate verification"),
    ("hardcoded-secret",
     re.compile(r"""(token|key|secret|password)\s*[=:]\s*["']?(sk-|pk_|AKIA)[A-Za-z0-9_-]{6,}"""),
     "a credential-shaped literal; use a placeholder or an env var"),
    ("world-writable", re.compile(r"chmod\s+(777|a\+rwx|o\+w)"),
     "world-writable permissions"),
    ("public-acl", re.compile(r"--acl\s+public-read|public-read-write"),
     "granting public access to a bucket"),
]

Each rule carries a name, a pattern and the reason, because a finding that does not explain itself gets suppressed rather than fixed.

Step 3: run it, and count carefully

python3 seclint.py

SEC  docs/quickstart.md:6:  pipe-to-shell: piping a downloaded script into a shell teaches an unverifiable install
SEC  docs/quickstart.md:14: tls-disabled: disabling certificate verification
SEC  docs/quickstart.md:15: hardcoded-secret: a credential-shaped literal; use a placeholder or an env var
SEC  docs/quickstart.md:21: world-writable: world-writable permissions
SEC  docs/quickstart.md:22: public-acl: granting public access to a bucket
FAIL: 5 finding(s)

Five findings. There are two hardcoded secrets in that page, on lines 7 and 15, and only line 15 was reported.

Step 4: the miss

line = "export WIDGET_TOKEN=sk-live-abc123def456"
print(bool(re.search(pat, line)))        # False
print(bool(re.search(pat, line, re.I)))  # True

WIDGET_TOKEN is uppercase and the pattern's alternation is lowercase. The rule was case-sensitive, and environment variables are conventionally uppercase, so the rule missed the single most common way a credential appears in a shell sample.

re.compile(r"""(?i)(token|key|secret|password)\s*[=:]\s*...""")

SEC  docs/quickstart.md:6:  pipe-to-shell: piping a downloaded script into a shell teaches an unverifiable install
SEC  docs/quickstart.md:7:  hardcoded-secret: a credential-shaped literal; use a placeholder or an env var
SEC  docs/quickstart.md:14: tls-disabled: disabling certificate verification
SEC  docs/quickstart.md:15: hardcoded-secret: a credential-shaped literal; use a placeholder or an env var
SEC  docs/quickstart.md:21: world-writable: world-writable permissions
SEC  docs/quickstart.md:22: public-acl: granting public access to a bucket
FAIL: 6 finding(s)

This is the third time case sensitivity has silently disabled a rule in this guide: once in a Vale rule on the style guide page, and twice here counting the rule and the finding it hid. For security rules it matters more, because the failure mode is a green build on a page that teaches a credential leak.

Step 5: fix the documentation, which is the point

cat > docs/quickstart.md <<'MDEOF'
# Quickstart

Install, verifying the download first:

```bash
curl -sSLO https://example.com/install.sh
sha256sum -c install.sh.sha256
bash install.sh
export WIDGET_TOKEN="$(cat ~/.config/widget/token)"
```

Connect from Python:

```python
import os
import requests

r = requests.get("https://api.example.com/widgets")
client = Client(token=os.environ["WIDGET_TOKEN"])
```

Grant access to the service account only:

```bash
chmod 750 /etc/widget
aws s3api put-bucket-acl --bucket widgets --acl private
```
MDEOF

python3 seclint.py; echo "exit=$?"

ok: 0 finding(s)
exit=0

Note what changed in the install step. The insecure version was shorter and the secure version teaches verification, which is the real tradeoff: secure samples are usually longer, and the pressure on a quickstart is always toward brevity.

What you built. A gate that fails a build on a sample readers should not copy, and a corrected quickstart.

docs.title: Rules worth encoding
docs.text:
Rule Catches Pipe-to-shell curl ... | sudo bash installs TLS verification disabled verify=False, --insecure, InsecureSkipVerify Credential-shaped literals sk-, pk_, AKIA, long hex after a key-ish name World-writable permissions chmod 777 Public bucket or object ACLs --acl public-read Long-lived credentials where short-lived exist A static key where OIDC is available latest tags in a security context Unpinned base images in a sample Secrets in a URL https://user:pass@host

Use (?i) on all of them. Environment variables are uppercase, Go field names are capitalised, and YAML keys vary.

docs.title: What this is not
docs.text:
Not this Why A code scanner for the product That is the security team's job on the real codebase A substitute for threat modelling It checks patterns, not design A claim of security review It is a floor; the pages may still advise badly

Be precise about that last one in an interview. The gate catches a list of known-bad patterns in samples. It does not mean the documentation gives secure advice, and a page can pass every rule while recommending an insecure architecture in prose.

docs.title: The other standards on NVIDIA's list
docs.text:
The bullet names four, and all four follow the same pattern:

Standard Static document Encoded as Security guidance "Be careful with credentials" The linter above Release readiness A checklist page A CI gate per item Onboarding A "getting started for writers" page A scaffold command plus local gates User stories A template in a wiki An issue template with required fields

The move is identical each time: find the part of the standard that is a rule, make it fail a build, and leave in writing only the part that needs judgment. Which is the same split as the style guide.

docs.title: Working with a security team
docs.text:
They give you You turn it into A policy document A rule list, and questions about the ambiguous parts An approved-patterns list Templates and scaffolds that produce them by default A finding on a doc page A rule, so the class cannot return A review requirement A gate plus a named reviewer for what the gate cannot judge

The third row is the one that compounds. A security finding on a single page is worth fixing once; converted into a rule it is worth fixing forever, and that conversion is the thing you are being hired to do rather than asked to do.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with blast radius. "Documentation samples are the most copy-pasted code in an organisation, and a sample reads as a recommendation. An engineer writing verify=False has made a local mistake; a quickstart doing it has made that mistake in every project that follows it, with official authority. So the security rules go in CI rather than in a page asking authors to be careful."

The follow-up is where the rules come from, and the good answer is the security team's own policy converted into patterns, plus every past finding on a doc page turned into a rule so the class cannot return.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Secure samples are longer. Verifying a checksum before running an installer is three lines where the insecure version is one, and the pressure on a quickstart is always toward brevity because time to first success is the metric. That tension is real, and the honest resolution is that the quickstart gets the secure version and the brevity is bought elsewhere, not by teaching a bad pattern.

One sharper point. Use case-insensitive patterns. My own rule for credential literals was case-sensitive and missed export WIDGET_TOKEN=sk-live-..., which is the single most common shape a secret takes in a shell sample, because environment variables are uppercase by convention. A security rule that silently matches nothing is worse than no rule, and you only find out by writing a fixture that must fail.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A sample linter in CI with a named rule list, plus one commit where it caught something in your own documentation.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path, and count the findings before reading step 4.
  2. Point the linter at a quickstart you own. Pipe-to-shell and credential literals are both common enough that you will probably find one.
  3. Take the last security finding anyone raised about your documentation and write it as a rule.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. The linter is committed as drills/security_lint.py and reproduces all three states in one run: five findings against six planted problems, six once the rule is case-insensitive, and none once the quickstart is actually repaired. A test asserts that the drill still prints the lines quoted above, in both directions, so the figures on this page cannot drift from the code that produces them.

What neither repository has is a security gate in its own CI, which the demonstrated page records: this is a linter with a fixture, not a policy applied to a real corpus. What travels is the honest account of the miss, which is the more useful half. Six problems planted, five found, and the sixth hidden by a case-sensitivity bug in the rule written to catch exactly that.

docs.title: SEO for documentation
docs.text:
Making a page findable by someone searching the problem rather than the product.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

Optimize documentation for search (SEO and GEO) and for AI assistants and coding agents through agentready, LLMdigestible content

Source: intel posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: Metadata for navigation and retrieval

Leads to: Crawlability and the agent-ready front door, Generative engine optimization

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Making a documentation page findable by someone who searches the problem rather than the product. Most developers do not navigate to your docs; they search an error message, a symptom, or a task, and land deep inside.

Documentation SEO is a narrow and unglamorous subset of SEO. There is no link building and no content marketing. It is mostly titles, descriptions, headings and URLs, done consistently, derived from a content model rather than hand-tuned per page.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Intel names it in a responsibility and again in minimum qualifications: "Experience optimizing technical content for search (SEO and GEO) and for AI assistants." That is unusual for an engineering-adjacent role and it tells you something about how Intel sees the job: the front door is a search result page they do not own.

On a Tuesday it is a specific recurring decision. An engineer titles a page "Configuration Options Reference". Nobody searches that. The developer who needs it is searching "widget server out of memory" or "how to set batch size", and your page ranks for neither because it contains the word "configuration" where the reader used the word "memory".

The reason this is supporting rather than core: once the content model requires a real title and summary, most of the mechanical work is a build step, and the rest is a writing habit covered by technical writing. But the habit is worth a page because the default failure is systematic. Documentation gets titled from the structure of the product and searched from the state of the reader, and nothing in a normal review catches the mismatch.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Generate the search-visible surface from the content model, then find the pages whose vocabulary does not match their readers'. Thirty minutes.

Step 1: a corpus with the usual problem

mkdir -p seo-drill/docs && cd seo-drill
cat > docs/configuration-reference.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Configuration Options Reference
summary: Reference for configuration options.
kind: reference
updated: 2026-10-26
---
# Configuration Options Reference

| Flag | Default |
|---|---|
| `max_memory_gb` | 16 |
| `batch_size` | 32 |

Setting `max_memory_gb` too low causes the server to exit during load rather
than at startup.
EOF

cat > docs/getting-started.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Getting Started
summary: Get started with the widget platform.
kind: tutorial
updated: 2026-10-26
---
# Getting Started

Install the CLI with `pip install widget`, then run your first inference.
EOF

cat > docs/troubleshooting-oom.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Fix an out-of-memory error under load
summary: Diagnose and fix a widget server that runs out of GPU memory under load but starts fine.
kind: how-to
updated: 2026-10-26
---
# Fix an out-of-memory error under load

If the server starts cleanly and dies under traffic, it is sized for startup
memory rather than peak.
EOF
ls docs/

Step 2: generate the search surface, do not hand-write it

cat > seo.py <<'PY'
"""Generate the search-visible surface from the content model.

Every field here is derived from front matter the content model already
requires. The reason to generate rather than hand-write: a per-page SEO
description written once at publication describes a page that no longer
exists, and nothing in the site contradicts it.
"""
import datetime as dt
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

BASE = "https://widget.example/docs"
SITE = "Widget platform"


def pages(docs: Path):
    for path in sorted(docs.glob("*.md")):
        text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        front, _, body = text.partition("---\n")[2].partition("\n---\n")
        yield path, yaml.safe_load(front), body


def head_tags(path: Path, meta) -> str:
    url = f"{BASE}/{path.stem}/"
    # The title tag is NOT the page title: it carries the site name for
    # recognition in a result list, and search engines truncate around 60
    # characters, so the distinctive part goes first.
    title_tag = f"{meta['title']} | {SITE}"
    return "\n".join([
        f"<title>{title_tag}</title>",
        f'<meta name="description" content="{meta["summary"]}">',
        f'<link rel="canonical" href="{url}">',
        f'<meta property="og:title" content="{meta["title"]}">',
        f'<meta property="og:description" content="{meta["summary"]}">',
        f'<meta property="og:url" content="{url}">',
    ])


def audit(path: Path, meta, body: str):
    """Report the mechanical problems, which are the ones worth automating."""
    problems = []
    title = meta["title"]
    summary = meta["summary"]

    if len(f"{title} | {SITE}") > 60:
        problems.append(f"title tag is {len(title) + len(SITE) + 3} chars, over 60")
    if len(summary) < 50:
        problems.append(f"description is {len(summary)} chars, under 50")
    if len(summary) > 160:
        problems.append(f"description is {len(summary)} chars, over 160")

    # The highest-value check: does the summary repeat the title and add
    # nothing? That is a description with no search surface of its own.
    title_words = {w.lower() for w in title.split() if len(w) > 3}
    summary_words = {w.lower() for w in summary.split() if len(w) > 3}
    new = summary_words - title_words
    if len(new) < 3:
        problems.append(
            f"description adds only {len(new)} new word(s) beyond the title"
        )

    if not body.strip().startswith("#"):
        problems.append("no H1")
    return problems


for path, meta, body in pages(Path("docs")):
    print(f"=== {path.name} ===")
    print(head_tags(path, meta))
    problems = audit(path, meta, body)
    if problems:
        for problem in problems:
            print(f"  SEO  {problem}")
    else:
        print("  SEO  ok")
    print()
PY
python3 seo.py

Step 3: the check that actually finds the real problem

The mechanical checks above catch lengths. The real failure is vocabulary, and it needs the reader's words as input.

cat > vocabulary.py <<'PY'
"""Find pages whose searchable text lacks the words readers actually use.

The queries are the input that makes this work, and they are not invented:
they come from search logs, support tickets and the zero-click queries nobody
exports. See docs-prioritization.
"""
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

# Real reader phrasings, with the page that should win each one.
QUERIES = [
    ("widget server out of memory", "troubleshooting-oom.md"),
    ("how to set batch size", "configuration-reference.md"),
    ("max_memory_gb default", "configuration-reference.md"),
    ("install widget cli", "getting-started.md"),
]


def surface(path: Path):
    """The text a search engine weights most: title, description, H1, headings."""
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    front, _, body = text.partition("---\n")[2].partition("\n---\n")
    meta = yaml.safe_load(front)
    headings = [l.lstrip("# ").strip() for l in body.splitlines() if l.startswith("#")]
    return f"{meta['title']} {meta['summary']} {' '.join(headings)}".lower()


surfaces = {p.name: surface(p) for p in sorted(Path("docs").glob("*.md"))}

for query, expected in QUERIES:
    terms = [t for t in query.lower().split() if len(t) > 2]
    scores = {
        name: sum(1 for t in terms if t in text) for name, text in surfaces.items()
    }
    best = max(scores, key=scores.get)
    hit = scores[best] > 0 and best == expected
    missing = [t for t in terms if t not in surfaces[expected]]
    print(f"  {'OK ' if hit else '   '} {query:<32} -> {best} ({scores[best]}/{len(terms)})")
    if missing:
        print(f"         {expected} is missing: {missing}")
PY
python3 vocabulary.py

Step 4: fix one page and re-measure

cat > docs/configuration-reference.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Server configuration flags
summary: Every server flag with its default, including batch_size and max_memory_gb, and what happens when each is set too low.
kind: reference
updated: 2026-10-26
---
# Server configuration flags

## batch_size

| Flag | Default |
|---|---|
| `batch_size` | 32 |

## max_memory_gb

| Flag | Default |
|---|---|
| `max_memory_gb` | 16 |

Setting `max_memory_gb` too low causes the server to exit during load rather
than at startup.
EOF
python3 vocabulary.py

What you built. A generated search surface, a length audit, and a vocabulary check driven by real reader phrasings.

Step 4 is the point, and the numbers are unambiguous:

Before After Queries routed to the right page 2 of 4 4 of 4 how to set batch size 0 of 4 terms matched 3 of 4 max_memory_gb default 0 of 2 2 of 2 Length audit on that page 2 problems ok

The page did not get better documentation. It got the reader's words into the places a search engine weights, by naming the flags in H2 headings and in the summary rather than only inside a table cell.

Two honest residuals. install widget cli still wins on 1 of 3 terms, because getting-started.md never says "install" or "CLI" in its title, summary or headings: it wins by default rather than by merit, and a competing page would take it. And how is missing from the fixed page, which is correct, since reference pages should not be titled as questions. The check reports it; you decide it does not matter. That is the right division of labour between a linter and a person.

docs.title: The fields that matter, and where they come from
docs.text:
Element Length Source Notes <title> under ~60 chars title + site name Distinctive part first; it gets truncated <meta name="description"> 50 to 160 chars summary Not a ranking factor; decides the click <link rel="canonical"> n/a page URL Essential with versioned docs H1 one per page the page title Must match the title's intent H2/H3 n/a the page's own structure Where task phrasing belongs URL slug short filename Stable; a renamed URL loses its ranking og: tags n/a title and summary Link previews in Slack and chat

Deriving all of these from two required fields is the whole trick. It means nobody writes a separate SEO description, which is the artifact that always goes stale.

docs.title: Where to put the reader's vocabulary
docs.text:
In order of weight:

  1. Title. "Fix an out-of-memory error under load" beats "Memory configuration".
  2. H2 headings. One per task or symptom. This is where "out of memory under load" lives.
  3. Description. The sentence that decides the click, in the reader's words.
  4. First paragraph. Answer the question; do not introduce the topic.
  5. The exact identifiers. max_memory_gb must appear as text, not only in a table cell nobody indexes well.

docs.title: Documentation-specific concerns
docs.text:
Concern Why it is different here Versioned docs Multiple URLs per page; canonical must point at the current version or you split your own ranking Deep landing Most arrivals are on an interior page, so every page needs orientation and a route onward Error messages Developers search the literal string. A page containing the exact message outranks a general one Generated reference Thousands of near-identical pages; thin-content risk, and canonicalisation matters Retired versions Retired pages that stay indexed outrank current ones

The error-message row is the cheapest high-value action in documentation SEO and almost nobody does it: put the literal text of common errors in the page that fixes them.

docs.title: What does not apply
docs.text: Not relevant Why Keyword density Write for the reader; the vocabulary check above is sufficient Link building Your docs rank on relevance and site authority you already have Content refresh for its own sake A updated date you bumped without changing anything is dishonest Long-form padding A reference page should be exactly as long as the interface

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with the vocabulary mismatch, because it is the documentation-specific insight. "Documentation gets titled from the structure of the product and searched from the state of the reader. A page called 'Configuration Options Reference' does not rank for 'server out of memory', and no review catches that because the page is correct. So I derive the title tag, description, canonical and Open Graph tags from the content model's required fields, and then run a separate check that takes real search queries and reports which pages lack the reader's words in their title, headings and summary."

The follow-up is "how do you get the real queries", and the honest answer is that most teams have them and nobody exports them. Site search logs, support ticket subject lines, and the zero-click queries from Search Console are all cheap and all underused. A list of fifty real phrasings is worth more than any amount of SEO advice, and gathering it is an afternoon.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Optimising for search vocabulary pulls titles toward symptoms and away from structure, and a corpus titled entirely by symptom is hard to navigate for someone browsing rather than searching. "Fix an out-of-memory error under load" is a better search result and a worse table-of- contents entry than "Memory". The resolution is usually that reference pages stay structural and how-to pages go symptomatic, which is Diátaxis deciding an SEO question, but it is a real tension rather than a free win.

One sharper point. The strongest observation is that documentation SEO and retrieval want the same thing for the same reason. Both are vocabulary-matching problems between a reader's phrasing and an author's. A summary written in the reader's words improves the search snippet, the retrieval snippet, the llms.txt annotation and the embedding, all at once, from one edit. That is why the content model's summary field is load-bearing far out of proportion to its size, and why "optimise for SEO and GEO" in Intel's posting is one task rather than two.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A generated head-tag build step, plus the vocabulary check run against real queries, plus one before-and-after page.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Export fifty real queries from any documentation site you can access, especially the ones with no click. Ten minutes, and it is the input everything else needs.
  2. Run the vocabulary check and list the pages whose surface lacks their own readers' words. That list is a prioritised backlog nobody else has.
  3. Generate the head tags from front matter and add a CI check that the descriptions are not all identical. The commonest real-world failure is a site serving one site-wide description on every page, which looks fine and destroys every snippet.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Describing title tags proves nothing. A vocabulary check driven by exported queries, a list of mismatched pages, and a measured before-and-after on one of them demonstrates that you treated findability as measurable.

docs.title: Single-sourcing and content reuse
docs.text:
Writing a fact once, and the new silent failure that reuse introduces.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

Not a quotation (adjacent)

Neither posting mentions single-sourcing. It is the mechanism behind every claim about documentation scaling, so it is here as the thing those claims depend on.

Prerequisites: Content models

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Writing a fact in one place and referencing it everywhere else, rather than copying it. Three mechanisms, in increasing order of power: includes, which pull a block of text into several pages; variables, which substitute a value such as a version number; and generation, which renders many pages from one template and one data source.

The reason it is worth a page of its own is that reuse introduces a failure mode that copied prose does not have. A duplicated paragraph goes stale. A broken include can make a page disappear, and the build may not mention it.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
It does not, by name. It is here because both postings make claims that depend on it. "A small team of educators operating with the reach of an organisation ten times larger", in Anthropic's phrasing. Or NVIDIA's "turn documentation, standards and tribal knowledge into tooling, templates and self-service paths". Both are statements about leverage, and leverage in a documentation corpus means not writing the same thing N times.

It also decides how expensive your localization is, since every duplicated paragraph is translated once per copy, and how coherent your corpus looks, since N copies of a fact diverge in N directions.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Measure duplication, set up includes, then find the silent failure. About thirty minutes.

Step 1: measure what is actually duplicated

Before adopting a mechanism, find out whether you have the problem. Normalise prose sentences outside code fences and count the ones that appear on more than one page:

norm = lambda s: re.sub(r"\s+", " ", s.strip().lower())
seen = collections.defaultdict(list)
for p in sorted(Path("docs").rglob("*.md")):
    # ... skip fenced lines, tables and headings ...
    for s in re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", prose):
        if len(norm(s).split()) >= 8:
            seen[norm(s)].append(p.name)

dupes = {k: v for k, v in seen.items() if len(set(v)) > 1}

prose sentences (8+ words): 3654
appearing on more than one page: 27

   40 pages: this concept is on the curriculum and the prose is not written yet
   40 pages: everything below comes from the registry, so it is accurate as far
   40 pages: the [page contract](../explanation/the-page-contract.md) applies t
    5 pages: neither posting names it; both describe the problem it solves.
    4 pages: you will be asked to do it; it is not the centre of the role.

Read that carefully, because the top three are not a problem. They appear on 40 pages each because they come from one generator template, which is single-sourcing working correctly: one definition, forty renders, and changing the sentence changes all forty.

The 5-page and 4-page entries are the real duplication: hand-written sentences copied between pages. Twenty-seven duplicated sentences out of 3,654 is a low rate, which is itself the answer for this corpus. Measure before you build.

Step 2: set up includes

mkdir -p ss-demo/docs ss-demo/snippets && cd ss-demo
cat > mkdocs.yml <<'EOF'
site_name: SS
markdown_extensions:
  - pymdownx.snippets:
      base_path: ["snippets"]
      check_paths: true
EOF
printf 'You need Python 3.10 or later and an access token.\n' > snippets/prereqs.md

cat > docs/a.md <<'EOF'
# Install

--8<-- "prereqs.md"

Then run the installer.
EOF

python3 -m mkdocs build -q
grep -c 'Python 3.10' site/a/index.html site/b/index.html

site/a/index.html:1
site/b/index.html:1

One source, two pages. The prerequisite now changes in one place.

Step 3: break the include, with the check on

printf '# Configure\n\n--8<-- "nonexistent.md"\n' > docs/c.md
python3 -m mkdocs build -q; echo "exit=$?"

ERROR - Error reading page 'c.md': Snippet at path 'nonexistent.md' could not be found
exit=1

Good. A missing include fails the build.

Step 4: break it again, with the default configuration

Remove check_paths: true, which is not the default:

python3 -m mkdocs build -q; echo "exit=$?"

exit=0

Exit zero. And the page that ships:

   page text: ''

Empty. The missing include was silently dropped, so docs/c.md published with nothing in its body, and the build said nothing at all.

That is the failure mode reuse introduces. A copied paragraph can go stale; a broken include can delete a page's content, and by default nobody is told. check_paths: true is not an optimisation, it is the thing that makes the mechanism safe.

What you learned. Measure duplication before adopting a mechanism, and when you adopt one, turn on its integrity check in the same commit.

docs.title: The three mechanisms
docs.text:
Mechanism Reuses Good for Cost Includes A block of text Prerequisites, warnings, shared procedures A page's content can vanish; see step 4 Variables A value Version numbers, product names, URLs Substitution is invisible in source Generation A whole page Indexes, API reference, matrices The generator becomes software you own

Generation is the most powerful and the most underused. This guide's coverage matrix, study plan, learning paths and 40-odd placeholders are all generated from one registry, which is why fieldguide build --check can fail when a committed view is stale.

docs.title: When reuse is wrong
docs.text:
Situation Why copying is better The two pages will diverge An include forces them to stay identical The shared text is one sentence The indirection costs more than the duplication The copies have different audiences Same facts, different framing, is not duplication It is an example Examples should suit their context

The first row is the one that bites. An include is a commitment that these passages are the same thing forever, and when one page needs a variation you get a parameterised include, then a conditional, and eventually a templating language inside your documentation.

docs.title: What reuse does to the rest of the pipeline
docs.text:
Concern Effect Chunking A source consumer sees the include directive, not the text Localization Reuse cuts translation cost proportionally; it is the biggest single lever Link checking Links inside an include resolve relative to the including page Review A reviewer sees a one-line diff whose effect is on 40 pages Freshness An included block's age is not the page's age

The chunking row deserves attention in an AI-ready corpus. Anything reading your Markdown source rather than your built HTML sees --8<-- "prereqs.md" instead of the prerequisite, so retrieval pipelines should be built on the rendered output when includes are in play.

docs.title: Integrity checks that are not optional
docs.text:
Mechanism Check Default pymdownx.snippets check_paths: true Off, and silent when off Sphinx .. include:: Warns on a missing file On, fails with -W Variables A check for undefined references Usually absent; write it Generation Regenerate in CI and fail if output differs You implement it

The last row is the one that makes generation trustworthy. Generating pages is easy; the hard part is guaranteeing that the committed output matches what the generator produces today, and that is a --check mode plus a CI step.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with measurement. "I measure duplication before adopting a mechanism. On this corpus, 27 of 3,654 prose sentences appeared on more than one page, and the biggest clusters were generated from one template, which is reuse working. The actual hand-copied duplication was tiny, so includes would have added indirection for very little."

The follow-up is about the risk, and this is the strong answer: reuse introduces a failure copying does not have. With pymdownx.snippets at its default settings, a missing include is silently dropped and the page ships with an empty body at exit zero. So the integrity check goes in with the mechanism, in the same commit.

The tradeoff to volunteer. An include is a commitment that two passages are the same thing permanently, and the pressure is always toward parameterising it when one page needs a variation. That road ends in a templating language inside your prose, which is worse than the duplication you started with. Reuse facts and procedures; do not reuse explanations, which legitimately differ by audience.

One sharper point. Generation is the mechanism people underuse. Includes reuse a paragraph; generation reuses a page's entire structure, and it is what makes an index, a coverage matrix or an API reference impossible to leave stale. It costs you a generator that is real software, and the discipline that makes it safe is a --check mode that fails when committed output has drifted.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A corpus with one reuse mechanism, its integrity check enabled, and a duplication measurement that justified choosing it.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run step 1 on your own corpus. The number will probably surprise you in one direction or the other, and either way it tells you what to do.
  2. If you already use includes, check whether path validation is on. For pymdownx.snippets it is off by default, and off means silent.
  3. Find the fact in your corpus that is copied the most times and single-source that one. Start with a version number or a prerequisite, not an explanation.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack single-sources page summaries through hooks/seo.py, so one front-matter field feeds the page, the meta description and the retrieval artifacts, which is recorded as a partial demonstration. This guide's own generation is the stronger example: four views and 40-odd placeholders from one registry, with fieldguide build --check failing in CI when committed output is stale.

docs.title: Extracting tribal knowledge
docs.text:
Getting what an expert knows out of their head and into something other people can use without them.

core · difficulty 2 · 3h

Turning documentation, standards, and tribal knowledge into tooling, templates, and self-service paths

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Leads to: Playbooks and decision guides, Working with engineers as sources

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Getting what an expert knows out of their head and into a form other people can use without them. Tribal knowledge is the subset of what a team knows that has never been written down, usually because the people who have it do not experience it as knowledge. It feels like common sense.

The work is an interview technique plus a judgement about what shape the result should take, and the second part is where most of the value is.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA names it twice. Once in the framing: "turning documentation, standards, and tribal knowledge into tooling, templates, and self-service paths, so fewer people have to ask how do I". Once as a responsibility: "Capture tribal knowledge from engineering, product, and operations, and turn it into playbooks, decision guides, and self-service paths".

Notice what the sentences have in common. Neither says "write it down". Both specify an output form, and none of the forms is a page. That is the distinctive thing about this role, and the thing most technical writers get wrong. The deliverable for tribal knowledge is often a template, a validator, or a decision tree. The knowledge in question is usually a judgement rather than a fact, and a page describing a judgement gets read once and forgotten.

On a Tuesday it looks like this. A staff engineer is the only person who knows which of four ways to configure a simulation is right for a given workload. Three teams ask her every quarter. The naive output is a page titled "Configuration options", which already exists and which nobody uses because it lists the options without ranking them. The useful output is a decision guide: four questions in order, each narrowing the choice, ending in one answer and the reason. That is the same knowledge and a different artifact, and only one of them stops the questions.

The second reason this matters: the knowledge is the thing the role is protecting against. A platform whose operational knowledge lives in four people's heads is one reorganisation away from losing it.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Run one extraction, on a real person, and produce something that is not a page. Forty-five minutes including the conversation.

Step 1: find the question, not the topic

Topics produce overviews. Questions produce usable artifacts.

mkdir -p tribal-drill && cd tribal-drill
cat > scope.md <<'EOF'
BAD SCOPE      "Tell me about our deployment process."
               Produces a 2,000-word overview nobody reads.

GOOD SCOPE     "What do you get asked about deployment that you wish
               people could answer themselves?"
               Produces the three things that actually recur.

THE PIVOT      Do not ask what they know. Ask what they get interrupted
               about. Interruptions are the measurable shadow of tribal
               knowledge, and the expert can list them instantly.
EOF
cat scope.md

Step 2: run the interview with the five questions

cat > interview.md <<'EOF'
# Extraction interview, 30 minutes

1. WHAT RECURS
   "What do people ask you more than once a month?"
   -> the list. Pick one. Do not try to cover all of it.

2. THE DECISION
   "When someone asks that, what do you need to know before you can
   answer?"
   -> these become the questions in the decision guide, in this order.

3. THE WRONG ANSWER
   "What do people do when they guess? What goes wrong?"
   -> the failure modes. This is the half that never gets written down
   and the half that makes the artifact trustworthy.

4. THE EXCEPTION
   "When is the usual answer wrong?"
   -> the thing that will make your first draft embarrassing if you
   skip it. Always ask it.

5. THE TELL
   "How do you know, looking at a request, which case it is?"
   -> the signal. Often something they have never articulated, and
   usually the single most valuable sentence in the interview.
EOF
cat interview.md

Step 3: write down what you heard, in their words, before you shape it

Do this before designing the artifact. Shaping while listening loses the exceptions.

cat > raw.md <<'EOF'
# Raw notes: batch size for inference workloads  (SME: A. Patel, 30 min)

RECURS      "Which batch size should I use" -- several times a month,
            from three teams.

DECISION    Needs to know: is latency user-facing? how much GPU memory?
            is the model quantised? is the traffic bursty?

WRONG       People copy the number from the tutorial (32). On a latency-
            sensitive endpoint that adds ~200ms p99. On a small GPU it
            OOMs at load, not at startup, so it passes smoke tests.

EXCEPTION   Quantised models tolerate much larger batches; the memory
            math is different and the tutorial number is far too low.

TELL        "If they mention a p99 target, it is latency-sensitive and
            the answer is almost always 1 or 2, whatever the memory
            allows."
EOF
cat raw.md

Step 4: choose the output form, then build it

cat > choose.md <<'EOF'
Is the knowledge...        Then the artifact is...
-------------------------  ------------------------------------------
a fact                     a reference entry
a procedure                a how-to guide
a JUDGEMENT between        a DECISION GUIDE
  known options
a judgement that can be    a VALIDATOR or a default in the tooling
  computed from inputs
a sequence under pressure   a PLAYBOOK
a convention people        a TEMPLATE
  keep getting wrong
EOF
cat choose.md

This one is a judgement between known options, so it is a decision guide.

cat > decision-guide.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Choosing a batch size
summary: Four questions that determine the batch size for an inference workload.
diataxis: how-to
audience: developer
source: A. Patel, platform team, 2026-10
---

# Choosing a batch size

Do not copy the number from the tutorial. The tutorial uses 32 because it is
convenient for a demo, and it is wrong for most production workloads.

## 1. Is anything waiting on the response?

If a user or a caller is waiting, you are latency-sensitive. **Use 1 or 2.**

The tell: if you have a p99 target, the answer is almost always 1 or 2,
whatever memory allows. Batching at 32 on a latency-sensitive endpoint adds
roughly 200ms at p99.

If nothing is waiting, continue.

## 2. Is the model quantised?

If yes, the memory arithmetic is different and the tutorial's number is far
too low. Start at 64 and raise it while watching memory.

## 3. How much GPU memory do you have at peak, not at startup?

Size for peak. The common failure is an out-of-memory error under load rather
than at startup, which means it passes a smoke test and fails in production.

## 4. Is the traffic bursty?

Bursty traffic with a large batch size queues. Prefer a smaller batch and more
replicas.

## If you get this wrong

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| p99 latency far above p50 | Batch size too high for a latency-sensitive path |
| OOM under load, fine at startup | Sized for startup memory, not peak |
| Throughput lower than expected on a quantised model | Batch size too low |
EOF
wc -l decision-guide.md

What you built. A page that answers a recurring question in the order the expert actually thinks about it, including the failure modes and the exception, with the source and date recorded in the front matter.

The source field matters more than it looks. Tribal knowledge has a shelf life, and a reader in two years needs to know who said this and when, so they can go and ask whether it is still true. That one line is the difference between a document and a captured claim.

docs.title: The five questions, and what each one is for
docs.text: Question Produces What do people ask you more than once a month? Scope, chosen by frequency rather than by topic What do you need to know before you can answer? The decision guide's questions, in order What goes wrong when people guess? Failure modes, which nobody writes down When is the usual answer wrong? The exception that saves your draft How do you tell which case it is? The signal, usually never articulated

docs.title: Choosing the output form
docs.text:
The knowledge is The artifact is A fact A reference entry A procedure A how-to guide A judgement between known options A decision guide A judgement computable from inputs A validator, or a better default in the tooling A sequence executed under pressure A playbook A convention people keep getting wrong A template A number that drifts A freshness check on the page

The fourth row is the one that distinguishes this role. If the judgement can be computed, the right output is code, not prose. If the tutorial's batch size is wrong for most workloads, the strongest fix is changing the default and warning on the bad combination, and the page becomes an explanation of a safe default rather than a warning about a dangerous one.

docs.title: Interview mechanics that matter
docs.text: Do Why 30 minutes, one question An hour on a topic produces an overview Record or take verbatim notes Their phrasing is usually better than yours, especially the tell Ask for the last time it happened Concrete incidents surface exceptions; general questions do not Write the draft, then have them correct it Experts review well and compose badly Send the draft within a day Their context decays fast Put their name and the date on it Captured knowledge needs provenance

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text: Failure What it looks like Interviewing the topic A 2,000-word overview that answers nothing specific Capturing the answer, not the decision "Use 16" with no account of when that is wrong Skipping the exception A guide that is confidently wrong for quantised models Writing a page when the fix was a default The questions keep coming because nobody reads the page No provenance In two years nobody knows whether it is still true Interviewing one person You have captured one person's opinion as doctrine

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Name the output form and why you chose it. "An engineer was being asked monthly which batch size to use. The page that existed listed the options without ranking them, so I built a decision guide with the four questions she actually asks, in order, plus the failure modes and the quantised-model exception. Then I argued for changing the tutorial's default, because the real problem was that the demo number was being copied into production."

That last move is what separates this from note-taking.

The follow-up is about experts who will not talk to you, or who talk and then never review the draft. The honest answer is that a thirty-minute meeting about one recurring question is an easy ask and a one-hour meeting about a topic is not, so scope is your main lever. Beyond that: write the draft wrong on purpose and send it, because experts who will not compose will happily correct, and a wrong draft generates a faster response than a request for information.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Extraction takes the expert's time, and the people with the most tribal knowledge are the most interrupted people on the team. You are asking for the scarcest resource in the building to reduce demand on itself, which is a good trade and an unobvious one. The way to make it land is to lead with the interruption count rather than with documentation: "you get asked this three times a month, let me take thirty minutes and make it stop."

One sharper point. Tribal knowledge is tribal for a reason, and the reason is usually that it is a judgement with exceptions, which is genuinely hard to write down and easy to write down badly. A confidently wrong decision guide is worse than no guide, because people follow it. This is why question four exists and why provenance is non-negotiable. Saying that demonstrates you understand why the knowledge was not already written down, which is a more sophisticated position than assuming nobody got round to it.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A decision guide with a named source and a date, for a question that genuinely recurred. Not an overview.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run one extraction on a real person. Thirty minutes, one recurring question, the five questions above. Produce something that is not a page if the knowledge is not a fact.
  2. Count the interruptions before and after. Ask the expert, a month later, whether the question stopped. That number is the whole argument, and it is what NVIDIA means by "measurable reductions in support load".
  3. Find one case where the answer was code. A judgement that could be a default, a warning, or a validator. Propose it. Being the documentation person who argues for changing a default rather than documenting it is memorable.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Everyone in this field says they interview subject matter experts. A decision guide with four ordered questions, an exception, a failure table and a named source is specific enough to be checked, and "she stopped getting asked" is the only outcome that matters.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
The artifact this produces is a page, and a page does not reveal how it was obtained. What would demonstrate the skill is the gap between what an expert said and what they knew, which only exists in the room.

What you need. An engineer who knows something undocumented, thirty minutes, and a prepared set of questions. No tooling. The scarce resource is the engineer's attention, which is why the preparation is the skill.

What a learner would do. Pick something in your own product that is undocumented because it is "obvious", and interview whoever knows it, using questions that cannot be answered abstractly:

What breaks most often, and what does the person do first?
Walk me through the last time this went wrong.
What do you know that is not written down anywhere?
What does everyone get wrong when they first use this?
If I changed this, what would you be worried about?

Then write the page, send it back, and count the corrections. The count is the measurement: a first draft from a good interview comes back with factual corrections, and one from a bad interview comes back rewritten.

What competence looks like.

Evidence Why it carries weight A page the expert approved with few edits The interview captured the right things A documented failure mode nobody had written You got tacit knowledge, not a restatement A second interview that was shorter You learned what to ask An expert who volunteers things afterwards The hardest signal to fake A question you stopped asking, and why The questions improve or they are a script

Why it does not commit to a repository. The page commits; the interview does not. A reader cannot tell whether a well-documented failure mode came from an engineer, from reading the source, or from a support ticket, and those represent very different skills. The one piece of evidence that would distinguish them, the correction count on the first draft, lives in a review thread.

The adjacent thing that is demonstrable. Reading the source to verify what you were told is a separate concept, reading code to verify, and the combination is what makes either trustworthy: an interview tells you where to look, and the code tells you whether the memory was right.

docs.title: Sphinx
docs.text:
The generator whose build fails when a symbol moves, and what that costs.

core · difficulty 3 · 6h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "static site generators (Sphinx, MkDocs, Docusaurus, or similar)"

Prerequisites: Choosing a static site generator, reStructuredText

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A documentation generator built around an intermediate representation called the doctree, which is what makes its distinguishing feature possible: typed cross-references that resolve against a symbol table. A reference to pkg.widget.retry is not a link to a URL you hoped would exist. It is a reference to a function, and if that function is renamed, the documentation build fails.

It is the strictest of the generators and the hardest to adopt, and those are the same fact.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA's documentation estate is Python and C++ tooling: Omniverse, Isaac Sim, OpenUSD. That is Sphinx territory and has been for twenty years, because Sphinx is the only common generator that treats API symbols as first-class objects with their own namespaces.

The thing being tested is whether you know what it buys. Anyone can describe Sphinx as "the Python one with RST". The useful answer is that its build is a correctness gate on the relationship between documentation and code. The honest version adds that mkdocstrings achieves the same gate for Python on MkDocs, and that what stays distinctively Sphinx is multi-language domains and cross-project checking through intersphinx.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Generate reference documentation from real source, then rename the function and watch the build fail. About forty minutes.

Committed as drills/sphinx_autodoc.py, which runs both states in one go. It needs sphinx and myst-parser, neither of which this guide depends on, so it is not in the test suite's default run; the page states what it prints and the drill is how you check that.

One thing changed when it was committed. The signature line below arrives as → rather than as a real arrow, because the extraction script strips tags and leaves entities alone. This page used to show the arrow. That is a trivial defect with a non-trivial consequence: a reader who follows the steps sees output that does not match what they were promised, and has no way to tell whether the difference matters.

Step 1: a package and a Sphinx project

mkdir -p sx-demo/src sx-demo/pkg && cd sx-demo
cat > pkg/widget.py <<'EOF'
"""Widget client."""


def retry(times: int = 5, backoff: float = 1.5) -> int:
    """Retry an operation.

    Args:
        times: How many attempts.
        backoff: Multiplier between attempts.

    Returns:
        The number of attempts made.
    """
    return times


class Client:
    """A client."""

    def connect(self, url: str) -> bool:
        """Open a connection."""
        return True
EOF

cat > src/conf.py <<'EOF'
import os
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.abspath(".."))
project = "W"
extensions = ["sphinx.ext.autodoc", "sphinx.ext.napoleon", "myst_parser"]
nitpicky = True
EOF

Three extensions and nitpicky = True. autodoc reads the source, napoleon understands Google-style docstrings, myst_parser lets the pages be Markdown, and nitpicky turns every unresolved reference into a warning.

Step 2: a page that pulls the reference out of the code

cat > src/index.md <<'EOF'
# API

```{eval-rst}
.. automodule:: pkg.widget
   :members:
```

See {py:func}`pkg.widget.retry` and {py:class}`pkg.widget.Client`.
EOF

sphinx-build -q -W -b html src out
echo "exit=$?"

exit=0

Check what it produced:

python3 - <<'PY'
import re
from pathlib import Path
html = Path("out/index.html").read_text()
plain = re.sub("<[^>]+>", "", html)
print(re.search(r"retry.{0,70}", plain).group(0))
for s in ("backoff", "Multiplier", "connect", "Parameters", "Returns"):
    print(f"  {s:12} {s in html}")
PY

retry(times: int = 5, backoff: float = 1.5) → int¶
  backoff      True
  Multiplier   True
  connect      True
  Parameters   True
  Returns      True

The full typed signature, the parameter descriptions, and the return documentation, all pulled from the source. Nothing about the signature was written by hand, so nothing about it can be out of date.

Step 3: the demonstration

Rename the function in the code and leave the documentation untouched, which is precisely what happens in a real refactor:

sed -i 's/^def retry(/def attempt(/' pkg/widget.py
sphinx-build -q -W -b html src out2
echo "exit=$?"

WARNING: py:func reference target not found: pkg.widget.retry [ref.func]
exit=1

The documentation build failed because a function was renamed in the code. An ordinary Markdown link cannot do this. [retry](api.md#retry) resolves against a heading slug, so after the rename the heading is attempt, the anchor dies, and MkDocs ships it even in strict mode.

But Sphinx is not alone in this, and it would be wrong to say so. MkDocs with mkdocstrings has its own cross-reference syntax, [text][symbol], and those are resolved against the collected objects: a reference to a renamed symbol produces Could not find cross-reference target, which --strict turns into a failed build. The comparison is drawn properly on generated API reference.

What remains genuinely Sphinx's is the breadth: multiple language domains in one corpus, and intersphinx extending the same checking across project boundaries. The rename demonstration is worth forty minutes either way, because it is the mechanism both approaches depend on.

Step 4: what the strictness costs, measured

drills/generator_build.py builds an identical corpus under both generators, bare, across three sizes:

  pages   mkdocs   sphinx cold   sphinx warm   warm vs mkdocs
    121     0.50          1.57          0.59   mkdocs 1.2x faster
    240     0.91          2.36          0.58   sphinx 1.6x faster
    480     1.94          4.10          0.65   sphinx 3.0x faster

One machine, one run; the shape is the claim and not the seconds.

The doctree that makes step 3 possible is also what makes incremental rebuilds possible, so MkDocs rebuilds everything every time and Sphinx rebuilds what changed. MkDocs' time therefore scales with the corpus and Sphinx's warm build is nearly flat, and the two cross just above a hundred and twenty pages.

This page used to quote a single row of that table, 0.58 against 3.52 seconds, and conclude "six times slower cold". The direction survives and the magnitude does not: cold Sphinx measures about three times MkDocs in steady state here, and the 3.52 was most likely a first-ever build paying for imports that were not yet in the filesystem cache. CI pays that first number on every run and a laptop pays it once, which is a distinction a single figure cannot carry.

The authoring loop, which is what the cost actually feels like:

  one page edited in 121: mkdocs 0.53s, sphinx 0.59s  (mkdocs 1.1x faster)
  one page edited in 480: mkdocs 1.78s, sphinx 0.70s  (sphinx 2.5x faster)

So "often the faster of the two in day-to-day authoring" was right, and only past a certain size. Below it MkDocs still wins, because rebuilding a hundred trivial pages costs less than Sphinx's fixed startup.

What you built. Reference documentation that cannot drift from its signatures, and a build that fails when code and docs disagree.

docs.title: What -W plus nitpicky catches
docs.text:
Defect Caught Link to a missing page Yes Link to a missing heading anchor Yes Page in no toctree Yes, toc.not_included Reference to a renamed symbol Yes, ref.func Duplicate label Yes A type annotation that does not resolve Yes, and this is the noisy one

The last row is why nitpicky is divisive. It flags every unresolvable type, including standard-library and third-party types Sphinx cannot find, so adopting it on an existing project means a session with nitpick_ignore. Worth it, but do not turn it on an hour before a release.

docs.title: The extensions that matter
docs.text:
Extension Does sphinx.ext.autodoc Pull docstrings and signatures from source sphinx.ext.napoleon Understand Google and NumPy docstring styles sphinx.ext.intersphinx Cross-reference other projects' symbols sphinx.ext.viewcode Link reference entries to highlighted source myst_parser Author pages in Markdown sphinx.ext.doctest Run the examples in your docs; see doctests sphinx-autobuild Live reload while authoring

intersphinx deserves attention. It lets a reference to str or to another library's class resolve to that project's documentation, which means cross-project references are also checked. Nothing in the Markdown world has an equivalent.

docs.title: Domains, which is the concept under the feature
docs.text: A domain is a namespace of object types and roles. py:func, cpp:class, js:method are all domain-qualified, so Sphinx can tell a Python Client from a C++ Client and check each against the right symbol table. On a codebase with multiple languages, this is the feature that makes a single documentation set coherent.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text: Cost Detail conf.py is a Python program Powerful, and a configuration file that can have bugs Learning curve Directives, roles and toctree before the first page Error vocabulary Messages are in docutils and Sphinx terms, not plain English Theme work is harder Fewer good themes, and customising them is more involved Cold builds are slower Measured above; mitigated by incremental rebuilds nitpicky adoption A real session of nitpick_ignore on any existing project

docs.title: Should a new project use it
docs.text: Yes No The deliverable includes API reference for a library The corpus is conceptual and narrative The code is Python, C++ or multi-language The site needs interactive components Symbols are renamed often enough to hurt The team has no Python experience You need cross-project references You need a site this afternoon

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the rename. "Sphinx's build fails when a function referenced in the docs is renamed in the code, because references are typed and resolve against a symbol table rather than a URL. That is not available in any Markdown generator, and on an API corpus it is the difference between documentation that drifts and documentation that cannot."

The follow-up is whether that means RST, and the answer is no: myst_parser lets contributors write Markdown while keeping domains, toctree and typed references. Knowing that is what separates a current answer from a 2015 one.

The tradeoff to volunteer. The doctree buys correctness and costs approachability. conf.py is a Python program that can have bugs, errors are reported in docutils vocabulary, and nitpicky on an existing project produces a wall of unresolvable standard-library types before it produces value. Sphinx is the right answer for a library and the wrong answer for a dozen conceptual pages.

One sharper point. intersphinx is the underrated piece. It extends reference checking across project boundaries, so a link to another library's class is verified rather than hoped for. In an ecosystem of related packages, that turns a set of separate documentation sites into something closer to one correct corpus, and almost nobody mentions it.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A Sphinx project with -W in CI, autodoc generating reference from source, and ideally nitpicky on.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Step 3 is the whole point, and seeing your own build fail on a rename is more persuasive than any description of it.
  2. Turn on nitpicky in a project you have and count the warnings. That count is the honest size of its reference debt.
  3. Add intersphinx pointing at the Python standard library and see how many previously unresolved types start resolving.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Neither of this guide's repositories is built with Sphinx, which the demonstrated page records, and that is a real gap for a role at a company whose documentation is Sphinx-shaped. Running it in a drill is not the same as owning a Sphinx corpus: nothing here involves a large conf.py, a custom extension, a theme fork, or intersphinx across teams, which is where the actual work is.

What is committed is the mechanism. drills/sphinx_autodoc.py renames a function and the build fails with py:func reference target not found and exit 1, against the same defect MkDocs publishes, and drills/generator_build.py measures what the doctree behind that costs and what it buys back incrementally. Both corrected this page: one fixed a quoted output line, the other replaced a six-times claim with a comparison that inverts.
