docs.title: Choosing a static site generator
docs.text:
The decision is about how much correctness the build checks, not about which syntax you prefer.

core · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "static site generators (Sphinx, MkDocs, Docusaurus, or similar)"

Prerequisites: Markdown and its dialects

Leads to: MkDocs and Material, Sphinx, Docusaurus, Antora and AsciiDoc, Versioned documentation

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The tool that turns a tree of source files into a website. It decides your Markdown dialect, your navigation model, your theming, your extension mechanism, and, least discussed and most important, how much of your corpus's correctness the build is willing to check.

NVIDIA names three by name. The useful skill is not having a favourite, it is being able to say what each one's build does and does not verify.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because the choice is close to irreversible and it is usually made by whoever set up the repository in week one.

Migrating a mature corpus between generators means rewriting every tool-specific construct, remapping every URL, rebuilding the navigation model and retraining contributors. People do not do it. So the generator you inherit is the generator you have, and the valuable thing is to know its blind spots well enough to close them with CI gates.

That framing is also the honest answer to "which would you choose". The differences in syntax and theming are small and mostly taste. The differences in what the build catches are large and measurable.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build identical content in two generators and compare what each one is willing to fail on. About thirty-five minutes.

Step 1: the same three defects in both

mkdir -p ssg/mk/docs ssg/sx/src && cd ssg

# MkDocs
printf 'site_name: W\n' > mk/mkdocs.yml
cat > mk/docs/index.md <<'EOF'
# Widget

See [the tuning bit](guide.md#tuning).
EOF
printf '# Guide\n\n## Setup\n\nContent.\n' > mk/docs/guide.md
printf '# Orphan\n\nNobody links here.\n' > mk/docs/orphan.md

# Sphinx, with MyST so the source is also Markdown
cat > sx/src/conf.py <<'EOF'
project = "W"
extensions = ["myst_parser"]
EOF
cat > sx/src/index.md <<'EOF'
# Widget

See [the tuning bit](guide.md#tuning).

```{toctree}
guide
```
EOF
printf '# Guide\n\n## Setup\n\nContent.\n' > sx/src/guide.md
printf '# Orphan\n\nNobody links here.\n' > sx/src/orphan.md

Two defects: a link to guide.md#tuning where guide.md has no Tuning heading, and a page in no navigation at all.

Step 2: ask both builds, in their strictest mode

( cd mk && python3 -m mkdocs build --strict >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "mkdocs --strict exit=$?" )
sphinx-build -q -W -b html sx/src sx/out >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "sphinx -W  exit=$?"

mkdocs --strict exit=0
sphinx -W  exit=1

WARNING: local id not found in doc 'guide': 'tuning' [myst.xref_missing]
WARNING: document isn't included in any toctree [toc.not_included]

MkDocs's strictest mode passes a corpus with a dead heading anchor and an unreachable page. Sphinx fails on both, and names them.

This is the measured version of the gap that link checking exists to close: the custom anchor checker on that page is necessary on MkDocs and redundant on Sphinx.

Step 3: measure what the stricter build costs

121 generated pages, same content in both:

mkdocs,  cold build          0.58 s
sphinx,  cold build          3.52 s
sphinx,  incremental rebuild 0.75 s

Sphinx is roughly six times slower cold, because it builds an intermediate doctree that makes cross-reference resolution possible. That doctree is also what gives it incremental rebuilds, which MkDocs does not have.

Step 4: find out what actually dominates build time

Same generator, same 121 pages, two configurations:

mkdocs, default theme, no extensions    0.6 s
mkdocs, Material theme, 12 extensions  16.0 s

Twenty-seven times slower, with the generator held constant. Your theme and extension set matter far more to build time than your choice of generator. Anyone comparing generators on speed without holding the theme constant is measuring the wrong thing.

What you learned. The real axis is how much the build verifies, the real cost of verification is a doctree and some seconds, and the headline speed numbers people quote are mostly about themes.

docs.title: What each build checks, measured
docs.text:
Defect MkDocs --strict Sphinx -W Link to a missing page Fails Fails Link to a missing heading anchor Passes Fails Page in no navigation Passes Fails Reference to a missing symbol Fails, with mkdocstrings autorefs Fails, with domains Duplicate label No such concept Fails

The second and third rows are what you have to replace with your own gates on MkDocs. The fourth row needs a tool that collects symbols: Sphinx natively, or MkDocs with mkdocstrings and its [text][symbol] references, which are checked. Plain Markdown links to generated anchors are not.

docs.title: The four, in one table
docs.text: MkDocs Sphinx Docusaurus Antora Source Markdown RST, or Markdown via MyST MDX AsciiDoc Runtime Python Python Node Node Cross-reference checking Pages only Pages, anchors, symbols Pages Pages, across repos Versioning A plugin A convention plus builds Built in Built in, first-class Multi-repository No No No Yes, its reason to exist Interactive components No No Yes No Setup cost Lowest Medium Medium Highest Best at Getting good fast API correctness Product sites Many repos, one site

docs.title: Choosing, honestly
docs.text:
Situation Choice A library's API docs, Python or C++ Sphinx A product site with interactive examples Docusaurus Documentation spread over many repositories Antora Anything else, and you want to be productive today MkDocs You inherited one Keep it, and close its gaps with gates

The last row is the most common real situation and the best interview answer.

docs.title: What you will have to build yourself, by choice
docs.text:
On MkDocs On Sphinx Anchor checking Little; the build covers it Orphan page detection Little Versioned docs, via a plugin A build-per-version convention A content model validator A content model validator Sample execution Sample execution

Both still need sample validation and cold-start testing. No generator checks whether your quickstart works.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with correctness, not syntax. "The difference that matters is how much the build verifies. MkDocs in strict mode ships a dead heading anchor and an unreachable page; Sphinx with -W fails on both and also fails on a reference to a symbol that moved. So the choice is really about how much of the gate suite you are going to write yourself."

The follow-up is usually about speed, and the honest answer corrects the premise. Sphinx is slower cold and has incremental rebuilds, but holding the generator constant and swapping a bare theme for Material and a dozen extensions cost twenty-seven times more than the generator choice did. Theme weight dominates.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Sphinx's correctness comes from a doctree, and the doctree is also its difficulty: conf.py is a Python program, errors are reported in its own vocabulary, and contributors meet directives before they meet their first page. MkDocs is dramatically easier to adopt, and you pay for that later in gates you write yourself. Both are defensible; pretending one is simply better is the tell.

One sharper point. Migration between generators effectively does not happen, so this reads like a high-stakes decision and mostly is not one: you will inherit a choice. The valuable skill is auditing what your generator's build does not check and closing those specific gaps, which is a concrete thing to have done and a much better interview answer than a preference.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A table like step 2's for the generator you actually use, with the gaps you closed and how.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Step 2 takes ten minutes and the result surprises most people who use MkDocs daily.
  2. Put a dead heading anchor into your own corpus and confirm whether your build catches it. If not, you have just identified your first gate.
  3. Time your build with your theme and again with the default theme. The ratio tells you where your build minutes actually go.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. This guide runs on MkDocs with Material, and it has a hand-written anchor checker, a fence gate and a render gate precisely because the build does not cover them. Being able to say "I chose this generator and here are the three checks I added to compensate" is the answer that demonstrates judgment rather than preference.

docs.title: Structured data and JSON-LD
docs.text:
Telling a machine what a page is and what kind of question it answers, in a format crawlers already parse.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

Not a quotation (derived)

Required by "a crawlable, agent-ready front door": the machine-readable half of SEO and GEO.

Prerequisites: Metadata for navigation and retrieval

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A block of JSON in the page's <head> describing what the page is, using a vocabulary crawlers already understand. For documentation that means TechArticle, with its title, description, modification date, and the facts a machine cannot infer from prose.

It is the only place where your content model becomes visible to something that fetches your HTML and does not run your search index.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Neither posting says "JSON-LD", which is why this is derived. Intel asks for "a crawlable, agent-ready front door" and for content optimized "for search (SEO and GEO) and for AI assistants and coding agents". Structured data is the mechanism that makes a page's type machine-readable to a consumer that is not your retriever.

What makes it supporting rather than core is that most of the benefit comes from one small block generated from fields you already require. The work is an afternoon, and then it is a build step.

On a Tuesday the reason it matters is narrower than SEO people claim. Your chunks carry the page type because you put it there. Your MCP server exposes it because you wrote the schema. A crawler that fetches the rendered page sees none of that, because diataxis: how-to lives in front matter that never reaches the HTML. So an external assistant reading your site cannot tell a reference page from an explanation page, and that is the single most useful distinction you have.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Generate JSON-LD from the content model, validate it, and show what a consumer learns from it that the HTML alone does not say. Thirty minutes.

Step 1: pages with a content model, and the HTML they would produce

mkdir -p struct-drill/docs && cd struct-drill
cat > docs/rotate-key.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Rotate a signing key
summary: Replace a signing key with a one-hour overlap and no downtime.
diataxis: how-to
audience: operator
updated: 2026-10-20
tags: [keys, security]
---
# Rotate a signing key

Run `widget keys rotate`. The old key stays valid for one hour.
EOF

cat > docs/why-overlap.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Why keys overlap for an hour
summary: The reasoning behind a one-hour overlap window rather than instant cutover.
diataxis: explanation
audience: operator
updated: 2026-10-20
tags: [keys, security]
---
# Why keys overlap for an hour

An instant cutover breaks any deployment mid-rollout.
EOF

cat > docs/keys-reference.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Key management commands
summary: Every key subcommand with its flags, defaults and exit codes.
diataxis: reference
audience: developer
updated: 2026-10-20
tags: [keys, cli]
---
# Key management commands

## widget keys rotate

Exits 0 on success, 2 on invalid arguments.
EOF
ls docs/

Three pages on one subject, with three different jobs. A crawler sees three pages about keys.

Step 2: generate the block from the model

cat > jsonld.py <<'PY'
"""Generate JSON-LD TechArticle blocks from the content model.

Every field comes from front matter the model already requires, which is the
whole design: nobody hand-writes structured data, so it cannot drift from the
page, and a page cannot ship without the fields the block needs.

The field doing the real work is `about`. Schema.org has no vocabulary for
"this is a how-to guide rather than an explanation", so the Diataxis type goes
in `about` as a readable statement of what kind of question the page can
answer. That is the one thing a crawler cannot infer from the prose.
"""
import json
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

BASE = "https://widget.example/docs"
SITE = "Widget platform"

#: What each page type can and cannot answer, stated for a machine.
ROLE = {
    "tutorial": "Tutorial: learning-oriented, assumes no prior context",
    "how-to": "How-to guide: task-oriented, gives steps for one goal",
    "reference": "Reference: factual description of the interface, no narrative",
    "explanation": "Explanation: design reasoning and tradeoffs, not instructions",
}

PROFICIENCY = {
    "new-user": "Beginner",
    "developer": "Expert",
    "operator": "Expert",
    "contributor": "Expert",
}


def block(meta, slug):
    url = f"{BASE}/{slug}/"
    return {
        "@context": "https://schema.org",
        "@type": "TechArticle",
        "headline": meta["title"],
        "description": meta["summary"],
        "url": url,
        "dateModified": str(meta["updated"]),
        "about": ROLE[meta["diataxis"]],
        "audience": {
            "@type": "Audience",
            "audienceType": meta["audience"],
        },
        "proficiencyLevel": PROFICIENCY[meta["audience"]],
        "keywords": ", ".join(meta.get("tags", [])),
        "isPartOf": {"@type": "WebSite", "name": SITE, "url": BASE},
        "inLanguage": "en",
    }


def head(meta, slug):
    """The whole machine-readable head, not only the JSON-LD."""
    url = f"{BASE}/{slug}/"
    tags = [
        f"<title>{meta['title']} | {SITE}</title>",
        f'<meta name="description" content="{meta["summary"]}">',
        f'<link rel="canonical" href="{url}">',
        f'<meta property="og:title" content="{meta["title"]}">',
        f'<meta property="og:description" content="{meta["summary"]}">',
        f'<meta property="og:type" content="article">',
        '<script type="application/ld+json">'
        + json.dumps(block(meta, slug), separators=(",", ":"))
        + "</script>",
    ]
    return "\n".join(tags)


def pages(root):
    for path in sorted(root.glob("*.md")):
        text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        yield path, yaml.safe_load(text.split("---")[1])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for path, meta in pages(Path("docs")):
        print(f"=== {path.name} ===")
        print(head(meta, path.stem))
        print()
PY
python3 jsonld.py

Step 3: validate it, because a silently invalid block does nothing

cat > validate.py <<'PY'
"""Check the generated blocks before publishing them.

Invalid structured data does not raise an error anywhere. It is ignored, and
the page looks fine, which is why this check exists at all.
"""
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from jsonld import ROLE, block, pages

REQUIRED = ("@context", "@type", "headline", "description", "url", "dateModified")
MAX_DESCRIPTION = 160

failures = []
blocks = []

for path, meta in pages(Path("docs")):
    data = block(meta, path.stem)
    blocks.append((path.name, data))

    for field in REQUIRED:
        if not data.get(field):
            failures.append(f"{path.name}: missing {field}")
    if data["@context"] != "https://schema.org":
        failures.append(f"{path.name}: wrong @context")
    if len(data["description"]) > MAX_DESCRIPTION:
        failures.append(
            f"{path.name}: description {len(data['description'])} chars, "
            f"over {MAX_DESCRIPTION}"
        )
    if data["about"] not in ROLE.values():
        failures.append(f"{path.name}: `about` is not a known page role")
    try:
        json.dumps(data)
    except (TypeError, ValueError) as exc:
        failures.append(f"{path.name}: not serialisable: {exc}")

# The check that matters most: descriptions must differ. A site serving one
# site-wide description on every page is the commonest real failure, it looks
# completely fine, and it destroys every snippet and every link preview.
descriptions = {name: data["description"] for name, data in blocks}
if len(set(descriptions.values())) < len(descriptions):
    failures.append(
        f"only {len(set(descriptions.values()))} distinct descriptions "
        f"across {len(descriptions)} pages"
    )

for failure in failures:
    print(f"JSON-LD  {failure}", file=sys.stderr)
print(f"{'FAIL' if failures else 'ok'}: {len(blocks)} blocks, {len(failures)} problem(s)")
sys.exit(1 if failures else 0)
PY
python3 validate.py; echo "exit=$?"

Step 4: show what a consumer learns from the block that the HTML does not say

python3 - <<'PY'
import json
from pathlib import Path

from jsonld import block, pages

print("A crawler reading only the rendered prose sees three pages about keys.")
print("Reading the structured data, it can route a question:\n")

questions = [
    ("how do I rotate a key", "How-to guide"),
    ("why is there an overlap window", "Explanation"),
    ("what exit code does rotate return", "Reference"),
]

blocks = {path.stem: block(meta, path.stem) for path, meta in pages(Path("docs"))}

for question, wanted_role in questions:
    match = [
        slug for slug, data in blocks.items()
        if data["about"].startswith(wanted_role)
    ]
    print(f"  {question!r}")
    print(f"    wants: {wanted_role}")
    print(f"    page:  {match[0] if match else 'none'}")

print("\nThe `about` field is the routing signal. Nothing else in the HTML")
print("distinguishes these three pages by what kind of answer they support.")
PY

What you built. Generated JSON-LD, a validator including the duplicate-description check, and a demonstration of the one field that carries information nothing else in the HTML does.

docs.title: The fields worth setting, and where each comes from
docs.text:
Field Source Why @type: TechArticle the page type The right schema.org type for developer docs headline title What a crawler shows description summary The snippet. Must be per-page url the page URL Canonical identity dateModified updated Freshness, which crawlers weight about diataxis What kind of question this answers. The one irreplaceable field audience.audienceType audience Who it is for proficiencyLevel derived from audience A schema.org field that happens to fit keywords tags Weak signal, free to emit isPartOf site config Groups the corpus

Every one is derived. Nobody hand-writes a structured-data block, for the same reason nobody hand-writes an API reference.

docs.title: Why about carries the Diátaxis type
docs.text:
Schema.org has no field for "this is a how-to guide rather than an explanation of the same subject". TechArticle has proficiencyLevel and dependencies, and nothing for genre.

So the type goes in about as a readable sentence. That is a slight misuse of the field and it is the best available option, because the alternative is losing the single most useful fact about a page at the HTML boundary. Worth saying out loud rather than pretending the vocabulary fits.

docs.title: Types other than TechArticle
docs.text:
Type Use for TechArticle The default for developer documentation HowTo A page with discrete numbered steps; supports step APIReference Generated API reference, as a subtype of TechArticle FAQPage A page of genuine question-and-answer pairs SoftwareApplication A product landing page, not a docs page BreadcrumbList Navigation position, emitted alongside

HowTo is tempting and usually not worth it: the step markup is laborious and the gain over TechArticle plus a good about is small. FAQPage has been abused enough that search engines discount it.

docs.title: What to validate, and why each check exists
docs.text:
Check Catches Required fields present A block missing headline is ignored silently @context is exactly https://schema.org A typo makes the block inert Description length under 160 Truncated snippets about is a known role A typo in the type, which defeats the point JSON serialises A date object that was never going to render Descriptions differ across pages The commonest real failure

The last row is the one to build first. A site serving its site-wide description on every page looks completely correct in a browser, passes every other check, and destroys every search snippet and every link preview. It is also the default behaviour of several static site generators unless you wire the per-page field through, which is a mistake this guide made in its companion project and only caught by looking at the rendered HTML.

docs.title: Honest limits
docs.text:
Claim Reality "It improves rankings" Not directly. It affects how results are displayed and parsed "Assistants read it" Some do; coverage is uneven and undocumented "about is the right field for genre" It is the least wrong field available "Rich results are guaranteed" No. Eligibility, not entitlement "More schema is better" Invalid or irrelevant markup is ignored at best

Present it internally as cheap, generated, and useful for parsing rather than as a ranking lever, because the ranking claim is overstated everywhere and someone in the room will know it.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with the boundary problem, which is the documentation-specific insight. "The page type is the most useful field in our content model, and it stops existing at the HTML boundary: front matter does not reach a crawler. So I generate a TechArticle block from the required fields and put the Diátaxis type in about as a readable sentence, since schema.org has no genre field. It is a slight misuse of about and the alternative is losing the distinction entirely. All of it is generated, and the check I care about most is that descriptions differ across pages, because a site-wide description on every page looks fine and destroys every snippet."

The follow-up is "does any of this actually do anything", and it deserves a straight answer rather than a defence. Structured data is not a ranking factor; it affects display eligibility and makes a page parseable without a crawler guessing from prose. The honest reason to do it is that it costs an afternoon, it is generated so it cannot rot, and it forces per-page descriptions, which is worth having regardless. If someone wants a ranking promise, they should not get one.

The tradeoff to volunteer. This is a second representation of facts that already exist in front matter, and a second representation can drift. Generating it removes most of that risk and not all: a change to the content model needs a corresponding change here, and nothing fails if you forget. Hence the validator, and hence keeping the block minimal. A sprawling structured-data block with fifteen fields is fifteen chances to drift for a benefit nobody has measured.

One sharper point. The strongest observation is that structured data is where you find out whether your content model survives contact with the outside world. Every field you cannot map onto a public vocabulary is a field only your own tooling can use, and that is fine for audience and genuinely awkward for page genre, which is your most valuable facet. Noticing that the thing you most want to tell a machine has no standard way to say it is a more interesting position than listing schema.org types, and it is the sort of gap a KnowledgeOps role is being hired to notice.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A generated block in a build step, with the validator, and specifically the distinct-descriptions check.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Step 4 is the demonstration: three pages on one subject, routed by about, which nothing else in the HTML supports.
  2. Check a real site for the duplicate-description failure. Fetch three pages of any documentation site and compare their meta descriptions. It is two minutes and the hit rate is high.
  3. Generate the block from front matter and gate it. Not hand-written, with the validator in CI. That is the difference between structured data and a snippet somebody pasted into a template once.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Listing schema.org types proves nothing. A generated block, a validator whose first check is that descriptions differ, and an articulated reason for putting the page genre in about demonstrates that you thought about what a machine can and cannot learn from your HTML.

docs.title: Style guides and terminology management
docs.text:
Splitting a style guide into the half a machine enforces and the half it cannot, and proving each rule fires.

supporting · difficulty 1 · 2h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "You're a writer who builds: as comfortable in Git, CI, or Python as in a style guide, and fluent with LLMs in daily work"

Prerequisites: Taxonomy and controlled vocabularies

Leads to: Prose linting with Vale, Security guidance as encoded standard

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The agreed rules for how your documentation is written: terminology, voice, person, capitalisation, how to format a command, when to use a note versus a warning. In practice it is two documents wearing one name, and separating them is most of the value.

One half is mechanical: terminology, deprecated words, heading case, acronym expansion. A machine enforces it, and a machine should, because humans are bad at it and it uses up the review attention that judgment needs. The other half is editorial: what to explain, how much, in what order, when an example beats a paragraph. No linter will ever check it.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA's phrasing is "as comfortable in Git, CI, or Python as in a style guide", which is a claim about range rather than about style guides specifically. The expectation is that you can both write the rules and implement them.

The thing that distinguishes experience here is knowing which rules are worth encoding and being willing to say that most style guides are too long to be used. A forty-page guide is a document people are told to read and do not. A twelve-rule linter plus two pages of editorial guidance is a thing that actually shapes a corpus.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Encode three classes of rule, then find out that one of them never fires. About twenty-five minutes.

Step 1: one rule per class of guidance

mkdir -p style-demo/docs style-demo/styles/House && cd style-demo

cat > .vale.ini <<'EOF'
StylesPath = styles
MinAlertLevel = suggestion
[*.md]
BasedOnStyles = House
EOF

cat > styles/House/Terms.yml <<'EOF'
extends: substitution
message: "Use '%s' rather than '%s'"
level: error
swap:
  Widget CLI: widget
EOF

cat > styles/House/Passive.yml <<'EOF'
extends: existence
message: "Possible passive voice: '%s'"
level: warning
tokens:
  - '\b(is|are|was|were|be|been|being)\s+\w+ed\b'
EOF

cat > styles/House/SecondPerson.yml <<'EOF'
extends: existence
message: "Address the reader as 'you', not '%s'"
level: warning
tokens:
  - 'the user should'
  - 'one should'
EOF

Three classes: terminology as an error, voice as a warning, person as a warning.

Step 2: a page that violates all three

cat > docs/a.md <<'EOF'
# Install

The Widget CLI is installed by the package manager.
The user should then run the setup command.
You can verify the result.
EOF

vale docs/a.md

 3:5   error    Use 'widget' rather than 'Widget CLI'   House.Terms
 3:16  warning  Possible passive voice: 'is installed'  House.Passive
✖ 1 error, 1 warning and 0 suggestions in 1 file.

Two findings. The page violates three rules.

Step 3: work out which rule is broken

SecondPerson did not fire, and line 4 is "The user should then run the setup command", which is exactly what it was written to catch.

The rule's token is the user should, lowercase. Vale's existence is case-sensitive by default, and the phrase occurs at the start of a sentence, so the text is "The user should". The rule matched nothing.

ignorecase: true

 4:1   warning  Address the reader as 'you', not 'The user should'  House.SecondPerson
✖ 1 error, 2 warnings and 0 suggestions in 1 file.

Now consider how you would have found that without looking. A rule that matches nothing produces no output. Vale does not warn that a rule is never satisfied, the build stays green, and the style guide claims a rule that is not being enforced. A silently dead rule is worse than no rule, because it buys false confidence.

The discipline that prevents it: every new rule ships with a fixture that should fail, and you confirm it fails before you trust it. The same practice the custom linters page arrives at, for the same reason.

Sentence-initial case is the specific trap to remember, because the phrases style guides most want to ban, "The user should", "Simply", "Note that", "In order to", overwhelmingly appear at the start of a sentence.

What you built. Three enforced rules, one near miss, and a rule about rules.

docs.title: What goes in which half
docs.text:
Mechanical, enforce it Editorial, write it down Canonical and deprecated terms What a page should explain and what to link Acronym expansion on first use How much background a reader needs Heading case When an example beats a paragraph Banned filler: "simply", "just", "obviously" How to order a procedure Product and feature name casing When a warning is warranted Code formatting conventions Tone for an error message Passive voice, as a warning Whether a page should exist

The split is also a split in medium. The mechanical half belongs in styles/, in version control, reviewed as code. The editorial half belongs in a short document, and short is the operative word.

docs.title: Rule levels
docs.text:
Level Use for Why Error, blocks the merge Terminology, product names, deprecated terms Not a matter of taste Warning Passive voice, person, sentence length A reasonable contributor could disagree Suggestion Readability scores Informational

The test is whether a reasonable contributor could disagree. If they could, it is a warning, because a build that fails on a defensible choice teaches people that the pipeline is an obstacle. And recall from prose linting that Vale's exit code tracks errors only, so this decision lives in each rule file rather than in a CI flag.

docs.title: Traps in rule authoring
docs.text:
Trap Effect Fix Case sensitivity Misses sentence-initial occurrences, which is most of them ignorecase: true Swap direction substitution keys are the bad form; reversing it silently never fires Test it Over-broad tokens Fires inside correct prose; people disable the rule Narrow, then re-measure No fixture A dead rule is indistinguishable from a clean corpus Ship a failing example Rules about code Vale excludes code by design A custom linter

Three of those five fail silently. That is the character of style automation: the failure mode is not noise, it is quiet absence.

docs.title: Terminology management
docs.text:
Artifact Job A glossary as data The canonical term and its deprecated forms A Vale substitution rule Stops new drift, per pull request A drift measurement Tells you how far the corpus already moved A decision record per term So the choice is not relitigated

The glossary is the artifact and the rules are generated from it, not the other way round. A corpus where the Vale rules are the glossary cannot answer "what is the canonical term for X" without someone reading YAML.

docs.title: How long a style guide should be
docs.text:
Length Outcome A page of editorial guidance plus linted rules Used Ten pages Skimmed once at onboarding Forty pages Cited in arguments, never read

If a rule can be enforced, enforce it and delete the prose about it. What remains in writing should be only the part that needs human judgment, and that is genuinely short.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the split. "A style guide is two documents. The mechanical half, terminology, acronyms, heading case, belongs in a linter, because humans enforce it badly and it consumes the review attention that judgment needs. The editorial half, what to explain and in what order, can only be written down. Most style guides fail because they mix the two and get long enough that nobody reads either."

The follow-up is how you know the rules work, and the answer is fixtures. I wrote three rules and one of them silently matched nothing, because Vale's existence is case-sensitive by default and the banned phrase appears at the start of a sentence. Nothing reported it. So every rule ships with an example that must fail.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Encoding a rule makes it rigid. A terminology rule banning "dataset" will flag a direct quotation from a third-party API genuinely called dataset, so you need a suppression mechanism, and then you have to watch how often it is used, because widespread suppression means the rule is wrong rather than the prose.

One sharper point. The dangerous failure in style automation is silence, not noise. Case sensitivity, a reversed substitution direction and an over-narrow token all produce a rule that fires on nothing, and a corpus with no findings looks identical to a corpus with no enforcement. A rule you have not seen fail is a rule you should not count.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A styles/ directory of rules you wrote, each with a fixture, and a short editorial document that contains only what the rules cannot.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Step 3 is the point, and the trap generalises past Vale.
  2. Take your current style guide and sort every rule into mechanical or editorial. The mechanical pile is your backlog; the editorial pile is your real style guide.
  3. For every rule you already have, write a line that should fail and check it does. Expect at least one surprise.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack carries four hand-written Vale rules with terminology as errors and style as warnings, and one of them caught the author's own hedge word in the README. That is the story to tell: not that the rules exist, but that one fired on the person who wrote it, which is the only proof that a rule is live.

docs.title: Support deflection
docs.text:
The deflection a corpus is capable of is measurable without a single ticket; the deflection it achieved is not measurable without a controlled comparison nobody runs.

core · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Measurable reductions in support load or onboarding time through self-service knowledge systems"

Prerequisites: Documentation analytics

Leads to: Repeat questions

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A question that documentation answered, so nobody had to answer it again. The claim is a counterfactual: this ticket would have been filed and was not, which is a statement about an event that did not happen, and that is why the metric is so often reported badly.

The useful move is to split it in two. Deflection capability is whether the corpus contains the answer and hands it over when asked, which is a property of the documentation and measurable today with no audience. Deflection achieved is whether support volume actually fell because of it, which is a property of the world and needs a comparison almost nobody sets up.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because it is the one documentation outcome that converts directly into money, which makes it the number a documentation team is funded by and the number it is most tempted to overstate.

NVIDIA's phrasing is careful: "measurable reductions in support load". Not "fewer tickets", which any release can produce by shipping fewer features, and not "a self-service portal", which is an artifact rather than an outcome. The word doing the work is measurable, and the honest answer in most organisations is that nobody has the baseline to measure against.

So the professional skill here is less about raising the number than knowing which half you are reporting, and saying so.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Measure the deflection a corpus is capable of, using no tickets, no analytics and no audience. About twenty-five minutes. The method is the point: it turns a counterfactual into two properties you can check.

Step 1: separate answerable from findable

A question becomes a support ticket for one of two quite different reasons. The documentation does not contain the answer, which is a content gap. Or it contains the answer and did not surface it, which is a retrieval gap. Those need opposite responses, and the ticket looks identical either way.

Both are checkable against a golden set:

whole = "\n".join(p.read_text() for p in Path("docs").rglob("*.md")).lower()

for case in cases:
    answerable = all(t.lower() in whole for t in case.must_contain)
    hits = index.search(case.question, limit=1)
    findable = bool(hits) and hits[0].source == case.expect_source

Step 2: run it

  the answer exists somewhere in the corpus:   20/20
  the right page is returned first:            13/20
  answerable but not findable:                  7/20

  deflection ceiling      100%   every question is answered by the corpus
  deflection achieved      65%   the reader is handed the right page
  avoidable support load   35%   of these questions

Seven of twenty questions have an answer in the documentation that the documentation will not give you. Those are the tickets worth caring about, because each one is a reader who would have been deflected by better ranking or better wording rather than by more writing.

The content gap is zero here, which is unusual and is an artifact of the golden set having been written from the corpus. On a real corpus with real queries that row is the interesting one, and it is the only row that calls for writing.

Step 3: notice what the number is not

Thirty-five per cent avoidable load is a statement about twenty questions chosen by the author of the corpus. It is not a prediction about ticket volume, for three reasons worth saying out loud:

the sample is 20 cases, author-written          one case is five points
no case is weighted by how often it is asked    all twenty count equally
no ticket queue exists for this project         nothing to validate against

Real deflection weights each question by frequency, and frequency comes from search logs or a ticket queue. An unweighted golden set treats a question asked four hundred times a month and one asked twice as equally important, which is exactly the error that makes documentation backlogs look nothing like support backlogs.

Step 4: the comparison that would measure the other half, and why it is rare

To claim deflection achieved you need tickets on a topic before a page existed and after, with everything else held still. In practice everything else moves:

release cadence     a quieter quarter lowers tickets with no docs change
traffic             more users raise tickets while deflection improves
support policy      a new triage rule reclassifies tickets out of the category
product changes     the feature that generated the tickets was fixed
seasonality         enterprise support volume is not flat across a year

Each of those moves ticket volume by more than a documentation page does. A before-and-after chart with none of them controlled is the standard artifact in this area, and it supports no causal claim at all.

What does work, in rough order of rigour:

  • A staged rollout, where the page is reachable for some locales or plans before others. This is the only option that gives you a control group.
  • Tagging tickets with whether the asker had seen the page.
  • Reporting the rate per thousand active users rather than the count.
  • Instrumenting documentation search for the question and reporting that query volume moved. Cheapest and most honest, as long as you call it what it is: a deflection proxy, not a deflection.

What you built. A deflection ceiling and an achieved figure from a corpus with no audience, a content gap separated from a retrieval gap, and an explicit list of the confounds that make the other half unclaimable.

docs.title: The two halves
docs.text:
Deflection capability Deflection achieved Property of The corpus The world Needs A golden set A controlled comparison Measurable today Yes Almost never Moves when You write or rank better Anything at all happens Honest claim "35% of these questions are avoidable" "We do not have the baseline"

Reporting the left column in the right column's language is the overstatement to avoid, and it is close to universal.

docs.title: Why a ticket arrived, and what each cause needs
docs.text:
Cause Detected by Fixed by The corpus lacks the answer The answerable check fails Writing The answer exists, ranked badly The findable check fails Ranking or vocabulary The answer exists, phrased in house terms Grounding fails on the right page One sentence, usually The reader never searched Nothing in the corpus Support workflow, not docs The reader did not trust it Nothing in the corpus Freshness signals, examples The answer is wrong A reader complaining Code-sample validation

The first three are a documentation role's work and are separable by measurement. The last three are the ones usually blamed and mostly are not documentation problems, which is worth having evidence about before that conversation rather than during it.

docs.title: Proxies, and how much to trust them
docs.text: Proxy Trust Why Deflection ceiling from a golden set High, for capability Deterministic and reproducible Zero-result searches High, for gaps A reader looking for something absent Search query volume for a topic Medium Directional, confounded by traffic Ticket rate per active user Medium Controls the biggest confound cheaply Page views on the answer page Low A view is not a resolution "Was this helpful?" Very low Measures mood Ticket count, uncontrolled None Moves for a dozen unrelated reasons

docs.title: What to say when asked for the number
docs.text: Asked Answer "How much did docs reduce support?" The capability figure, and that achieved needs a baseline "Can we get that baseline?" Yes: tag tickets, or stage the rollout "Just give me a percentage" The capability figure, labelled as capability "Our competitor claims 40%" Ask what they controlled for

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the split, because it is the part most people have not separated. "Deflection capability is whether the corpus contains the answer and surfaces it when asked. That is a property of the documentation and I can measure it today with no audience. Deflection achieved is whether support volume fell, which is a property of the world and needs a controlled comparison. I report the first and say plainly that I do not have the second."

The follow-up is how you measure the first. Against a golden set, separate answerable from findable. On mine every question is answered somewhere in the corpus and the right page comes back first for thirteen of twenty, so seven questions have an answer the documentation will not hand over. Those seven are the deflectable load, and they need better ranking or better wording rather than more writing, which is a different backlog from the one people expect.

Volunteer the weakness of your own number. Twenty author-written cases, unweighted, so a question asked four hundred times a month counts the same as one asked twice. Real deflection weights by frequency, and frequency needs search logs or a ticket queue. Without them the figure is a ceiling rather than a forecast, and I would rather say that than quote it as one.

The point to make about the uncontrolled chart. A before-and-after ticket graph is the standard artifact here and it supports no causal claim, because release cadence, traffic, triage policy and seasonality each move ticket volume further than a documentation page does. The cheapest real improvement is reporting the rate per thousand active users instead of the count, which controls the largest confound for no extra instrumentation.

One sharper point. The difference between a content gap and a retrieval gap is invisible in the ticket and decisive for what you do next, and almost no support taxonomy records it. A corpus that answers everything and surfaces nothing looks exactly like a corpus with holes in it, and the two call for opposite work: one needs a writer, the other needs a synonym.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A deflection ceiling computed from your own golden set, with the answerable and findable columns kept separate.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Predict the ratio between answerable and findable for your corpus, write the two numbers down, then compute them. Mine were 20 of 20 against 13 of 20, and the second is the one that funds work.
  2. Take your last ten support tickets and label each as content gap, retrieval gap, or not a documentation problem. Ten is enough to discover which of the three you have been assuming.
  3. Convert any deflection figure you currently report into a rate per active user. If the trend reverses, the previous chart was measuring growth.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. The measurement above runs against docpack's twenty-case golden set and its twelve pages and is reproducible from the repository: a ceiling of 100 per cent, an achieved figure of 65 per cent, and a gap of seven named cases. What does not exist is a ticket queue, an audience, or any baseline, so nothing here is a claim about support volume, and the demonstrated page records the achieved half as having no demonstration in either repository.

docs.title: A systems mindset
docs.text:
Fixing the condition that produced a defect rather than the defect, and knowing when not to.

core · difficulty 2 · 2h

A systems mindset: you fix the class of problem, not just the instance

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Leads to: Giving architecture owners implementation feedback, Prioritizing documentation work

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Treating a defect as evidence about the process that produced it. You fix the broken link, and then you ask what allowed a broken link to reach a reader, and you change that.

The second half is what makes it a mindset rather than a slogan: it includes knowing when the answer is "nothing, this was genuinely a one-off", because building a system for every instance is its own failure.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA names it as a required trait and spells it out, which is unusual for a soft requirement. The surrounding language explains why: "We build systems where the right way is easier than the wrong way", and "turning documentation, standards, and tribal knowledge into tooling, templates, and self-service paths, so fewer people have to ask how do I".

Read those together and the role becomes clear. This is not a documentation job with some automation attached. It is a job whose output is mechanisms, and pages are one kind of mechanism among several.

On a Tuesday it is a fork in the road, several times a day. Someone reports that a code sample in the quickstart no longer runs. The instance fix is five minutes. The class fix is a test that executes every sample, which is an afternoon and which means that specific report never happens again. Doing the instance fix feels responsive and leaves you doing it again next quarter.

The reason it is tagged core rather than filed as attitude: it is the thing that determines whether your backlog shrinks. A documentation team that only does instance fixes has a backlog that grows with the product. A team that converts recurring instances into gates has a backlog that grows with the novelty of the product, which is much slower.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Take one instance, find its class, and build the smallest gate that closes it. About thirty minutes.

Step 1: the instance

mkdir -p systems-drill && cd systems-drill
mkdir -p docs
cat > docs/install.md <<'EOF'
# Install

Run `pip install widget`.
EOF
cat > docs/configure.md <<'EOF'
# Configure

First, [install the widget](install.md). Then see the
[tuning guide](tuning.md) for performance options.
EOF
ls docs/

tuning.md does not exist. That is the instance. The instance fix is obvious: create the page or remove the link.

Step 2: ask the question that turns it into a class

cat > analysis.md <<'EOF'
INSTANCE   A link in configure.md points to a page that does not exist.

Q: What allowed this to reach a reader?
A: Nothing checks whether internal links resolve.

CLASS      Any link to a nonexistent page, in any page, ever.

Q: What is the smallest thing that makes the class impossible?
A: A check that resolves every internal link, run before merge.

Q: What does the gate NOT cover?  (Ask this, always.)
A: External links. Anchors within a page. Links in generated output.
   Images. Redirects that resolve but go somewhere wrong.
EOF
cat analysis.md

That last question is the one people skip, and it is what separates a gate from a false sense of security. A link checker that silently ignores anchors will convince a team that links are handled.

Step 3: build the gate

cat > check_links.py <<'PY'
"""Fail if any internal Markdown link points at a file that does not exist."""
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

LINK = re.compile(r"\[[^\]]*\]\((?!https?://|mailto:)([^)#]+)(?:#[^)]*)?\)")

def main(root: Path) -> int:
    broken = []
    for page in sorted(root.rglob("*.md")):
        for target in LINK.findall(page.read_text(encoding="utf-8")):
            if not (page.parent / target).resolve().exists():
                broken.append(f"{page}: {target}")
    for item in broken:
        print(f"broken link  {item}", file=sys.stderr)
    print(f"{'FAIL' if broken else 'ok'}: {len(broken)} broken internal link(s)")
    return 1 if broken else 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(Path(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "docs")))
PY
python3 check_links.py docs

It fails, naming the file and the target.

Step 4: confirm the gate works in both directions

A gate you have only seen fail is half-tested. The dangerous failure is a gate that passes when it should not.

printf '# Tuning\n\nSet the batch size.\n' > docs/tuning.md
python3 check_links.py docs

# And now the case the gate does NOT cover, which you wrote down in step 2.
cat >> docs/configure.md <<'EOF'

See [the batch size section](tuning.md#batch-size).
EOF
python3 check_links.py docs
echo "^ passed, but #batch-size does not exist. Known gap, not a surprise."

What you built. A gate that makes one class of defect impossible, plus a written record of what it does not cover. The record is the deliverable that distinguishes this from enthusiasm: you now know that anchors are unchecked, so when an anchor breaks nobody concludes the link checker is broken, and the next increment is obvious.

docs.title: The four questions, in order
docs.text: Question Purpose What allowed this to reach a reader? Finds the missing gate rather than the bad actor What is the smallest thing that closes the class? Prevents building a platform to fix a typo What does the gate not cover? Stops false confidence, names the next increment Is this class worth a gate at all? The brake. Some instances are genuinely singular

docs.title: Instance and class, worked examples
docs.text:
Instance Class The gate A broken link Any unresolvable internal link Link checking A sample that no longer runs Any sample drifting from the API Code-sample validation A quickstart that fails on a clean machine Any undeclared dependency Cold-start testing A page using "repo" where the glossary says "repository" Terminology drift Prose linting A page with no owner and no review date Unmaintainable content Content model with a required updated A page nobody can find Structure invisible to search Metadata and findability The same question in support three times Missing self-service path Repeat-question analysis A release shipped undocumented Docs outside the definition of done Release readiness

That table is most of what both postings are asking for, which is why this page is short and the others are long.

docs.title: When the instance fix is correct
docs.text:
Worth stating plainly, because this mindset has a failure mode:

  • The class has one member. A typo in a page title is a typo.
  • The gate would cost more than the defects. A linter for a three-page site.
  • You do not understand the class yet. Two instances is not a pattern; building a gate on a guess produces a gate people route around.
  • The gate would be unreliable. A check that fails spuriously trains people to ignore red builds, which is worse than no check. This is the big one.
  • The real fix belongs to someone else. If the class is "the API changes without warning", a documentation gate is a workaround and the conversation belongs with engineering.

docs.title: The strongest version of the idea
docs.text:
A gate catches a defect after someone makes it. The better move, where it is available, is to make the defect unrepresentable: a closed vocabulary means an invalid page type cannot be written down, not merely that it is caught. A generator means a conforming page is the path of least resistance.

NVIDIA's phrase for this is "systems where the right way is easier than the wrong way", and it is a stronger claim than validation. Validation makes the right way mandatory, which is a different and more annoying thing.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Tell a two-level story with a number. "A reader reported a broken sample. I fixed it, then wrote a test that extracts and executes every Python block in the docs. It found four more that day. Then I added a skip marker with an assertion that skips stay under a quarter of the samples, because an escape hatch with no limit becomes the default."

That third sentence is the signal. It shows you expect your own mechanism to be worked around and designed for it.

The follow-up is "when have you over-engineered this", and an interviewer who asks it is testing for judgement rather than enthusiasm. Have a real answer. The most common honest one in this field is a linter rule too aggressive for its corpus, producing dozens of warnings everyone learned to ignore, which left the corpus worse than before because now there was a check that meant nothing.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Every gate is permanent friction on everyone who contributes afterwards, and the people who pay it are not the people who benefited from it. A check that saves you an hour a quarter and costs eleven contributors thirty seconds a day is a net loss that will never show up in any metric you look at. Gates need the same scrutiny as features, including the question of what to remove, which is why retiring content and retiring checks are the same discipline.

One sharper point. The highest-leverage version of this mindset is applied to social problems, not technical ones. "An engineer rewrote a page badly" has a class, and the class fix is usually a template or a review checklist rather than a conversation. Most documentation people apply systems thinking to pipelines and instance thinking to humans. Saying that out loud is unusual and it is the thing NVIDIA's "collaborative style" bullet is circling.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A commit pair: the instance fix, and the gate that closes its class. In the same history, visible as two commits.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path, then find a real instance. Any project. Fix it, then write the smallest gate. Twenty lines is fine; the point is not the sophistication.
  2. Write down what the gate does not cover, in the gate. A comment or a README line. This is the cheapest credibility available on this page, because almost nobody does it and it is immediately recognisable as the work of someone who has been burned.
  3. Find one gate to remove. A check that has never caught anything, or whose warnings everyone ignores. Removing it is the same skill pointed the other way, and it is the harder half to demonstrate. If you cannot find a check that has never caught anything, you have either a young pipeline or no record of what your gates catch, and the second is the more common answer.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. "I think in systems" is a claim anyone can make. A repository where you can point at the red build, the fix, and the gate that followed is not. The strongest version includes a gate you later deleted.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
A repository can hold the output of this thinking and not the thinking. What would demonstrate it is a record of decisions and their consequences, which is a thing you accumulate rather than build.

Where the skill is exercised. In the choice to fix a class rather than an instance. In noticing that two unrelated-looking failures share a cause. In declining to add a check because the check would be ignored.

What a learner would do. Take the last five defects you fixed, in anything, and for each write down the instance you fixed and the class it belonged to. Then ask which of the five you closed at the class level. Most people find one. That ratio is the measurement, and it is available today without any tooling.

Then do the inverse on something you own: find a check that fires often and ask what it is really telling you. A link checker that reports twenty dead links a month is not a link problem, it is a publishing problem, and the systems answer is to find out what keeps breaking them.

What competence looks like.

Evidence Why it carries weight A fix whose commit message names the class The class was seen, not just the bug A check added after a defect, in the same change The instinct is present, not retrofitted A check removed because it was noise Harder than adding, and rarer Two problems diagnosed as one cause The actual skill A deliberate decision not to automate Judgment rather than reflex

What this guide can point at instead. The closest thing to evidence here is the pattern in its own history. A prerequisite label was standardised and asserted in a test rather than corrected on one page. A word-count gate was re-derived after a generator was added. A fence parser was written after three naive versions returned plausible wrong numbers. A Related section was promoted from convention to contract once one page was found without it. Each of those is an instance closed as a class, and the record of them is the nearest a repository gets.

Why it is still not a demonstration. Those decisions are visible in hindsight and the reasoning is not. A reader cannot tell from the commit whether the class was seen at the time or found later during an audit, and in at least two of those four cases it was found later. Saying so is the only honest version of this page.

docs.title: Taxonomy and controlled vocabularies
docs.text:
Closing a vocabulary so values can be relied on, and checking that something actually reads it.

core · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Information architecture skills: content modeling, taxonomy, and metadata for both navigation and machine retrieval"

Prerequisites: Content models

Leads to: Style guides and terminology management, Detecting terminology drift

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The set of agreed terms your content is classified by, and the decision about which of those sets are closed. A closed vocabulary has a fixed list of permitted values and a check that rejects anything else. An open one is a text field people type into.

That distinction is the whole concept. An open vocabulary is a suggestion. A closed one is a guarantee, and a guarantee is the only thing a pipeline can be built on.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA names taxonomy between content modeling and metadata, which is where it belongs: the model says a field exists, the taxonomy says what may go in it, and metadata is the result.

The practical stake is filtering. "Show me the how-to pages for operators" is answerable only if diataxis and audience are closed, because a query against an open field has to guess at spellings, synonyms and capitalisation. Every retrieval feature in the AI-ready category is a filter over a vocabulary, so a corpus with open vocabularies caps how good retrieval can get no matter which model is behind it.

The second stake is that closing a vocabulary forces a decision. Arguing about whether a page is a tutorial or a how-to is a useful argument, and an open field lets everybody avoid having it.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Close a vocabulary, then discover the failure a closed vocabulary does not protect against. About twenty-five minutes.

Step 1: see what a real corpus's vocabularies look like

import collections
import re
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

fields = collections.Counter()
values = collections.defaultdict(collections.Counter)
pages = 0
for p in sorted(Path("docs").rglob("*.md")):
    m = re.match(r"^---\n(.*?)\n---\n", p.read_text(), re.S)
    if not m:
        continue
    pages += 1
    for k, v in (yaml.safe_load(m.group(1)) or {}).items():
        fields[k] += 1
        if isinstance(v, list):
            for item in v:
                values[k][str(item)] += 1
        elif isinstance(v, (str, bool)) and len(str(v)) < 30:
            values[k][str(v)] += 1

121 pages

field        pages  coverage  values
title          121      100%  free text
summary        121      100%  free text
diataxis       121      100%  reference(53), explanation(46), how-to(22)
audience       121      100%  developer(100), new-user(13), operator(5), contributor(3)
concept         64       52%  64 distinct
tags            64       52%  core(43), ai(21), supporting(19), qa(14), dac(14) +3 more
generated       53       43%  True(53)

Two vocabularies look healthy: diataxis with three values and audience with four, both at full coverage. tags sits at 52 per cent, which means it cannot be depended on for anything, exactly as the content model page argues about optional fields.

Step 2: look harder at the healthy-looking one

diataxis: reference on 53 pages. Split that by whether the page was generated:

(gen_types if fm.get("generated") else hand_types)[fm.get("diataxis")] += 1

generated pages by diataxis: {'reference': 53}
hand-written by diataxis:    {'how-to': 22, 'explanation': 46}

Every generated page is reference. No hand-written page is.

So in this corpus diataxis: reference did not mean reference documentation. It meant "generated stub", because the placeholder generator hardcoded the value. The vocabulary was closed, every value was legal, and the field was lying on 44 per cent of the pages.

A closed vocabulary guarantees values come from the list. It guarantees nothing about whether they are true.

Step 3: find out why nobody noticed

grep -rn "diataxis" src/fieldguide/*.py hooks/*.py mkdocs.yml

src/fieldguide/generate.py:144:        "diataxis": "reference",
src/fieldguide/scaffold.py:102:        "diataxis: explanation",

Two writers, zero readers. Nothing consumed the field: not navigation, not search, not a hook, not a validator. A vocabulary nobody reads is a vocabulary that is already wrong, and nothing exists that would tell you.

That is the general rule worth taking away. What keeps a vocabulary honest is not the list of permitted values. It is a consumer that breaks when the values are wrong.

Step 4: make the value honest

A generated stub has no Diátaxis type, because it has no content. Claiming one is the lie, so add the value that is true:

DIATAXIS = ("tutorial", "how-to", "reference", "explanation", "placeholder")

# in the placeholder generator
"diataxis": "placeholder",

all pages by diataxis:  {'how-to': 22, 'explanation': 46, 'placeholder': 53}
generated pages:        {'placeholder': 53}

placeholder is not part of Diátaxis. Adding a value the framework lacks is the right call when the alternative is a value that is wrong: the vocabulary describes your corpus, not a book.

Step 5: give it a reader, so it cannot drift again

if isinstance(data, dict) and "diataxis" in data:
    if data["diataxis"] not in DIATAXIS:
        out.append(f"{page}: diataxis is {data['diataxis']!r}, "
                   f"which is not one of {list(DIATAXIS)}")

  FIRES: diataxis is 'refrence', which is not one of ['tutorial', 'how-to', ...]

Plus a regression test asserting that no generated page claims a type it has not earned. The field now has a consumer, so a typo or a hardcoded default fails a build.

What you learned. Closing a vocabulary stops illegal values. Only a consumer stops untrue ones, and a field nothing reads drifts immediately and silently.

docs.title: What to close and what to leave open
docs.text: Field Closed? Why Page type (diataxis) Yes Three or four values, and filters depend on it Audience Yes Small set; open produces "devs", "developer", "Developers" Status or lifecycle stage Yes A workflow with unlimited states is not a workflow Product area or component Yes, from the product's own list It must match what engineering calls it Tags or keywords Usually open, and therefore mostly useless See below Title, summary Open They are prose Author Open, or a people directory Not a classification

docs.title: Why free tags disappoint
docs.text:
tags above sits at 52 per cent coverage with eight distinct values. A tag vocabulary fails in a predictable sequence: it is optional, so half the corpus omits it; it is open, so synonyms accumulate; nothing depends on it, because it is unreliable; and because nothing depends on it, nobody maintains it.

If you want tags to work, close the list and require them. If you are not willing to do both, the honest move is to delete the field rather than keep a half-populated one implying a classification nobody can trust.

docs.title: The three properties a vocabulary needs
docs.text:
Property Without it Closed Synonyms and spellings accumulate, so filters miss Required Absent half the time, so nothing can depend on it Consumed Nothing breaks when values are wrong, so they go wrong

All three, or you do not have a vocabulary. The third is the one teams skip, and the one this guide got wrong across 53 pages.

docs.title: Taxonomy against its neighbours
docs.text:
Concept Is about Taxonomy Which terms are permitted, as classification Style guide Which terms to use in prose Terminology drift Whether the corpus still obeys either Metadata The values actually attached to pages Content model Which fields exist at all

Taxonomy and style guide overlap without being the same thing. access token as the canonical term in prose is a style decision; audience: operator as a permitted classification value is a taxonomy decision. Confusing them produces a style guide full of metadata rules nobody can enforce.

docs.title: Who owns the vocabulary
docs.text:
The product's own terms are not yours to invent. If engineering calls a component ingest-gateway, your component vocabulary uses that string even if a nicer name exists, because a classification that disagrees with the product is one readers cannot map onto anything.

Where there is no external source of truth, as with page type and audience, you own it, and the right size is the smallest set that supports a filter somebody actually wants.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with filtering, not tidiness. "Closing a vocabulary is what makes filtering possible: 'how-to pages for operators' is answerable only if those two fields have fixed value sets. Every retrieval feature is a filter over a vocabulary, so open vocabularies cap how good retrieval can get regardless of the model."

The follow-up that separates experience from theory is what keeps a vocabulary honest, and the answer is a consumer. I had a closed, fully populated diataxis field whose value was wrong on 44 per cent of pages, because a generator hardcoded one value and nothing read the field.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Every closed vocabulary is an argument you have to have, and then a constraint contributors live with. A vocabulary that is too small forces pages into the wrong bucket, and the mitigation is to add the value that is true rather than making authors lie. placeholder is not in Diátaxis, and adding it beat having 53 pages claim to be reference documentation.

One sharper point. Free-tag fields are where taxonomies go to die, and the failure is mechanical rather than cultural: optional means half-populated, half-populated means nothing can depend on it, and nothing depending on it means nobody fixes it. Either close the list and require it, or delete the field.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A closed vocabulary, a check that rejects values outside it, and something that consumes it.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run step 1 against a corpus you own and print the value distribution for every field. Skew is the signal: one value dominating usually means a default somewhere.
  2. Grep for readers of your most important metadata field. If writers outnumber readers, that field is already wrong.
  3. Pick your least reliable vocabulary and either close and require it, or remove it. Both are improvements; leaving it half-populated is not.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack validates five front-matter fields, two of them closed vocabularies, rejected in CI. The more useful story is this one: a closed vocabulary that was fully populated, entirely legal and wrong on 53 pages, found by comparing the value distribution between generated and hand-written pages, and fixed by adding an honest value plus a consumer that fails the build.
