docs.title: Technical writing as a craft
docs.text:
Writing that a competent stranger can act on without asking you a question.

core · difficulty 2 · 8h

Strong technical writing and information architecture skills for developer documentation

Source: intel posting, verbatim

Leads to: Giving architecture owners implementation feedback

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Writing that a competent stranger can act on without asking you a question. The test is behavioural rather than aesthetic: not whether the prose reads well, but whether the reader does the right thing next.

It is a craft in the specific sense that it improves with deliberate practice on feedback, and that people who are good at it can say why a sentence is wrong.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Both postings list it as a minimum qualification. Intel asks for "strong technical writing" in the same breath as information architecture; NVIDIA opens with "You're a writer who builds" and wants eight years in technical writing or developer documentation.

This guide's first version covered pipelines, retrieval, taxonomy and validators and had no page for writing well. That was its worst gap, and the reason it was easy to fall into is worth naming: everything else in this field is more legible. A chunker either works or does not. A link checker either fails the build or does not. Prose quality has no test suite, so it quietly becomes the thing nobody budgets for while everyone agrees it matters.

On a Tuesday this is less glamorous than the postings suggest. An engineer hands you four paragraphs about a new flag. The paragraphs are accurate. They also open with implementation history, use three names for the same thing, bury the one command a reader needs in the middle of the third sentence, and never say what happens if you get it wrong. Turning that into a page someone can act on, in twenty minutes, without losing anything true, is the job. You will do it several times a day.

The second reason it is core: in a role where you build the validators, your own writing is the reference implementation. A style rule you cannot follow is a style rule the team will litigate.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
No installation, which makes this the one golden path in the guide that is pure practice. About thirty minutes, and it still ends in a measurement.

Step 1: get a page that is accurate and unusable

mkdir -p writing-drill && cd writing-drill
cat > before.md <<'EOF'
# Configuring Retry Behaviour

Historically the widget client did not retry at all, which caused problems
during the 2024 migration when the upstream service was being restarted
frequently. We subsequently added retry logic, and after some discussion
about whether the backoff should be linear or exponential, exponential was
chosen. The retry configuration is controlled through the client
configuration object, which also controls other things like timeouts, and
users should be aware that the retry count does not include the initial
attempt, so a retry count of 3 means 4 total requests will be made. It is
generally recommended that you do not set the retry count very high because
this can cause the client to block for a long time, and in some cases it may
be better to fail fast and let the caller decide. The maximum is 10.
EOF
wc -w before.md

Nothing in that paragraph is false. A reader who needs to set a retry count has to read 150 words and do arithmetic.

Step 2: four passes, in this order

Order matters: reorganising sentences you are about to delete is wasted work.

cat > passes.md <<'EOF'
1. CUT      Remove what the reader does not need in order to act. History,
            decision records and hedging all go. Target: half the words.
2. ANSWER   Put the thing they came for in the first sentence.
3. NAME     One term per concept, every time. No synonyms for variety.
4. FAIL     Say what goes wrong, and what to do about it.
EOF
cat passes.md

Step 3: do the passes

cat > after.md <<'EOF'
# Configure retry behaviour

Set `retries` on the client. The default is 3.

    client = WidgetClient(retries=3)

`retries` counts retries, not attempts: `retries=3` makes up to 4 requests.
The maximum is 10.

## Choosing a value

| Situation | Value |
|---|---|
| A caller is waiting on the response | 1 to 2 |
| Background job that can afford to wait | 3 to 5 |
| Upstream is known to restart often | up to 10 |

Retries use exponential backoff, so a high count blocks for a long time. If the
caller handles failure better than the client can wait, prefer failing fast
over raising this.

## Why exponential backoff

See the retry design note.
EOF
echo "before: $(wc -w < before.md) words"
echo "after:  $(wc -w < after.md) words"

Step 4: measure the thing that matters

Word count is a proxy. The real test is how far a reader travels before they can act.

python3 - <<'PY'
import pathlib

def words_before_the_answer(path, marker="retries"):
    text = pathlib.Path(path).read_text()
    index = text.find(marker)
    return len(text[:index].split())

for name in ("before.md", "after.md"):
    print(f"{name:<12} {words_before_the_answer(name):>3} words before the answer")
PY

What you built. The same facts, with the reader reaching the answer in a fraction of the distance, plus two things the original lacked entirely: a table for choosing a value, and a statement of what goes wrong.

Note that the rewrite is not merely shorter. The history moved to an explanation page rather than being destroyed, which is Diátaxis doing the work. Keep both files: a before-and-after you can show is the most persuasive artifact in this whole category.

docs.title: The four passes
docs.text: Pass Question Typical cut Cut Does the reader need this to act? Implementation history, decision narrative, hedging, apologies Answer Is the thing they came for first? Move the command or the value to sentence one Name One term per concept? Synonyms introduced for variety Fail What goes wrong, and then what? Usually missing entirely

docs.title: Sentence-level habits that carry most of the weight
docs.text:
Habit Instead of Write Active voice for instructions "The flag should be set" "Set the flag" Second person "Users can configure" "Configure" Present tense "The client will retry" "The client retries" Condition first "Run drain if deploying a schema change" "Before a schema change, run drain" Say the number "A reasonably high value" "Up to 10" One idea per sentence Three clauses and a however Three sentences

Condition-first is the least obvious and the most valuable. A reader scanning for their situation needs to know whether a sentence applies to them before they read it.

docs.title: Words that signal a problem
docs.text:
Word What it usually hides "simply", "just", "easy" A step the author stopped seeing "should" Nobody checked whether it does "note that", "it is important to" Something belonging earlier, or in a callout "etc.", "and so on" The author did not finish the list "robust", "seamless", "powerful" Nothing. Delete "obviously", "of course" The reader is about to feel stupid

These are exactly what a Vale rule catches, which is the link between this page and the automation half of the job.

docs.title: What technical writing is not
docs.text: Not Difference Good prose Literary quality is irrelevant; actionability is not Brevity A reference page should be exhaustive. Short is a means Simplification Never make it less true to make it shorter Explaining everything An explanation inside a how-to guide is a defect

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Do not call your writing clear and concise; everyone does. Describe a specific edit and its cost. "The page documented a flag accurately in 150 words of history. I moved the history to an explanation page, put the default in the first sentence, added a table for choosing a value and a line on what happens if you set it too high. The reader reaches the answer in one sentence instead of five, and nothing true was lost."

The follow-up is usually "how do you get engineers to write documentation". The answer that lands is that mostly you do not, and designing around that is the skill. You take their accurate, badly organised paragraph as a source rather than a draft, and you ask them to review for accuracy rather than for style. An engineer will happily confirm a number is right. They will not happily restructure a page.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Editing someone else's writing hard enough to make it usable costs political capital every time, and the cost is highest with the people whose expertise you most need. There is a real version of this job where you keep every contributor happy and the documentation stays bad. The mitigation is to move standards into linters and templates, so the rule is impersonal and the argument happens once against the rule rather than weekly against a person. That is the systems mindset applied to a social problem.

One sharper point. The hardest part of technical writing is not sentences, it is knowing what the reader does not know, and it is hard because writing a page destroys your ability to judge it. Once you understand the system, the gap you left is invisible to you. Nothing fixes that from the inside, which is the real argument for cold-start testing and for watching someone new follow your page without helping them. Saying that connects the craft to the automation, which is the whole pitch of both roles.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A before-and-after, with the reasoning. Not a writing sample: a sample shows you can write, which is table stakes. An edit shows you can diagnose.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path on a real page. Find a genuinely bad page in a project you know, rewrite it with the four passes, and write three sentences on what each pass removed. Twenty minutes, and the highest-value portfolio item on this page.
  2. Encode one of your own rules as a linter. Take a habit you care about, hedge words or synonym drift, and write the Vale rule. A writer who ships their style guide as code is making precisely the argument both postings are hiring for.
  3. Watch someone follow one of your pages without helping them. Note where they stop, then fix the page rather than explaining it. That note is more convincing about your judgement than any finished page. Predict where they will stop before you watch. Being wrong about that is the point of doing it with a person rather than from the page.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Anyone can produce a polished page. The signal is being able to say what is wrong with a page and in what order you would fix it, and having an example where you were the one who was wrong. If the "before" is always someone else's writing, that is a smaller claim than one where it is yours.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
This one cannot be demonstrated by a repository anywhere, not for want of tooling. A repository can show that a page exists, conforms and is accurate; it cannot show that a reader understood it, and understanding is the claim.

Where the skill is actually exercised. In an edit of someone else's draft, where the measure is whether the author accepts the change and can say why. In the gap between a first draft and a third. In the decision to cut a section that took a day to write.

What a learner would do. Take a page you did not write and that works, and rewrite it badly on purpose: bury the first instruction under motivation, move the expected output away from the command, replace the reader's word with the precise term everywhere. Then read both aloud. The exercise is instructive in the direction people do not try, because the defects you introduce deliberately are the ones you stop introducing accidentally.

Then the reverse: take a page that does not work, and fix it without adding words. The constraint is the whole exercise. Most bad documentation is bad by addition, and the instinct to explain more is the instinct to resist.

What competence looks like, in evidence someone else can see.

Evidence Why it carries weight A diff that shortens a page and improves it The rarest and most convincing artifact An author thanking you for a cut They had to agree, which is the test A page whose support questions stopped Indirect, and the only outcome measure A style decision you reversed, with the reason Shows the judgment is live rather than inherited Writing that survives a hostile review Review is the nearest thing to a reader

Why none of that commits to a repository. The diff is in someone else's project. The acknowledgement is in a review thread. The support question that stopped is an absence, and absences do not appear in version control. This is the honest reason this concept has no demonstration here and would have none anywhere: the evidence exists, it is just not the kind of thing you can clone.

What a corpus can show is the mechanisable part, which is why this guide enforces a page contract, a duration, a stated result and a verification section. Those are the floor. The craft is what happens above it, and the distance between a page that satisfies the contract and a page that works is the whole subject.

docs.title: Templates and scaffolding
docs.text:
Generating a page that already satisfies the contract, and the gate a helpful template quietly weakens.

core · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Encode standards (user stories, release readiness, onboarding, security guidance) into templates, validators, and guided workflows rather than static documents"

Prerequisites: Content models

Leads to: Guided workflows

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A command that produces a new page already shaped correctly: the required front matter present, the required sections in the required order, the cross-references computed, and a prompt in each section saying what belongs there.

The difference between a template and scaffolding is that a template is a file you copy and scaffolding is a program that generates one. The program can fill in what it knows, which on a corpus with a content model is most of the metadata.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA's bullet says templates rather than static documents, which is the whole argument. A style guide tells an author what a page should contain, and is read once. A scaffold hands them a page that already contains it, and is used every time.

The deeper reason is that it makes the standard the path of least resistance, which is NVIDIA's other phrase: build systems where the right way is easier than the wrong way. An author who runs fieldguide new gets the contract for free. An author who copies a neighbouring page gets whatever that page had.

The failure mode this page is really about is more interesting: a scaffold is so helpful that it can accidentally satisfy the checks that were supposed to hold the author to a standard.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Scaffold a page, check it against the validator, then find out what the scaffold is doing to your own quality gate. About twenty-five minutes.

Step 1: generate a page from the registry

fieldguide new docs-analytics --dry-run

---
title: Documentation analytics
summary: 'TODO: one sentence on what documentation analytics is and why this role needs it.'
diataxis: explanation
audience: developer

# Documentation analytics

`core` · difficulty 2 · 4h

> Instrument documentation analytics and convert findings into improvements to
> docs, samples, and tooling

> Source: intel posting, verbatim

**Prerequisites:** [Documentation CI](documentation-ci.md)

**Leads to:** [Measuring AI answer quality](ai-answer-quality.md), [Search and
query log analysis](search-log-analysis.md), [Support deflection](support-deflection.md),
[Time to first success](time-to-first-success.md), ...

Four things were computed rather than typed: the tags from category and tier, the posting quote verbatim from the registry, the prerequisites, and the concepts that depend on this one. None of them can be wrong, because none of them were transcribed.

Step 2: the prompts, which are the interesting part

## What it is

<!-- Define it in two sentences, for someone who has heard the
term in a meeting and not admitted they do not know it. No history, no
motivation, no list of benefits.

The failure mode here is writing the Wikipedia opening: a definition so
careful it is useless. Prefer the sentence you would actually say out loud.
-->

Each section carries a prompt and a named failure mode. That is the part worth copying. "Define it in two sentences" is a brief; "the failure mode is the Wikipedia opening" is the thing that actually changes what gets written, because it names the mistake the author is about to make.

Step 3: check the scaffold against the validator

A scaffold and a validator are separate programs with separate ideas of a valid page. If they drift, your tooling tells contributors to run a command whose output your own CI rejects. So test every one:

for c in [x for x in reg.concepts if x.status == "planned"]:
    text = render_concept_page(reg, c.id)
    heads = _headings_outside_fences(text)
    missing = [s for s in REQUIRED_SECTIONS if s not in heads]
    order = [heads[s] for s in REQUIRED_SECTIONS if s in heads]
    assert not missing and order == sorted(order)

planned concepts: 27
scaffolded pages failing the section contract: 0

Twenty-seven for twenty-seven. This check belongs in CI, not in a one-off script, because the two modules are edited independently.

Step 4: now measure what the scaffold did to your word gate

The contract says a page marked complete must be at least 450 words, which exists to stop a stub wearing a label. Measure a fresh scaffold against it:

scaffold word count: min=372 max=402   (complete minimum is 450)

Comfortable, apparently: no scaffold can pass as complete. But count where those words are:

COMMENT = re.compile(r"<!--.*?-->", re.S)
total    = len(text.split())
stripped = len(COMMENT.sub(" ", text).split())

concept                     total  outside comments  in comments
sample-apps                   376                87          289
templates-scaffolding         385                96          289
docs-analytics                400               111          289

289 of about 380 words are prompt text inside HTML comments, and the gate was counting them. So the arithmetic an author faced was:

real prose required to cross the 450-word gate: ~74 words

Seventy-four. A gate meant to require a substantial page was 84 per cent pre-satisfied by the template's own instructions, so two paragraphs and a status change would mark a page complete with most of its prompts unanswered.

Two good ideas, a helpful template and a word-count gate, combining into a weak gate. Neither is wrong on its own.

Step 5: fix the measurement, not the template

HTML_COMMENT = re.compile(r"<!--.*?-->", re.S)

def prose_words(text: str) -> int:
    """Count words a reader would see, excluding HTML comments."""
    return len(HTML_COMMENT.sub(" ", text).split())

scaffold raw words:   376
scaffold prose words: 87
real prose needed:    363 (was 74)

The threshold did not move. What the threshold means changed, from 74 words of prose to 363.

What you built. A scaffold that computes what it can and names the failure modes, a CI check that it agrees with the validator, and a word gate that measures prose rather than instructions.

docs.title: What a scaffold should compute rather than ask for
docs.text:
Field Source Tags, category, tier The registry entry Title The registry entry Required sections The page contract Prerequisites and dependents The knowledge graph A source quotation The registry's demanded_by Date fields The clock Summary, body The author; these are the actual work

Anything on the top half that an author types is something they can get wrong. The bottom two rows are where human effort belongs, and a scaffold that pre-fills them with plausible text is worse than one that leaves a TODO.

docs.title: What makes a prompt work
docs.text:
Weak prompt Better "Describe the concept" "Two sentences, for someone who heard it in a meeting" "Add examples" "The shortest exercise that produces a working result" "Keep it concise" "The failure mode is the Wikipedia opening" "Explain the benefits" Delete; nobody needs a benefits section

Naming the failure mode is the highest-leverage sentence in a template, because an author about to make a mistake rarely knows which mistake it is.

docs.title: Template, scaffold, generator
docs.text:
Is Drifts because Template A file you copy Nothing enforces that you copied the current one Scaffold A program producing a new file It can disagree with the validator Generator A program producing pages from data Committed output can go stale

Each step up removes a class of drift and adds a program to maintain. The scaffold-versus-validator agreement from step 3 is the drift you take on by moving from a template to a scaffold, and it is cheap to check.

docs.title: Mechanisms worth encoding this way
docs.text: Standard Scaffolded as Page contract fieldguide new <concept> Content model Front matter pre-filled and validated Security guidance Approved patterns in the sample stub Release readiness A checklist issue template Playbooks A node-and-outcome skeleton Pull request expectations A template asking the judgment questions

docs.title: Keeping it honest
docs.text: Rule Why CI asserts the scaffold satisfies the validator They are separate programs Prompts live in comments, not placeholder prose Placeholder prose gets published Comments are excluded from word counts See step 4 TODO markers fail a complete status Otherwise they ship The scaffold is the documented way to start A scaffold nobody runs is a template

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with least resistance. "A template rather than a static document means the standard arrives as a working file instead of as a page somebody read once. The scaffold computes everything it can from the content model, so metadata cannot be mistyped, and each section carries a prompt that names the failure mode rather than restating the requirement."

The follow-up is drift, and the answer is that a scaffold and a validator are two programs with two ideas of a valid page, so CI asserts that scaffolded output passes validation. Twenty-seven for twenty-seven, checked on every build rather than once.

The tradeoff to volunteer. A scaffold is code you own, and it has to be version-aware: when the page contract changes, every page generated by the old scaffold is now non-conforming and nothing tells you which ones. A template has the same problem and no way to detect it, which is the argument for the scaffold, but neither solves it.

One sharper point, and the best thing here. A helpful template can quietly weaken your quality gates. Mine put 289 of roughly 380 words into prompt comments, and because the word-count gate counted raw words, an author needed only 74 words of real prose to mark a page complete. The fix was to count prose rather than instructions, which left the threshold unchanged and changed what it meant from 74 words to 363. The lesson generalises: when you add a generator, re-derive every metric that counts the generated artifact.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A new command in a repository of yours, a CI step asserting its output passes your validator, and a word count that excludes the template's own text.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Step 4 is the one worth doing on your own tooling.
  2. Check whether your scaffold's output passes your own validator. If nobody has checked, assume it does not.
  3. Add a named failure mode to the three prompts in your template that produce the worst writing. It is the cheapest editorial intervention available.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack has docpack new <type> --title, which serialises front matter with yaml.safe_dump after an f-string version broke on its own default placeholder, and this guide's fieldguide new is checked against the validator in CI for every planned concept. The story to tell is step 4: the scaffold was quietly supplying 84 per cent of a gate meant to hold authors to a standard, and nothing was wrong with either piece on its own.

docs.title: Detecting terminology drift
docs.text:
Measuring how consistently a corpus uses its own vocabulary, and finding where it stopped.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "Automate the content lifecycle with LLMs and scripting, from drafting and updating to auditing, with checks for freshness, code accuracy, and terminology drift, and human review where judgment matters"

Prerequisites: Taxonomy, Prose linting with Vale

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Measuring, across a whole corpus, how often each concept is referred to by its agreed name versus by something else. A Vale rule catches a deprecated term in one pull request. Drift detection answers the different question of how far the corpus as a whole has already moved, which pages are worst, and whether the situation is improving.

The distinction matters because the two produce different actions. A linter finding is a fix. A drift measurement is a decision: rename the thing, update the glossary, or accept that the term you chose lost.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA names it alongside freshness and code accuracy as one of three things the content lifecycle should be audited for. All three share a shape: the individual page was correct when written, and the world moved.

Terminology drift is the one that damages trust fastest, because it is invisible page by page. Every page is internally consistent. The reader meets access token in the quickstart, API key in the reference and auth token in the troubleshooting guide, and has to work out whether those are three things or one. Nothing is wrong; the corpus is just no longer speaking with one voice, and a reader who cannot tell whether two names mean the same thing stops trusting any of them.

It also breaks retrieval, which is why it sits next to the AI-readiness work. A search for access token cannot rank a page that calls it an API key, and embeddings blur the distinction without resolving it. Three names for one concept means a retriever has three weaker clusters instead of one strong one.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Measure drift against a glossary, then discover that the naive measurement flatters you. About thirty minutes.

Committed as drills/terminology_drift.py, which walks all four states in one run. Tests assert it still prints the tables below, and that the glossary and three sample pages it measures are the ones this page tells you to write.

Step 1: a glossary as data

mkdir -p drift-demo/docs && cd drift-demo

cat > glossary.yaml <<'EOF'
terms:
  - canonical: widget
    deprecated: [Widget CLI, widget-cli, WidgetCLI]
  - canonical: data set
    deprecated: [dataset, data-set]
  - canonical: access token
    deprecated: [API key, apikey, auth token]
EOF

cat > docs/a.md <<'EOF'
# Install
Install widget, then create an access token.
EOF
cat > docs/b.md <<'EOF'
# Configure
Point the Widget CLI at your dataset. Use your API key.
EOF
cat > docs/c.md <<'EOF'
# Troubleshoot
If widget-cli fails, check the auth token and the data-set path.
EOF

Three pages, deliberately inconsistent, which is what a real corpus looks like after two years and nine contributors.

Step 2: the obvious measurement

Count canonical uses, count deprecated uses, divide. Running that version produces this:

canonical        conformant  total   rate  variants
widget                    3      5    60%  Widget CLI(1), widget-cli(1)
data set                  0      2     0%  dataset(1), data-set(1)
access token              1      3    33%  API key(1), auth token(1)

Sixty per cent conformance on widget. That number is wrong, and wrong in the flattering direction.

Step 3: find out why

python3 - <<'PY'
import re
from pathlib import Path
pat = re.compile(r"\bwidget\b", re.I)
for p in sorted(Path("docs").rglob("*.md")):
    text = p.read_text()
    for m in pat.finditer(text):
        print(f"{p}: ...{text[max(0, m.start() - 12):m.end() + 12]!r}...")
PY

docs/a.md: ...'all\nInstall widget, then creat'...
docs/b.md: ...'e\nPoint the Widget CLI at your'...
docs/c.md: ...'bleshoot\nIf widget-cli fails, '...

Two of the three "conformant" matches are the canonical term matching inside its own deprecated variants. \bwidget\b matches the Widget in Widget CLI and the widget in widget-cli, because a hyphen is a word boundary.

This is not a quirk of this example. The canonical term is a substring of its deprecated forms most of the time, because deprecated forms are usually the canonical term plus something: a suffix, a hyphen, a product word. So the naive measurement systematically counts drift as conformance, and the worse the drift the more it flatters you.

Step 4: mask before you count

# drift.py
import re
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

terms = yaml.safe_load(Path("glossary.yaml").read_text())["terms"]
rows, per_page = [], Counter()

for entry in terms:
    canon = entry["canonical"]
    # Longest first, so "API key" is consumed before any shorter variant.
    deprecated = sorted(entry["deprecated"], key=len, reverse=True)
    variants, conformant = Counter(), 0

    for page in sorted(Path("docs").rglob("*.md")):
        text = page.read_text()
        for bad in deprecated:
            pattern = re.compile(r"\b" + re.escape(bad) + r"\b")
            found = pattern.findall(text)
            if found:
                variants[bad] += len(found)
                per_page[str(page)] += len(found)
            # Mask it so the canonical count cannot see it.
            text = pattern.sub("\x00" * len(bad), text)
        conformant += len(re.findall(r"\b" + re.escape(canon) + r"\b", text, re.I))

    total = conformant + sum(variants.values())
    rows.append((canon, conformant, total, variants))

print(f"{'canonical':16} {'conformant':>10} {'total':>6} {'rate':>6}  variants")
for canon, ok, total, variants in rows:
    rate = f"{100 * ok // total}%" if total else "n/a"
    v = ", ".join(f"{k}({n})" for k, n in variants.most_common())
    print(f"{canon:16} {ok:>10} {total:>6} {rate:>6}  {v}")
print()
print("worst pages:", ", ".join(f"{p} ({n})" for p, n in per_page.most_common(3)))
drifted = sum(sum(v.values()) for _c, _o, _t, v in rows)
print(f"\n{'FAIL' if drifted else 'ok'}: {drifted} deprecated usage(s)")
raise SystemExit(1 if drifted else 0)

python3 drift.py

canonical        conformant  total   rate  variants
widget                    1      3    33%  Widget CLI(1), widget-cli(1)
data set                  0      2     0%  dataset(1), data-set(1)
access token              1      3    33%  API key(1), auth token(1)

worst pages: docs/b.md (3), docs/c.md (3)

FAIL: 6 deprecated usage(s)

widget drops from 60 per cent to 33 per cent, which is the true figure. The masking also gives you the two outputs that make this actionable: a per-term rate, and a ranked list of which pages to fix first.

Step 5: confirm it goes green

printf '# Configure\nPoint widget at your data set. Use your access token.\n' > docs/b.md
printf '# Troubleshoot\nIf widget fails, check the access token and the data set path.\n' > docs/c.md
python3 drift.py

widget                    3      3   100%
data set                  2      2   100%
access token              3      3   100%

ok: 0 deprecated usage(s)

What you built. A measurement with a direction, which is what makes drift a managed quantity rather than a complaint. Run it on a schedule and the rate over time tells you whether the glossary is winning.

docs.title: Linting versus drift detection
docs.text:
Vale rule Drift measurement Scope One pull request The whole corpus Output A finding to fix A rate and a ranking Runs On every change On a schedule Answers Did this diff regress? How bad is it, and where? Blocks a merge Yes, for terminology No Needs a glossary Implicitly, in the rule Explicitly, as data

Build both. The linter stops new drift; the measurement tells you about the drift you already have, which the linter will never mention because those pages are not being changed.

docs.title: What the rate tells you to do
docs.text:
Conformance Interpretation Action Above 95% The term is established Keep the linter, stop measuring 60% to 95% Real drift, fixable Fix the worst pages, keep the gate Below 60% The glossary lost Reconsider the canonical term 0% with usages The canonical name is aspirational Someone renamed it in a document and nowhere else

That last row happens more than it should. A term is changed in a style guide, nobody updates the corpus, and a year later the canonical name exists only in the glossary. The measurement makes that visible in one run.

docs.title: Counting traps
docs.text:
Trap Effect Fix Canonical matches inside its variants Inflates conformance Mask deprecated forms first Overlapping variants Double counts Match longest first Code samples and identifiers False positives on api_key Exclude fenced blocks, or treat identifiers as a separate vocabulary Quoted third-party names Flags correct prose An allow-list, plus a suppression comment Case-insensitive canonical Widget and widget merge Decide whether casing is part of the term

The third one is the most common in developer documentation. access token in prose and ACCESS_TOKEN in a sample are both correct, and a checker that does not separate prose vocabulary from code identifiers will drown you.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with retrieval, not consistency, because it is the stronger argument and the one that connects to the rest of the job. "Three names for one concept means a retriever has three weak clusters instead of one strong one, so drift degrades search and assistant answers before anyone complains about style."

The follow-up is how you decide what the canonical term is, and the honest answer involves usage data rather than preference: what the product calls it in the UI, what support tickets call it, what the search logs show people typing. A glossary that disagrees with all three will lose.

The tradeoff to volunteer. A drift report is only as good as its glossary, and maintaining a glossary is real ongoing work that nobody is assigned. If you automate the measurement without owning the glossary, you get a dashboard measuring a stale list. Say that the glossary is the artifact and the script is the easy part.

One sharper point. The naive measurement flatters you in proportion to how bad the drift is, because the canonical term is usually a substring of its own deprecated forms. A conformance number produced without masking is not conservative, it is biased toward good news, which is the worst property a quality metric can have.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A glossary in version control, a script that reports a rate per term and a ranked list of pages, and a before-and-after number.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. Step 3 is the part worth your time: watch the canonical term match inside its own variants.
  2. Write a ten-term glossary for a corpus you already have, and run the measurement. The first number is almost always worse than the team's estimate, which is the point.
  3. Pick the term with the lowest rate and decide, in writing, whether to fix the corpus or change the glossary. That decision is the deliverable.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. A rate measured twice, with work in between. One measurement is a complaint; two measurements and a glossary commit are a managed quantity. Nothing in this guide's own repositories demonstrates this yet, which is recorded honestly on the demonstrated page rather than implied.

docs.title: Time to first success
docs.text:
The best metric in this field, and worth exactly as much as the path you instrumented: a cold-start test passed in nine seconds while a real reader never succeeded at all.

core · difficulty 2 · 3h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "measure time-to-first-success, support deflection, repeat questions, and AI answer quality"

Prerequisites: Documentation analytics, Golden paths

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The elapsed time between a developer deciding to try something and that developer having it work. Intel writes the same idea as a design goal, "from a clean environment to a working result", and NVIDIA writes it as a metric. It is the same quantity from two sides.

It is the best single number in developer documentation, because it is the only one that cannot be satisfied by a well-written page. Prose quality, link health, sample correctness and search ranking are all inputs to it, and none of them substitutes for it.

Defining it requires two decisions, and both are where the metric usually goes wrong: when the clock starts, and what counts as success.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because every other documentation metric can be green while nobody can get started.

A corpus can be complete, correct, linked, linted, searchable, fully tested, and still leave a competent developer with nothing working after twenty minutes. Time to first success is the metric that refuses to be fooled by that, which is precisely why it is uncomfortable to adopt: it is the one number that can make a quarter of good work look insufficient.

NVIDIA lists it first of four, ahead of deflection and answer quality, and that ordering is defensible. Deflection measures the load you removed from someone else. First success measures whether the thing works for the person in front of you.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Measure it on a real repository, discover the measurement passed while a real reader failed, and work out why. About thirty minutes, and the finding is the most useful thing in this category.

Step 1: instrument it properly

A cold-start test is time to first success, automated. The companion repository has one: it creates an empty directory, builds a fresh virtual environment, installs the package the way a reader would, and runs the tutorial's commands in order, asserting the output the tutorial promises.

bash scripts/coldstart.sh

==> Cold environment at /tmp/tmp.7SDBOfrJoQ
==> Tutorial step 1: create a virtual environment and install
==> Tutorial step 1: verify the CLI is on PATH
docpack --help works
==> Tutorial step 3: pack it
packed 2 pages into 4 chunks -> dist
output matches what the tutorial promises
==> Tutorial step 4: inspect the artifacts
dist/llms.txt present
dist/chunks.jsonl present
dist/llms-full.txt present
chunks.jsonl has the documented shape
==> COLD START PASSED: a reader following the tutorial reaches the documented result

EXIT=0  ELAPSED_S=9

Nine seconds, exit zero. A reader goes from an empty directory to three artifacts whose shape is asserted. By any reasonable reading, time to first success is nine seconds and the metric is excellent.

Time the steps individually, though, and the nine seconds turns out to be almost entirely one step. A second run on a different machine, with each ==> banner timestamped:

  [+   0.0s  step  0.0s]  Cold environment at /tmp/tmp.XqTcyx6tJH
  [+   0.0s  step  0.0s]  Tutorial step 1: create a venv and install
  [+  11.6s  step 11.6s]  Tutorial step 1: verify the CLI is on PATH
  [+  11.7s  step  0.1s]  Tutorial step 2: create the documentation tree
  [+  11.7s  step  0.0s]  Tutorial step 3: pack it
  [+  11.8s  step  0.1s]  Tutorial step 4: inspect the artifacts
  [+  11.8s  step  0.0s]  Tutorial step 5: break it on purpose
  [+  12.6s  step  0.7s]  COLD START PASSED
TOTAL 12.7s

Of 12.7 seconds, 11.6 are pip install: 91 per cent. Everything the tutorial actually teaches, creating a tree, packing it, inspecting the artifacts and breaking it on purpose, takes 0.4 seconds in total.

Two things follow, and the second is the one worth keeping. The headline figure is machine-dependent, nine seconds here and 12.7 there, so quoting it to two significant figures is false precision; the composition is stable and the total is not. And the only lever on this number is the dependency install, because rewriting every word of the tutorial could not move four tenths of a second. A metric whose single component you cannot influence by doing your own job well is a metric about somebody else's work.

Step 2: a real reader arrives

The same day, the project's first real reader worked through the repository. Every command he ran exited zero. He then reported that he had no idea what the library did or what he should be looking at.

commands run:        9
commands failing:    0
first success:       never reached

Both measurements are correct. The cold-start test is not lying, and neither is the reader.

Step 3: find out why the instrument missed it

The cold-start script runs the tutorial's command sequence. The reader followed the README's quick start, which is a different sequence entirely:

quick start, in the order a reader meets it:
   1. docpack docs --check                   report
   2. python -m pytest -q                    report
   3. python scripts/check_links.py          report
   4. vale docs/                             report
   5. mkdocs build --strict                  artifact: site/
   6. docpack eval evals/golden.yaml         report
   7. bash scripts/coldstart.sh              report
   8. docpack new how-to --title ...         artifact: a page
   9. docpack docs --out dist                artifact: 3 files
  10. python mcp_server/server.py            artifact: a running server

commands that produce something: 4/10, at positions 5, 8, 9, 10
the first four, consecutively, produce nothing but reports

The command that makes the library's actual output is ninth of ten. The first four are validators that print "ok". A reader working down that list in order spends their entire first impression watching a corpus check itself.

So the repository had two front doors, instrumented one of them, and the metric was silently absent on the other. Not wrong: absent. There was no number for the README path at all, and nothing to notice.

Step 4: instrument the other door

The README's quick start cannot be executed end to end (one step needs a separately installed prose linter), but the property that failed is checkable without running anything:

#: Commands that leave the reader holding something.
PRODUCES_SOMETHING = ("docpack docs --out", "docpack search",
                      "docpack new", "mcp_server/server.py")

first = [c for c in commands if not c.startswith("pip install")][0]
assert any(first.startswith(p) or p in first for p in PRODUCES_SOMETHING), (
    f"the first quick-start command after install is {first!r}, which only "
    "reports. Lead with a command that leaves the reader holding something."
)

Run against the README as the reader found it:

old README first command: 'docpack docs --check'
would the gate pass? False

And against the rewritten one, where the quick start is split into commands that make something and commands that check something:

6 passed

A test that would have caught the failure before a human had to. Cheap, and it exists only because somebody said something.

Step 5: what the two numbers mean together

instrumented path:    9 seconds
unmeasured path:      never

Time to first success is not a property of a product. It is a property of a route through a product, and a product has as many of those as it has entry points: the README, the tutorial, the package registry page, the --help output, the first search result, whatever an assistant says when asked.

Reporting a single number means having chosen a route, usually the one you wrote the test for, which is the route you understand best and therefore the one least likely to fail.

Step 6: the definitions that decide the number

Two choices do most of the work, and defaults tend to flatter.

Decision Flattering default Honest version Clock starts First command of the tutorial Arrival at the front door Success means The command exits zero The reader has a result they recognise

The second row is this whole page. Nine of nine commands exited zero, and the reader had no result he recognised, because exit codes are a property of programs and recognition is a property of people.

What you built. An automated cold-start measurement at nine seconds, a documented case of that measurement passing while a real reader never succeeded, a diagnosis naming the uninstrumented entry point, and a test that closes it.

docs.title: Defining the two endpoints
docs.text: Clock starts at Measures Use when Arrival at the docs The whole funnel, including navigation The honest default First command of a quickstart Quickstart quality alone Comparing quickstarts After install The API's own learnability Install is somebody else's problem Account creation Onboarding including provisioning There is a signup Success means Strength Weakness A result the reader recognises The real thing Needs a judgment per task An asserted output Automatable Can pass with no comprehension Exit code zero Trivial to measure See step 2 The reader says they are done Honest Needs a reader A telemetry event Scales Instruments one surface only

docs.title: How the metric fails
docs.text: Failure What it looks like Fix One route instrumented A good number and unhappy readers Instrument every entry point Success defined as exit zero Green runs, confused people Define success as a recognised result Measured only on the author's machine Passes forever A clean environment per run Measured once Passes forever In CI, on every change Averaged across audiences Nothing actionable Segment, or pick one Measured and not acted on A dashboard Cut steps before first success

docs.title: Reducing it, in order of effect
docs.text:
Change Why it works Delete a step before first success The only reliable lever Remove a choice before first success A decision costs more than a command Show expected output after each command Removes "did that work?" Lead with the command that produces something See step 4 Defer configuration until after first success Most of it is not needed yet Supply a working default A placeholder the reader must replace is a step Shorten the install Usually the largest single block

The first two are the whole list in practice. Prose improvements move this number much less than people expect, which is unwelcome news for a writing team and the reason the metric belongs next to the tooling.

docs.title: What it does not tell you
docs.text:
Not measured Needs Whether they understood it Assessment Whether they came back Retention Whether the second task was easy A second measurement Whether they needed help Support deflection Why they gave up A person, or a session recording

A fast first success followed by a wall is a real pattern, and this metric reports the good half of it.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with why it is the best metric and what it costs. "It is the only documentation number that cannot be satisfied by a well-written page. Prose quality, link health, sample correctness and search ranking are all inputs; none substitutes. Which is also why it is uncomfortable: it can make a quarter of good work look insufficient."

Then the story, because it is the strongest thing I have in measurement. I automated it as a cold-start test: empty directory, fresh environment, install the way a reader would, run the tutorial's commands, assert the promised output. Nine seconds, exit zero. The same day, the first real reader ran nine commands, had every one exit zero, and told me he could not tell what the library did. Both measurements were correct.

The diagnosis is the part worth remembering. The cold-start test ran the tutorial's sequence; he followed the README's quick start, where the first four commands are validators that print "ok" and the command producing the library's actual output is ninth of ten. The repository had two front doors and I had instrumented one, so on the other the metric was not wrong, it was absent. An uninstrumented entry point is where this number silently does not exist, and that is the general lesson: time to first success is a property of a route through a product, not of the product, and a product has as many routes as entry points.

The fix, and the tradeoff. I added a test that reads the README's quick start and fails unless the first command after install produces something; it fails on the old README and passes on the rewritten one. The tradeoff is that this is a proxy. It checks the ordering of a list, not whether a human recognises the result, and the only instrument that checks the second one is a human. So the proxy goes in CI and the human channel stays open, because the proxy exists only because a person spoke up first.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A cold-start script in CI that runs from an empty environment and asserts a promised output, plus a check on whichever entry point it does not cover.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run your quickstart in a fresh container, timing it, and write the number down. Predict it first. The gap between your prediction and the measurement is the finding, not the measurement.
  2. List your entry points: README, tutorial, registry page, --help, first search result. Mark which ones have ever been tested. One of five is the usual answer, and the untested four are where the metric is absent rather than bad.
  3. Count how many commands a reader runs before anything they can look at appears. If the answer is more than one, reorder the list; it is the cheapest improvement available in this entire category.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. scripts/coldstart.sh is in the companion repository, runs in CI, and passed in nine seconds with exit zero on the run quoted above. The reader failure is equally real, reported by the first person to follow the README, and the test added in step 4 is in tests/test_doc_samples.py and verified to fail against the previous README. What is missing is any measurement over more than one reader: n is one, so nothing here supports a claim about distributions, medians or trends, and the demonstrated page records the cold-start half as demonstrated and the reader-side half as not.

docs.title: Designing tutorials
docs.text:
Measuring how long a tutorial leaves the reader without feedback, which is where its defects hide.

core · difficulty 2 · 4h

Asked for by name

Intel: "Write and maintain reference documentation, tutorials, and sample walkthroughs that assume no prior context"

Prerequisites: Diátaxis

Leads to: Sample walkthroughs

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A lesson. The reader follows it to learn, and the working thing at the end is evidence that they learned rather than the point of the exercise. That is what separates it from a quickstart, which optimises for the working thing and teaches as little as it can get away with.

Intel's phrase is "assume no prior context", which is the hard constraint. The design question this page is built on is narrower and measurable: how long does your tutorial leave the reader with no way to tell whether it is working?

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because a tutorial is where a reader decides whether the product is for them, and because its failures are structural rather than stylistic.

The common structural failure is sequencing. An author who knows the architecture builds it in architectural order: configuration module, then domain logic, then the interface, then run it. That is how you would build it if you already understood it, and it means the reader types for twenty minutes before anything can possibly produce output. Every mistake they make in those twenty minutes surfaces at once, at the end, attributed to the wrong place.

That is a measurable property, not a matter of taste, which is what the golden path demonstrates.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Measure blind-run length on two tutorials, then watch what a long one hides. About forty minutes.

Step 1: the same tutorial, sequenced two ways

The architectural ordering, eight steps, output only at the end:

mkdir -p tut-demo && cd tut-demo
cat > tut-bad.md <<'MDEOF'
# Build a sync tool

## Step 1
```bash
mkdir sync && cd sync
```
## Step 2
```bash
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
```
## Step 3
```bash
pip install widget click
```
## Step 4
```bash
mkdir src tests
```
## Step 5
```bash
cat > src/config.py <<'EOF'
DEFAULTS = {"retries": 5}
EOF
```
## Step 6
```bash
cat > src/sync.py <<'EOF'
from .config import DEFAULTS
def run(): return DEFAULTS
EOF
```
## Step 7
```bash
cat > src/cli.py <<'EOF'
import click
@click.command()
def main(): print(run())
EOF
```
## Step 8
```bash
python -m src.cli
```
```
{'retries': 5}
```
MDEOF

And the same lesson sequenced so that something runs immediately, then grows: step 1 gets a working command-line tool that prints a message, step 2 adds the configuration.

Step 2: measure the blind run

A step gives feedback when it shows expected output, which by this guide's convention is an untagged fence alongside the commands:

OPEN = re.compile(r"^```(\w*)\s*$", re.M)

def has_output_block(step):
    openers = OPEN.findall(step)[::2]   # fences alternate open/close
    return any(t == "" for t in openers)

fb = [has_output_block(s) for s in steps]
longest = cur = 0
for f in fb:
    cur = 0 if f else cur + 1
    longest = max(longest, cur)

tut-bad.md     steps= 8 feedback_at=[8] first=8 longest_blind_run=7
tut-good.md    steps= 2 feedback_at=[1, 2] first=1 longest_blind_run=0

Seven steps on faith against zero. The first number to care about is first: the reader of the bad tutorial has no evidence anything works until step 8.

Step 3: follow the bad tutorial exactly and see what happens

python -m src.cli; echo "exit=$?"

exit=0

Nothing. No output, no error, exit zero. The reader has done eight steps and the tutorial's final command produces silence, so they cannot tell whether they succeeded, mistyped something, or are looking at a broken tutorial.

The cause is that step 7 wrote a click command and no if __name__ == "__main__" guard, so python -m imports the module and exits.

Step 4: add the guard, and find the next defect

cat >> src/cli.py <<'EOF'
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
EOF
python -m src.cli

    def main(): print(run())
                      ^^^
NameError: name 'run' is not defined

A second defect: step 7's cli.py never imports run from sync.py. And behind it sits a third, which only surfaces after that one is fixed, because config.py as written would be imported for a name it does define but sync.py imports under a different spelling in the typo variant of this exercise.

Three independent defects, stacked across seven unverified steps, and the first symptom was silence. Any one of them would have been obvious the moment the reader ran something. The sequencing is what let them accumulate.

Step 5: the rule that follows

Order the tutorial so that something observable happens as early as possible, and keep the blind run short:

Metric Target Steps before first observable output 1 Longest run of steps with no output 1, or 2 at most Final step produces something Always; silence is not success

The reordering is not cosmetic. The good version reaches a working command-line tool in step 1 and then changes it in step 2, which is more work to write and strictly better to follow, because every defect is attributable to the step that introduced it.

What you built. A measurement that turns tutorial sequencing from a stylistic preference into a number, and a demonstration of what the number predicts.

docs.title: Tutorial against its neighbours
docs.text: Tutorial Quickstart How-to Walkthrough Goal Learning Working, fast One task done Understanding existing code Reader builds Yes, incrementally Minimal Nothing new Nothing Explanation Essential Almost none Brief Essential Detours If they teach Never No Not applicable Length As long as the lesson Shortest possible One task One sample

docs.title: Design rules that hold up
docs.text:
Rule Why Something runs in step 1 See the golden path Every step is verifiable So defects are attributable One new idea per step Two ideas per step means an ambiguous failure Build up, do not reveal A finished file dropped in teaches nothing The reader types, you explain Not the other way round Nothing unexplained "Assume no prior context" State the time and the result up front So the reader can decide to start

The "build up, do not reveal" rule is where architectural ordering comes from and where it goes wrong. Building up is right; building up in the order you would build it is not, because that order defers running anything.

docs.title: What to cut
docs.text:
Cut Where it goes Alternatives and platform variants A how-to Why the design is the way it is An explanation Every option on every command Reference Error handling the lesson does not need A later tutorial Production concerns An operations guide

A tutorial that handles errors properly is a tutorial nobody finishes. Say that you are deliberately omitting it, and link where it is covered.

docs.title: Testing a tutorial
docs.text:
Check Catches Cold-start test Undeclared dependencies, missing steps Output assertion per step The silent-success failure in step 3 Blind-run measurement Sequencing that hides defects A reader who does not know the product Everything else, and nothing else can

The last row is irreplaceable. Blind-run length tells you where defects can hide; only a real learner tells you whether the explanation lands.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the measurement. "The structural failure in tutorials is sequencing. An author who knows the architecture builds it in architectural order, so the reader types for twenty minutes before anything can produce output. I measure the longest run of steps with no observable result: on an eight-step tutorial written that way it was seven, and three independent defects were hiding in it with silence as the only symptom."

The follow-up is the difference from a quickstart, and the answer is the goal: a tutorial optimises for learning and may take a longer route if the detour teaches; a quickstart optimises for working and teaches as little as it can. Merging them produces a page too long to be one and too thin to be the other.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Keeping the blind run short costs you refactoring inside the tutorial: the good version builds a working thing in step 1 and then rewrites part of it in step 2, which is more words and feels less elegant than building the final structure once. Some readers notice and object. It is still right, because attributable failure is worth more than elegance in a document whose readers are guaranteed to make mistakes.

One sharper point. Silence is not success. A tutorial whose final command produces no output cannot tell the reader anything, and it will hide real defects indefinitely: mine exited zero with three bugs in it. Every step that runs something should show what the reader will see, and the final step most of all.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A tutorial with output shown at every step, a cold-start test, and a measured blind-run length.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the blind-run measurement over a tutorial you own. Anything above 2 is worth reordering.
  2. Follow your own tutorial in a fresh environment and note the first point at which you could tell it was working. That number is the one readers feel.
  3. Check that your final step produces output. Silent final steps are common and they make the whole tutorial unfalsifiable.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. docpack's docs/tutorials/getting-started.md is the demonstration, recorded on the demonstrated page: five steps, nine code blocks, one route, no choice offered before first success, with scripts/coldstart.sh running the whole thing in a fresh virtual environment and asserting the exact output it promises. What is missing is a reader: the blind-run count is zero. The number is the claim worth making, because it is checkable by anyone who disagrees.

docs.title: OpenUSD and Omniverse
docs.text:
USD's whole model is a resolution order, and the surprising part is that the first sublayer wins, not the last.

context · difficulty 2 · 4h

Asked for by name

NVIDIA: "familiarity with USD, Omniverse, Isaac Sim, or ROS"

Leads to: Robotics simulation

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
OpenUSD is a scene description format and, more importantly, a composition engine: several files each state opinions about the same objects, and USD resolves them into one scene at read time. Omniverse is NVIDIA's platform built on it, where the composition happens live across applications.

The format is the easy half. Everything that confuses people, and everything a documentation role has to explain, is the resolution: when two files disagree, which one wins.

context tier means the goal is to follow a conversation and know what you do not know, not to ship scene code.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Because NVIDIA lists USD among the things to be familiar with, and because the documentation failure around it is unusually clear-cut.

USD's reference material describes composition as a set of arcs: sublayers, references, payloads, inherits, variant sets, specialises. Each is documented accurately. A reader finishes knowing six mechanisms and still cannot answer the only question they came with, which is why their override is being ignored.

That gap is the documentable thing. The arcs are a feature list; the reader needs an ordering.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a layered stage and find out which opinion wins. About twenty-five minutes, and the second result is the one worth remembering.

pip install usd-core

Step 1: a base asset, and an override that does not touch it

base = Usd.Stage.CreateNew("base.usda")
arm = UsdGeom.Cube.Define(base, "/Robot/Arm")
arm.GetPrim().CreateAttribute("payload_kg", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.Float).Set(2.5)

over = Usd.Stage.CreateNew("studio.usda")
over.GetRootLayer().subLayerPaths = ["./base.usda"]
ov = over.OverridePrim("/Robot/Arm")
ov.CreateAttribute("payload_kg", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.Float).Set(4.0)

base.usda        payload_kg = 2.5
studio.usda      payload_kg = 4.0   <- the override wins

base file on disk, unchanged:
          custom float payload_kg = 2.5

That is the point of the format in one result. A studio changes a vendor's asset without editing the vendor's file, and the vendor can ship an update.

USD will also tell you exactly where a value came from, which is the single most useful debugging call in the API:

for spec in attr.GetPropertyStack(Usd.TimeCode.Default()):
    print(spec.layer.identifier, spec.default)

  studio.usda                  4.0
  base.usda                    2.5

Step 2: two layers disagree, and the ordering is not what you expect

Two sublayers, both setting speed, one to 10 and one to 20:

root.GetRootLayer().subLayerPaths = ["./a.usda", "./b.usda"]

subLayerPaths = ['./a.usda', './b.usda']   a sets 10, b sets 20
  resolved speed = 10
  stack, strongest first:
    a.usda       10.0
    b.usda       20.0

subLayerPaths = ['./b.usda', './a.usda']   the same two files, reordered
  resolved speed = 20

The first sublayer wins. Not the last.

That is the opposite of nearly every ordering a developer already knows. CSS later-wins, a shell source later-wins, #include later-wins, a dict update later-wins, a Docker layer later-wins. Here the list is strongest-first, and a reader who assumes otherwise has a scene that silently uses the wrong value, with no error anywhere.

Step 3: a local opinion beats a reference

inst.GetPrim().GetReferences().AddReference("./asset.usda", "/Asset")

reference only:          mass = 100
local opinion added:     mass = 7   <- local beats the reference

This is the LIVRPS ordering: Local, Inherits, Variant sets, References, Payloads, Specialises, strongest first. Six arcs, one order, and knowing the acronym answers the override question that the six individual arc pages do not.

Step 4: what this says about documenting it

The reference material was accurate throughout. What was missing is a page that leads with the order and demonstrates the counter-intuitive case, because the counter-intuitive case is the one that generates the support question.

A golden path for USD is three files and one printed resolution, and it is worth more than six accurate arc pages. That is the general shape of this problem. A reader whose mental model is wrong in one specific way needs that specific correction, and complete reference material will not deliver it.

What you built. A layered stage, an override that leaves its base file untouched, the resolution order printed from the API, and the one ordering fact most newcomers get backwards.

docs.title: The arcs, in strength order
docs.text:
Arc Use Mnemonic position Local opinions Direct edits in this layer L, strongest Inherits Class-like shared edits I Variant sets Switchable alternatives V References Pulling in another asset R Payloads References you can defer loading P Specialises Fallbacks that stay weaker S, weakest

Within the local layer stack, earlier sublayers are stronger. Both orderings have to be known; neither is guessable.

docs.title: References against payloads
docs.text:
Reference Payload Loaded Always On request Use for Composition you always need Heavy geometry Cost Paid at open Deferred

A scene that opens slowly is usually references where payloads belong, and that is the commonest performance question in USD documentation.

docs.title: Terms worth recognising
docs.text:
Term Means Prim A node in the scene hierarchy Attribute, relationship A prim's typed value, or its link to another prim Stage The composed result of one or more layers Layer One file of opinions, .usda text or .usdc binary Opinion A value stated by a layer, which may lose Over An edit to a prim defined elsewhere Schema A typed API over prims, such as UsdGeom Stage traversal Walking the composed hierarchy

.usda is text and diffable; .usdc is binary and is not. For documentation work, always show .usda.

docs.title: Where Omniverse sits
docs.text:
Layer What it is OpenUSD The open format and composition engine Omniverse Kit NVIDIA's application framework over USD Connectors Live sync between Omniverse and other tools Isaac Sim A robotics simulator built on Kit

Being clear about this boundary matters in writing: a reader's problem is often with USD and not with the vendor platform, or the reverse, and the two have separate documentation sets and separate failure modes.

docs.title: What usually goes wrong
docs.text:
Symptom Cause "My override is ignored" Sublayer ordering, or a weaker arc "The value changed when I added a file" A stronger opinion appeared "It works for me and not in the pipeline" A different layer stack "The scene takes a minute to open" References where payloads belong "The diff is unreadable" .usdc instead of .usda

Every row is a resolution question, which is the argument for leading the documentation with resolution.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with composition rather than the format. "USD is a scene format and really a composition engine: several files state opinions about the same objects and USD resolves them at read time. So a studio can override a vendor's asset without touching the vendor's file, and the vendor can still ship updates. The format is the easy half."

The concrete thing to bring. The first sublayer wins, not the last. I checked it by building two layers that disagree and reordering them, and the resolved value flips. That is the opposite of CSS, #include, shell source and Docker layers, so a developer's existing intuition is reliably wrong in one specific direction, and they get a silently incorrect scene rather than an error.

The documentation point, which is the reason this is worth discussing in an interview. USD's reference material documents six composition arcs accurately, and a reader finishes it able to name all six and unable to answer why their override is ignored. The arcs are a feature list; what the reader needs is the resolution order, LIVRPS, plus a demonstration of the counter-intuitive case. Three files and one printed resolution beat six accurate arc pages, and GetPropertyStack prints exactly where a winning value came from, which is the first thing I would put in a troubleshooting page.

Be honest about the depth. I have composed layers, resolved overrides and read the API; I have not shipped a production scene graph, tuned payload loading on heavy assets, or used Omniverse itself. For this role that is the right amount: enough to write the page that is missing and to know which questions to take to an engineer.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. Three .usda files and a script that prints the resolution order, which fits in a gist and demonstrates the thing newcomers get wrong.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Install usd-core and run step 2. Predict which sublayer wins before you run it; the prediction is the exercise.
  2. Call GetPropertyStack on an attribute with more than one opinion. It is the answer to most USD support questions and it is not where a newcomer looks.
  3. Write the paragraph that states the resolution order and names the intuition it violates. It is the page that does not exist.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Every result above was executed against usd-core 0.26.11 on this machine, and the files are three short scripts. What is absent is the platform: no Omniverse, no Kit, no live Connector, no heavy asset, and no production pipeline, so this is familiarity with the composition model rather than experience of the product. The demonstrated page records it that way, and context tier is the honest claim.
