docs.title: User stories as a documentation standard
docs.text:
Using the story format as a validator on documentation scope rather than as a planning ritual.

supporting · difficulty 1 · 2h

Encode standards (user stories, release readiness, onboarding, security guidance) into templates

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: The format "as a role, I want to do something, so that outcome", used here as a constraint on documentation scope rather than as a planning artifact. A page that cannot be stated as one story is usually more than one page.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA lists it first among the standards to encode "into templates, validators, and guided workflows rather than static documents". That placement is the interesting part. User stories are normally a product-planning artifact, and NVIDIA is asking for them as something a template enforces.

Read that way, the requirement makes sense. The story format is a cheap test for the most common documentation defect, which is a page with no single reader in mind. "As a developer, I want to configure retry behaviour, so that transient upstream failures do not surface to my callers" is a page. "Retry and timeout configuration and the connection pool" is three.

On a Tuesday it is a scoping conversation that takes ninety seconds instead of twenty minutes. An engineer asks for a page about the inference server. You ask who wants what, and it turns out there are two readers: an operator who wants to size a deployment, and a developer who wants to send a request. Those are two pages and neither was going to be well served by one.

This is tagged supporting rather than core because the underlying skill is Diátaxis and content modelling; the story format is a convenient front end to both. Worth two hours, not more.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Use the format as a validator on a real page set. Twenty minutes.

Step 1: write the stories for pages that already exist

mkdir -p story-drill && cd story-drill
cat > stories.md <<'EOF'
Try to state each existing page as exactly one story.

PAGE: "Inference server configuration"
  As an operator, I want to size a deployment, so that it handles peak load.
  As a developer, I want to send my first request, so that I know it works.
  As an operator, I want to tune batching, so that throughput improves.
  -> THREE stories. Three pages, or one page with three sections and a
     reader who has to filter.

PAGE: "Configure retry behaviour"
  As a developer, I want to configure retries, so that transient upstream
  failures do not reach my callers.
  -> ONE story. The page is correctly scoped.

PAGE: "Troubleshooting"
  As ... anyone, I want ... to fix whatever is broken, so that ... it works.
  -> NO story. The format fails here, and that is a real limit rather than
     a defect in the page. Troubleshooting is indexed by symptom, not by goal.
EOF
cat stories.md

Step 2: make the test mechanical

mkdir -p docs
cat > docs/retries.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Configure retry behaviour
diataxis: how-to
audience: developer
story:
  role: developer
  wants: configure retry behaviour
  so_that: transient upstream failures do not reach my callers
---
# Configure retry behaviour
EOF

cat > docs/inference-server.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Inference server configuration
diataxis: how-to
audience: operator
---
# Inference server configuration
EOF

cat > check_stories.py <<'PY'
"""Require a single, well-formed story on every how-to and tutorial page.

Reference and explanation pages are exempt: a reference page serves every
reader with a question, and demanding one role for it would be false.

The check is deliberately shallow. It cannot tell whether the story is
honest, only whether somebody was made to write one, which is most of the
value: the format's benefit is the thirty seconds of thought at authoring
time, not the stored text.
"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

NEEDS_STORY = {"how-to", "tutorial"}
AUDIENCES = {"new-user", "developer", "operator", "contributor"}


def main(docs: Path) -> int:
    failures = []
    for page in sorted(docs.glob("*.md")):
        front = yaml.safe_load(page.read_text(encoding="utf-8").split("---")[1]) or {}
        if front.get("diataxis") not in NEEDS_STORY:
            continue

        story = front.get("story")
        if not story:
            failures.append(f"{page.name}: a {front['diataxis']} page needs a story")
            continue
        for field in ("role", "wants", "so_that"):
            if not story.get(field):
                failures.append(f"{page.name}: story is missing {field!r}")
        if story.get("role") not in AUDIENCES:
            failures.append(
                f"{page.name}: story role {story.get('role')!r} is not a declared audience"
            )
        if story.get("role") != front.get("audience"):
            failures.append(
                f"{page.name}: story role {story.get('role')!r} disagrees with "
                f"audience {front.get('audience')!r}"
            )

    for failure in failures:
        print(f"STORY  {failure}", file=sys.stderr)
    print(f"{'FAIL' if failures else 'ok'}: {len(failures)} story problem(s)")
    return 1 if failures else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(Path("docs")))
PY
python3 check_stories.py

Step 3: split the page the check found

cat > docs/size-a-deployment.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Size an inference deployment
diataxis: how-to
audience: operator
story:
  role: operator
  wants: size a deployment
  so_that: it handles peak load without over-provisioning
---
# Size an inference deployment
EOF
cat > docs/send-first-request.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Send your first inference request
diataxis: tutorial
audience: developer
story:
  role: developer
  wants: send a first request
  so_that: I know the server is working
---
# Send your first inference request
EOF
rm docs/inference-server.md
python3 check_stories.py

What you built. A check that fails when a task page has no single reader, and a page set where the split was forced by the format rather than argued about. The cross-check between story.role and audience is the part worth keeping: it catches a page that declares one audience and tells a story about another, which is a reliable sign the page is serving two.

docs.title: The format, and what each part constrains
docs.text:
Part Constrains Failure if vague As a role Who the page is for A page written for everyone, filtered by nobody I want to do something The page's scope, one goal Scope creep into adjacent tasks So that outcome Whether the goal is worth documenting A page about a capability nobody needs

The third part is the one people skip and the one that catches the worst waste. If you cannot finish "so that", the page may be documenting something because it exists rather than because anyone needs it.

docs.title: Where the format applies and where it does not
docs.text:
Page type Story? Why How-to guide Yes, exactly one The reader arrived with a goal Tutorial Yes, one, and the author owns it The reader has no goal yet Reference No Serves every reader with a question Explanation No The reader wants understanding, not a task Troubleshooting No Indexed by symptom rather than by goal

Demanding a story on a reference page produces a fake one, which is worse than none: it trains authors to satisfy the field rather than to think.

docs.title: Honest limits
docs.text:
Limit Consequence The check verifies presence, not honesty An author can write a vague story to pass The format is weak for troubleshooting Two whole page types are exempt It is a planning artifact borrowed into docs Teams that dislike agile ritual will resist the name One story per page is sometimes wrong A genuinely shared task across two roles

The last row is real. "As a developer or an operator, I want to read the logs" is a legitimate single page, and the strict one-role rule would split it pointlessly. A good check warns rather than blocks on that case.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Frame it as a scope test, not as a planning practice, because that is what distinguishes the documentation use from the product-management use. "I require a story on how-to and tutorial pages, and I cross-check the role against the declared audience. It is a cheap test for the commonest defect, which is a page with two readers. The inference server page turned out to be three stories, so it became two pages and a reference."

The follow-up is likely to be sceptical, some version of "is this not bureaucracy?" Agree partly. The honest position: the value is in the ninety seconds of thought at authoring time, and the stored field is mostly a way to make that thinking non-optional. If a team already scopes pages well, the field is overhead. It earns its place on a corpus with many authors of varying experience, which is exactly the NVIDIA situation.

The tradeoff to volunteer. This is a required field, and every required field is friction on every contributor forever. On a corpus of twenty pages with one author it is pure cost. It also invites gaming: an author who wants to ship writes a vague story, the check passes, and now there is a field full of noise that a later reader might trust. That failure is worse than not having the field, which is why this is supporting and why the check should be scoped to the two page types where the format actually fits.

One sharper point. The useful insight is that the story format and Diátaxis are checking the same thing from different directions. Diátaxis asks what kind of page this is; the story asks who wants what. A page that fails one usually fails the other, and the story version is easier to explain to an engineer who has never heard of Diátaxis and is not going to read a framework. Using it as the friendly front end to a stricter model underneath is a genuinely practical move.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. The check, scoped to the right page types, plus one page you split because the format forced it.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Write stories for ten existing pages. Twenty minutes. Count how many need more than one; in most corpora it is a third or more, and that number is the finding.
  2. Add the field and the check to a real repository, exempting reference and explanation. The exemptions are what make it credible.
  3. Split one page because the stories forced it, and link the before and after. The split is the evidence; the field is just the prompt.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. User stories are a well-worn format and claiming to use them signals nothing. Using them as a validator on documentation scope, with the two page types where they do not apply explicitly exempted, shows you have thought about the format's limits rather than adopted it.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
The format is trivial to show and the discipline is not. Writing user stories proves nothing; using them to refuse scope is the skill, and refusal needs someone to refuse.

What you need. A documentation request from someone who wants more than the reader needs.

What a learner would do. Take a documentation task as it arrived, write the reader's story for it, and then list what the task asked for that the story does not justify. Take that list to whoever asked.

What you would see.

Outcome What it means Scope agreed down The story did its work Scope defended with a different reader Good: now you have two stories, both written Scope defended with "it should be complete" The format has found an unstated goal A page type the story cannot describe The format's limit, and worth writing down

The last row matters most and is where most advocacy for this format stops. A reference page has no user story worth writing: nobody reads a parameter table as a journey. Knowing which page types the format does not fit is the evidence that you use it rather than recite it.

Why it does not commit. The story commits; the conversation where it changed somebody's mind does not. The nearest available artifact is a scope decision recorded with its story beside it, in a tracker rather than a repository.

docs.title: Vector stores and hybrid search
docs.text:
Where the vectors live, and why a documentation corpus needs lexical search alongside them rather than instead.

core · difficulty 3 · 5h

Not a quotation (derived)

The retrieval half of a RAG pipeline, which NVIDIA names as a way to stand out.

Prerequisites: Embeddings

Leads to: RAG pipelines

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A store that holds vectors and answers "which of these is closest to this one" quickly, plus the metadata needed to filter before ranking. Hybrid search is running a lexical index alongside it and combining the results, because the two methods fail on different queries.

For a documentation corpus, hybrid is the default and vector-only is the mistake.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Neither posting names a vector store, which is why this is derived. NVIDIA asks for RAG pipelines twice and for content "structured and packaged for RAG", and this is where the packaged content ends up.

What makes it core is the decision rather than the database. The database choice barely matters and people spend all their time on it; the hybrid decision matters enormously and people skip it. The reason is covered in embeddings: a developer's question turns on flag names, version numbers and negations, and those are precisely what embeddings blur. A documentation search that cannot reliably find max_memory_gb when asked about max_memory_gb is broken in a way no amount of reranking fixes.

On a Tuesday it is a triage question with a clear procedure. A developer searched an exact error string and got nothing useful. Was the chunk missing (a chunking problem), outranked (a fusion problem), or did the vector search simply never surface it because the string is rare and semantically unremarkable? The third is the common one and the fix is a lexical index, not a better model.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build a BM25 index, a vector index, and a fused one, then find the queries each gets wrong. About forty minutes, dependency-free: the "vectors" here are deterministic and local, so the comparison is reproducible and needs no model download.

Step 1: a corpus with the vocabulary that breaks each method

mkdir -p store-drill && cd store-drill
cat > chunks.json <<'EOF'
[
  {"id": "c1", "text": "Set batch_size on the client. The default is 32.", "kind": "reference"},
  {"id": "c2", "text": "If your p99 is too high, reduce the batch to 1 or 2. Larger batches wait for the batch to fill before running.", "kind": "how-to"},
  {"id": "c3", "text": "Set max_memory_gb to cap GPU memory. The default is 16.", "kind": "reference"},
  {"id": "c4", "text": "Set max_memory_mb on the legacy 1.x client. Removed in 2.0.", "kind": "reference"},
  {"id": "c5", "text": "Quantised models tolerate much larger batches because the memory arithmetic differs.", "kind": "explanation"},
  {"id": "c6", "text": "The cache is enabled by default. Pass cache=False to turn it off.", "kind": "reference"},
  {"id": "c7", "text": "Exit code 2 means the arguments were invalid.", "kind": "reference"},
  {"id": "c8", "text": "A GPU is more efficient per item on a larger batch, which is why batching raises throughput.", "kind": "explanation"}
]
EOF
python3 -c "import json; print(len(json.load(open('chunks.json'))), 'chunks')"

Step 2: BM25, which is the baseline worth beating

cat > bm25.py <<'PY'
"""BM25 in about thirty lines, with no dependencies.

Worth implementing once rather than importing, because the two corrections it
makes are the two that matter and both are invisible in a library call:

  idf    a term appearing in every chunk carries almost no signal
  length normalisation, so the longest chunk does not win every query
"""
import json
import math
import re
from collections import Counter

K1, B = 1.2, 0.75


def tokenize(text):
    """Lowercase alphanumeric runs, keeping underscores so flag names survive.

    Splitting on underscore would turn `max_memory_gb` into three common
    words and destroy the one thing lexical search is good at.
    """
    return [t for t in re.findall(r"[a-z0-9_]+", text.lower()) if len(t) > 1]


class BM25:
    def __init__(self, chunks):
        self.chunks = chunks
        self.docs = [Counter(tokenize(c["text"])) for c in chunks]
        self.lengths = [sum(d.values()) for d in self.docs]
        self.avg = sum(self.lengths) / len(self.docs)
        df = Counter()
        for d in self.docs:
            df.update(d.keys())
        n = len(self.docs)
        self.idf = {
            t: math.log(1 + (n - c + 0.5) / (c + 0.5)) for t, c in df.items()
        }

    def search(self, query, limit=3):
        terms = tokenize(query)
        scored = []
        for chunk, doc, length in zip(self.chunks, self.docs, self.lengths):
            score = 0.0
            for t in terms:
                f = doc.get(t, 0)
                if not f:
                    continue
                norm = 1 - B + B * (length / self.avg)
                score += self.idf.get(t, 0.0) * (f * (K1 + 1)) / (f + K1 * norm)
            if score > 0:
                scored.append((score, chunk))
        scored.sort(key=lambda s: -s[0])
        return scored[:limit]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    index = BM25(json.load(open("chunks.json")))
    for query in ["max_memory_gb default", "my p99 is too high", "exit code 2"]:
        print(f"\nQ: {query}")
        for score, chunk in index.search(query):
            print(f"   {score:5.2f}  {chunk['id']}  {chunk['text'][:58]}")
PY
python3 bm25.py

Step 3: a deterministic stand-in for vector search

What this toy can and cannot show

A real embedding model is far better than what follows, and this page is careful about which conclusions the toy can support.

It can show the token-blur failure, because that failure comes from representing text as a point in a topic space, which the toy also does. That is the result step 4 measures.

It cannot win a quality comparison against BM25. Its vocabulary is a hand-written cue list, so on anything outside that list it returns nothing, and a horse race between the two here would be measuring the author's cue list rather than dense retrieval. The author's attempt to run one produced BM25 winning 6 of 7, which is a fact about the toy and not about embeddings.

For a real quality comparison, run the embeddings golden path with an actual model on your own vocabulary.

cat > vectorish.py <<'PY'
"""A deterministic, dependency-free stand-in for dense retrieval.

Each chunk becomes a vector over TOPICS rather than over words, by counting
cue words per topic. That reproduces the two properties of a real embedding
model that this page is about:

  it matches on MEANING    "p99 too high" finds a chunk about latency even
                           with almost no shared words
  it blurs EXACT TOKENS    max_memory_gb and max_memory_mb land in the same
                           place, because both are about memory limits

A real model does this far better and for the same structural reason. Using a
toy keeps the comparison reproducible and keeps the lesson about retrieval
design rather than about model choice.
"""
import json
import math
import re

TOPICS = {
    "latency": ["p99", "latency", "wait", "high", "fast", "slow", "responsive"],
    "batching": ["batch", "batch_size", "batches", "batching", "throughput", "32"],
    "memory": ["memory", "gpu", "cap", "max_memory_gb", "max_memory_mb", "gb", "mb", "16"],
    "config": ["set", "default", "pass", "client", "flag", "option"],
    "errors": ["exit", "code", "invalid", "arguments", "error", "removed"],
    "caching": ["cache", "enabled", "disable", "off"],
}


def embed(text):
    words = set(re.findall(r"[a-z0-9_]+", text.lower()))
    vec = [
        float(sum(1 for cue in cues if cue in words)) for cues in TOPICS.values()
    ]
    n = math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in vec))
    return [x / n for x in vec] if n else vec


def dot(a, b):
    return sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))


class VectorIsh:
    def __init__(self, chunks):
        self.chunks = chunks
        self.vectors = [embed(c["text"]) for c in chunks]

    def search(self, query, limit=3):
        q = embed(query)
        scored = [
            (dot(q, v), c) for v, c in zip(self.vectors, self.chunks) if dot(q, v) > 0
        ]
        scored.sort(key=lambda s: -s[0])
        return scored[:limit]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    index = VectorIsh(json.load(open("chunks.json")))
    for query in ["max_memory_gb default", "my p99 is too high", "exit code 2"]:
        print(f"\nQ: {query}")
        for score, chunk in index.search(query):
            print(f"   {score:5.3f}  {chunk['id']}  {chunk['text'][:58]}")
PY
python3 vectorish.py

Step 4: fuse them, and measure all three

Reciprocal rank fusion is the default worth starting from: it combines rankings rather than scores, so it does not care that BM25 returns 7.4 and cosine returns 0.83.

cat > hybrid.py <<'PY'
"""Compare BM25, dense, and reciprocal rank fusion on the same queries.

RRF scores a document as the sum over retrievers of 1 / (k + rank). Combining
RANKS rather than SCORES is the whole trick: BM25 scores are unbounded and
cosine scores sit in [-1, 1], so any weighted sum of the raw numbers is
arbitrary and needs retuning whenever either side changes.
"""
import json

from bm25 import BM25
from vectorish import VectorIsh

RRF_K = 60

QUERIES = [
    ("max_memory_gb default", "c3", "exact flag name"),
    ("max_memory_mb", "c4", "NEAR-IDENTICAL legacy flag"),
    ("exit code 2", "c7", "exact error code"),
    ("my p99 is too high", "c2", "rare token, shared"),
    ("switch off the cache", "c6", "paraphrase"),
    ("why does batching help throughput", "c8", "a why question"),
]


def ranked_ids(hits):
    return [c["id"] for _, c in hits]


def rrf(*rankings):
    scores = {}
    for ranking in rankings:
        for rank, cid in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
            scores[cid] = scores.get(cid, 0.0) + 1.0 / (RRF_K + rank)
    return sorted(scores, key=lambda c: -scores[c])


chunks = json.load(open("chunks.json"))
lexical, dense = BM25(chunks), VectorIsh(chunks)

totals = {"bm25": 0, "dense": 0, "hybrid": 0}
print(f"{'query':<34} {'want':<5} {'bm25':<6} {'dense':<6} {'hybrid':<6} note")
print("-" * 92)

for query, expected, note in QUERIES:
    l = ranked_ids(lexical.search(query, limit=5))
    d = ranked_ids(dense.search(query, limit=5))
    h = rrf(l, d)

    results = {}
    for name, ranking in (("bm25", l), ("dense", d), ("hybrid", h)):
        top = ranking[0] if ranking else None
        results[name] = "OK" if top == expected else (top or "none")
        if top == expected:
            totals[name] += 1

    print(f"{query:<34} {expected:<5} {results['bm25']:<6} "
          f"{results['dense']:<6} {results['hybrid']:<6} {note}")

print("-" * 92)
n = len(QUERIES)
print(f"{'totals':<34} {'':<5} {totals['bm25']}/{n}    "
      f"{totals['dense']}/{n}    {totals['hybrid']}/{n}")
PY
python3 hybrid.py

Step 5: look closely at the one case dense loses

python3 - <<'PY'
import json

from bm25 import BM25
from vectorish import VectorIsh

chunks = json.load(open("chunks.json"))
lexical, dense = BM25(chunks), VectorIsh(chunks)

query = "max_memory_mb"
print(f"Q: {query}\n")
print("  dense ranking:")
for score, chunk in dense.search(query, limit=3):
    print(f"    {score:.3f}  {chunk['id']}  {chunk['text'][:52]}")
print("  lexical ranking:")
for score, chunk in lexical.search(query, limit=3):
    print(f"    {score:.2f}   {chunk['id']}  {chunk['text'][:52]}")
PY

What you built. Three retrievers, and one measured failure that is the whole argument for hybrid search.

The totals are 6/6 lexical, 5/6 dense, 6/6 hybrid, and the totals are not the finding. Step 5 is. Asked for max_memory_mb, the dense retriever returns:

Rank Chunk Score Text 1 c3 0.928 Set max_memory_gb to cap GPU memory 2 c5 0.707 Quantised models tolerate larger batches 3 c4 0.408 Set max_memory_mb on the legacy 1.x client

The correct answer is third, behind a chunk about a different flag and a chunk about quantisation. Lexical search puts it first, alone, at 2.06, and fusion recovers it.

That is a developer asking about a flag and being told about a different flag, confidently. It is the single most common serious failure of vector-only documentation search, and it is why "which vector database" is a far less interesting question than "is there a lexical index at all".

Note also that lexical scores 6 of 6 here. BM25 is a strong baseline on a documentation corpus and is frequently better than the dense-only system a team spends a quarter building. Any claim that embeddings improved retrieval needs the BM25 number next to it, which is what retrieval evaluation is for.

docs.title: The other half: exact against approximate
docs.text:
Everything above is about ranking. A vector store exists for a different reason, which the eight-chunk corpus is too small to show: it does not compare the query to every vector. drills/vector_store.py measures what that costs, over 4000 chunks in 64 dimensions with an IVF index, clustering the vectors and probing only some clusters.

The vectors there are hashed, not learned: each chunk's tokens are feature hashed into 64 dimensions with a signed hash and L2-normalised. No model, no weights, nothing downloaded.

  IVF: 64 clusters, smallest 32, largest 102, mean 62 vectors
  exact: 0.15 ms per query, recall@10 1.000 by definition

  nprobe  scanned  recall@10  ms/query  speedup
       1       67     0.548      0.02    7.6x
       2      133     0.772      0.03    4.9x
       4      263     0.888      0.02    6.3x
       8      521     0.988      0.04    4.1x
      16     1017     1.000      0.09    1.7x
      32     1995     1.000      0.20    0.8x
      64     4000     1.000      0.44    0.4x

The table is one run's output. Its exact measurements can vary across numerical environments; the stable result is the shape of the curve and the full-probe recall. Milliseconds and speedup also vary by machine.

Three things in that table are worth more than the headline.

The knee. Recall climbs steeply and then flattens: probing 8 of 64 clusters scans 13 per cent of the corpus and recovers 98.8 per cent of the exact answer. That ratio, not the absolute numbers, is what makes an approximate index worth operating, and it is why nprobe is the first dial to look at when retrieval quality is disappointing.

Past the knee it is slower than brute force. At nprobe 32 and 64 the speedup is 0.8x and 0.4x: the index is doing more work than scanning everything, because gathering candidates from clusters costs more than the comparisons it saves. A vector store tuned to its maximum recall is a slower exact search with extra steps, and that configuration is easy to arrive at by raising nprobe until quality complaints stop.

Probing every cluster returns exactly the exact answer, which sounds like a truism and is the reason this drill found a bug in its own measurement rather than in the index. The first version reported 0.924 recall at full probe. An index cannot lose recall against itself, so the number was measuring the measurement: len(set(found) & set(truth)) / k is wrong whenever scores tie, and this corpus ties constantly, so the identity of the top ten was arbitrary among equals while the tenth-best score was not. Scoring against the k-th best score fixes it, because an answer tied with a true answer is a true answer. Any recall@k figure quoted without saying how ties were handled should be read with that in mind.

docs.title: What the hashed stand-in does and does not preserve
docs.text:
The drill's second half tried to show hybrid search beating either half, and could not. That failure is the clearest statement of where this substitution stops.

  retriever  identifier     paraphrase     both
  lexical    1.000          0.135          0.568
  dense      0.880          0.000          0.440
  hybrid     0.935          0.065          0.500
Preserved by hashed vectors Why Exact search yes Exhaustive comparison is exhaustive for any vectors Approximate recall loss yes It comes from partitioning a set of points, not from their origin The recall-latency curve yes Same reason Token blur partly Hash collisions blur unrelated tokens; a model blurs related ones, which is a different cause with a similar effect Semantic matching no A hash has learned nothing. cache and invalidate are as far apart as cache and banana Any quality comparison no It depends entirely on the above

The paraphrase column shows the consequence: lexical scores 0.135, dense scores zero, and fusing two retrievers that both fail produces a third that also fails. Hybrid search wins when the two halves fail on different queries, and the dense half earns its share by knowing that "too much ram" and memory are related. This one cannot know that.

The identifier column is the sharper result. Dense scores 0.880, nearly as well as BM25, and a dense retriever is not supposed to be good at exact identifiers; that failure is most of what this page is about. It scores well because feature hashing sends one token to one dimension, so a one-identifier query is a near-one-hot vector and the search is a lexical lookup wearing vector clothes. A stand-in that accidentally reproduces the opposite of the behaviour you are demonstrating is worse than no stand-in, which is why the hybrid argument above uses the cue-based toy, which at least has a topic space, and why any real quality claim needs a real model.

docs.title: Why hybrid, in one table
docs.text:
Query type Lexical Dense Example Exact identifier strong weak max_memory_gb Exact error string strong weak exit code 2 Version number strong weak "2.4 vs 2.3" Rare term strong weak a one-off API name Paraphrase weak strong "turn the cache off" vs cache=False Symptom with no shared words weak strong "my p99 is too high" Synonym weak strong "repo" vs "repository" Negation and polarity weak weak "supported" vs "deprecated"

The last row is the honest one: neither method handles polarity, so the fix there is writing and metadata, not retrieval. Anyone claiming hybrid search solves negation has not tested it.

docs.title: Fusion methods
docs.text:
Method How When Reciprocal rank fusion Sum of 1/(k+rank) per retriever The default. No score calibration needed Weighted score sum a * bm25 + b * cosine Only after normalising; needs retuning constantly Cascade Lexical to shortlist, dense to rerank Large corpora, latency budget Rerank the union Cross-encoder over the top k of both Highest quality, slowest, most expensive

RRF with k = 60 is the standard starting point and is usually good enough that tuning it is not where your time should go.

docs.title: Store options, which matter less than people think
docs.text:
Option Good for Watch out for In-process (numpy, faiss, sqlite-vec) Under ~1M chunks, which is most docs No built-in metadata filtering in some Postgres with pgvector You already run Postgres; real SQL filters Index tuning on large tables Dedicated (Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus) Large corpora, hybrid built in A service to operate Hosted (Pinecone, Turbopuffer) Not wanting to operate one Cost per query, data leaving Search engines (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Typesense) Hybrid in one system Heavier to run

For a documentation corpus of a few hundred thousand chunks, the honest answer is that an in-process index plus a lexical index in the same process is sufficient, fast, and much easier to debug than a service.

docs.title: Filtering before ranking
docs.text:
The most important feature after hybrid search, and the reason the content model exists:

# docpack: skip
results = store.search(
    query_vector,
    filter={"kind": "how-to", "audience": "developer", "visibility": "public"},
    limit=5,
)

A filter is a hard constraint. Hoping the ranking noticed the page genre is not, and for restricted content the difference is an access-control boundary rather than a quality preference.

Check that your store filters before it searches, not after. A store that retrieves the top 100 and then filters can return fewer than you asked for, or nothing, while the right answer sat at rank 150.

docs.title: Operational things that cause incidents
docs.text: Thing Consequence Changing the embedding model Every stored vector is incomparable; full re-embed Changing the chunker Same, plus every id changes unless ids are content-derived Thresholding on absolute score Scores are not comparable across queries No updated in the metadata Cannot discount stale content at query time Re-indexing on every commit Avoidable with stable chunk ids

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with hybrid and with the specific failure. "For documentation I would not ship vector-only search. A developer asking about max_memory_gb has to get the page about max_memory_gb, and dense retrieval puts that nearly on top of max_memory_mb. So BM25 plus dense, fused with reciprocal rank fusion, which combines ranks rather than scores so nothing needs calibrating. The store choice is almost incidental: an in-process index is enough for a few hundred thousand chunks, and what I care about is whether it filters on metadata before ranking rather than after."

The follow-up is "which vector database", and the interesting move is to decline the premise politely and name the two things that actually matter: hybrid support and filter-before-rank. Then give a real answer anyway, because refusing to choose reads as evasion: Postgres with pgvector if they already run Postgres, an in-process index if the corpus is small, a search engine like OpenSearch if they want hybrid in one system.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Hybrid search is two indexes to build, two to keep in sync, and two to debug, and it roughly doubles your retrieval infrastructure for a gain that is invisible on the queries you tested with. There is also a subtler cost: fusion makes results harder to explain. With BM25 alone you can say which terms matched; with RRF over two retrievers the answer is "it was third in one list and first in the other", which satisfies nobody when a stakeholder asks why the assistant said something wrong.

One sharper point. The strongest framing is that a vector store is a cache of a decision you made earlier. Every vector in it is downstream of a chunking choice and a model choice, and neither is visible once the vectors are stored. So the operational discipline that matters is not tuning the store, it is making the inputs reproducible: pinned model, content-derived chunk ids, and a re-embed that is a deliberate migration rather than a surprise. Teams that treat the store as the system discover this when a model update quietly degrades retrieval and nothing in their dashboards explains why.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A scored comparison of lexical, dense and fused retrieval on your own corpus, with the per-query losses visible.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path. The six-query table is the deliverable: it shows the two methods failing on disjoint sets, which is the argument.
  2. Redo it with your product's identifiers. Your flag names, your error codes, your version strings. The dense column gets worse and the case for hybrid gets stronger.
  3. Check filter-before-rank in whatever store you use. Query with a filter that matches only a handful of chunks and ask for twenty results. If you get fewer than exist, it filters after. Writing that test down is a small, specific thing most people never check.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Naming vector databases proves you read a comparison post. A per-query table showing exactly which queries dense retrieval loses on your own vocabulary, and a stated conclusion about hybrid, demonstrates you measured it.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
The mechanics of this page turned out to be demonstrable without a model, and drills/vector_store.py now does it: the exact-against-approximate measurement above is a real index over real vectors, because recall and latency depend on the geometry of the points rather than on where they came from.

What remains blocked is the half where learned geometry matters, which is every quality comparison. The drill's second half measures the boundary rather than asserting it, and the table above records which properties survive the substitution. What follows is how to run the part that does not.

What you need. The embedding setup from embeddings, plus any vector store with an approximate index: FAISS or hnswlib locally, or a hosted store if you want to measure network latency too. A corpus of at least a few thousand chunks, since approximate indexes behave like exact ones on small collections and the whole point is what happens when they stop.

What you would run. Index the same vectors twice, exactly and approximately, then measure the agreement between them and the cost of each.

exact  = numpy_bruteforce(vectors)            # ground truth, O(n) per query
approx = hnswlib.Index(space="cosine", dim=384)
approx.set_ef(ef)                             # the recall/latency dial

What you would see.

Observation Rough magnitude What it tells you Exact search, 10k chunks single-digit milliseconds Below ~100k chunks, exact is often fine Approximate search under a millisecond The gain, which arrives later than people expect Recall at ef=10 against exact 0.85 to 0.95 Approximate means wrong sometimes, by design Recall at ef=200 0.99 or better The dial, and what it costs in latency Build time for the index seconds to minutes Why reindexing is an operational event Hybrid lexical-plus-vector hit@1 better than either alone The result this page exists to argue for

The third row is the one to internalise: an approximate index returns the wrong neighbour a measurable fraction of the time, and no amount of evaluation of your model will reveal it, because the defect is in the index.

The measurement that matters most. Run a query whose answer depends on an exact token, a flag name or an error code, and compare the three rankings: lexical only, vector only, hybrid. Vector-only will often miss it entirely while scoring something topically adjacent highly, which is the failure mode that makes a demo look good and production look broken.

How you would know it had failed. A recall of exactly 1.0 at a low ef means the corpus is too small for the approximate index to matter, so the measurement is not testing anything. Identical results from lexical and vector search mean one of the two is not actually running. And a latency figure that does not change with ef means the dial is not wired to the query path.

docs.title: Versioned documentation
docs.text:
Publishing a site per release, and the duplication that nobody measures until it is large.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 3h

Not a quotation (adjacent)

Neither posting mentions versioned documentation. It is unavoidable for any platform that ships releases, which is both of these, so it is here on the grounds that the work requires it.

Prerequisites: Choosing a static site generator

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Publishing more than one copy of the documentation, one per release, so a reader on version 2.3 is not told how 2.4 behaves. In practice: a URL per version, a switcher in the page, an alias such as latest or stable, and a default that the bare domain redirects to.

The mechanism is simple. The consequences, which are what this page is about, are a per-version duplication cost that is almost always larger than people expect and a content problem that no tool solves.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
It does not ask, and the banner says so. But both postings describe platforms that ship releases, and documentation for a platform that ships releases needs versioning the moment a reader can be on an older one.

The judgment being tested, if it comes up, is when not to version. Versioning multiplies the corpus you maintain, and a team that versions everything from day one ends up with five copies of a conceptual explanation that was never version-specific, four of which are now wrong and none of which anybody is updating.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Deploy two versions, then measure what you just published. About thirty minutes, and the measurement is the interesting part.

Step 1: a site and two releases

mkdir -p ver-demo/docs && cd ver-demo
pip install --quiet mkdocs mike
git init -q && git config user.email d@e.f && git config user.name dev
printf 'site_name: W\n' > mkdocs.yml
printf '# Widget 2.3\n\nThe retry default is 3.\n' > docs/index.md
git add -A && git commit -qm init

mike deploy 2.3
printf '# Widget 2.4\n\nThe retry default is 5 (changed from 3).\n' > docs/index.md
mike deploy --update-aliases 2.4 latest
mike set-default latest
mike list

2.4 [latest]
2.3

Two versions, with latest pointing at 2.4.

Step 2: look at what was published

git ls-tree -r --name-only gh-pages | grep -E "index.html|versions.json|^latest"

2.3/index.html
2.4/index.html
index.html
latest
versions.json

A directory per version, a versions.json that feeds the switcher, a root index.html that redirects, and latest. Check what latest actually is:

git ls-tree gh-pages latest

120000 blob 7208c218... latest

Mode 120000 is a symlink. Aliases cost nothing, which is worth knowing before someone proposes avoiding them to save space.

Step 3: measure the duplication

git ls-tree -r -l gh-pages | python3 -c "
import sys, collections
tot = collections.Counter(); files = collections.Counter()
for line in sys.stdin:
    p = line.split(maxsplit=4)
    if len(p) < 5 or not p[3].isdigit(): continue
    top = p[4].strip().split('/')[0] if '/' in p[4] else '(root)'
    tot[top] += int(p[3]); files[top] += 1
for k in sorted(tot):
    print(f'  {k:10} {files[k]:4} files  {tot[k]:>9} bytes')
"

  (root)        4 files       538 bytes
  2.3          31 files   1993207 bytes
  2.4          31 files   1993258 bytes

Two megabytes per version for a one-page site. Split it by kind:

  HTML content:       11591 bytes (0%)
  theme assets:     1981667 bytes (99%)

Ninety-nine per cent of each version is the theme: webfonts, CSS, JavaScript, the search index runtime. The content is eleven kilobytes.

So versioning does not duplicate your documentation. It duplicates your theme. Ten versions is twenty megabytes, of which nineteen point eight is the same webfonts ten times over.

Step 4: decide what that means

For most projects: nothing. Twenty megabytes of static files is free, and the sentence above is not an argument against versioning.

It matters in three places. Clone times for the publishing branch grow linearly, and gh-pages with fifty versions becomes genuinely slow to fetch. Deployment time grows with it. And a CDN caching per version sees no reuse across versions, because the asset URLs differ by directory.

The mitigation, if you need one, is to prune old versions on a published policy rather than to avoid aliases or to hand-manage assets:

mike delete 2.1 2.2

What you built. Two versions, a switcher, and the knowledge that the per-version cost is your theme rather than your prose.

docs.title: Tooling by generator
docs.text:
Generator Mechanism MkDocs mike, deploys a directory per version to gh-pages Sphinx Build per tag or branch, assembled by convention or sphinx-multiversion Docusaurus Built in: npm run docusaurus docs:version 2.4 snapshots into the repository Antora Versions are branches; its model is version-first

Docusaurus and Antora make this ordinary. The other two bolt it on, and the difference shows up in whether a version is a directory in your source tree or a build artifact.

docs.title: What to version and what not to
docs.text:
Version it Keep one copy API reference Conceptual explanation Configuration options and defaults Architectural overviews Install and upgrade instructions Contribution guides Anything stating a default or a signature Glossary and style guide Tutorials that run real commands Marketing and landing pages

This table is the whole judgment. Versioning a page that was never version-specific creates N copies that drift, and the drifted copies are worse than no versioning at all because they carry a version number that implies someone checked.

docs.title: Decisions to make once, and write down
docs.text:
Decision Common answer What the bare domain shows The latest stable release Alias names latest for newest, stable if they differ Whether to publish pre-release docs Yes, unlisted, behind an explicit URL How long old versions live Supported releases plus one Whether old versions get fixes Security and factual corrections only Whether old versions are indexed No; canonical to latest

That last row is the one that gets missed and the one with the most visible consequence. Without canonical tags pointing at the current version, search engines index all of them and readers arrive on 2.1 through a search result. It is the same mechanism as the preview indexing problem and the same two-line fix.

docs.title: The banner nobody adds
docs.text: A reader who lands on an old version from a search result has no idea they have done so. A version banner on every non-latest page, saying which version this is and linking to the current one, costs a template change and prevents the single most common versioned-docs support ticket.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with what to version rather than how. "The mechanism is a directory per release and a switcher, and every generator has it. The decision that matters is what gets versioned: reference, defaults and install instructions yes; conceptual explanation no, because five copies of an architecture overview means four stale ones carrying a version number that implies somebody checked."

The follow-up is often about cost, and the measured answer is more interesting than the guess. The duplication is almost entirely the theme, not the content: I measured 99 per cent of each version as webfonts, CSS and JavaScript, with eleven kilobytes of HTML. It matters for clone and deploy times rather than for storage.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Versioning multiplies the maintenance surface and gives you no mechanism for keeping the copies consistent. A fix to a tutorial that applies to three supported versions is three pull requests, and in practice it is one, applied to latest, with the other two quietly left wrong. Anyone who says versioning is cheap has not maintained a correction across four branches.

One sharper point. Old versions are indexable by default and will outrank your current page for some queries, because they have had longer to accumulate links. Canonical tags to the current version plus a banner on non-latest pages is the fix, and almost nobody does either until a support ticket arrives.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A versioned site with aliases, a documented retirement policy, canonical tags on old versions and a version banner.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run the golden path and the measurement in step 3. The 99 per cent figure is the thing to quote.
  2. On any versioned docs site you can reach, check whether old versions carry a canonical tag or a banner. Usually neither.
  3. Write the two-column table above for a product you know. The disagreements about which column a page belongs in are the valuable part.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Neither of this guide's repositories is versioned, which the demonstrated page records, and for a single-version project versioning would be theatre. What travels is the measurement and the judgment table: knowing that the cost is theme duplication and that the hard part is deciding what not to version.

  • Crawlability, why old versions need canonical tags

docs.title: Working with engineers as sources
docs.text:
Getting accurate information from people whose job is not documentation, repeatedly, without becoming a burden.

core · difficulty 2 · 3h

Partner with Engineering, Product, Security, Developer Relations, and Partner Programs so every release ships documented, discoverable, and supportable

Source: nvidia posting, verbatim

Prerequisites: Extracting tribal knowledge, Reviewing documentation

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Getting accurate information from people whose job is not documentation, repeatedly, over years, without becoming the person they avoid. It is the ongoing relationship rather than the one-off interview.

The mechanics matter more than the rapport. A process that asks engineers for the cheapest thing they can give is worth more than being well liked.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
NVIDIA lists five partner functions by name and attaches an outcome to the partnership: "so every release ships documented, discoverable, and supportable". Intel's version is "Partner with engineering, product, and developer advocates so each new capability ships with tested documentation."

Both are asking for the same thing, which is that documentation stops being a thing that happens after a release and becomes a thing the release cannot ship without. That is a relationship problem before it is a process problem.

On a Tuesday it is an asymmetry you have to design around. You need forty minutes of a staff engineer's attention; she is on call, mid-migration, and has three reviews waiting. Documentation is somewhere below all of it on her list, and reasonably so. Any process that depends on her prioritising your work above hers will fail, so the design constraint is to need less from her, not to persuade her to care more.

The thing that changes this permanently is being useful to them first, and the most reliable way is reading the code yourself. A writer who arrives with "the page says 30, the constructor says None, which is right?" is asking for ten seconds. A writer who arrives with "can you explain timeouts to me" is asking for forty minutes. Same page, same outcome, two hundred times the cost.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Build the three mechanisms that make engineer time cheap, and measure the ask. Thirty minutes.

Step 1: price every way of asking

mkdir -p source-drill && cd source-drill
cat > asks.md <<'EOF'
| How you ask                                  | Their cost | Reliability |
|-----------------------------------------------|------------|-------------|
| "Can you explain X to me?"                    | 40 min     | medium      |
| "Can you review this page?"                   | 15 min     | medium      |
| "Is this specific sentence right?"            | 2 min      | high        |
| "The docs say 30, the code says None. Which?" | 10 sec     | high        |
| A PR they only have to approve                | 30 sec     | high        |
| A CI failure naming the file and the line     | 0 min      | high        |

The last row is the goal. Every mechanism below moves an ask one row down.
EOF
cat asks.md

Note that the cheap asks are also the more reliable ones. An engineer confirming a specific number is operating on knowledge they can check. An engineer explaining a subsystem from memory is reconstructing.

Step 2: a review request they can answer in two minutes

The trick is to ask for accuracy only, and to mark exactly where you are unsure.

cat > review-request.md <<'EOF'
# Review request: "Configure retry behaviour"

I am not asking about wording. Three claims to confirm or correct:

1. `retries=3` makes 4 total requests (retries exclude the initial attempt).
   -> correct / wrong: ___

2. The maximum is 10, enforced client-side.
   -> correct / wrong: ___

3. Backoff is exponential with no jitter.
   -> correct / wrong: ___

One thing I could not determine from the code:
   Does the retry budget reset per call or per session?  ___

Everything else is my problem. If all three are right, reply "all good".
EOF
cat review-request.md

Step 3: a template that collects what you need at the moment they know it

The cheapest information is captured when the engineer is already thinking about the change, in a field they are already filling in.

cat > pr-template.md <<'EOF'
<!-- .github/pull_request_template.md, docs section -->

## Documentation

- [ ] No user-visible change
- [ ] Docs updated in this PR
- [ ] Docs issue filed: #____

If a default, limit, or error type changed, say so here. One line is enough;
we will write the page.

Changed defaults or limits:
EOF
cat pr-template.md

That last prompt is the whole mechanism. One line at the moment of the change is worth an hour of archaeology later, and it is a smaller ask than a review.

Step 4: the gate that removes the ask entirely

mkdir -p docs
cat > docs/retries.md <<'EOF'
---
title: Configure retry behaviour
verified_against: widget.client.WidgetClient
verified_on: 2026-10-26
claims:
  retries_default: 3
  retries_max: 10
---
# Configure retry behaviour

Set `retries` on the client. The default is 3; the maximum is 10.
EOF

cat > check_claims.py <<'PY'
"""Compare documented numeric claims against the implementation.

This is the mechanism that converts a recurring human ask into a build
failure. Nobody has to remember to tell the docs team that a default
changed, because the build says so.
"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

# Stands in for `inspect.signature` against the real client. In a real repo
# this imports the module and reads the defaults.
ACTUAL = {"retries_default": 5, "retries_max": 10}


def main(page: Path) -> int:
    front = yaml.safe_load(page.read_text(encoding="utf-8").split("---")[1])
    claims = front.get("claims", {})

    failures = []
    for name, documented in claims.items():
        actual = ACTUAL.get(name)
        if actual is None:
            failures.append(f"{name}: documented {documented}, not found in the code")
        elif actual != documented:
            failures.append(f"{name}: documented {documented}, code says {actual}")

    for failure in failures:
        print(f"CLAIM DRIFT  {page.name}: {failure}", file=sys.stderr)
    print(f"{'FAIL' if failures else 'ok'}: {len(claims)} claims checked, "
          f"{len(failures)} drifted")
    return 1 if failures else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(Path("docs/retries.md")))
PY
python3 check_claims.py

What you built. Three mechanisms at descending cost, and one gate that costs nothing. The gate is the one that matters: the engineer who changed the default from 3 to 5 did not have to remember you existed, and the build told you anyway.

That is the same move as the systems mindset, applied to a social dependency rather than a technical one, and it is the thing that makes this relationship sustainable over years.

docs.title: The escalation, cheapest first
docs.text: Mechanism Their cost Use when A CI check on a documented claim zero The claim is numeric or structural A docs field in the PR template 10 seconds Any user-visible change A specific yes/no question 2 minutes You read the code and one thing is ambiguous A marked-up review request 5 minutes A page with several claims A 30-minute extraction interview 30 minutes Tribal knowledge, once per topic An open-ended explanation 40 minutes You are new, and sparingly

docs.title: How to ask for a review
docs.text: Do Why Ask for accuracy, not wording Style is your job; they will not do it and should not Mark the claims you are unsure about Scopes the review to minutes Say what you could not determine Invites the one answer only they have Offer "all good" as a valid reply Lowers the floor on responding Send a draft, not a request for information Experts correct well and compose badly

docs.title: Things that destroy the relationship
docs.text: Mistake Effect Asking to be taught what the code would have told you You become the expensive channel Asking for wording feedback They disengage from the parts that matter Open-ended "any thoughts?" requests Unbounded, so deferred forever Publishing an unreviewed claim as verified Breaks trust once, permanently Reporting their mistake to their manager Never recoverable Asking the same thing twice because you did not write it down Signals their time is cheap

docs.title: The partner functions NVIDIA names, and what each wants
docs.text:
Function What they need from docs What they can give you Engineering Accuracy they did not have to write Defaults, error paths, the exception Product A documented path at launch Which capability matters, and when Security Guidance that does not teach a bad pattern Review of anything about credentials or data Developer Relations Something to point at in a talk Direct developer feedback Partner Programs Content partners can use externally The partner-specific constraints

Reading that table as five different asks rather than one is most of release readiness.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like. Lead with the cost reduction, not the rapport. "I stopped asking engineers to explain things and started asking them to confirm specific claims, after reading the code first. A review went from forty minutes to two. Then I put the numeric claims in front matter and added a check comparing them against the signatures, so for those the ask went to zero and the build tells me when a default changes."

The follow-up is about the engineer who will not respond, and it is the real question. The honest answer has layers. First, make the ask smaller: a two-minute yes/no gets answered when a review request does not. Second, go where they already are, which usually means a comment on their pull request rather than a message in a channel. Third, publish with the gap marked: a page that says "the retry budget's scope is unconfirmed" is better than a page that guesses, and it is often what finally prompts a correction. What does not work is escalation, which buys one response and costs the relationship.

The tradeoff to volunteer. Every mechanism that reduces the ask shifts work onto you. Reading the code before asking is slower for you and faster for them. Writing the draft first means you write things that turn out to be wrong. That trade is correct, because your time is the cheaper resource and because the alternative is a documentation process that stalls whenever someone is on call, but it does mean the honest version of this job involves doing more of the work than the org chart suggests.

One sharper point. The strongest version is that you are not trying to make engineers care about documentation. That is the trap, and it is where most documentation advocacy goes. You are trying to make the correct thing cost them nothing: a field in a template they already fill in, a check that fails without anyone's attention, a question answerable in ten seconds. Caring is not a mechanism. Saying that plainly is unusual and it is exactly what NVIDIA's "systems where the right way is easier than the wrong way" means when applied to people.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A pull request template with a docs field, or a claim-checking gate, plus one marked-up review request. Small artifacts, specific, and they demonstrate the design instinct rather than the social skill.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Rewrite a review request you have sent into the three-claim form above. Ten minutes, and the difference is immediately visible.
  2. Add a docs section to a PR template in any repository you can touch, with the "changed defaults or limits" prompt. That one line is the highest ratio of value to effort on this page.
  3. Build the claim gate. Put one numeric claim in front matter and check it against the code. It is twenty lines and it is the thing that proves you think about this structurally rather than socially.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. Everyone says they collaborate well with engineers. A PR template diff, a two-minute review request, and a check that fails when a default drifts are three things an interviewer can look at, and together they make a much more specific claim than any description of your working style.

docs.title: How this would be demonstrated elsewhere
docs.text:
This is the concept most thoroughly removed by a single-author repository. Everything about it is the behaviour of two parties, and here there is one.

What you need. Engineers who own code you document, and enough standing that a request of yours costs them something they will still pay.

What a learner would do. Make the smallest possible ask three times and measure the response. A two-minute review request with the specific question attached, not "please review". Then record whether it came back, how fast, and whether the answer was usable.

What you would see.

The ask Typical response Why "Please review this page" Slow, or never It is an unbounded request "Is this default still 30 seconds?" Fast, and usable Bounded, checkable, cheap to answer "I documented this and it took four paragraphs; is the design right?" Engaged It arrives as an observation, not an opinion A PR that fixes the code's docstring Merged You did the work

The pattern is that an engineer's willingness tracks how specific the ask is, not how important you say it is. The fourth row is the strongest move available and the one documentation people use least.

Why it does not commit. The artifact is a merged pull request in a repository you do not own and a response time in someone's review queue. What a repository of your own can show is the habit's residue: checks that encode a question an engineer answered once, so nobody has to ask again.

  • Freshness monitoring, where claim checking scales to

docs.title: Workshops and hands-on labs
docs.text:
A three-hour workshop covers about one step of a thirty-four-hour path, so the design question is which step genuinely needs a room.

supporting · difficulty 2 · 4h

Adjacent, not quoted

Neither posting mentions workshops. A standard developer-relations deliverable, and the only setting where you can watch a reader fail.

Prerequisites: Learning paths and curriculum, Reproducible environments

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A fixed block of time in which a group works through material together, with someone present who can unblock them. The defining constraint is not the content, it is synchrony: everyone has to be at the same place at the same time, so the slowest person sets the pace and any environment failure strands one attendee while the room moves on without them.

Everything that makes workshop design different from writing a tutorial follows from that constraint.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
Two reasons, and only one of them is about teaching.

The honest teaching reason is that a room is the only place you can watch people fail. Assessment over a corpus tells you whether your tasks are well formed; it cannot tell you where readers get stuck. Twenty people attempting your quickstart in front of you produces that information in forty minutes, and it is the highest-quality signal available anywhere in this job.

The other reason is that workshops are a developer-relations deliverable with a conference schedule attached, which means the date is fixed before the content exists. Worth naming, because it drives the characteristic failure: a workshop scoped as though it were a tutorial, discovered on the morning to be three times too long.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
Measure the two things that decide whether a workshop works: what the environment costs, and how much material fits. About thirty minutes, and both numbers are worse than people expect.

The second half is committed as drills/workshop_arithmetic.py, which computes it from the registry rather than quoting a figure. The first half is not, and cannot be: it needs a network, a stopwatch and a particular machine, and the numbers below are one run on one of them. Treat the shape as the claim and the seconds as an anecdote.

Step 1: time the setup, in ideal conditions

This is a quiet cloud machine with a warm package index and a fast link, which no attendee will have. Nothing checks these seconds, so do not reuse them:

python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install mkdocs mkdocs-material pyyaml pytest

venv_create_s=3
pip_upgrade_s=3
deps_install_s=14
packages_installed=34
bytes_on_disk=94697572
first_build_s=0  rc=0
total_s=21

Twenty-one seconds. The number that matters is underneath it:

requested=4   installed=34

Four packages asked for, thirty-four installed. The failure surface of this workshop is thirty-four independent resolutions, not four, and every one can resolve differently on an attendee's laptop depending on their Python version, their existing site-packages, their corporate proxy, and what pip decides is newest that morning.

Ninety-five megabytes per attendee, times a room.

Step 2: remove the network from the room

The mitigation is to resolve the dependency graph once, in advance, and ship the result:

pip download --dest wheelhouse mkdocs mkdocs-material pyyaml pytest
pip install --no-index --find-links wheelhouse mkdocs mkdocs-material pyyaml pytest

wheelhouse_build_s=2   files=33   bytes=28411989
offline_install_s=6    rc=0       packages=34

Six seconds instead of fourteen, 28 MB on a stick or on a laptop serving the room, and, more importantly, the same thirty-four packages for everybody. The resolution happened once, on a machine you could inspect.

That last property is the whole value. Speed is a bonus; determinism is the reason, because a workshop where two attendees have different transitive dependencies is a workshop where you debug one laptop while eighteen people watch.

Step 3: the arithmetic that kills most workshop plans

This guide's first-week path is ten concepts. drills/workshop_arithmetic.py reads them out of the registry, so the numbers below are the current ones rather than the ones that were true when this page was written:

  Technical writing as a craft                     8h
  Treating docs, setup and samples as one product  3h
  Docs-as-code                                     2h
  Markdown and its dialects                        2h
  Git authoring workflows for writers              4h
  Diátaxis                                         2h
  Choosing a static site generator                 3h
  MkDocs and Material                              4h
  Link checking                                    2h
  Documentation CI                                 4h
                                            total 34h

A three-hour workshop, after setup and questions, offers perhaps two hours of hands-on time.

two hours against the 34-hour first-week path: 6%
shortest path in the guide: domain-context, 6 concepts, 24h (8%)
concepts in this corpus of 3h or less: 48/106

That second line is here because of a mistake. This page used to call first-week the shortest path in the guide, which it was, until a six-concept domain path was added and took the title by ten hours. The claim was prose, the answer was in concepts.yaml, and nothing connected them, so the page was wrong for as long as it took somebody to compute it. The drill now prints the shortest path by name and a test compares it to this block, which is the only reason the sentence you are reading is true.

Note which direction the correction goes. The shortest path in the guide is twenty-four hours, so two hours of hands-on time is eight percent of it rather than six. The superlative was wrong and the argument got worse.

A three-hour workshop covers about one step of a ten-step path. Not a compressed version of the path. One step of it.

Most workshop abstracts promise the path. The abstract is written in June for a conference in October, it says "learn to build and ship a documentation pipeline", and in October somebody tries to deliver thirty-four hours in three.

Step 4: the design consequence

If a workshop is one step, the only question worth asking is which step needs a room, and the answer is not the most important step.

Needs a room:   failure is confusing, recovery needs judgment, and
                seeing the person next to you helps
Does not:       mechanical, well documented, succeeds first time

On this path, "Documentation CI" needs a room, because its failures are environmental and a stuck attendee cannot read their way out. "Markdown and its dialects" does not, however foundational, because a page explains it perfectly and nobody gets stuck.

That inverts the usual instinct, which is to start at step 1 and get as far as possible. Starting at step 1 spends the room's scarce resource, a person who can unblock you, on the material least likely to need one.

Step 5: what to do with the other nine steps

Send them. A workshop that covers one step well and hands out a path for the rest is honest; a workshop that gallops through ten produces twenty people with a broken environment and a folder they will not reopen.

The handout is the artifact that survives the room, which is the argument for having the written path exist first. A workshop built on top of a curriculum is an afternoon's work. A workshop that is the curriculum gets rebuilt every time it is delivered.

What you built. A measured setup cost of 34 packages and 95 MB per attendee, an offline wheelhouse making it deterministic in six seconds, and the arithmetic showing a three-hour workshop is one step of a ten-step path.

docs.title: A three-hour block, honestly budgeted
docs.text:
Minutes Spent on Notes 20 Environment, including the two people it fails for Always; plan it rather than absorb it 10 What we are building and why Shorter than you want it to be 100 The hands-on material The entire teaching budget 20 Questions, and the slowest finishers Not optional 30 Overrun nobody planned Something will go wrong

The last row is the one people leave out, and it is why workshops overrun, rather than any individual mistake inside them.

docs.title: Environment strategies
docs.text:
Strategy Cost in the room Determinism Fails when "Install these four packages" 15 to 40 minutes None Always, for somebody Wheelhouse on a stick or local server Under a minute High Someone has the wrong Python Container image, pre-pulled Under a minute Very high Docker is absent or disallowed Hosted environment per attendee Zero Total The venue wifi dies Attendees set up beforehand Zero, for the prepared None Half of them do not

The last row is the plan most workshops actually have, and the honest reading is that it is not a plan. Pair it with one of the others.

docs.title: What needs a room
docs.text:
Needs it Does not Failure modes that are confusing Anything that works first time Judgment calls with no single right answer Mechanical procedure Work people will not start alone Work they will happily read Anything where watching a neighbour helps Reference material Material where you need to watch them Material you already have feedback on

The bottom-right cell is the trap: well-understood material is the most comfortable thing to teach and the least worth the room.

docs.title: Workshop against the alternatives
docs.text:
Tutorial page Screencast Workshop Pace The reader's The video's The slowest attendee's Scales Indefinitely Indefinitely 20 to 30 Cost per delivery Nothing Nothing A day Shows where people stick No No Yes, immediately Survives the day Yes Yes Only the handout does

The fourth row is why workshops earn their cost even when the teaching is mediocre, and the fifth is why the handout matters more than the slides.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Prevention Setup eats an hour Step 2, plus a greeter who starts people early Scoped as a path, delivered as a sprint Step 3's arithmetic, before the abstract One broken laptop stops the room A spare hosted environment, and permission to move on Everyone finishes at a different time A stated stretch task for the fast Nobody asks anything A planted checkpoint question, not an invitation The material exists only as slides Write the path first

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
Lead with the arithmetic, because it is the thing nobody has done. "A three-hour workshop has about two hours of hands-on time, and the shortest path through my curriculum is thirty-four hours. So a workshop is one step of a ten-step path rather than a compressed version of it, and the design question becomes which step needs a room, not how fast I can go."

The follow-up is usually environments, and this is where the numbers are. I asked for four packages and got thirty-four installed, 95 MB per attendee: thirty-four independent resolutions that can differ on somebody's laptop. So I resolve once in advance and ship a wheelhouse, 28 MB, six seconds, offline, and the same thirty-four packages for everybody. Speed is a bonus; determinism is the reason, because the alternative is debugging one laptop while eighteen people watch.

The non-obvious design point. The step that needs the room is rarely the most important one. It is the one where failure is confusing and recovery needs judgment. Foundational material that a page explains perfectly is the most comfortable thing to teach and the worst use of the only resource a workshop has.

The tradeoff to volunteer. A workshop costs a day and reaches twenty people; a page costs a day and reaches thousands. The honest justification is not teaching efficiency, it is that a room is the only place I get to watch people fail, and that is feedback no analytics produce. A team running one workshop a quarter purely to collect it, and publishing a page from what it learned, would be making the right trade.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact. A wheelhouse or image that installs offline, a timed run of it, and a workshop plan whose hands-on minutes are written next to the hours of material it claims to cover.

Three things to do, in order:

  1. Run pip download against your own workshop's dependencies and count the files. Write your prediction down first; the gap between four and thirty-four is this page's whole subject.
  2. Take your next workshop abstract and divide its promised scope by two hours of hands-on time. A ratio much over one means the abstract is already wrong, and it is far cheaper to fix in June than in October.
  3. Ask which step of your material genuinely needs a person in the room. If the answer is "all of it", the material has not been written down yet, and writing it is the actual task.

What makes it credible rather than decorative. The setup measurements were executed: 34 packages and 94,697,572 bytes from four requested, a wheelhouse of 33 files and 28 MB built in two seconds, an offline install in six. The path arithmetic comes from this guide's own registry. What has not happened is a workshop, so the claims about what needs a room are reasoning from the design rather than observation, and the demonstrated page records workshops as having no demonstration in either repository.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
Every concept prints whether a posting asked for it in those words, and why that distinction is not averaged away.

Every concept in this guide carries a tag saying how strong its claim on your time is.

Tag Meaning Count quoted A verbatim phrase from one of the two job postings 90 derived The posting requires this, but these are not its words 4 adjacent Neither posting mentions it; the named work is impossible without it 12

The tag is printed on every row of the coverage matrix and at the top of every concept page. fieldguide check requires one, along with a quote, on every concept.

docs.title: Why this is worth the clutter
docs.text:
A curriculum assembled from job postings has an obvious failure mode: the author's existing interests quietly become requirements. The posting says "information architecture", and forty pages later the guide is teaching a specific taxonomy methodology the author happens to like, with the posting's authority borrowed for all of it.

Printing the provenance makes that move visible. When a page says adjacent, it is saying: no employer asked for this, I am asserting that you need it, and you may disagree. Twelve of the 106 concepts are in that position, and a reader who wants only what the postings demand can skip them and know exactly what they skipped.

The same logic applies to derived, which is the larger and more interesting category. 4 concepts are here because a posting requires the capability without naming the concept. NVIDIA asks for RAG pipelines, so embeddings and vector stores are derived: you cannot build the first without the second two, but NVIDIA never wrote the word "embeddings". That inference is almost certainly correct and it is still an inference.

docs.title: What a second pass against the source text changed
docs.text:
The first version of this registry was built from notes rather than from the postings themselves, and it is worth recording what happened when both postings were read again in full, because the result is the best available argument for tracking provenance at all.

Fifty-one concepts had the wrong tag. Most were understated: the postings name docs-as-code pipelines, Git authoring, Markdown/RST, Sphinx, MkDocs, Docusaurus, knowledge architecture, Vale, llms.txt, documentation analytics, the sample-app gallery and the AI software stack in so many words, and all of those had been filed as derived.

Eight were overstated in the other direction, which matters more. Localization, accessibility, versioned documentation, OpenAPI, single-sourcing, screencasts, workshops and assessment design had been filed as things a posting required. Neither posting mentions any of them. They are now adjacent, which means: one person thinks you need this, and no employer said so.

Twenty-three concepts were missing entirely, including three that are core: technical writing as a craft, which both postings list as a minimum qualification; reading code to verify accuracy; and judging where AI can be trusted.

The ratio moved from 41 quoted out of 83 to 90 out of 106. The curriculum did not get more rigorous, it got more honestly labelled, and the eight demotions are the part worth dwelling on. An unchecked registry drifts toward whatever the author already believed, with the posting's authority attached.

A guide that quietly presented all three tags as "what the job requires" would be more persuasive and less true. The cost of the distinction is a cluttered table and a reader who has to think about which claims to accept. That seems like the right trade for a document whose entire subject is how to make knowledge trustworthy.

docs.title: How to read a weak claim
docs.text:
An adjacent tag is not a warning that the concept is unimportant. Diátaxis is tagged adjacent, and it is the single most useful thing on this list: neither posting names it, and both describe at length the problem it solves. Markdown is adjacent too, and you will not get through a day in either role without it.

What the tag tells you is where the authority comes from. For quoted, an employer. For adjacent, one person's judgement about what the work requires. Decide how much that is worth to you, which is a decision you can only make if somebody tells you which it is.
