docs.title: The page contract
docs.text:
Seven required sections in a fixed order, enforced in CI, and the reasoning behind each one.

Every concept page in this guide answers the same seven questions in the same order. fieldguide check rejects one that does not, and fieldguide new generates the headings so nobody has to remember them.

  1. What it is
  2. Why the job asks for it
  3. The golden path
  4. Reference
  5. How to talk about it
  6. How to prove it

docs.title: Why a fixed order rather than a suggested one
docs.text:
A reader working through thirty pages of a reference corpus spends attention on two separate things: the subject, and figuring out where in this particular page the thing they want is. The second is pure overhead, and it is paid again on every page.

A fixed contract pays it once. By the third page a reader knows that the command they can paste is under "The golden path" and the interview answer is fifth, and they can skip directly. That is the entire benefit, and it only exists if the order is actually reliable, which is why it is a build failure rather than a style note.

This is Diátaxis logic applied inside a page instead of across a tree. Diátaxis separates the four kinds of documentation into separate documents because mixing them serves nobody. A concept page in a study guide is a deliberate exception: the reader wants orientation, a tutorial, reference, and argumentation about one narrow subject, in one sitting. The contract keeps them separated within the page rather than interleaved, which is the thing Diátaxis is actually objecting to.

docs.title: What each section is for, and how it usually fails
What it is
docs.text:
Two sentences, for someone who has heard the term in a meeting and did not admit they were lost. No history, no motivation, no benefits.

The failure mode is the Wikipedia opening: a definition so hedged and complete that it conveys nothing. "Diátaxis is a systematic framework for technical documentation authoring" is correct and useless. Prefer the sentence you would say out loud to a colleague.

docs.title: Why the job asks for it
docs.text:
The posting quote is already printed at the top of the page. This section explains the work behind it: what does someone in this role do on a Tuesday that requires this?

The failure mode is restating the quote. If this section can be deleted without losing information, it was not written.

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
The shortest real exercise that produces a working result. Commands to paste, and what the reader should see after each one.

Three rules, and they are rules rather than preferences:

  • It starts from a clean environment. The commonest documentation failure in existence is a quickstart that works because the author installed something months ago and forgot.
  • It ends in something observable. Not "you now understand chunking", but a file on disk, a number printed, a page rendered.
  • The author has run it, in that order, in that environment. A golden path nobody has walked is fiction with good formatting.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
The facts worth looking up later: vocabulary, options, defaults, gotchas.

The failure mode is narrative. Nobody reads this section; they scan it and leave. Tables, definition lists, and short rows beat paragraphs.

docs.title: How to talk about it
docs.text:
What a competent answer sounds like, and what the follow-up question will be.

Every one of these must include a tradeoff. Reciting what a thing does is not signal, because anyone can read the documentation an hour before the interview. Knowing what it costs, and when you would not use it, is the thing that cannot be faked, and it is the question a good interviewer asks second.

docs.title: How to prove it
docs.text:
The artifact that demonstrates the concept without the reader having to assert it: a repository, a file, a measured number, a commit.

It has to be specific enough to act on today. "Build a RAG pipeline" is not a proof. "Write twenty questions with their expected source pages, score recall@3, and publish the number including the bad one" is.

docs.title: How it is enforced
docs.text:
fieldguide check reads every page belonging to a concept whose status is past planned and checks:

  • all seven headings are present, matched as ## <exact text>
  • their positions in the file are in contract order
  • a page marked complete is at least 450 words

The word count is a crude proxy and is meant to be. It does not detect a bad page; it detects a page marked complete that is obviously a stub, which is the specific dishonesty worth automating against. Judging whether a page is good is a review problem, and no linter is going to take it over.

docs.title: The honest limitation
docs.text:
A contract this rigid is wrong for some concepts. Several of the domain-context entries, such as OpenUSD or robotics simulation, do not have a meaningful golden path at this guide's level of detail: the useful content is orientation and vocabulary so you are not lost in a room full of specialists. Those pages have a "golden path" section because the contract demands one, and on the weakest of them it is the least valuable section on the page.

The alternative was a second contract for context-tier concepts, which means two shapes for a reader to learn and a conditional in the validator. That seemed worse than a handful of thin sections, but it is a judgement call rather than an obvious win, and a reader who finds those sections padded is not wrong.

docs.title: Why the curriculum is a data file
docs.text:
A checklist nobody can verify reports completion it has not earned, so this one is validated in CI.

The obvious way to build this guide is a Markdown page with 106 checkboxes on it. Someone ticks one when they write a page.

That version is worse than having no checklist, and it is worth being precise about why, because the same failure runs through most documentation projects.

docs.title: What a hand-maintained checklist actually reports
docs.text:
A checkbox records an intention at the moment someone typed it. It does not record the state of the repository. Within a month the two have diverged in every direction at once:

  • A page was written and nobody ticked the box.
  • A box was ticked and the page is three paragraphs of TODO.
  • A page was renamed and the link under its ticked box is dead.
  • A concept turned out to be two concepts and the single box still says done.
  • Someone added a page for a concept that was never on the list.

None of these are visible. The index page looks authoritative, which is precisely the problem: it is the page a reader trusts most and the page most likely to be wrong. A reader who follows a tick to a stub learns not to trust the index, and after that the index is decoration.

docs.title: What the registry does instead
docs.text:
concepts.yaml holds the curriculum as structured data: 106 concepts with a category, a tier, a difficulty, a time estimate, prerequisites, the job posting line that justifies the concept, and a status.

fieldguide check then refuses to let the registry and the repository disagree:

The claim What catches a false one This concept is covered The page must exist, unless status is planned This page belongs here Every page must have a concept in the registry This concept is complete A complete page under 450 words is rejected This page follows the contract All seven required sections, in order This path is teachable No concept before a prerequisite the path also teaches This graph is followable No cycles, no dangling prerequisites A posting asks for this Every concept needs a source, provenance, and a quote

The coverage matrix, the learning paths, and the full ordering are all generated from the registry. They are views, not copies, so there is no state in them that can drift. CI runs the generator with --check and fails if a committed view is stale, which closes the last gap: changing the registry without regenerating.

docs.title: It caught four real mistakes immediately
docs.text:
This is the part that justifies the machinery rather than merely describing it.

Two learning paths taught a prerequisite too late. The first-week path taught link checking before documentation CI, and the educator path taught reproducible environments before cold-start testing. Both were flagged on the first run.

Both turned out to be wrong dependencies, not wrong orders. Thinking about it, you run a link checker on a tree long before you own a pipeline, so link checking depending on documentation CI was backwards. And a reproducible environment is how you make cold-start testing meaningful, so that edge pointed the wrong way too. The validator reported a symptom in the paths; the bug was in the model. That is the ordinary experience of working with a validated schema, and it is the argument for having one: the error surfaced somewhere cheap.

The page-contract check and the stub check both found what they were built for while the first pages were being drafted.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
Honesty requires the other column.

Adding a concept is now a two-step operation: edit the registry, then run the generator. A contributor who edits a generated page by hand loses the work. The banner on every generated page exists because of that, and a banner is a weaker guard than a lock.

The schema has opinions, and some of them will be wrong. tier has three values and difficulty has three levels, which is a forced simplification of something continuous. A concept that is genuinely between core and supporting gets rounded, and the rounding is invisible to a reader.

Eighty-three concepts in one flat namespace is near the limit of what this model carries well. There is no sub-categorisation and no notion of a concept that is a special case of another. At two hundred concepts this file would need to become a directory, and the generator would need to grow a notion of hierarchy it currently does not have.

And a validated curriculum is still only one person's curriculum. Nothing here checks whether these are the right 106 concepts. The registry makes the list consistent and honest about its sources. It cannot make it correct, and no amount of schema will.

The coverage matrix is a reference: it lists everything and assumes you know what you need. A path is the other thing a learner wants, which is somebody else's opinion about the order.

Paths overlap on purpose. A concept that appears in four of them is load-bearing, and that is worth knowing before you pick where to start.
